To summarize, safety is a physical property of a system and not a sentiment, and it rests on principles that can be learned and checked. Electrical safety keeps leakage current small, gives it a harmless path through the protective earth conductor, holds conductive surfaces at one potential through bonding, isolates the supply where the patient is most vulnerable, and classifies every applied part so that only the right accessory touches the heart. Gas safety rests on compression, on identity, on the pin index that prevents a wrong connection, and on the fact that oxygen accelerates fire rather than causing it. Alarms are a chain that must be designed, tested, and set for the individual patient, and alarm fatigue is a hazard in its own right. Human factors, labeling, and the read-back habit prevent the errors that no alarm can detect, and incident reporting with a culture that answers every report is how a hospital and a clinic both learn. Radiation protection is time, distance, and shielding, measured by a dosimeter and confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, while falls, entrapment, burns, and the injuries that staff suffer while moving patients are equipment problems with equipment answers. The field variant gives up the infrastructure, the service contract, and the central alarm, and demands in their place discipline, redundancy, and understanding. In the chapters that follow, every device is described with the same questions in mind: what can it do to the patient, what can the operator do to it, what alarm announces the failure, what consumable keeps it honest, and what check proves it is ready.

# Chapter 4 — The Lifecycle of Equipment

A machine in a hospital is not an event but a biography. It begins as a need, becomes a budget line, arrives in a crate, is bolted to a floor, is used by hands that did not choose it, and ends as scrap or as a spare part inside another machine. Most equipment failures are not electronic failures at all but failures of supply, training, maintenance, and documentation. Wear itself is physical: surfaces rub, seals harden, solder joints fatigue, batteries lose capacity, and sensors drift as their materials age. Corrosion eats contacts, dust blocks filters, heat cooks the electrolyte, and moisture finds every crack. The discipline that follows a device from first idea to final disposal is called the lifecycle.

The first stage is not procurement but an honest recognition of a need. Someone must ask what problem the machine solves, how often that problem occurs, who will operate it, who will repair it, and what happens on the day it breaks. The real question is never only whether a clinic can afford to buy a machine, but whether it can sustain one. A hospital-grade device assumes a building that can feed it: stable electricity at the correct voltage and frequency, clean water, drainage, compressed air, vacuum, and a supply chain that delivers filters and reagents on time. Before writing a specification, the buyer should walk the route the machine will take and check each of those requirements. A need that cannot be sustained is a future piece of furniture, and the graveyards behind clinics are full of machines that answered a question nobody had asked carefully.

For every device there is a second device hidden inside it, and that second device is the consumable. An analyzer is really a pump, a lamp, and a set of reagents; an ultrasound machine is a console, a probe, and a bottle of coupling gel; a ventilator is a turbine, a circuit, a filter, and a humidifier chamber. The purchase price is only the entrance fee, and the true cost of ownership is paid over the whole life of the machine in consumables, service, calibration, electricity, water, staff time, and downtime. That cost is estimated by listing every expense the device will generate in a year and dividing it by the number of patients it will actually serve. A cheap device with expensive consumables can cost more per patient than an expensive device with cheap ones. A machine that is too expensive to run is a machine that is not available, however modern it looks on arrival.

Procurement begins with a specification written around the clinical need rather than around a catalog. It should state what the device must measure or do, with what accuracy and over what range, in what environment, and by whom it will be operated. It should name the consumables, the service, the training, the documentation, and the warranty, including the response time for a breakdown. It should describe the electrical supply, whether single phase or 3 phase, at what voltage and frequency, because a machine built for 60 hertz will not behave correctly on a 50 hertz supply, a requirement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase and again before the first patient. It should state the gas connections and cylinder fittings, so that they match what the hospital actually has. A specification written in the language of the clinic rather than the salesman is the buyer's only real protection.

The tender is the formal contest in which suppliers offer to meet that specification, and it is where good intentions are most often lost. Evaluation must compare not only the offered price but the offered life: the consumable pack, the service visit, the spare parts, the distance to the nearest engineer, and the years the maker promises to keep supplying. A showroom demonstration proves very little, because a device can perform beautifully on a stable bench and fail in a dusty room on an unstable supply. The buyer should ask for the service history of the model and the name of a reference site where it has worked for several years. The lowest price is not the lowest cost, and the machine nobody can service is the most expensive machine in the building.

The field variant of procurement inverts almost every one of those assumptions. A mobile or frontier clinic usually cannot host a tender, cannot demand a reference site, and cannot wait for a service visit. It must therefore choose devices that are simple, robust, repairable with common tools, and tolerant of dust, heat, humidity, and unstable power. What it needs is not maximum capability but minimum complexity: fewer moving parts, fewer proprietary connectors, and fewer sealed modules that cannot be opened. It should prefer devices that run on a widely available battery format, that charge from a solar panel, and that can be repaired locally rather than returned to a capital city. The field buyer is really buying a relationship with a supply chain, and the machine is only the visible part of that relationship.

Acceptance testing begins the moment the crate is opened, and its purpose is to prove that the device that arrived is the device that was ordered and that it works as promised. A machine travels by ship, truck, and hand, so it may have been dropped, stored in the rain, built for a different voltage, or configured in a way nobody intended. The test verifies the model and accessories against the purchase order, inspects the housing, cables, connectors, and seals, and confirms that the manual, the certificate, and the service contact are present. The device is then powered up and made to perform a known measurement against a known reference, so that a reading can be trusted rather than merely believed. Electrical safety belongs here too, because the protective earth must be intact and the leakage current within the limits the manufacturer states and the local standard requires.

Installation places the device in the environment it will live in, and commissioning proves that device and environment work together. The room must supply what the machine demands: the correct circuit and grounding, the correct gas outlet or cylinder connection, adequate ventilation, a stable temperature, acceptable humidity, and enough space for the operator to work and reach the patient. A large imaging device may also need floor reinforcement, radiation shielding, cooling, and a dedicated power feed, and each requirement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the room is prepared. Heavy equipment should be anchored, and cables routed so that nobody trips and no bed crushes them. Commissioning includes the first full function test in place, the setting of language and units, and entry into the equipment register. The moment to discover that the doorway is too narrow is before the machine is inside the room.

Inventory is the memory of the hospital, and without it no maintenance system can exist. Every device should carry a unique identifier that survives cleaning, linked in a register to its description, maker, serial number, location, custodian, purchase date, warranty, and full service history. A device without a number cannot be found, cannot be scheduled, and cannot be proven to have been maintained. The register also reveals the pattern of loss: pumps that migrate to another department, monitors that are borrowed and never returned, and accessories thrown away with the packaging. A hospital-grade register is usually electronic, searchable, and reconciled by physical count at intervals, with every discrepancy investigated. A field clinic can keep the same discipline with a paper ledger, a painted number, and a monthly walk through the rooms. What cannot be found cannot be maintained.

Training is not an accessory to the device but one of its components, and a machine handed over without it is only half delivered. Its purpose is to build a working mental model in the operator, so the person understands what the device is doing, what normal looks and sounds like, and what early failure looks like. A good handover covers the start-up sequence, the daily checks, the meaning of the settings, the alarms and their correct responses, the cleaning that is allowed, and the faults that require a technician rather than a nurse. It should be practical, repeated, and recorded, with a competency check rather than a signature on an attendance sheet. At least one person on each shift should be a designated superuser who can teach others and who knows whom to call. A device is only as safe as the least trained person who will be left alone with it.

Calibration is the process that keeps a measurement honest. Its physical basis is comparison: an instrument is made to measure a known reference, and the difference between what it reads and what the reference states is recorded, so that its error becomes known and can be corrected. The reference must itself be traceable, meaning it has been compared, step by step, with a national or international standard, and each comparison is documented. Drift is why calibration is repeated, because sensors age, amplifiers wander, mechanical parts wear, and the link between a physical quantity and an electrical signal slowly changes. Calibration is not verification, which only checks that a device still reads within tolerance, and it is not adjustment, which changes the device to restore agreement. Intervals are set by the manufacturer and by the risk of the device, and each interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is relied upon.

The devices that most need calibration are those whose numbers become decisions. Sphygmomanometers, thermometers, infusion pumps, defibrillators, gas analyzers, laboratory analyzers, and dialysis machines all belong to this group, and each has its own reference and tolerance. A defibrillator is checked by delivering a stored charge into a test load and measuring the energy in joules, and the acceptable error must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is cleared for use. An infusion pump is checked by measuring the volume it actually delivers over a set time, because a pump that under-delivers silently changes every dose in the ward. The general rule is that the more directly a number drives a drug dose or an energy delivery, the more often it must be questioned.

The field variant of calibration is a compromise openly made rather than a failure hidden. Where no traceable reference exists, a clinic can still cross-check one device against another, keep a dedicated reference instrument that is never used on patients, and send that instrument to a regional laboratory for periodic comparison. Simple physical checks remain valuable: a thermometer against the freezing and boiling behavior of water at the local altitude, a scale against a known mass, and a pressure cuff against a second cuff and a careful manual reading. The limits of these substitutes must be written down, because a cross-check between two equally drifted instruments proves only that they agree. An uncalibrated device used knowingly is a named risk, while the same device used unknowingly is a trap.

Preventive maintenance is the work done before a fault becomes a failure, and its logic comes from the way machines wear. Many components fail on a curve that begins with early failure, settles into a long plateau, and then rises sharply as wear accumulates, and replacing the wearing parts on schedule keeps the device on that plateau. Preventive maintenance includes inspection, cleaning, lubrication, tightening, testing, and replacement of parts with a known life, such as filters, seals, tubing, batteries, lamps, and probe covers. It includes the functional test of every alarm, because an alarm that has never sounded is an untested safety system and tends to be found silent on the worst possible day. The interval is set by the manufacturer and the intensity of use, and it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, since a device used continuously needs attention far sooner than one used occasionally. The common operator error is postponing maintenance while the machine is busy, which is precisely when wear accumulates fastest.

Failure modes cluster in the places the designer could not protect. Cables break where they bend, connectors corrode where liquid collects, seals leak where they are compressed, filters block where dust is drawn in, and circuit boards fail where heat has nowhere to go. A battery is a consumable that looks like a permanent part: its capacity falls with every cycle, it ages even when unused, and it fails fastest at high temperature and at full charge. A device always left plugged in may carry a battery that has never been exercised, and the first time it is needed on transport it may fail within minutes. The operator's contribution to reliability is not repair but early reporting, because a new noise, a new smell, or a slightly different reading is the cheapest warning a device will ever give. The safety hazard here is the gradual and invisible decline that leaves the machine looking exactly as it always did.

Every device has a short list of things the operator must check before it touches a patient, and that list belongs on the machine or in the log rather than in memory. The check begins with the physical state: plug, cable, housing, connectors, probe, cuff, tubing, and seals, looking for cracks, exposed conductors, discoloration, moisture, or residue from the last cleaning. It continues with power and self-test, battery charge, the presence and expiry date of consumables, and the correct selection of patient size or operating mode. Alarm limits should be set deliberately for this patient and provoked once to prove they sound, because a threshold that is not confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol is only a hope. Settings left from the previous patient are a frequent and dangerous error, especially on ventilators, pumps, and monitors, where the wrong mode can be delivered with complete confidence. If anything fails the check, the device must be removed, tagged, and reported, and the temptation to use it just this once must be treated as the hazard it is.

Characteristic alarms teach an operator what a device is worried about, and each one has a correct response. A low battery alarm means the machine is warning before it stops, and the answer is to connect it rather than to silence it. An occlusion alarm on an infusion pump means the pressure in the line has risen, and the answer is to examine the line, the cannula, and the clamp rather than press start repeatedly. An air-in-line alarm means the sensor has seen a bubble, so the line must be stopped and the air removed before restarting. A sensor fault or a calibration due alarm means the measurement itself is suspect, and the machine is telling the truth about its own limits. The common operator error with every alarm is silencing it and continuing, which converts a warning into an unnoticed event.

Cleaning and reprocessing belong to the lifecycle because they are the most frequent form of wear a device will ever experience. The physical principle is that soil, salt, and protein must be removed before any disinfectant can work, because organic material shields the organisms beneath it and consumes the chemical meant to kill them. Cleaning therefore precedes disinfection, and disinfection precedes sterilization where sterilization is required, and each step must reach every surface that will contact the patient. An instrument that will enter sterile tissue must be cleaned, inspected, and sterilized, often in a steam cycle at 134 degrees Celsius for several minutes, a cycle that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The materials constrain what may be applied, because alcohol cracks some plastics, chlorine corrodes metal and ruins some seals, and water enters anything not sealed against it. Every device has an ingress rating and a list of approved agents, and these must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any liquid is applied.

The biomedical engineering department is the institution's memory and skill for all of this work. It receives new equipment, performs acceptance testing, maintains the register, schedules preventive maintenance, calibrates what it can and contracts what it cannot, repairs what is repairable, investigates incidents, trains users, manages spare parts, and recommends decommissioning. It usually keeps a small equipment library of pumps, monitors, and beds that can be lent during a repair, which is one of the cheapest ways to reduce the clinical cost of downtime. Its most valuable product is not the repair but the trend: the model that fails repeatedly, the cleaning method that damages a surface, and the training gap that keeps producing the same user error. A hospital without this function does not avoid the work, because it distributes the work invisibly among nurses who have no time for it.

A clinic without a biomedical engineering department must build a substitute, and the substitute can be surprisingly effective if it is deliberate. The usual arrangement is a named person with a written role, a basic toolkit, a multimeter, a maintenance schedule pinned to the wall, and a telephone relationship with a regional workshop or the maker's service line. Consumable parts and the most common spares should be held locally, because a journey of 200 kilometers for a fuse is a day of lost care. Simple tasks can be delegated to trained users: cleaning, the alarm test, the battery check, cable inspection, and recording faults in a log. More complex work should be sent out early rather than attempted late, because an amateur repair on a device that delivers energy or measures a dose can turn a fault into an injury.

Repair against replacement is a decision made on evidence rather than sentiment. The questions are whether the repair restores the device to its specified performance, whether parts are available in useful time, whether the cost is a sensible fraction of an equivalent replacement, whether the device is still clinically needed, and whether the maker or regulator has withdrawn it for safety. A device becomes unsafe to keep when its failure could harm a patient and cannot be reliably repaired: cracked insulation, an alarm that no longer sounds, a radiation output beyond tolerance, a pressure vessel past its test date, a swelling battery, or a fault the maker will never correct. Such a device must be removed immediately, tagged with the reason and date, and stored where it cannot quietly return to the ward. The temptation in a low-resource setting is to keep a marginal device alive, and that temptation must be named as a hazard, because the machine that is almost working is often more dangerous than the one that is clearly broken. A repaired device must be tested against its specification before returning to use.

Decommissioning is the orderly end of the biography, and it begins with a decision that is written down. The device is removed from the active register, its location and final state recorded, and any patient data it holds erased according to the rules that govern the electronic health record and the local privacy law. Its special contents must be handled before the metal: batteries, mercury switches and thermometers, refrigerants, compressed gas cylinders, oils, and any sealed radioactive source, each with its own route and record. A radiation source cannot simply be sold or dumped, and the responsible authority must be involved before anything moves. Useful parts may be harvested, manuals and accessories kept as spares for surviving units, and the remainder sent to electronic waste recycling or another licensed route. The removal must be complete, because a decommissioned device left in a corridor will eventually be plugged in by someone who does not know why it was retired.

Cannibalization is the practice of taking parts from one device to keep another alive, and it is neither shameful nor safe by itself. It is rational when a model is out of production, the part cannot be bought, and the donor device is beyond repair, because the alternative is two dead machines instead of one working one. It becomes dangerous when the donor is merely inconvenient, when worn parts are moved into a working machine, when the swap changes calibration without verification, and when the change is not written down. A cannibalized device may pass every function test and still be unreliable, because the transplanted part carries the wear of its previous life and the machine has lost the traceability that proves it was assembled as designed. The safe version keeps a controlled store of harvested parts, pairs each with its donor and condition, and verifies the function and calibration of the recipient after the swap. In a field clinic cannibalization is often the only repair available, which makes discipline around it more important and not less.

Disposal is the last physical stage, and it is a clinical and environmental act rather than a housekeeping one. Devices that have contacted blood, body fluids, or infectious material must be decontaminated before they leave the building, and the waste they generate must be separated into the streams local rules define: general, infectious, sharps, chemical, pharmaceutical, and radiological. Electronic waste must not be burned in the open, because the plastics release toxic fumes and the batteries can ignite, and a lithium battery crushed in a landfill is a fire waiting for a reason. Metals can be recovered, and in some settings that recovery is a livelihood, which makes removing hazardous components before sale a matter of public safety. A device that disappears without a record has not been disposed of, because it has only been lost.

Donation is one of the largest sources of equipment in low-resource settings and one of the largest sources of unsustainability. The failures are consistent and well known: the device arrives without consumables, without a manual, without a service history, and without anyone trained to use it. It may be built for a different electrical supply, gas fitting, cylinder valve, language, or clinical practice, and it may already be at the end of its supported life when shipped. The receiving clinic often pays transport, customs duty, and storage, so a gift can cost more than a purchase and deliver less. A clinic that accepts a donation should inspect it before it is sent, require the documents and a service record, identify the consumables and their supplier, and confirm that someone can maintain it. It is entirely legitimate to refuse a donation that cannot be sustained, and to ask instead for the consumable budget that would make an existing device work.

The field variant compresses every stage of the lifecycle and places it in the hands of a few people. Acceptance testing becomes a careful inspection on a table, because there is no engineering department to call, and the person who unpacks the device must check the voltage setting, the battery, the accessories, and the basic function before the crate is discarded. The register is a notebook or a card taped inside the carrying case, listing the device, its number, its faults, and the name of whoever fixed them. Preventive maintenance is a daily and weekly ritual performed by the user, and the person who cleans the device is the one most likely to notice the crack, the noise, and the failing battery. Repair is tiered: the user changes what the manual allows, a district technician handles the next level, and the device travels to the capital only when nothing else can be done. In this setting the lifecycle is not a department but a habit.

Across every stage, 3 failures repeat themselves, and naming them is the purpose of this chapter. The first is the machine used without being understood, which happens when training is treated as optional and the manual is written in a language the operator does not read. The second is the machine maintained only after it fails, which converts a cheap scheduled part into an expensive repair and a period of unavailable care. The third is the machine nobody owns, which drifts between rooms, loses its accessories, and is discovered with a fault no one reported. The characteristic alarm of a neglected device is rarely dramatic; it is the low battery, the calibration due, and the sensor fault that everyone has learned to dismiss. The operator error joining all three is the assumption that a machine which turns on is a machine that can be trusted.

Documentation is what turns a collection of machines into a managed system, and it is also what protects patients when something goes wrong. The equipment register, maintenance log, calibration certificate, acceptance test record, training record, and disposal record together form the legal and clinical history of the device, and they are the first things requested after an incident. That history also makes recalls possible, because a manufacturer's safety notice can be acted on only if the affected serial numbers and their locations are known. In a hospital these records live in a maintenance management system and increasingly connect to the electronic health record. In a field clinic the same records live on paper, in a bound book that stays with the equipment. The deepest point of the lifecycle is that maintenance is clinical care performed in advance, because the nurse who checks the suction before the airway is needed is practicing medicine.

To summarize, the life of a medical device runs from recognition of a need through specification, procurement, acceptance, installation, training, inventory, calibration, preventive maintenance, repair, and finally decommissioning and disposal, and every stage determines whether the machine will be safe when a patient needs it. The hospital-grade device depends on infrastructure, consumables, documentation, and a biomedical engineering department, while the field variant depends on simplicity, repairability, local skill, and a supply chain that can actually reach it. The physical realities are wear, drift, corrosion, battery aging, and contamination, and the human realities are operator error, alarm fatigue, skipped maintenance, and the machine nobody owns. The operator's own responsibility is the pre-use check: cables, housing, battery, consumables, correct settings, and an alarm provoked and heard. Every setting, interval, temperature, and threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because no number in a book can replace the document that belongs to the machine.

# Chapter 5 — Hospital Beds and Patient Handling

The hospital bed is not furniture but a machine, and every part of it exists to solve a problem of force. A body lying still still presses downward with its whole weight, and that weight passes through the skin, the soft tissue, and the bone onto whatever surface supports it. A flat, hard surface concentrates that load on the few places where the skeleton is close to the skin, while a soft surface spreads it over a wider area but lets the body sink into a hollow. The frame carries the load, the moving sections change its direction, the mattress distributes it, and the side rails and brakes keep the whole assembly where it was put. Every adjustment described in this chapter is a setting, and every setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

A manual bed is the purest expression of the mechanism. Its frame is a rectangular steel or aluminum chassis on 4 casters, with a head section, a seat section, and a leg section hinged to each other. Cranks at the foot of the bed turn shafts that drive worm gears or screw jacks, and each turn of the handle raises or lowers a section by a fixed distance. A ratchet holds the section at the height chosen, and the patient's weight is what the gear train must overcome, which is why a bed loaded with a heavy patient is far harder to crank than an empty bed. The common operator error is to leave the crank handle protruding into the walkway, where it catches a passing hip or a swinging door and bends the shaft or breaks the handle. The characteristic sign of a failing manual bed is a crank that turns freely without moving the section, which usually means a stripped gear or a sheared pin rather than a problem the user can repair. The angle each section reaches, whether 30 degrees for a backrest or 45 degrees for a knee break, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the graduations on an old bed may no longer be honest.

An electric bed replaces the crank with a motor and a linear actuator, a threaded rod that extends and retracts inside a tube when the motor turns it. The characteristic alarm is a warning tone or a flashing indicator when the actuator is overloaded, when the handset is disconnected, or when the battery is too weak to answer the button. The common operator error is to keep pressing a button against a mechanical stop, which stalls the motor and heats the windings rather than protecting them. The height range, the backrest angle, and the battery capacity printed in the manual are settings that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The intensive care bed is the same machine with more of everything. It is usually longer and wider, rated for a much heavier patient, and built so that a radiograph cassette can slide beneath the mattress without lifting the patient. Many intensive care beds carry a built-in scale, which works by measuring the load at each corner of the frame and summing the 4 readings, and this is why the bed must be level and the patient still before a weight is trusted. The characteristic alarm is the scale fault or the bed exit alert, the latter triggered by a sensor pad or by a load change when the patient tries to climb out. The weight limit of such a bed may be 250 kilograms or more, and that figure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the bed is used, because the limit includes the mattress, the rails, and every pump hung on the frame.

Side rails look like a simple safety feature and are in fact among the most serious hazards in the ward. They are barriers, but a barrier with gaps, and a patient whose body is small, confused, or frail can slide through the gap between the rail and the mattress, or between 2 sections of rail, and become trapped by the neck or the chest. The danger is greatest with a mattress that is too thin for the rail, with a rail that is not locked in its raised position, or with a rail raised only along a single edge so that the patient tries to climb over the other. The correct response to a patient who keeps climbing out is not more rails but a proper assessment and, where needed, a low bed, a mat on the floor, or a bed exit alarm. The common operator error is to treat raised rails as a restraint and to leave them up for a patient who is fully mobile, which increases the fall from a greater height when he climbs over. Any gap measurement quoted for a rail and mattress combination must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, since a rail matched to the wrong mattress is the failure that causes the injury.

The brakes and casters decide whether the bed stays where it is put. A caster is a small wheel in a swiveling fork, and a brake is usually a cam or a lever that presses a pad against the tread, or a lock that drops a pin into the wheel. Braking a single wheel of the 4 is not the same as braking the bed, because the frame can still pivot around the locked wheel, which is why the rule is to apply the brakes on all 4 casters, and on most beds to press the pedal at the head end and the foot end in turn. A bed on a polished floor with wet wheels can travel several meters from a single push, and a patient stepping onto an unbraked bed is a classic cause of a fall and of a staff back injury. The common operator error is to leave the brake pedal in the mid position, where it looks applied but holds nothing, or to brake only the wheels along a single edge. The braking mechanism on a bed that has been dragged through detergent and disinfectant for years may need adjustment, and the inspection interval for that adjustment must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Position is the reason the bed has sections at all, and each position is a controlled application of gravity. Raising the backrest shifts the patient's weight onto the sacrum and the heels, and raising the knee break keeps him from sliding down the bed, but the pair together create shear, a force that pulls the skin sideways across the mattress and damages it from within. The Trendelenburg position tilts the whole bed head down, which uses gravity to drain the airway or to shift the abdominal contents upward, while the reverse Trendelenburg tilts the foot down and is used to relieve pressure on the diaphragm in a patient who cannot breathe lying flat. A tilt of 15 to 30 degrees is the range usually quoted for these positions, and that angle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard of a steep head-down tilt is that the patient slides toward the head of the bed, that the diaphragm is pushed up, and that a full stomach can reflux into the airway. The common operator error is to reach for the Trendelenburg position as a reflex in every collapse, when in many cases it delays compressions and does nothing for the cause.

The mattress is where the body actually rests, and its job is to keep the interface pressure between skin and surface below the pressure at which capillaries close. A foam mattress distributes load by compressing where the body is heaviest and springing back where it is light, and its quality is measured by density and by the way it recovers rather than by its softness in the hand. A mattress that is too thin or too soft lets the sacrum, the heels, and the shoulder blades press almost directly onto the bed frame, and it is at those 4 or 5 points that pressure injury begins. A cover that is waterproof keeps fluids out but also keeps air in, so a mattress with a torn or wrinkled cover traps moisture and heat against the skin and multiplies the damage. The thickness and the load rating of the mattress must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the mattress must be matched to the bed frame and to the side rails, because the 3 are designed as a single system.

Pressure-relieving surfaces go beyond foam by changing the pressure under the patient over time. A static surface uses a material that flows, such as viscoelastic foam, gel, or air cells linked to each other, to spread the load over a larger area. An alternating pressure mattress is built from parallel air cells that inflate and deflate in cycles, usually of several minutes, so that any single patch of skin is loaded and then released; the physical principle is that even a short period of unloading restores blood flow to the tissue. A low-air-loss system is different: it keeps the cells inflated but forces air through small perforations to evaporate moisture from the skin, which addresses maceration rather than pressure alone. The inflation pressure, the cycle duration, and the alarm threshold on such a pump must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because an under-inflated cell that touches the frame transfers the patient's weight straight to it.

The pump of a powered mattress is a small blower or compressor, and it is the part that fails first. Its filter clogs with lint and dust, its hose splits at the connector, and its alarm sounds when the pressure in the circuit falls below the set point, which usually means a leak, a disconnected cell, or a patient who has slid off the surface onto the frame. The characteristic alarm is therefore a low pressure tone, sometimes with a flashing light, and the correct response is to look for the leak rather than to silence the pump. The common operator error is to lay the mattress hose across the floor where it is stepped on, or to set the pump on the bed frame where it falls, and both produce the same low pressure alarm within hours. The filter change interval and the pressure setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A powered surface that has been running without its filter for a year is not a pressure-relieving device; it is a noisy mattress.

Stretchers and trolleys are beds designed around movement rather than rest. Their frames are lighter, their wheels are larger and often of different sizes at the 2 ends so that the trolley can be steered, and most carry a brake and a steering lock on separate pedals. They add a head-end section that raises for transport, side rails that fold flat, and a mattress that is thinner because it must be light enough for 2 people to lift. The common operator error is to push a loaded trolley at a run while a single staff member steers and nobody watches the patient's arms, which are the first thing to strike a doorframe. The safe working load of the trolley and the pressure of its hydraulic system must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A wheelchair is a chair on 2 large wheels and 2 small ones, and its physics are dominated by where the weight sits. The large wheels carry the occupant, the small casters steer, and the rear axle position decides how much effort the user needs to push and how easily the chair tips backward. Its brakes are not brakes in the vehicle sense; they are parking locks that press on the tire, and they do nothing to slow a moving chair, which is why a wheelchair on a slope must be controlled by hand or by an attendant. An examination couch is a fixed or adjustable table, often with a backrest and a leg rest, and its height is chosen so that the examiner can work at a comfortable angle, commonly between 70 and 90 centimeters, a dimension that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error with both devices is to ignore the weight limit, which on a standard wheelchair may be around 120 kilograms, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and to overload it without noticing the frame flex.

Weight limits are engineering statements, not suggestions, and the label on the frame is the place to find them. The rating refers to the whole load: the patient, the mattress, the pumps, the monitors, the traction frame, and anything else hung on the bed. A bed rated at 150 kilograms that carries a 130 kilogram patient, a 15 kilogram mattress, and 2 infusion pumps is already at or beyond its rating, and the failure that follows is a bent frame, a cracked weld, or a collapsing leg. The common operator error is to assume that a bed which has held a heavy patient before will hold another, and to skip the label because the bed looks substantial. The rating and the labeling convention for a given frame must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and where the label is missing, the bed should be treated as unrated until the manufacturer or a biomedical engineer can say otherwise.

Moving a patient is a problem in friction and leverage. The load is the patient's body, the lever is the staff member's spine, and the force needed rises steeply as the load is held farther from the body; that is why reaching across a bed to lift is far more damaging than lifting the same weight close to the chest. Friction between the patient and the sheet is what makes a slide so hard, and the whole family of transfer aids exists to reduce that friction or to change the direction of the effort. A sliding sheet, made of a smooth low friction fabric, lets 2 people move a patient who could not be lifted by 4, and a transfer board bridges the gap between bed and chair so that the patient slides rather than is carried. The common operator error is to pull a patient by the arms or by the shoulders, which loads a joint that is not designed to carry the body, instead of using the sheet and a coordinated count. The safe working load of every transfer aid must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A hoist changes the direction of the effort from horizontal to vertical, so that a motor and a sling carry the patient instead of the staff member's back. A mobile hoist is a wheeled frame with a mast, a boom, and a spreader bar from which the sling hangs, and a ceiling lift is the same mechanism fixed to a track above the bed, which removes the need to push a heavy frame across the floor. The sling is the critical part: it must match the patient's size and the lift's attachment points, and a sling that is too small, wrongly threaded, or worn at the seams can release its load without warning. The characteristic alarm is an overload tone or a low battery warning.. The common operator error is to leave a patient suspended in a sling while attending to something else, or to use a damaged sling because a replacement is not in the cupboard. The lifting capacity, the battery charging routine, and the sling inspection interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Because a bed is shared by a succession of patients, its cleaning is a clinical procedure and not a housekeeping afterthought. The frame, the rails, the handset, the crank handles, and the casters are touched constantly and carry organisms from the previous occupant, and the mattress cover is the surface with which a broken or moist skin is in contact for hours. Cleaning usually means detergent first to remove organic soil and then a disinfectant rated for the organisms of concern, applied for the contact time on its label, and the contact time itself must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to spray disinfectant onto the handset and the motor housing, where liquid enters the switches and causes corrosion or an electrical fault, instead of wiping a dampened cloth over a closed surface. A mattress with a compromised cover, or a foam core that has been wet, is a reservoir that no amount of surface cleaning will make safe.

Preventive maintenance for beds and handling equipment is mostly inspection, lubrication, and replacement of small parts. The biomedical technician or the maintenance officer checks the welds and the frame for cracks, tests each caster and brake, tightens the bolts that hold the sections and the rails, inspects the handset cable for cuts, and loads the actuator or the hydraulic ram to see whether it holds. Consumables include mattress covers, foam cores, air cells, pump filters and hoses, hoist slings, sliding sheets, transfer boards, caster wheels, brake pads, and the batteries in handsets and hoists. The maintenance interval is set by the manufacturer and by the intensity of use, and it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol rather than assumed from the last workshop visit. The common operator error is to report a fault only when the bed stops working, so that a brake that needed adjustment for months becomes a fall, and a hose that needed a new filter becomes a burned out pump.

Beds fail in a small number of characteristic ways, and each has a signature. A manual bed whose backrest sinks under the patient has a worn ratchet or a slipping clutch. An electric bed that moves in a single direction has a failed limit switch or a broken wire in the handset. A bed that drifts on the floor has a brake that is not engaging, and a bed that veers sideways has a caster that has seized. A mattress that bottoms out under the sacrum has lost its foam resilience or its air pressure, and a pump that runs continuously without inflating the cells has a leak or a blocked filter. A hoist that descends slowly under load has a worn battery or a damaged actuator, and a hoist that will not lift at all may simply be on its emergency lowering function. Any pressure, angle, or load value used to diagnose or adjust these faults must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device returns to a patient.

Before a bed is given to a patient, the operator must walk around it and test what the patient will depend on. The brakes are applied on all 4 casters and the bed does not move when pushed. The side rails rise, lock, and descend smoothly, and the gap between rail and mattress is small enough that no body part can pass through. The mattress is the right size for the frame, its cover is intact, and the foam or the air cells have not collapsed. The bed is at the correct height for the patient to get in and out with his feet on the floor, and the call bell, the light, and the table are within reach. Any height, angle, or gap figure the check relies on must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and any fault found must be reported and the bed taken out of service rather than handed over with a warning.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the bed becomes an object that must be carried, improvised, or done without. The classic field stretcher is a canvas sheet stretched between 2 poles, with a second sheet or a blanket laid over it, and its whole value is that it is light, repairable with a needle, and can be carried by 2 people through a door or a forest track. A locally welded frame takes the opposite approach: a workshop copies the geometry of a hospital bed from steel tube, adds a hinged backrest and holes for the pins, and produces a device that is strong and cheap but has no standardization, no weight rating, and no manual. Its welds, its pin positions, and its tube thickness are the entire safety case, and they must be verified against the local protocol by a competent technician before it takes a patient. The characteristic failure is a welded joint that cracks at the point where the backrest hinge meets the frame, which happens suddenly and without any alarm to warn the staff. Where no frame exists, the rope bed is a woven platform of cord or webbing on a timber frame, and it is only as good as the knots and the timber that hold it.

The ground is the final field variant, and it must be described honestly, because a patient on a mat on the floor is receiving care on the oldest and least capable of all surfaces. A thin mat over earth or concrete concentrates pressure at the sacrum, the heels, and the hips within hours, and the lack of airflow and the inability to turn the patient easily make moisture and shear worse. There is no backrest, so the head cannot be raised for eating, breathing, or conversation, and there are no rails, so a confused patient rolls into whatever is beside him. There is also a matter of dignity: the height of a bed places a patient at the level of the caregiver's hands and eyes, and the floor places him below everyone who comes to help, which changes how he is spoken to and how often he is checked. Where the ground must be used, a thick mat or a stack of blankets, a regular turning schedule written on the wall, and a low platform of boards or bricks are the minimum that converts a floor space into something resembling a bed. Any turning interval or mat thickness chosen in the field must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and where neither exists, it must be set by the most experienced clinician present and recorded.

The field variant gives up precision, alarms, and the assumption of power, and it demands skill, inspection, and improvisation in return. Without motors there are no overload alarms, so the staff must judge the load by eye and by feel, and a frame that creaks under a heavy patient is a warning that only a person can hear. Without adjustable air cells there is no way to unload a pressure point except by turning the patient, so the turning schedule becomes the pressure-relieving device and the person who keeps it becomes the pump. The field kit that answers this is small: a canvas stretcher, a set of sliding sheets, a transfer board, and a rope or a set of straps for lifting. What the field configuration requires above all is that someone inspects it before every use, because nothing in it will announce its own failure.

Protecting the mover is as much a part of patient handling as protecting the patient. The injury that ends a career is rarely a single dramatic lift; it is a disc or a muscle damaged by years of small, awkward transfers, and it appears as back pain that the staff member works through until he cannot. A handling program therefore reduces the number of manual lifts by design: it puts a hoist or a ceiling lift within reach of every bed that needs it, it keeps sliding sheets and boards where they are used, and it trains staff in the specific moves their ward actually performs rather than in a general lecture. The common failure of such a program is equipment that is present but unusable, a hoist with a flat battery, a sling in the wrong size, or a board stored in a locked room, and staff who then lift by hand because it is faster. The load limits and the training requirements of any handling program must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the hospital bed is a machine for carrying a body, and every part of it answers a force. The frame and the casters carry the load and keep it still, the sections redirect gravity into the positions the patient needs, the mattress spreads the load below the pressure that closes capillaries, and the rails, the brakes, and the hoists stand between the patient and a fall. The electric bed adds motors, handsets, and batteries, and with them the alarms that say when an actuator is overloaded or a handset is unplugged, while the manual bed keeps the same geometry in a form that fails in ways a user can sometimes see. The powered mattress adds movement and airflow, and it brings a pump, a filter, and a low pressure alarm that must never be silenced without finding the leak. The field variants, the canvas stretcher, the welded frame, the rope bed, and the ground, do the same job with fewer parts and no alarms at all, which is why they demand more inspection and more turning, not less. In every setting the rule is the same: check the device before the patient depends on it, keep the weight inside the label, and treat every setting, angle, pressure, and load limit as a number to be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 6 — Vital Sign Monitoring

Vital signs are the small set of numbers that tell a clinician whether a body is governing itself: temperature, blood pressure, pulse and oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, and carbon dioxide in the breath of a sedated or seriously ill patient. Each number comes from a transducer that converts a physical quantity into a readable signal, accurate in one range and misleading outside it. This chapter takes the instruments one at a time, principle before clinical use, then the hospital-grade device with its infrastructure and consumables, then the field variant and what it gives up. Hazards, characteristic alarms, and habitual operator errors are named where each device is described.

Body temperature is a balance between heat produced by metabolism and heat lost to the environment, and the core stays in a narrow band while skin and limbs vary widely. A thermometer reads its own sensor at equilibrium with the tissue, or the infrared energy the tissue radiates, never the body directly. Clinical thermometry uses three families: thermal expansion of a liquid in a narrow bore, change in electrical resistance as a material warms, and emission of infrared radiation from a surface. Each has a different response time, site, and way of being wrong, so the dwell time or temperature threshold used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Mercury expands as it warms and is forced up a narrow bore beside a printed scale, and a constriction below the bulb holds the column so that the highest temperature is retained. Its accuracy is excellent, but mercury is a neurotoxin, a broken tube scatters droplets that evaporate, and glass in the mouth of a confused patient invites injury. The common errors are reading too early, failing to shake the column down, and reading the meniscus at the wrong angle. There is no alarm, only the silent error of a premature reading, so the required dwell time of several minutes must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The digital probe replaces the column with a thermistor whose electrical resistance falls predictably as it warms, and many devices predict the final temperature from the rate of change without waiting for equilibrium. Sites are the mouth, the armpit, and the rectum, each with an offset from core temperature that the operator must apply. The consumables are single-use probe covers that form the barrier and must not be doubled, because two layers slow the response and bias the reading. A low battery or out-of-range alarm means the reading cannot be trusted, and site offsets and concern thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The tympanic thermometer measures infrared energy radiated by the tympanic membrane, which shares its blood supply with the hypothalamus and tracks core temperature closely. A thermopile converts received energy into a temperature once emissivity and probe temperature are known, so the device is fast and needs no mucosal contact. Accuracy depends on pulling the pinna back to straighten the canal, aiming at the membrane, and keeping the canal free of wax, and the common errors are aiming at the canal wall and omitting the single-use cover. The fever threshold used to act must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The temporal artery thermometer reads infrared emission along a swept path over the forehead and temple, where the superficial temporal artery runs close to the surface. Because the artery carries blood near core temperature, a correct sweep from the forehead to behind the ear approximates the core and depends far less on probe angle. The technique is one continuous stroke with the hair parted and the skin dry, and stopping the sweep, pressing too hard, and scanning over hair are the habitual errors. Sweat or a cold forehead after outdoor exposure produces a low reading that may hide fever, and any treatment threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The chemical dot thermometer is a strip of heat-sensitive material, often a matrix of squares that each change color at a slightly different temperature, so it reports a band rather than a number. It is cheap, powerless, unbreakable, and useful for screening many people or for sending a mother home with a means of checking her child. Its accuracy is poor near the thresholds that matter, it is single-use, and its calibration drifts if it is stored hot, so a box left in a parked vehicle may be useless. Common errors are reading in dim light, using the wrong dwell time, and using a strip past its expiry date, and storage temperature and the action threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the field, every thermometer is a contest between dust, heat, and the battery, since glass breaks, a digital probe needs covers and power, an infrared device needs a clean lens, and chemical dots need shade and a cool box. The field substitutes are a hand on the abdomen, a careful axillary reading taken the same way every time, and the picture of a child who is hot, lethargic, and not feeding. What the field gives up is precision, and what it demands instead is consistency of site, dwell time, and device. Every temperature threshold that leads to treatment must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Blood pressure measurement begins with a physical act, because a cuff is inflated until it exceeds the pressure inside the artery and the artery is occluded. As the cuff deflates, the turbulent jet of returning blood is heard through a stethoscope as sounds that appear, soften, and finally disappear, with the first appearance read as systolic and the disappearance as diastolic. Three instruments measure the cuff pressure itself: a mercury column by the height of liquid metal pushed up a tube, an aneroid gauge by the deformation of a sealed metal element, and an automated device by the small oscillations the artery transmits into the cuff. The diagnostic and treatment thresholds used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The mercury sphygmomanometer is a vertical tube, a reservoir, a bulb, a valve, and a cuff joined by tubing, read by eye against a scale. Its virtue is that it reports a length of mercury, a quantity that cannot drift, so a clean and correctly zeroed instrument is a reference for checking others. Its hazards are the roughly one kilogram of toxic mercury it contains and the fragility of its glass, and it must be checked for a broken column, bubbles, oxidized mercury, and leaks in the tube and valve. Common errors are deflating too quickly to hear the sounds, letting the mercury rest below the zero mark, and using a cuff too small for the arm, and any pressure used to diagnose or to treat must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The aneroid sphygmomanometer replaces the column with a circular gauge in which a curved, sealed metal element straightens as pressure enters and drives a needle across a dial. It is light, cannot spill mercury, and is the device most often found in a clinic bag, but its mechanism drifts with age, drops, and heat, usually reading low. Common errors are a gauge that does not rest at zero, a bent needle or cracked glass, and a cuff left folded for years so that the bladder perishes. A gauge should be checked against a known good reference at zero and across its range, and calibration intervals and the acceptable error must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The automated oscillometric device pumps the cuff, then releases the pressure in steps while a sensor watches the small pulsations that each heartbeat adds to the cuff. Those oscillations grow to a maximum and then fade, and the pressure at the maximum corresponds closely to mean arterial pressure, from which an algorithm estimates the systolic and diastolic values. The method removes the observer's ear but also the observer's judgment, and it is less reliable with an irregular rhythm, in shock with low flow, in certain hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and in a moving patient. Common errors are measuring through clothing, an arm hanging below heart level, talking during the measurement, and kinked tubing, and inflation and alarm limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cuff is not an accessory but part of the instrument, and its size determines the result, so the bladder should encircle about 40 per cent of the limb circumference and wrap about 80 per cent of the way around. Too narrow a cuff for a large arm reads falsely high, because more pressure is needed over a smaller contact area, and too wide a cuff for a small arm reads falsely low, because pressure is spread along a longer segment of artery. Manufacturers mark cuffs with a range of limb circumferences and often a color code, and common errors are an adult cuff on a child, a child cuff on an adult because it fits more comfortably, and not measuring the arm at all. Cuff size ranges and the correction they imply must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Even with the right cuff and a calibrated device, technique changes the number, so the patient should rest for 5 minutes, sit with the back supported and the feet flat, and keep the arm supported at heart level. The bladder belongs over the brachial artery with its lower edge about 2 to 3 centimeters above the crease of the elbow, and deflation for an auscultatory reading should run about 2 to 3 millimeters of mercury per second. An auscultatory gap, a silent interval between the sounds, causes the systolic value to be underestimated if the cuff is inflated only slightly above the expected pressure. Talking, an unsupported back, crossed legs, a full bladder, and a cold room all raise the pressure. The rest period, deflation rate, repeat interval, and thresholds used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of blood pressure equipment is mostly a search for leaks and drift, because cuff, tubing, and valve are rubber and fabric that perish, and a leak makes the pressure fall faster than intended. A simple leak test is to inflate the cuff, close the valve, and watch whether the pressure holds, and the cuff should be inspected for a cracked bladder, a frayed closure, and perished tubing at the connectors. An aneroid gauge should be checked against a reference at more than one pressure, and an automated device for the accuracy of its cuff and the integrity of its hose and connector. Devices in daily use belong on a calibration schedule with a written log, and calibration intervals and the acceptable error must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the field, mercury is too fragile and heavy and an automated device needs batteries and an intact cuff, so an aneroid gauge or a battery-operated oscillometric device is usual. Neither can be sent away for calibration every year, so the field demands a local reference, meaning a second device kept clean and handled carefully, cross-checked against the first, with a written note whenever the two disagree. The palpation method, in which the operator inflates the cuff and feels the pulse return at the wrist, gives a systolic value only, but it needs no stethoscope and no quiet room and it beats no measurement at all. What the field gives up is traceability, and what it demands is the same technique, limb, and cuff for the same patient, and the action thresholds derived from those readings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The pulse oximeter rests on an optical fact, because oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently. It shines two wavelengths through a translucent part of the body, one near 660 nanometers that deoxygenated blood absorbs more strongly and another near 940 nanometers that oxygenated blood absorbs more strongly, and measures how much light reaches a detector on the other side. The signal has a steady part from skin, bone, and non-pulsatile blood and a small pulsatile part that rises and falls with each heartbeat, and the device uses only the pulsatile part, which is why a good oximeter shows a pulse waveform. The ratio of the wavelengths becomes a saturation value through an empirical curve built from healthy volunteers, and that value says nothing about how much hemoglobin is present or how much oxygen reaches the tissues, and alarm limits and the values used to act must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A transmission probe places the light source and the detector on opposite sides of a finger or an earlobe, while a reflectance probe places both on the same surface of the forehead or the chest, and infants wear a wrap around a foot or a toe. Reusable probes are robust but must be cleaned between patients, while single-use adhesive probes reduce cross-contamination and stay in place on a moving patient but cost money and cannot be reused. The safety hazard is pressure, because a probe left too long or applied too tightly can injure skin and underlying tissue, especially in a small child or a patient with poor circulation, so the site must be inspected and rotated. Common errors are a probe too large or too small for the digit, a cable trapped under the patient, and cleaning the sensor with a solvent that damages its optical surfaces, and rotation intervals and cleaning agents must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The pulse oximeter is the vital sign instrument most likely to report a confident wrong number. Movement makes the pulsatile signal unstable, cold causes vasoconstriction and a poor signal even in a well oxygenated patient, and nail polish and artificial nails absorb the wavelengths used. Poor perfusion from shock, low cardiac output, or severe anemia reduces the signal, venous congestion from a tight probe confuses the algorithm, and ambient light or electrical interference adds noise. Carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin are misread as normal saturation, so carbon monoxide poisoning may show a reassuring number, and the common operator error is to trust the number without looking at the waveform and the perfusion at the site. Alarm thresholds and the response to a poor trace must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic alarms of a pulse oximeter are a low saturation alarm, a pulse rate alarm, and a probe-off or low-perfusion alarm, and each asks the operator to look at the patient rather than the screen. A saturation threshold is often set near 90 per cent for an adult, but the correct value depends on the patient and the setting and must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Common errors are silencing an alarm without examining the patient, setting limits so wide that they never fire, and setting them so narrow that they fire constantly and train the staff to ignore them. When a reading is doubtful, the operator should check the waveform, warm the limb, move the probe to another site, and compare the result with the patient's breathing, color, and conscious state, because a pulse oximeter monitors rather than diagnoses.

In the field the oximeter is often the only continuous monitor available and also the most fragile, since a handheld battery device survives dust and a drop but its probe is the weak point, with a cable that breaks at the connector and optical surfaces that scratch. A reusable clip probe needs careful cleaning and a spare, and a supply of adhesive wraps is worth carrying because they keep a child's foot still. Solar charging and a stock of batteries are part of the equipment, since a device that cannot be charged will fail at night, and cold hands make warming the limb a routine step. What the field gives up is the hospital's continuous multi-parameter display, and what it demands is a disciplined spot check with the waveform inspected and the result written down, and the limits used for action must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Capnography measures carbon dioxide in the breath and belongs beside the other vital signs because it shows whether the airway is patent and whether air is reaching the alveoli. Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light strongly at a wavelength near 4.3 micrometers, so a mainstream device measures across a chamber in the breathing circuit while a sidestream device pulls a sample through a thin tube to a bench instrument protected by a water trap and a filter. The output is the capnogram, which rises as the patient exhales, plateaus as alveolar gas passes the sensor, and falls sharply as the next breath begins. The value at the end of the plateau, the end-tidal carbon dioxide, approximates alveolar and therefore arterial carbon dioxide, and alarm limits and interpretation thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The practical difficulty of capnography is water and secretions, because a sidestream sampling line is narrow and saliva, mucus, or condensed water can block it, producing a flat line that looks exactly like apnea. The water trap is a consumable that must be emptied or changed as its design requires, and the sampling line is single-use and should be replaced when contaminated or when the waveform degrades. A nasal cannula with a sampling port monitors a sedated patient who is breathing spontaneously, while an airway adapter with a mainstream sensor monitors a ventilated patient. Common errors are treating a blocked line as a clinical event, skipping zeroing where the design requires it, and leaving the sensor where it is heated or soiled, and replacement intervals and alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic alarms of a capnograph are apnea, a low end-tidal value, and a high end-tidal value, with a low alarm often set near 25 millimeters of mercury and a high alarm near 50 millimeters of mercury. Both values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use because they differ with the patient and the setting. A sudden loss of waveform during airway management usually means the tube has moved, but it can also mean a disconnected circuit or a blocked line, so the operator must check the patient first and the tubing second. A rising value suggests hypoventilation or rebreathing, a falling value suggests hyperventilation or reduced cardiac output, and a sudden rise during chest compressions is a recognized sign that circulation has returned, so the waveform and not the single number carries the information.

In the field, continuous capnography is rare because it needs a battery, a supply of sampling lines, and a device that survives being carried, so the substitute is the colorimetric detector. That detector is a single-use device between the circuit and the patient, containing an acid-sensitive chemical that changes color with carbon dioxide, and the color swings with each breath so that the change over several breaths confirms the airway is in the trachea. It reports a range rather than a number, has a limited life once opened, and is sensitive to heat and expiry, so it must be stored within its stated range and checked before use. A handheld electronic capnograph with disposable lines is the middle option, and what the field gives up is the continuous trend while what it demands is the discipline to confirm placement and ventilation at the moment that matters, and storage temperature, expiry, and response time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The respiratory rate is the vital sign that changes first in a deteriorating patient and the one most often estimated rather than measured. It should be counted for a full 60 seconds while the patient remains unaware, because people breathe differently when observed, and counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by four multiplies the error. A newborn breathes much faster than an adult and the normal range narrows with age, so the same number means different things in different patients. The common operator error is to copy the number from the last chart entry, which is serious because the respiratory rate triggers escalation in most early warning systems, and escalation thresholds and normal ranges must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Several devices count the respiratory rate automatically, including impedance pneumography through two electrocardiogram electrodes that detects the change in chest impedance, a capnograph that derives the rate from the carbon dioxide waveform, a strain gauge belt that measures the change in length as the body moves, and acoustic or radar devices that listen without touching the patient. All are defeated by movement, coughing, poor electrode contact, and the irregular breathing of a partly obstructed patient. The common error is to accept a displayed rate when the underlying waveform is noisy. Alarm limits and the apnea interval used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the field the respiratory rate is measured by a watch and a hand, because the health worker places a hand on the chest or the abdomen, watches the rise and fall, and counts for a full minute. There is no device to fail and no battery to die, but there is also no alarm to call attention to a patient deteriorating between visits, so a small notebook and the observation chart record the value and the time. A pediatric counting aid or a simple timer supports the count, and a pulse oximeter with a respiratory rate display can supplement it when it works. What the field gives up is automation, and what it demands is the discipline to count every time and compare the number with the previous one, and escalation thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Every instrument in this chapter touches the patient, and every one can carry organisms from one person to the next, so reusable cuffs, thermometer probes, oximeter probes, and device surfaces must be cleaned between patients with an agent compatible with the materials. Single-use items, including probe covers, adhesive oximeter wraps, capnography sampling lines, water traps, and chemical dot thermometers, are used once and discarded, and a clinic that reuses them trades a small saving for an infection. Consumables must be stored within their stated temperature range, rotated so that the oldest are used first, and checked for expiry before they reach the patient, because a thermometer without a cover or an oximeter without a probe is out of service. Storage conditions, cleaning agents, contact times, and the compatibility of each product with each device must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of monitoring equipment is mostly batteries, calibration, and inspection, and it is cheap compared with the cost of a missed deterioration. Batteries must be charged on a schedule, tested at the start of a shift, and replaced before they fail, because a monitor that dies during a transport is worse than no monitor. Devices with a calibration requirement, including automated blood pressure monitors, capnographs, and some infrared thermometers, belong on a documented schedule with results written in a log. The failure modes to hunt are the silent drift of a gauge, a cracked cuff, an intermittent cable, a blocked sampling line, and a flat battery, and calibration intervals, acceptable error, and the self-test procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Before any device in this chapter is used on a patient, the operator must check a short list, because the cuff must match the limb, the device must rest at zero or pass its self-test, the probe must be clean and the right size, covers and wraps must be in place, and the battery must be charged. Alarm limits must be set to the patient rather than left at the factory setting, the patient must be identified, and the technique must be the one the device assumes. The reading must be compared with the patient and with the previous reading rather than copied onto the chart, and any value that contradicts the clinical picture must be repeated with a different device or site before it is acted on. Every threshold, interval, and limit named in this chapter is a starting point that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the instruments of vital sign monitoring are physical transducers first and clinical tools second, and a listener who understands the expansion of mercury, the deformation of a metal element, the oscillations inside a cuff, the absorption of two wavelengths of light, and the absorption of infrared by carbon dioxide can predict how each one will fail. The hospital-grade versions assume calibration services, clean power, a stock of covers and sampling lines, and staff trained to set alarm limits deliberately, while the field versions assume none of that and demand consistency, spare batteries, careful technique, and the honesty to record an approximate value as approximate. Every device carries a hazard, a characteristic alarm, and a habitual operator error, and safe use begins with the operator looking at the patient rather than at the number. The trend and the combination of signs are more informative than any single measurement, so no setting, pressure, temperature, or alarm threshold should be taken from memory, because each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 7 — Patient Monitors
