A patient monitor is a machine that watches the body and turns its activity into lines and numbers. It is worth saying at the outset what the monitor actually does, because its name is misleading. The monitor measures very little by itself. Every channel begins with a sensor that converts one physical event into a small electrical signal: a voltage generated by heart muscle on the skin, a pulse of light passed through a fingertip, a pressure wave carried along a column of fluid, a change in the absorption of infrared light in a breath. The monitor receives those signals, amplifies them, removes what does not belong, converts them into digits, and presents the result on a screen. This is why a fault in a sensor can look exactly like a fault in a patient, and why an experienced clinician always asks which of the two is more likely before reacting.

The screen is the part everyone recognizes: a dark panel with bright traces, numbers beside each trace, and a row of small symbols for alarms and battery state. Most hospital monitors use a liquid crystal display, LCD for short, lit from behind by a light emitting diode, LED, so that it can be read at an angle in a bright room. The traces scroll from right to left, and the speed of that scroll is a setting. The numerics are updated on their own schedule, often once every second, and they can freeze in a plausible position when a sensor fails, which makes a still number far more dangerous than an empty one. The listener should picture a monitor as two different devices sharing one case, a waveform display for shape and rhythm, and a numeric display for trend and threshold. Reading only the numbers is a common and quiet error, because the shape of a waveform carries information that no number can hold.

Behind the screen sit the modules, the removable blocks that give the monitor its channels. A basic unit may hold only electrocardiography and cuff blood pressure. A fuller chassis accepts a plug in module for invasive pressures, another for exhaled carbon dioxide, another for temperature, another for cardiac output or depth of anesthesia. Each module has its own connector block on the front or side, its own patient cable, and often its own calibration and self test. The physical hazard at this level is electrical. The patient cable is designed to isolate the patient from the mains supply, and any monitor that has been dropped, wetted, or repaired outside the manufacturer's instructions may leak current. Every electrical safety parameter and test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is returned to a patient.

Inside the chassis the signal path is much the same for most channels. The sensor voltage passes through an amplifier that raises a signal measured in millionths of a volt to something a circuit can use, then through filters that remove muscle noise, mains hum, and drift, then through an analog to digital converter that samples the signal many times each second. A typical electrocardiography channel samples hundreds of times per second, for example 500 times per second, and the sampling rate, the filter settings, and the display gain are all configurable. These are settings, and every one of them must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The chassis also holds the alarm logic and the network connection, which is why a monitor with a dead network card can still display perfectly while no one at a distance can see it. Standards from the International Electrotechnical Commission, IEC, and the International Organization for Standardization, ISO, describe how these devices must behave, but a standard on paper does not inspect a cable.

The electrocardiography channel, ECG for short, is the channel most people mean when they say monitor. Heart muscle generates a small voltage as it depolarizes, and that voltage spreads through the body to the skin, where electrodes pick it up. Because the signal arrives at different skin points at slightly different times and sizes, the monitor can subtract one electrode from another and build a view of the heart's electrical activity from a particular direction. A 3 electrode set gives a single view, a 5 electrode set gives several, and the classic 10 electrode arrangement gives the 12 views of a diagnostic ECG. The monitor is not a diagnostic ECG machine, but it uses the same physics. The quality of the trace depends first on the skin, second on the electrode, and only third on the electronics.

An electrode is a small disc of silver and silver chloride with a conductive gel, pressed onto clean dry skin. Skin is a poor conductor, so the person applying the electrode should abrade the surface lightly, remove oil, and clip hair rather than shave it, because a nick can bleed and a bleeding site conducts badly. The lead wires then carry the signal to the module, and those wires are the most common point of failure in the whole system. A loose electrode, a dried gel, a cracked wire, or a wire crossing another produce artifact: a wandering baseline, a thick fuzzy trace, or a spike that looks like a dangerous rhythm. The characteristic alarm is the lead failure alarm, which the monitor sounds when it cannot find a stable electrical path. The common operator error is to blame the monitor and change the lead wire when the real fault is a dry electrode under a sweating patient, and the hazard is a decision made on a trace that was never the heart.

Blood pressure by cuff is the second everyday channel. The cuff is a bladder inside a fabric sleeve, wrapped around the upper arm and inflated above the systolic pressure, then deflated slowly while a pressure sensor watches the small oscillations that the artery transmits into the cuff. This is why the method is called oscillometry, and why it estimates rather than measures. The cuff must fit the arm: a bladder that is too narrow reads falsely high, and one that is too wide reads falsely low, so the correct bladder width is roughly 40 per cent of the arm circumference, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator errors are placing the cuff over clothing, wrapping it loosely, letting the arm hang, and leaving the cuff on a limb that carries an intravenous line. The characteristic alarm is the cuff overpressure or cuff timeout alarm, which protects the arm from a bladder that will not stop inflating.

Invasive arterial pressure is the third pressure channel and the most demanding. A catheter sits in an artery, connected by stiff tubing full of saline to a transducer, a small chamber whose diaphragm flexes as the pressure wave arrives and converts that movement into a voltage. The monitor displays a waveform with a sharp upstroke and a dicrotic notch, and it derives the systolic, diastolic, and mean pressures from that wave. Two rituals make the reading trustworthy: leveling the transducer at the level of the heart, and zeroing it to the atmosphere. The tubing must be short, stiff, and free of bubbles, because a soft or bubbly system damps the wave and understates the systolic pressure. A square wave test, performed by briefly flushing the line and watching how fast the trace settles, tells the operator whether the system is damped or resonant. The transducer position, the flush pressure, and the test criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hazards of an arterial line belong with the line, not with a later chapter. If the tubing disconnects, the artery can bleed quickly and invisibly under drapes, so the line is always secured, labeled, and inspected. If air enters, it can travel, and if the line is flushed carelessly, a bolus of saline or clot can reach the hand or the brain. Infection follows any line that stays in place, so the insertion site is observed every shift. The characteristic alarms are the low pressure alarm, which may signal a disconnected line, and the high pressure alarm, which may signal an occluded catheter or a patient who is coughing. The common operator error is to silence a low pressure alarm before looking at the arm, when the correct sequence is to look at the patient, then the tubing, then the screen.

Oximetry is the channel that most changed how clinicians think, because it made continuous oxygen monitoring possible without a blood sample. A probe shines red light and infrared light through a translucent part of the body, usually a fingertip, and a detector on the other side measures how much of each wavelength arrives. Oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorb those two wavelengths differently, so the ratio of the two signals reveals the proportion of hemoglobin that is carrying oxygen. Only the pulsatile part of the signal is used, the part that swells with each heartbeat, and this is why a poor pulse gives a poor reading. Probes exist for the finger, the ear, the forehead, and the newborn foot, and each has its own placement rule and its own risk of pressure injury. The alarm limits and the averaging time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The errors of oximetry are worth memorizing because they all produce a confident number that is wrong. Motion makes the probe read a moving finger rather than a pulse. Cold, low blood pressure, and vasoconstriction reduce the pulsatile signal until the monitor either drops the reading or latches onto a poor one. Nail polish, artificial nails, dirt, and bright light can distort the optics. Carbon monoxide poisoning and abnormal hemoglobin can make the saturation look reassuring while the patient is starved of oxygen, and a probe placed on a limb with a blood pressure cuff cycling above it will read the cuff, not the patient. The characteristic alarm is the low saturation alarm, and it is the alarm most often silenced without a look at the patient. A default low saturation limit is often near 90 per cent, and that example, like every default threshold for that alarm, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The temperature channel is small but not trivial. A thermistor or a thermocouple changes its electrical behavior as it warms, and the monitor converts that change into a temperature after the probe's own characteristics have been entered or recognized. Skin probes lie on the surface and read low; core probes sit in the esophagus, the bladder, the rectum, or the nasopharynx and read closer to the body's true center. The difference between the two is itself useful information, because a rising skin to core gap suggests poor perfusion. Probes are fragile, they are a known source of pressure injury in the mouth and rectum, and they are a documented route for cross infection when they are reused without proper reprocessing. A usual alert range is 36 to 38 degrees Celsius, and those temperature limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Exhaled carbon dioxide is the channel that proves a tube is in the windpipe and that the lungs are moving air. Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light at a specific wavelength, so a small sensor or a sampling line pulls a breath into a chamber and measures how much light is absorbed. The result is a waveform with a flat start, a steep rise, a plateau, and a steep fall, and the highest point of the plateau is the end tidal value. A sudden drop to zero in a patient with a breathing tube is a disconnection or a lost airway until proved otherwise. A gradual rise may mean the patient is not breathing enough, and a rising value during chest compressions is a sign that the compressions are working. The end tidal value in a healthy resting adult is usually between 35 to 45 millimeters of mercury, and that range, the sampling rate, and the calibration method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The practical problems of capnography are mostly plumbing. Water vapor from the breath condenses in the sampling line, so a water trap collects it and must be emptied before it fills and blocks the airway. Secretions, blood, and vomit can block the line, giving a flat trace that looks like apnea. The characteristic alarm is the apnea alarm or the low end tidal alarm, and both must be answered by looking at the patient's chest and at the tube before the sensor is touched. The common operator error is to accept a flat trace as a technical fault and disconnect the circuit, when the correct first act is to confirm ventilation by hand and by sight.

Alarms are a subsystem, and the monitor's alarm system is the part most likely to hurt a patient by being ignored or disabled. Most monitors grade alarms by priority: a lethal rhythm, a very low saturation, or an apnea is highest; a mild limit breach is lower; a technical fault is lower still. The screen shows the priority by color and the speaker changes tone, and the alarm settings include limits, volume, delay, and whether the alarm is on at all. Default limits are written for an average adult and are wrong for many patients, so the discipline is to set limits deliberately for the person in the bed and to write them down. Typical default limits for an adult might be a systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury, a mean pressure below 65 millimeters of mercury, or a saturation below 90 per cent, and those example figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Alarm fatigue is the predictable result of too many false alarms, and it harms people when staff stop looking up. The hazard is a monitor whose alarm has been silenced or whose limits were widened to stop a nuisance, and every limit, delay, and volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Central stations and telemetry extend the monitor beyond the bedside. A central station is a computer that receives the waveforms from many bedside monitors over the hospital network and displays them on one large screen, usually with a technician or a nurse watching. Telemetry is a small transmitter worn by a walking patient that sends a single ECG view by radio to a receiver. Both systems introduce delay: the picture at the central station is a little behind the picture at the bedside, and a network fault can leave the bedside monitor perfect while the central station shows a frozen patient. The characteristic hazard of the central station is the belief that someone is watching, and the common operator error is to treat the screen as a substitute for walking to the bed. Monitoring a patient means touching the patient; watching a screen means watching a screen.

Every monitor carries a battery, and the battery decides what happens during transport. Older units use sealed lead acid cells, newer ones use lithium chemistry, and their runtime varies with the number of channels, the screen brightness, and the age of the cells. A monitor that has been on charge for months may still hold only a few minutes, because capacity falls silently with every cycle. Before any transport, the operator confirms the charge state, carries a spare battery where the design allows, and knows which channels will be shed to extend runtime. The hospital supports the bedside unit with an uninterruptible power supply, UPS, and a circuit on the emergency generator, but neither follows the patient to the scanner. The advertised runtime, which may be given as 4 to 8 hours, and the low battery alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning between patients is where a monitor becomes an infection risk. The screen, the case, the buttons, the cables, and the reusable sensors all touch hands that have touched patients. The manufacturer's approved disinfectant is the only safe choice, because alcohol, bleach, and quaternary ammonium compounds attack different plastics, soften cable jackets, and cloud screens at different rates. Cuffs are a special problem: the fabric holds moisture, the bladder holds air, and a cuff wiped only on the outside has not been cleaned. Cables should be wiped along their whole length, connectors inspected for corrosion, and probes cleaned according to their own instructions. Contact times, which are often stated as 1 minute for a wipe and 10 minutes for a soak, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is a hurried wipe of the screen while the cable, the cuff, and the probe go untouched to the next patient.

The consumables of monitoring are few, but their failure is frequent. Electrodes come in adult, pediatric, and neonatal sizes with different gel formulations, and their gel dries with time and heat, so stock must be rotated and expiry dates read. Lead wires and patient cables fail at the connector and at the point where they bend, and a spare set is part of a functioning monitor. Cuffs come in a range of sizes and must be matched to the arm; probes exist for every site and every age; carbon dioxide sampling lines and water traps are single use in most designs. Recording paper, where a monitor still prints, is thermal and fades with light and heat. Storage should be dry, out of direct sun, and away from the disinfectant shelf, because vapor ages adhesive and gel.

Maintenance and calibration are what keep the numbers honest. A preventive schedule checks the case, the screen, the connectors, the cables, the battery, and the alarm speaker, and it tests the module against a simulator: a device that generates a known ECG, a known pressure, and a known saturation. The pressure channel is checked against a manometer or a calibrated reference, the cuff is checked for leaks, and the electrical safety test measures leakage current at the points the standard requires. Calibration intervals, commonly every 6 to 12 months, and the tolerances and safety limits themselves must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The records matter as much as the tests, because a monitor without a maintenance history cannot be trusted in a crisis and cannot be defended in an inquiry.

The characteristic failures of a monitor are worth listing because they repeat. A cracked or delaminated screen loses a corner of the display. A battery that no longer holds charge cuts transport short. A module fails its self test and takes one channel with it. A cable breaks internally and produces artifact only when the patient moves. A monitor with a full memory or a corrupted configuration may freeze the display or forget the alarm limits, and one with a failed network card drops off the central station without any bedside warning. The common operator error in all of these cases is to keep using the device because it looks alive. The safe response is to move the patient to a working monitor, label the faulty unit, and remove it from service.

The field variant of this chapter is the portable monitor of a mobile or frontier clinic. It is a single box with a handle, a smaller screen, and a battery that must last a day, and it usually offers ECG, cuff blood pressure, oximetry, and temperature, with exhaled carbon dioxide appearing only on the better models. It gives up a great deal: the invasive pressure module, the central station, the telemetry link, the printer, the large screen with room for many traces, and the service contract. Its sampling and filtering are simpler, so its traces are noisier. Its cuffs and probes are reusable and must survive dust, heat, and repeated disinfection. Its internal battery is often the only power source, and a monitor that cannot be charged overnight is a monitor that stops working at the worst moment.

What the field monitor demands instead is discipline. Someone must own the charging routine, the spare battery, and the solar panel, because a portable monitor is only as reliable as the last person who plugged it in. The case must be padded and carried, not thrown into the back of a vehicle, and the screen must be protected from sun and from impact. Consumables must be adapted: reusable cuffs in the sizes the clinic actually sees, a supply of electrodes stored away from heat, and a cleaning routine that uses what is available without destroying the plastic. Settings, alarm limits, and battery thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and in a field clinic the local protocol may be a single laminated sheet that someone wrote carefully.

The field alarm problem is different from the hospital one. There is no central station, so the alarm must be loud enough to cross a small ward and distinctive enough to be recognized from a distance, and the staff may be one person who is also mixing a drug. Sharing one monitor between several patients creates its own hazards, because the cable and the cuff travel and carry organisms with them. The common error is to leave a monitor on a patient who no longer needs it, which exhausts the battery and trains everyone to ignore the alarm. The characteristic hazard is an alarm that is not heard because the device is under a blanket, in a corridor, or on a bench across the room.

When the battery finally dies, manual observations replace the machine, and they are not a lesser form of medicine. The pulse is counted by palpation for a full minute, the respiratory rate is counted by watching the chest, blood pressure is taken with an aneroid manometer and a stethoscope, temperature is taken with a clinical thermometer, and consciousness, urine output, and skin color are recorded on paper. The manual schedule is written down with a time for each set of observations, and the trend matters more than any single value. The aneroid gauge itself must be checked against a known reference, and the cuff sizes are the same sizes the monitor used. Manual observation demands attention, but it demands nothing from the electricity supply.

To summarize, a patient monitor is a set of sensors and a screen, and the sensors are the part that fails first. The hospital-grade device brings modules, invasive channels, a central station, and a service contract, and it repays that infrastructure with precision. The field variant brings a handle and a battery, and it repays that simplicity with demands on the person who carries it. In both settings the same rules hold: set alarm limits deliberately, look at the patient before the screen, clean every surface between patients, calibrate on schedule, and keep a manual observation routine ready for the moment the battery dies.

# Chapter 8 — Basic Examination Tools

Basic examination tools are the small instruments that extend the unaided senses of the examiner. Each couples a property of the body to a sense and bends sound, light, or touch into a form the ear, the eye, or the hand can read. A stethoscope gathers faint pressure waves, an otoscope concentrates light, a reflex hammer delivers an impulse, and a tape compares the body against a known length. Because they are simple they fail quietly, so this chapter describes each hospital-grade tool and then its field substitute, naming the hazard, the common error, and the warning sign of each.

Sounds inside the chest are pressure waves of very small amplitude, and they reflect back when they meet the skin, because the change from tissue to air is abrupt. The stethoscope defeats that boundary. Its chest piece collects the vibrations, a closed column of air carries them up the tubing, and earpieces seal the ear canal against room noise. The diaphragm is a taut disc pressed firmly to the skin and answers the higher sounds of breathing and most murmurs, while the bell is an open cup pressed lightly that answers the low sounds of blood flow.

Using the instrument well depends on knowing which face is listening. The diaphragm needs enough pressure to seal, while the bell needs only light contact, because pressing the bell stretches the skin into a diaphragm and hides the low murmurs the examiner wants. The common operator error is exactly this. The instrument is shared, so the chest piece and tubing are wiped between patients with the disinfectant named in the local protocol, and any cleaning agent must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Tubing cracks and develops pinholes where it bends, and a pinhole weakens the instrument without making it look broken, while hardened earpieces stop sealing. The characteristic warning sign is not an alarm but a change in sound that becomes obvious when the 2 ears are compared. The checks are to look along the tubing for cracks, listen with both earpieces at once, and confirm that the diaphragm is neither torn nor hardened. The interval for those checks must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The electronic stethoscope replaces the air column with a microphone, an amplifier, and headphones. The microphone contacts the skin, the signal is filtered and amplified, and the sound reaches the ear at a volume the examiner can adjust. A quiet murmur can be made audible, the signal can be stored, and the instrument can feed a recording or a remote consultation. Its characteristic alarm is a low-battery tone or a flashing indicator, and its common error is to trust the volume control so far that a genuine sound and an amplified artifact cannot be told apart. The housing is wiped rather than immersed, and any battery or cleaning agent must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a field clinic the stethoscope is often the cheapest single-head instrument available, sometimes a single-tube model with a plastic chest piece and stiff tubing. It gives up the choice of face, and with it the deliberate separation of low and high frequencies, so the examiner must learn what it can and cannot hear. It also gives up durability, because the chest piece cracks and the thin tubing splits at the bend. Where a fetal heartbeat must be heard, the acoustic fetal stethoscope, a simple funnel pressed on the abdomen, needs no tubing and gives a clear low sound to a trained ear. Any specification or replacement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The otoscope turns a small lamp into a beam and a cone into a speculum. Light from a bulb or a light-emitting diode travels along the handle and head, is directed down a funnel-shaped speculum, and illuminates the ear canal while a magnifying lens enlarges the view. The speculum is tapered so that it seats in the opening of the canal, and it must be wide enough to see past its own walls and narrow enough to enter without pain. The pneumatic attachment adds a rubber bulb and a tube, and its principle is that a sealed column of air can test the mobility of the eardrum, because a squeeze of the bulb changes the pressure and a healthy eardrum moves while a stiff or perforated one does not. Any bulb specification and any cleaning or sterilization cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Using the otoscope requires a technique the design assumes. The examiner selects the largest speculum that will enter comfortably, braces the back of the hand against the patient's cheek or temple, pulls the pinna upward and backward in an adult and backward and downward in an infant, and advances only as far as the canal allows. The brace is a safety device, because a patient who turns the head can drive a rigid speculum through the eardrum if the examiner's hand is free in the air. The common error is to push toward the eardrum instead of following the curved canal, and the second is to choose a speculum so small that it fits easily but shows nothing. Cerumen, a failing bulb, and a dim light limit the view rather than announce themselves, so the warning sign is a dark field that the examiner wrongly blames on the patient. Specula are single-use or reprocessed according to the local protocol and the lens and head are wiped between patients, with any bulb, cleaning agent, or sterilization cycle confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The ophthalmoscope solves a harder optical problem, because the examiner must look into the eye almost along the line by which light enters it. Its essential target is the red reflex, the soft red glow that appears when light returns from the retina, and the same instrument inspects the optic disc, the retinal vessels, and the macula. The apertures change the beam, so a small round spot is used through an undilated pupil, a larger spot gives a wider view once the pupil is dilated, a red-free filter removes red light to make vessels stand out, and a fixation target gives the patient something to look at. The lenses are measured in diopters, and the setting that matches a particular patient and examiner must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the examination is relied upon.

The technique the ophthalmoscope assumes is easy to describe and easy to get wrong. The examiner holds it in the right hand for the right eye and the left hand for the left eye, keeps it close to both faces, and follows the red reflex at about 15 centimeters before moving in toward the pupil. The common error is to flood the eye with a wide bright beam, which makes the patient blink and squeezes the pupil to a pinhole so that nothing can be seen. The characteristic warning sign of a failing instrument is a dim or uneven beam, usually an aging bulb or a dirty window. The forehead rest and housing are cleaned between patients, with any bulb, battery, aperture, or lens specification confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The reflex hammer is a controlled mechanical impulse in the shape of a small mallet. Its head strikes a tendon and stretches the muscle spindle, the spindle sends a burst of signals along a sensory nerve to the spinal cord, and the cord returns a signal that makes the muscle contract. The technique that makes the test meaningful is a short, loose swing of the wrist that delivers a brisk tap rather than a heavy blow, with the limb relaxed and supported, because a tense muscle cannot show its reflex. The common error is to strike too hard or repeatedly, which produces pain and voluntary guarding that the examiner misreads as a reflex. Because the hammer has no alarm or calibration, the warning sign of a problem is a difference between the 2 sides caused by technique rather than by the patient, with the strength of the tap confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the finding is trusted.

The tuning fork is a piece of metal shaped so that it vibrates at a single known frequency when struck. The 2 tines swing toward and away from each other, the stem transmits that vibration into whatever it touches, and the frequency is fixed by the length, thickness, and material of the tines. A clinical set commonly contains forks at 128 hertz, 256 hertz, 512 hertz, and 1024 hertz, and the frequency of each fork and the tests performed with it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the examination is interpreted. In the first hearing test the fork is held near the ear canal and then its stem is pressed against the mastoid bone behind the ear, and the patient reports which sound lasts longer. In the second test the vibrating stem rests on the middle of the forehead and the patient reports which ear hears it better, which helps separate a problem of the outer or middle ear from one of the inner ear.

The results depend entirely on how the fork is excited and held. The correct stroke is a firm tap against the heel of the hand or a rubber pad near the elbow, and the correct hold is by the stem alone, because a finger touching a tine stops the vibration. The common error is to strike the fork against a hard metal or wooden surface, which gives a loud overtone instead of a clean tone, or to strike so hard that the tines are damaged and the pitch changes. A fork that has been dropped may be cracked at the stem, and a cracked fork sounds dull, so the warning sign is a tone that dies quickly and unevenly. Tuning forks are cleaned by wiping and never by immersion, and their storage, replacement interval, and cleaning agent must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A penlight concentrates a small battery current into a narrow beam that can be aimed at a pupil to test the light reflex, at the skin to look for a rash, or through the mouth or sinuses to transilluminate tissue, so that a fluid-filled cavity appears dark against a glowing field. The tongue depressor holds the tongue down and out of the line of sight so that the throat can be seen without provoking a gag. The common error with the depressor is to push it too far back on the tongue, which causes retching and can injure the mouth if the patient bites down. The common error with the penlight is to shine it from an angle that puts the examiner's own shadow across the view, or to use a beam so wide that the pupil is flooded. Both items touch mucous membranes, so a wooden depressor is used once and discarded, a plastic one is reprocessed or discarded according to the local protocol, and the penlight is wiped between patients.

A measuring tape is a physical standard carried to the patient. The tape is marked in equal divisions, usually centimeters and millimeters, and a measurement is a comparison between the patient and those divisions, so the only thing that makes a tape trustworthy is that its length does not change. A cloth or paper tape stretches with use and moisture, and a stretched tape reads high, which is a silent error no examiner can see. Tapes come in different forms for different jobs, including a firm tape for limb circumference, a narrow flexible tape for the head and chest of an infant, and a long tape for the length of a child. The measurement depends on the landmark, because a mid-upper-arm circumference or a head circumference means nothing unless the tape is placed at exactly the point the local protocol defines. The common errors are to use a stretchy tape, to measure over clothing, to pull until the tissue is compressed, and to read the wrong mark, with the specification, the landmark, and the cleaning agent confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the measurement is used to make a decision.

The neurological pin and the cotton wisp test the sensory side of the nervous system, which no machine in this book can examine for the clinician. A pin delivers a sharp stimulus and a wisp of cotton delivers a light touch, and the patient's report of what is felt and where maps the pathway from skin through peripheral nerve and spinal cord to brain. The common error is to push the pin hard enough to draw blood or to test so lightly that nothing is felt anywhere, since a test that is too weak is as misleading as one that is too strong. A disposable pin is used for one patient and discarded, a reusable pin must be disinfected between patients because any object that breaks the skin can carry infection, and a cotton wisp is used once or replaced.

Examination gloves are a barrier, and their principle is that a continuous, intact film of polymer does not let organisms pass from the patient's skin to the examiner's hands or the other way. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, so hands are cleaned before they go on and after they come off, and a single pair is used for a single patient and then discarded. The common error is to wear one pair through a whole round of patients, or to touch a telephone, a keyboard, or a door handle with a contaminated glove and then continue the examination, because the glove then carries organisms exactly as a bare hand would. The examination surface has its own rule, since a couch, a table, or a chair is touched by every patient, and a paper cover, a clean sheet, or a disinfectant wipe is the barrier between them. The choice of glove material, the cleaning agent, and the interval for changing covers must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the examination begins.

Every small tool in this chapter is cleaned and reprocessed according to a rule that depends on what it touches. A tool that touches intact skin needs cleaning and low-level disinfection, one that touches mucous membranes needs a higher level, and one that enters sterile tissue must be sterile. The principle is that disinfection reduces the number of organisms while sterilization removes or destroys all of them, and that a disinfectant works only after the surface has been cleaned of blood, wax, and oil, because organic material shields organisms from the chemical. Contact time matters as much as the chemical, and the time, concentration, and temperature of any disinfectant or sterilization cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the process is trusted. A tool whose reprocessing method is unknown should not be used on the next patient.

Between 2 patients the smallest tools carry the greatest risk, because they are touched, shared, and forgotten. The sequence that works is to keep clean items away from contaminated ones, to clean the hands between patients, and to reprocess or discard each tool according to what it touched. The common error is to clean the visible tool and forget the invisible one, the telephone, the pen, the door handle, and the earpieces handled while the stethoscope was put away. The warning sign of a broken routine is a tool that is warm from the previous patient or still damp from a hasty wipe, and both are reasons to stop and clean properly.

Storage keeps a small tool working, and the enemies of small tools are heat, moisture, sunlight, and dust. Instruments are kept in a clean, dry case where the tubing is not kinked, the specula are protected, and the bulbs are not crushed, and batteries are stored outside the device when it will not be used for some time, because a leaking cell destroys the contacts. The common error is to fit the wrong bulb or battery because it fits the socket, which can damage the instrument or produce a light too dim to be useful. A simple inventory with a spare bulb, a spare battery, a set of specula, and a replacement set of earpieces prevents most of the interruptions that make an examination incomplete.

The same tools must be adapted to very different patients, and the smallest patients punish the largest errors. An infant or small child needs a stethoscope with a smaller chest piece, because a large diaphragm covers the whole chest and blends the sounds of both lungs and the heart into one. An infant needs the smallest otoscope speculum, and the ear is pulled backward and downward rather than upward because the canal is straighter and shorter. The tape for an infant is narrow and flexible so that it can follow the curve of the head and chest, and the landmarks for the head, the chest, and the mid-upper arm differ from those of an adult. The correct size, the landmarks, and the cleaning method for each patient group must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile clinic or a frontier health post the instruments are fewer, lighter, and chosen for what they can survive rather than for what they can hear or see. The field kit usually holds one stethoscope, one otoscope or a substitute for it, a penlight, a supply of tongue depressors, a tape, gloves, and a small power source, packed so that it can be carried on a bicycle or a shoulder bag. What the field gives up is precision, the right instrument for the task, the spare part, and the certainty that the next patient will find a clean tool. What it demands instead is skill, because the examiner's own senses and memory carry the work the missing instrument would have done, and discipline, because an improvised tool must still be cleaned and used with the same care as a manufactured one.

The flashlight built into a mobile telephone replaces the penlight for many field examiners, and its physics is the same light-emitting diode in a smaller package. It gives up the shaped beam of a clinical penlight, the colored or red-free filter, and the ability to be cleaned as a sealed instrument, because the telephone is a porous object that should not be wiped with aggressive chemicals. The common error is to hold the telephone so close that the examiner's fingers and shadow block the view, or to use the brightest setting, which makes the patient turn away and closes the pupil. The warning sign of a failing telephone light is a beam that flickers or dims when the telephone moves, which usually means a weak battery or a loose connection. The telephone must be cleaned according to its own instructions and kept out of the examination field where it can contaminate the gloves.

The camera of a mobile telephone can serve as a magnifier, and its principle is that a small lens focuses an image onto a sensor and the image can be enlarged on the screen, stored, and shown to another clinician. In the field this turns a telephone into an improvised otoscope for the outer ear, a magnifier for a skin lesion, a reader for a faint label, and a means of sending a picture to a distant colleague for advice. It gives up the stereoscopic view, the controlled illumination, and the magnification of a true instrument, and it adds a hazard, because a photograph can flatter a lesion or hide its depth. The common error is to rely on digital zoom, which enlarges the pixels rather than the optics and produces a blurred picture that looks detailed on a small screen. The warning sign of a poor photograph is uneven light, a color cast, or a shadow across the subject, all of which change what the remote colleague is being asked to judge.

An improvised tuning fork is one of the more demanding substitutions, because the pitch of the substitute is not known. Any stiff metal object that vibrates, a heavy table fork, a spoon, or a piece of spring steel, can produce a tone when struck, and the vibration can be felt when its base is pressed against a bone. It cannot be used for the tuning fork tests of hearing, because those compare air conduction with bone conduction at a known frequency, and an uncalibrated piece of metal gives neither the frequency nor the purity the comparison requires. Other substitutions follow the same logic, because a rolled cone of paper with a flashlight behind it forms a crude speculum, the edge of a hand or the head of a stethoscope can elicit a reflex, and a length of string laid along a limb and measured against a ruler can replace a tape. Each demands that the examiner knows what the real instrument would have shown, states the limitation in the record, and confirms every frequency, method, and cleaning rule against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field kit lives or dies by its consumables and its power. Specula, wooden depressors, cotton, alcohol wipes, gloves, replacement earpieces, bulbs, and batteries are the items that run out first, and a kit that is not restocked becomes a bag of useless instruments. The common field error is to store the kit with the batteries inside, so that a leaking cell corrodes the contacts and the tool is found dead at the moment it is needed. Another error is to reuse a single-use speculum or a wooden depressor because the supply is low, which is exactly the moment when the risk of transmission is highest. The warning sign of a failing field light is a beam that is yellow rather than white or that dims when the lamp is moved, and the response is to replace the battery or the bulb before the next patient.

Every measurement and observation made with these small tools ends as a record, and the record is part of the device system. A head circumference, a limb circumference, a reflex grade, the result of a hearing test, and the appearance of an eardrum are written into a chart or an electronic health record, or EHR, and the value depends on the units, the landmark, and the date being stated. Around that record sits a program of maintenance, in which a scheduled round checks the stethoscope tubing and earpieces, the otoscope bulb and lens, the ophthalmoscope beam and lenses, the hammer for cracks, the tuning forks for a clean tone, the penlight for a steady beam, and the tapes for stretch and legibility. The common failure of such a program is to treat these small tools as consumables that need no attention, so that they are replaced only when they break and never when they quietly degrade.

Almost none of the tools in this chapter has an alarm, and that absence is the central safety fact of the chapter. A monitor announces a failing battery and a ventilator announces a disconnected circuit, but a stethoscope with a pinhole, an otoscope with a failing bulb, an ophthalmoscope with a dirty window, and a tape that has stretched all continue to look and feel exactly as they should. The examiner therefore has to be the alarm, and the only way to be the alarm is to test the tool deliberately rather than to assume that yesterday's performance continues today. The simple tests are a visual inspection, a comparison with a second instrument, and a check against a known standard, and they take less time than the examination itself. The common error is to explain away a poor finding as a difficult patient, a narrow canal, a small pupil, or a quiet chest, when the difficulty lies in the tool.

Returning to the field, the value of these tools is not that they are simple but that they are the only instruments that always work. The field examiner must therefore protect them with the care a hospital gives to a scanner, because a cracked tube or a dead battery ends the diagnostic capability of an entire clinic. The substitutes described here, the telephone light, the telephone camera, the rolled paper speculum, and the improvised vibrating metal, are honest tools as long as their limits are stated and their hygiene is maintained. What they demand is a clear understanding of what each can show and what each can hide, and the discipline to record the difference, with every substitute, cleaning method, and improvised material confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

To summarize, the basic examination tools are small devices that extend the ear, the eye, and the hand, and each works by a physical principle that can be stated plainly. The stethoscope couples chest vibrations to a column of air and offers a bell for low frequencies and a diaphragm for high ones, the otoscope funnels light into a narrow canal, and the ophthalmoscope follows the path of light into the eye to find the red reflex. The reflex hammer delivers a controlled stretch, the tuning fork supplies a known frequency, and the penlight, the tongue depressor, the tape, the pin, and the cotton wisp test the surface of the body against simple standards. In the field the same work is done with a telephone light, a telephone camera, a paper cone, and a piece of vibrating metal, each of which gives up precision and demands skill in return. Whatever the setting, every specification, every cleaning method, and every threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the tool is used on a patient.

# Chapter 9 — Vascular Access

Every route into the circulation begins with one physical idea, a tube placed inside a blood vessel so that fluid can travel along a path that skin would otherwise seal. Flow through a narrow tube depends enormously on its width, because the radius enters the resistance calculation raised to the fourth power. Halve the internal diameter and resistance rises about sixteen times, so the difference between two neighboring gauge sizes is far larger than the number on the package suggests. Around that idea sit a pressure gradient, a length of soft tubing, a vessel wall, and a fluid with its own thickness, and any one of them can defeat the others. A clinician who cannot draw blood back through a fine cannula should suspect the diameter before the syringe.

A vein is not a rigid pipe but a soft collapsible tube with thin walls, low pressure, and valves, so it flattens when tissue presses inward. An artery is the opposite object, with a thick muscular wall, a high pulsatile pressure, and a deeper position that makes it harder to find and more dangerous to puncture. Because a vein collapses, access depends on filling it, and the tourniquet does this by blocking outflow while leaving inflow open. Left in place too long, it raises the pressure until fluid leaks into the tissue around the vein. Every tourniquet time and pressure limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Vascular access is the family of devices that make a temporary or long-lasting door into that system. The hospital keeps a graded inventory: short plastic cannulas for the hand and forearm, long catheters whose tips rest in the great veins near the heart, midline catheters that stop short of the chest, implanted ports hidden beneath the skin, stiff arterial catheters for pressure watching, and intraosseous needles that enter the marrow rather than a vessel. Each step buys reliability, duration, or monitoring, and also a larger infection risk and a greater chance of serious harm. The choice is never the biggest device that fits but the smallest that will do the job for as long as the job requires. Each rung is described here first as the hospital device and then as the field variant used in a mobile or frontier clinic.

The peripheral cannula is the most common device in the hospital and the one most often taken for granted. It is a thin plastic tube mounted over a hollow metal needle, with a transparent flashback chamber at the back and an angled bevel at the tip. The chamber fills with blood the instant the tip enters the vein, and the operator then advances the plastic off the needle and connects the hub to a cap or an extension set. The design carries three jobs at once: cut a small hole, leave a soft tube where the metal was, and seal against the skin so nothing leaks out or enters. The operator who feels resistance is usually feeling the vessel wall rather than the lumen.

Cannulas are named by gauge, and the naming runs opposite to intuition, because a larger gauge number means a smaller internal diameter. A 14 gauge cannula is for rapid fluid or blood, a 20 gauge is an everyday adult size, and a 26 gauge is fine enough for a fragile neonatal vein. Each gauge carries a colored hub that follows a published international color code, so orange, grey, green, pink, blue, yellow, and violet each belong to a size, and the color is a label rather than a guarantee. Standard lengths run from about 2 to 5 centimeters, and a stiff plastic threads easily while a softer polyurethane is kinder to the vein wall over days. Every gauge, length, and material choice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The veins that suit a cannula are the ones a person can see and feel, such as the dorsal veins of the hand, the forearm veins, and the large vein in front of the elbow. The rule is to start as far from the heart as the treatment allows and to move toward it only when a distant site has failed, because each failed attempt scars the vessel it touched. A vein that is firm, cord-like, red, or painful is already inflamed, and skin that is broken, infected, or burned is never a site. Certain limbs are off limits, including an arm with a dialysis fistula, an arm on the same side as a removed breast with lymph nodes taken, a paralyzed arm, and a limb swollen from poor lymphatic drainage. A cannula placed there can destroy the only route a patient has for dialysis.

Insertion is a sequence of small decisions rather than one motion. The operator fills the vein with a tourniquet, chooses the straightest segment, cleans the skin and lets the antiseptic dry, and enters at a shallow angle with the bevel facing up. The flash of blood confirms the tip is in the lumen, and only then is the plastic advanced while the needle is held still. The common operator error is to push the whole assembly forward after the flash, which drives the needle through the far wall and leaves the plastic outside the vein. Another is to withdraw the needle while the plastic is only partly in, which drags the sharp point back through the soft tube and shaves its tip.

The hazard that belongs with every sharp placed in a vein is the injury the operator can suffer while placing it. A needle that has just been inside a patient carries that patient's blood, and a hand that recaps it or drops it into a pocket transfers the risk to whoever handles laundry or waste. A safety cannula that retracts or shields its needle reduces this, but its protection is defeated by habit, whether by holding the device in the mouth, laying it on the bed, or engaging the safety too late. The discipline is one sharp, one use, and immediate disposal into a rigid container at the point of use. The needle is never recapped, bent, or removed from the plastic by hand.

Keeping a cannula in place is a mechanical problem rather than a clinical one. Every time the patient moves a wrist or flexes an elbow, the tube pivots in the skin, the tip pistons in the vessel, and the entry point slowly widens. A transparent dressing lets the operator see the site without lifting it, and a manufactured stabilization device grips the hub and spreads the pull across a wider area of skin. Tape alone is a poor substitute, because it loosens when damp and a loop around a limb can act as a tourniquet. The dressing is changed when it is soiled or loose, and the site is inspected every shift. Dressing intervals, often every 5 to 7 days for a transparent dressing and every 2 days for gauze, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Extravasation is the failure mode that turns a routine cannula into an emergency. It happens when the tip leaves the lumen and fluid continues to flow into the tissue, because the pump keeps pushing while the pressure it senses is still below its occlusion threshold. The early signs are pain, a cool or taut swelling, and a slowing infusion, while the later signs are blistering, blanching, and a hard area that may go on to die. Some medicines are vesicants, meaning they destroy tissue on contact, which makes extravasation a chemical burn rather than a mechanical one. The characteristic alarm is the occlusion alarm of the infusion device, and it sounds late, after the tissue is already flooded. The common operator error is to reset the pump and continue when the rate falls, instead of stopping, disconnecting, and looking at the limb.

Flushing a catheter is a small procedure with real physics behind it. The pressure a syringe generates depends on the force of the hand and on the area of the plunger, so a small syringe concentrates the same force onto a smaller area and produces a much higher pressure than a large one. A 1 milliliter syringe can therefore exceed the pressure a thin catheter wall can tolerate, rupturing the catheter or forcing clot into the circulation. A 10 milliliter syringe is usually the safe adult choice, and that size and the maximum pressure stated by the maker must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A steady push with a brief pause clears the catheter wall better than a smooth stream, and finishing with positive pressure prevents blood from being drawn back into the tip.

After the flush comes the lock, the small volume of fluid left in the catheter to keep it open between uses. Two solutions dominate: ordinary saline, and saline with a small amount of the blood thinner heparin. The choice depends on the device and the patient, and a typical heparin lock may contain 10 to 100 units per milliliter in a volume of 3 to 5 milliliters, figures that vary so widely they must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The connector at the end of the line also touches blood, so it is scrubbed with antiseptic and allowed to dry before every entry, a practice called scrubbing the hub. Needleless connectors reduce sharp injuries but add a hidden surface where blood can stagnate, and their scrub time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A cannula that stays in place can inflame the vein, a condition called phlebitis, through chemical irritation from the fluid and mechanical irritation from the tube. The classic signs are pain along the vein, redness, warmth, and a palpable cord under the skin. Infection can follow phlebitis, and bloodstream infection from even a peripheral cannula is possible, which is why the site is inspected every shift. The device is removed at the first sign of phlebitis, infiltration, or leakage, and it is removed as soon as it is no longer needed rather than left in place as insurance. Routine replacement intervals, often every 72 to 96 hours, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The central venous catheter is the next rung, and the physical difference is position rather than size. It is a long soft tube inserted through a large vein in the neck, the chest, or the groin and advanced until its tip rests in the great vein just above the heart, where flow is fast and the vessel is wide. That position makes it useful: a medicine that would burn a small vein is diluted in a torrent of blood, fluid can be given at a high rate, and the pressure inside the chest can be measured directly. Central catheters are described by their number of separate channels, or lumens, usually 1 to 4, and by their length, often 15 to 30 centimeters. Each lumen has its own hub and lock, and a mistake in one can contaminate the others. The number of lumens, the length, and the French size, often 4 to 8 French, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The sites used for a central catheter each carry their own anatomy and their own characteristic harm. The internal jugular vein runs down the side of the neck beside the carotid artery, and the operator can often see it, but the artery lies close and can be entered by mistake. The subclavian vein passes under the collarbone, which gives a stable tunnel that is hard to infect, but the needle travels near the top of the lung and can cause a collapsed lung called pneumothorax. The femoral vein in the groin is easy to reach in an emergency, but it is close to the skin, moist, and colonized by bacteria, so it carries the highest infection risk. The choice among the three is guided by the patient's anatomy and the availability of ultrasound.

Almost all central catheters are placed by a technique named after Sven Seldinger, and each step exists to make the next one safer. A thin needle enters the vein, and a flexible wire is passed through it into the vessel, soft enough to follow the curve of the vein without tearing it and stiff enough to guide the rest. The needle is removed, a dilator is threaded over the wire to widen the track through the skin, and the catheter is slid over the wire into place before the wire is withdrawn. The wire is the safety line, because it keeps the track open and keeps the catheter on course. The common operator error is to lose control of the wire, either letting it advance into the heart or pulling it out while the catheter is short of position. A wire that cannot be accounted for is a reason to stop and image.

Because central catheters reach the heart, they carry the most serious infections in the hospital, and the insertion bundle is the set of practices that reduces them. The bundle usually means hand hygiene before and after, full sterile barrier including cap, mask, gown, and a large drape, skin preparation with an antiseptic that is allowed to dry, the widest possible choice of site, ultrasound guidance, and a daily review of whether the line is still needed. When ultrasound is used, the probe is enclosed in a sterile cover with sterile gel, because gel and probe surfaces that touch the skin can carry organisms into the track, and the cover and gel choice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The antiseptic is frequently a chlorhexidine solution at 2 per cent, and its strength and required drying time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A central line placed in a hurry without a barrier will earn its infection within days.

Three hazards deserve to be named at the point of insertion rather than the point of harm. The first is the collapsed lung that follows a needle grazing the pleura, which is why the patient is watched and imaged after a subclavian or jugular attempt. The second is arterial puncture, which produces a bright red pulsatile return and, if unrecognized, leaves a catheter sitting in an artery. The third is air embolism, and its physics is the reason the patient is placed head down before a central line is opened, because the chest cavity has a slight negative pressure during breathing and an open hub below the height of the heart can suck air into the vein. The characteristic alarms are the air in line alarm of the infusion device and the low pressure alarm of a pressure monitoring system. Every alarm threshold and response protocol must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

After insertion, the position of the tip is confirmed before the line is used for anything that could injure the heart. A chest image shows the catheter against the anatomy, and the tip should sit at the junction of the great vein and the right atrium rather than inside the heart, where it can irritate the rhythm or perforate the wall. The tip can migrate later, because a cough, a deep breath, or a raised arm can move it several centimeters, which is why the external length is recorded at insertion. Daily care then keeps the outside world away from the blood: the dressing and connectors are changed on schedule, unused lumens are locked, and the necessity of the line is reviewed every day. Dressing and connector intervals, often every 5 to 7 days for the dressing and every 3 to 7 days for the connector, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The peripherally inserted central catheter, PICC for short, is a long thin tube placed in a vein of the upper arm and threaded centrally until its tip reaches the same great vein as a conventional central catheter. Its physics is a compromise: it avoids the neck and chest entirely, so it cannot cause a collapsed lung, but it travels a longer distance through smaller veins, so it more readily causes a clot along its path. The vein is measured with an ultrasound probe, and the catheter is chosen to occupy only a fraction of the vein's width, because a catheter that fills the vessel leaves no room for blood to flow. A typical PICC is 50 to 60 centimeters long and 4 to 6 French in diameter, and those figures and the measurement method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A PICC suits weeks to months of therapy.

The midline catheter and the implanted port sit on either side of the PICC in duration and complexity. A midline is placed in the same arm veins but is shorter, and its tip stops in the upper arm rather than the chest, so it cannot carry the concentrated solutions that a central tip can dilute, though it suits ordinary antibiotics or fluids over one to four weeks. An implanted port is a small chamber with a self-sealing rubber septum placed beneath the skin, which gives it a lower infection risk and almost no care between uses, so it suits months or years of intermittent therapy. Access requires a special non-coring needle whose side opening and flat tip push through the septum without cutting a plug of rubber, while an ordinary sharp needle will core the septum and destroy the seal. The common operator errors are to treat a midline as a central line and to access a port without confirming the needle is fully seated.

The arterial line is a different instrument because it measures rather than delivers. A small stiff catheter sits in an artery, connected by short stiff tubing full of saline to a transducer, a chamber with a flexible diaphragm that moves as the pressure wave arrives and converts that movement into an electrical signal. The monitor draws the wave and derives the systolic, diastolic, and mean pressures from it, and the shape of the wave carries information no number can hold. Two rituals make the reading trustworthy: leveling the transducer at the height of the heart, and zeroing it to the atmosphere so the monitor knows where zero is. The leveling point is often described as the phlebostatic axis at the fourth intercostal space, and that landmark, the zeroing procedure, and the flush pressure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The tubing in an arterial system must be short, stiff, and free of bubbles, because of the physics of a vibrating column of fluid. A soft or bubbly system absorbs the sharp edge of the pressure wave, a fault called damping, and it understates systolic pressure while overstating diastolic. A system that is too stiff or too long can instead ring, a fault called resonance, which exaggerates the systolic peak. The square wave test reveals both: the operator briefly opens the fast flush valve, sending a flat-topped pressure step into the tubing, and watches how the trace settles. A good system settles in one or two small oscillations, a damped system climbs slowly and flattens, and a resonant one oscillates for several cycles. The flush pressure and the test criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hazards of an arterial line belong with the line itself. If the tubing disconnects at the hub, the artery can bleed quickly and, under a drape or a sleeve, invisibly, so the line is always secured, labeled, and inspected. If the catheter blocks, the tissue beyond it loses its blood supply, which is why the fingers or toes are checked for color, warmth, and pulse every shift. If air enters during a flush, it can travel to the hand or, rarely, to the brain, so the line is never left open to the air. The characteristic alarm is the low pressure alarm, which may signal a disconnected line, and the common operator error is to silence it before looking at the arm. Sampling from the same line requires the syringe to be prepared with a small amount of heparin, any air bubble to be removed at once because air changes the gas values, and the puncture site to be pressed firmly after the needle is withdrawn, typically for 5 minutes and for 10 minutes or more when blood clots slowly, times that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Intraosseous access ignores veins entirely, and its principle is that the marrow cavity of a long bone is a rigid chamber filled with a spongy network of small vessels that does not collapse when the circulation fails. In shock, the peripheral veins empty, but the marrow space still connects to the central circulation through veins that do not depend on blood pressure, so a needle through the tough outer cortex reaches the heart even when every surface vein has vanished. The device is either a manual needle with a removable trocar or a powered drill that spins a designed needle through the cortex in seconds, and needle sizes run from about 15 gauge to 18 gauge with lengths from about 15 to 45 millimeters, chosen by tissue depth and site. In adults the usual sites are the upper shin bone below the knee, the upper arm bone, and the lower shin bone above the ankle, while in children the shin bone is first choice. Correct placement is confirmed by the needle standing without support and by a flush that runs without swelling the tissue, and every size, depth, and site rule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The complications of intraosseous access are the price of its speed. Fluid or medicine that leaks out of the cavity can raise the pressure in the muscle compartment and cut off its blood supply, the bone can become infected with osteomyelitis, and a poorly aimed needle can fracture it. The characteristic alarm is the high pressure alarm of the infusion device, which sounds when fluid is going into tissue instead of marrow, and the common operator error is to accept a needle that wobbles or a flush that meets resistance. A needle left in place is also a route for infection, so it is removed as soon as a reliable intravenous route is established, usually within 24 hours, and that dwell time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. In a frontier clinic the ladder is shortened, and intraosseous access becomes the emergency default, because there is often no ultrasound probe, no experienced operator, and no time to wait. A powered drill depends on batteries that lose their charge silently in heat, so spare cells and a manual needle are carried together, and every battery state must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Peripheral access in the field is a skill of the hands rather than the screen. Without an ultrasound probe, the operator relies on a tourniquet, gravity, warmth, and gentle tapping to make a vein visible, and on the fingertips to judge its depth. The external jugular vein in the neck is often visible when arm veins have collapsed, but it lies close to the carotid artery and the airway, and when nothing can be found the clinician must decide quickly between an intraosseous needle, a surgical cutdown, and transfer. Central access in a frontier clinic is rare and should be rare, because a cutdown demands sterile gloves, an anesthetic, a scalpel, forceps, and a catheter that may be improvised poorly. Securement changes too, because transparent dressings and sterile applicators are replaced by gauze and tape, which hold moisture, loosen when wet, and can tear fragile skin. A port or a PICC without its proper supplies is often best left alone until the patient reaches a better facility, and every substitute considered must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of vascular access are many, and their storage decides whether they work. They include cannulas in every gauge, central catheter kits with their wires and dilators, PICCs and midlines, non-coring needles, arterial catheters and transducer sets, intraosseous needles, syringes, flush vials, antiseptics, dressings, securement devices, and tourniquets, and most are single use, so a torn or damp wrapper is a discard. Heat and sunlight age the plastic and dry the lubricant on a needle. Cleaning divides these items into two groups: needles, cannulas, catheters, flush vials, and dressings are used once and discarded, while transducers, tourniquets, and probes are cleaned or disinfected according to their own instructions, and any reprocessing method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Maintenance is the maintenance of attention: each shift the operator checks the site, the labels, the locks, and the spare stock. The failure modes form a short catalogue, in which the catheter can leave the vessel, block, inflame the vein, become infected, admit air, or injure the operator, and each is made more likely by haste and an unclean hub.

To summarize, vascular access is a ladder of devices built on one physical truth, that flow through a narrow tube depends on its width. The peripheral cannula is the everyday tool, placed by hand, secured by dressing, flushed and locked with care. The central catheter reaches the great veins and buys dilution and monitoring at the price of infection, collapsed lung, and air embolism. The peripherally inserted central catheter and the midline trade location for duration, the implanted port hides beneath the skin and needs its special needle, the arterial line measures rather than delivers and lives or dies by leveling and zeroing, and the intraosseous needle finds the one space that does not collapse. In a frontier clinic the ladder shortens to the devices that need no power, no imaging, and no sterile supply chain, and intraosseous access becomes the emergency default. Whatever the setting, the operator's duties are the same: confirm every setting and threshold against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, know the hazard before it happens, look at the patient before the screen, and remove the device as soon as it is no longer needed.

# Chapter 10 — Infusion Devices

An infusion device is any apparatus that moves fluid into a patient at a rate someone has chosen and can defend. Fluid flows from a place of higher pressure to a place of lower pressure, and the volume delivered in a given time depends on that pressure difference and on the resistance of the tubing. In a gravity set the pressure comes from height, and a column of fluid standing 1 meter above the vein produces roughly 74 millimeters of mercury, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. In a pump the pressure comes from a motor that squeezes or pushes the fluid, and the machine meters volume rather than trusting height. Every device in this chapter is one of those two ideas, and the hazard is always the same, because the amount delivered can differ from the amount intended.

The gravity set is the simplest complete device in the hospital and the measure against which every other system is understood. It is clear plastic tubing, usually polyvinyl chloride, PVC for short, with a spike that pierces the fluid bag, a drip chamber below it, a filter in the line, a roller clamp as the regulator, and a connector that locks into the cannula. The drip chamber is a flow indicator and an air trap, because air from an empty bag rises and collects there instead of reaching the patient. A typical filter has a pore size of 15 micrometers, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it holds back glass, rubber, and precipitate. Injection ports allow a drug to be added without a new puncture, and each port is a place where contamination can enter. The common operator error appears at the first step, spiking the bag with the roller clamp open so that fluid and then air run down an unconnected line.

Because the drip chamber makes drops, the gravity set measures rate without electricity. The set is calibrated so that a known number of drops makes 1 milliliter, and that number is the drop factor, commonly 10, 15, 20, or 60 drops per milliliter, a calibration that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A set of 60 drops per milliliter is called a microdrip set, and its small drops allow finer control of slow infusions. The operator counts drops for 1 minute and converts the count into a rate using the drop factor and the prescribed volume and time. A misplaced decimal or a mistaken drop factor changes the dose by a factor of ten, and the mistake is invisible once the fluid has run in. The characteristic alarm of a gravity set is not a sound but the attention of the nurse, and the common error is to set the clamp by eye once and never count again.

When a small controlled volume must be given, the hospital uses a burette set or volume control set. A graduated chamber of 100 or 150 milliliters, a capacity that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, is filled from the main bag, and only the fluid inside that chamber is connected to the patient. This lets the nurse give a measured volume of a diluted drug and then stop, which is why the set is used for children, for potent drugs, and for infusions where a rapid bolus would be dangerous. The physics is unchanged, because the chamber still empties by gravity through the same roller clamp. The hazard is the clamp between the main bag and the chamber, which, if left open, turns a guarded volume into a free-running infusion, and leaving it open is the common error.

A gravity infusion has no alarm, and this absence defines how it must be watched. The hazards are air embolism, unnoticed occlusion, infiltration of fluid into tissue, phlebitis along the vein, and free flow from a clamp left open. Air embolism occurs when air enters a vein in quantity, usually through a disconnected or badly primed line or a central catheter whose hub is open to the air. Infiltration begins as swelling, coolness, or pain at the cannula site, which is why the site is inspected at a frequency that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An occlusion is quiet, because the chamber stops, the site looks unchanged, and the patient receives nothing. The common error is to trust the bag and the clock rather than the chamber and the arm, so the ward routine becomes the only alarm the set has.

The volumetric infusion pump removes the arithmetic and the eye from the gravity set. Its mechanism is peristalsis, the principle a gut uses, because a row of small fingers or cams presses the tubing closed in sequence and each step pushes a fixed small volume along the line. The pump counts steps and therefore measures what it has delivered rather than inferring it from drops, and it uses either a dedicated cassette with valves or a channel that squeezes ordinary tubing. The rate is set in milliliters per hour, and a typical range runs from 1 to 999 milliliters per hour, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pump is accurate only with the tubing it was calibrated to use, so loading another pump's set can change the delivered volume while the display still looks correct. The safety hazard of the device is the free-flow state, when the tubing leaves the pump and the line becomes a gravity set with no regulator.

Modern pumps protect themselves with sensors, and understanding each one explains the alarms it raises. An air-in-line sensor passes ultrasound across a small section of tubing, where fluid carries the sound and air reflects it, and the change trips the alarm. An occlusion sensor reads pressure, and it may look upstream toward the bag, where an empty bag or a closed clamp raises the alarm, or downstream toward the patient, where a kink or a clotted cannula does.
