The occlusion threshold is often adjustable, for example between 100 and 500 millimeters of mercury, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Raising that threshold to the maximum to silence a recurring alarm is the common operator error, because it makes the pump tolerate a real obstruction. The characteristic alarms of the pump family are air in line, downstream occlusion, upstream occlusion, door open, battery low, and pump error.

The alarms of a volumetric pump must be answered in a fixed order, and it is not the order the sound invites. The line is clamped first, because a pump that has stopped may release the tubing and let gravity take over. The patient is examined second, for the cannula site, the arm, the breathing, and the color, because an alarm may be the first sign of an infiltration that has been developing for an hour. The line is checked third, for kinks, closed clamps, a full chamber, and a bag that has run dry, and only then is the pump examined. Good sets carry an anti-free-flow clamp that closes when the tubing is released, a feature that must be tested and never disabled, a requirement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to silence the pump and walk away, which turns a brief interruption into an unmeasured infusion.

The hospital pump is only as good as the consumables that join it to the patient. Each pump family uses a dedicated administration set or cassette that carries the priming volume, the filter, the injection ports, and the connector the calibration assumes, and priming must fill the whole line before it is connected. Extension sets, stopcocks, and needleless connectors add dead space, and every added connection can separate or become contaminated. A set is changed on a schedule set by policy, commonly every 24 hours for a continuous infusion and sooner for blood, lipid, or suspected contamination, and that schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The line is labeled at the pump and at the patient with the drug and the rate, because a tangle of identical tubing is a recognized cause of the wrong drug reaching the wrong lumen. The common error is to add a second infusion to a set already in use, mixing two drugs in one line and losing the ability to stop either alone.

A syringe pump is the precision instrument, and it gains accuracy by giving up volume for control. The syringe is held in a cradle, its plunger is captured by a driven screw, and a stepper motor advances that screw at a chosen linear speed, so flow equals the cross-sectional area of the barrel multiplied by the speed of the plunger. The pump must know which syringe it is pushing, and it asks the operator to select the size and the model, because the barrel's diameter is part of the arithmetic. Because the barrel is narrow, the volumes are small and the steps are fine, and rates as low as a fraction of a milliliter per hour are possible, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. This is why syringe pumps carry vasoactive drugs, insulin, and opioids, and the characteristic alarms are occlusion, plunger not engaged, syringe dislodged, and near end of infusion. The physical hazard is siphoning, because a syringe above the patient whose plunger is not firmly held can let fluid run by gravity at an uncontrolled rate, and the common error is to seat the syringe without confirming that its flange and plunger are captured.

Patient-controlled analgesia, PCA for short, is designed around the patient's own hand, and its safety lies in the limits locked inside it. The machine is a syringe pump or a small volumetric pump with a handset that carries a single button, and the patient presses it to request a small bolus of analgesic. The pump enforces three boundaries, the size of the bolus, the lockout interval during which no second bolus is given, and a cumulative limit over a set period, and each of these values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. These settings sit behind a locked access, often a key, a code, or a physical cover, so the patient cannot change them. The hazard is not the machine's arithmetic but the people around the bed, because a relative who presses the button on the patient's behalf can cause sedation and respiratory depression, and that is the most common operator error in PCA care. The characteristic alarm is the occlusion alarm, and the monitoring that accompanies a PCA is the sedation score and the breathing rate.

Enteral feeding pumps look like infusion pumps and are deliberately made to be different. They move liquid nutrition, water, or medication into the stomach or small intestine through a feeding tube, and their sets are wider, differently connected, and built to tolerate a thicker fluid. The mechanism is usually peristaltic, the rate is set in milliliters per hour, and a typical range runs from 1 to 300 milliliters per hour, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard that defines this device is the wrong route, because an enteral set connected to an intravenous line delivers food into the bloodstream and is a recognized fatal event, which is why adapters that defeat the differently shaped connectors are dangerous. Aspiration is the second hazard, and it follows a displaced tube, a patient lying flat, or a stomach that is not emptying. The characteristic alarm is the occlusion or empty container alarm, and the common error is to hang the feed without first confirming that the tube is still in the stomach, so the operator's checks are the tube position, the residual volume, and the elevation of the head of the bed.

The elastomeric pump is the device for places where electricity is a rumor, and it contains no motor, no battery, and no keys. Its engine is a stretched elastic membrane inside a rigid housing, filled under pressure at the pharmacy or the factory, and its recoil pushes the fluid out at a nearly constant pressure. The rate is set not by a controller but by a flow restrictor, a very narrow tube of precise length and diameter at the outlet, whose resistance fixes the flow for a given fluid and temperature. Because the driving force is elasticity and the restriction is fixed, the delivered rate depends on the viscosity of the drug and on the temperature, and a rise of a few degrees Celsius thins the fluid and speeds the flow, a sensitivity that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is that silent variation, and the common error is to store a filled pump against the body or in the sun. The characteristic signal is not an alarm but the visible collapse of the balloon, which tells the observer the dose has been delivered.

A blood or fluid warmer is a heat exchanger that prevents the patient from losing temperature when a large volume enters a vein. Two fluids at different temperatures, separated by a conducting wall, move toward a common temperature, and the warmer uses a water bath, a dry heating plate, or a countercurrent path beside a warmed stream. The target is body temperature, near 37 degrees Celsius, and a warmer is set to bring fluid to that point rather than above it, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The upper limit matters because warming blood above about 41 degrees Celsius causes hemolysis, a ceiling that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the damaged cells release potassium and free hemoglobin. The hazard is the overheated unit or the bag placed on a radiator, and the characteristic alarm is the over-temperature alarm. The common error is to warm a bag on a radiator or in a sink of hot water, and the field version is a basin of warm water or a warm pack that demands a thermometer rather than a thermostat.

The infusion stand or pole is the least respected piece of equipment in this chapter and the cause of a recognizable class of injury. It is a vertical pole with a telescoping section, several hooks, and a weighted base, usually with five legs and small casters, and its stability depends on the width of the base and the height of its center of gravity. Hanging a pump high on the pole raises the center of gravity, which is why every pole carries a weight limit and a maximum number of pumps, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A rolling pole that crosses a threshold or a wet floor can catch a caster and go over, dropping a pump onto the patient, the line, or the nurse's foot. The common error is to push a heavily loaded pole by its top or to hang extra pumps on a pole designed for one, and the daily check is short, because the casters roll and lock, the base is intact, and the hooks are not bent.

Behind every hospital pump lies an infrastructure the operator rarely sees and always depends on. The pumps draw power from the wall, and in an intensive care unit they are commonly plugged into a circuit supported by an uninterruptible power supply, UPS for short, so a brief failure of the mains does not stop a vasoactive drug. The pharmacy prepares the drugs, and the ward supplies the sterile single-use tubing, filters, connectors, and labels whose packaging must be intact and whose expiry date must be in the future. Many pumps carry a drug library, a stored list of standard concentrations with limits, and the operator must select the correct entry rather than override it, with every pressure limit and alarm threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Cleaning and maintenance decide whether the pump is still the device the manufacturer calibrated, so the housing, keypad, door, and cradle are wiped with the approved disinfectant and the pump is never immersed. The parts that soil most are the parts that fail, namely the door seal, the occlusion sensor and air sensor windows, and the tubing channel, and the common error is to leave a cracked case or a swollen battery in service.

Alarm handling is a skill, and it begins with the refusal to press the silence button first. The sounds a pump makes are information, because air in line points to the bag or the priming, a downstream occlusion points to the cannula or the patient's arm, an upstream occlusion points to a closed clamp or an empty bag, a battery alarm points to a socket, and a pump error points to the device itself. The trouble-shooting sequence is therefore physical before electrical, so the operator looks at the patient, then along the whole line, then at the bag and the chamber, and only then at the screen. Alarm fatigue is the quiet hazard, because a pump that alarms often is a pump whose alarms are ignored, and the response to a nuisance alarm is to find its cause rather than raise a threshold, with every adjustable threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to restart the pump to clear an alarm without correcting the condition, which resets the alarm and hides the problem. The failure modes are few, because over-infusion follows a programming error, a miscalculated drop rate, a raised threshold, a siphon, or an open clamp, while under-infusion follows an occlusion, a kink, an empty bag, or a dead battery, and most are prevented by watching the site, confirming the rate, and never leaving a line unclamped.

The daily check is the ritual that makes an infusion safe, and it takes only a few minutes when done the same way every time. The operator confirms the patient, the drug, the concentration, the route, the rate, and the volume to be infused against the written order, and reads the values back aloud when a second person checks a high-alert drug. The pump is checked for a mains connection, a charged battery, a set within its labeled use-by date, a primed and bubble-free line, and a chamber at its marked level. The site is inspected for redness, swelling, coolness, pain, or leakage, and the line is followed from the bag to the patient to confirm that every connection is tight and no clamp is closed by accident. The alarm function is tested at the start of the shift on many protocols, and every rate limit and occlusion threshold used in the check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to perform the check from memory, which is how a decimal point and a drop factor change places.

The field variant of an infusion device begins with what the field does not have. A mobile clinic or a frontier health post usually lacks reliable mains power, dedicated pump tubing, calibrated cassettes, a pharmacy that prepares standard concentrations, and a technician who can service a peristaltic mechanism. What it has instead is a gravity set, a bag, a vein, a watch, and a person who can count, and in the field the gravity set is not a backup but the ordinary instrument. The field gives up the pump's memory, its alarms, and its precision, and it demands arithmetic, a written rate, and a person who watches. The bag is hung as high as the situation allows, because the height sets the pressure and therefore the rate, and the drop factor is read from the packaging. If the packaging is missing, the operator calibrates the set by counting how many drops fill a known volume, then converts the prescribed volume into drops per minute and counts for a full minute. The rate is recounted after every bag change and at intervals that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because in the field the observer is the alarm.

The wide-open clamp is the field's characteristic catastrophe, and it is worth describing precisely. A roller clamp opened fully offers almost no resistance, so a full bag of 1,000 milliliters, a volume that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, can empty into an adult in a few minutes at a height of 1 meter. This happens when a clamp is knocked by a passing patient, when a clamp that no longer grips is kept in service, or when a hurried operator opens the clamp to catch up a delayed infusion. The consequences range from fluid overload and pulmonary edema to an air embolism if the bag empties and the line is not clamped, and the common error is to widen the clamp to catch up without ever remeasuring the new rate. The safeguards are physical and procedural, so the operator uses a clamp that grips, keeps it turned toward the closed position when not adjusting it, never leaves a full bag running unobserved above a patient, and prefers the narrowest tubing that will carry the required flow. Field improvisation also raises pressure, whether by raising the bag or by wrapping a blood pressure cuff around it, and any external pressure applied to a fluid bag must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When a field clinic does have a battery pump, the battery becomes the central consumable. The device is charged whenever the sun or a generator allows, a spare battery or a charged power bank is carried, and the pump is used only for drugs whose interruption would harm the patient, because a pump that dies mid-infusion is worse than a gravity set that never needed power. The elastomeric pump is the field's answer to this problem, since it carries its own stored energy in a stretched membrane and needs nothing from the grid, while enteral feeding is usually done by gravity with a syringe and a funnel. Warming is done in a basin of water or with a warm pack, and the operator must use a thermometer to be sure the fluid does not exceed a safe temperature, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Infection control is harder, because the field may reuse tubing and connectors when supplies run out, and every reuse is a trade between scarcity and sterility, so a reused set is flushed, inspected, and stored dry, its ports are disinfected before every access, and it is replaced at the earliest opportunity. The common error is to keep a set in service because it looks new, when the part that matters is the inside of the connector.

The final safeguard in every setting is the person at the bedside, and the human factors of infusion care deserve the same attention as the mechanics. Labels must be legible and complete, tubing must be traced rather than assumed, and high-alert drugs must be checked by two people who read the values aloud and compare them with the order. Training should cover the arithmetic of drop rates, the loading of each pump used in the facility, the meaning of each alarm, and the physical signs of infiltration and overload. Documentation should record the drug, the concentration, the rate, the volume, the start time, the site, and every change, and equipment failures belong in the incident system rather than in the corridor. Every default value, alarm threshold, and concentration stored in a pump library must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator error that outranks all the others is silence, which is not reporting the alarm that kept sounding or the clamp that would not hold.

To summarize, an infusion device is a way of turning pressure into a measured dose, and the two sources of that pressure are height and a motor. The gravity set, its drip chamber, its drop factor, and its roller clamp remain the physical foundation on which every pump is built, which is why counting drops is still a clinical skill worth keeping. The volumetric pump, the syringe pump, the patient-controlled analgesia pump, the enteral feeding pump, the elastomeric pump, and the blood warmer each add control in exchange for consumables, power, and maintenance. The safety hazard is almost always a mismatch between the intended and the delivered amount, the common operator error is a rate that was set once and never verified, and the characteristic alarms of the pump family are air in line, occlusion, door open, and battery low. The hospital supports these devices with power, dedicated sets, a pharmacy, a drug library, and a technician, while the field replaces them with arithmetic, observation, and a clamp that is never trusted, so the discipline that unites both halves is to know the rate, watch the site, clamp the line, and never leave an infusion to look after itself.

# Chapter 11 — Syringes, Needles, and Injection Devices

A syringe is a pump worked by the human hand, and a needle is the hole through which its output escapes. Together they are the smallest delivery system in the hospital and the one used most often, because almost every drug that cannot be swallowed must be pushed through the skin or into a vein. This chapter describes the physical act of injection before the clinical habits that surround it, then takes the hospital-grade syringe, needle, and injection device apart piece by piece. It then turns to the field clinic, where the same act is performed with fewer devices, more reuse, and a much narrower margin for error, and where a single contaminated needle can undo a year of careful work. The safety hazard, the common operator error, and the characteristic warning sign are named with each device rather than gathered at the end.

Pressure applied to a liquid that fills a closed space is transmitted through it in every direction without appreciable loss, a principle named for Blaise Pascal. A syringe exploits this by giving the hand a large flat plunger to push and giving the fluid a very small hole to escape through. The force of the thumb is spread over the area of the plunger, producing a modest pressure in the barrel, and that same pressure acts on every square millimeter of the needle channel. The volume that leaves the needle is exactly the volume the plunger displaces as it travels down the barrel, which is why the graduation printed on the barrel can be trusted as a measure rather than a guess. Nothing about the injection is mysterious, because the device converts a small force over a large area into a large force over a small area, and the hand that understands this pushes steadily instead of jerking. Any pressure, volume, or dose setting named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The rate at which fluid leaves a needle is governed ferociously by the width of its channel. Flow rises with the fourth power of the internal radius, so doubling the diameter of the channel multiplies the flow for the same pressure by roughly 16, and halving it divides the flow by the same enormous factor. Length works the other way, because a longer needle resists flow in direct proportion to its length, and the thickness of the fluid matters as well, which is why a thick oily preparation is far harder to push than salt water. In practical terms this explains why a 21 gauge needle empties a syringe in a few seconds while a 27 gauge needle of the same length demands patience and a firmer thumb. It also explains the danger of forcing a plunger, because when the needle is blocked or buried in tissue the pressure rises inside the barrel, the hub may separate from the tip, and the joint fails under the hand. Needle gauge, needle length, and the fluid being given must all be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The syringe itself is a clear barrel of known cross-section, a plunger with a soft elastomer seal at its tip, a flange at the top for the fingers, a graduated scale along the side, and a tip at the bottom that receives the needle. The seal is what makes the device a pump, because it must slide easily and still resist the pressure of injection, and a seal that has dried, swollen, or been lubricated with the wrong substance will leak at the moment of use. The tip comes in 2 main forms. A luer slip is a smooth taper that grips the needle hub by friction alone, and a luer lock adds a threaded collar that screws the hub down so the joint cannot separate under pressure. The taper is a precision fit made to a fixed angle, and mixing parts from different makers defeats it, so the pairing of a syringe and a needle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Volumes run from 1 milliliter for a fine dose through 2, 3, 5, 10, and 20 milliliters to 50 milliliters for irrigation and aspiration. The rule of thumb is to choose the smallest syringe that holds the dose, because a wide barrel magnifies every error of the thumb.

A syringe never delivers quite everything it holds, because a small volume remains in the tip and in the hub of the needle after the plunger reaches the end of its travel. This dead space is a real amount of drug, on the order of a few hundredths of a milliliter in a conventional device and much less in a low dead space design that narrows the tip and fills part of the hub. The difference matters for expensive medicines, for vaccines where every dose must count, and above all for the small volumes given to infants, where the retained amount can be a visible fraction of the intended dose. A prefilled syringe avoids the problem differently, because the manufacturer fills and seals the barrel, and the operator has only to expel the air and inject. Air in the barrel should be cleared before injection by holding the device upright and advancing the plunger until a bead of liquid appears at the bevel, and the volume of that clearing step must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A needle is a hollow steel tube cut at an angle at one end and fixed into a molded hub at the other. The cut end, the bevel, is ground in facets so that the tip is sharp and the opening faces the tissue being entered, and the sharpness of that geometry, not the diameter of the shaft, decides how much force the skin demands. The hub carries a color that follows an international convention keyed to gauge, and the convention is useful for sorting a drawer but must never replace reading the label, because makers differ and a color remembered wrongly becomes the wrong needle. Gauge is a measure of the outside diameter of the shaft, and the numbers run backwards, so a 30 gauge needle is far finer than a 14 gauge needle. The finest gauges, from 30 down to 27, belong to intradermal and subcutaneous work, including insulin; the middle range, from 25 to 21 gauge, suits most intramuscular and intravenous injections; and the wide bores, from 20 down to 14 gauge, are reserved for rapid fluid, blood, and the aspiration of thick material. Every gauge and length mentioned here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Length is chosen as carefully as gauge, because the needle must reach its target layer without passing through it. Subcutaneous injections use short needles of roughly 6 to 16 millimeters, intramuscular injections in an adult use 25 to 40 millimeters, and a patient with thick subcutaneous fat may need a longer needle than the standard one to reach muscle at all. The bevel must face upward, toward the surface of the skin, because that orientation lets the point enter cleanly and the opening glide under the skin rather than tear it. Turning the bevel downward is one of the most common operator errors, and it produces a painful injection, a nick in the tissue, and sometimes a failed puncture. The needle must also be inspected before use for a bent shaft, a burr on the bevel, or a loose hub, since a bent needle tracks a curved path and a burred point tears as it enters. Needle length, insertion angle, and the choice of bevel orientation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Several needles exist for work that never touches a patient. A filter needle contains a small mesh inside its hub that traps glass fragments when a drug is drawn from a glass ampoule, and it is used for the drawing step only, because the filter would blunt the therapeutic dose if the same needle were used to inject. A blunt fill needle has no cutting bevel and is used to draw from a rubber-stoppered vial, where a sharp point would slice a core of rubber that then floats in the solution. That coring is a genuine hazard, and its characteristic sign is a small dark speck in the fluid or a fragment lying against the wall of the syringe, so the solution must be inspected again after drawing. A vented needle or a vented vial adapter lets air into the vial as fluid leaves, which equalizes the pressure and prevents the frothing and the spray that otherwise soak the stopper. Reconstitution devices and vial adapters go further by joining 2 vials, or a vial and a diluent container, so that the transfer needs no exposed needle at all. Filter pore size, adapter compatibility, and the technique for each device must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Safety-engineered needles exist because the moment of greatest danger is the moment between the injection and the disposal. Their designs differ but their principle is the same, because after the injection the sharp is either drawn back inside the barrel, covered by a sleeve that slides forward, or folded behind a hinged shield, so that no hand ever approaches the point. A needleless system removes the sharp altogether by placing a smooth valve or a blunt connector on the line, allowing drugs to be drawn and injected through a closed pathway. Protection is routinely defeated by habit. Operators still recap needles two-handed, they leave the safety device unactivated because it slows the case, they push the shield only partway so that the point remains exposed, or they remove a needle from a syringe before disposal so that the sharp travels loose. The characteristic sign is the absence of the audible click or the visible lock that tells the operator the shield has engaged, and any device that does not click has protected no one. Activation technique and disposal requirements for each safety device must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A needlestick injury transfers a small volume of blood directly into the tissues of the worker, which is why it is treated as a serious exposure rather than a minor cut, and why human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C are the infections that shape practice around it. The immediate response is to wash the wound, report it, and follow the local exposure protocol, but the better answer is that the injury should not happen at all. The sharps container is the device that prevents it, and its essential property is that it sits at the point of use, within arm's reach of the injection, so that no one carries an exposed needle across a room. The container is puncture resistant, leak proof, closable, and marked with a fill line, and it must be replaced when it reaches about three quarters full rather than pressed down or shaken to make more space. Nothing is ever retrieved from a sharps container by hand, and a container that is overfilled or left open is a hazard in its own right. Fill levels, closure requirements, and the disposal chain must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The insulin pen is a syringe made convenient, and it is a good example of how a device succeeds by rearranging the same physics. A spring-loaded or screw-driven piston in the pen advances a cartridge that holds several hundred units of insulin, and a dose dial on the end clicks as it is turned so that the patient can hear and feel the amount selected. The needle is a short, very fine one, usually in the 4 to 8 millimeter range, and it screws onto a threaded collar over the rubber septum of the cartridge. It is changed for every injection, because a reused pen needle is dull, contaminated, and a path for infection. The pen fails in particular ways. A blocked or bent needle leaves the dose inside the cartridge while the dial still clicks, and the characteristic warning sign is the absence of a bead of insulin when the operator performs the priming step before injection. An air bubble, a partly used cartridge, or a dial turned the wrong way can produce a dose that is small or absent. Unopened cartridges are stored cold, usually between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, while a pen in use is kept at room temperature for a limited number of days, and both the storage temperature and the in-use period must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. One pen belongs to one patient, because blood can travel backward into the cartridge.

An autoinjector is a spring-loaded syringe that fires its needle and delivers its dose in one action, and it exists for the emergency in which the patient or a bystander cannot manage a conventional injection. The device holds a prefilled syringe, a compressed spring, and a trigger, and pressing the device against the thigh releases the spring so that the needle enters and the drug is pushed through automatically. Its characteristic sounds are a click at the moment of firing and often a second signal when the injection is complete, and some devices also show a color change in a window that confirms the dose has left. The common operator errors are to fire the device into the wrong site, to fire it through clothing when the design requires bare skin, to remove it immediately instead of holding it in place for the full dwell time, and to place the thumb over the trigger end of a device held backwards. Dwell time, injection site, and storage temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An autoinjector that has been frozen or overheated may fail silently at the exact moment it is needed, so its storage and its expiry deserve the same attention as the drug inside it.

The syringes made for pumps are the same object refined to a tolerance that a hand does not need. A pump drives the plunger with a motor that knows the exact cross-section of the barrel, so it can compute a volume from the distance it travels, and for that calculation to be true the barrel must be straight, the plunger must move with even friction, and the device must recognize the syringe size loaded into it. A syringe that is too small, too large, or of a type the pump does not recognize will produce a false rate, and a modern pump displays a syringe recognition error rather than proceed. The characteristic alarms of a syringe pump are the occlusion alarm, which sounds when the pressure in the line exceeds a set limit, and the air-in-line or near-empty alarm, which sounds as the syringe empties. The common operator error is to silence an occlusion alarm and increase the rate instead of looking for the clamped tube or the displaced cannula that caused it. Occlusion pressure limits, alarm thresholds, and the accepted syringe list must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The reuse of a needle or a syringe is a practice that survives wherever supply is uncertain, and it fails for physical reasons that no amount of care can remove. A needle is sharpened to a fine bevel that dulls with a single passage through skin, and a resharpened point cannot reproduce the original facets, so a reused needle demands more force, causes more pain, and tears rather than cuts. The lumen of a fine needle is a long narrow channel that cannot be brushed, so blood and tissue remain inside it even after soaking, and the plastic hub and the barrel have crevices that no rinse reaches. Heat does the rest of the damage, because the temperatures that kill organisms also deform plastic, soften the seal, and cloud the graduation. Sterilization therefore offers a device that is neither clean nor accurate, and prions and some resistant organisms survive cycles that would ordinarily be adequate. The older reusable glass syringe with its ground glass plunger and metal needle is still found in some settings, and its parts can indeed be autoclaved, but the ground joint wears with every cycle until the fit leaks and the needle lumen remains as unreachable as ever. The correct rule is that a needle and a syringe are single-use devices, and any decision to reprocess one, together with the sterilization cycle, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumable side of this chapter is a discipline of checking rather than repairing. Before an injection the operator confirms that the packaging is intact and dry, that the sterile indicator has changed as it should, that the expiry date has not passed, and that the drug in the syringe matches the order in both name and dose. The syringe is inspected for a cracked barrel, a plunger that sticks or moves too freely, a legible scale, and a tip that holds the needle without wobble. The needle is inspected for a straight shaft, an unbent bevel, and a hub that seats fully, and the injection site is inspected for the skin condition that decides the technique. The parts that touch the patient only indirectly, the pen body, the pump cradle, and the connector valve, are wiped between patients with the disinfectant named in the local protocol. Stock is stored dry, out of sunlight, and within a temperature range the manufacturer defines, and it is rotated so that the oldest batch is used first. Sharps containers are checked on every shift for fill level and closure, and any container that is cracked is replaced rather than taped. Storage temperature, expiry intervals, and batch rotation rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The failure modes of the injection set are quiet, and most of them are visible to a careful eye. A plunger seal that has lost its lubrication drags and then releases in a jump, delivering a bolus instead of a steady push. A barrel that has been cracked by freezing leaks at the flange, and the leak is discovered only by the wet glove. A luer joint that has been cross-threaded holds until the pressure rises and then separates, spraying the contents. A needle pushed through a stopper without a fill needle carries a rubber core into the tissue. A syringe loaded upside down in a pump is recognized as the wrong size or delivers at the wrong rate. The characteristic alarms of the powered devices, the pump occlusion tone and the silent failure of a pen to prime, are the sounds and the silences that tell the operator something has gone wrong. Any pressure limit, alarm threshold, or rate setting associated with these failures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a field clinic the disposable syringe is the whole delivery system, and it arrives through a supply chain that may fail for months at a time. The result is that the same device is asked to do more, and the discipline that keeps it safe is stated as one needle, one injection, one disposal. That sentence is not a slogan but a chain of custody, because a needle is taken from a sealed package, used once, and placed immediately into a container, with no step in which it is set down on a tray, tucked into a pocket, or handed to another person. Where immunization programs cannot rely on this discipline, they use an auto-disable syringe, whose plunger locks at the end of the stroke so that the device cannot be used a second time even by accident. The World Health Organization recommends such devices for immunization for exactly this reason. The supply, the storage, and the disposal of every one of these devices in a field setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where disposable devices run out, the field does what it can, and most of what it can do is not sterilization. Boiling a needle in water at 100 degrees Celsius kills many organisms but leaves the lumen uncleaned, dulls the point, and does nothing about the blood inside the hub. Passing a needle through a flame chars the residue and destroys the temper of the steel, so that the point bends on the next insertion. Soaking in bleach corrodes the metal and leaves a residue that is painful in tissue, while the cleaning that must precede disinfection is exactly the step that a narrow needle makes impossible. Sharpening a needle on a stone can restore a point that a finger can feel, but it cannot restore the shape of the bevel, and the resharpened instrument tears rather than cuts. The improvised sharps container of a field clinic is often a sturdy plastic bottle or a sealed metal tin, and its value depends entirely on its being kept closed, kept away from children, and carried to a safe disposal site when full. Any boiling time, chemical concentration, or reprocessing method considered in the field must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Storage in the field is the part of the injection chain that fails first, because heat and freezing destroy the drug before the device ever reaches the patient. Insulin and most vaccines must be held cold, and a vaccine that has been frozen by an ice pack pressed against the vial may look normal and be useless, which is why a freeze indicator or a thermometer in the carrier matters more than the container itself. Multi-dose vials exist for economy in mass campaigns, and they are safe only when each entry uses a new sterile needle, the septum is disinfected before every puncture, and the vial is discarded at the interval the manufacturer sets. The shared vial and the shared needle are the 2 ways in which a campaign spreads infection rather than preventing it. Where large numbers must be injected quickly and supplies are scarce, needle-free jet injectors push a fine stream of liquid through the skin at high pressure, which removes the sharp but introduces the problem of the reusable nozzle and the contamination it can carry between patients. Cold chain temperature, multi-dose vial expiry after opening, and nozzle disinfection must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator checks in the field are the same as in the hospital, with the safety net of a supervisor and a maintenance department removed. The drug is read aloud against the order, and the label is read a second time by whoever is present, because the vial that looks like another vial is the classic error of a busy clinic. The dose is drawn in front of the patient wherever the patient can see it, the needle is shown to be new before the skin is prepared, and the sharp goes into the container before anything else is touched. The site is chosen with the same care as in a hospital, and the patient is watched for a few minutes afterward, because a reaction to an injection can begin within seconds and the field clinic may be far from help. Where an autoinjector is the emergency device on the shelf, its expiry and its storage temperature are checked as often as the drugs beside it, since a device that has been cooked in a vehicle will not fire as designed. Every dose, expiry date, and observation period named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the syringe is a hand pump that turns a small force into a precise volume, and the needle is a precision channel whose diameter, length, and bevel decide how the dose enters the body. The hospital-grade set adds engineered safety, color-coded gauges, filter and fill needles, vial adapters, pens, autoinjectors, and pump syringes, each with its own alarm or characteristic sign, and each depending on consumables that must be in stock before the patient needs them. The field set gives up the engineered safety and the redundancy of supply, and demands in their place an unbroken discipline of one needle, one injection, one disposal, backed by cold storage, honest record keeping, and a sharps container that is never filled past its line. The hazards are the same everywhere, the needlestick, the reused sharp, the wrong dose, and the injection into a blocked or unsterile site, and the defense is the same as well, because the operator who understands the physics, inspects the device, reads the label, and confirms every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use is the one who prevents them.

# Chapter 12 — Fluids, Blood, and Blood Products

Every fluid that reaches a patient arrives inside something, and here the container matters as much as its contents. A bag, a bottle, or a blood collection bag holds a column of liquid whose weight creates pressure at its outlet, and that pressure drives the fluid through tubing, a filter, and into a vein. Raise the container and the pressure rises, lower it and the pressure falls, and squeeze it and the pressure rises without any change in height. The solutions divide into crystalloids, water with small dissolved particles that cross capillary membranes, and colloids, which carry large molecules that stay in the circulation and hold water by osmotic attraction. Blood is a third case, a living tissue that must be collected, tested, cooled, warmed, and given within strict limits, and every storage temperature, flow rate, pressure, and alarm threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The flexible crystalloid bag is the most familiar container in the hospital. It is usually made of polyvinyl chloride, a soft plastic that can be heat sealed and squeezed without cracking, with a large spike port for the giving set and a smaller medication port with a rubber septum under a clear plastic overwrap. The bag carries graduations and a label with the solution name, volume, concentration, additive, lot number, and expiry, and before use the operator confirms that the fluid is clear, the overwrap is intact, the ports are capped, and the expiry is in the future, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The rigid bottle behaves differently because it does not collapse, so a vacuum forms above the falling fluid and stops the flow unless air enters, which is why a bottle is hung with a vented set whose air inlet carries a filter. The common errors are to use a bag that has been frozen or dropped, whose hairline port crack leaks only later, to choose a fluid by its shelf position rather than by reading the label, and to hang an unvented bottle and then wonder why the drip chamber has stopped.

The solutions themselves are devices with labels, and the labels are not interchangeable. Sodium chloride at 0.9 per cent is the reference isotonic fluid, balanced electrolyte solutions disturb the acid and base balance less when large volumes are given, and dextrose solutions expand the circulation poorly because the sugar is metabolized and the water spreads through the body. Bags compounded by a pharmacy carry a second label that can fall off, and potassium-containing fluids deserve particular care, because a rapid infusion can stop the heart. Every concentration and rate limit for these solutions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to choose a bag by its shelf position or packaging color rather than by reading it.

Colloid solutions work by oncotic pressure rather than by volume alone. The capillary wall lets water and small ions pass but holds back large molecules, so albumin, gelatin, dextran, or a synthetic starch stays in the vessel and draws water toward itself, and a smaller volume expands the circulation more than the same volume of crystalloid. Each colloid carries its own dangers, since gelatin and dextran can cause anaphylaxis, dextran can interfere with crossmatching, and starches have been associated with kidney injury and impaired clotting. The operator checks the label, concentration, expiry, and clarity, and every volume limit and infusion rate must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to treat a colloid as a stronger crystalloid and give it freely, when its place is narrow and its cost is high.

Blood is not a solution but a living tissue, and the bag that collects it is a small system rather than a container. A collection bag is a set of two to four plastic bags joined by integral tubing, with the primary bag holding a citrate anticoagulant before the donation begins. The citrate binds calcium and stops clotting, and its volume is matched to the volume of blood to be collected, while the bag is rocked during collection so that every drop meets the anticoagulant and no clot forms. Short lengths of tubing, called segments, are sealed off from the main bag and remain attached, and each segment holds a representative sample so the blood bank can test the unit without opening it, with every collection volume and anticoagulant ratio confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error at the donor's arm is to let the tubing kink or the bag lie still, which wastes a donation.

Everything that happens to a unit afterward depends on a number. At collection the bag receives a unique donation number, printed on the bag, repeated on every segment, on the paperwork, and on the crossmatch sample tubes, and the label records the blood group, the Rhesus factor written Rh, the component, the volume, the anticoagulant, the collection and expiry dates, and the storage temperature range. The number is the thread that ties the unit to the patient, and the most serious error in transfusion medicine is not a laboratory mistake but an identity mistake, in which a correct unit reaches the wrong patient because a number was copied by hand without a second check. The characteristic alarm of this system is a mismatch at the bedside, a bag whose number, group, or expiry does not agree with the paperwork or the wristband. That mismatch must stop the transfusion before the line is connected, and the identity check itself, along with every date and storage temperature printed on the label, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

One donation becomes several components because blood separates by weight. Spun in a centrifuge, the dense red cells move to the bottom, a thin layer of white cells and platelets gathers above, and the lighter plasma stays at the top, and the blood bank draws these layers off in sequence to produce packed red cells, platelet concentrate, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate. Red cells are stored between 2 and 6 degrees Celsius, platelets between 20 and 24 degrees Celsius with gentle agitation for a shelf life of only several days, and plasma frozen at minus 18 degrees Celsius or colder, and every one of those ranges and times must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. This is why a power failure threatens the inventory before it threatens the patient.

The blood bank refrigerator is a precision instrument that looks like a domestic appliance. It holds red cells near 4 degrees Celsius by circulating cold air through the cabinet, and the circulation matters as much as the cooling, because a still refrigerator develops warm and cold pockets and cells in the warm corner age faster. Its safety features are what make it a medical device: an independent thermometer whose probe sits among the bags, a continuous chart recorder or an electronic data logger, and an alarm that sounds on high temperature, low temperature, and power failure, with a battery that keeps it alive when the mains is gone. Every alarm threshold, recording interval, and battery test schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator records the temperature at fixed intervals, confirms that the independent thermometer agrees with the display, and the common error is to trust the display alone and silence a sounding alarm.

Two more machines complete the storage chain. The plasma freezer pulls its contents down quickly and holds them far below freezing, because rapid freezing protects the clotting factors that plasma is given to replace, and it carries the same independent thermometer, recorder, and battery-backed alarm as the refrigerator. The platelet agitator rocks a flat tray gently back and forth, usually a few cycles per minute, to keep platelets suspended and let them exchange gas through the permeable bag, and a stalled agitator is an alarm condition rather than a convenience. Because platelets are stored warm and their permitted storage time is short, they are the component most vulnerable to bacterial growth. Every freezer temperature and agitator setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common errors are a stalled agitator nobody notices and a freezer inventory that no one has checked.

Between the blood bank and the ward there is a journey, and the journey is part of the device. A unit leaves the refrigerator in an insulated box with a sealed lid, cooled by ice packs wrapped so that they do not touch the bag directly, because frozen red cells hemolyze and a bag pressed against bare ice can freeze at the point of contact. At the receiving end the nurse reads the temperature, inspects the bag for leaks, clots, discoloration, and a broken seal, confirms the number and the expiry, and starts the transfusion promptly. The usual rule is that a unit out of controlled storage for more than 30 minutes may not be returned, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to carry a unit in a pocket or on a car seat while finishing another task, and the result is a unit that is either discarded or, worse, given.

The transfusion set is the consumable that turns a bag into an infusion, and its central component is a filter. A filter is a screen with holes of a chosen size, and a standard blood administration set carries a screen with pores between 170 and 260 micrometers, large enough to pass red cells and small enough to catch clots and debris, while a finer screen of about 20 to 40 micrometers is used where microaggregates are a concern and a leukoreduction filter removes white cells by adhesion. Both of those pore sizes must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Pediatric sets have a smaller priming volume and often a graduated burette so that a small volume can be measured without wasting a whole unit, and pump sets for blood use tubing whose diameter and elasticity match the pump that squeezes it. The common operator error is to use an ordinary crystalloid set for blood, where the filter is too coarse to protect the patient.

Flow through a transfusion line obeys the same physics as any other fluid, and the numbers surprise people. Resistance rises steeply as a tube narrows, so a cannula of 14 gauge carries far more flow than one of 22 gauge, and the difference grows with the length of tubing, which is why a long extension set can halve the rate of a gravity transfusion. That is the purpose of the pressure infuser, a cuff that wraps around the bag and inflates to a chosen pressure, commonly around 300 millimeters of mercury, a target that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The device causes two classic accidents, air embolism when the bag empties and the pressure pushes air down the line, and over-infusion when the cuff stays inflated. The operator must watch the gauge, never let the bag empty completely, and never pressurize without a gauge, because a hand can generate pressures far above any safe target.

The rapid infuser is the hospital's answer to hemorrhage, and it is a system rather than a single device. It draws fluid or blood from bags and from a reservoir through wide tubing, passes it over a high-capacity heater, removes air in a chamber with a level sensor, and pumps it into the patient through a large-bore catheter at several hundred milliliters per minute, far beyond any gravity set. The characteristic alarms are air in line, over-temperature, occlusion, and reservoir empty, and an air detector, a temperature control, and an occlusion detector stand behind them, with every threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to connect a rapid infuser to a small peripheral cannula, which defeats the flow and can rupture the vein.

A blood warmer is a heat exchanger whose only job is to stop a cold fluid from cooling the patient. Two fluids at different temperatures, separated by a conducting wall, move toward a common temperature, and the warmer arranges that contact in one of three ways: a water bath that pumps warmed water through a jacket, a dry heat plate that presses against the bag or tubing, or an in-line cassette inside a warmed block immediately before the fluid enters the patient. The target is body temperature, and the danger is the upper limit, because red cells are damaged by heat and warming blood above roughly 41 degrees Celsius causes hemolysis, a ceiling that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm of a powered warmer is an over-temperature alarm, sometimes with an independent cut-out whose setting must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to warm a bag on a radiator, in a sink, or in a microwave, where the temperature is unknown and uneven.

Cell salvage recovers the patient's own blood and returns it, which removes the compatibility problem and reduces the demand on the blood bank. Its physical principle is density separation in a spinning bowl, where shed blood is sucked from the surgical field with a drip of anticoagulant and collects in a reservoir with a filter that holds back clots and tissue. From the reservoir the fluid is pumped into a centrifuge bowl, where the dense red cells pack against the wall while the lighter plasma, wash solution, and debris are displaced to a waste bag, and the concentrated cells are reinfused through a filter. Every pressure, speed, and anticoagulant ratio must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the alarms include air in the line and a full waste bag. The common operator error is to salvage from a field contaminated with bowel contents or from a patient with a malignancy or an active infection, where the recovered blood should not return.

The blood bank laboratory is a room full of devices that make antibodies visible. When an antibody meets its matching antigen on a red cell surface, it links several cells into a lattice, and that lattice is large enough to be seen as clumping, or agglutination, against a light or under a microscope. The simplest method reads that clumping by eye on a white tile, and modern laboratories use a column of gel or glass beads where agglutinated cells are trapped at the top and free cells travel to the bottom. The equipment behind these methods includes a refrigerated centrifuge, a water bath or incubator held at 37 degrees Celsius, a cell washer, calibrated pipettes, a reagent refrigerator, and a well-lit reading station. Grouping uses anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D reagents with the patient's own cells, a reverse grouping with known cells, an antibody screen, and finally the crossmatch, and every reagent's storage temperature, the 37 degrees Celsius incubation, and every expiry must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

All of this equipment is worthless if the sample in the tube is not the patient's. A blood sample for grouping and crossmatching must be labeled at the bedside, at the moment it is drawn, with the patient's full name, a unique identifier, the date and time, and the name of the person who drew it, and a tube without that label must be rejected rather than used. Many services require two separate samples from two separate venipunctures for a first crossmatch, precisely because a single mislabeled tube is the classic route to a fatal reaction. The common operator error is to prepare labels in advance or write them from memory in a busy room, and every sample acceptance rule and repeat-testing interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The last step in the chain is the bedside check, and it is performed by people rather than by a machine. Two trained people confirm the patient's identity from the wristband and by asking the patient, compare it with the compatibility label and the unit number, check the blood group and the expiry, inspect the bag for leaks, clots, or discoloration, and record baseline vital signs before the line is opened. The transfusion then begins slowly, at a rate that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the first 15 minutes are the most dangerous because a severe hemolytic reaction usually declares itself early. The nurse stays with the patient through that period, watching for fever, chills, rash, back pain, breathlessness, falling blood pressure, and dark urine. Any of those signs stops the transfusion at once, keeps the vein open, and sends the unit, the set, and the paperwork back to the blood bank with a reaction report, because the characteristic alarm of transfusion is the patient and the common operator error is to leave the bedside during those first minutes.

When a reaction is reported, the blood bank investigates with its own devices. The clerical check comes first, because a surprising number of apparent reactions are identity errors, and the laboratory then repeats the patient's group and the unit's group, performs a direct antiglobulin test to look for antibody coating the red cells, inspects the plasma for the pink discoloration that indicates hemolysis, and cultures the unit if bacterial contamination is suspected. The results decide the diagnosis and the patient's future treatment, which is why the bag is never discarded and every reaction is entered in a register. The World Health Organization recommends that every country operate a national blood system with a reporting scheme for adverse events, so that the same error is not repeated in the next hospital, and local reporting duties must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A transfusion service rests on infrastructure that the ward never sees, and its reliability is built from ordinary maintenance and an inventory of consumables. The blood bank needs power that survives an outage, usually a circuit supported by an uninterruptible power supply and a generator, because a freezer that warms over a weekend destroys an inventory that took weeks to collect. Refrigerators and freezers are temperature mapped so that every shelf position is known, alarm systems are tested at intervals that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and data loggers are checked against a reference thermometer. Cleaning is part of maintenance, since spilled blood is removed with the approved disinfectant, door gaskets are wiped so that they seal, condenser coils and air filters are cleaned so that the compressor can reject heat, and the inside of a refrigerator is never scrubbed with a harsh agent. The consumables run from blood administration sets and filter sets to collection bags with anticoagulant, crossmatch tubes, antisera that must stay cold, insulated boxes with ice packs, and the plastic overwrap that keeps plasma ports out of a thawing bath. The centrifuge needs special care, because an unbalanced rotor damages its bearings, and the common errors include recording a temperature from memory, silencing an alarm, and defrosting a freezer without moving the inventory to a monitored alternative.

The failure modes of this system can be sorted by which link has broken. The cold chain fails when power is lost, a door is left open, a freezer is overfilled, or a box sits in the sun, and the result is blood that is warm, blood that is frozen, or blood that has grown bacteria. The machine fails when a compressor, a thermostat, an alarm battery, or an agitator motor gives way, often without warning, which is why the independent thermometer and the written record are the real safety devices. The laboratory fails when a reagent is expired, a centrifuge is unbalanced, or a result is misread, and the people fail when the wrong sample is drawn, the wrong unit is issued, the first minutes of a transfusion are unobserved, or a reaction is dismissed as a fever from something else. The clinical outcomes have physical names: hemolysis with free hemoglobin and potassium, a hemolytic or febrile reaction, bacterial sepsis, circulatory overload, citrate toxicity, and air embolism.

The field clinic usually has no blood bank, and that single absence reorganizes everything. There is no inventory, no crossmatched unit waiting in a refrigerator, no component therapy, and often no laboratory that can type blood and screen for antibodies on demand. What the field has instead is a donor, often a relative of the patient, a cool box or a small refrigerator, a rapid test or a set of grouping reagents, and a clinician who must decide whether the risk of transfusing is greater or smaller than the risk of waiting. The field gives up the inventory, the screening, and the second pair of experienced eyes, and it demands donor selection, testing, labeling, and close observation in their place. Even the simplest field transfusion involves numbers, and every hemoglobin threshold, volume, and storage temperature in this half of the chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The walking donor is a person well enough to give blood and close enough to give it now, and selecting that person is the field substitute for a blood bank's testing. The donor is questioned and examined for age within an accepted range, a weight above a stated minimum, a hemoglobin measured from a finger-prick sample against a threshold the facility has set, a normal pulse and blood pressure, no fever, no recent illness, no recent donation, and no medication that would harm a recipient. Every one of those thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a donor who is anemic, infected, or too small is a danger to the recipient and to themselves. The donation uses a sterile collection bag with anticoagulant that is kept moving so that blood and citrate mix, and the bag is labeled at the bedside with the donor's identity, the time, the volume, and a unique number that is also written in the register beside the patient's name. The common operator error is to accept a donor on the strength of appearance alone, and the second error is to fail to record who gave the blood and when.

Some testing must precede any field transfusion, and its purpose is to avoid giving a unit that will destroy the patient's red cells. The patient and the donor are each grouped for the A, B, and O antigens and for the Rhesus factor using antisera on a tile or a card, and the patient's plasma is tested against the donor's cells in a crossmatch, on a tile, in a tube, or on a rapid test strip, to look for the clumping that predicts a reaction. Reading agglutination requires good light and a magnifying lens or a microscope, and the result is recorded before the unit leaves the donor's side, because minutes can matter in a hemorrhage. Expired, warm, or contaminated reagents give misleading answers, and every reagent's storage condition, reading time, and interpretation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Where no grouping or crossmatch is possible at all, a group O Rh negative unit is the emergency choice for the widest range of recipients, but this is a calculated risk, and the common operator error is to accept a single weak or ambiguous reading under pressure rather than repeating the test.

When the field has a tested donor and a patient who needs blood, the administration must still obey the physics of the hospital. Ideally the blood is collected into a bag with anticoagulant and given through a blood administration set with a filter, because a filter protects the patient from clots and a bag lets the volume and the rate be seen and controlled. Passing blood directly from donor to recipient through a short set without a collecting bag is the oldest method and the most dangerous, because the volume is unmeasured, the anticoagulant is absent or improvised, air can enter, and a crystalloid set has no blood filter. Storage is the field's hardest constraint, so a cool box with wrapped ice packs and a thermometer, or a solar refrigerator designed for vaccines, must be monitored with an independent thermometer and the reading written down at intervals that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Whole blood in a citrate solution has a shelf life measured in weeks, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while warming is done in a basin of warm water or against a warm pack with a thermometer to keep the fluid below its safe limit, a limit that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A pressure infuser is improvised from a blood pressure cuff with its own gauge rather than a hand, and the field's final safeguard is the record, because the donor register and the patient's chart are the only crossmatch that survives the night.

To summarize, this chapter has been about containers, tubing, filters, refrigerators, and freezers rather than about the drugs inside them, because those objects determine what the patient actually receives. A crystalloid bag or bottle delivers fluid by height and pressure, a colloid adds the physics of oncotic attraction, and a blood collection bag adds anticoagulant, integral segments, and a number that must follow the unit to the bedside. The transfusion set's filter, the pressure infuser's gauge, the rapid infuser's air detector, the blood warmer's temperature limit, and the cell salvage circuit's centrifuge each exist to make an old physical process safer, while the blood bank's refrigerators, freezers, and agitators are medical devices whose alarms, records, and independent thermometers are the real inventory. The safety hazard is the wrong unit or the wrong temperature, the common operator error is an unchecked identity or an unobserved first 15 minutes, and the characteristic alarm of a transfusion is the patient rather than a machine. The field variant gives up the inventory, the component therapy, and the laboratory, and demands donor selection, testing before transfusion, and a written record instead, with every threshold there confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 13 — Medication Management

Medication management is the system that keeps a drug safe from the shelf to the patient, and its physical problem never changes. A medicine is a chemical quantity that must be identified, counted, held within a narrow band of temperature and light, and matched to one named person at one named time. The clinical shorthand is the five rights, meaning the right patient, the right drug, the right dose, the right route, and the right time, and every cabinet, label, seal, and scanner in this chapter exists to make one of those five verifiable rather than remembered. The stakes are asymmetric, because a missed dose may be survived while a doubled dose may not. The characteristic hazard is not one dramatic failure but a chain of small ones, a label read too quickly, a vial that resembles its neighbor, a refrigerator that warmed overnight, a seal nobody checked. The characteristic alarm is rarely a siren, because most of this equipment fails quietly, and a good system is built to make the quiet failure visible.

Unit-dose packaging is a small piece of material engineering that performs a large amount of safety work. A tablet is placed in a thermoformed plastic cavity, a foil lid is heat sealed across the top, and the card is printed with the drug name, the strength, and a lot number. The cavity holds one dose, so nobody has to count, and the foil lid gives tamper evidence, because a broken seal is visible before the drug is touched. Cold-form foil laminates aluminum between plastic layers and is used for drugs damaged by moisture, oxygen, or light, because the metal layer is an almost perfect barrier to all three. The price of this protection is infrastructure, since the ward needs a packaging machine, a heat sealer, a printer, a cleaning routine, and a pharmacist who confirms that the tablet inside matches the label outside. The common operator error is to tear a card open in a hurry and lose the part of the label that carries the strength, leaving a bare tablet whose identity must be guessed. A drug without its label is not a drug but a mystery.

Strip packaging applies the same idea in a continuous form. A roll of foil passes through a machine that forms pockets, drops one unit into each pocket, and seals a lidding layer over the top, leaving a strip that can be torn at perforations. The strip is efficient to produce and compact to store, and its perforations let a nurse detach one dose without opening the rest. Its weakness is that the printed identity often repeats only once across several doses, so a detached end pocket may carry no name at all. Repackaging from a bulk bottle into a pill organizer creates the same danger in a different place, because once a tablet leaves its original container the only record of what it is becomes the new label. The common operator error is to transfer several tablets first and label the pockets afterwards, which is how one drug ends up in another's space. The rule is to label the new container before the first tablet leaves the old one.

The printed label is the single most important information device in medication management. It is usually a pressure-sensitive sheet of paper or synthetic film, printed by a thermal printer, a laser printer, or a handwriting pen, and its adhesive must survive refrigeration and humidity without curling off the vial. A compliant label carries the patient's full name and a second identifier, the drug name, the strength or concentration, the total volume, the diluent if one was used, the route, the time of preparation, the expiry of the preparation, and the name of the person who prepared it. Trailing zeros and abbreviations are dangerous, so a dose is written as a whole number with its unit in full, and the word units is never shortened, because a hurried hand can turn a short form into a zero. Tall man lettering, in which a few letters of similar drug names are printed in capitals, uses shape difference to separate products. Color is a tempting cue and an unreliable one, because colors fade and because a color-blind operator sees none of it. The common operator error is the handwritten label written after the syringe is already filled, when the telephone has rung twice.

Because human reading is the weak link, the hospital adds a machine that reads for it, and the physical basis of that machine is the barcode. A barcode is a pattern of dark bars and light spaces whose relative widths encode characters, and a scanner works by shining light at the pattern and measuring how much reflects back, since a dark bar absorbs and a light space reflects. A laser scanner sweeps a beam across the symbol and detects the returning light, while an imager captures the whole pattern as a picture and decodes it in software, so the imager tolerates a curved vial and a smudged label better. A linear symbol holds a limited amount of data, and a two-dimensional grid holds far more, which is how a small square on a vaccine vial can carry a lot number and an expiry date. Every symbol carries a check character, so the software can reject a misread rather than pass it on. The common operator error is to scan the barcode on the outer carton rather than the one on the unit dose, which defeats the purpose of the check.

Barcode medication administration joins the drug to the patient through the same optical principle applied twice. The operator scans the barcode on the patient's wristband, scans the unit dose, and the software compares both against the prescribed order held in the electronic health record, EHR for short. If the drug, the dose, the route, or the time does not match the order, the screen and the speaker raise a mismatch alert, and the operator is expected to stop and resolve it rather than continue. The system is only as good as the identifiers it reads, so a crumpled wristband, a wet label, or a dead scanner battery turns a verified dose back into a remembered one. The characteristic failure is the workaround, in which staff scan a barcode kept on a card on the wall, or scan several doses at the end of a shift to clear the queue, and the check becomes a formality. Overrides exist for genuine emergencies and are logged, and a rising override rate is treated as a system alarm rather than as an operator failing. The safety hazard is automation complacency, because an operator who trusts the scanner stops reading the label.

The automated dispensing cabinet is the hospital's physical answer to keeping many drugs available and counted at once. It is a locked steel cabinet divided into drawers and pockets, each pocket latched by an electromechanical device and released only after the software receives a valid order and a valid identity. The operator enters a password or presents a fingerprint, the machine opens exactly one pocket, and the transaction is recorded against that person's name and that patient's record. Some cabinets verify the count by weighing each pocket, because the change in mass after a removal reveals how many units left, and some use radio frequency identification, RFID for short, in which a tag on each package answers a radio query so the cabinet knows what is present without being opened. The advantage is not convenience alone but an auditable trail, since every removal, return, and waste is time-stamped. The common operator error is to remove a dose and forget to record the return when the patient refuses it, which leaves a discrepancy that can never be cleared. The characteristic alarms are a drawer left open, a count that does not reconcile, and a cabinet that has lost its network connection and is running on a local list.

Before the cabinet, and still beside it in many wards, stands the plain locked cupboard that holds ward stock. Its parts are a lockable door, adjustable shelves, a shelf label for every drug, and a ledger in which receipts and issues are written by hand. Its strength is that it needs no power, no network, and no software, so it survives a blackout and a server failure, and its weakness is that its accuracy depends on the handwriting and honesty of the people who use it. The physical principles that matter are separation and labeling, because look-alike containers should sit on different shelves and high-alert drugs should be physically apart from ordinary ones. The common operator error is to return a partly used container to the wrong labeled space, so that the shelf label and the contents no longer agree. The operator check is a periodic read of the shelf against the ledger, and an unlabeled or mismatched container is removed rather than left for the next person to reason about.

The crash cart is the medication system compressed into an object that must work on the worst day of the year. It is a wheeled cabinet whose drawers are arranged in the order a resuscitation team reaches for things, with airway equipment at the top, drugs in the middle, and intravenous supplies and a defibrillator at the sides. Its identity is not the cabinet but the seal, a numbered tamper-evident tie or a breakable lock that passes through the drawers, so that one glance tells the team the cart has not been opened since it was checked. When the seal is broken for a real resuscitation, the cart is swapped for a sealed one at the earliest opportunity, and the used cart is restocked and resealed by a named person. The common operator error is to break the seal for one item and quietly reseal the cart without a full restock, so that the next arrest finds a gap.
