The characteristic alarm is the broken or missing seal found during a routine check, and the sealed emergency box is the same logic made portable. Every check interval and restocking rule for a cart or box must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Refrigerated storage rests on a physical cycle the operator should be able to picture. A compressor compresses a refrigerant gas, the gas condenses to a liquid and releases heat at the coils behind the cabinet, the liquid passes through an expansion valve, and inside the evaporator it boils back into a gas while absorbing heat from the interior. The thermostat cycles the compressor on and off to hold a set point, and air circulation spreads the cold so that the top and bottom shelves differ as little as possible. Many pharmaceutical refrigerators contain sealed bottles of water or glycol, which act as thermal ballast, because a large mass of liquid changes temperature slowly and carries the cabinet through a door opening or a short power cut. The drugs that need this protection typically require a range of 2 to 8 degrees Celsius, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to place drugs against the back wall or directly under the evaporator, where the local temperature can fall below freezing even while the cabinet thermometer reads correctly. The characteristic alarm is the high-temperature alarm, triggered by a probe above the range or by a door left open, and it must be answered by checking the drugs rather than by silencing the sound.

The vaccine cold chain adds a biological dimension to the physics, because vaccines are damaged in two opposite directions. A live attenuated vaccine loses potency when it is warm, since heat denatures the proteins and slowly kills the weakened organism, and the rate of that damage roughly doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius of extra warmth, a relationship that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A vaccine adsorbed onto an aluminum adjuvant is instead damaged by freezing, because ice crystals break the adsorption and the adjuvant clumps, and a vaccine that has been frozen may never be restored, however good it looks. This is why freeze-sensitive vaccines are never placed in direct contact with ice packs, and why a cold box uses a conditioned ice pack, one that has been left at room temperature until the surface no longer frosts. The cold chain is managed as a continuous record of temperature from the factory to the child's arm, and any break in that record is treated as a possible loss. The safety hazard is a vaccine that still looks like a vaccine and no longer protects, and the common operator error is to add extra ice in the belief that colder is safer.

Two small devices make heat and freeze damage visible on the vial itself. A vaccine vial monitor is a square of heat-sensitive material printed on the label, whose color darkens steadily as it accumulates heat exposure, and it is read by comparing the square with the circle printed beside it. When the square is as dark as the circle, the vial has received more heat than the vaccine can tolerate and must be discarded, and the correct reading of the monitor must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A freeze indicator is a small device that changes color or bursts irreversibly if the vial has been frozen, and it is the only way to prove that a freeze-sensitive vaccine stayed liquid. Where no indicator exists, the field uses the shake test, in which a suspect vial and a known frozen control are shaken side by side, because a thawed adsorbed vaccine settles as a flocculent sediment. The test is a heuristic rather than a proof and must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic error is to read the monitor after loading the carrier, when a damaged vial is already inside.

The cold box, the vaccine carrier, and their coolant packs are simple thermal machines. Water absorbs a large amount of heat when it melts, so a frozen ice pack held at 0 degrees Celsius, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, keeps absorbing heat while it turns to liquid, which is why it holds a low temperature far longer than its mass alone would suggest. A carrier is an insulated box with a tight lid, usually molded foam or a vacuum panel, loaded with packs arranged around the vaccines so that no vial touches a pack directly. In a fixed field clinic the same job is done by a solar direct drive refrigerator, which uses panels to freeze water or a phase-change material around the cabinet and then cools the interior from that stored cold, so it runs through the night without a battery. A gas absorption refrigerator uses heat from a flame or a heater to drive an ammonia and water cycle with no compressor at all, which is why it survives where electricity does not. Hold times, pack counts, and loading patterns must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to open the lid at every stop, so that the interior warms while the packs still feel cold.

Temperature monitoring turns all of this storage into evidence. A data logger is a small battery-powered instrument with a sensor, a memory, and often a liquid crystal display, LCD for short, and it records temperature against time so that an excursion can be seen, timed, and judged. Its battery must be fresh, its memory must be downloaded on a schedule, and its sensor must not sit against the cabinet wall or in the door. Temperature mapping measures the cabinet at many points while it is loaded and running normally, because the coldest and warmest spots are rarely where the shelves suggest, and the map determines where drugs may and may not be stored. The common operator error is to record a temperature taken at a convenient time rather than the minimum and maximum of the whole interval, which hides a night-time excursion. Every logging interval, alarm threshold, and calibration schedule mentioned here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A controlled substance safe is a storage device whose physics is entirely about delay and proof. It is a heavy steel box with a lock, often mounted to the wall or floor, and it is frequently double locked, meaning it sits inside a locked room and has its own lock as well. The purpose is not merely to prevent theft, since a determined intruder can defeat most boxes with time and tools, but to make the time and the tools visible and to force every access through a documented act. Access is limited to a small number of named people, and many facilities require two people present for a controlled count, which converts a solitary temptation into a witnessed transaction. The safe must be anchored, because a box that can be carried away is a box that can be opened elsewhere. The characteristic alarm of a modern safe is a door-open alert or a tamper signal, and the characteristic failure is a discrepancy found at the shift count. The operator must never share a key or a code, and the access rules of the safe must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The register that accompanies the safe is the audit trail, and its logic is a running balance. Every line records the date, the time, the patient, the drug, the dose given, the amount removed, and the amount discarded, and the arithmetic of the balance is checked line by line because a single unexplained unit is an incident. A dose that is drawn and not given must be wasted in the presence of a witness, and both people sign, because an unwitnessed waste is indistinguishable from a diversion. A spill or a broken ampule is handled the same way, with the volume or the fragments accounted for and witnessed, and never simply rinsed away. The register is reconciled at every shift change, and the count is performed by two people who each sign the total. The common operator error is a late entry written from memory at the end of a busy shift, which introduces an error that can no longer be traced. The safety hazard is diversion, and the only reliable defense is a culture in which an unexplained unit is reported immediately rather than quietly corrected.

Expiry checking is a routine rather than an event, because every drug is slowly changing from the moment it is manufactured. Chemical degradation follows the same general rule as vaccine damage, in that heat accelerates it, while light breaks down some molecules and moisture hydrolyzes others, which is why so many drugs are stored in amber glass or sealed foil. A manufacturer's expiry date assumes correct storage, so a drug kept warm or damp has effectively lost part of its shelf life even though the printed date has not arrived. The physical check uses stock rotation, in which new stock goes behind old stock so that the oldest is used first, and a recurring sweep in which every shelf, box, and bag is read for dates and the short-dated items are pulled forward. The common operator error is to check only the front row of a shelf and miss the expired vial behind it. A multi-dose vial carries a separate in-use period after it is first opened, commonly 28 days for many preparations, and every expiry sweep interval and beyond-use period must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of this equipment is mostly inspection, but inspection of parts that fail slowly. The refrigerator's condenser coil, door gasket, drain, and defrost cycle decide its performance, and a schedule that cleans the coil and checks the gasket at defined intervals prevents most warm-cabinet events. Temperature probes need periodic calibration against a reference thermometer, because a probe reading 1 degree low will allow the cabinet to run 1 degree warm without ever alarming. The automated cabinet needs its drawers lubricated, its latches inspected, its weighing pockets checked for drift, its software updated, and its supply protected, since a sudden outage can corrupt a count. The barcode scanner needs a clean lens, a charged battery, and software that still understands the symbols in use, and the printer needs its ribbon or thermal paper and a print head free of debris, because a faint label will be misread. The consumables that keep the system alive are labels, ribbon or thermal paper, wristbands, numbered seal tags, logger batteries, thermometers, ice packs, cold box liners, and the paper or electronic registers. A ward that runs out of labels will start writing on tape, so the consumable list is also a safety list. Every maintenance interval, calibration tolerance, and cleaning agent must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the operator must check, and when, is best learned as a rhythm. At the start of every shift the controlled substance count is reconciled by two people, the refrigerator temperature is read and recorded, the high-temperature alarm is confirmed to be armed, and the crash cart seal is inspected and its number logged. Every day the refrigerator's minimum and maximum readings are noted and reset, expiring items are rotated forward, and any drug delivered from pharmacy is put away under its correct name. Every week the crash cart and emergency boxes are checked against their lists, the data logger is downloaded where it is not networked, and the cabinet discrepancy report is reviewed. Every month the full expiry sweep is performed, the controlled registers are audited against the physical count by a second person, and the scanner and printer are cleaned. The common operator error is to sign a check that was not performed, which converts a real safety system into a record of optimism. Every check interval and alarm threshold used by the facility must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant begins with the lockable cupboard, and its differences from the hospital are differences of proof rather than of purpose. The field cupboard is often a metal cabinet with a padlock, or a wooden box with a hasp, standing in a room that is itself lockable, and it is stocked by a single clinical officer who also dispenses, administers, and documents. What it gives up is the automated count, the barcode, the network, and the pharmacist's independent review, because none of that infrastructure exists at the end of the road. What it demands instead is an unbroken written record, a named custodian who is accountable for the key, and a discipline of physical separation that substitutes for the software. Separation matters more in the field, not less, because the cupboard may hold drugs whose packaging looks alike, and a single shelf label in faded ink is the only cue. The characteristic failure is not a crash but a slow drift, in which the ledger and the shelf disagree by a few units that nobody can explain. The operator must count the cupboard on a schedule, and the storage conditions and shelf life allowed in the field must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The paper register and the vaccine carrier are the field's substitutes for the hospital's electronic checks and its refrigerator. The register records the date, the patient, the drug, the dose, the route, the time, and the balance remaining, and the balance is recalculated and initialed at the end of each day. Its advantage is that it needs no electricity, and its disadvantage is that it has no automatic check, so an error persists until an honest count reveals it. The vaccine carrier is a small insulated box with conditioned ice packs, a foam liner, and a thermometer visible without opening the lid, and carrying it to a village means managing three enemies at once, which are ambient heat, direct sun, and freezing damage from the packs themselves. The field rule is to keep the carrier in the shade, off the hot floor of a vehicle, and closed except when a dose is actually drawn. Where no carrier exists, an unglazed clay pot with wet sand between two walls substitutes evaporative cooling, but it cannot hold a fixed temperature and it fails in humid weather. Every hold time, pack arrangement, and temperature limit for a carrier must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, medication management is a chain of proof that begins at a manufacturer and ends at a patient's mouth or vein. Its physical foundations are the sealed unit dose and its label, the optical barcode and the machine that reads it, the latched drawer of the automated cabinet, the numbered seal that proves a crash cart complete, the vapor compression cycle and its thermal ballast that hold a refrigerator between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the phase change of water that makes an ice pack useful. The safety hazard is a chain of quiet failures rather than one loud one, the common operator error is the check performed after the fact or not at all, and the characteristic alarms are the refrigerator high-temperature alert, the open drawer, the count discrepancy, the barcode mismatch, and the broken seal. The hospital supports these devices with pharmacy oversight, power, networks, calibrated probes, and a trained technician, while the field replaces them with a lockable cupboard, a paper register, a conditioned ice pack, a vaccine carrier, and a named person who counts. The discipline that unites both halves is unchanged, which is to identify the drug, count it, keep it in its range, write it down, and verify it against the patient before it is given.

# Chapter 14 — Oxygen Systems

Oxygen is a drug, and in most hospitals it arrives in a heavy steel cylinder rather than a paper packet, so the person who gives it must also understand a machine. The physical principle is a gradient, because oxygen crosses from the alveolus into the blood only when its partial pressure there is higher than in the blood returning to the lungs. Room air contains about 21 per cent oxygen, which is enough for a healthy person at rest but not for a lung that is blocked, flooded, stiff, or poorly perfused, so the patient breathes faster to compensate. Adding oxygen to the inspired gas raises the alveolar partial pressure, restores the gradient, and buys time while the underlying problem is treated. Every device here, from the bulk tank to the smallest nasal prong, exists only to control that fraction and to deliver it at a flow the patient can tolerate.

The gas must be obtained, stored, and moved, and pressure is what makes this possible. Oxygen is held as a compressed gas in steel or aluminum cylinders, as a cryogenic liquid in an insulated vessel, in a piped supply generated centrally, or in a concentrated stream made at the bedside from room air. A compressed cylinder is filled to roughly 2000 pounds per square inch, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A gas follows a simple relationship, because pressure multiplied by volume stays constant when the temperature does not change, so gas squeezed into one tenth of its volume exerts ten times the pressure. When the valve opens the gas expands toward atmospheric pressure and rushes out, and the regulator tames that rush into a steady, measured flow.

Cylinders come in a family of sizes, chosen by how the gas will be used rather than by clinical preference. The smallest hold a few hundred liters and are carried by hand for resuscitation or transport, the middle sizes sit on a trolley, and the largest stand nearly a meter tall and are chained to a wall. Manufacturers and national systems name them differently, sometimes by a letter and sometimes by the water capacity in liters, and that capacity is the multiplier that converts pressure into usable gas. Every cylinder must carry its own identity, which means the gas name, the concentration, the batch, the filling pressure, and the date of the last hydraulic pressure test. Color coding of the shoulder and body is a useful first glance, but conventions differ between systems and are no substitute for reading the label.

The top of the cylinder carries the valve, and this is where most handling errors begin. The valve is a metal block screwed into the neck, with a stem that opens and closes the gas path, an outlet port, and a safety disc that bursts if internal pressure rises beyond the design limit, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Large cylinders open with a handwheel and smaller ones with a key or spanner, and the rule is to open slowly, because a sudden blast of high-pressure gas can ignite any trace of oil it meets. A cylinder stored in the cold may read low until it warms, and one left on its side can discharge debris when opened carelessly, so the valve should be closed and the cap replaced before the cylinder is moved. The connection to the regulator is protected by the pin index system, in which two holes on the valve face match two pins on the yoke, and oxygen has its own positions so that a regulator for another gas cannot be seated. The seal is a compressible washer that must be present, intact, and free of grease, because worn pins, removed pins, or a wrongly filled cylinder all defeat the interlock. If a regulator does not seat easily, the operator must stop and find out why rather than forcing it.

The regulator and the flowmeter turn storage into therapy. The regulator uses a diaphragm and a spring to reduce high cylinder pressure to a low working pressure, and a well-made unit does this in two stages so that flow does not drift as the cylinder empties. The high-pressure gauge reads what is left, while a second gauge or the flowmeter reads what is going to the patient. The common flowmeter is a tapered tube with a small ball inside, and the gas lifts the ball to a height proportional to the flow. The ball is read at its top edge, the tube must be held upright and calibrated for oxygen alone, and the setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The duration of a cylinder is calculated. The full contents in liters equals the water capacity in liters multiplied by the filling pressure in bar, or in customary units the pressure in pounds per square inch divided by 14.7 gives the number of atmospheres. A simpler field method uses a cylinder factor, a fixed number belonging to each size, so that minutes remaining equals the gauge pressure in pounds per square inch multiplied by that factor and divided by the flow in liters per minute. A medium cylinder with a factor of about 0.3 and a gauge reading of 2000 pounds per square inch delivering 5 liters per minute would last roughly 120 minutes, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator should write the start time and the flow on the cylinder tag, because the calculation assumes a full cylinder and an accurate flowmeter, and both assumptions deserve suspicion.

Because oxygen supports combustion, the handling rules around cylinders are not decoration. Oxygen does not burn, but it lowers the temperature at which other materials ignite and makes any fire burn hotter and faster. Oil and grease are the classic enemies, and a single fingerprint of lubricant on a valve, a regulator, or a tool can start a fire when gas is released quickly. Smoking, open flames, and electrical sparks must be kept away from every cylinder and every oxygen-enriched surface. Cylinders must be stored upright and secured with a chain or strap, separated from flammable gases such as acetylene or hydrogen, and during transport the valve must be closed and the cap in place. An oxygen-enriched room is one in which clothing, bedding, and hair burn with terrifying speed, so ventilation and the removal of ignition sources matter as much as the equipment.

The piped oxygen system replaces the bedside cylinder with a wall outlet and is the standard of care in any large hospital. The gas comes from a central source, which may be a bulk liquid oxygen tank with its own evaporator, a manifold of large cylinders, or an on-site generating plant, and the source is duplicated so that one failure does not stop the supply. A typical pipeline delivers a working pressure of about 50 pounds per square inch to the terminal units, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The gas travels through copper or stainless steel pipe installed and tested under standards that forbid contamination with oil or debris, and a second source is kept ready to take over automatically or by a simple valve change. The whole system is monitored, because the failure of a pipeline is a silent event until a patient needs oxygen.

The terminal unit at the wall is where the clinician meets the pipeline, and it is built so that the wrong device cannot be plugged in. The outlet is a gas-specific socket, and the connector is keyed by a diameter index safety system that admits only the matching gas. A quick-connect fitting locks with a quarter turn, and the flowmeter hanging below it is usually the same tapered tube with a ball. Some outlets supply air or vacuum as well as oxygen, and the three look similar enough that the index system is the only reliable distinction. The operator must check that the flowmeter is seated, that gas flows when the valve is opened, and that the ball moves freely, with the setting confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The piped system carries its own alarms, and the clinician must know what they mean before they sound. An area alarm panel near the ward entrance and a master alarm at the engineering desk monitor pipeline pressure and, in some systems, oxygen concentration. A low-pressure alarm sounds when the supply falls below the set threshold, and a high-pressure alarm sounds when it rises above the design limit, and both thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic sound is a repeating electronic tone with a flashing indicator, and the correct response is not to silence it but to establish whether patients are receiving gas and to switch to cylinders. The alarm does not always mean the supply has failed, because a closed valve, a leaking terminal unit, or a maintenance isolation can produce the same reading.

Between the pipeline and the cylinder stands the oxygen concentrator, which makes its own oxygen from the air in the room. The active material is a synthetic zeolite, a mineral with a vast internal surface of tiny pores that trap nitrogen molecules in preference to oxygen. A compressor pushes filtered room air into one of two sieve beds until the zeolite is saturated with nitrogen, and the oxygen-rich gas that passes through is collected in a reservoir. While the first bed loads, the second is vented to the atmosphere and releases its nitrogen, and the two beds alternate every few seconds so that the flow never stops. This cycle is called pressure swing adsorption, and its output is not pure oxygen but a stream of about 90 to 96 per cent, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A concentrator is a small factory with filters, moving parts, and its own failure modes, and it earns its place only when it is maintained. The intake filter sits behind the cabinet and collects dust and lint, and a clogged filter reduces flow and raises the working temperature. The sieve beds have a finite life and slowly lose capacity, so the delivered concentration falls before the machine stops entirely. The compressor wears, the cooling fan clogs, and internal tubing can develop a leak that lets the product gas escape. A concentrator also has alarms for low concentration, low flow, power failure, and high temperature, and the exact thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The concentrator is unusually sensitive to its environment, and its great enemies are dust and altitude. Dust clogs the intake filter and contaminates the sieve beds, so a machine used in a dusty setting needs its filter cleaned far more often than the manual suggests. Altitude matters because the concentrator works on the percentage of oxygen it can extract from the air, and although it still produces about 90 per cent oxygen, the total amount the patient receives at a low flow is lower when the air is thin. Heat and humidity shorten the life of the compressor and encourage condensation in the tubing. The tubing itself adds resistance, and a very long line reduces the flow that reaches the patient, so its length and internal diameter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Liquid oxygen is used by large hospitals and by patients who need a portable supply with a high capacity for its weight. Oxygen becomes a pale blue liquid at about minus 183 degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and in that state it occupies a small fraction of the volume of the gas. It is stored in a double-walled vacuum-insulated vessel, and a little is allowed to boil off through a coil so that pressure builds and pushes the gas to the point of use. The bulk tank stands outside the building and connects to the pipeline, and a portable unit can be filled from it for a patient going home. The hazards are cold and concentration, because spilled liquid causes frostbite and the boiling gas enriches the surrounding air, and their maintenance belongs to trained engineering staff rather than the ward.

Once the gas reaches the patient, the delivery device decides how much of it enters the lungs, and the physics divides these devices into two families. Low-flow devices, such as the nasal cannula and the simple face mask, provide less gas than the patient inhales, so the rest is drawn from room air and the inspired concentration depends on how deeply and how fast the patient breathes. High-flow devices, such as the venturi mask and heated high-flow nasal therapy, provide more gas than the patient can inhale, so room air is excluded and the concentration is fixed by the device. This distinction explains why the same flow produces different concentrations in different patients and why a breathless patient may receive less oxygen than the flowmeter suggests. The operator should choose the device by the concentration required rather than by habit, and should confirm every flow and concentration against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The nasal cannula is the most common oxygen delivery device in the world, and it is two soft prongs on a light tube under the nose. Flows of 1 to 6 liters per minute are typical, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the inspired concentration rises from roughly 24 per cent at 1 liter per minute to about 44 per cent at 6 liters per minute. The rule of thumb is that each liter per minute adds about 4 per cent, but the figure varies with the breathing pattern and is only an approximation. The nasopharynx acts as a small reservoir that stores oxygen between breaths, which is why the cannula achieves more than the flow alone suggests. The prongs must point into the nostrils rather than against the septum, and a cannula left kinked under a pillow or a shoulder is a common and invisible cause of desaturation.

The simple face mask covers the nose and mouth and holds a small volume of gas in front of the face, but it has no reservoir and no valves. Flows of 5 to 10 liters per minute are used, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the inspired concentration usually falls between 35 and 60 per cent. The mask must never be run below about 5 liters per minute, because at a low flow the patient re-breathes carbon dioxide collected in the mask and the dead space becomes harmful. The reservoir mask, often called a non-rebreather, adds a soft bag that holds oxygen between breaths, and one-way valves stop exhaled gas from entering it. Flows of 10 to 15 liters per minute are used, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the concentration can exceed 80 per cent when the mask seals well. The bag must be seen to fill before the mask is placed on the face and must not collapse completely, because an empty bag means the patient is pulling room air. The valves are thin plastic flaps that can stick or invert, and a mask whose valves are wet or distorted will not do its job.

The venturi mask solves the problem of variable performance with a physical effect described in the eighteenth century. When gas is forced through a narrow orifice its speed rises and its pressure falls, and the low-pressure jet drags room air in with it, a process called entrainment. The mask has a jet of fixed size and an entrainment port of fixed size, so the ratio of oxygen to air is fixed and the concentration is fixed as long as the total flow exceeds the patient's peak inspiratory flow. The usual jets give concentrations of about 24, 28, 31, 35, 40, and 60 per cent, and each value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator error is to mix parts of different masks, to block the entrainment ports, or to run the device below the minimum flow marked on the jet.

Heated high-flow nasal therapy takes the cannula idea and adds flow, heat, and humidity, and it has become the bridge between simple oxygen and mechanical ventilation. A blender mixes oxygen and air to a chosen concentration, a heater warms the gas to near body temperature, and a humidifier saturates it with water vapor, so flows of up to 60 liters per minute can be tolerated through a soft nasal interface, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Because the flow exceeds the patient's inspiratory demand, the concentration is stable, and the high flow also washes carbon dioxide out of the upper airway and provides a small positive pressure. The device demands care, because the circuit must be drained of condensate, the temperature must be set within the maker's range, and the interface must not injure the nose. Water in the circuit and an overfilled humidifier are the commonest faults.

Humidification and nebulization are the two ancillaries that keep the upper airway from drying and deliver medication to it. A bubble humidifier is a bottle of sterile water that the oxygen passes through on its way to a mask or cannula, and it adds water vapor but very little heat. Heated humidifiers are used with high-flow therapy and with ventilators, and they use a heated plate and a temperature probe to control the water content of the gas. Nebulizer drivers are small compressors, or the oxygen flow itself, and they push gas through a jet that breaks a liquid drug into a mist the patient inhales. All of these share the same consumables, which are the water chamber, the tubing, the mask or mouthpiece, and the filters, and their flow and temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Oxygen is a drug with a dose and a toxicity, and the goal is always the lowest concentration that achieves the target. Prolonged breathing of a high concentration can injure the lung directly, causing chest discomfort, cough, and diffuse damage resembling acute lung injury, and it can wash nitrogen out of the alveoli so that they collapse, a condition called absorption atelectasis. At very high partial pressures, as in a hyperbaric chamber or a diving accident, oxygen can cause central nervous system toxicity with visual changes, twitching, and seizures. In the premature newborn, excessive oxygen can damage the developing retina and cause lifelong visual loss, which is why the target in that group is deliberately narrow. For most adults the target is an arterial oxygen saturation between 94 and 98 per cent, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, with lower targets for some patients who retain carbon dioxide.

Fire is the hazard that makes oxygen different from every other drug, and the rules that prevent it are absolute. Oxygen is an oxidizer rather than a fuel, but a fire in an oxygen-enriched atmosphere burns far hotter and faster, and materials that would normally smolder can flare. Grease, oil, and petroleum jelly must never touch a cylinder valve, a regulator, a flowmeter, or the face of a patient receiving oxygen, and alcohol-based hand rub must dry completely before the hands go near a mask. Smoking and open flames are forbidden wherever oxygen is in use, and electrical equipment must be in good repair, because a spark from a worn plug is enough. The diathermy machine, also called the electrosurgical unit, is a particular danger because it produces sparks and heat, and oxygen should be discontinued for as long as is clinically safe before a procedure near the airway, with the decision confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Static electricity can also ignite a fuel in an enriched atmosphere, so bedding and clothing should not be rubbed near a cylinder.

The common operator errors in oxygen therapy are few, and they are repeated in every hospital. The first is to run out of gas, which happens when no one calculates cylinder duration or checks the gauge at the change of shift. The second is to deliver the wrong concentration, which happens when a low-flow mask is used for a patient who needs a controlled fraction or when the flowmeter is read at the wrong part of the ball. The third is to lose the gas between source and patient, through a kinked tube, a disconnected humidifier, a leaking washer, or a mask sitting on the chin. The fourth is to forget the backup, so that a power failure stops a concentrator, and the fifth is to silence the alarm, which hides the information it was designed to give.

The check that prevents these errors follows the gas from source to patient, and it is repeated before every use and at every shift. The cylinder or wall outlet must be identified as oxygen, the gauge or flowmeter must be read and recorded, and the flow must be set and confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The regulator or flowmeter must be seated without a leak, the tubing must be free of kinks and cracks, and the delivery device must match the concentration required. The humidifier, if used, must hold sterile water and sit below the level of the patient, and the saturation, respiratory rate, and work of breathing must be observed together. The spare cylinder, tubing, and mask must be within reach, and the alarm must be audible and tested if the system has one.

Consumables in oxygen therapy are simple, cheap, and constantly used, and their management is what keeps the therapy safe. Nasal cannulas, simple masks, reservoir masks, venturi masks, and their tubing are usually single-patient items, replaced at the interval the maker and the local protocol specify, and a soiled or cracked device is replaced at once rather than cleaned for reuse. Humidifier chambers and sterile water are single-use, and refilling a chamber rather than replacing it is a common source of infection. The reusable parts, including the regulator, the flowmeter, the cylinder valve, and the concentrator cabinet, are wiped with a cloth dampened with a compatible disinfectant, and the intake filter is cleaned or replaced according to its type. Reusable components meant to be reprocessed must be cleaned first and then disinfected or sterilized by a validated method, with the cycle confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the oxygen system is built from what can be carried, powered, and repaired, and it gives up a great deal. The usual configuration is a portable oxygen concentrator charged by a solar panel during the day and by a battery at night, with a small cylinder as the reserve for resuscitation and transport. The concentrator is lighter and inexhaustible compared with cylinders, but it delivers a limited flow, its concentration falls with altitude and dust, and it stops when the battery is empty. A pulse-dose conserver releases a bolus only when the patient inhales, which stretches the oxygen in a cylinder several times further, but it requires a nose-breathing patient and it fails silently in a mouth breather. Cylinders are refilled by a cascade from a larger supply, and the motorcycle that carries them straps them upright in padded panniers with the valve closed and the cap fitted. The field system demands a maintenance routine that a hospital can delegate and a clinic cannot, with filters cleaned weekly, batteries cycled, tubing inspected, a written log kept, and every setting confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

At the destination the equipment must be assembled in a clean, shaded place, with the concentrator on a hard surface and the tubing kept off the ground. Heat, rough roads, and altitude all raise the pressure inside a cylinder and stress the valve, so a cylinder that has been dropped must be inspected before it is refilled. A carrier that takes two cylinders allows one to be in use and one in reserve, which is the difference between a functioning service and an interrupted one. The field clinician should also carry a self-inflating resuscitation bag as the fallback that works with no gas, no power, and no battery. Every pressure and flow used in this setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the reserve must never be spent on anything but a patient.

To summarize, oxygen therapy is a chain that begins with a source under pressure and ends at the patient's nose, and each link has its own physics, its own consumables, and its own failure. A cylinder stores gas by pressure and is emptied by flow, so its duration must be calculated and its identity, seal, and valve checked. A pipeline delivers gas from a central source through keyed outlets and monitored alarms, and its silence must never be mistaken for its health. A concentrator makes oxygen from room air through a zeolite sieve, it depends on electricity, clean filters, and a realistic flow setting, and a liquid system stores oxygen cold and demands trained handling. The delivery device decides whether the concentration is variable or fixed, and the venturi mask and heated high-flow nasal therapy are the tools of precision. Fire safety and the rules against grease, oil, and sparks apply to every one of these systems, and in the field the same chain is rebuilt from a concentrator, a solar panel, a battery, and a motorcycle with cylinders. Whatever the setting, the discipline is the same: identify the gas, calculate the supply, set and confirm the flow, watch the patient, and keep a reserve ready.

# Chapter 15 — Airway Management

An airway device is any instrument that keeps the path between the outside air and the lungs open, and the whole family follows from one physical fact. The upper airway is a soft, collapsible tube, and in a person who is unconscious or deeply sedated the muscles that hold it open relax, so the tongue falls backward against the throat. Air must travel from the higher pressure of the atmosphere toward the lower pressure the chest creates, and no amount of oxygen at the mask will help if that path is pinched shut. Every device here holds soft tissue out of the way, seals over the entrance to the voice box, or passes a tube through the vocal cords. The most feared event in this field is a tube placed in the food pipe while the team believes it is in the windpipe, and every habit described here exists to prevent that error. The pressures, volumes, sizes, and temperatures named below must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To use these devices well, the operator carries a short map of the airway in mind. Air enters the nose or mouth, crosses the pharynx, and reaches the larynx, where the epiglottis, a leaf-shaped flap, guards the entrance to the trachea. The vocal cords lie just below, and beyond them the trachea divides into the two main bronchi at a ridge called the carina. Behind the larynx lies the esophagus, normally closed and easy to enter by mistake, and its position is the reason a tube can pass smoothly and still be in the wrong place. In adults the distance from the teeth to the vocal cords is roughly 15 centimeters, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A tube advanced too far enters the right main bronchus more often than the left.

The simplest device is the oropharyngeal airway, a rigid curved plastic channel that follows the curve of the tongue and holds it forward. It is made in a series of lengths, and the correct one is chosen by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, a measurement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The principle is mechanical, because the device occupies the space the tongue would otherwise fill, so the tongue cannot fall back and air passes around the channel. A device that is too short pushes the tongue backward and worsens the obstruction, and one that is too long can press on the epiglottis or enter the larynx and provoke spasm. It is inserted along the roof of the mouth and rotated into place. It holds tissue but does not seal, so it offers no protection against vomit or blood.

The oropharyngeal airway is the wrong device for a patient who still has protective reflexes, because a conscious or lightly sedated person will gag, retch, and may vomit or develop a spasm of the vocal cords. The operator must judge the depth of unconsciousness before inserting it, and the common error is to force it into a patient who is only partly unresponsive. The device does not prevent aspiration, so a patient wearing one still needs to lie on the side or be watched for vomiting. Cleaning is by hand washing followed by high-level disinfection or sterilization, and the temperature and duration of that cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant is a single rigid airway carried in a bag, and its danger is that one size must serve every patient.

The nasopharyngeal airway is a soft tube passed through a nostril into the pharynx, and it is tolerated by patients who would never accept the rigid oral device. Its principle is that it slips behind the tongue and holds the soft palate and the tongue base forward from inside the air column, and because it is soft it moves with the tissues. It is measured from the tip of the nostril to the tragus of the ear, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it is chosen by internal diameter or by length in the French scale. It must be lubricated with a water-soluble gel and advanced gently along the floor of the nostril with a slight rotation, never forced, because the lining of the nose bleeds easily. The contraindications are a suspected fracture of the base of the skull, a severe bleeding disorder, and a blocked or deformed nasal passage.

Ignoring those contraindications is the common operator error, and it can drive the tube into the cranial cavity through a fractured skull base or start a hemorrhage in a patient whose blood does not clot. Petroleum jelly must never be used as the lubricant, because it damages many plastics, so a water-soluble gel is correct, a point that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The tube is secured at the nostril with a manufactured flange and tape, and the position is rechecked after every movement of the patient. In the field the device is often improvised by cutting a softened endotracheal tube to the measured length, a practice that demands a smooth cut and the same lubricant. The improvisation gives up the flange and the exact sizing, and it demands that the cut end be inspected for sharp edges.

The supraglottic devices sit above the larynx and solve the airway problem without ever showing the operator the vocal cords. The best known is the laryngeal mask airway, a wide tube whose end carries a small elliptical mask with an inflatable rim that sits over the entrance to the larynx and forms a low-pressure seal around it. The principle is a seal rather than a plug, because the inflated rim presses against the pharynx and closes the space around the laryngeal inlet, so positive pressure from a bag reaches the lungs. It is made in sizes numbered from 1 to 5, matched roughly to the weight of the patient, and both the sizes and the weights must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The mask is deflated, lubricated, and slid along the hard palate until resistance is felt, and only then is the rim inflated with the recommended volume of air. The seal is limited, and if the pressure needed to move air rises above the seal pressure, often around 20 centimeters of water, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, gas leaks out instead of entering the lungs.

The characteristic failure of a supraglottic device is therefore a poor seal, and it has two sounds, an audible leak around the mask as the bag is squeezed and a gurgling of gas entering the stomach that distends it and raises the risk of vomiting. The common operator error is to overinflate the rim in an attempt to stop the leak, which presses harder against the pharyngeal tissues without improving the seal. The device does not protect the airway against regurgitated stomach contents, so it is a rescue tool and a bridge rather than a substitute for a tube with a sealed cuff in a patient at high risk of aspiration. A rising airway pressure alarm on the ventilation device, if one is in use, is often the first sign that the seal has failed, and the second sign is a falling oxygen saturation. The operator's response is to stop squeezing, recheck the position and the size, and prepare the next device rather than to add more air.

Several refinements of the laryngeal mask airway are now standard in hospital practice. A second-generation device adds a separate channel that reaches down to the esophagus, so that any regurgitated fluid can be diverted away from the larynx and vented, and it adds a bite block that keeps the tube from being occluded by the teeth. An intubating version is shaped so that an endotracheal tube can be passed through it and guided toward the vocal cords, which makes it a useful bridge when the cords cannot be seen. Reusable versions are made of silicone and are sterilized by steam at 134 degrees Celsius for a cycle whose temperature and duration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the rim is checked for cracks before every use. The field argument for this family is strong, because it needs less skill and less equipment than passing a tube through the cords.

A laryngoscope is the instrument that turns a hidden opening into a visible one, and its principle is direct mechanical displacement. The operator places a rigid blade in the mouth, advances it along the tongue, and lifts the handle upward and forward, which pulls the tongue and the jaw forward and brings the larynx into a straight line of sight. A curved blade is placed into the vallecula, the pocket between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, and lifting there pulls the epiglottis aside indirectly. A straight blade is placed directly under the epiglottis and lifts it, which is often preferred in infants and in patients with a long, floppy epiglottis. The light at the tip comes either from a small bulb on the blade or from optical fibers fed by the handle, and the handle holds the batteries. The most common equipment failure at the worst possible moment is a dead battery or a loose bulb, so the light is tested before every attempt and spare batteries and a spare handle travel with the set.

The characteristic hazard of the laryngoscope is mechanical rather than electrical, because the upper front teeth are the fulcrum a hurried operator instinctively uses. The blade must be used as a lever against the jaw, never against the teeth, and the common operator error is to pry backward on the handle when the view is poor, which chips or dislodges teeth that can then fall into the airway. The video laryngoscope removes the need for a straight line of sight by placing a small camera and a light at the tip of the blade and showing the image on a screen. It improves the view in many difficult patients and reduces the force applied to the teeth, but it adds a screen, a battery, and a cable, and it fails when the battery is flat or the lens is coated with blood. The operator must look at the screen rather than into the mouth, and that change of habit is itself a common error during the first attempts.

The endotracheal tube is the definitive airway, and its principle is simple, because a flexible tube passed between the vocal cords into the trachea creates a sealed conduit through which the lungs can be inflated and which is protected from the contents of the stomach. The tube is sized by its internal diameter in millimeters, and adult sizes commonly run from 7.0 to 8.0, with smaller sizes for children chosen by age, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Around the lower end sits a cuff, a thin balloon inflated through a small channel to a pilot balloon outside the mouth, and the cuff seals the trachea against the tube. Modern cuffs are high in volume and low in pressure, and the recommended cuff pressure is commonly between 20 and 30 centimeters of water, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A small side opening near the tip, called a Murphy eye, allows air to pass even if the main opening is pressed against the tracheal wall.

Three simple tools make the difference between a failed and a successful attempt. The stylet is a malleable metal rod inserted into the tube to give it a chosen shape, and its tip must stay inside the tube, because a projecting wire can cut or perforate the airway. The bougie is a long, thin, flexible introducer with a curved tip, and it is passed through the cords when the view is poor; its entry into the trachea is often felt as clicks as the tip rides over the cartilage rings, and the tube is then threaded over it. A curved intubating forceps, traditionally called a Magill forceps, guides a tube or a nasal tube through the cords and removes a foreign body, and it works because its long curve follows the pharynx while the operator's hand stays outside the line of sight. A tube exchanger is a long hollow catheter passed through an existing tube before that tube is removed, so the new tube can be railroaded over it and the airway is not lost in between. The common error with all of these tools is to use force when the view is poor, which drives the instrument into tissue instead of guiding it.

Confirming that the tube is in the trachea is the single most important act in this chapter, and no single sign is trustworthy on its own. Listening over both sides of the chest and over the stomach is traditional, and it is unreliable because breath sounds can be conducted from one side to the other and because a tube in the esophagus can produce sounds that imitate them. Watching the chest rise, seeing the tube mist with each breath, and listening for air escaping are useful supporting signs, and none of them settles the question. The reference standard is the detection of carbon dioxide in the exhaled gas, because carbon dioxide comes from the body and is present in every breath from the lungs, while the esophagus contains none. A small colorimetric detector clipped between the tube and the bag changes color in the presence of carbon dioxide, and its color change over several breaths must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A capnograph draws that concentration as a waveform against time, and a sustained waveform across many breaths is the most reliable confirmation available outside direct vision of the cords.

The carbon dioxide detector can lie in both directions, and knowing how it lies is part of using it. A very low reading, or none at all, may occur during cardiac arrest, when almost no blood reaches the lungs, so a negative result in a patient with no circulation does not prove that the tube is misplaced. A false positive can occur when the tube has just been in the esophagus after the patient swallowed air containing carbon dioxide, and the color then fades over a few breaths. The rule that protects the patient is to keep watching the waveform or the color for several breaths and to recheck after every movement, after every transfer, and after any sudden change in the patient's condition. Any loss of the carbon dioxide signal is treated as a lost airway until proven otherwise, and the alarm on the monitor is the falling oxygen saturation, which is a late and dangerous sign of a misplaced tube.

A tracheostomy tube is placed directly through the front of the neck into the trachea, and it exists for patients who need a secure airway for weeks or months or who have an obstruction above the larynx. The tube has an outer cannula that stays in the trachea, an inner cannula that can be lifted out for cleaning, a cuff on some designs, a flange that rests against the skin, and ties that hold the whole assembly in place. The inner cannula is removed and cleaned on a schedule, commonly every eight hours, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because dried secretions narrow the tube silently and can block it completely. The cuff pressure is checked with a gauge and kept in the same low range as an endotracheal cuff, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The stoma is cleaned and dressed, and a spare tube of the same size and one size smaller must live at the bedside.

Tracheostomy care is a routine that conceals an emergency, and the operator's checks are the defense. The obturator, the rounded guide used to insert the tube, must be at the bedside, because without it a replacement tube cannot be threaded back through the stoma. A source of suction, a manual resuscitation bag, and oxygen must be immediately available, and the alarm that matters most is the patient's own breathing, because a blocked inner cannula announces itself as increasing effort and noisy breathing rather than as a machine alarm. The common operator error is to clean the inner cannula less often than the schedule requires because the patient looks comfortable, and the second common error is to change the ties without a second person holding the tube. A late, brisk bleed from the stoma is an emergency because a fistula can form between the trachea and a major artery.

The surgical airway is the last resort, and it exists for the situation in which the upper airway cannot be opened, a tube cannot be passed, and the patient cannot be ventilated by any other means. The principle is to enter the airway below the vocal cords through the cricothyroid membrane, a small, relatively bloodless sheet of tissue stretched between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. The operator identifies the membrane in the midline of the neck, stabilizes the larynx with one hand, and either passes a needle, a guidewire, and a dilator to make a passage for a small tube, or makes a short incision and inserts a small cuffed tube directly. The tube used is much smaller than an oral tube, commonly 6.0 millimeters internal diameter, a size that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazards are bleeding, damage to the cartilages, and placement outside the trachea, and in small children the membrane is tiny and the procedure is far more dangerous. The common operator error is delay, because the decision is postponed while other attempts continue and the patient's oxygen falls.

The consumables that surround these devices matter as much as the devices themselves, and they are the items that run out first in a busy unit. Gloves, eye protection, and a gown protect the operator from the blood and secretions that accompany every airway attempt, a working suction unit with a rigid catheter is essential before any attempt begins, and oxygen tubing, a mask, and a self-inflating bag with a reservoir feed the patient during and between attempts. A tube of the chosen size, a syringe for the cuff, a water-soluble lubricant, a stylet, a bougie, a carbon dioxide detector, and a stethoscope complete the set, together with tape or a tie to secure whatever is placed. Every one of these items has an expiry date, and every setting, pressure, and alarm threshold associated with them must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Contaminated tubes, suction catheters, and gloves are discarded as clinical waste, and hand hygiene before and after every contact remains the simplest and most effective measure in the room.

Reprocessing the reusable parts is where cross-contamination is prevented or allowed. Laryngoscope blades and handles are wiped free of visible soil, cleaned, and then disinfected or sterilized, and the cycle, the temperature, and the concentration of the disinfectant must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A common and costly error is to immerse a blade still wet with disinfectant into the handle, because the fluid runs into the battery compartment, corrodes the contacts, and destroys the light that the next patient will need. The blade and the handle are separated before cleaning, the batteries are removed and checked, and the handle is wiped rather than soaked. Reusable supraglottic devices are washed, inspected for cracks and leaks, and sterilized by steam at 134 degrees Celsius for a cycle whose temperature and time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Single-use tubes, stylets, suction catheters, and detectors are discarded after each patient, and no amount of cleaning makes them safe to reuse.

Before any airway is managed, the operator performs a check that is short, spoken, and systematic. Suction is switched on and tested against the hand, oxygen is flowing and the reservoir of the bag is full, and a bag and mask of the right size are assembled and squeezed once to confirm the valves move. The laryngoscope light is clicked on and the brightness is judged, spare batteries and a spare handle are within reach, and a tube of the expected size and one size smaller are checked by inflating the cuff and watching the pilot balloon hold its shape. A stylet is prepared but kept inside the tube, and a bougie, a lubricant, and a carbon dioxide detector are laid out with a syringe for the cuff. Intravenous access, monitoring, and the drugs for sedation and paralysis are confirmed with the team, and the plan for a failed attempt is stated aloud, including a limited number of attempts, commonly three, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Pre-oxygenation before the attempt buys time, and the operator must recognize the features that predict difficulty, including a short neck, a large tongue, and limited mouth opening.

Airway devices fail in a small number of recognizable ways, and each has a signature the listener can learn. A tube can be obstructed by thick secretions, by a kink at the teeth, by a cuff that has herniated over the tip, or by the patient biting it closed, and the sign is a sudden rise in the pressure needed to move air together with a fall in oxygen saturation. A tube can become dislodged outward until the cuff sits at the cords, and the sign is a new leak and a change in the sound of the breathing. There can be a leak from a torn cuff, announced by the loss of the seal and by a pilot balloon that will not stay inflated. The bag can fail to refill because a valve is stuck, and the mask can fail to seal because it is the wrong size or the patient has no teeth. The most dangerous failure of all is unrecognized misplacement, which shows no mechanical sign and is caught only by the carbon dioxide detector and repeated examination.

The field decision is which of these devices earns its place in a bag carried up a mountain, and the answer is driven by weight, volume, power, and the skill of the person who will use it. The reliable core is a self-inflating bag with masks, a small set of oral and nasal airways, two or three sizes of supraglottic device, a small number of endotracheal tubes, a laryngoscope with spare batteries or a battery-powered video device that can be recharged from a portable power bank, a carbon dioxide detector, and a manual suction pump. A cricothyrotomy kit is carried by those trained to use it, and a spare tube and a means of securing it are always included. Where no device is available the operator still has the hands and the position, because a head tilt with a chin lift or a jaw thrust pulls the tongue forward and the recovery position keeps the tongue and vomit away from the opening. What this kit gives up is the range of a hospital trolley, the monitoring, the humidification, and the sterile processing, and what it demands instead is that every item be checked before departure and that the carrier maintain the skill to use it. A device carried for years without practice is a liability rather than a safety net, and a clinician who once intubated regularly may go months without passing a tube, so scheduled practice on a model matters as much as the equipment list.

To summarize, airway management is a family of devices built on three physical ideas, holding the soft tissue of the upper airway open, sealing over the larynx without seeing it, and passing a tube through the vocal cords to replace the upper airway. The oral and nasal airways hold the tongue forward but seal nothing, the supraglottic devices seal over the larynx and tolerate only limited pressure, and the endotracheal tube seals inside the trachea and remains the definitive airway when it is placed correctly. Around these devices sits a set of consumables, a laryngoscope whose light and batteries must be tested, and a carbon dioxide detector whose signal is the only reliable proof of placement. Tracheostomy tubes and surgical airway kits extend the same principles to the neck and to the last resort, each with its own hazards and its own checks. In the field, the choice is governed by weight, power, and skill rather than by ambition, and the kit that is carried must be the kit that is practiced. Every size, pressure, volume, temperature, and alarm threshold in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a number on a package is not a substitute for the number in the protocol.

# Chapter 16 — Ventilation

Breathing is a mechanical event before it is a chemical one, and every machine in this chapter reproduces that event from outside the body. A healthy person breathes because the diaphragm drops and the rib cage lifts, lowering the pressure inside the chest below the pressure of the atmosphere, so gas flows down that gradient into the alveoli and expiration follows as the elastic lung recoils. The work of breathing is the price of moving gas against the resistance of the airways and the stiffness of the lung and chest wall, and illness raises that price until the patient cannot pay it. A ventilator is any device that takes over or supports that work, and the manual bag, the transport machine, and the intensive care unit ventilator are all members of one family. Pressure, volume, flow, and time are the four quantities behind every setting on these machines.

A stiff lung and chest wall need a large pressure to move a small volume, which is called compliance, while narrow airways force gas to be pushed harder for the same flow, which is called resistance. Compliance and resistance together set a time constant, so a lung with a long time constant needs more time to exhale before the next breath. A ventilator can control the volume it delivers and let the pressure rise as it will, or control the pressure and let the volume follow, and these are the two fundamental strategies of mechanical breathing. A fixed volume pushed into a stiff lung raises the pressure, and a fixed pressure into a stiff lung lowers the volume, so the same dial setting produces different results in different patients and the patient must be watched rather than the number.

The self-inflating bag is the most important breathing device in the world, because it works when everything else has stopped. It is a bag of flexible rubber or silicone that springs back into shape after it is squeezed, and that elastic recoil is its physical principle, because the re-expanding bag draws gas in, which the operator then pushes through a one-way valve into the patient. Sizes follow the patient: a small bag of about 250 milliliters for a newborn, a medium bag of about 500 milliliters for a child, and a large bag of about 1600 milliliters for an adult, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The bag needs no compressed gas and no electricity, and it delivers room air to a patient whose lungs have stopped moving, but a small bag used on an adult will not ventilate adequately and a large bag used on a newborn can injure the lung.

Three parts of the self-inflating bag fail in their own ways. The patient valve is a one-way valve at the mask or tube end that lets gas into the patient and directs exhaled gas out through a side port, so if it sticks or is assembled wrongly the patient receives little or nothing. The inlet valve opens as the bag refills so that fresh gas enters and exhaled gas does not return, and a torn or dirty inlet valve lets the patient rebreathe carbon dioxide. The reservoir is a soft bag or corrugated sleeve behind the inlet valve that holds a reserve of oxygen, and the oxygen tubing feeds it from a cylinder or wall outlet at a flow of 10 to 15 liters per minute, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, so a bag run without its reservoir delivers only room air.

Before use the operator should squeeze it with the patient port occluded and watch for the valve to move, listen for the leak of a cracked bag, and confirm that the reservoir fills. The common error is to hold the mask loosely against the face so that most of the gas escapes around the seal, and the correct technique is to lift the jaw forward with one hand while the other holds the mask down and squeezes. Squeezing too fast and too deeply drives gas into the stomach, causes vomiting and aspiration, and raises the pressure in the chest until the blood returning to the heart falls. A bag can also be reassembled with its valves reversed by a well-meaning cleaner, so a reprocessed bag must be tested before it returns to the trolley, and reusable bags are washed, disinfected to the highest level appropriate to their material, dried, and stored open.

The flow-inflating bag looks like a self-inflating bag and behaves completely differently, and knowing the difference is a mark of competence. It is soft and thin-walled, with no elastic recoil, so it does not refill by itself; it stays partly inflated only while gas flows into it continuously, and the operator controls the pressure by how firmly the patient port is occluded with the thumb. Squeezing raises the pressure, releasing the thumb lets the lung empty, and the feel of the bag tells the operator how well the lung is filling, which is why it is prized in anesthesia for children and for patients with poor compliance. It can supply continuous positive airway pressure by itself, but if its gas supply fails the bag deflates and the patient receives nothing, and the common error is to wait for it to refill on its own.

The transport ventilator carries ventilation between the intensive care unit, the imaging suite, the operating room, and another hospital. Its gas may come from small cylinders of compressed oxygen and compressed air, or from a turbine that spins at high speed and draws the breath from room air while blending oxygen into it, which frees the machine from a compressed air supply and lets it run on a battery and a single oxygen cylinder. Battery life is measured in hours rather than days, with a typical endurance of 2 to 6 hours, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it falls as the oxygen concentration, the positive end-expiratory pressure, and the minute volume rise. Its modes are deliberately few, usually volume control, pressure control, and a spontaneous or continuous positive airway pressure mode, without the fine synchrony of a full intensive care machine. The settings for tidal volume, respiratory rate, positive end-expiratory pressure, and inspired oxygen must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and rechecked after every move.

In a moving ambulance the flow sensor can drift, the circuit can disconnect at a hidden joint, and the oxygen cylinder can empty faster than the gauge suggests because the machine draws a higher flow than the planned minute volume. The characteristic alarms of the transport ventilator are the high-pressure alarm when the circuit kinks against a stretcher rail, the low-pressure or disconnect alarm when a fitting separates, and the low-battery alarm that gives only a short warning before the machine stops. The operator must test the machine with a test lung before leaving, confirm that the alarm is audible above the engine, and carry a self-inflating bag and a spare cylinder as the guaranteed fallback. The common error is to trust the display during the move instead of checking chest movement, oxygen saturation, and exhaled carbon dioxide, so a transport begun without this discipline leaves the patient watched by no reliable observer.

The intensive care unit ventilator is a life-support device of the same rank as a dialysis machine, and it deserves to be understood as a system rather than a box. Gas arrives from the wall pipeline as oxygen and as medical air, and a blender mixes them to the chosen fraction of inspired oxygen; valves then regulate flow, an inspiratory sensor measures the volume on its way to the patient, and an expiratory valve and a second sensor measure the gas coming back. The breath is generated by a piston, a bellows, a compressor with proportional valves, or a turbine, and most intensive care unit ventilators have an internal battery that allows 30 to 60 minutes of continued ventilation during a power failure, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The gas supply, the electricity, the battery, and the alarm system are all part of the therapy, and the machine must be calibrated and self-tested at intervals set by its maker.

The modes of ventilation are the rules by which the machine decides when to give a breath and how large it should be, and their names describe the rule rather than the disease. In assist-control mode the machine delivers a full breath at a set rate and also delivers one whenever the patient triggers it, so the patient can increase the rate but cannot reduce the size of the breath. In volume control the machine pushes a fixed tidal volume at a set flow over a set time, and the pressure rises or falls as the resistance and compliance of the lung dictate; a typical adult setting is 6 to 8 milliliters per kilogram of predicted body weight, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. In pressure control the machine holds a fixed pressure above the baseline for a set time, and the volume delivered depends on the patient's lung, so a leak or a stiff lung produces a smaller breath without any change on the dial. The respiratory rate is set between about 10 and 20 breaths per minute in a typical adult, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the fraction of inspired oxygen is set to the lowest value that achieves the target oxygen saturation.

Two further modes let the patient do more of the work and are used to separate a patient from the machine. Synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation delivers a set number of full breaths, each synchronized to the patient's own effort so that the machine does not fight the patient, and between them the patient may breathe spontaneously. Pressure support adds a fixed boost to every spontaneous breath, and its level is usually adjusted between 5 and 20 centimeters of water, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Positive end-expiratory pressure holds a baseline pressure in the airway at the end of expiration so that the alveoli do not collapse, and it is commonly started at 5 centimeters of water and adjusted upward, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. These modes demand a reliable respiratory drive, so they are not used in a deeply sedated or paralyzed patient, and the operator error is to choose a mode by habit rather than by the patient's effort, which produces a patient who fights the machine.

Three pressures inside a ventilated lung matter more than all the others. The peak inspiratory pressure is the highest reached during a breath, the plateau pressure is held briefly when flow stops and reflects the stretch of the alveoli, and the positive end-expiratory pressure is the baseline remaining at the end of expiration. A plateau pressure above 30 centimeters of water is associated with injury to the lung, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the difference between the plateau pressure and the positive end-expiratory pressure, called the driving pressure, is kept as low as the patient allows. When a patient breathes rapidly and the lung has a long time constant, gas can be trapped and the end-expiratory pressure can rise above the set value, a condition called auto-positive end-expiratory pressure, which reduces the blood returning to the heart and lowers the blood pressure, and the high-pressure alarm is the signature of this problem.

Non-invasive ventilation supports breathing without a tube in the trachea, and its physics is the physics of a splint. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers a single steady pressure throughout the breath, usually set between 4 and 15 centimeters of water, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and that pressure holds the small airways and alveoli open, reduces the work of breathing, and can keep an obstructed upper airway from collapsing during sleep. The interface decides the success of the therapy: a well-fitted nasal mask, an oronasal mask, a full-face mask, or a helmet, chosen for the patient's face and for the pressure required. A leak at the edge of a mask is not a small nuisance, because the machine cannot distinguish the gas that leaks from the gas the patient receives, so the pressure and the volume at the patient fall silently, and the common error is to tighten the straps until the skin breaks down.

Bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP) adds a second pressure to the idea of CPAP, and that second pressure is what makes it a ventilator. The higher pressure, called the inspiratory positive airway pressure, helps the breath enter, and the lower pressure, called the expiratory positive airway pressure, keeps the airway open during expiration, so the difference between them is the amount of support the patient receives.
