Typical settings are an inspiratory pressure between 8 and 20 centimeters of water and an expiratory pressure between 4 and 10 centimeters of water, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and because the patient triggers every breath the mode is comfortable and is widely used for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and for pulmonary edema. The hazards are those of CPAP and are worse, including a leaking mask, a patient who vomits into a sealed interface, and a stomach distended by gas, and a patient who is drowsy or not improving within the first hour needs reassessment for an invasive tube.

The circuit is the set of tubes that carries gas from the machine to the patient and back, and its design has clinical consequences. A dual-limb circuit has a separate inspiratory limb and expiratory limb joined at a Y-piece, with one-way valves that keep the two streams apart, and it allows the exhaled volume to be measured accurately. A single-limb circuit carries gas to the patient and relies on a deliberate leak at the mask or an exhalation valve near the patient to let gas out, and it is lighter and easier for non-invasive ventilation but less precise for monitoring. The tube is corrugated plastic that can stretch, kink, or disconnect, and its expiratory limb collects water as the warm humidified gas cools, so the circuit must be positioned so that condensate drains away from the airway and replaced at the interval the maker and the local protocol specify.

A ventilator delivers dry gas, and the nose and upper airway that normally warm and moisten inspired air are bypassed by the tube, so humidity must be added. The heated humidifier passes the gas over a chamber of sterile water on a heated plate, and a temperature probe at the patient end controls the plate so that the gas arrives warm and saturated; the usual target is a temperature near 37 degrees Celsius at the airway, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The alternative is a heat and moisture exchanger, a small cartridge of foam or paper between the tube and the circuit that captures heat and water from the exhaled gas and returns them to the next breath, and it needs no power and no water but adds resistance and dead space. The heated humidifier risks a burn to the airway if the probe fails, and the exchanger risks blockage when secretions dry inside it, so water in the circuit, a dry chamber, and a cartridge left beyond its rated life are three of the most preventable faults in ventilation.

Filters sit at the boundary between the patient and the machine and do two jobs at once, protecting the patient from the machine and the machine from the patient. A mechanical filter is a dense mat of fibers that traps particles and microorganisms, and an electrostatic filter uses a charged medium to attract particles too small to be caught mechanically. A filter in the inspiratory limb protects the patient, while a filter in the expiratory limb, or at the expiratory valve, protects the machine and the ward, and in a patient with a transmissible respiratory infection the expiratory filter is the single most important infection control measure in the circuit. Filters have a rated life measured in hours or days, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a wet, blocked, reused, or autoclaved filter is no longer a filter, so every filter should be inspected at the start of each shift.

The alarms of a ventilator are its language, and every one names a specific physical event rather than a vague malfunction. The high-pressure alarm sounds when the pressure in the circuit rises above the set threshold, and it usually means a kink, a blocked tube, secretions, a cough, or a stiffening lung, while the low-pressure or disconnect alarm sounds when the pressure or volume falls below the threshold and means a leak, a separated circuit, a displaced tube, or a patient who has stopped triggering the machine. The apnea alarm reports that the patient has stopped breathing for longer than the set interval, usually 15 to 30 seconds, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the inspired oxygen concentration alarm, the power failure alarm, and the battery alarm each report a different failure whose threshold must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic operator error is to silence an alarm without looking at the patient, so the correct habit is to go to the patient first, check the chest and the circuit, and then read the screen.

At the extreme end of respiratory support stands extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, a technology that removes gas exchange from the lung altogether. Blood is drained from a large vein, pumped through a membrane oxygenator that adds oxygen and removes carbon dioxide across a thin permeable film, warmed, and returned to the patient, so that the lung can rest while it heals or while a transplant is arranged. The circuit needs a pump, an oxygenator, a heat exchanger, large cannulae, and a supply of oxygen, and the patient usually needs continuous anticoagulation to keep the circuit from clotting. The infrastructure it demands is the real subject: a trained perfusion team at the bedside continuously, a supply of blood products, a laboratory that can measure clotting within minutes, a protected power supply, and a spare circuit ready to be exchanged, with blood flow rates of 2 to 5 liters per minute in adults that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A ventilator that is not maintained is a ventilator that will fail at the worst moment, and its maintenance is mostly a matter of consumables and of checking what wears. The breathing circuit, the humidifier chamber, the heat and moisture exchanger, the filters, the flow sensors, the expiratory valve membrane, the oxygen sensor, and the internal battery all have a limited life, and each has a replacement interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Flow sensors are delicate and are damaged by water, secretions, and rough handling, so a sensor that has been dropped or allowed to get wet must be recalibrated or replaced, and the internal battery ages quietly and may hold only a fraction of its rated time after a few years. The exterior, the screen, and the trolley are wiped with a compatible disinfectant, the intake filter is cleaned or changed on schedule, and the compressor, the valves, and the internal tubing belong to the biomedical technician, whose service intervals are set by the maker and recorded in the equipment register.

The pre-use check of a ventilator is a fixed sequence that follows the gas from the wall to the patient, and it takes only a few minutes when it is done in the same order every time. The operator confirms that the machine is plugged into the correct outlet, that the gas hoses are connected to oxygen and to medical air and not crossed, that the cylinder reserve is full, and that the internal battery is charged, and then inspects the circuit for cracks, for a secure connection at every joint, and for a water trap that is empty and correctly positioned. The machine is run through its self-test with a test lung attached, and the operator watches for a leak, for an accurate delivered volume, and for the alarm to sound when the test lung is squeezed or removed. The alarms are tested deliberately, because an alarm that cannot be made to sound will not sound when it matters, and the thresholds and the settings are checked against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use and against the written order for the patient.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the ventilator is a different animal, and the difference is measured in what it cannot do. The usual field machine is a compact turbine or compressor-driven device in a padded case, powered by a rechargeable battery and a solar panel, with a single gas inlet for oxygen enrichment and no dependence on a compressed air pipeline. It gives up the precise flow sensing, the fine synchrony, the full alarm set, and the control of humidity that a hospital machine provides, and it typically offers only volume control, pressure control, and a spontaneous or continuous positive airway pressure mode. Its oxygen consumption is often higher than the operator expects, so a cylinder that would last hours on a hospital machine may last a fraction of that time, and its battery life depends on the mode, the pressure, and the temperature, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When the field ventilator is absent or has failed, the fallback is the manual bag, and around it a set of simpler supports a clinic can build. CPAP can be improvised for a newborn with a bubble circuit, in which the expiratory limb of a nasal interface is placed under a measured depth of sterile water so that the depth sets the pressure: a depth of 5 centimeters of water gives about 5 centimeters of water of pressure, a relationship that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The oxygen source may be a concentrator, whose limited flow must be shared with the circuit, and the interface is a short pair of nasal prongs that must not block the nose, while the circuit demands a steady supply of sterile water and a person who watches the chest and the bubble pattern continuously because the system has no alarms of its own. For an older child or an adult, a tight-fitting mask with a controlled leak and a continuous flow from a concentrator can provide a crude CPAP, but the pressure is unknown and the choice between a machine and a manual bag is often settled by the state of the battery.

The manual bag is what remains when everything else fails, and it is the one ventilator that has never needed electricity, a compressor, or a service contract. Its discipline is simple to state and hard to perform: the operator holds the mask with a proper seal, lifts the jaw, squeezes at a rate of about 10 to 12 breaths per minute for an adult, a rate that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and watches the chest rise with each squeeze rather than the bag. The volume delivered is judged by the visible chest movement and the feel of the bag, because a bag has no display and no flow sensor, and the common error is to squeeze harder than the lung can accept, so two rescuers and a change of operator every few minutes keep the quality of the breaths from falling. In a prolonged resuscitation the operator should watch for the stomach filling with gas, for a chest that rises on one side only, and for an oxygen saturation that fails to improve, because the manual bag is also the correct answer during a ventilator failure.

Maintenance in the field is a routine built from what is available, and it is the difference between a machine that lasts and a machine that becomes furniture. Filters are washed or replaced on the maker's schedule, batteries are cycled and stored charged, the circuit is inspected for cracks before every use, and the machine is protected from dust with a cover when it is not running. Cleaning follows the same principles everywhere: the external surfaces and the reusable patient interface are cleaned first to remove organic material, then disinfected with a compatible product, and then dried, while single-use items are discarded rather than reprocessed. Reusable components that are meant to be sterilized must be reprocessed by a validated method, with the cycle confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the written log of checks, faults, and repairs is the only way an absent engineer can understand what has been happening.

The hazards of mechanical ventilation are grouped around pressure, volume, oxygen, infection, and power. Too much pressure or too much volume injures the lung and can rupture it, producing air around the lung or in the chest wall, while too much oxygen over days injures the lung and, in a premature newborn, damages the retina, so the fraction of inspired oxygen is lowered as soon as the oxygen saturation allows. A patient who lies ventilated with a tube in place is at risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia, which is reduced by hand hygiene, by keeping the head of the bed raised, by oral care, and by avoiding unnecessary circuit changes. A circuit that disconnects, a tube that is displaced, a battery that empties, and a gas supply that fails are the mechanical emergencies, and the common operator errors repeat across every setting: the wrong mode, an alarm silenced, a humidifier run dry, a mask strapped too tight, and a bag squeezed too hard.

To summarize, ventilation is the replacement or support of the work of breathing, and every device that does it manages pressure, volume, flow, and time. The self-inflating bag turns the elastic recoil of a rubber bag into a breath that needs no gas and no power, while the flow-inflating bag trades that independence for a controllable pressure that demands a continuous supply. The transport ventilator buys portability by giving up modes, precision, and endurance, and its battery and gas supply must be planned before the journey rather than discovered on the way. The intensive care unit ventilator is a system of blender, valves, sensors, circuit, humidifier, filters, and alarms, and CPAP and BIPAP support the breath through an interface whose fit decides the outcome. In the field the same tasks are met with a rugged machine, a bubble circuit, a solar panel, and a manual bag, and the manual bag is never obsolete. Whatever the setting, the discipline is identical: confirm every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, check the whole chain from gas supply to chest movement, watch the patient rather than the dial, and keep a hand-ventilation plan ready for the moment the machine stops.

# Chapter 17 — Suction, Nebulizers, and Chest Drainage

Three families of equipment share this chapter because they share one physical idea, which is that gas and liquid move from a place of higher pressure to a place of lower pressure. Suction lowers the pressure at the tip of a tube below the pressure of the room, so the atmosphere pushes air, blood, vomit, or secretions into the tube. A nebulizer drives a gas through a narrow opening and uses that fast stream to tear a liquid drug into a mist that the patient's own breath carries into the airway. Chest drainage restores a one-way path for air or fluid to leave the pleural space, where the pressure is normally a little below atmospheric pressure. Each system is described twice, first in its hospital form with pipelines and single-use consumables, and then in its field form, where the work is done with a hand pump, a bottle, and sterile water.

Suction is not a force that pulls material toward a machine. It is the removal of gas from a closed space so that the pressure inside falls, after which the higher pressure outside pushes whatever lies at the opening into the tube. A pump creates the difference, a regulator decides how large it will be, a canister receives what is removed, and a catheter carries the opening to the place that must be cleared. The flow depends on the pressure difference, the length and internal diameter of the tubing, and the resistance of the catheter, so a long narrow tube joined to a weak pump moves little material no matter what the gauge says.

In a well-resourced hospital the suction arrives at the bedside through a central vacuum pipeline. Two or more pumps in a plant room draw air from a receiver tank, and filters and traps protect them from liquid and dust. The pipework runs to terminal units at the wall, each a gas-specific socket keyed by a diameter index safety system so that oxygen or air cannot be plugged into it by mistake. The pipeline carries an area alarm panel, usually near the ward entrance, and a low-vacuum alarm sounds when the level falls below the set threshold, with the threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The response is to establish whether patients are receiving suction and, if not, to move to a portable unit, because a closed isolation valve or a leaking terminal can produce the same reading.

The regulator tames the pipeline into a usable level, and it hangs below the wall outlet or sits on the lid of the canister. Inside it a diaphragm and a spring oppose the vacuum, so turning the dial changes the point at which the two forces balance and therefore the suction that reaches the patient. The gauge is commonly marked from 0 to 300 millimeters of mercury, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Continuous suction holds the set level, while intermittent suction switches it on and off on a timed cycle, and the mode must be chosen deliberately rather than left wherever the previous user placed it.

The canister is the collection vessel, designed so that a handling mistake does not reach the pump. It is a rigid jar of about 1 to 3 liters, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, with an inlet for the patient tubing and an outlet for the vacuum line, and most modern systems line it with a disposable bag. A float valve rises with the fluid and closes the outlet when the jar is nearly full, and a hydrophobic filter stops liquid and aerosol from entering the pipework. Overfilling can spill into the vacuum line and contaminate the whole pipeline, and a canister struck by a trolley can pour its contents back through the patient tubing, so the jar must hang on the wall or stand below the level of the chest.

The connecting tubing is thick-walled and non-collapsible, usually about 6 to 8 millimeters in internal diameter and 1.5 to 2 meters long, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. It must be transparent enough that the operator can see fluid moving through it. Longer tubing adds resistance and reduces the flow that reaches the patient, which is why a tube coiled on the floor is a common cause of ineffective suction. A kinked tube is the classic silent failure, because the pump runs, the gauge reads correctly, and nothing arrives at the tip. The tubing is a single-patient item and is replaced when soiled or cracked.

Suction catheters are soft tubes with a rounded tip, side openings, and a connector at the machine end, and they are sized in French units, which describe the external circumference. Sizes commonly run from 5 to 18 French, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the rule for airway suction is that the catheter should be no larger than one half the internal diameter of the artificial airway. The catheter must reach the carina, which the operator estimates by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe and then to the sternal notch. Vacuum is applied only while the catheter is withdrawn, never while it is advanced, and each pass should be brief and followed by rest and oxygen. For the mouth a rigid tip with a single large opening is used instead, and it is never passed into the nose, where it can tear the mucosa.

For the ventilated patient, disconnecting the breathing circuit to pass a catheter is dangerous, and the closed suction system avoids it. The catheter is enclosed in a transparent sleeve and stays attached to the airway between uses, so the circuit is never opened and the positive end-expiratory pressure is never lost. A thumb port lets the operator advance the catheter and apply suction, and an irrigation port allows sterile saline to clear the tube. Closed systems are replaced at a defined interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. When sputum is needed, a small trap is inserted between the catheter and the canister so the specimen is collected sterile, sealed, labeled, and sent to the laboratory without delay.

Where no pipeline exists, an electric suction unit is a self-contained machine with its own pump, motor, canister, and regulator. A rotary vane pump may be oil-lubricated or run dry, and the motor is cooled by a fan and protected by a thermal cutout that opens the circuit when it becomes too hot. A battery version is built for transport, and its runtime falls as the battery ages and as the canister and filter add resistance. The characteristic alarm is the thermal cutout, which stops the machine rather than warning, and the response is to switch to a backup unit. The oldest device, and still the most reliable without electricity, is the manual pump, worked by a foot bellows or a hand piston, and its level is lower and less steady but it needs no power. The other powerless option is a Venturi device, in which compressed oxygen or air is forced through a narrow jet and drags a vacuum with it, with a driving flow typically 10 to 15 liters per minute, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Suction of an airway is never a neutral act, and its hazards must be named at the machine rather than deferred. The first is a fall in blood oxygen, because the catheter occupies the airway and the vacuum removes the oxygen in it, so the patient should be pre-oxygenated and each pass kept short, commonly under 15 seconds, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The second is a vagal response, in which suction slows the heart and drops the blood pressure. The third is direct injury to the mucosa, which bleeds and then swells and narrows the airway. The fourth is infection carried on the catheter, the canister, or the hands. The commonest operator error is to believe that stronger suction is better suction, when a vacuum at its maximum tears tissue and removes more oxygen than secretion, and the correct habit is to use the lowest level that clears the material.

Cleaning is what keeps the next patient safe. After each use the liner and tubing are discarded, and the canister is washed with warm water and detergent, rinsed, disinfected with a compatible product, and dried, with the contact time and concentration confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The lid, float valve, and hydrophobic filter are inspected, and a wet or clogged filter is replaced because it blocks the vacuum while a missing one sends fluid to the pump. In a mobile or frontier clinic the suction system is assembled from what can be carried, usually a foot or hand pump driving a single bottle, with a rigid tip for the mouth and a few soft catheters for the airway. A 12 volt pump run from a vehicle or solar-charged battery gives a steadier vacuum but adds a battery to cycle and a pump to keep dry, while a Venturi device run from an oxygen cylinder is strong enough for resuscitation but empties the cylinder quickly. The field demands that every part be washed and dried, every filter inspected, every battery logged, and a manual pump kept as the fallback that cannot fail.

A nebulizer turns a liquid medicine into a cloud of droplets small enough to be carried into the lower airway, and the size of those droplets decides where the drug lands. Droplets larger than about 5 micrometers, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, tend to strike the walls of the mouth and throat and never reach the lung. Droplets of about 1 to 5 micrometers travel with the airstream into the bronchi and the alveoli, and droplets smaller than about 1 micrometer may be exhaled before they deposit. Three mechanisms make this cloud, namely a fast jet of gas, a vibrating crystal, and a vibrating mesh, and each produces a different droplet spectrum and a different set of maintenance problems.

The jet nebulizer is the classic and the cheapest. A compressor or a cylinder pushes gas through a very narrow opening, and as the gas accelerates its pressure falls, so liquid is drawn up a capillary tube into the stream and torn apart into droplets. A baffle in the path removes the largest droplets and returns them to the reservoir, so the same liquid is recycled until it is used up. The compressor usually delivers about 6 to 8 liters per minute, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, the chamber is filled with about 2 to 5 milliliters of solution, and a treatment commonly lasts 5 to 10 minutes. Jet nebulizers are robust and inexpensive, but they waste drug, because much of it remains in the chamber.

The ultrasonic nebulizer makes its mist with sound rather than with gas. A piezoelectric crystal is driven by an electrical oscillator at a frequency of roughly 1 to 3 megahertz, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the crystal vibrates against a thin layer of liquid. The vibration sets up standing waves, and at their crests the liquid breaks into fine droplets that rise as a visible mist. The output is higher and quieter than that of a jet device and the treatment is faster, but the vibration warms the solution and can degrade some drugs, especially proteins, and the crystal and its coupling surface need careful cleaning. The device stops producing mist when the liquid level falls too low.

The mesh nebulizer is the newest of the three and the one that has travelled furthest into the field. A plate pierced with thousands of tiny tapered holes is vibrated, either by a piezoelectric ring around it or by a small pump that pushes the liquid through the holes, and each hole produces a droplet of very uniform size. The device is small, quiet, battery powered, and delivers a large fraction of the drug with very little left in the reservoir, which matters when the medicine is expensive or scarce. Its weakness is the mesh itself, which clogs with dried drug, with salt, and with sticky solutions, and which must be rinsed and dried after every use. The characteristic fault indicator is a blocked mesh warning or a low battery signal, and both must be treated as an instruction to stop and clean or recharge.

The nebulizer chamber is connected to the patient by a mask, a mouthpiece, or a T-piece with tubing, and the choice changes how much drug is delivered. A mouthpiece with a good seal gives the most reliable dose in a cooperative adult, while a mask is used for children, for the breathless, and for anyone who cannot hold a mouthpiece. Between the chamber and the patient there is often a short length of wide tubing and sometimes a one-way valve, and exhaled gas and condensation must escape so the patient does not re-breathe carbon dioxide. After every use the chamber, the mask or mouthpiece, and the tubing are washed in warm water and detergent, rinsed, disinfected if the maker allows it, and dried completely, because a damp nebulizer grows organisms that are then inhaled into the lung.

For a drug supplied in a pressurized canister, the spacer is often a better delivery device than a nebulizer. When the canister is pressed, a measured dose of drug and propellant leaves the valve at high speed, and without a spacer much of it strikes the back of the throat. A spacer is a plain tube or chamber that holds the cloud while the propellant evaporates, so the particles become smaller and slower and the patient can inhale the whole dose in one or two quiet breaths. A valved holding chamber adds a one-way valve at the patient end, which keeps the drug in the chamber during exhalation and makes the device usable by a young child. Where no spacer is available, a clean plastic bottle of about 500 milliliters can be made into a chamber, with a hole cut to accept the inhaler and the joint sealed with tape. The improvised chamber is not valved, and it must be clean, dry, and replaced when cracked.

The common operator errors in nebulization are simple and repeated. The first is to fill the chamber beyond the marked line or to mix drugs without checking compatibility, so the output falls and the mixture becomes unpredictable. The second is to run a compressor with a clogged intake filter, which reduces flow and droplet production and overheats the motor, and the third is to leave the tubing full of condensation so the patient inhales water rather than mist. The fourth is to dry the parts with a towel, which leaves lint and organisms, or to store them damp in a closed bag. The safety hazard that follows is infection of the lower airway with organisms that grew in the device. Some compressors carry a thermal cutout as their only alarm, and a mesh device may signal a blocked mesh or a low battery, and every such threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the nebulizer is usually a small compressor run from a vehicle battery through an inverter, from a solar-charged battery, or from a foot pump in an emergency. A mesh device powered by a rechargeable battery is increasingly common, because it is light, quiet, and parsimonious with the drug, but it depends on a charged battery and a clean mesh. An oxygen-driven jet nebulizer needs no electricity at all, but it consumes oxygen at 6 to 8 liters per minute, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it will empty a small cylinder during a single treatment. The field demands a cleaning routine that a busy ward can forget and a lone clinician cannot, namely wash, rinse, disinfect where possible, and air dry, with each part stored dry and protected from dust.

Chest drainage begins with a small space that is almost invisible when it is healthy. The pleural space is a thin layer of fluid between the lung and the chest wall, and the pressure within it is normally a little below atmospheric pressure, which is what holds the lung expanded against its own elastic recoil. If air enters the space, as after a puncture or a burst bleb, or if blood, pus, or lymph collects there, the lung is pushed away from the chest wall and collapses, and breathing becomes difficult and inefficient. A chest drain reopens a path from that space to the outside and then controls the direction of flow, so air and fluid can leave but nothing can be drawn back in. The system therefore has three parts to think about, namely the pleural space, the atmosphere, and the one-way valve between them.

The chest tube itself is a soft, flexible tube of silicone or polyvinyl chloride, and it is sized in French units, with common adult sizes running from about 20 to 40 French and smaller sizes used in children, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A straight tube has several side openings near its tip, called drainage eyes, and a stripe of radiopaque material along its length so its position can be seen on a radiograph. A pigtail catheter is thinner, coiled at the tip, and designed for air or for a small collection, and it is usually placed over a guide wire rather than by cutting. Some tubes carry a sharp inner trocar that helps guide the tube through the chest wall, and that trocar is also the source of the most serious injuries, because it can be pushed into the lung or the heart.

Once the tube is in place it must be held there, because a tube that slips out is both a treatment failure and a new open wound. The tube is fixed with a heavy suture through the skin and around the tube, and the site is covered with an occlusive dressing that keeps air from entering around the tube while allowing the tube to leave it. The dressing is changed with a sterile technique, the skin is inspected for infection, and the suture is checked for security at every shift. The tube is connected to the drainage system with a connector of the correct size, and the connection must be locked and taped so it cannot separate when the patient moves. A loose connection, a stretched suture, and a dressing that has come away are the three commonest mechanical failures of chest drainage.

The simplest and most important part of the drainage system is the underwater seal, and it works by the same principle as a valve in a drainpipe. The end of the tube from the patient is held below the surface of a small volume of sterile water, so that when the patient exhales or coughs, air and fluid push out through the water, and when the patient inhales, the water is drawn back up the tube and seals it before air can enter. The depth of the tube below the surface is usually about 2 centimeters, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a deeper seal makes the patient work harder to push air out and a shallower one can be lost with a tilt. The water column also moves slightly with each breath, and that gentle rise and fall, called tidaling or swinging, is the sign that the tube is still open.

Modern hospital systems combine three functions in a single molded unit. The first chamber collects the fluid and is marked with a scale so the output can be measured. The second chamber is the underwater seal, with its 2 centimeters of water that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it shows both the swing of breathing and any continuous bubbling that means air is still leaking. The third chamber controls suction, either by a column of water set to about 10 to 20 centimeters of water, a value that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, or by a dry regulator and a dial, called a dry suction system. Before molded units existed, the same three functions were performed by three separate glass bottles. The first bottle collects the drainage, the second holds the underwater seal, and the third is the suction control bottle, and the three-bottle system works when assembled correctly, but it is fragile, it tips easily, and every joint is a place where air can enter or fluid can spill.

For transport and for walking patients, the water seal is replaced by a one-way valve, usually a flattened tube with a flexible membrane inside that opens in one direction only. The valve allows air and fluid to leave but not to return, it cannot spill, and it cannot be lifted above the chest and then drain back into the patient, which makes it the safest choice when a patient must be moved between buildings or in a vehicle. It gives up the information that the water seal provides, because there is no column to swing and no bubbles to watch, so the clinician can judge the drain only by the amount of fluid in the bag and by the patient's condition. The valve must be kept free of kinks and blood clot, and its direction of flow must be confirmed before it is connected, because a valve fitted the wrong way blocks the drain completely.

The chest drain is monitored by watching and measuring rather than by listening for a tone, though some electronic drainage systems do provide alarms for an occluded tube or a persistent air leak, with thresholds that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The first sign to check is the swing of the water column, because a column that has stopped moving usually means the tube is blocked or kinked, or that the lung has re-expanded. The second is bubbling, which is normal for a short time after insertion and afterwards means a continuing air leak. A blocked drain can allow air to collect under pressure in the pleural space, and that tension pushes the heart aside, a pattern that requires immediate decompression. Draining a long-standing collection too quickly can pull fluid into the lung, a condition called re-expansion pulmonary edema, so the rate is often limited, with the limit confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The common operator errors in chest drainage are almost all positional. The first is to lift the drainage unit above the level of the patient's chest, for example to hang it on a stand or carry it up a stair, which lets fluid run back into the pleural space. The second is to clamp the tube while the patient is moved or the dressing is changed, because a clamped drain cannot relieve a tension pneumothorax. The third is to strip or milk the tube to clear it, a practice that generates very high negative pressure and can injure the lung. At every shift the operator confirms that the unit is upright and below the chest, that the water seal is at its marked level, that the connections are locked, that the dressing is intact, and that the tube is not kinked, and the output and any swing or leak are recorded. The drainage unit is replaced when it is full, broken, or at the interval the maker and the protocol specify.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the drainage system is built from a bottle, a tube, and sterile water, and it must be built correctly or not at all. A clean bottle is filled with sterile water to a marked depth, the tube from the patient is passed through the cap and its tip held 2 centimeters below the surface, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the bottle is placed below the level of the chest. The cap must be sealed around the tube, because an open bottle is an open pneumothorax, and the bottle must be marked with the time and the starting level so the output can be measured. Where a commercial one-way valve is available it is preferred for transport, because it cannot spill or drain back. Where no sterile water and no clean bottle exist, a chest drain cannot be improvised, and the patient must be moved to a place where one can be placed.

To summarize, suction, nebulization, and chest drainage are three ways of managing pressure and flow around the airway and the pleural space. Suction works by lowering pressure at the tip of a tube so that the atmosphere pushes material out, and it demands the lowest effective vacuum, the shortest pass, and a clean canister and filter. Nebulization works by breaking a liquid into droplets of a size that will reach the lung, and it demands the correct fill volume, an unobstructed jet, crystal, or mesh, and a device that is washed and dried after every use. Chest drainage provides a one-way path for air and fluid to leave the pleural space, and it demands a system that stays upright, below the chest, unkinked, and sealed. In every setting the operator who understands the pressure gradient recognizes failure before the patient does, and every setting, pressure, and interval named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 18 — Respiratory Diagnostics

Breathing looks effortless and is in fact a problem in fluid mechanics, and every instrument in this chapter is an attempt to measure one part of that problem. Air moves into the lung only because the pressure inside the chest falls slightly below the pressure in the room, and it moves out again because the elastic recoil of the lung raises the pressure above the room. The rate at which the gas travels is the flow, the amount that has passed is the volume, and the two are linked by a simple relationship, because flow is the rate of change of volume. The opposition to that movement is the resistance of the airways, and the stiffness of the lung and the chest wall is the compliance. Disease changes one or more of these numbers by narrowing the tubes, stiffening the tissue, weakening the muscles, or destroying the surface where gas exchange happens. A respiratory diagnostic device does not look for a disease by name; it measures pressure, flow, volume, or the concentration of a gas, and the clinician reads the pattern. Understanding which of these the instrument actually senses is what separates a trustworthy result from a plausible-looking number.

The spirometer is the central instrument of lung function testing, and the first thing to understand is that most modern spirometers are flow meters that calculate volume rather than volume collectors that measure it directly. A pneumotachograph places a small, known resistance in the path of the breath and measures the tiny pressure difference that develops across it. When the flow is smooth and orderly the pressure difference is proportional to flow, a condition called laminar flow, and the instrument can then be calibrated with a known volume of air pushed through it by a syringe. A screen of fine mesh, a bundle of parallel tubes, or a small hole can all serve as that resistance, and each behaves predictably only within a limited range of flows. A turbine or vane spirometer instead lets the breath spin a light rotor and counts the rotations, while an ultrasonic spirometer measures the time taken by pulses of sound to cross the moving stream. All of these approaches answer the same question in different ways, and each has a characteristic weakness that the operator must know.

A complete spirometer is a chain of parts, and every link can degrade the result. At the patient end there is a mouthpiece, usually a disposable rigid tube or a flanged cardboard type, and between the mouthpiece and the sensor sits a filter that traps particles and microorganisms. The filter adds a small resistance and a small dead space, and a wet, clogged, or wrongly seated filter changes both, so the filter specified by the maker must be used and the resistance it adds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Beyond the sensor there is the tubing, which must be short, wide, and free of kinks, because a long narrow hose distorts the flow signal and encourages water to collect. The console holds the pressure transducer, the amplifier, and the processor, together with sensors for room temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure. A calibration syringe of exactly 3 liters is the standard tool for checking the sensor, a nominal value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it must be stored where its plunger seal cannot dry out or crack. Consumables include mouthpieces, filters, nose clips, and the disinfectant for the sensor head, and a spirometer without them will be idle within a week.

The maneuver itself is the part of spirometry that depends most on the patient and the coach, and a poor maneuver produces a wrong diagnosis rather than a missing one. The patient sits upright, applies a nose clip, seals the lips tightly around the mouthpiece, breathes in fully to total lung capacity, and then blasts the air out as hard and as long as possible until no more will come. The effort must be maximal from the opening instant, because the volume expelled in the first second is the number most often used, and a slow start understates it badly. The patient then breathes in fully again so that the maneuver can be repeated, and the series is performed at least 3 times until the best 2 efforts agree closely, a requirement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A bronchodilator may then be given and the test repeated after a fixed interval, so that a change in the numbers can be attributed to the drug, and the interval and the dose must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The coach must demonstrate, encourage, and watch the screen rather than the patient's face, because the shape of the curve tells immediately whether the effort was acceptable. A leak at the lips, an extra breath in the middle, or a tongue partly blocking the mouthpiece all spoil the effort, and the quality messages on the display should be read rather than dismissed.

Quality criteria exist because a spirometer will happily report a number from a worthless effort, and the criteria are mathematical rather than a matter of opinion. The back-extrapolated volume, found by extending the steepest part of the curve back to the start, shows how much air escaped before the blast began, and a large value means a hesitant start. The effort must last long enough for a plateau to appear, otherwise the patient simply stopped early and the total is falsely low. Repeatability means that the best 2 acceptable efforts differ by only a small margin, and the acceptable margin must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The great hazard of the procedure is infection, because a forced exhalation turns whatever is in the airway into a fine mist that reaches the sensor, the tubing, and the room, so a filter and careful hand hygiene are not optional. The common operator error is to accept the first effort because it looks reasonable, and the second common error is to mistake a leaking mouth seal for genuine obstruction. A spirometer signals its displeasure with prompts such as blow harder, blow longer, or a message that the effort was not acceptable, and the quality limits and alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The peak flow meter is the simplest respiratory diagnostic instrument in existence, and its principle is a variable opening. As the patient blows through the device, a piston, a vane, or a small flap is pushed against a spring or along a calibrated slot, and the distance it travels depends on the greatest flow reached during the blast. The reading is held by a ratchet or a marker until it is reset, so the patient and the clinician can both see it, and the scale is usually printed in liters per minute with numbered bands alongside. The device measures only one point, the highest flow achieved, and it says nothing about the total volume or the shape of the effort, which is both its strength and its limitation. Because the measurement depends on effort and technique, the patient must stand or sit upright, take the deepest possible breath, seal the lips, and blow as hard and as briefly as possible, and the best of 3 attempts is recorded, a convention that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Each patient should have a personal best, established while well, so that later readings can be expressed as a fraction of it rather than compared with a stranger's prediction. The common operator error is to read the marker after the patient has already lowered the device, or to let the patient blow with the tongue partly in the way, and both produce a number that is low for the wrong reason.

In asthma care the peak flow meter earns its place by being cheap, portable, and repeatable in the patient's own hands, and by turning a symptom into a number that can be followed over time. A fall in the peak flow often begins hours or days before the patient feels breathless, so a daily morning reading can warn of deteriorating control while there is still time to act. Action plans therefore divide the personal best into zones, most often a green zone of normal function, a yellow zone of caution, and a red zone of danger, and the boundaries and the instructions attached to each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. During an acute attack the peak flow helps to grade severity and to show whether treatment is working, and a value that fails to improve after repeated bronchodilator doses is a strong argument for transfer to a higher level of care. The hazard is a false sense of security, because a patient who cannot perform the maneuver properly, or who uses a meter clogged with dust, may record a low value while well or a falsely acceptable value while ill. Meters must be washed or wiped according to the instructions supplied with them, allowed to dry completely, and compared with a second meter when results seem inconsistent, and a cracked or sticky meter must be discarded rather than repaired. The characteristic failure is silent rather than audible, because there is no alarm, only a scale that sticks, which is why the operator must test the device before it is trusted.

Pulse oximetry was introduced as a monitor, but in respiratory diagnostics it becomes a measuring instrument, and its physics must be understood before its numbers are believed. The sensor shines light of 2 wavelengths, one red and one infrared, through a translucent part of the body, usually a fingertip, and a detector on the other side measures what survives the journey. Oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorb those wavelengths differently, and the ratio of the absorbed amounts is converted into a percentage saturation. The device separates the pulsatile part of the signal, which comes from arterial blood arriving with each heartbeat, from the steady part, which comes from skin, bone, and venous blood, and that separation is why a good pulse waveform is required for a good reading. This is also why the technique fails in the cold, in shock, with movement, with dark nail polish, and with a badly placed sensor, because in each case there is too little pulsatile signal for the arithmetic to work. The reading is a saturation and not a content, so a patient with severe anemia can show a normal percentage while carrying far too little oxygen in absolute terms. It also cannot distinguish oxygen from carbon monoxide, because the 2 forms of hemoglobin look alike to the 2 wavelengths, so a survivor of a fire may show a reassuring number while being poisoned. The characteristic alarm is the low saturation tone or message, and the threshold that triggers it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The walk test turns oximetry from a snapshot into a diagnostic procedure by adding exertion, and it is one of the most useful low-technology tests in respiratory medicine. The standard version asks the patient to walk as far as possible along a measured corridor for 6 minutes, and the distance covered, the lowest saturation reached, the heart rate, and the symptoms are all recorded, with the exact duration and the stopping rules confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A fall in saturation during walking, particularly below the threshold set by the local protocol, which must itself be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, identifies a patient who desaturates with activity and who may benefit from oxygen away from the bed. A simpler version, sometimes called the step test or the shuttle walk, is used where there is no corridor, and it still reproduces the essential feature, which is that the measurement is taken while the patient works rather than while the patient rests. A continuous recording during the walk is more informative than a single reading at the end, because the lowest value often occurs during the effort and recovers within seconds of stopping. The common operator error is to let the patient stop at the first sign of breathlessness, which conceals the very desaturation that the test was designed to find, or to hold the sensor still with a hand, which removes the pulse and blanks the display. The operator must also record whether the patient used oxygen during the walk, because a test performed on oxygen answers a different question from one performed on room air.

Blood gas analysis measures the pressures and the acidity of arterial blood directly, and it does so with electrodes rather than with light. The sample is drawn into a syringe, introduced into a small chamber, and brought into contact with a series of sensors, each of which produces a tiny electrical signal in proportion to the quantity it senses. The acidity is measured with a glass electrode, a thin membrane of special glass across which hydrogen ions distribute themselves and create a voltage that the instrument compares with a stable reference. The partial pressure of carbon dioxide is measured with a modified glass electrode covered by a membrane that lets the gas diffuse into a thin film of bicarbonate solution, where it changes the acidity, and that change is read as a voltage. The partial pressure of oxygen is measured with a different electrode, in which oxygen diffuses through a membrane and is consumed at a small electrode, producing a current proportional to the amount arriving. Newer analyzers use fluorescent dyes printed on a disposable cartridge, where the presence of a gas or an ion changes the light the dye emits, and optics replace the wet electrodes.

A blood gas analyzer is only as good as its calibration, its quality control, and the sample that reaches it. The instrument holds a set of calibration gases and buffer solutions, and it performs a full calibration at intervals, with a shorter calibration before each sample, and the composition, the values, and the schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Control material with known values is run at fixed intervals and after every maintenance visit, and the results are charted, because an analyzer can drift slowly and still appear to work. The sample syringe is itself a critical consumable: it must contain a small amount of an anticoagulant, usually a salt of heparin, it must be sealed against air, and it must be mixed by gentle rolling rather than shaking. Air bubbles are the classic error, because a bubble exchanges gas with the blood and falsely raises the measured oxygen pressure while lowering the carbon dioxide pressure, and a bubble left in a syringe for a few minutes can change the interpretation entirely. The sample must be analyzed quickly, and the acceptable delay and the acceptable temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the cells in the blood continue to consume oxygen and produce carbon dioxide after the sample is drawn. The operator must also confirm that the sample is arterial, which is judged from the color and the pulsatile flow at the time of puncture and from the plausibility checks built into the analyzer, since a venous sample sent as arterial is a dangerous misdiagnosis waiting to happen.

Maintenance of a blood gas analyzer is a discipline of membranes, fluids, and cleanliness, and its failures are usually gradual rather than sudden. The electrode membranes are thin films that can dry out, crack, or become coated with protein, and each of these faults produces a drifting or sluggish reading rather than an obvious breakdown. The reference electrode and the internal filling solutions must be replenished on schedule, and the tubing, the clot traps, and the sample path must be flushed and cleaned to remove fibrin and blood cells, because a partial blockage can produce a falsely low oxygen reading and erratic results. The instrument must be kept at a stable temperature, because the electrodes are sensitive to it and the sample is warmed to the electrode temperature during analysis, and the set temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Waste fluid and rinse solutions must be emptied and replaced, and the used syringes and needles must be handled as infectious material. The characteristic alarms include a calibration failure, an electrode drift or slope error, a sample error when the analyzer detects a clot or too little blood, a low reagent warning, and a temperature warning, and every threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to keep reporting results after a calibration flag has appeared, or to override a quality control failure because the sample, in the operator's judgment, is urgent. A result from an analyzer whose control material is failing is not a result at all, and the correct response is to suspend testing, use a backup analyzer or send the sample onward, and write the event in the log.

Exhaled carbon dioxide measurement sits between monitoring and diagnosis, and it deserves attention here because it answers questions that oximetry cannot. The usual instrument is an infrared analyzer, which passes a beam of infrared light through a small chamber filled with the patient's breath and measures how much of one particular wavelength is absorbed by carbon dioxide molecules, because the absorption is proportional to the number of molecules in the path. The sample may be drawn through a thin tube to a remote chamber, or the chamber may sit directly in the breathing circuit, and a filter and a water trap protect the optics from mucus and condensation. The result is displayed as a waveform and as a number, the end-tidal value, which is the concentration at the very end of exhalation when the gas has come from the deepest part of the lung. The difference between that value and the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide is normally small, and a widening gap suggests that some of the exhaled gas is coming from parts of the lung that are not exchanging gas well, which is a ventilation problem rather than a metabolic one. A flat waveform, a sudden fall, an unexpected rise, or the loss of the characteristic shape all carry meaning, and a colorimetric detector that changes color on contact with the gas is the simplest field version. In diagnostics the measurement is used to confirm that a breathing tube is in the airway, to follow the severity of an asthma attack, and to judge the response to treatment, and the normal range and the alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Bronchoscopy is the invasive end of respiratory diagnostics, and it exists because some questions can only be answered by looking inside the airway and taking a piece of it. The flexible instrument is a long tube built around bundles of glass fibers, and it works by total internal reflection, because light travelling along a fiber strikes the boundary at a shallow angle and is reflected back into the fiber rather than escaping, so an image can be carried around a curve without lenses along the way. One bundle carries light from the console to illuminate the airway, and a second bundle, with its fibers arranged in the same order at both ends, carries the image back to the eyepiece or the camera. A separate channel runs the length of the scope for suction, for the passage of instruments, and for the instillation of fluid, and a set of wires at the tip allows the operator to bend the end in one or 2 directions. The rigid instrument is a hollow metal tube with a lens and a light source, and it gives a wider view and a larger working channel at the cost of requiring deep anesthesia and an extended neck. The consumables are numerous, including biopsy forceps, cytology brushes, needles for sampling through the airway wall, grasping tools, guide wires, specimen containers, and a suction trap. The field variant of this instrument barely exists, and its absence is one of the sharpest limits on what can be diagnosed far from a referral hospital.

The hazards of bronchoscopy are immediate and must be managed during the procedure rather than after it. Bleeding can follow a biopsy, particularly in a patient with a clotting problem, and the operator must be ready to instill a cold solution, to suction, and to press on the area, with the exact agents and the protocol confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Spasm of the vocal cords and coughing are provoked by the instrument touching them, and the oxygen saturation commonly falls because the scope occupies part of the airway and suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Monitoring of saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure, and the presence of resuscitation equipment, are part of the procedure and not a separate concern. The characteristic alarm is the falling saturation tone or the low saturation message on the monitor, and it must be treated as an instruction to withdraw the scope, suction briefly, and give oxygen, not as a signal to continue and watch. The common operator error is to advance the scope against resistance, which can perforate the airway, or to use suction continuously, which collapses the airway, damages the lining, and provokes bleeding. Cleaning is a multistep process: bedside pre-cleaning of the insertion tube, leak testing before immersion, manual brushing and flushing of every channel, enzymatic cleaning, rinsing, high-level disinfection or sterilization, drying, and vertical storage, and the concentrations, the contact times, and the temperatures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A leak test is the single most valuable step in that sequence, because fluid entering a damaged scope destroys the optical bundle, and a scope that fails its leak test must be removed from service at once.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the respiratory diagnostic toolkit shrinks to almost nothing, and the clinician must decide what to carry and what to do without. A peak flow meter, a pulse oximeter, a watch, a measuring tape for the walk test, and a supply of mouthpieces and filters weigh little and cost little, and together they cover a surprising amount of respiratory assessment. What disappears is the blood gas analyzer, the spirometer with its calibration syringe, the exhaled carbon dioxide monitor, and the bronchoscope, each of which needs electricity, reagents, calibration gases, trained maintenance, and a patient volume large enough to keep it honest. The respiratory rate counted over a full minute, the use of the muscles of the neck and ribs, the ability to speak in whole sentences, the position the patient chooses, the color of the lips, the presence of sweating, and the response to a trial of oxygen all carry information that a machine would otherwise supply. Because these signs are judged by the observer, they must be recorded at each visit in the same way, so that change over time, rather than any single reading, drives the decision. Where an arterial blood gas is impossible, the clinician reasons from the pattern: a patient who is breathless at rest, who cannot finish a sentence, or whose saturation falls with the slightest effort is treated as seriously ill and moved onward, while a patient whose saturation is stable and whose work of breathing is normal can be observed and treated locally. The absence of a number is a real loss, and the honest response is to say so and to transfer the patient when the clinical picture is uncertain.

Whatever survives in the field must be maintained with the same seriousness as a hospital instrument, and the checks are simple enough to be done on every clinic day. The pulse oximeter needs clean and undamaged sensors, a battery that holds its charge, and a check that the displayed pulse matches the pulse felt by hand, and a device whose readings cannot be reproduced must be taken out of use. The peak flow meter needs a free-moving piston or vane, a clean mouthpiece area, and a periodic comparison with a second meter, and it must be stored where it cannot be crushed or filled with dust. A portable spirometer with a disposable flow sensor needs fresh sensors, a charged battery, a check with a known volume, and a clean and dry sensor port, and its results must be read only when the quality message or the curve shows an acceptable effort. Consumables must be counted before the clinic, because a missing mouthpiece or a dead battery turns a diagnostic visit into a wasted journey, and the stock must be rotated so that expired filters and sensors are not carried for months. The operator must also know the failures that mimic disease, because a battery losing power can make a spirometer under-report, a dirty sensor port can make it over-report, and a cold finger can make an oximeter under-report, and each of these errors sends the clinical reasoning in the wrong direction. Every device should carry its own log of checks, faults, and repairs, and any instrument that fails a check must be labeled and set aside rather than used with an explanation. Where no spirometer is available at all, the peak flow meter and a careful bronchodilator trial remain the substitute, and the change in peak flow after treatment is the most useful single piece of evidence the clinic can generate.

To summarize, respiratory diagnostics begins with the simple physics of pressure, flow, and volume, and each instrument in this chapter senses one of these quantities and converts it into a number. The spirometer measures flow across a known resistance and adds it up over time to obtain volume, and its value depends entirely on a maximal effort that meets defined quality criteria. The peak flow meter measures one point of that effort against a spring or an opening, and it is most useful as a personal baseline tracked over time rather than as a single reading. Pulse oximetry uses 2 wavelengths of light and the pulsatile signal to estimate saturation, and the walk test extends it into a diagnostic procedure by adding exertion. Blood gas analyzers use electrodes or fluorescent dyes to measure acidity and the partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide directly, and they are only as reliable as their calibration, their quality control, and the care taken with the sample. Exhaled carbon dioxide measurement adds a view of ventilation and of the shape of the breath, and bronchoscopy adds direct vision and tissue at the cost of sedation, bleeding, infection, and a demanding cleaning routine. In the field the toolkit contracts to a peak flow meter and an oximeter, and clinical reasoning must take over from the missing laboratory, with serial observation, a measured walk, and the honest recognition of uncertainty guiding the decision to treat locally or to transfer.

# Chapter 19 — ECG and Cardiac Diagnostics

The heart is a moving battery, and the electrocardiogram, ECG for short, is what that battery looks like from the surface of the body. Each heartbeat begins as a wave of activation that sweeps through the atria and ventricles, and because the body is a volume conductor of salt water, the resulting voltage changes spread outward to the skin. Two electrodes at different points therefore sit at slightly different voltages at the same instant, and the instrument measures only that difference, amplifies it many thousands of times, and plots it against time. The signal at the skin is tiny, on the order of 1 millivolt, and the usual gain makes 1 millivolt of input produce a deflection of 10 millimeters on the record, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Direction matters as much as size, because activation moving toward an electrode gives an upward deflection while activation moving away gives a downward one.

The recording chain is a series of links, and each link can spoil the result on its own. At the patient end sits the electrode, a conductive pad that turns the ionic current of the skin into the electronic current of the wire. Above it are the adhesive and the conductive gel, which hold it in place and bridge the dry outer skin. A lead wire then carries the tiny voltage to a differential amplifier that compares each pair of inputs and rejects the interference common to both, which is why a clean trace is possible in a room full of lights and pumps. The amplifier passes only the frequencies of interest, commonly a diagnostic range of 0.05 to 150 hertz with a notch filter at 50 or 60 hertz, and every bandwidth, filter setting, and gain value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The machine drives a thermal printer or fills a screen, and it should emit a calibration pulse of exactly 1 millivolt before and after a recording, a reference that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The standard diagnostic recording uses 10 electrodes to produce 12 views. Four electrodes sit on the limbs, and the right leg electrode serves mainly as a neutral reference. From those 4 points the machine calculates 6 frontal views, in which lead 1 compares the right arm with the left arm, lead 2 compares the right arm with the left leg, and lead 3 compares the left arm with the left leg. Three augmented leads reweight the same inputs into the augmented right arm lead, the augmented left arm lead, and the augmented left leg lead. Six further electrodes cross the chest, from chest lead 1 beside the breastbone to chest lead 6 in the mid axillary line, and each looks at the heart from a different angle. Lead 2, lead 3, and the augmented left leg lead face the inferior wall, the chest leads face the anterior and lateral walls, and lead 1 with the augmented left arm lead faces the high lateral wall, so the pattern of abnormality is itself a map of where the trouble lies.

Placement is not a formality, because a tracing made 2 centimeters too high or with 2 wires exchanged can imitate a serious disease that is not present. The limb electrodes go on soft tissue rather than bone, and the chest electrodes follow the spaces between the ribs at the positions the machine expects. The classic operator error is exchanging the left and right arm wires, which inverts lead 1 and can suggest a lateral problem while concealing a real one, and the second is placing all 6 chest electrodes too low on the abdomen, which flattens the anterior views. The machine cannot detect either mistake, because the electrodes are connected and the trace looks plausible, so the operator must read the positions from the machine's diagram and inspect the patient rather than the screen. When the standard 12 views are not enough, electrodes are added deliberately, mirrored onto the right side of the chest for the right ventricle or placed posteriorly for the back wall. More leads mean more wires and a greater chance of a loose connection, and the positions and their number must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The ECG machine is deceptively safe because it only listens, but a patient connected to it is part of an electrical circuit and the connection is a real hazard. Every electrode and lead wire brings the patient into contact with a mains powered instrument, so the machine must be properly grounded, its cables must be undamaged, and its leakage current must be tested at the intervals its maker specifies. A fault leaking current into a patient with a catheter inside the heart can provoke a fatal rhythm disturbance. The patient must never be connected to a machine whose case is cracked, whose cable is frayed, or whose plug bypasses the earth connection, and electrodes must not be placed over broken skin or a rash. The characteristic alarms are the lead off message, the low battery warning, the paper out message, and the rhythm alarms of a monitor with a heart rate limit, and every threshold and message must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to silence a lead off alarm, tape the cable, and continue recording, because the resulting flat line can be read as a pause in the heart rather than a loose wire.

Electrode quality decides more tracings than any electronic setting, and the electrode is the consumable that must never be improvised. A disposable electrode is a pad carrying a metal stud, a conductive adhesive, and a gel that may be wet, semi solid, or solid. A wet gel conducts well but dries out once the package is opened, while a solid gel lasts longer and grips the skin less strongly. The gel must be moist across the whole contact area, the adhesive must be pressed firmly to the skin, and the electrode must be within its expiry date, because an expired electrode may already have lost its moisture and will produce a wandering baseline that looks like disease. Single use electrodes are discarded after one patient, and reusable suction electrodes or limb plates are cleaned and fitted with fresh gel or a fresh strap for every recording. Chest hair, sweat, cream, and powder all separate the gel from the skin, so the site may be clipped rather than shaved, wiped with an alcohol pad, and dried, and the local skin care protocol must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Artifact is any mark on the tracing that did not come from the heart, and recognizing it is the difference between a clinician and a machine operator. Baseline wander is a slow undulation caused by breathing, a loose electrode, or a shivering patient, and it can hide the elevated or depressed segment between the S wave and the T wave that matters most. Muscle tremor is a dense fuzz from a tense patient, and it is reduced by warming the room, resting the hands, and asking the patient to relax rather than by turning up a filter. Interference from the mains appears as a fine ripple at 50 or 60 hertz and is usually caused by a dried electrode, a coiled lead wire, or a cable lying across a power supply. Motion from a cough or a mobile telephone can imitate a dangerous rhythm, and a poor contact can produce a flat line that mimics a pause. The operator must correct the cause at the patient, because a filter that hides tremor can also flatten the wave the clinician is looking for, and the filter settings and acceptable noise limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A poor tracing does not announce itself; it becomes a wrong decision with the confidence of a real recording. A wandering baseline from a dry electrode can be read as an injury of the inferior wall and lead to a transfer or a treatment that was never needed, while a flat line from a disconnected wire can be read as a stopped heart. A muscle tremor can be mistaken for a fast irregular rhythm, and an inverted lead from exchanged arm wires can be mistaken for an old scar. The operator must therefore look at every tracing before it leaves the room, check that the calibration pulse is square and of the expected height, check that the baseline is steady in every view, and repeat the recording if any part is uninterpretable. A repeat costs minutes while a wrong decision costs a great deal, and the repeat should be documented with the reason it was made. A tracing sent for a remote opinion must be complete and legible, with the patient's identifier, the date, the time, and the recording settings visible on it, and the local retention rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of an ECG machine is mostly cleanliness, inspection, and a battery that is always ready. The housing, the keyboard, and the screen are wiped with the disinfectant the maker approves, and no liquid is allowed to enter the connectors or the printer, because the lead wire socket is the part most easily damaged by fluid. Lead wires are inspected along their whole length for cracks and loose connectors, since a single broken strand can produce an intermittent trace that appears only when the patient moves. The battery of a portable unit is charged before every shift, its contacts are cleaned, and a spare battery is carried wherever the unit is used away from a socket. Thermal paper is stored away from heat and sunlight, because it darkens with age and a faded strip cannot be read. A calibration pulse and a short test recording are made at the start of every day, and the intervals for electrical safety testing, calibration verification, and battery replacement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Most ECG failures are gradual, and the operator is the only detector. The first group is contact failure, in which electrodes dry out, gel migrates, adhesive lifts, or a strap loosens, and it appears as a wandering baseline, a lead off alarm, or a trace that changes when the patient is touched. The second is conductor failure, in which a lead wire breaks inside its insulation, a connector corrodes, or a socket loosens, and it appears as one view that fails while the others remain clean. The third is instrument failure, in which the amplifier drifts, the printer darkens the paper unevenly, or the software freezes, and it produces a tracing that is internally consistent but wrong. A fourth group belongs to the user and includes the wrong filter, the wrong gain, the wrong paper speed, and the wrong patient identification. Any unit that fails a check is labeled, removed from service, and repaired, and an intermittent fault is written down with the conditions in which it appeared.

When the heart produces its evidence over hours rather than seconds, the recording must move with the patient, and the ambulatory recorder does exactly that. A Holter recorder is a small battery powered unit worn on a belt or a shoulder strap, connected to the chest by 3 to 7 electrodes that give 2 or 3 simultaneous views, and it stores every beat of a full day or more in solid state memory rather than on paper. The patient keeps a diary of symptoms, meals, exercise, and medication times, and that diary is what turns a mark on the record into a clinical event. The value of the recording is decided in the first 10 minutes, when the operator prepares the skin, avoids muscle that will move, secures the wires with loops of tape, tests every channel, and records the exact start time. The common operator error is to send a patient home with a channel that is already noisy, because the whole day will be wasted. The characteristic alarms are the lead off alert, the low battery warning, and the memory full message, with the recording duration and every alarm threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Not every symptom happens within a single day, and the event recorder is the answer to the symptom that appears once a week. An external event monitor stores a short strip from before and after the patient presses a button, capturing the heart's activity at the moment of the symptom. A wire free patch recorder is worn continuously for up to 2 weeks and combines the long wear of an ambulatory recorder with an event button that marks the moment. An implantable loop recorder placed under the skin of the chest can watch for 3 years or more, which makes it the tool for the rare fainting episode no external recorder catches. Each device trades the completeness of the continuous recording for the length of the observation, and the recording duration and the event detection settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.
