Exercise makes the heart reveal a shortage that rest conceals, and the exercise stress test is the deliberate production of that situation. When the patient works against a treadmill or a cycle, the muscles demand more oxygen and the heart rate and blood pressure rise. A narrowed coronary artery that was adequate at rest can no longer supply the region it feeds, which shows itself as a change in the electrical pattern before the patient feels pain. The workload is increased in stages, each lasting a set number of minutes, and the protocol, the increments, and the stage duration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A cycle ergometer keeps the upper body stable and measures the work in watts, while a treadmill reproduces daily exertion more faithfully. Throughout the test the operator records a full 12 view ECG continuously, samples the blood pressure at fixed intervals, and watches the patient's face, gait, and speech. The usual endpoint is a target heart rate calculated from the patient's age, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, or a stopping sign such as chest pain, a dangerous rhythm, or a fall in blood pressure.

Some patients cannot exercise, and the stress laboratory must be able to provoke the heart by drug instead. A pharmacological test infuses an agent that raises the heart rate and the force of contraction, or that dilates the coronary arteries and reveals a difference in blood flow between regions. The agent, the dose, the infusion rate, and the duration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An agent that increases the work of the heart can provoke an injury, a rhythm disturbance, or chest pain, and a dilating agent can cause flushing, breathlessness, and a fall in blood pressure, so monitoring matches that of exercise. The drug is given through a secure intravenous line, an antidote for the dilating agents must be immediately available, and a physician trained in resuscitation must remain in the room. A stress laboratory is an emergency room that usually has no emergency, so a defibrillator, a resuscitation bag with masks, suction, oxygen, a crash cart, and a working telephone are checked before the first patient of the day. The characteristic alarm is the monitor's rhythm alarm with its heart rate limits and its low saturation alarm, the hazard is the exercise induced heart attack, and the common operator error is to let the patient grip the treadmill handrails.

Echocardiography answers the questions the electrical tracing cannot, because it shows muscle, valves, and the movement of blood rather than the timing of activation. The instrument works like a depth sounder, because a crystal that changes shape when a voltage is applied is made to vibrate at millions of cycles per second and to produce a voltage when it is squeezed. The pulse of sound it sends into the chest is partly reflected at every boundary where the stiffness of the tissue changes, and the time taken for the echo to return gives the depth of the boundary. The same crystal listens between pulses, so rapid repetition produces a moving image the eye reads as real time motion. The frequency of the sound decides the central trade off, because a higher frequency gives a finer image but penetrates less deeply while a lower frequency reaches the far side of the heart with less detail. The operator therefore chooses a probe and a frequency for the patient's size and the depth of interest, and the frequency, the depth, and the image settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The echocardiography machine offers several ways of using the same echoes. In motion mode a single line of the image is followed over time and the movement of each structure is plotted as a wavy line, which measures the motion of a valve leaflet or a chamber wall. In the cross sectional mode many lines are combined into a fan shaped image that the operator sweeps through the heart, and this is the mode used to judge chamber size, muscle thickness, valve shape, and the squeezing of the ventricles. Doppler modes add the motion of the blood itself, using the fact that sound reflected from moving cells changes its frequency by an amount proportional to the speed of the movement. Pulsed wave Doppler measures flow at one chosen depth up to a speed limit set by the pulse rate, continuous wave Doppler measures the highest speeds without that limit but cannot say at what depth they occurred, and color Doppler paints the same information across the image in shades of red and blue, with every mode setting, angle, and gain value confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A cardiac ultrasound examination is only as good as the window the operator finds and the probe that fits there. The standard transthoracic probe is a small phased array crystal steered electronically to sweep the beam through a sector, and it is pressed between the ribs beside the breastbone, below the breastbone, and at the apex of the heart, because bone blocks sound and air scatters it. A coupling gel fills the microscopic gap between probe and skin, and without it almost all of the sound is reflected at the first boundary and the screen stays black, so the gel is a consumable of the same importance as the electrode. The transesophageal probe is mounted on a flexible gastroscope and looks at the heart from inside the esophagus, where no rib or lung intervenes, at the cost of sedation and of a demanding cleaning routine. Every examination should be documented with a set of standard views, the measurements taken, the reason for the study, and the operator's impression. The images and report are stored in the picture archiving and communication system, PACS, which accepts the standard format of the digital imaging and communications in medicine, DICOM, with the naming and retention rules confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Stress echocardiography joins the exercise or the drug to the image, and it looks for a segment of muscle that stops moving when the heart is asked to work harder. The same views are recorded before the stress, at each stage, and immediately afterward, and the comparison is made between a segment that contracts well at rest and the same segment under load, because a region supplied by a narrowed artery loses its movement before it is permanently damaged. The useful window closes within a minute or 2 of stopping as the heart rate falls, so the images are acquired in a fixed order and compared honestly. A contrast agent may be used when the plain image is poor, and the agent is a suspension of tiny gas bubbles with a thin shell that scatters sound far more strongly than blood or tissue. Those bubbles are destroyed by the sound beam and by the lungs, so they are given intravenously as a slow injection and imaged within minutes, and the dose, the injection rate, and the imaging settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is an allergic reaction that can be severe, so the patient is screened for previous reactions and resuscitation equipment is at hand, while the common operator error is to compare images taken from different positions or depths.

The echocardiography probe is the most fragile expensive object in the room. The face of the probe is a delicate lens that must never be dropped, scraped, or rested on a hard surface, and the cable must be supported so that its weight does not hang from the connector. Cleaning begins at the bedside with removal of the gel, using a soft cloth and the approved disinfectant, and the probe is wiped without being immersed beyond the line marked on its shaft, since fluid entering the handle destroys the electronics. Transesophageal probes must be leak tested before every immersion, cleaned of all biological material, and then given high level disinfection or sterilization, with the concentration, the contact time, the temperature, and the rinsing steps confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Probes are stored hanging vertically so that they are not coiled or crushed, and a probe that shows a broken element, a dark band in the image, or a failed leak test is removed from service at once. The characteristic alarms include a probe over temperature warning and a system or image fault message, and the temperature limit and every alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile clinic or a frontier hospital the full diagnostic machine is usually absent, and the ECG contracts to a rhythm monitor that a single trained operator can carry and trust. The field instrument is commonly a small battery powered monitor with 3 electrodes that produce 1 or 2 views, a screen that can be read in daylight, and a rhythm alarm with a heart rate limit. Its purpose is narrower than diagnosis: it answers whether the rhythm is fast, slow, regular, or dangerously chaotic during a treatment or a transfer. Its electrodes are the same disposables used in the hospital, but heat, dust, and repeated use of one site make them fail sooner, so the operator carries twice as many as the count suggests. Its battery may be the only power for the day, so the unit is charged whenever a socket or a solar panel is available, and the charging state is recorded rather than assumed. Because the screen is small and the trace is often noisy, the operator places the electrodes carefully, keeps the patient still for the initial recording, and stores a baseline strip of that patient's normal rhythm, with the alarm thresholds set to the patient and every limit confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The smartphone has become a genuine field instrument, and it earns that place through 2 mechanisms that must not be confused with one another. A small handheld unit with 2 metal contacts records a single view when the patient touches it with the fingers of both hands or when it is laid against the chest, and a miniature recorder with 2 or 3 adhesive electrodes sends a continuous rhythm to the telephone by a short range radio link. Both methods record a real electrical signal that can be printed, stored, and sent for an opinion, and their tracings are adequate for rhythm but not for fine detail, which still requires a proper 12 view recording. The single most valuable habit in field cardiac diagnosis is the repeat tracing, because a first tracing made in a hot, crowded room with a nervous patient is often uninterpretable. The repeat is made after the patient has rested, after the skin has been prepared again and the electrodes changed, and after any obvious interference has been moved away. If a rhythm is fast, the repeat shows whether it is sustained, and if a tracing suggests an injury, the repeat shows whether the finding is stable rather than a single artifact, with every device limit and alarm threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field kit lives or dies by its consumables, so electrodes, gel, alcohol pads, clippers, tape, spare lead wires, a charged battery, and a means of storing images are all checked before the clinic. Heat dries the gel, softens the adhesive, and drains the batteries, so the kit is stored out of direct sun and the oldest electrodes are used first. Without a cardiologist and without a full machine, the field clinician must decide what can be answered locally and what must be referred. A single view can show a rate, a regularity, the width of the Q, R, and S spike, and the small wave that precedes each beat, enough to recognize many dangerous rhythms and to choose a treatment or a transfer. What it cannot do is localize an injury, measure an interval that needs several simultaneous views, or detect a change that appears in only one of 12 positions, and the clinician must say so plainly rather than guess. The absence of a number is a real loss that must be admitted in the notes, because a confident diagnosis made from an uninterpretable strip is more dangerous than an honest uncertainty, and the service intervals and tolerance limits of every field device must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the ECG records the small voltage that a moving wave of cardiac activation produces at the skin, and every lead is a viewpoint rather than a picture. The hospital machine depends on good electrodes, prepared skin, intact lead wires, a verified calibration pulse, and correct filter and gain settings, and most of its failures are contact and conductor faults the operator must find. Artifact imitates disease, and a poor tracing accepted without question leads to a wrong decision, so every tracing is inspected, repeated when unclear, and documented with the conditions in which it was made. The recording extends in time through ambulatory and event recorders, and it extends in provocation through exercise and drug stress testing, which must be conducted with the resuscitation readiness of an emergency room. Echocardiography adds structure and flow through reflected sound, and its modes, probes, contrast agents, and demanding cleaning routine each carry their own hazards and operator errors. In the field the ECG contracts to a single view on a small monitor or a telephone, and the discipline that replaces the missing machine is skin preparation, a stored baseline, and the habit of the repeat tracing, with every setting, threshold, dose, cycle, and temperature named in this chapter confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 20 — Defibrillators and Pacing

The heart is an electrical organ before it is a pump, and defibrillation overwhelms a chaotic rhythm with one brief, organized wave of current. In normal conduction, depolarization sweeps through the muscle in order, each cell contracting after its neighbor, so the chambers empty and fill usefully. In ventricular fibrillation that order collapses into many small re-entrant circuits wandering at random, so the tissue quivers rather than squeezes. The only escape is to depolarize a critical mass of muscle at the same instant, which extinguishes every circuit at once and lets the heart's own pacemaker tissue restart. What the machine controls is not voltage but current density inside the chest, and the current that reaches the heart depends on the resistance of the path, called transthoracic impedance. That impedance is set by the chest wall, the lungs, the heart, the size and position of the electrodes, the pressure applied, and above all by how well skin and electrode conduct. A listener who understands that the dial controls stored energy while the heart receives current will see why the same setting succeeds in one patient and fails in the next.

The electrodes are part of the electrical circuit, and their size, position, and contact decide how much current the heart sees. A large electrode spreads the current over a wider area, lowering the impedance and reducing the risk of a skin burn, while a small one concentrates the current and raises the impedance. Firm pressure improves contact, which is why the paddles are pressed down hard, and a hairy or wet chest with poor adhesion behaves like a small electrode. One electrode below the right collarbone and the other at the left side below the armpit sends the current roughly along the long axis of the heart, while a front and back placement sends it from another direction. Both positions work, but the operator must never allow the 2 electrodes to touch, because contact shorts the current across the skin. The hazard of a misplaced or heavily gelled electrode is a burn or a shock that misses the heart, and the common error is to press the paddles together or let gel bridge the gap between them.

A defibrillator is essentially a capacitor, charged over several seconds from a battery or from the mains and then discharged across the chest in a few thousandths of a second. The energy stored is described in joules, and the energy that reaches the heart is only a fraction of it, because some is lost inside the machine and much depends on impedance. Nominal first shock energies for an adult commonly lie between 120 and 200 joules for a biphasic device and up to 360 joules for a monophasic one, and every one of those figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The shape of the discharge in time is the waveform, and the oldest form is monophasic, in which current flows one way and stops, usually requiring high energies. The modern form is biphasic, in which the current reverses partway through the pulse, lowering the threshold and allowing success with less energy and less injury. Many machines also measure the impedance and adjust the duration or the voltage to compensate, so a thick chest may receive a longer pulse than a thin one. The common misunderstanding is that a higher number on the dial always means a stronger shock, when a well shaped lower energy pulse may succeed where a poorly shaped higher one fails.

The manual defibrillator is the hospital-grade instrument, and it usually combines a monitor showing an electrocardiogram, a defibrillator, and often a pacing unit. The front carries the electrocardiogram trace, the energy controls, a charge control, and either 2 paddles or a pair of adhesive pads on cables. The paddles are pressed firmly onto the chest, and the operator holds clear while calling a warning and checking that nobody is touching the patient, the bed, or a wet surface. The stored energy is lethal if it crosses a person's heart, so every member of the team must be clear before the discharge control is pressed, and the operator must be able to see every pair of hands. A thin layer of conductive gel must lie between electrode and skin, because dry contact burns and concentrates the current, while excess gel can bridge the electrodes and divert the current across the chest. The characteristic alarm is the rising charge-ready tone, and its absence after charging is a machine fault that must be treated as a failure rather than as a slow patient. The common error is to charge before the team is ready, which wastes battery and creates a charged device in a crowded room, and the second is to discharge while a colleague still touches the patient.

Synchronized cardioversion times the discharge to the patient's own electrical cycle rather than delivering it at random. The machine reads the electrocardiogram, marks each tall R wave, and delays the discharge by a few thousandths of a second so that it falls outside the vulnerable part of the cycle, where a shock can provoke ventricular fibrillation. The synchronizer is used for rhythms that still produce a pulse, such as atrial fibrillation and unstable organized rapid rhythms, and never for ventricular fibrillation, where there is no R wave to sense. Sedation and analgesia are needed whenever the patient is conscious, and the drugs and their doses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The starting energy for cardioversion is usually lower than the energy used for defibrillation, and that energy and any step up must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to leave the synchronizer switched on after a cardioversion, because the machine will then refuse to discharge during a later arrest while it waits for a marker that never comes. The alarm that matters is the message that no marker has been detected, and the operator must check the sync indicator before every shock rather than trust memory.

Children change both the physics and the settings, because a small chest has a lower impedance and less muscle to depolarize. Manual machines offer smaller pediatric paddles or pads, and some use an attenuator that reduces the delivered energy to a fraction of the selected value, so the attenuator must be fitted correctly. Automatic machines often ship with a pediatric attenuator, a key, or a switch, and the age or the weight at which it is used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The nominal child energy is chosen by weight, and that weight-based dose and the maximum permitted energy must both be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Placement in a small chest may be front and back rather than front and side, so that the 2 electrodes do not touch and short the current across the skin. The hazard is contact between the pads, and the common error is to use adult pads on a small child without an attenuator, delivering far more energy than was intended.

The automated external defibrillator removes the decision from the operator's hands, using an algorithm that analyzes the electrical signal for a shockable rhythm. The operator attaches 2 adhesive pads, one below the right collarbone and one at the left side, switches the device on, and follows voice prompts ordering everyone to stand clear while the rhythm is analyzed. The algorithm looks for the coarse, irregular activity of ventricular fibrillation and the fast, wide complexes of pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and advises a shock only for those 2 patterns, leaving every other rhythm to be treated by cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Movement, compressions, and a loose electrode corrupt the analysis, which is why the device orders hands off the patient, and a team that ignores that order may cause a shockable rhythm to be misread as a normal one. After a shock the device prompts for a fixed period of compressions and then analyzes again, and that compression interval and the whole sequence must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is the spoken order to stand clear followed by the shock advisory, while a problem with the pads is announced as a message to check them. The common error is to interrupt compressions for too long while the pads are found, because every second without circulation lowers the chance that the next shock will succeed.

Every automated external defibrillator runs a self-test on a schedule, checking its circuitry, its battery, and its pads, and displays a readiness symbol. Some units test daily, some weekly, and some run a partial test daily and a fuller test at a longer interval, and the schedule and its meaning must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The battery is a sealed pack rated for years of standby, and the pads are sealed in foil with an expiry date, so readiness depends on both of them as much as on the electronics. A device with out of date pads may still show readiness on some models and will still fail to shock, which is why the dates must be read by a person rather than inferred from a light. Some units store a record of their self-tests for later interrogation, and that record is the only proof that the checks actually happened. The common failure in a well-run hospital is a battery taken for another device and never returned, and the common failure in a neglected cupboard is a readiness symbol that was assumed rather than seen.

The consumables of defibrillation are few, cheap, and fatal to omit, and the first is the pad or the gel that makes the electrical contact. Adhesive pads carry their own gel, are sealed in foil, and bear an expiry date, and an expired pad loses moisture, adheres poorly, and raises impedance so that less current reaches the heart. Bottled gel for paddles dries, thickens, and becomes contaminated once it is opened, and a bottle whose contents have separated must be discarded rather than stirred back into use. Monitoring electrodes are needed at the same time as the pads, because the machine must show a rhythm before and after the shock. A single-use razor belongs in the kit, because hair under a pad adds impedance and weakens adhesion, and gauze and scissors are equally ordinary and equally necessary. Thermal printer paper, a spare battery, a test load for the technician, a pediatric attenuator, and pacing cables complete the list, and the stock level and replacement interval of each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The used pads and packaging are contaminated with the patient's blood and sweat and belong in the clinical waste stream, and the daily check must confirm the pad dates, the gel, the battery, and the readiness symbol.

In the hospital the defibrillator is one part of an organized system, and the system is what makes it usable within seconds. The device lives on a crash cart or in a wall bracket in every area where a patient may arrest, including the emergency department, the intensive care unit, the catheterization laboratory, and every general ward. The cart carries the pads, the gel, the electrodes, the razors, the suction, the airway equipment, and the drugs, and it is sealed with a numbered tag so that a missing item is visible before the arrest rather than during it. The defibrillator is kept connected to the mains so that its battery stays charged, and many hospitals put that socket on an emergency power circuit, an arrangement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The team is organized as well, with defined roles for compressions, airway, drugs, and the defibrillator, and the person on the defibrillator calls the shocks aloud so that the others can time their work around them. The machine records the rhythm, the shocks, and the times, and that record is filed with the patient's notes and often into the electronic health record. The characteristic failure of the system is a cart whose seal was broken days ago and never replaced, so that the next arrest begins with a search for a pad.

The daily check of a hospital defibrillator is a short ritual that a nurse can perform, and its purpose is to find the failure before the arrest. The operator looks at the readiness indicator, switches the device on, verifies that a rhythm appears on the screen, checks the date and time, confirms the pads and the gel, and confirms that the battery is charged and correctly seated. The biomedical technician performs deeper tests on a schedule with a defibrillator analyzer that measures delivered energy, pulse duration, peak current, and the impedance of a simulated patient. The delivered energy must fall within the tolerance set by the maker, and that tolerance and the test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The technician also verifies the synchronizer with a simulated electrocardiogram, tests the pacing output into a load, and checks the leakage current of the patient circuit. The battery fails most often, because it ages silently whether or not the machine is used, and a pack charged daily for years still holds less and less. The written record of these tests is the only proof that the device was verified, and an untested machine that looks clean is not a tested machine.

The maintenance failure discovered during a resuscitation is almost always a flat battery, a dried pad, a loose electrode, or a cable cracked inside its insulation. Each is invisible in a cupboard and obvious in an arrest, and each can be prevented by a check that takes less than a minute. A flat battery is the most common, because a device left on its charger in a warm cupboard may still lose capacity, and a spare pack never rotated may be as old as the machine. A dried pad comes next, because the foil was opened and imperfectly resealed, or the pad was stored in heat and the gel that should conduct became a dry film. A loose electrode is third, because the trace depends on skin contact, and a patient being moved, compressed, and shocked will shed electrodes. The cracked cable is the most treacherous, because it passes every test while it lies still and fails the moment it is pulled across a chest. The defense is the daily check, the documented functional test, and a spare device or a spare set of consumables within reach.

Cleaning after use is quick but must be done properly, because the same machine may be needed within minutes and one patient's residue must not become the next patient's hazard. The paddles are wiped free of gel, dried, and inspected for a dried film or a brown pit on the electrode surface, either of which reduces contact. The housing is wiped with the approved disinfectant, and liquid must never be poured onto the machine or allowed to run into the vents, because fluid in the high-voltage section can cause a short or a shock to the next operator. The cables are wiped along their length, uncoiled, and inspected for cracks and exposed conductors, because a cable that fails only when it is bent will pass every test and fail every arrest. Abrasive agents, solvents, and excessive moisture must be avoided as the maker directs, with the cleaning agent and the contact time confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The used pads are discarded, the gel bottle is closed, and the machine is returned to its charger, and if it was used on a patient with a transmissible infection the local decontamination rules apply, confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Transcutaneous pacing uses the same large adhesive pads but delivers a much smaller current, repeated at a set rate, to capture the ventricles when the heart's own conduction has failed. The machine generates pulses of a few tens of milliamperes, each lasting a few thousandths of a second, large enough to depolarize muscle through the chest wall and small enough to avoid injury. The operator sets a rate and an output, attaches the pads, and increases the output until each pulse produces a wide complex on the screen and a pulse that can be felt at the wrist. That moment is capture, and it is the only proof that the machine is truly pacing rather than merely stimulating the chest wall. Typical outputs range from about 40 to 70 milliamperes and typical rates from 60 to 80 per minute, and both figures, together with the method of confirming capture and the sedation needed, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The discomfort is severe, because the current contracts every skeletal muscle in the chest and the diaphragm with every pulse, so analgesia and sedation are essential and the patient must be warned. The characteristic alarm is the message that capture has been lost, and the common error is to trust the pacing spike on the screen as proof of capture, when the spike proves only that the machine discharged.

An implanted pacemaker is a small sealed generator under the skin of the chest, connected by insulated leads that pass through a vein into the right atrium, the right ventricle, or both. The generator senses the heart's own electrical activity and delivers a tiny pulse only when a beat is missing, which is called demand pacing, and it can also pace at a fixed rate when it is programmed to ignore what it senses. The device is programmed before implantation and can be reprogrammed later by a programmer, a dedicated computer with a wand or a cable that communicates with the generator through the skin. The programmer also reads the stored history, including the rate, the recorded episodes, and the remaining battery voltage, and interrogation is the only way to know what an implanted device is doing. A magnet placed over the generator closes a switch inside it and forces a fixed, asynchronous rate, and the effect of the magnet and the rate it produces must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Electrosurgery, magnetic resonance imaging, large magnets, and strong radio transmitters can all interfere with an implanted device, because the circuit may mistake them for the heart's own signal or may reset itself. The interference may make the device withhold a beat, pace too fast, or change to a default mode, so the return pad of an electrosurgical unit is kept far from the chest and the device is interrogated after any procedure that could have disturbed it.

An implanted cardioverter defibrillator is a pacemaker with a wider mandate, because it senses the same signals but is permitted to treat dangerous rhythms rather than only to support a slow one. When it recognizes a rapid rhythm it may first try a burst of fast pacing called antitachycardia pacing, which is painless, and only then deliver an internal shock. The internal shock is far smaller than an external one because the current passes directly between the lead and the generator, but the patient feels it as a blow to the chest that may be repeated several times. Interrogation reveals how many episodes occurred, what therapy was delivered, and whether any shock was appropriate, and that record guides every later decision about drugs and programming. A magnet over the device usually suspends the shock function while leaving pacing intact, and that behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. If external defibrillation is needed, the adhesive pads are placed front and back so that the current does not pass through the generator, and they are never placed directly over it. After any resuscitation or electrosurgery the implanted device must be interrogated, because a shock or an electromagnetic field can change its programming and leave the patient unprotected without anyone noticing.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the defibrillator is almost always an automated external defibrillator, because it is the only version that a small team can use safely without a physician at the bedside. The field device gives up the screen, the manual energy selection, the synchronized cardioversion, and the transcutaneous pacing of the hospital machine, and in exchange it offers a sealed case, a long shelf life, and a voice that tells an untrained rescuer what to do. Its pads are chosen for long life and a wide temperature range, its battery is rated for years of standby rather than for many shocks, and its self-test runs without anyone thinking about it. The advantage is decisive, because a nurse or a clinical officer who has never interpreted a rhythm can still deliver a shock within the first minutes. The price is that the device cannot treat a fast rhythm that still produces a pulse, cannot pace a slow heart, and cannot show the team the rhythm, so a patient who needs cardioversion or pacing must be moved to a hospital that holds the manual machine. The field unit depends entirely on consumables that must be replaced on schedule, and the expiry dates of the pads and the battery are the single most important information written on the case. Heat, humidity, dust, and the vibration of a vehicle all age the device, and the rule in the field is that it is checked at the start of every shift and after every journey, with the check written down.

Where a trained operator does exist, a manual defibrillator belongs in the field kit as well, because it can do what the automated device cannot and the clinical difference is real. The field manual device is usually a compact battery-powered monitor with paddles or pads, a small screen, a recorder, and sometimes pacing, and it gives up the large display, the mains supply, and the printer of the hospital unit. It demands a trained operator on every shift, a disciplined battery rotation, a stock of pads and gel that does not expire unnoticed, and the self-control to discharge only when the whole team is clear. It also demands a working electrocardiogram, because a manual shock without a rhythm is a blind shock, and the electrodes, the cables, and the screen are therefore part of the defibrillator rather than optional accessories. The team must know in advance which device is primary, where the pads are stored, how the battery is charged from a vehicle or a solar panel, and who is responsible for the daily check when the usual nurse is away. A device that depends on one trained person is fragile, so at least 2 members of the team should be able to use it and the skill must be refreshed on a fixed schedule. The honest field position is that an automated defibrillator with fresh pads and a charged battery saves more lives in most remote settings than a manual machine that nobody present has been trained to use.

The maintenance of a field defibrillator is mostly the work of the people who carry it, because the biomedical technician may visit once a year or never. The operator must check the readiness symbol, the expiry dates of the pads and the battery, the case and its seal, the gel if paddles are used, and every cable, and must record the check with a name and a date. The self-test is the device's own maintenance system, and its result must be read rather than assumed, because a machine that blinks a readiness light while its pads are 2 years out of date is ready to monitor and unable to shock. The characteristic failures in the field are a battery that has lost capacity after repeated partial charging, pads whose gel has dried in the heat, a screen that cannot be read in direct sunlight, and a cable crushed in a vehicle door. When the self-test fails, the device must be withdrawn from service and labeled, and the failure must be reported rather than hidden, because a machine quietly left on the shelf is a machine that will fail at the worst possible moment. The team must also plan for the case in which the device works but the operator does not, so practice with the actual machine, the actual pads, and the actual battery is part of maintenance in the fullest sense.

To summarize, a defibrillator stores electrical energy in a capacitor and releases it in a few thousandths of a second to depolarize a critical mass of heart muscle at once, and almost everything else about the device follows from that single fact. The hospital manual defibrillator adds a monitor, a synchronizer for cardioversion, pediatric energy control, and transcutaneous pacing, and it needs mains power, a biomedical service schedule, and a trained operator who can read the rhythm on the screen. The automated external defibrillator gives up the screen and the manual controls, and in exchange it lets a small team in a remote clinic deliver a shock within the first minutes, which is the interval that decides survival. The hazards are the charged capacitor and the wet or gel-bridged chest, the operator errors are charging too early, shocking into a vulnerable part of the cycle, leaving the synchronizer on, and mistaking a pacing spike for capture, and the alarms are the charge-ready tone, the stand clear prompt, the loss of capture message, and the low battery warning. The consumables are pads, gel, monitoring electrodes, batteries, printer paper, and razors, and their expiry dates and stock levels decide whether any of the rest of it works. The maintenance failure found during a resuscitation is almost always a flat battery, a dried pad, a loose electrode, or a cracked cable, and the daily check exists to find it the day before instead. If the reader remembers only one instruction, let it be that no setting, energy, rate, threshold, or interval in this chapter may be used from memory, and that each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 21 — Resuscitation Equipment

Resuscitation equipment is not one machine but a system of parts that must work together within minutes, and its physical principle is that two failures kill at the same time. The first is the failure of ventilation, because without a moving column of gas the alveoli receive no fresh oxygen and the blood leaving the lungs carries nothing usable. The second is the failure of circulation, because a stopped heart delivers no oxygen to the brain even when the lungs are full. Chest compressions squeeze the heart between the sternum and the spine and raise the pressure inside the chest so that blood is pushed out and flows back as the chest recoils. Every device here restores one of those two functions or keeps the brain alive while both are restored, and the arrangement of the equipment matters as much as the equipment itself. A resuscitation is a race against the metabolism of the brain, which tolerates only a short interruption of flow.

The crash cart turns that collection of parts into something a team can use in the dark. It is a cabinet on four casters, usually waist high to chest high, with a flat lipped top, three to five drawers that grow deeper toward the bottom, and a handle for pushing. Two casters swivel and two are fixed, with brakes, because the cart must turn a corner and cross a threshold without being lifted. The top carries the defibrillator on a bracket, a monitor, a small oxygen cylinder in its own holder, and a suction unit with a canister. The shallow upper drawers hold airway items and drugs, while the deep lower drawers hold fluids, giving sets, suction catheters, and spare tubing. The exact layout of every drawer must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the cart is placed in service.

The order of the drawers is a deliberate use of spatial memory, because under stress the mind loses the ability to search systematically. A team that has opened the same cart in the same order many times reaches for a laryngoscope, a syringe, or a fluid bag along a path the hand already knows, without the eyes leaving the patient. Every cart in an institution should therefore be laid out identically, and a cart borrowed from another department can slow a team even when nothing is missing. The numbered single-use seal through the hasp completes that discipline, because it cannot be reopened without leaving evidence of the fact. The commonest error in the whole system is the hurried clinician who takes one item during an arrest and pushes the drawer shut with the same seal, leaving a gap nobody discovers until the next patient needs it. The seal number, the lock, and the inspection interval must be confirmed against the local protocol before the cart enters service.

The defibrillator sits on the top surface because it is the only device on the cart that can restart a heart, and its physical principle is the capacitor. Two conducting plates separated by an insulator store charge and release it across the chest in a few thousandths of a second, and that stored energy is measured in joules. A typical adult biphasic shock delivers 120 to 200 joules, an energy level that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pads are adhesive electrodes that both sense the rhythm and carry the shock, so their gel must be moist and their expiry date current, because a dried pad burns the skin and conducts poorly. The characteristic sound is a rising charge tone followed by a discharge, while a steady low-battery tone warns that the device may not deliver its full stored energy. A shock advisory that keeps repeating means the algorithm still detects a treatable rhythm.

The oxygen supply on the cart is a small cylinder with a regulator and a flowmeter, and its physics is the release of a compressed gas. The cylinder holds gas at many times atmospheric pressure, the regulator reduces that to a safe working level, and the flowmeter, a tapered tube with a small ball, shows the rate in liters per minute. A common resuscitation flow is 10 to 15 liters per minute through a reservoir mask, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is a cylinder that only reads full because the gauge was never checked, and the commonest error is to open the valve part way, which starves the flowmeter and lets the reservoir bag collapse. A low-pressure whistle or a gauge that falls during use is the characteristic alarm, and the correct response is to switch to the spare cylinder rather than hunt for a leak. Every cylinder should be exchanged at the end of a call.

Suction keeps the airway clear of blood, vomit, and secretions, and it works by a pressure difference between the patient's airway and a collection jar. A pump or wall vacuum line removes air from the jar, so fluid is drawn through the catheter because the pressure inside the tubing is lower than the pressure in the mouth. The vacuum is set on a regulator, usually between 80 and 120 millimeters of mercury for an adult, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A manual suction unit replaces the pump with a hand-operated piston or bellows and is the fallback when there is no vacuum line and no electricity. The characteristic alarm is the float valve of a full canister, which rises and blocks the suction path with a sudden loss of vacuum, and the commonest error is to keep suctioning through a full jar. The catheter must be measured against the patient before insertion, because one driven too deep can injure the airway or provoke a slow heart.

The bag-valve-mask is the most important single object on the cart, and it works by elastic recoil rather than by any motor. Squeezing the self-inflating bag pushes its volume through a one-way valve into the mask, and when the hand releases the bag springs back and draws the next breath through an inlet valve while the patient valve closes so exhaled gas leaves by a separate port. A reservoir bag or an oxygen inlet raises the delivered concentration toward 100 per cent when the flow is high enough, a target that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The mask must seal over the bridge of the nose and the cleft of the chin, and the usual technique is a two-hand grip with a jaw thrust while an assistant squeezes the bag. The hazard is gastric insufflation, in which gas forced too fast enters the esophagus, distends the stomach, and pushes the diaphragm up so the lungs cannot fill. The characteristic failure is silent, because a leaking mask raises no alarm, only poor chest rise and a falling oxygen saturation.

The oral and nasal airways are simple plastic tubes that hold the tongue away from the back of the throat, and their principle is geometry. In an unconscious patient the tongue falls backward because the muscles that hold it forward have lost their tone, and a curved tube placed over the tongue follows the arc of the mouth and pharynx. An oral airway is measured from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, and sizes are marked in millimeters or by color, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A nasal airway is a soft beveled tube passed along the floor of the nose, and it is tolerated by patients who still have a gag reflex. The commonest error is an airway so long that it pushes the epiglottis down over the larynx instead of lifting it, and the second is placing an oral airway in a patient awake enough to vomit. The supraglottic airway forms a low-pressure seal above the larynx with a soft cuff that inflates behind the tongue, and its sizes are chosen by body weight, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A tracheal tube is the definitive airway because it seals the trachea with a cuff and protects the lungs from stomach contents. The physics is a balloon against a tube wall, and the cuff is inflated until the space around the tube closes, typically to a pressure of 20 to 30 centimeters of water, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Tube sizes are given as the internal diameter in millimeters, so a typical adult tube is 7 to 8 millimeters, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The laryngoscope is a handle of batteries and a blade with a light, and a video laryngoscope puts a camera at the blade tip and shows the cords on a screen when the neck cannot be moved. Placement must be confirmed by watching the chest rise, listening over both lungs and over the stomach, and above all by detecting exhaled carbon dioxide with a colorimetric detector or a waveform capnograph. A dead battery in the laryngoscope handle is the classic maintenance failure discovered during a resuscitation.

The drug compartment carries a small pharmacy chosen for speed, and the first principle of that pharmacy is concentration. Drugs arrive as a glass ampoule that must be snapped open, a powder that must be dissolved, a rubber-capped vial from which a dose is drawn, or a prefilled syringe that needs no preparation. The commonest resuscitation drug is adrenaline, also called epinephrine, and it exists in at least two strengths, one of which is meant to be diluted before intravenous use, so the label must be read at arm's length and then again at the syringe. A common dilution is 1 milligram of adrenaline in 10 milliliters for a bolus and 1 milligram in 1000 milliliters for an infusion, and every concentration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Other drugs usually present include amiodarone for a shockable rhythm, atropine for a slow heart, sodium bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, dextrose, and naloxone for opioid overdose. The hazard is the wrong dilution, which is the same as the wrong drug.

The prefilled syringe removes preparation from the most hurried moment in medicine, and its physics is a plunger in a sealed barrel. Because the maker filled and sealed it, the volume and concentration are fixed and the operator needs only to connect the syringe to a port and push. The trade is cost and shelf life against seconds, so each hospital must decide which drugs are worth carrying prefilled, and the expiry dates on prefilled syringes are shorter than many people expect. The drug drawer is arranged by color coding, dividers, and labels that print the differing parts of similar names in larger letters, and the compartments follow the order in which the drugs are likely to be needed. The commonest error is not a wrong drug but a missing one, because a vial returned to the wrong compartment makes the next search slower. An opened ampoule, a punctured vial, or an unlabeled syringe is waste and must be removed and recorded rather than left for the next team.

Circulation equipment begins with access, and access is a problem of flow. A peripheral cannula lets fluid and drug enter the circulation, and its size is given in gauge, where a smaller number means a larger bore, so a 14 gauge cannula carries far more than a 22 gauge one. Flow through any tube depends far more on its radius than on its length, which is why a short wide cannula in a large vein outperforms a long narrow catheter at the same pressure. When no vein can be found, an intraosseous needle is driven into the marrow cavity of a long bone, usually the upper tibia or the humerus, and the cavity acts as a non-collapsible vein that a falling blood pressure cannot shut. Adult needles are commonly 15 or 25 millimeters long and 15 gauge, measurements that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is a needle that passes through the bone or an entry site that becomes infected.

Fluids are carried as bags of crystalloid solution, and getting them in quickly is again a problem of pressure. A bag hung high on a pole flows because gravity provides the pressure, but the rate is usually limited by the narrowest part of the giving set, so a pressure cuff around the bag or a hand pump on the tubing raises the driving pressure. A rapid infusion device warms and pumps fluid at high flow and is reserved for massive hemorrhage, while a simple blood warmer with a coil is the common substitute. The commonest error is to expect a narrow cannula to deliver a rapid bolus, which it cannot, and the second is to forget that an unspiked bag may contain a drug someone added. Every pressure, rate, and temperature used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the same rule applies to the volume of any bolus given to a child.

The compression feedback device measures what the hands are actually doing, and it works with a small accelerometer and a force sensor inside a pad or a puck. The accelerometer detects the depth and rate of each compression, and the force sensor detects whether the chest is fully released, because a hand resting on the chest during recoil stops the heart from refilling. The usual targets are a depth of 5 to 6 centimeters and a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute with full recoil, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is a spoken prompt or a changing tone telling the operator to push harder, to push faster, or to release fully, and a device that never complains is often one placed under the patient out of position. The commonest operator error is to silence the tone as an annoyance, when it is the only objective witness of compression quality in the room. The device is an aid and not a substitute for rotation, because the compressor tires and quality falls.

The mechanical compression machine replaces the tired human hand with a motor and comes in two broad forms. The piston device presses a pad down on the sternum at a set depth and rate, while the load-distributing band wraps around the chest and tightens cyclically, and both depend on a battery and on strapping that holds the patient in one position. Its principle is repetition without fatigue, because the machine never tires and never leans on the chest, and it frees one member of the team for other tasks. The hazards are a piston set too low and pressing on the abdomen, a band that slips up onto the neck or down onto the belly, and a battery that empties during a long resuscitation. The characteristic alarms are a low-battery tone and a device fault tone, and the thresholds for both must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The commonest operator error is to apply the device without pausing compressions for longer than a few seconds.

The checklists, the seal, and the expiry dates make a cart trustworthy, and they work on the principle that a closed drawer cannot be seen. The daily and shift check follows a fixed route: the seal number is read against the log, the lock is tested, the defibrillator runs its self-test, the pads and their expiry dates are inspected, the oxygen pressure is recorded, the suction is run, the laryngoscope light is switched on, the bag is squeezed to test its valves, and the drugs are counted. Expiry dates are managed by rotation on a first in and first out rule, because a deep drawer can hide expired ampoules beneath fresh ones and the only defense is to empty each compartment and rebuild it in order. The commonest error is to check the front row and the outward-facing labels, since the items that fail are the ones that cannot be seen. A cart without a completed log is treated as unchecked, and every pressure and expiry interval used in the check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The pediatric cart differs from the adult cart in scale and in logic, because a child is not a small adult. Every device is duplicated in smaller sizes, so there are masks from newborn to adolescent, airways in a range of lengths, tracheal tubes from 2.5 millimeters upward, smaller self-inflating bags of about 250 milliliters, and smaller suction catheters, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The defibrillator uses pediatric pads with a smaller contact area, and the energy selected is usually 2 joules per kilogram for the first shock, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Drugs are almost always diluted because the dose is calculated per kilogram, and the cart usually carries a length-based tape that estimates weight from height and prints each dose in a colored band. The characteristic hazard is the decimal point, because a misplaced point can multiply a dose tenfold. A child also consumes the small sizes faster than an adult consumes the large ones.

The failures that matter most are discovered during a resuscitation, and they are almost always the same handful. A laryngoscope whose battery was left switched on in the drawer is dead when it is needed, an oxygen cylinder used for transport was never exchanged, pads whose gel has dried adhere poorly and burn the skin, a suction canister left full has no vacuum at all, and a compression device has a battery that no longer holds charge. The characteristic alarms each mean something specific: the defibrillator gives a rising charge tone, a discharge, and a steady low-battery tone, the compression device signals a low battery or a fault, the suction unit blocks at the canister float, the oxygen system falls silent at the gauge or whistles, and the monitor repeats a lead-off beep. Every one of those thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The commonest error is to silence the alarm without naming its cause, which turns a warning into silence, and the correct habit is to say the alarm aloud and assign someone to fix it. A cart can also be too heavy to move or blocked by a bed.

Maintenance is a scheduled program with a biomedical technician, and it exists because a device that is never used still ages. The defibrillator is tested at intervals for delivered energy, and the interval and method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a capacitor that has drifted may deliver far less than its display promises. Batteries are the shortest-lived part of almost everything on the cart and are replaced on a calendar rather than on failure, with the replacement date written on the casing. Mechanical compression devices need their straps and contacts inspected, feedback devices need their calibration verified against a known reference, suction regulators need their gauges checked, and the cart itself needs its wheels and latch maintained. Cleaning follows the same division as every department, so laryngoscope blades are cleaned of all visible soil and then disinfected or sterilized by a validated method, often by steam at 134 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes or at 121 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes. Those cycles, and every disinfectant contact time used on the cart, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of the crash cart are ordinary and inexpensive, and their management is what keeps the expensive machines useful. The list includes gloves and other personal protective equipment, syringes and needles, alcohol swabs, gauze, tape, a tourniquet, intravenous cannulae, intraosseous needles, fluid bags and giving sets, airways, tracheal tubes, suction catheters, defibrillator pads, batteries, a sharps container, biohazard bags, and the forms for recording the event. Infection is a real hazard of resuscitation because the work is fast, close, and often bloody, so gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection go on before contact even though the delay is genuine. The commonest injury is a needle left on a tray or recapped by hand, which is why a sharps container must sit within arm's reach of the drug drawer and must never be overfilled. Documentation turns the event into information that can be reviewed, and a designated recorder writes the times of the arrest, of each drug, of each shock and its energy in joules, and of the return of circulation as they happen. The record is entered into the electronic health record afterwards, the cart is restocked and resealed, and the new seal number is written in the log on the same shift.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the resuscitation kit is a soft bag that one person can carry, and its principle is that everything must work without a wall, a pipe, or a mains outlet. The bag is a rucksack or shoulder satchel with padded compartments and a reflective strip, and it holds a self-inflating bag with masks in several sizes, a set of oral airways, a pocket mask, a manual suction pump, a small oxygen cylinder with a regulator, a portable automated external defibrillator, intraosseous needles, a tourniquet, gauze and dressings, a few essential drugs, and a laminated checklist. The weight is the central design problem, because a bag that is too heavy is left in the vehicle, so the field kit is built around what the first responder can carry for a kilometer. Every pressure, flow, and energy setting in the bag must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The bag is repacked in daylight after every call, against the written list, because a soft bag has no drawers to keep an item in its place.

The field variant gives up a great deal, and an honest list of the losses is more useful than optimism. There is no mechanical compression machine, no multiparameter monitor, no rapid infusion device, no blood bank, no cold chain for temperature-sensitive drugs, no piped suction, no wall oxygen, and usually no waveform capnography to confirm a tracheal tube. What remains is the hand, the bag, the defibrillator, and a small set of drugs, and the discipline that replaces the missing hardware is rotation of the compressor. Because no device measures the quality of compressions, the team must change the person compressing every 2 minutes, an interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the leader must count aloud. A mechanical metronome or a timer with an audible tone substitutes for the feedback device, and a written tally of shocks and drugs substitutes for the monitor's memory. The field kit therefore demands more skill from the operator, not less, because there is no alarm to announce a failure.

Some equipment cannot be carried at all, and the field clinician must know that boundary before the patient arrives. Pacing, invasive monitoring, mechanical chest compression, blood products, surgical airways beyond a basic cricothyrotomy kit, and any device needing a stable mains supply are hospital resources, and a resuscitation that needs them must move toward the hospital rather than wait for the equipment to arrive. The decision to transport is itself a clinical decision made early, and the field kit must include the means to keep the patient alive during the movement, which means a bag, an oxygen cylinder, a defibrillator, and secured access. The commonest error in this setting is to spend time on a procedure the kit cannot support while the transport window closes. Every drug, energy level, and interval used during transport must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field environment attacks the kit in ways a hospital cart never experiences, so the maintenance routine is built around weather rather than around a calendar. Heat softens the adhesive of defibrillator pads and shortens the life of batteries, dust clogs suction filters and valve seats, humidity corrodes contacts and grows mold inside tubing stored damp, and altitude changes the pressure inside a partly used cylinder. Batteries are charged from a solar panel where mains power is absent, and the state of charge is written on a tag at the end of each day, because a discharged defibrillator is an empty bag with a handle. Restocking happens after every call, in daylight, from the written list, and the seal or zip tie is replaced and its number logged. A field kit checked once a week is not checked, and the person who carries it must confirm that every setting and expiry date in it has been confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A resuscitation succeeds or fails as a team, and the equipment exists to give each role its own instrument. One person compresses, one manages the airway, one operates the defibrillator and the monitor, one gives drugs and manages access, one keeps time and records, and one leads by stepping back and calling the plan aloud. The cart is arranged so that each of these people reaches a different part of it without colliding, which is why the compressor stands at the chest and the drug person stands at the drawer behind the shoulder. Closed-loop communication is a piece of equipment as real as the laryngoscope: the leader names the task and the person, the person repeats it back, and the person reports when it is done. The commonest organizational error is the silent room in which everyone works hard and nobody knows what has been given. The final guarantee of readiness is practice rather than purchase, because a cart that has never been opened in a drill is a cabinet of unverified assumptions, and regular simulation with the actual cart exposes the jammed wheel and the drug nobody can find.

To summarize, resuscitation equipment is a system built around two physical failures, the failure to move gas and the failure to move blood, and every item on the cart answers one of them. The crash cart is a cabinet with a fixed geography, a numbered seal, and a checklist, and its drawers hold the airway, the drugs, the circulation supplies, and the bulk items in an order the hand can learn. The defibrillator stores energy in a capacitor, the bag inflates by elastic recoil, suction works by a pressure difference, and the intraosseous needle turns the marrow into a vein. Compression feedback devices and mechanical compression machines protect the quality of a task that tires the human hand, while the pediatric cart duplicates everything in smaller sizes with doses calculated by weight. The cart is kept trustworthy by the daily check, by date rotation, by scheduled maintenance, by disciplined cleaning and reprocessing, and by honest recording after every event. In the field the same system shrinks into a bag that one person can carry, it gives up the monitor, the pipeline, the blood, and the machine, and it demands instead a timer, a counted rotation, a charged battery, and the judgment to move early. Whatever the setting, the discipline is the same: know the order of the cart, check the seal, confirm every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, watch the chest and the clock, and restock before the next patient.

# Chapter 22 — Cardiac Catheterization and Interventional Tools

The cardiac catheterization laboratory is a room built around one large machine. Its purpose is to see the inside of blood vessels and the chambers of the heart while a physician works within them. The physical principle is differential attenuation, because a beam of X-rays is absorbed in different fractions by structures of different density. Bone and metal absorb a great deal, soft tissue and blood absorb little, and an iodinated liquid absorbs far more than the blood it displaces, so an injected vessel appears dark against a pale field.

The images are made while they are needed rather than afterwards, which is what makes the procedure interventional. Fluoroscopy is X-ray imaging performed at a low dose for each frame and displayed continuously. The operator therefore sees a moving picture rather than a single exposure. The older detector was an image intensifier, a vacuum tube that turned the pattern into a small bright image for a camera to record. The modern detector is a flat panel of semiconductor material that converts X-rays directly into an electrical charge at every pixel.

A fixed angiography system is usually mounted as a C-arm, a curved gantry holding the tube on one side and the detector on the other. The gantry rotates to give many angles of view without moving anyone, and a biplane system has 2 arms roughly perpendicular to each other. The patient lies on a table that can be raised, tilted, and floated, so its top slides and a catheter can be advanced without moving the patient. The table has a stated weight limit and must be locked while the patient is positioned. That limit, the allowable tilt, and the floating function must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Several features of the system reduce the radiation received by the patient and the staff. Collimation narrows the beam to the region of interest, and added filtration removes the low-energy X-rays that would be absorbed in the skin. Pulsed fluoroscopy produces brief exposures instead of a continuous beam, and last image hold keeps the final frame on the screen with the beam off. The system displays fluoroscopy time, the dose area product, and often an estimated skin dose. The frame rate, the dose for each frame, and the warning level at which the system alerts the operator must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Radiation protection here is a set of habits and devices checked before every case. The operator and the assisting staff wear lead aprons covering the torso and the gonads, a thyroid shield covering the neck, and leaded glasses that protect the lens of the eye. A lead skirt hangs from the table edge to shield the legs, and distance remains the most powerful protection because dose falls steeply with the square of the distance from the beam. Each person wears a dosimeter badge, and the dose limits and the badge exchange interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Pregnancy changes the calculation for both the patient and the staff. A woman who may be pregnant should be identified before the procedure begins, and the decision to proceed is made with the fetal dose weighed explicitly. The beam should be collimated tightly and the pelvis shielded where the examination allows. A pregnant staff member should be reassigned away from the beam or wear a second dosimeter under the apron. The occupational dose limit for a declared pregnant worker must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and skipping this conversation is one of the more serious operator errors in the room.

The contrast injector makes angiography possible without a human hand on a syringe. To render a coronary artery opaque for a fraction of a second, contrast must be delivered at a high flow rate and at a pressure well above what a hand can generate. The injector holds a large syringe in a cradle, and a motorized piston drives the plunger at a programmed flow rate. The flow rate in milliliters per second and the pressure limit in pounds per square inch at which the motor stops must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The injector carries 2 characteristic hazards, and both have alarms. The first is air, because a bubble driven into a coronary artery can stop the heart, and most modern injectors detect it so the air alarm halts the injection. The second is extravasation, because contrast delivered outside the vessel dissects into the tissue and can cause severe injury that the machine cannot see. A pressure limit alarm during a coronary injection usually means a blocked or engaged catheter, and it must never be overridden. The air alarm, the pressure limit, and the over-temperature alarm of a contrast warmer must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The contrast medium is a consumable with its own storage rules and its own risks. It is an iodinated solution, and the iodine makes it opaque to X-rays, so its concentration determines how dark the vessel appears. The bottle is kept warm so it is less viscous and flows more easily through a narrow catheter, and a dedicated warmer holds it at a set temperature. Contrast is drawn up through a spike or a closed transfer device and purged of air before it reaches the injector. That set temperature, the over-temperature alarm, and the expiry check before every case must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Every case begins with access, and the vascular sheath holds that access open. A sheath is a short plastic tube with a hemostasis valve at its hub and a side arm for flushing. A dilator passes through it so the tapered tip can be advanced over a wire without tearing the vessel. Sheaths are sized in French, where one French equals one third of a millimeter, and the common coronary sizes are 5 French, 6 French, and 7 French. The size must match the largest device that will pass, and the flush pressure and the sheath size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A sheath is removed at the end of the case, when bleeding is most likely. Manual compression is held over the puncture point until hemostasis is achieved, and then a pressure dressing is applied. A closure device may be used instead, either a suture-based or a collagen-based plug, and each has its own failure modes. A sheath left in place for a long procedure can kink and will then accept neither a wire nor a balloon. The compression time, the closure device instructions, and the dressing schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The guidewire is the device that leads everything else. It has a central core of stainless steel or nickel titanium alloy that carries the push, a coiled or braided wrap that gives flexibility, and a shaped tip the operator bends before insertion. The diameter is usually 0.014 inch for coronary work and 0.035 inch for larger vessels, and the length is chosen so a device can be advanced over it while a length still protrudes. Guidewires are single-use devices, and a resterilized wire loses its coating, its tip shape, and its fatigue life. A fractured wire can leave a fragment in the coronary circulation that only a snare or an operation can retrieve. The diameter, the length, the tip shape, and the reuse policy must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Diagnostic and guiding catheters are distinguished almost entirely by their curve. A diagnostic catheter is shaped so its tip can be seated briefly in a coronary opening. A guiding catheter is stiffer and larger in bore so it can sit coaxially and support balloons and stents. Common shapes include a curve for the left coronary artery, a curve for the right, and a pigtail whose curl keeps the tip off the vessel wall. The catheter is advanced over a wire rather than pushed blindly, and when it is seated the pressure trace is watched for damping and for the waveform change that signals the tip is against the wall. Damping means the catheter is blocked against the vessel, so the catheter curve, the size, and the exchange technique must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The balloon is the tool that opens a narrowing, and its behavior is governed by compliance. A compliant balloon stretches as pressure rises, so its diameter grows with every increment and it can dilate a range of sizes. A non-compliant balloon holds its diameter nearly constant, so the final size can be known and not exceeded. Each balloon has a nominal pressure at which it reaches its stated diameter and a rated burst pressure above which it may rupture. A rupture in a coronary artery releases contrast and debris and can dissect the vessel, so the nominal pressure, the rated burst pressure, and the inflated diameter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The inflation device is a syringe with a screw thread and a pressure gauge. The screw thread gives a large mechanical advantage, so a small turn of the handle produces a large change in pressure. The device is filled with a mixture of contrast and saline, usually 1 part contrast to 2 parts saline, so the balloon is visible while it is inflated. A common operator error is to overfill the device, leaving no room to draw negative pressure, so the balloon cannot be deflated quickly. The mixture ratio, the gauge range, and the maximum pressure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A stent is a metal scaffold mounted on a balloon or a delivery catheter and left in the vessel to hold it open. The balloon-expandable stent is crimped onto a balloon and expanded by inflating it, and the self-expanding stent is compressed inside a sheath and springs open when withdrawn. A drug-eluting stent carries a medication in a polymer coating that reduces tissue regrowth, and that coating can be damaged by rough passage or a dry wipe. A stent can dislodge during passage through a tight curve, so the operator confirms under fluoroscopy that it lies across the lesion with adequate margins before inflation. After deployment the balloon is withdrawn and inspected to confirm the stent is no longer on it, and the stent diameter, the deployment pressure, and the inventory check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Hemodynamic monitoring rests on one small component, the pressure transducer. The transducer is a strain gauge whose electrical resistance changes when fluid pressure stretches it, and it is connected to the patient through a column of fluid. Because it measures pressure relative to the air on its other side, the system must be referenced to a fixed external point. That point is the phlebostatic axis on the chest wall, a level that approximates the right atrium, and the transducer is placed there and zeroed to the atmosphere. The square wave test flushes the system briefly and watches the trace, because a properly damped system shows a sharp rise and 1 or 2 small oscillations. A trace that rises and falls slowly is overdamped, usually because of a bubble, a clot, or a kink, and blood left to stagnate clots and can be flushed into the patient. The reference level, the zeroing technique, the square wave criteria, and the tubing change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

With a reliable pressure signal, the laboratory measures the pressures and flows that guide the decision. A catheter passed into the right side of the heart gives right atrial, right ventricular, pulmonary artery, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures. The shapes of those waveforms reveal narrowing of valves, shunts between chambers, and the filling of the heart.
