The common operator error at this stage is starting the scan before checking that the arms are out of the beam, which produces a streak artifact and often forces a repeat examination.

Four numbers dominate the dose a patient receives: the tube voltage, usually between 80 and 140 kilovolts, the tube current in milliamperes, the time the beam is on, and the pitch, which is the distance the table moves per rotation divided by the width of the beam. Slice thickness, usually between 0.5 and 5 millimeters, sets the detail available, and a thin slice through a large volume costs more dose than a thick slice through the same volume. A pitch greater than one shortens the scan and lowers dose but may leave gaps in the data that reconstruction must interpolate. Every one of these settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the difference between a diagnostic scan and an unnecessarily high dose is a set of numbers chosen by a human being.

Dose is reported in milligray for the radiation delivered to a specific tissue, and in millisievert for the biological effect when tissue sensitivities are taken into account. A chest radiograph delivers on the order of 0.1 millisievert, while a CT scan of the chest delivers roughly 7 millisieverts, and a multiphase abdominal study can exceed 20 millisieverts, and each of these figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazard is not a burn or a shock; it is a small, cumulative, stochastic risk of cancer that no patient can feel and no operator can see, which is why it is so easy to ignore. The scanner should display and archive a dose report for every examination, and the operator error that matters most is repeating a scan without a new clinical reason, because a repeat doubles the dose to the same patient for no new information. Children, pregnant patients, and patients having repeated follow-up are the groups in which the justification must be argued most carefully, and their protocols must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Intravenous contrast is what turns a CT scan from an anatomical map into a physiological one, and a powered injector is what makes contrast delivery reproducible. The injector is a programmable pump that holds a syringe of contrast and a syringe of saline, and it delivers a chosen volume at a chosen flow rate, typically between 2 and 5 milliliters per second, followed by a saline flush, and that rate must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Timing is everything, because an arterial phase, a portal venous phase, and a delayed phase each require the scan to begin at a defined interval after the injection, and many scanners use bolus tracking, in which a low-dose monitoring sequence watches the contrast arrive in a chosen vessel and starts the scan when the density crosses a threshold. The characteristic alarm of this part of the examination is the injector pressure limit alarm, which sounds when the line is occluded or the cannula has moved out of the vein. The hazard the operator must fear is extravasation, the leakage of contrast into the tissue around the vein, which causes pain and swelling and demands that the injection stop at once, that the arm be elevated, and that the event be documented.

The control console is where the operator stands, behind a lead-glass window or in an adjoining room, and it carries the scan prescription, the contrast timing, the image display, and the emergency controls. A clearly marked emergency stop button halts the gantry and the table instantly, and every operator must know its location before the first patient of the day rather than during the first emergency. Scanner alarms are named for the fault they detect, and the ones an operator will meet are the tube heat alarm, the rotation fault alarm, the table limit alarm, the injector pressure alarm, and the motion or gating alarm. The most dangerous alarm is the one that never sounds, because a scanner can produce a complete and well-formed image from a failing detector without any warning, which is why daily quality control on a phantom matters more than any single reading on the console. The common operator error is quiet rather than dramatic: accepting an image because it looks familiar, choosing a protocol from memory, or scanning a region that another examination has already covered, and every alarm threshold and time limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Image quality in CT is a balance among noise, spatial resolution, and dose, and every artifact is the visible signature of that compromise. Motion artifact appears as blurring or as ghosted bands, and it comes from breathing, swallowing, cardiac motion, or a patient who is cold and shivering on the table. Beam hardening appears as dark bands between two dense objects, typically between the bones at the base of the skull or across a shoulder, because the low-energy part of the beam is absorbed first and the remaining beam is harder than the reconstruction assumes. A ring artifact, a perfect circle centered on the isocenter, is the classic sign of a single miscalibrated detector channel, while a streak artifact radiating from metal or from a surgical clip can be reduced by angling the gantry, increasing the tube output, or applying a metal artifact reduction algorithm. Photon starvation, a mottled noise through a very thick body part, is a sign that the protocol was written for a smaller patient.

The X-ray tube is a consumable with a finite life, and its end is usually announced by a rising heat load, a falling output, and a gradual loss of contrast in the images. The anode and its bearing wear, the vacuum slowly degrades, and the focal spot spreads until the resolution the protocol expects is no longer produced. Detector maintenance is quieter but equally decisive, because the detector array must be calibrated against known attenuation, and a channel that drifts produces the ring artifact already described. An air calibration, performed with the gantry empty, and a phantom calibration, performed with the manufacturer's test object, are the routines that keep the numbers honest, and the interval and method for each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The reconstruction computer needs maintenance as well, because software versions, filter files, and geometry tables can become corrupted, and a mismatch between the calibration table and the current configuration produces images that look real and measure wrongly. A quality assurance program should record tube output, noise, uniformity, spatial resolution, and slice thickness at fixed intervals, so that a slow drift appears as a trend rather than as a failure.

The consumables of CT scanning are ordinary items with serious consequences. They include the intravenous cannula, the extension tubing and the injector syringe set, the contrast medium itself, saline, the pressure-resistant connectors, and the adhesive dressing that holds the cannula in place. Add the electrocardiogram electrodes when the scanner gates to the heartbeat, the respiratory belt, the positioning foam, the table covers, and the disinfectant wipes used between patients. Contrast medium must be stored within its temperature range, protected from light, and checked for the expiry date before every single use, because a degraded agent provides poor opacification and wastes a dose of radiation. The injector tubing is single use and must be discarded even when the examination is abandoned, the syringe in the injector must never be refilled for a second patient, and sharps from cannulation go into a puncture-resistant container at the point of use.

Cleaning the scanner is a patient safety task rather than housekeeping. The table top, the pads, the positioning aids, the injector head, and the gantry surfaces are touched by every patient, and they must be cleaned and disinfected between examinations with an agent compatible with the manufacturer's materials, because some disinfectants cloud the detector covers or crack the table pad. The bore, the control knobs, the touch screen, and the keyboard deserve the same treatment, and the disinfectant contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, includes gloves for handling contrast and body fluids and a gown or apron wherever splashing is likely, and the operator at the console is not exempt from hand hygiene between patients. Patients with a known transmissible infection do not need a special machine, but they do need a defined cleaning sequence and, where the procedure generates droplets, a mask and eye protection, and the cleaning record belongs in the log.

A CT scanner is not simply bought and installed; a room is built around it. The gantry and the table are heavy, the gantry alone often between 1,500 and 2,500 kilograms, and the floor must be rated for that concentrated load, which may require a reinforced slab beneath the finished surface. Power is the second demand, because the tube generator draws a large current for short periods, so the supply must be sized for peak load rather than average load, and a voltage drop during a rotation degrades image quality without an obvious alarm. Cooling is the third, because a rotating anode converts most of its energy into heat, and the room needs either a chilled water circuit or a substantial heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, or HVAC, capacity, with temperature and humidity held in a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Humidity control prevents condensation and static discharge, an uninterruptible power supply, or UPS, protects only the console and the computer rather than the tube, and the radiation shielding in the walls, floor, ceiling, and lead-glass window must be designed by a qualified medical physicist for the scanner's output and the occupancy of the neighboring rooms.

The reconstruction workstation is the other half of the scanner, and it is where an examination becomes a diagnosis. From the raw projection data it produces the reconstructed slices, and from those slices it produces the coronal, sagittal, curved, and three-dimensional views that a clinician actually reads. The images travel as Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine, or DICOM, objects, and the picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, stores, distributes, and retrieves them, so a failure of that link can make a perfectly good scan invisible to the person who needs it. The workstation also generates the dose report, the structured record of the radiation the patient received and the protocol that delivered it. Post-processing tools, including vessel analysis and artificial intelligence, or AI, assisted detection, are aids rather than replacements, and the operator should verify that the correct patient identity travels with every image, because a mislabeled examination can be read as another person's anatomy.

The field position must begin with an uncomfortable fact: a full CT scanner does not travel, and no amount of improvisation makes it portable. The gantry, the high-voltage generator, the cooling loop, the shielding, and the floor loading together add up to a fixed installation that costs more than many district hospitals spend on all their other equipment. A remote or mobile clinic therefore does not own a CT scanner, it owns a relationship with one. What the field service can own is a compact head scanner, a small machine built specifically to image the brain, which weighs a few hundred kilograms rather than a few tonnes and can be moved in a reinforced vehicle or installed inside a shipping container. Even that machine demands a stable power supply, a cool and dry space, a trained operator, and a maintenance contract that reaches the site, and the distinction that matters is between the scanner designed for the field and the full scanner that is merely hoped to be.

The compact head scanner gives up a great deal in order to gain its mobility. Its bore is small, often just large enough for a head and a pair of shoulders, so it cannot examine the chest, the abdomen, or the pelvis, and it cannot comfortably admit a patient on a ventilator with a full monitoring array. Its detector coverage is limited, its rotation is slower, and its tube operates at a lower output, so the images are noisier and the fine detail that a full scanner delivers through the base of the skull is simply absent. It usually reconstructs a narrow set of standard brain windows rather than a full library, it may not support the contrast phases that a body scan requires, and its table limit may exclude an obese or unstable patient on mechanical grounds alone. Its dose for a head examination is broadly comparable to a full scanner's head protocol, and every setting on it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the field variant demands instead is discipline in everything that surrounds the machine. It demands a power supply that is either genuinely stable or backed by a properly sized generator and an uninterruptible supply for the computer, because a brownout during a rotation ruins the study and abuses the tube. It demands a room that can be kept cool and dry, because a container in the sun becomes an oven and a humid climate corrodes the electronics. It demands a trained radiographer or clinical officer who can position a head, recognize motion artifact, and decide when an image is not good enough, since there is no physicist in the next room, and it demands a supply chain for the disposable head holders and the cleaning agents. It demands a service plan with spare parts held locally, because a scanner that must be shipped abroad for repair is a scanner that stops working for a year, and above all it demands a clear referral rule, so that cases beyond its ability are identified early and sent onward rather than scanned badly.

A remote clinic with no scanner at all does something more useful than pretending: it triages. The clinician in the field examines the patient, records the history and the vital signs, and decides whether the presentation is one that CT would change. A suspected stroke, a head injury with a falling level of consciousness, a suspected tuberculosis cavity, or an unexplained abdominal mass may justify a journey, while a simple fracture, a pneumonia, or a migraine usually does not. Plain radiography, ultrasound, and careful clinical examination answer many of the questions that a scanner would be asked, and a portable ultrasound probe is the diagnostic device that genuinely travels. Where a scan is required, the clinic stabilizes the patient first, arranges transport with a trained escort who carries the referral question in writing, and checks kidney function before any intravenous contrast. Teleradiology, in which images are transmitted for reading at a distance, turns a scanner in one city into a service for a whole province, provided the images carry the right identifiers and the report returns to the right clinician.

The operator's daily check is the cheapest safety device in the room. Before the first patient, the operator confirms that the gantry rotates smoothly, that the lasers align with the isocenter, that the table travels its full range and returns to zero, that the emergency stop functions, and that the intercom and the patient observation camera work. The warm-up routine must be completed exactly as written, because a cold tube asked for a high-output protocol may fail or produce unstable output, and the warm-up interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The air calibration status, the last phantom quality control result, and the dose display should be checked and logged, and any deviation reported rather than repeated. Contrast stock, injector syringes, cannulas, and the emergency drugs and airway equipment must be present and in date, the patient identity, the pregnancy question, the allergy history, the kidney function, and the presence of any metal implant must be confirmed before the table moves, and the operator should look at the patient and not only at the screen.

The failure modes of a CT scanner can be read from the outside. A tube nearing its end shows a longer warm-up, more frequent heat alarms, and images that look softer than the previous week's, and then one morning it simply stops. A detector that drifts draws its ring across every image, and the ring's position identifies the channel at fault, while a slipping or misindexed table makes every slice a little wrong in the same direction, which is easy to miss precisely because the error is uniform. A cooling failure raises the tube temperature, triggers an over-temperature alarm, and eventually forces the scanner to refuse a scan, while a power disturbance resets the console and can leave a reconstruction incomplete. A corrupted calibration file produces plausible images with wrong numbers, and that is the most dangerous failure of all, so the daily phantom check catches the quiet failures while the operator's attention catches the loud ones.

In the field, maintenance is a matter of survival and must be planned before arrival. The compact scanner needs a service schedule, a set of consumable parts such as the tube, the detector module, and the cooling filter, and at least one local technician trained to replace them. The most common field failures are power quality, heat, dust, and humidity, in that order, and each has a cheap defense in a voltage stabilizer, a shaded and ventilated enclosure, a filtered air intake, and a dehumidifier. Calibration must be repeated after any transport, because the geometry shifts, and the calibration phantom must travel with the machine. The operator keeps a log of every examination, every fault, and every calibration, since that log is the only maintenance history the machine will ever have, consumables must be ordered with enough lead time to survive a broken supply road, and when a remote scanner fails the entire referral pathway fails with it.

To summarize, the CT scanner is a mathematical instrument built around a rotating X-ray tube and a ring of detectors, and it produces a computed slice rather than a photograph. Its speed comes from the slip ring and multislice detection, its contrast from a timed intravenous injection, and its images from a reconstruction that can be tuned, filtered, and reformatted long after the patient leaves the table. The safety hazard is the radiation dose, delivered silently and cumulatively, and the operator error that matters most is the unnecessary or repeated scan. The characteristic alarms are the tube heat alarm, the rotation fault, the table limit, and the injector pressure alarm, and behind them the daily phantom check is the routine that finds the quiet faults. The infrastructure is a room built around a heavy, hot, and power-hungry machine, and the consumables are cannulas, contrast, injector tubing, electrodes, and cleaning agents whose availability decides whether any of the rest of it works. The field variant is a compact head scanner, or more often a referral pathway that uses plain radiography, ultrasound, and teleradiology instead of a scanner that cannot travel, and no setting, dose, temperature, time, pressure, or threshold in this chapter may be used from memory.

# Chapter 26 — MRI

Magnetic resonance imaging, called MRI, begins with the nucleus of ordinary hydrogen, which is a single proton and behaves like a very small spinning magnet. In tissue at rest those protons point in every direction, so their tiny fields cancel and the body is magnetically silent. Inside a strong static magnetic field a small excess of protons aligns with the field, and this faint imbalance is the only source of everything the scanner later shows. Each aligned proton precesses around the direction of the field like a tilted spinning top, at a frequency fixed by the strength of that field. A burst of radiofrequency energy at that frequency tips the protons away from their resting direction, and as they relax back they re-emit radiofrequency energy that a coil can detect. The machine exists to create the field, to disturb the protons in one chosen place at a time, and to listen to the answer, and the finished picture is a map of how quickly those protons give their energy back.

The static field comes from a superconducting electromagnet, in which a coil of alloy wire is cooled until its resistance falls to nothing, so a current launched into it circulates for years without any power supply. A vessel of liquid helium around the coil, wrapped in vacuum and radiation shields, holds the winding at about 4 kelvin, close to absolute zero, and because the current persists the magnet is never switched off and cannot simply be unplugged. That one fact governs the safety of the whole department. Field strength is measured in tesla, and a clinical scanner commonly runs between 0.5 tesla and 3 tesla, so the contour at which the field falls to 5 gauss, still strong enough to pull a ferromagnetic object from a hand, is called the five gauss line and forms the practical edge of the danger zone. That line does not respect walls, floors, or ceilings, and a scanner on an upper floor projects its field into the room below. The field strength, the position of the five gauss line, and every related warning threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Spatial information comes from three sets of gradient coils, one for each direction in space, which superimpose a small deliberate variation on the main field. Where the field is slightly stronger the protons precess slightly faster and where it is weaker they precess slightly slower, so the frequency of the returning signal encodes the position of the protons that produced it, and switching the gradients in a planned order labels every volume element. Each rapid switch makes the coil assembly hammer against its mountings, and the knocking or buzzing is not a fault but a consequence of the physics. The noise rises with the strength and speed of the sequence and can reach levels loud enough to damage hearing, so every patient must wear protection that fits and is rated for the noise the scanner produces. Earplugs go in before the patient enters the room, headphones are added on top, and the patient is told that the sound is expected so that it does not provoke movement or panic. The gradient strength, the slew rate, the noise level, and the attenuation rating of the protection must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The radiofrequency system has two halves, a transmit path that delivers the tipping pulse and a receive path that listens to the answer. Transmission is usually performed by a large coil built into the scanner, because it must create a uniform field across the whole region examined, and the energy deposited in the patient by that transmission is called the specific absorption rate. Too much deposited energy heats tissue, and the tissues most at risk are those with poor blood flow. The receive side is where the art of the examination lies, because the coil that listens must lie as close to the anatomy as possible, so a head examination uses a snug head coil, a knee uses a wrap or a rigid knee coil, and a wrist or an ankle uses a small surface coil. A coil that is switched off, unplugged, badly seated, or damaged produces a dark band, a region of noise, or no image at all in the part it was meant to cover. The coil and its position, the permissible specific absorption rate, and every displayed energy limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the commonest operator error here is to choose a demanding sequence without reading the display that warns of it.

When the tipping pulse ends the protons return to their resting alignment, and the time constant of that recovery along the main field is the longitudinal relaxation time while the time constant of the decay across the field is the transverse relaxation time. Fat, muscle, cerebrospinal fluid, and edema differ in these values, so they look different from one another even though all are mostly water, and by choosing how long to wait and how long to listen the operator weights the image toward one relaxation time, the other, or the density of protons. The patterns of pulses and listening intervals are called sequences. A spin echo sequence uses a second pulse to undo the loss of signal from an uneven field and gives robust contrast at the price of a long scan, while a gradient echo sequence is faster but more sensitive to field unevenness. An inversion recovery sequence nulls the signal from one tissue, which is how fat is made to disappear and how fluid is made to stand out. The timing values, the sequence library, and the weighting chosen for each clinical question must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The signal that leaves the patient is not an image but a set of measurements of frequency and phase across the whole field of view, stored in a mathematical data space filled line by line. Reconstruction converts that space into the familiar grid of picture elements, and the same data can be reprocessed with different filters or shown in different planes. A scan interrupted before enough lines are collected cannot be reconstructed at all, which is why sudden movement at the end of a long sequence wastes the whole sequence. Every examination is a negotiation among contrast, resolution, scan time, and noise, and no setting improves all four at once, because finer resolution means smaller volume elements and less signal from each of them. A scanner asked to do too much at low field will always be beaten by a modest protocol performed well at the field it has. The resolution, the number of signal averages, and every acquisition time displayed must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital machine lives in a room that is part of the device, and the room is kept free of anything that could become a projectile. The magnet has a cylindrical bore, commonly between 60 and 70 centimeters across, and the patient is carried into it on a table whose movement is measured in millimeters so that the region of interest ends up at the center of the field. The table has a weight limit often lower than a hospital bed, so a heavy patient must be weighed or moved with a transfer device rather than tested against the limit. Positioning is a discipline of stillness, because a patient who is uncomfortable will move and a patient who moves will spoil the study, so the body is made straight, the region of interest is centered on the coil, and padding is placed so that nothing presses over a long scan. Arms are kept clear of the bore wall and clear of the coil, because a limb touching either can pick up energy and become warm. The bore diameter, the table weight limit, the patient's position, the padding, and the coil placement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Access to a magnetic resonance suite is organized into four zones, and knowing which zone you are in is the first safety skill. Zone 1 is the public area outside the suite, where no special control applies, and zone 2 is the reception and screening area, where the questionnaire is completed and checked. Zone 3 is the control room, where the scanner is operated and where a trained person can still intervene, and it is a restricted area. Zone 4 is the magnet room itself, entered only by staff who are trained and formally authorized, by a patient who has been screened, and by nobody else. The locked doors, the warning signs, and the list of authorized persons must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A person who does not know which zone they are standing in has already defeated the model.

The screening questionnaire is the most important object in the department, and it is never skipped, never delegated to an untrained clerk, and never completed on the patient's behalf. It asks about surgery, implanted devices, foreign bodies, metal in the eyes from grinding or welding, tattoos, pregnancy, and anything the patient remembers being put inside the body, and a patient who cannot answer reliably is screened with the help of a relative or a written record, or is not scanned. Certain implanted devices make the scanner dangerous rather than merely unsuitable, because a cardiac pacemaker or an implanted defibrillator may be damaged or may deliver inappropriate therapy, and an intracranial aneurysm clip from an older material can twist or dislodge. Cochlear implants, neurostimulators, medication pumps, and some dental work each carry their own rules, and even a device described as safe for MRI must be verified as safe for the specific field strength and examination. An intraocular foreign body can move inside the eye and cause blindness, so any history of metal in the eye requires imaging or an ophthalmic review before the patient approaches the magnet. Every implant must be identified by name, material, and documentation, and its condition confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The projectile hazard is the one that kills, because a ferromagnetic object near the magnet is accelerated toward the bore with a force that grows as it approaches. Any object containing iron, nickel, or cobalt, or certain stainless steels, may fly, including oxygen cylinders, scissors, keys, tools, and mop buckets, and such an object crosses the room in a fraction of a second and cannot be caught. The published accidents include a patient struck by an oxygen cylinder carried into the room and staff pinned by furniture, and these are why the rules are written in blood. The commonest operator error is not the dramatic one but the ordinary one, a person who steps into the magnet room with a forgotten object because the door was open, and a second error is to assume that a device labeled safe for magnetic resonance is safe at any field strength and with any sequence. The answer is a written check at the door by a trained person, backed by a handheld ferromagnetic detector whose characteristic alarm sounds when metal is present, and the correct response is to stop, remove the object, and re-screen. The use of the detector, its sensitivity, and the objects it may miss must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The magnet is kept cold by liquid helium, and a quench is the sudden loss of that cooling, when the superconducting coil becomes resistive and its enormous stored energy turns the liquid instantly into gas that must leave through a vent pipe. A quench may happen spontaneously or may be triggered by the quench button, which exists for the single emergency in which a person is pinned against the magnet, and that button must never be pressed for a fire, for a distressed patient, or to end a scan. The helium released is lighter than air and odorless and does not announce itself to a person breathing it, because as it expands it pushes oxygen out of the room and a person can lose consciousness without any warning sensation of suffocation, so an oxygen monitor in the magnet room and in any space through which the vent passes is a required device whose alarm threshold must be set and verified. The cryogenic system has its own alarms, in which a low cryogen level warns that a refill is needed, a cold head or compressor alarm warns that the refrigerator has stopped, and a magnet rundown alarm means a quench has occurred and the room must be evacuated. The commonest operator failure here is to silence a warning and keep scanning, which converts a planned refill into an emergency. The quench procedure, the button locations, the oxygen alarm threshold, and the response time for each alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Contrast in MRI changes the magnetic behavior of nearby water protons rather than absorbing X-rays, so the agents used are a different family of molecules. A gadolinium containing agent works because the gadolinium ion is strongly paramagnetic and shortens the relaxation time of the water around it, brightening the tissue where it accumulates, and the free ion is toxic so it is held inside a chelating molecule whose stability determines the risk. Agents differ in whether they remain in the blood vessels or spread into the space between cells, and the choice depends on the question asked. The most serious risk is in a patient whose kidneys cannot clear the agent, because a prolonged dwell time allows the chelate to break down and the released ion to deposit in tissue, producing an illness called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis that thickens the skin and can involve internal organs. A patient with known kidney disease or an uncertain kidney history must have kidney function measured before an agent is given, while immediate reactions such as hives and nausea are managed with observation and a true anaphylactic reaction requires the same emergency response as any other. The agent, its concentration, the injected dose in millimoles per kilogram of body weight, and the emergency drugs must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Claustrophobia is a genuine barrier to care rather than a character flaw, and a substantial minority of patients find the bore intolerable. The patient is told beforehand what will happen, how long each sequence takes, that the noise is normal, and how to call for help, and a panic button that works inside the magnet is placed in the hand before the scan begins. An open or short bore magnet, a mirror that lets the patient see out, a familiar person in the room, and a calm voice through the intercom solve most cases, and the choice to scan a frightened patient by force is never correct. Children need a different plan because they cannot lie still for a long sequence, and a child who is prepared, shown the room, and scanned with a short protocol may succeed without any drug. When sedation is required, the anesthetic equipment and the monitor must be compatible with the magnetic field, and the anesthetist must understand that a ferromagnetic cylinder cannot enter the room. The sedation protocol, the compatible equipment, and the pediatric dose of any agent must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Monitoring a patient inside the magnet is a specialized problem, because ordinary monitors contain iron and ordinary leads can act as an antenna. A patient who needs continuous observation requires equipment formally rated as safe or conditional for the magnetic field, used at the field strength and in the position the rating permits. An electrocardiogram, called ECG, is possible with compatible equipment, though the trace is often distorted by the flow of blood in the field, and pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and capnography each have a maximum cable length and a routing rule. Radiofrequency energy can also burn skin, and the burn is almost always caused by a conductive loop, because a cable that touches the patient and then the bore, or that crosses another cable, concentrates energy at the point of contact. A coil cable, an ECG lead, or a monitoring wire laid carelessly across the skin can produce a serious burn in a patient who cannot feel it. The rule is that no cable touches the skin unless it must, that cables run without crossing the body, and that padding separates the patient from the bore wall, and the compatibility rating, the routing, and the skin inspection after each scan must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A magnetic resonance room is a radiofrequency fortress, because the signal it listens to is weaker than the radio and television broadcasts that fill the air, so the walls, floor, ceiling, and door are lined with a continuous conductive layer, usually copper, whose seams are bonded so that no gap can leak. Every penetration for a pipe or a cable is fitted with a waveguide that lets the service through while blocking the frequencies of interest, and a break in the shield appears as a stripe or a shower of noise across every image. The magnet also needs services most hospital rooms were never designed to provide, including chilled water and a compressor for the cold head, a stable electrical supply sized for the gradients, and an uninterruptible power supply for the control console and the cryogenic monitoring. It needs helium delivered by road on a schedule, with a storage vessel and a transfer line, because a magnet that runs out of helium quenches, and that supply chain is the most fragile part of the installation. The floor must carry the concentrated weight of the magnet, and the room needs ventilation for released gases and for heat. The shield integrity, the chilled water temperature, the electrical load, the floor loading, and the helium delivery interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of a magnetic resonance department are modest in appearance and absolute in function, and a missing item can cancel a scheduled scan. Every patient needs hearing protection in the correct size, an intravenous cannula and tubing for contrast, a skin preparation and dressing for the puncture, and pads, straps, and wedges to hold the position, while the contrast agent is stored according to its label, checked for clarity and expiry, and drawn up as a single dose for a single patient. Compatible monitoring electrodes and cables, a working call button, and a charged and tested ferromagnetic detector belong to the same list. Cleaning a magnetic resonance room has one rule that overrides every other consideration, which is that no cleaning equipment containing ferromagnetic metal may ever be taken past the zone 3 door, because a mop with a metal bucket and a floor polisher are projectiles. The table, the coil surfaces, the bore liner, and the patient handling aids are wiped between patients with a disinfectant the maker of the equipment allows, and coils are handled gently because their conductors and tuning components are fragile. The expiry date, the storage temperature, the dose of every agent, the concentration and contact time of each disinfectant, and the list of approved cleaning equipment must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of a magnetic resonance scanner is mostly the maintenance of its cold chain and its coils, and it is performed by engineers with equipment that never enters the magnet room. The helium level is recorded and the vessel refilled on a schedule, the cold head and compressor are serviced, the water cooling loop is checked for flow and temperature, and the magnetic field is checked for homogeneity with a phantom and measured against a baseline so that a distance in the picture matches a distance in the patient. Every coil is tested individually, because one failing element in an array degrades part of every examination performed with it. The failure modes announce themselves first as changes in the image, so a motion artifact appears as blur or ghosting that repeats in the direction of the movement, a zipper artifact is a line of noise caused by a radiofrequency leak from the door or a cable, and a dark band that appears with one coil and disappears with another proves the coil is at fault. A cold head that becomes unusually loud, a compressor that runs continuously, or a rising helium boil off rate are early warnings of cryogenic failure rather than of image quality. The refill interval, the field homogeneity tolerance, the signal to noise baseline, and the escalation procedure for a cryogenic alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator's start of shift check is short, deliberate, and recorded, and it is the habit that prevents most accidents. The zone doors are confirmed locked, the warning signs and lights are working, the ferromagnetic detector is charged and tested against a known object, and the screening forms are stocked in every required language. The quench button is confirmed present and unobstructed, the oxygen monitor is reading and its alarm is tested, the emergency contacts for the cryogenic system are posted, and the helium level, compressor status, and coils are checked. The patient list is reviewed in advance so that implants, contrast, sedation, and monitoring needs are identified before the patient arrives. An emergency inside the magnet room is unlike any other emergency in the hospital, because the first instinct of a rescuer may be the thing that kills, so a patient who collapses in the bore must be brought out before resuscitation begins and no ferromagnetic defibrillator, oxygen cylinder, or stretcher may cross the five gauss line. If a person is pinned by a ferromagnetic object and cannot be freed, the quench button is pressed as a last resort, accepting the loss of the magnet to save that person, and the evacuation route, the approved resuscitation equipment, and the quench decision criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Staff who work in the suite are screened like patients, because a technologist with a pacemaker or a ferromagnetic implant must not enter zone 4, so each person authorized to enter signs a screening declaration and reports any new implant. Training covers the zones, the questionnaire, the projectile hazard, the quench, the oxygen alarm, the emergency procedure, and the recognition of a failing image, and it is repeated on a defined interval, while a visitor, a cleaner, or an engineer must be escorted and screened before crossing the line. The finished examination is a set of images plus the information that makes them interpretable, so the images travel to the picture archiving and communication system, called PACS, along with the sequence parameters, the field strength, the coil used, the contrast agent and its dose if any, and any adverse event. The technologist records the screening result, the sedation given, the repeat, and the clinical question, because a reader who does not know what was being looked for may miss the finding that answers it. The last and most important piece of equipment is the trained person, because the examination is safe only as long as someone is thinking about safety at the door. The training content, the re-screening interval for staff, the escort rule, the data fields required in the record, and the retention period must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the magnetic resonance device is usually a low field scanner, and its physics is the same while its compromises are large. Such a scanner may use a permanent magnet or a resistive electromagnet rather than a superconducting one, so it needs no liquid helium, no quench pipe, and no compressor, and it can be sited in a room a hospital scanner could never use. Field strength is commonly in the range of 0.2 tesla to 0.5 tesla, and the lower field reduces the signal available for every image. A permanent magnet cannot be turned off, so the safety perimeter and the screening rules survive in full even though the field is weaker, and the same questionnaire is used without exception. A dedicated extremity scanner is the other field relevant variant, built to image a hand, a wrist, or a knee rather than a whole body, and its magnet is small and often open, so the patient sits beside it and places the limb into the gap. That arrangement is closer to a radiographic examination than to a tunnel, so claustrophobia nearly disappears and the fringe field is small enough that the room needs less control. The field strength, the limb to be examined, and the safety perimeter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the low field variant gives up is signal to noise before anything else, and almost every other loss follows from that one. Finer resolution and thin slices become difficult, so small structures and subtle lesions may not be visible at all, and fat suppression becomes less reliable when so many examinations depend on making fat dark so that fluid or a lesion stands out. Sequences that require many rapid switches of the gradients are slow and limited by heating, so functional work, angiography, and cardiac imaging may be impossible. What it demands instead is time, patience, and discipline, because scan times are longer, motion is punished more severely when the signal is weak, and coil placement is even more critical. Quality assurance in the field is a written record and a simple phantom rather than a service contract, so a standard test object is scanned at fixed settings on a regular schedule and compared with the previous set. Where no scanner exists at all, the honest work is to answer the question with the equipment in hand and to refer the rest, and the referral decision turns on the question, the urgency, and whether the answer will change management. Every benchmark, interval, acquisition time, and safety rule used in the field must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, magnetic resonance imaging places the patient in a strong static field, tips the hydrogen protons with a pulse of radiofrequency energy, locates them with gradients, and listens with a coil to the signal they return, so the picture is a map of relaxation rather than a shadow of absorption. The static field in tesla, the gradient coils and their noise, the coils chosen by body part, and the sequence that weights the image are the working parts of the hospital machine, while the four zone model, the screening questionnaire, the five gauss line, the quench button, and the oxygen monitor are the working parts of its safety. A ferromagnetic object in the wrong hands becomes a projectile, a gadolinium agent in a failing kidney becomes a poisoning, and a cable looped across the skin becomes a burn, so the hazard, the alarm, and the operator error are named before the patient is placed in the bore. The field variant trades signal, speed, and fine detail for a low field magnet that needs no helium, and in exchange it demands longer scans, stricter positioning, and the same absolute screening discipline. In every setting the rule is the same: no one enters zone 4 unscreened, nothing ferromagnetic crosses the line, and every setting, alarm threshold, and agent dose is confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a patient is scanned.

# Chapter 27 — Ultrasound

An ultrasound image begins with a crystal that changes shape when an electric field is applied to it and produces a voltage when squeezed, and that reversible property is the piezoelectric effect. A short electrical pulse makes the crystal ring at a chosen frequency, and the ringing leaves the surface as a pressure wave that travels into the body. Every boundary between materials of different acoustic impedance reflects part of that energy back, and because sound crosses soft tissue at roughly 1540 meters per second, the time until each echo returns becomes depth while its strength becomes brightness. Every pixel is therefore an inference from timing rather than a photograph, and the assumed speed of sound and the depth scale must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Frequency decides both what can be seen and how deep it can be seen, because a higher frequency has a shorter wavelength and resolves smaller detail yet is absorbed and scattered faster. A lower frequency penetrates farther but blurs small detail, because its longer wavelength cannot separate structures that lie close together. The usual compromise is 2 to 5 megahertz for the abdomen, 7 to 12 megahertz for superficial structures, and higher still for the eye, and each range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Attenuation rises with frequency and with depth, which is why the machine amplifies late echoes more than early ones and why a higher frequency aimed at a deep structure shows less rather than more.

A modern probe is an array of many small elements, each pulsed slightly later than its neighbor, and by delaying pulses across the face of the array the machine shapes a beam, focuses it at a chosen depth, and steers it without any moving part. The same delays applied in reverse during reception make the array listen preferentially to echoes from one direction, which is how a stationary probe sweeps a sector through the body. Behind the elements a backing block shortens the pulse for finer depth resolution, while in front a matching layer eases sound into skin and a plastic lens protects the layers beneath. A damaged element, a cracked lens, or a broken wire removes part or all of one line of the image, so the probe is the most fragile part of the machine, and the element count, the array geometry, and the electrical drive must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Probe shapes follow the anatomy they must serve, and the frequency, the insertion depth, and the disinfection level for any of them must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A linear array fires its elements in a straight line for a rectangular image and serves superficial structures such as vessels, tendons, the thyroid gland, and the breast, while a curvilinear, or convex, array curves its face for a fan shaped field and is the general abdominal and obstetric probe for the liver, the kidneys, and the uterus. A phased array has a small footprint and steers electronically through a sector, letting it look between the ribs at the heart, and it is the standard cardiac probe. A transvaginal probe is a long narrow high frequency device shaped for insertion into the vagina to view the uterus and ovaries from a few centimeters away, a transesophageal probe on a flexible gastroscope lies in the esophagus behind the heart during surgery, and intracavitary and endorectal probes apply the same idea to the rectum and prostate.

The console converts echoes into a readable image, and its controls are few but decisive. Gain is overall amplification and sets the brightness of the picture rather than the truth of it, so too much fills the screen with noise and too little hides real structures. Time gain compensation is a row of sliders that amplifies late echoes from deep tissue more than early ones, depth sets how far the machine listens, and focus places the narrowest part of the beam where detail matters. Output power is the strength of the transmitted pulse and changes what the patient receives rather than what the screen shows, so it is kept as low as the image allows, and the gain, the time gain compensation, the depth, the focus, and the output power must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The preset menu holds starting points, one for each probe and examination type, so the operator does not rebuild the image from scratch. The cardiac preset selects the cardiac probe, a low frequency, a fast frame rate, a small sector, and a Doppler mode for fast flow, while the abdominal preset selects a convex probe, a slower frame rate, and a deeper field. A preset is only a starting point, because body size, bowel gas, and organ depth still demand adjustment, and a preset copied from another machine will not transfer its numbers. The commonest misuse of the console is to correct a poor image with gain alone, which brightens noise without recovering information, when the true fault is poor coupling, the wrong probe, or the wrong preset, and every preset, its probe pairing, and the values it loads must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The machine displays the same echoes in several ways, and each mode answers a different question. Brightness mode draws each echo as a bright dot whose position shows depth and produces the familiar gray cross sectional image, while motion mode records one line of that image over time so a vertical strip shows how a structure moves, which is still used to measure the rate of a fetal heartbeat or the excursion of a valve leaflet. Doppler modes use the change in frequency, or phase shift, of echoes from moving red blood cells to measure the speed and direction of flow, and color Doppler paints those velocities as a colored map while spectral Doppler plots them over time as a waveform. Power Doppler shows the presence of flow rather than its direction and is more sensitive to slow flow in small vessels, and the mode, the sample volume, the angle of insonation, and the velocity scale must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Doppler deserves its own caution because it concentrates energy in time and can reach the highest acoustic outputs the machine produces. Pulsed wave Doppler sends bursts from one element and listens with the same one, so it measures flow at a chosen depth but only up to a limited velocity before the reading wraps around, an error called aliasing. Continuous wave Doppler transmits and receives with separate elements at the same time, so it measures very fast flow without aliasing but reports everything in the beam without depth resolution. The angle between the beam and the direction of flow changes the measured velocity by a cosine term, and at angles greater than about 60 degrees the number becomes too unreliable to report, so the angle correction, the sample volume, the velocity scale, and the exposure limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The safety hazard of ultrasound is easy to forget because nothing is felt at the time, yet the beam deposits energy as heat and can exert mechanical forces at microscopic gas bubbles. The thermal index estimates the temperature rise the beam could produce, and the mechanical index estimates the likelihood of cavitation, the formation and collapse of small bubbles that can damage tissue. Both rise when output power and dwell time increase, and both matter most where the beam is held still, as in fetal scanning, ocular scanning, and long Doppler studies, so the habit is to use the lowest output that answers the question and to keep the dwell time short. The mechanical index, the thermal index, and the exposure time limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Electrical safety is a second hazard, because a cracked lens or damaged cable can leak current, and probe overheating is a third whose characteristic alarm is a probe temperature warning that cuts the transmission off.

The commonest operator error in ultrasound is not a wrong button but a wrong assumption, and it usually begins with coupling. A thin, uneven, or dried film of gel lets air sit between probe and skin, and air reflects almost all the sound, so the operator turns up the gain and produces a bright noisy image from almost no signal. The second error is reading a single view as the whole truth, because a structure can look normal in one plane and be abnormal in the next, so every important finding should be seen in at least two planes. The third is accepting an image that was never saved, because an interpretation that is not documented cannot be reviewed later, and the characteristic alarm is a disconnected probe message or a probe identification failure when the connector is not fully seated. The thresholds and the correct response to each alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning a probe is a clinical procedure because the same device touches every patient, and the method depends on what it touched. A probe that has touched only intact skin needs a wipe with a compatible disinfectant between patients, while one that has entered a body cavity or contacted mucous membrane is a semicritical device needing a high level of disinfection, and one used in a sterile field needs a sterile sheath and sterile gel. The lens and housing are fragile, because many disinfectants craze the plastic, cloud the lens, and eventually crack the seal that keeps fluid out, and the maker states which chemicals are compatible, so the list must be checked before any new disinfectant is introduced. Transesophageal and intracavitary probes need particular care, because their long flexible shafts can be kinked, their controls can be flooded, and their connectors must never be immersed, and the contact time, the concentration, the temperature, and the compatibility of the disinfectant must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables are cheap and indispensable, and running out of one stops the examination as surely as a power failure. Coupling gel excludes air from the space between probe and skin, and it must be water based, acoustically matched, and free of bubbles, while oily or scented products damage some lenses and dry out quickly. Where gel is unavailable, clean water, a water soluble lubricant, or a thin film of vegetable oil will carry sound, though water runs off, lubricant may contain substances the maker forbids, and oil can stain and degrade the lens. A standoff pad lifts very superficial structures into the focal zone, and probe sheaths, sterile gel, sterile covers, and a needle guide are needed in a sterile field, with the expiry dates, the concentrations, and the compatibility of all of these confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A complete examination follows a fixed order, and the order is what makes it repeatable. The patient is positioned so the target organ lies within reach, the area is exposed, gel is applied, and the probe is placed with its orientation marker matched to the marker on the screen. The operator scans systematically rather than hunting for the expected finding, adjusting depth, focus, and gain as the anatomy changes, and comparing right with left. Measurements are made on a frozen image with electronic calipers, and each should be taken in the plane that truly contains the structure, because an oblique cut exaggerates a length. Images and clips are labeled, dated, and stored with the patient's identity, and the report separates what was seen from what it might mean, with the depth, the focus, the gain, the storage format, the required image set, and the labeling rules confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Artifacts are not rare faults but predictable consequences of how sound behaves, and a beginner who does not recognize them will diagnose diseases that are not there. Acoustic shadowing appears when a dense structure such as a stone, a bone, or a calcified plaque absorbs or reflects the beam so completely that everything behind it is dark, and the beginner reads that dark band as a mass or as fluid. Posterior acoustic enhancement is the opposite, a bright band behind a fluid filled structure because fluid weakens the beam less than the tissue around it, and a beginner can mistake it for a solid lesion. Reverberation appears as evenly spaced parallel lines at a fixed depth, produced when the pulse bounces between two strong reflectors such as the probe face and a fascial layer, and comet tail and ring down artifacts are short bright streaks from metal or air that hide the structure being examined. Every one of these must be recognized before it is reported, and the display settings that create or reduce them must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Mirror image artifact most often deceives a beginner, because it looks exactly like real anatomy. When a strong flat reflector such as the diaphragm lies between the probe and a structure, returning echoes can bounce a second time and appear on the far side of the reflector, so a liver lesion or a pleural collection seems to exist on the wrong side of a boundary. Refraction and speed error artifacts bend the apparent position of structures when the beam crosses an interface at an angle or passes through tissue whose true speed of sound differs from the value the machine assumes. Slice thickness artifact comes from the finite width of the beam, which averages echoes from tissue beside the plane of interest and can fill a simple cyst with fake internal echoes, while aliasing turns a fast jet into a reversed waveform that looks like a different disease. The honest defense is to change the approach, the probe angle, or the window, because an artifact usually moves when the operator moves, and the settings that affect these artifacts must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Ultrasound is used in almost every specialty, and in several it has replaced procedures that once required radiation or surgery. In obstetrics it dates a pregnancy from the length of the embryo, checks the number of fetuses, follows growth, locates the placenta, measures the fluid around the fetus, and guides a needle for amniocentesis, while Doppler of the umbilical artery gives information about the placental circulation. In gynecology a transvaginal probe examines the uterus and ovaries, characterizes a cyst, follows a follicle, and guides the retrieval of eggs for assisted reproduction, and in cardiology the phased array probe measures chamber size, wall thickness, and valve motion while Doppler quantifies the velocity of flow across a narrowed or leaking valve. In emergency and general medicine a rapid bedside scan looks for free fluid in the abdomen, blood around the heart, fluid in the chest, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and in vascular practice it maps the veins for a clot and follows a graft or a dialysis fistula, with the specific protocols, the required views, and the measurement thresholds confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Other specialties use the same physics for narrower purposes. In urology a probe measures the prostate, estimates residual urine in the bladder, and guides a biopsy, while in musculoskeletal practice a high frequency linear probe examines tendons, ligaments, joints, and nerves and can guide an injection or a nerve block. In anesthesia and intensive care it helps place a central line under direct vision, confirms the position of a tube in the airway, and assesses the lungs for fluid or collapse. In pediatrics it examines the infant hip, the neonatal brain through the fontanelle, and the urinary tract, and its lack of ionizing radiation is a particular advantage in a growing child. In ophthalmology a very high frequency probe measures the length of the eye and examines the retina when the cornea or lens is opaque, and in breast care it characterizes a lump and guides a core needle biopsy, with the probe frequency, the needle guide, and the sterility requirements confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital grade machine is a cart with a large display, a keyboard, a trackball, several probe ports, and a computer inside. It needs a stable mains supply, and in a busy department it is usually plugged into a circuit backed by an uninterruptible power supply, called a UPS, because a machine that loses power during an examination may lose the study. It needs a dedicated examination table with a cleanable surface, a screen for privacy, dim lighting so the display can be read, and enough space for the operator to stand on both sides of the patient. Its images travel over the hospital network in the standard format of Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine, called DICOM, and are filed in the picture archiving and communication system, called PACS, where the report and the images meet the patient's record. It needs a gel warmer, a supply of probe covers and disinfectant, a waste bin, a rack to store probes, and hand hygiene materials and personal protective equipment, called PPE, within reach, and the voltage, the power rating, the network configuration, and the storage pathway must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Between the cart and the pocket device sit two more classes of machine, and the difference is mostly the display and the software. A point of care device is a compact unit, often with a sealed keyboard and a touch screen, designed for the bedside, the emergency department, or the intensive care unit, and its presets are simplified so a non specialist can answer one narrow question quickly. A handheld unit is smaller still, sometimes no larger than the probe itself, and it either has a tiny built in screen or sends the image by a cable or wireless link to a mobile telephone or tablet, where an application performs the processing. Both classes accept a limited number of probes, both usually lack the full measurement package of a cart machine, and both depend on a battery and on software updates that the user must actually install. The advantage is that the machine reaches the patient rather than the patient reaching the machine, and the battery capacity, the charging cycle, the wireless configuration, and the software version must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance is mostly inspection and restraint, because the electronics are sealed and the vulnerable parts are the probe and the cable. Every probe is examined in good light before each shift for cracks in the lens, a lifted seal, a kink, a worn strain relief, or a bent connector pin, and any probe that fails is withdrawn until tested, because a damaged probe is both an infection risk and an electrical risk. A tissue equivalent phantom or small test object is scanned at intervals to check that the same structure produces the same brightness and the same measured distance, and the record of that test is what proves the machine has not drifted. Dead elements show as dark vertical bands in a uniform phantom image, and a probe that has lost a group of elements may still produce a convincing picture of the wrong anatomy, while cable and connector faults often appear only when the cable is flexed, so the electrical safety test, the calibration interval, the phantom test, and the inspection schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The failure modes of ultrasound are few and each has a signature. A probe with dead elements produces fixed vertical dark lines that stay in the same place whatever the patient and whatever the depth. A break in the cable produces a sudden loss of signal when the cable is bent, and the characteristic alarm is a disconnected probe message or a blank image with a fault code. Fluid that has entered a cracked lens or flooded connector produces an image that fades, flickers, or fills with noise, and a probe in that condition must never be used on a patient, because the same defect that lets fluid in can let current out. A console that overheats may shut down or lose its image storage, a battery that no longer holds charge turns a portable machine into one that must be carried with its power supply, and a software fault can freeze the image while the machine continues to transmit. The fault codes, the temperature limits, the shutdown thresholds, and the battery replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator's start of shift check takes a few minutes and prevents most of the day's failures. The machine is switched on and allowed to complete its self test, the date and time are verified, and the patient identification fields are cleared of the previous patient. Each probe that will be used is connected, inspected, and briefly tested on a known structure, and its preset is confirmed correct, while the display is checked for uniformity and for any dark band that suggests a dead element. The trackball, keyboard, freeze button, and measurement calipers are exercised, the supply of gel, probe covers, disinfectant, and cleaning wipes is confirmed, and the battery of any portable unit is confirmed charged with its charger present. The previous day's studies are confirmed to have reached the picture archiving and communication system, because an unsent study may have to be repeated, and the self test, the probe check, the cleaning materials, and the storage confirmation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the ultrasound variant is usually a single handheld probe paired with a small screen or a telephone, powered by a battery bank that may itself be charged from a solar panel. The device gives up the cart, the large display, the several probe ports, the full measurement package, the image archive, and the reporting software, and in exchange it fits into a bag, runs for hours without mains power, and can be carried to a patient who cannot be moved. The most common configuration is a convex probe for the abdomen and obstetrics and a linear probe for superficial work, and the choice of which to carry is a decision about which questions the clinic must answer. The image is smaller and dimmer than a cart image, and the operator often works with daylight falling on the screen, which reduces the apparent contrast and makes a marginal finding harder to see. A gel substitute is often necessary, and the battery capacity, the charging arrangement, the probe selection, and the gel substitute must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the field unit demands instead of infrastructure is discipline, and the discipline is mostly about power, cleanliness, and interpretation. Power must be managed as a clinical supply, which means charging whenever a source is available, carrying a charged spare, avoiding deep discharge, and protecting the battery from heat, because a battery left in a hot vehicle loses capacity permanently. Cleanliness must be improvised without cutting corners, so a probe that has touched skin is wiped between patients, and a probe used inside a body cavity is covered with a sheath and then disinfected to the highest level the setting allows. Protection of the probe is a daily habit, because a handheld unit is dropped, sat upon, and packed against hard objects, and a cracked lens in a remote clinic may end the ultrasound service for months. Interpretation is the hardest demand, because a handheld image is easy to obtain and hard to read, and the operator must know the limit of his or her own skill, with the charging routine, the disinfection level, the sheath, and the referral criteria confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field clinic commonly sends images or short clips to a distant reviewer, and that practice has real value and real limits. A compressed image sent over a weak mobile link loses resolution and may lose the measurement scale, so the reviewer must be told the probe used, the depth, the patient's age and sex, and the exact question being asked. A telephone photograph of a screen is a triage aid rather than a diagnostic study, and it should decide whether a patient must travel, not exclude a serious condition at home. Where a data link exists, a short clip is more informative than a still image for anything that moves, such as a fetal heart or a valve, and the file should be sent in a standard format where the software allows it. Documentation in the field is often the weakest point, because a study that is not written down cannot be compared at the next visit, so the operator should record the date, the probe, the findings, the images saved, and the name of anyone who reviewed them, and the referral pathway and the transmission format must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the field the handheld probe earns its place through a small number of high value questions. It can confirm a pregnancy and estimate its age, locate a fetal heartbeat, check the position of the placenta, and measure the fluid around the fetus, which guides a decision about referral before labor begins. It can look for free fluid in the abdomen after trauma, for fluid around the heart, and for an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and it can guide a needle into a joint, an abscess, or a vein when blind puncture would be dangerous. It can examine the gallbladder, the kidneys, and the bladder, and it can show a deep vein clot in a leg, which is otherwise a clinical guess. What it cannot do reliably in inexperienced hands is exclude disease, because a negative handheld scan is not the same as a negative full examination, so the operator must treat the device as a question answerer and not as a verdict and must confirm the specific protocols and measurement thresholds against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The last component of an ultrasound service is the trained person, and ultrasound is unusual in that the same machine produces a useful examination or a dangerous one depending entirely on the operator. Training must cover the physics well enough that the operator understands depth, attenuation, and artifacts, the anatomy of the regions being scanned, the standard views and how to obtain them, the controls and why each is adjusted, and the safety limits of acoustic output. Competence is best proved by a period of supervised scanning with a logbook of examinations and images reviewed by an experienced teacher, because a certificate without practice does not produce a safe operator. Periodic refresher training matters more in ultrasound than with many devices, because the operator's skill decays when the case mix is narrow and because new presets and new probes change the technique. Every service should have a written scope of practice stating which examinations each operator may perform and which must be referred, and the training requirements, the supervision period, the logbook, and the scope of practice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, ultrasound is a pulse of sound reflected from boundaries of differing acoustic impedance, and the machine turns the delay into depth and the strength into brightness. The frequency of that pulse fixes the trade between resolution and penetration, the array of crystals focuses and steers it, and the console controls gain, time gain compensation, depth, focus, and output power to make the returning echoes readable. The probe's shape follows the anatomy, coupling gel excludes the air that would reflect the beam, and the modes of brightness, motion, and Doppler answer different questions while the mechanical index and the thermal index warn of the energy being delivered. Artifacts such as shadowing, enhancement, reverberation, and mirror image can imitate disease, so every finding must be confirmed in more than one plane, and the same probe that touches every patient must be cleaned and disinfected according to what it touched and what its maker permits. In the hospital the machine is a cart with a network, an archive, and an uninterruptible power supply, while in the field it is a handheld probe with a battery bank, a gel substitute, and a distant reviewer. In every setting the rule is the same: use the lowest output that answers the question, keep the dwell time short, treat the probe as the fragile instrument it is, and confirm every setting, threshold, and disinfection cycle against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a patient is scanned.

# Chapter 28 — Nuclear Medicine and PET

Nuclear medicine images radiation that begins inside the patient rather than a beam aimed through the patient, and that inversion explains nearly everything about the machines that follow. A radionuclide is an unstable atomic nucleus that emits a particle or a photon as it reaches a more stable state, and when it is attached to a compound the body handles in a particular way the combination is called a radiopharmaceutical. Such an agent is a tracer rather than a drug, because the quantity given is far too small to have any pharmacological effect, yet its photons escape through the overlying tissue to a detector outside the body. The detector records the position and the number of those photons, so the picture maps where the tracer concentrated rather than showing a shadow of what stood in the beam, which is why these images are grainy compared with a radiograph. Every tracer, activity, and imaging time named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A nucleus can decay in several ways, and the choice of radionuclide follows from the manner of decay and the energy of what comes out. In one common mode a nucleus rearranges its own protons and neutrons and emits a photon of pure electromagnetic energy, called a gamma ray, whose predictable energy can be counted and located from outside the body. In positron emission a proton becomes a neutron and a positron, and the positron travels a few millimeters through tissue before meeting an electron, after which the two annihilate and produce two photons of 511 kiloelectron volts flying apart almost exactly opposite to each other, an energy that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The half-life is the time in which half of the atoms present will have decayed, and there is also a biological half-life, the time the body takes to clear half of the compound, with the physical and biological values combining into an effective half-life always shorter than either alone, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Production begins far from the imaging room, in a nuclear reactor or a cyclotron. A reactor makes nuclides by bombarding a stable target with neutrons, which is how iodine-131 and several therapeutic agents are produced, while a cyclotron accelerates charged particles into a target and is the usual source of fluorine-18 and other positron emitters.
