Most hospitals never see either machine, because the commonest imaging nuclide, technetium-99m, arrives through a generator on a bench in the hot laboratory, where molybdenum-99 with a half-life of about 66 hours decays into technetium-99m with a half-life of about 6 hours. The eluate is washed out with sterile saline once or twice a day, and the first elution carries the most activity. Every generator has a limit on the molybdenum that may break through into the eluate, and that breakthrough must be tested before the eluate reaches a patient, because molybdenum adds dose without adding image, with the elution efficiency and breakthrough limit confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The dose calibrator turns a prescription in megabecquerels into a measured volume in a syringe, and it is the first quality control device of the department. It is a gas-filled ionization chamber with a well in the top, and when a radioactive source sits in the well the radiation ionizes the gas and the resulting current is displayed as activity. The reading depends on the geometry of the source, so a syringe lying flat, a syringe upright in a holder, and a vial of different shape give different readings for the same radioactivity. The commonest operator error in nuclear medicine is to measure a dose in one geometry and inject it in another, or to leave the cap and needle shield in the well and count their attenuation as part of the dose. A daily constancy check with a sealed long-lived source proves the instrument has not drifted, and the characteristic alarm is a high background or an over-range indication that must stop the work rather than be silenced, with the calibration factors and constancy limits confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The patient's journey has three parts, and each has its own equipment and safety question. Before anything is injected the patient is identified against the request and asked about pregnancy and breastfeeding, because a radiopharmaceutical given to a pregnant woman irradiates the fetus and a tracer excreted in milk reaches the infant. A thyroid blocking agent may be given before certain examinations to protect the thyroid from free iodine. The injection is usually intravenous, and the activity is drawn behind a lead shield, checked against the prescription, and recorded with the time so decay between measurement and injection is accounted for. Then comes the uptake period, minutes or hours depending on the tracer, during which the patient waits in a designated area and is asked to drink water and empty the bladder, because a full bladder obscures the pelvis and receives unnecessary dose. The scan comes last and demands that the patient lie still for many minutes in a machine that may feel close and sound noisy, with the blocking dose, injected activity, and scan duration confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The gamma camera is the workhorse of single photon imaging, and it converts the position and energy of each arriving photon into a signal a computer accumulates into a picture. Its first element is the collimator, a thick plate of lead pierced by thousands of parallel holes, which admits only photons traveling roughly perpendicular to the crystal and absorbs the rest. The collimator gives the camera its sense of direction and makes it insensitive, because most photons emitted by the patient strike lead between the holes and are lost. Behind it sits a large crystal of sodium iodide activated with thallium, which absorbs a photon and converts its energy into a brief flash of visible light that an array of photomultiplier tubes detects, the relative brightness of neighboring tubes being used by position logic to calculate where the event occurred. A pulse height analyzer compares the total energy of the event with the expected energy of the radionuclide and rejects events outside a chosen window, so scattered radiation and background are separated from true gamma rays, with the energy window and collimator choice confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Collimators are exchanged for different examinations, and the choice follows the energy of the radionuclide and the resolution the question requires. A low energy collimator has thin septa and many small holes and gives the best resolution for technetium-99m, whose principal photon energy is about 140 kiloelectron volts, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A medium or high energy collimator has thicker septa and fewer, wider holes, because the higher energy photons of iodine-131 or indium-111 would penetrate thin septa and blur the image in a fog of septal penetration, while a pinhole collimator magnifies a small organ such as the thyroid. The most damaging operator error is to scan with the wrong collimator for the radionuclide in use, because the image still looks like an image, and the loss of contrast and the false counts are easy to blame on the patient rather than the mistake. A dropped collimator may have bent septa invisible to the eye, so it is inspected rather than merely dusted, with the septal thickness and usable energy range confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Quality control of a gamma camera is a daily and monthly ritual, because a camera can drift silently while still producing plausible pictures. The daily uniform flood image, made with a uniform source, reveals a photomultiplier tube that has failed, a crystal damaged by moisture, or an energy correction out of date. The energy spectrum of each radionuclide is checked and the peak position adjusted, because a drifting peak throws the energy window off the photopeak and lets scattered events into the image. Uniformity, spatial resolution, spatial linearity, sensitivity, and energy resolution are measured on a written schedule, and any result outside the tolerance set by the manufacturer must be corrected before patients are scanned. The characteristic alarm on a modern camera is a detector or energy warning at the console, and the correct response is to stop imaging and repeat the quality control rather than accept the study, with those tolerances confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Single photon emission computed tomography adds depth to the planar image by rotating the camera around the patient and reconstructing the data mathematically. The camera head orbits the body and collects a series of projections, each a planar image from a different angle, and the computer combines them into slices through the organ of interest. The reconstruction is usually iterative, because the algorithm models photon attenuation and scatter and adjusts its estimate until it matches the measured projections, and modern systems also correct for attenuation by the patient's own tissue. The first dominant error is patient motion, because a few centimeters of movement between projections produce streaks and false defects that resemble disease, and the second is a miscalibrated center of rotation, which produces artifacts that can mimic a lesion. The patient is therefore positioned securely and watched throughout the orbit, the center of rotation is measured and corrected on a written schedule, and the number of projections and the attenuation correction method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Positron emission tomography, called PET, detects the annihilation event rather than the emitted positron, and this indirectness is the source of both its power and its complexity. A positron travels a few millimeters through tissue until it meets an electron, and the two annihilate and convert their combined mass into two photons of 511 kiloelectron volts traveling in nearly opposite directions, an energy that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A ring of detectors surrounds the patient, and when two detectors on opposite sides record a photon within a few nanoseconds of each other the system accepts the event as a coincidence and draws a line between them. Coincidence detection replaces the physical collimator of the gamma camera and explains why a PET scanner is far more sensitive than a single photon camera, since no lead is needed to establish the direction of the photons. Random coincidences arise when two unrelated photons arrive inside the timing window and scattered coincidences when one photon is deflected before detection, and both are corrected during reconstruction, while attenuation is measured with a computed tomography scan, called CT, on the same bed. The coincidence timing window, the energy window, and the attenuation correction method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The detectors of a PET scanner are dense scintillator crystals arranged in blocks and coupled to photomultiplier tubes or solid state light sensors, and the crystal must stop 511 kiloelectron volts radiation efficiently as well as emit light quickly. The crystals are packed into rings around the bore, and the patient table moves through the ring in bed positions so that a whole body image can be assembled, while time of flight detection measures the tiny difference in arrival time between the two photons and localizes the annihilation along the line of response. A modern scanner is usually combined with a CT scanner in the same gantry, so a short CT scan is performed first for attenuation correction and anatomical localization and the two image sets are fused for reading. The characteristic alarm of a PET scanner is a detector block warning or a coincidence timing failure, and it must be investigated before the patient is injected, because an injected dose cannot be recovered. The scan time per bed, the reconstruction parameters, and the detector performance limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The most widely used PET tracer is fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose, a glucose analog in which one oxygen atom has been replaced by a positron emitting fluorine atom. It is made in a cyclotron, and its half-life of about 110 minutes governs the logistics of a PET service, because a dose must be produced, tested, transported, injected, and imaged within a few hours. Fluorodeoxyglucose enters cells through the same transporters as glucose, is phosphorylated by the same enzyme, and then cannot proceed along the metabolic pathway, so it is trapped inside the cell in proportion to that cell's glucose metabolism, which is why tumors, infected tissue, and active brain regions appear bright. Because the tracer competes with the patient's own glucose, a high blood glucose level depresses uptake into tumors and produces a misleading scan, so patients fast and a blood glucose measurement is taken before the injection. Insulin moves the tracer into muscle and fat, so a patient who has recently taken insulin or eaten may show intense muscle uptake that obscures the findings, with the injected activity, fasting interval, blood glucose limit, and uptake time confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hot laboratory is where radiopharmaceuticals are received, prepared, measured, and drawn into syringes, and it is designed to contain contamination rather than merely store material. Its walls, floor, and bench are smooth and non-absorbent so a spill can be wiped up, and its surfaces are covered with disposable absorbent paper changed whenever it is soiled. Radiopharmaceuticals are kept in lead pots behind a lead brick wall or in a shielded safe, syringes are carried in a lead or tungsten shield, and vials are handled with tongs rather than fingers. The fume hood protects the product from the operator and the operator from the product, and it runs at a negative pressure so that airborne radioactivity is drawn away from the breathing zone. Everyone who enters wears gloves, a laboratory coat, and a dosimeter, and the room is surveyed with a contamination monitor at the end of each working day, with the shielding thickness, hood airflow, acceptable contamination level, and wipe test frequency confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of nuclear medicine are cheap individually and indispensable collectively, and a single missing item can stop a patient list. There are sterile syringes and needles of several sizes, sterile vials, sterile saline for elution, and alcohol swabs handled on an absorbent pad that catches drips, together with lead or tungsten syringe shields, lead pots, transport containers, forceps, and vial holders. There are disposable gloves, laboratory coats, eye protection, absorbent bench covering, and a spill kit containing absorbent pads, tongs, bags, and a contamination monitor. There are the patient care items, including cannulae, adhesive dressings, warm blankets, pillows, positioning aids, and the urinary collection bags needed when a patient cannot control the bladder. There are the dose labels, activity record forms, the instruction sheets given to a patient after a therapy dose, and the sharps containers and radioactive waste bags that receive everything at the end, with the sterility, expiry date, and labeling of every syringe confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Radioactive waste is not removed but held until it is no longer radioactive, and the storage room is therefore part of the equipment. Solid waste goes into lined bins, liquid waste into shielded tanks or decay sinks, and sharps into a rigid container that is itself labeled as radioactive. The rule of thumb is to store the waste for at least 10 half-lives of the radionuclide present and then survey it before release, and the exact holding time and release level for each nuclide must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Iodine-131 is the difficult one, because its 8 day half-life means contaminated items may be held for weeks, and patients treated with it excrete radioactivity in urine, saliva, and sweat for several days. Cleaning a camera or a table after a patient with incontinence begins with gloves and an absorbent pad, continues with a detergent that lifts the material rather than spreading it, and ends with a survey of the area. Blood, urine, and vomit are all potentially radioactive after a dose, so the cleaning materials themselves become radioactive waste.

Radiation protection for staff rests on three variables, and every habit in the department manages one of them. Time is the first, because the dose received is proportional to how long a person stays close to the source, so injections are quick, rehearsed, and never performed with a colleague standing nearby. Distance is the second, because the dose rate falls steeply with separation, so a syringe is carried at arm's length and a patient is spoken to from the doorway. Shielding is the third, and it is why the syringe shield, the lead pot, and the lead-lined wall exist. Each worker wears a whole body dosimeter and, when handling large activities, a ring badge on the hand that receives most exposure, and the badges are read regularly because a dose never measured is a dose that can never be reduced. A declared pregnancy changes the working pattern, and any dose limit approached or exceeded triggers an investigation, with the dose limits and investigation levels confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The people who live with a patient are exposed after the patient goes home, and the equipment of their protection is a written instruction and a nurse who explains it. After a diagnostic scan the activity is small and the risk negligible, but after treatment with iodine-131 the patient remains a moving source for days, and the instructions are specific. The patient may be asked to sleep in a separate bed, keep a certain distance from children and pregnant women, use a separate toilet and flush it twice, and wash soiled linen separately, and the numbers attached to each instruction must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The commonest failure is a patient who cannot read the written sheet, or who is too polite to ask what it means, so the instruction is spoken and then checked by asking the patient to explain it back. The real hazard is not the trained worker, who is monitored and rotates away from the source, but the child held on a lap the evening after a therapy dose.

Two smaller instruments support nuclear medicine by measuring radioactivity outside the imaging room, and both need their own care. The well counter contains a sodium iodide crystal with a hole through it, and a small sample of blood, urine, or tissue placed in the well is surrounded by the crystal, which detects a large fraction of the emitted photons. It is used for blood volume, glomerular filtration, and other measurements where activity in a sample is counted against a standard, while the uptake probe is a collimated detector placed against the neck to measure the fraction of an administered iodine dose taken up by the thyroid. Both are energy sensitive, so both are checked with a source of known activity and their energy window and background verified before a patient is counted. The characteristic error with either device is a change in geometry, because moving a sample tube or the probe changes the count rate without any change in the patient, with the counting time, background subtraction method, and calibration factor of each instrument confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Nuclear medicine equipment needs scheduled maintenance, and every operator should be able to name its failure modes. The camera crystal is hygroscopic, so a crack or a failed seal lets moisture in and produces a cold spot or a spreading discoloration that no software can repair, which is one reason a camera room is kept at a stable temperature and humidity. A photomultiplier tube can fail or become noisy, which appears as a hole or a bright spot on the flood image, and the tube is replaced by an engineer rather than adjusted by the operator. The collimator is heavy and easily damaged, the gantry and table carry motors and position sensors that drift and fail, and the detectors of a PET scanner contain thousands of crystals and light sensors whose gains must be checked and corrected. The dose calibrator is the instrument most often neglected because it always appears to work, yet a drifting calibrator changes every dose in the department at once, with service intervals, calibration frequencies, and the acceptance tolerances that follow any repair confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A short start of shift check catches most of the faults that would otherwise spoil a day of imaging. The operator confirms that the dose calibrator is switched on, that its background reading is at the expected level, and that the daily constancy check with the sealed source agrees with the previous day's value. The camera is checked for the correct collimator, the energy peak is verified for the radionuclide in use, and the morning flood image is inspected before the first patient rather than after the last. The survey meter is switched on, tested against its check source, and its battery confirmed, because a survey meter with a dead battery gives false reassurance, and the generator is eluted according to schedule with the breakthrough test recorded. The patient list is checked for the correct tracer, activity, and timing, and the pregnancy and breastfeeding questions are asked and documented for every patient of childbearing age, with the energy peak, constancy limit, breakthrough limit, and background level confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The first field variant is not a frontier clinic at all but a large vehicle, because the smallest practical version of this imaging is a scanner that travels between hospitals. A mobile PET and CT unit is built into a trailer or container and carries the scanner, a small hot laboratory with a shielded bench, a dose calibrator, and a waiting area for patients. It gives up the cyclotron and the radiochemistry laboratory, so it depends entirely on delivered doses of fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose, whose short half-life and tight delivery schedule dictate the whole day, and it gives up the hospital's stable power and cooling, so it carries its own electrical supply and air conditioning. It demands that the receiving site provide a parking place with power, water, and a route wide enough for a stretcher, and the dose rate at the outer wall is surveyed whenever the unit is parked near another building or a public path. Because the equipment is moved, its alignment, energy calibration, and image quality are rechecked at every new site, and those checks and their tolerances must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A district hospital may support a much smaller service, and the compromises there are a lesson in what the physics actually requires. Such a service usually has a technetium-99m generator, a single-head gamma camera, a dose calibrator, a well counter or an uptake probe, and one lead-lined room that serves as hot laboratory and imaging room together. It gives up the cyclotron, the PET scanner, and the radiochemistry, so it performs planar and single photon emission computed tomography studies of thyroid, bone, kidney, and heart rather than metabolic whole body imaging, and it depends on a trained technologist who can recognize a failing photomultiplier tube rather than on a service contract that arrives within hours. The generator must be delivered on a schedule that respects its own decay, which makes a reliable supply chain as essential as the camera itself, and the activity available on any given day must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic nuclear medicine does not travel, and honesty about that fact is more useful than a modified machine. There is no generator, no hot laboratory, no shielded room, and no way to manage radioactive waste, and a radiopharmaceutical that cannot be delivered within its useful half-life cannot be used at all. Ultrasound answers many of the questions a thyroid scan or a renal scan would have answered, because it shows the size, structure, and blood flow of an organ without any radiation at all, and it is the single most valuable imaging device in a remote setting. Plain radiography answers questions about bone, lung, and bowel, and a CT scanner at a referral center answers questions about the brain, chest, and abdomen, while laboratory tests substitute for some functional studies, because a thyroid stimulating hormone level or a renal function panel may answer the clinical question an uptake measurement would have answered. The decision to refer is itself a piece of equipment and should be made early rather than after several days of tests that cannot settle the diagnosis.

Sending a patient for nuclear medicine from a remote clinic is a logistical exercise, and the equipment that makes it work is mostly paper and communication. The referral note must state the clinical question, the relevant history, the tests already done, and whether the patient can lie still and cooperate, because a scan without that information may answer the wrong question. The appointment must be timed with the tracer's half-life in mind, since a dose prepared for a morning appointment is useless to a patient who arrives in the afternoon, and the travel plan must include the return journey, because a patient who has received a therapy dose should not sit for hours on public transport beside other passengers. Images travel better than patients in some cases, and where a picture archiving and communication system, called PACS, is available the images are sent in the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine standard, called DICOM, rather than photographed, because a photograph of a screen loses the quantitative information on which interpretation depends. Where no such link exists, films or a disk may be carried by hand, and the appointment timing, the transport restrictions after a therapy dose, and the data format accepted by the receiving center must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, nuclear medicine images radiation that starts inside the patient, using a radiopharmaceutical whose radionuclide decays with a known half-life and emits photons a detector can locate. The gamma camera collimates those photons with a lead plate, converts them to light in a sodium iodide crystal, and positions each event with photomultiplier tubes, while single photon emission computed tomography rotates the camera and reconstructs slices and PET detects the two opposed photons of an annihilation event in coincidence and merges that metabolic image with CT. The supporting instruments matter as much as the camera, because the dose calibrator measures what is injected, the well counter and the uptake probe measure activity in a sample and in an organ, and the hot laboratory keeps the radioactivity where it belongs. The hazards are contamination, unnecessary dose to staff and families, and the silent drift of an instrument that still produces a plausible picture, and the defenses are time, distance, shielding, monitoring, and a written daily check routine that is actually followed. Among the commonest operator errors are the wrong collimator, the wrong geometry in the dose calibrator, an unasked pregnancy question, and a patient who moves during a long acquisition, while in the field none of this travels, so the clinic substitutes ultrasound, radiography, CT at a referral center, and laboratory tests and relies on an early and honest referral. Every setting, activity, energy, and threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 29 — Mammography, DEXA, and Specialized Imaging

Most imaging machines can be pointed at almost any part of the body, but a small group is built to answer one question extremely well, and mammography, bone densitometry, and the specialized units around them are the clearest examples. The reason is contrast, because the difference between one soft tissue and another, or between bone mineral and the fat around it, is far smaller than the difference between bone and air. To see such a faint difference the machine trades flexibility for optimization, using a narrow energy band, a short distance to the detector, and a fixed geometry. The benefit is the detection of a disease that is otherwise silent, and the cost is a room of its own, a phantom, and a strict quality program. This chapter describes those machines and their failures, and then describes what a mobile or frontier clinic can carry in their place.

The breast is a difficult radiographic subject because nearly everything inside it attenuates X-rays almost equally. Contrast comes from two measures at once, from photons of low energy, where small differences in absorption are magnified, and from compression, which spreads the tissue thinner and separates structures that would otherwise overlap. The mammography tube is therefore dedicated to a narrow band of low energy photons, with an anode of molybdenum, and sometimes rhodium or tungsten, whose characteristic emission lies at about 17 to 20 kiloelectronvolts at a tube voltage usually between 25 and 32 kilovolts, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The focal spot is very small, about 0.1 millimeter for magnification views and about 0.3 millimeter for contact views, dimensions that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The window is beryllium because glass would absorb the very photons the examination needs, and the anode must cool between patients because the weak beam needs a long exposure.

Compression is the most important action the technologist performs, and it is a mechanical intervention with a measured force. The paddle descends under motor power, and the force it applies is displayed in newtons, with a typical examination using roughly 100 to 200 newtons, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Compression thins the breast so that less radiation is needed, spreads the glandular tissue so that overlapping structures separate, and holds the breast still so that motion does not smear the image. Excessive force causes pain, bruising, and in a woman with an implant the risk of rupture, while the common operator error runs the other way, because too little compression produces a soft and unreadable image at a higher dose. The paddle must release instantly when the pedal or the emergency release is pressed, and that release is tested every day, a routine that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Between the breast and the detector lies an anti-scatter grid of fine lead strips that absorbs photons deflected inside the breast. Scatter carries no positional information and veils the faint contrast between glandular tissue and fat, so the grid is essential, and it usually moves during the exposure so that its own lines do not appear. Behind the detector the automatic exposure control ends the exposure when a preset quantity of radiation has arrived, and it therefore adapts the technique to the thickness and composition of each breast. The dose is reported as the mean glandular dose, usually between 1 and 3 milligray for a single view, and that value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An automatic exposure control that has drifted silently changes every dose in the room, and only a phantom of known thickness and composition will reveal it.

The receptor has passed through the same generations as general radiography, with film, photostimulable phosphor plates, and flat panels of amorphous selenium or a scintillator on a thin film transistor array. A digital panel reads each picture element within seconds and sends it to the picture archiving and communication system, called PACS, and the elements are commonly between 50 and 100 micrometers, a dimension that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Digital detectors hide overexposure, because a detector that receives too much radiation still produces a clean looking image. Tomosynthesis refines the same machine, because the tube sweeps through an arc, commonly 15 to 50 degrees, and makes between 10 and 25 low dose exposures whose shift and addition bring one thin plane into focus and blur the rest, and those values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The listener should picture a fan of thin slices through the breast, each a few millimeters thick, but the longer compression and the reconstruction mean more data and a longer reading time.

The examination is a set of views, and each view is defined by the anatomy it must show. The craniocaudal view compresses the breast from above, and the mediolateral oblique view compresses it from the side at an angle that follows the pectoral muscle, so that the muscle appears as a triangle at the top of the image. The common operator error is poor positioning, above all an oblique view with too little pectoral muscle, which leaves the upper outer quadrant unexamined and is a well documented reason for a cancer found between screens. The hazard is radiation risk, weighed differently because the breast is radiosensitive and the examination is offered to women who feel well, so a screening program fixes an age range, an interval, and a dose for each view, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pregnancy question is asked before the examination, the characteristic alarm is a tube overload tone or a fault message that stops the exposure, the correct response is to let the tube cool rather than repeat at once, and the emergency compression release is tested before the first patient.

A dedicated mammography room is arranged around the posture of the patient and the reach of the technologist. The machine is a single column with the tube above, the detector below, the paddle between them, a pedal for height, and hand controls on both sides, while the console may sit behind a lead glass screen. The room also holds a magnifier, a chair, a private changing area, and a viewing station whose monitor is calibrated for reading. The consumables are a gown, a skin wipe, and a single use paddle cover for every patient, a permitted disinfectant for the detector window, and for biopsy a sterile drape, a local anesthetic, needles commonly between 14 and 9 gauge, a vacuum canister, specimen containers with fixative, and marker clips. The gauge, depth, and throw of every needle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the list ends with sharps containers, hand hygiene supplies, and a written record of every specimen and marker.

Cleaning here is patient safety rather than housekeeping, because bare skin presses against the same surfaces all day. The paddle, detector window, face shield, and handles are wiped between patients, the paddle cover is changed even when the skin looked clean, and the biopsy tray and needle guide are disinfected after every procedure. The concentration, contact time, and material compatibility of every disinfectant must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Quality control is unusually strict because the contrast is faint, so a phantom containing simulated fibers, specks, and masses is imaged at a fixed technique and scored against previous images, the compression force is measured with a calibrated scale, and the reading monitor receives a luminance and gray scale check. A warning from the quality control software, or a phantom that fails its scoring criteria, is a fault to be investigated rather than a nuisance to be cleared.

A dying tube arcs, heard as a sharp crack and shown as a fault code, and an aged tube loses output so that the automatic exposure control raises the dose. A compression mechanism that drifts applies less force than the display claims, a flat panel with dead elements shows the same dots on every image, and a scratched plate shows a line that travels with the plate rather than with the machine. The viewing station is a common source of silent failure, because an uncalibrated monitor or a bright room changes the decision of the reader with no technical alarm at all. The start of shift check covers the whole chain, warming up the tube, raising and lowering the paddle, testing the emergency release, imaging a phantom, and confirming that the images of the last patient reached PACS. The warm-up, phantom schedule, and daily check list must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When an image shows something suspicious, the next device takes a piece of it, because a needle must reach a lesion a few millimeters across inside a moving organ without cutting anything it should not. Guidance relates the lesion to a coordinate system the operator can see, either stereotactically with pairs of angled X-ray views or in real time under ultrasound, and the choice follows the lesion. A stereotactic system exploits the geometry of two eyes, because two angled images of the same compressed breast reveal the depth of the lesion from its displacement, and the machine computes three coordinates and drives a needle guide to that point on a prone table. The common operator error is to accept a lesion that is not clear in both angled views, or to let the breast shift between the scout image and the sampling, because the computed depth then points at normal tissue. Bleeding, infection, and a needle advanced too far into the chest wall are the hazards, the characteristic alarm is a position or verification failure that stops the sequence, and the needle gauge, depth of throw, and verification sequence must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A vacuum assisted device collects more tissue than a spring loaded needle through a single insertion, drawing tissue into a side aperture with vacuum while a rotating cutter advances. The operator can rotate the aperture and take many cores around the lesion, which is why the technique can remove a small mass completely and why it samples a cluster of microcalcifications well. A small metal marker clip is then deployed, because the lesion may no longer be visible after sampling and the clip identifies the site for later surgery and for the pathologist. The common operator error is to lose track of the clip or to omit the image that proves its position, and every specimen must be radiographed or examined to prove that the lesion itself was sampled. The needle size, the vacuum level, the number of cores, and the clip deployment must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Breast ultrasound rests on the reflection of high frequency sound at the boundaries between tissues, and its physics explains both its strengths and its blind spots. A probe emits short pulses of sound, commonly between 7 and 15 megahertz, and the returning echoes are timed to build a picture of depth, a frequency range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A higher frequency gives finer resolution but is absorbed more quickly, so the frequencies that suit the superficial breast would fail at the depth of the abdomen. The method is real time and free of ionizing radiation, it shows whether a mass is solid or fluid, and it is the natural guide for a needle, but it cannot reliably show microcalcifications. The probe is a semi-critical device, so it is wiped and disinfected between patients, the gel is never taken from a large multiuse container onto broken skin, and the common operator error is to press so hard that the breast is flattened and the lesion is displaced.

Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry, called DEXA, solves a problem of two unknowns with two measurements. Attenuation depends both on the amount of material and on its atomic composition, so a single measurement cannot separate bone mineral from the soft tissue around it. If the same region is measured at two different photon energies, the soft tissue contribution can be calculated and subtracted, leaving the bone mineral content. The energies used are commonly around 40 and 70 kiloelectronvolts, produced by switching the tube voltage or by filtering the beam, and those values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The result is not a true density but an areal density, the bone mineral content divided by the projected area, reported in grams per square centimeter, a unit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The densitometer is a table, an arm carrying a collimated source and a detector, and a computer that moves the arm across the patient. A pencil beam system moves the source and detector together in a raster, while a fan beam system sweeps a wider fan and scans faster, which reduces the chance that the patient will move. The standard sites are the lumbar spine and the proximal femur, because those are where a fragility fracture most often occurs and where the reference data are strongest. The result is compared with a reference database matched to the sex and the ethnic group of the patient, and this is where a machine can be badly misused, because a database from a different population gives a number that looks precise and means something else. The report must state the site, the value, the comparison score, and any artifact that limits the analysis, and the reference database, the sites measured, the scan length, and the analysis thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Quality control for DEXA is built around a phantom that contains a known amount of bone mineral, usually simulated vertebrae embedded in a block of tissue equivalent plastic. The phantom is scanned on a fixed schedule, and its measured mineral content is plotted on a control chart, so that a slow drift of the calibration, the detector, or the software is detected before it changes a patient result. The acceptable variation is small, a few per cent over the life of the machine, and the control limits, the scanning frequency, and the reference values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is a phantom result outside the control limits, and the correct response is to stop patient scanning and investigate rather than to repeat the phantom until a better number appears. The same discipline applies to the precision of the operator, because a technologist whose positioning varies will produce a variation larger than the disease being followed.

The radiation hazard of DEXA is minute, but not every hazard of the examination is radiation, because a patient left on the table while the arm moves can be struck by the arm. The common operator error is misanalysis rather than bad scanning, because an edge placed through a vertebra, a rib or the iliac crest included in the bone map, or a compressed vertebra left in the calculation will change the result in either direction. Metal implants, a recent contrast study, and severe degenerative change all inflate the measured density, and the report must say so rather than presenting the number as if it were clean. Consumables are modest, consisting of a cover on the table for each patient, a positioning block for the leg, a foot support, and disinfectant wipes, and the table pad is cleaned between patients because skin and feet touch it. Failure modes are quiet, because a drifting detector or a stale calibration shifts every result, a table that travels at the wrong speed stretches the skeleton, and an edited analysis template places the bone edges wrongly, so the daily check includes a phantom scan, an inspection of the table and arm, a review of the templates, and a reading of the control chart, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy uses sound to break a stone without an incision, and its principle is the focusing of energy in space and in time. A generator creates a pressure pulse of very short duration, and an ellipsoidal reflector or an acoustic lens brings the waves to a focus, so that a large area of low pressure at the skin becomes a small point of very high pressure inside the body. The pulse is commonly between 30 and 100 megapascals at the focus and lasts only a few microseconds, and the stone fractures because the sudden change of pressure creates tensile stress within it while the surrounding tissue tolerates the same wave, and that pressure range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The three common sources are the spark gap, which discharges a high voltage across electrodes in water, the electromagnetic source, which drives a metal membrane with a coil, and the piezoelectric source, which makes an array of crystals expand together. The patient is coupled to the wave path through a water bath or a water filled cushion, and any air between the cushion and the skin reflects the wave and wastes the treatment.

The first hazard of lithotripsy is cardiac, because a shock wave passing through the chest can trigger a disturbance of the heart rhythm. The pulse is therefore delivered in synchrony with the electrocardiogram, called ECG, and gated to a point in the cycle when the heart is electrically quiet, and a patient with a cardiac pacemaker needs a cardiology opinion first. Other hazards are pain, which requires analgesia and often sedation, blood in the urine that clears in a day or two, and rarely a hematoma around the kidney. The common operator error is poor coupling, because a fold of the cushion, a bubble of air, or a smear of soap reduces the energy reaching the stone and leads the operator to raise the output unnecessarily. The characteristic alarms are a gating failure, a coupling or water fault message, and an electrode wear warning, and the gating window, sedation plan, maximum energy, electrode replacement interval, and water quality must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The radiotherapy simulator is a diagnostic X-ray unit built to imitate the geometry of a treatment machine, and it answers one question before treatment begins, which is where exactly the beam will enter the patient. It has the same rotational gantry, table movements, and often the same lasers and isocentric distance as the treatment unit, but it uses kilovoltage X-rays and a flat panel or image intensifier instead of a therapy beam. The field edges are set with lead shutters, the patient is marked on the skin with ink or small tattoos, and verification images are stored so the position can be reproduced on the treatment machine. Alignment depends on the isocenter, the point around which the gantry and table rotate, and a laser that has drifted by even 1 or 2 millimeters moves every field in the department, a distance that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is that a mark on the skin looks authoritative even when it is wrong, so the common operator error is a field marked from a mislabeled image, and the isocentric distance, laser alignment, shutter calibration, and marking procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Computed tomography, called CT, has largely replaced the radiographic simulator for planning, because a scan gives the planner the density of every tissue along the beam path as well as the geometry. The older simulator survives where a CT scanner is not available or where a simple field must be verified quickly, and its quality control resembles that of a radiographic room but with an obsession about geometry. The isocenter is measured with a front pointer, the lasers are checked against a fixed reference, the light field is compared with the radiation field, and the table travel is measured in all three directions. A mechanical fault that would be trivial in a diagnostic room becomes serious here, because an error of a few millimeters becomes the same error in the treatment of every patient, and the characteristic alarms are a door interlock, an exposure fault, and a laser or gantry warning. The isocenter tolerance, laser check, field size test, and table travel limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

All of these units share a pattern the listener can carry from one machine to the next, because each one fixes its geometry, narrows its energy band, and defends that design with a phantom, a control chart, and a dedicated room. Each one also concentrates the skill of the operator, so that a technologist who works only in that room can be excellent while a visitor can be dangerous. The reading environment belongs to the device as much as the machine does, because a calibrated monitor and a dim room are part of the imaging chain in mammography and densitometry reporting. When any of these devices is absent the clinical question does not disappear, and the field must answer it with different equipment. Mammography itself does not travel, because the machine is heavy, it needs a stable power supply, its detector is fragile, and its quality control needs a phantom and a service visit, so a working unit in a remote setting should be protected rather than moved.

Portable bone densitometry is the field variant that travels best, because the physics of two energies can be squeezed into a small device that measures the heel, the forearm, or a finger. The machine is a bench top or handheld unit with a small source and detector, a cradle for the limb, and a battery or a mains adapter, and it reports an areal density within minutes. What it gives up is the axial skeleton, because the spine and the hip cannot be measured by a peripheral device, and the diagnosis and monitoring of treatment are defined at those axial sites. What it demands instead is honesty about the reference database, since a peripheral measurement compared with a database from another population may be meaningless. The site measured, the reference database, and the interpretation limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the report must state that the result is a screening estimate.

Portable ultrasound is the workhorse of breast assessment where mammography cannot reach, because a handheld unit with a linear probe can show a palpable mass, distinguish a cyst from a solid lesion, guide aspiration, and measure a lesion for later reassessment. What it gives up is the detection of microcalcifications, the reproducibility of a standard set of views, and the archival image a reader can review later, because a handheld examination is only as good as the person holding the probe. What it demands instead is a trained and supervised operator, a written record of the probe position and the finding, clean gel, a disinfected probe face, and a referral pathway for every lesion that cannot be resolved on the spot. Infection control is the hazard that portable ultrasound brings to the field, because a probe that is wiped once a day, a large container of gel that is refilled rather than replaced, and a machine carried between wards all transfer organisms from one patient to the next. The remedy is a single patient wipe for the probe, a small gel bottle for one patient where possible, hand hygiene before and after every examination, and a clean cover for any probe that touches broken skin, and the gel, disinfectant, and cover must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where no mammography exists, a clinical breast examination by a trained examiner can find a mass that is large enough to feel. A fine needle aspiration with an ordinary syringe can show whether a lump is a cyst, an abscess, or a solid tumor, which is information that ultrasound alone cannot give. The limits must be spoken aloud, because a normal examination does not exclude an early cancer, a sample can be inadequate or falsely reassuring, and neither method can find a cluster of microcalcifications. Lithotripsy cannot be improvised either, because it demands a focused pressure pulse, a water coupling system, and a source that erodes as it works, so a stone that needs shock wave treatment must be referred while a stone causing obstruction with infection is drained first. Radiotherapy planning follows the same logic, because a mark made without the geometry of the treatment machine is worse than no mark at all, so the field sends a complete record with the patient, and the referral criteria and record format must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Quality assurance in the field is proved with a simple phantom, a fixed setting, and a written record rather than with a service contract. A portable ultrasound unit is checked against a tissue equivalent phantom, so that a failing probe or a drifting gain announces itself before a patient is examined, and a portable densitometer is checked with its own calibration block against the value from the week before. Troubleshooting begins with the question of whether the fault is in the machine, the operator, or the environment, because a blurred image may come from a cracked probe, a bad coupling layer, or a setting changed by the previous user. A unit that reports a calibration failure is not repaired by repeating the test, because the warning exists to prevent a wrong measurement from reaching a patient, so the device is labeled out of service and referred to a biomedical technician when the fault cannot be identified. Power, storage, and people are the rest of the system, because a portable unit is ruined by a voltage spike, a leaking battery, or a hot vehicle, while training, supervision, and a culture in which uncertainty is spoken aloud are the real equipment of the remote clinic.

To summarize, a specialized imaging device is a general purpose machine deliberately narrowed so that a faint contrast becomes visible. The mammography tube uses a low energy beam from a molybdenum or rhodium target, a small focal spot, a moving grid, an automatic exposure control, and a paddle that compresses the breast at a measured force, while digital detectors and tomosynthesis separate superimposed planes and a guided needle takes the tissue that the image has found. Bone densitometry uses two photon energies to subtract soft tissue from bone mineral and compares the areal density with a reference database, while lithotripsy focuses an acoustic pulse onto a stone and the radiotherapy simulator reproduces the geometry of a treatment machine. Every one of these devices has a characteristic hazard, a common operator error, and an alarm that should be obeyed, and every one depends on cleaning, consumables, quality control, and a start of shift check that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. In the field the honest survivors are portable ultrasound and peripheral bone densitometry, used by trained hands for triage and referral, while mammography, lithotripsy, and the simulator stay in the hospital and the patient travels to them.

# Chapter 30 — PACS and Imaging Information Technology

A picture archiving and communication system, called PACS, takes an image from the moment an exposure ends and keeps it available, findable, and readable for the life of the patient record. The principle behind it is easy to forget, because a medical image is not a photograph but a rectangular grid of numbers, and every decision made from it is made from those numbers. Once an image exists as numbers it can be copied without loss, sent through a cable, stored on a disk, and compared with an older study. Every parameter, capacity, compression level, brightness setting, and alarm threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The image begins as a measurement of how much signal reaches each small region of the patient, whether that signal is a beam of radiation, a radio wave, or a returning echo. Each measurement is written into a matrix counted in picture elements, so a chest image may be 2,000 picture elements across, and the number of gray shades each element can take is its bit depth. Contrast is therefore not fixed at acquisition but chosen later by the reader, which is the most important consequence of the digital form. The bit depth, matrix size, and reconstruction parameters of each modality must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The standard format that carries these numbers between machines is called Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine, called DICOM, and its design explains why equipment from different makers can usually talk to one another. A DICOM object is a self describing file, a header of tagged fields followed by the pixel values, where each tag has a number and a defined meaning, so the header records the patient's identity, the modality, and the acquisition settings. Images are organized beneath it in a hierarchy of study, series, and instance, each level carrying a unique identifier generated so that no two objects anywhere can collide. The tags, their permitted values, and the matching rules of those identifiers must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The order that starts an examination usually lives in the hospital information system, and the bridge between that system and the imaging equipment is a messaging standard called Health Level Seven, called HL7. A message carries the patient's identity and the requested examination to the imaging system, which turns it into a worklist that the technologist sees at the console of the modality, so the technologist selects the correct entry instead of typing the details. A worklist that fails to refresh leaves yesterday's names on the screen or an empty list, and the characteristic alarm is a query failure or a stale list warning at the console. The message fields and the refresh interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest and most damaging operator error in this chain is to bypass the worklist and type the patient's details by hand, or to pick the wrong name from a list of similar names. A name spelled differently in two systems, a date of birth in the wrong order, or an identifier read from the wrong wristband can all put a study under the wrong person, and the error is invisible in the image itself. The hazard is not only the mislabeled patient but also the missing study for the patient who should have been imaged, because a clinician who finds no image may repeat the examination and add dose. The written identification routine and the acceptable matching fields must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Once the images are accepted, the modality sends them onward, and the path they take is called the acquisition to archive chain. A larger department usually sends first to a verification station where a technologist checks the study for completeness and correct labeling before releasing it to the long term store. The exchange is a request and a response, in which the sender offers the objects, the receiver acknowledges them, and the receiver may commit to having stored them durably before the modality deletes its local copy. A modality that fills its own disk because nobody cleared the queue will refuse the next patient, so the outgoing queue must be watched, and the chain steps and commitment rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Compression is where bandwidth and storage are traded against diagnostic detail, and the distinction that matters is whether the process is reversible. Lossless compression rewrites the numbers more compactly and restores them exactly, usually achieving a modest reduction, and it is the default for images that may be measured. Irreversible compression discards detail the eye is unlikely to miss and can reduce a file greatly, but it alters the numbers, so measurements and computer aided detection may change with it and it must not be applied to quantitative work without a written policy. The permitted method and ratio for each examination type must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The archive is the hospital's memory for images, and it consists of servers running the archiving software and disk arrays holding the data, arranged so that a failed disk can be replaced without losing a study. Older studies migrate to slower and cheaper storage or to tape while recent ones stay on fast disk, and growth is relentless because every year adds more examinations. The characteristic alarm of an archive is a capacity threshold warning followed by a refusal to accept new studies when the last reserve is consumed. A backup is not a copy that exists but a copy that can be restored, so the archive keeps more than one copy, on separate storage and ideally in a separate building, because fire, flood, theft, and electrical damage take the primary copy and its neighbors together. The practice that proves a backup is the scheduled restore test, in which a sample of studies is recovered onto a spare system and found complete and readable, while physically separated copies are also the defense against extortion software. The retention periods, backup schedule, separation distance, and restore test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The workstation is where an image becomes a diagnosis, and a viewing program opens a study with a hanging protocol, a set of rules that lays out the series in the order the reader wants them. It allows several studies of the same patient to be scrolled together, so that today's image is compared with last year's in the same position, and it shows the series as a stack that can be paged through until the finding is located. It also reconstructs slices in other planes from the same acquired data and fuses one examination with another on the shared position data. The default layout, comparison rules, and available reconstructions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Windowing shows most clearly why a digital image behaves differently from a film, and it follows from the way stored numbers are mapped to visible brightness. The stored values span a wide range, but a screen can show only a limited number of gray shades, so the software chooses a window, a band of stored values, and stretches that band across the display while everything below becomes black and everything above becomes white. The center of the window sets which tissue is given middle gray and the width sets how much contrast is shown, and the same stored image therefore supports several appearances. The program also measures, converting picture elements into physical length using the spacing recorded in the header and rendering the stack into a rotatable volume. The window and level values, measurement conventions, calibration factors, and saved presets must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The diagnostic display is a liquid crystal display, called LCD, and it is a different class of device from an office screen. A liquid crystal cell does not emit light of its own, but twists to control how much light from a light emitting diode, called LED, backlight passes through a polarizing filter. The luminance of the panel, the uniformity of the backlight, and the contrast between the darkest and brightest regions all affect whether a faint lesion can be seen, and the display is calibrated so that the gray shades it shows follow the standard display function. A display drifts as it ages, so a scheduled quality control program uses a photometer to measure the luminance at several brightness levels and a test pattern to reveal banding, smudges, and dead picture elements. The ambient light in the room is part of the system, because a bright window or ceiling lamp reflected in the glass reduces the perceived contrast. The commonest operator error is to read on an ordinary office screen, an uncorrected mobile screen, or a display whose calibration has lapsed, and the characteristic reminder is a calibration due warning that should stop reading rather than be dismissed, with the calibration interval, luminance targets, and ambient light level confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Teleradiology sends the images away from the building, and the physical limit that governs it is bandwidth, the rate at which data can cross the link. A study of several hundred megabytes over a slow connection takes many minutes, and a queue of studies can exhaust a link shared with other hospital traffic, so transmission is often scheduled after hours or prioritized by urgency. The link is usually a wired connection in which a cable carries signals to a switch and the switch forwards them by address, and it may cross an encrypted tunnel so that images are unreadable to anyone between the two sites. The link capacity, encryption method, and priority rules for urgent studies must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Because bandwidth is finite, the reporting workflow is designed around what can be sent and when. The images may cross the link compressed, the report returns through the hospital information system as a structured message, and the acknowledgment that a report has been received is as important as the report itself. A preliminary verbal report by telephone may save a life when the link is down, but it must be written down and later matched to the final report, because a message passed verbally is easily lost or altered. A study that is sent but never acknowledged leaves the referring clinician waiting, so the receiving service keeps a list of unread studies, and the characteristic alarm is a rising count of unread examinations. The compression settings and turnaround targets must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Film printing has not disappeared, and the printers that survive are dry thermal devices that use heat rather than wet chemistry. A thermal print head is a row of tiny heating elements that transfer dye or develop a silver based layer in the film as it passes, and the density of each spot is set by the heat applied to it. The printer is calibrated so that the densities it produces match the display, because a film that is too dark or too light forces the clinician to guess, and the print head and its rollers accumulate dust and must be cleaned on schedule. The consumables are the film in its several sizes and the donor materials. The density, film size, and cleaning interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The network is not an accessory to the imaging chain but the chain itself, and its design decides whether the department can work. A hospital network is built in layers, with cabling running from each device to a switch, switches connecting to one another and to a central router, and the imaging traffic separated from other traffic so that a large transfer does not starve the clinical systems. Wireless links are convenient for a portable device but they are shared and variable, so a fixed workstation or an archive is connected by cable, and every connection has a backup path because a single switch or cable can isolate an entire room. The server room itself needs an uninterruptible power supply, called UPS, cooling from the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system, and limited logged access. Network addresses, battery test interval, room temperature alarm threshold, and access rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Images and reports are among the most sensitive records a hospital holds, and the security that protects them rests on three ideas, that only the right people may see them, that every access must be recorded, and that the data must remain unreadable to anyone who intercepts it. Access begins with a unique account for each user and a password that is not shared, because a shared login makes the audit trail worthless, while a smart card or a token adds a second proof of identity. The audit trail records who opened which study and when, encryption protects data in transit and at rest, and backups are kept in a form that extortion software cannot reach. The password policy, audit retention, and encryption standard must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Availability is the property that clinical decisions depend on, and it is measured rather than assumed. A well designed service removes single points of failure, so there are two servers, two network paths, and duplicate power supplies, and the software moves the workload to the surviving side when one fails, a behavior that must be tested rather than trusted. Monitoring watches disk space, queue lengths, response time, and temperature, and it raises an alert before a user notices a problem, because a slow archive is a warning while an unavailable archive is a crisis. The measure that matters to the ward is the number of minutes in a month when a clinician could not see an image, so the failover test interval, monitoring thresholds, and accepted downtime target must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Downtime procedures are the equipment that keeps a hospital working when the electronics do not, and they are useless if they are first read during the outage. The written plan names who decides that the system is down, who is called, how long the switch to paper will last, and how the work is recorded while the network is unavailable. Radiographers keep a paper log of every examination with the patient's identifier, the time, and the body part, and after recovery comes the reconciliation, in which each paper entry is matched to its study and each study is verified as archived. A study produced during downtime can otherwise be lost forever, so the plan is rehearsed at least once a year, and the notification list and reconciliation method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of this chain is mostly preventive and mostly unglamorous, and it is the part most often neglected because everything appears to work. The schedule covers the archive servers and their disks, the network switches and their power supplies, the workstations, the printers, and the display calibration, and each item has an interval, a task, and a record. Dust is the quiet enemy of every one of these, because it blocks airflow in a server, fouls a connector, and scratches a print head. Every device also has a characteristic way of failing, since the archive fails by filling, the network fails by isolating one room, the display fails by drifting silently, the printer fails by streaking, and the modality fails by keeping images in a queue nobody reads. The service intervals and spare parts list must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator's start of shift check catches most of the faults that would otherwise waste a day, and it takes only minutes. The technologist confirms that the modality is on the worklist, that the list shows today's patients and not yesterday's, and that the archive is reachable by sending a test object or opening the most recent study. The outgoing queue is inspected for unsent studies, the free space on the archive is read, the calibration status of the display is noted, and the printer is checked for film and for a clean test print. The server room temperature and the status of the uninterruptible power supply are glanced at, and any warning is written in the log rather than dismissed. The worklist query interval, acceptable free space level, and test object must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of this chapter are few and cheap, and a single missing item can still stop the service. They include the film and donor materials for the thermal printer, the cleaning kits for print heads and display glass, the lint free cloths, and the approved cleaning solution. There are the removable storage media used to carry studies out of the building, the labels and wristbands with their printed identifiers, and the barcode and radio frequency identification, called RFID, supplies that link a patient to an order. There are also the batteries for the uninterruptible power supply, the patch cables and connectors that seem to vanish, and the blank paper logs for the downtime box. The expiry dates, cleaning agents, and labeling supplies must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning the hardware of the imaging chain is a clinical task with a technical edge. Keyboards, mouse, console, and tablet are wiped with a compatible disinfectant between users, and the correct agent is chosen after checking the maker's list, because alcohol attacks some plastics, bleach corrodes metal, and a wet cloth can drive liquid into a vent. Display glass is cleaned with a soft dry cloth first and an approved solution applied to a cloth rather than sprayed onto the panel, since fluid running into the bezel can damage the backlight, and cables are inspected rather than scrubbed. The cleaning agents, dwell times, and approved surfaces must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the archiving chain described above does not exist. There is no archive, no radiologist on site, no reliable network, and often no electric supply stable enough to run a server, so the entire information system for imaging is reduced to what can be carried and what can be transmitted. What survives is the image itself and a way to move it, whether a film, a memory card, or a photograph taken from a screen. An improvised transfer that violates the standard can still save a life, and the same transfer can also hide a fracture, mislabel a patient, or expose a record to strangers, so the acceptable compromises must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant most often seen is a photograph of a screen taken with a mobile telephone and sent through a messaging application over a weak link, and it breaks the standard at every level. The photograph captures only the window that happened to be displayed, so the reader cannot change the window and cannot see the tissue that was mapped to black or to white, and it captures a perspective view of a panel, so distances are distorted and geometric measurements are meaningless without a known scale in the frame. The link compresses the picture irreversibly and may reduce it to a small number of picture elements, so fine detail is destroyed and compression artifacts can mimic or hide a line. The metadata is lost entirely, because the header does not survive the camera, and the patient's name may travel visibly in the corner of the frame while the file carries no verifiable identity.

When a photograph must be used, discipline turns a poor copy into a defensible one, and the rules are easy to remember. The camera is held square to the screen and steady, the room light is dimmed so that no reflection crosses the image, and the frame includes the whole image rather than a corner of it. The screen is set to the window the radiologist would want, usually the standard soft tissue or bone setting for that examination, and the brightness is not adjusted afterward, because any enhancement is irreversible. A ruler or a known object is included if a measurement may be requested, the patient's identifier is either fully visible or fully excluded but never partly legible, and the picture is sent with the clinical question, the date, and the sender's identity. The display setting and frame contents must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where no worklist exists, the paper request form becomes the worklist, and it must carry the fields a digital list would have carried. The form names the patient, the identifier, the date of birth, the requesting clinician, the clinical question, and the examination requested, and it stays with the patient or in a single bound book rather than on loose slips that blow away. The radiographer enters the same details into the modality by hand, which is precisely the step that causes wrong patient studies, so a second person reads the details back before the exposure is made, and a serial number is written on the form and on the image so that the two can be reunited later. The fields required on the form, the verification routine, and the retention of the book must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A district hospital may run a small version of the full chain, and its compromises are instructive. Such a site might have one modality, one workstation, and a single archive server in a locked room, with images kept on local disks and copies written to removable drives carried to a second building each evening. It gives up the redundancy and automatic migration of a large archive, so capacity is managed by hand and old studies are deleted only under a written retention policy and only after a verified copy exists elsewhere. It also gives up the specialist engineer, so the local technician must recognize a failing disk, a full volume, and a failing battery and must be able to restore a backup. The retention policy, backup rotation, and deletion procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where no network connects two sites, the study travels physically, and the equipment of that journey is a disk, a memory card, or a film jacket in the hands of a person. A disk carried by hand delivers more data in an hour than a weak link delivers in a day, provided it is labeled, protected, and signed for at both ends. The hazard is the loss of the medium or the loss of the chain of custody, because an unlabeled disk in a bag is both a privacy breach and a missing study. The receiving site must be able to read the format written by the sending site, which is why the universal standard is used, and the labeling, encryption, and accepted file format must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a truly remote clinic there is no archive at all, and the film jacket in a cupboard is the only record. The radiographer keeps a logbook of every exposure, files the film in a numbered jacket, and becomes, in effect, both the archive and the worklist at once, so that log must be protected by training, supervision, and a second copy. Images and reports leave by telephone, by short message with a photograph, or with the patient on the next transport, and the receiving clinician is told explicitly what was seen, what was not seen, and what could not be assessed. The referral note must state the clinical question, the relevant history, the results of tests already done, and the patient's ability to lie still.
