Ultrasound answers many questions without film, and a referral to a center with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging is planned early rather than after a trial of treatment, so the logbook fields, referral content, and transport of the film must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the image that leaves a modality is a grid of numbers with a header describing them, stored in the standard called DICOM, and the worklist built from messages in the standard called HL7 ties those numbers to the correct patient. The archive holds them on servers and disk arrays and is only as good as its tested backup and its separated copy, while the workstation turns them back into a picture through windowing and measurement and the diagnostic display must be calibrated. Teleradiology carries them over a link whose bandwidth and compression set the limits of the reporting workflow, film printing survives in the thermal printer, and the whole service depends on network design, security, privacy, cooling, power, and a written downtime procedure that is rehearsed rather than discovered. The hazards are the wrong patient in the header, the uncalibrated screen, the unacknowledged study, the untested backup, and the unprotected record, while the commonest operator errors are hand typing an identity, ignoring the outgoing queue, dismissing a calibration warning, and reading on an ordinary screen. In the field none of this infrastructure travels, so a photograph of a screen over a weak link, a paper logbook, a labeled disk carried by hand, and an early referral take its place, and every one of those substitutes violates the standard in a way that must be understood rather than ignored. Every parameter, capacity, compression level, brightness setting, and alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 31 — Specimen Collection

Specimen collection is the equipment and technique of the pre analytical phase, the part of the laboratory process that happens before any machine touches the sample. It is where most laboratory errors are born, because a result can be measured perfectly and still be wrong. The fault may lie in the tube, the volume of blood, the mixing, the warmth of the journey, or the label. This chapter treats those tools as physical objects, from the evacuated tube and the winged needle to the culture bottle, the swab, the specimen jar, and the insulated transport box. Every setting, volume, temperature, and time limit named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A specimen is not a fixed photograph of the patient but a living chemical system that keeps reacting after it leaves the body. Cells in a tube of blood consume glucose, and once the blood clots the serum no longer represents the plasma that circulated. Bacteria in urine multiply, potassium leaks out of cells and rises in the plasma, and clotting factors decay unless the calcium that drives clotting is bound. Warmth and delay accelerate every one of these changes, so the container, the additive, the fill volume, the storage temperature, and the transport time are part of the test itself. All of these must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The ordinary blood tube is an evacuated cylinder closed by a rubber stopper, and its working principle is a pressure difference. Most of the air is removed at manufacture, so when a needle already inside a vein pierces the stopper, atmospheric pressure drives blood into the lower pressure inside. That vacuum sets the volume the tube will accept, which is why it fills to a printed line and stops, and why a tube that has lost its vacuum through a cracked stopper or a hot store draws slowly or not at all. The stopper color is a code naming the additive inside, and the additive is the real difference between one tube and another. The vacuum, the additive expiry, and the fill line must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The additives are chemical tools chosen to preserve one property of the blood at the expense of others. A red stopper carries no additive or a fine clot activator powder and the blood clots so that serum can be tested, while a gold stopper adds a gel that traps cells below the serum when the tube is spun. A green stopper carries heparin, which blocks the cascade that builds a fibrin mesh, and a light blue stopper carries sodium citrate, which binds the calcium that clotting requires. A lavender or pink stopper carries ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid, which holds calcium more tightly still and preserves cell shape for counting, and a gray stopper carries fluoride and oxalate, which stop cells from consuming glucose. The additive and its concentration in each tube must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Because a needle passes through several stoppers, a trace of one additive can be carried into the next tube, and that trace is enough to corrupt a result. The order of draw prevents this cross contamination, and the tubes whose tests are most easily disturbed are filled first. Blood culture bottles come first, then citrate, then plain serum, then heparin, then ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid, and finally fluoride oxalate. The fill volume matters just as much, because a citrate tube is made for nine parts blood to one part citrate, so a half filled tube is over diluted and its clotting times are falsely prolonged. The order of draw, the fill volumes, and the acceptable tolerance must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The needle is a short steel tube with a slanted tip, and its behavior follows from fluid mechanics, because flow through a narrow tube falls steeply as the diameter shrinks. A fine needle fills a tube slowly, and pulling harder on a syringe across it tears red cells and releases their contents into the plasma. That change, called hemolysis, makes potassium appear high and makes many chemistry results unreliable. Diameter is stated in gauge, and a 21 gauge needle is common for routine adult collection, while a 23 gauge needle serves fragile veins at the cost of a slower draw. The holder grips needle and tube as one rigid assembly, and the gauge, the length, and the safety mechanism must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A winged set replaces the rigid assembly with flexible tubing, a small needle with two plastic wings, and a connector for a holder or a syringe. The wings let the collector steer the needle into a shallow or rolling vein, and the tubing can be taped flat so the needle stays still while tubes are changed. The price is dead space, because the blood filling the tubing never reaches the tube, and the first tube may be diluted by fluid already in the line. A small needle on a winged set attached to a vacuum tube can also hemolyze the sample, and the hazard is the needlestick, which loose tubing makes more likely. The gauge and the tubing volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Capillary collection is used when the patient is an infant, a small child, or an adult whose veins will not yield. A lancet makes a small incision in a bed of capillaries, and the drop that appears is a mixture of capillary blood with a little interstitial fluid and, if the site is squeezed, with fluid from the cells. Warmth brings blood to the surface, and the heel or the side of a finger is chosen to avoid bone and the dense nerve supply of the fingertip pad. The first drop is wiped away, and later drops are touched to the lip of a small tube rather than scooped, because scooping adds air and starts clotting. The lancet depth, the site, and the number of drops required must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The technique of the draw is part of the equipment, because a good tube handled badly produces a bad specimen. The tourniquet distends the vein and must be released as soon as blood flows, since one left in place for minutes concentrates cells and raises potassium. The site is cleaned and allowed to dry, and the vein is not touched afterward with a bare finger, which is the commonest source of skin contamination. The patient's identity is checked before the needle is uncovered, by asking the patient to state a name and comparing it with the wristband and the request. The tourniquet time, the number of attempts, and the identification routine must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A blood culture bottle is a sealed vessel of nutrient broth with a headspace of gas, and it is designed to be an incubator for whatever microorganisms the blood contains. It holds an anticoagulant, a medium that supports growth, and often a resin or charcoal material that absorbs the antibiotics the patient is receiving. The monitoring instrument watches for the physical signs of growth and raises a positive alert when it suspects that organisms are multiplying. The most important variable is the volume of blood placed in the bottle, because the number of organisms in adult blood is often extremely small, and the blood volume and the number of bottles in a set must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Skin preparation for a blood culture is more demanding than for an ordinary draw, because the culture will grow whatever enters the bottle, including the bacteria that live harmlessly on the skin. The site is cleaned with friction in a spiral from the center outward, and the agent is allowed to dry completely, because a wet site carries disinfectant into the bottle and a site wiped dry carries skin organisms back to the surface. The commonest operator error is to draw the culture through an existing intravenous line rather than a fresh site, which produces a false positive result. The second commonest is to take only one set, when two sets from separate sites are needed to separate true infection from contamination. The preparation agents, the drying time, and the number of sets must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A swab is a sampler rather than a container, and its job is to lift material from a surface and keep the organisms in it alive until they reach the laboratory. The transport medium is the part most often misunderstood, because a bacterial medium holds salts, a buffer, and sometimes charcoal to absorb substances that would kill the organisms, while a viral medium holds salts, protein, and antibiotics that suppress bacteria but keep viruses intact for the molecular test. A swab sent dry, in the wrong medium, or kept warm for a day delivers a dead or overgrown sample. The medium, the storage temperature, and the contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The urine container is a sterile screw topped jar, and much of what makes a urine result trustworthy happens before the jar is closed. A clean catch midstream specimen is the standard, because the first part of the stream washes the urethra and the middle part best reflects the bladder. The preservative depends on the test, since boric acid holds the bacterial population steady while an acid preservative stops chemical and hormonal change during a day of collection. The patient washes the genital area, begins urinating into the toilet, passes the container into the stream without touching the inside, and closes it before the stream ends. The preservative, the volume, and the maximum delay must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A stool container is a clean wide mouthed jar with a tight lid, and the parasitology pot is a smaller version that may contain a fixative. The physical state of the specimen matters here more than in almost any other test, because the motile forms of some parasites lose their shape within a short time, so a fresh warm specimen examined promptly is worth more than a preserved one examined late. The fixative, usually formalin, hardens the organisms so their form survives the journey and the concentration step. Stool must not be collected from toilet water or mixed with urine, and it must travel in a container that does not leak, because it carries a heavy load of infectious organisms. The fixative, the volume, and the maximum delay before examination must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A tissue pot is a wide mouthed container of formalin, and its purpose is to fix a fragment of tissue so that its structure survives the journey to the pathology laboratory. Formalin is a solution of formaldehyde gas in water, and it links the proteins of the tissue to one another, which stiffens the tissue and stops the enzymes that would otherwise digest it. The volume of formalin must be generous, because the fixative must diffuse from the surface to the center of the specimen, and a crowded pot leaves the middle unfixed and rotting. The container is filled only partly and closed firmly, because formalin vapor irritates the eyes and airways, and the handler wears gloves and eye protection and works with ventilation. The formalin concentration, the ratio of fixative to tissue, and the fixation time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A sputum container is a wide mouthed sterile jar with a screw cap, and its value depends entirely on whether the material inside is sputum from the airways or saliva from the mouth. Sputum is thick, coughed up from deep in the chest after several deep breaths, and carries the organisms and cells the test is looking for, while saliva is thin, watery, and full of mouth flora, so a specimen of saliva can give a result that means nothing. When a patient cannot produce sputum, a trained operator may induce it with a fine mist of salty water breathed from a nebulizer for a few minutes, though that produces a cloud of infectious droplets. It is therefore done in a well ventilated room or outdoors and away from other patients, and the operator wears a mask, eye protection, and a gown. The nebulizer concentration, its duration, and the required volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.


The transport box is the part of the chain easiest to neglect and hardest to improvise, and its physics are those of insulation and phase change. A rigid insulated box slows the movement of heat in both directions, and a cold pack holds the interior near a chosen temperature by absorbing heat as its contents change phase. A pack that has melted no longer holds that temperature, and a pack straight from a freezer can freeze the specimen against the wall, which bursts red cells and destroys the cells a count requires. A temperature logger or a simple maximum and minimum thermometer inside the box is the only honest record of the journey. The temperature range, the number of cold packs, and the monitoring method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Every analyte has a stability, and that is why the laboratory writes a time limit beside each specimen type. Glucose in a tube without preservative falls steadily as the cells consume it, so a sample delayed for hours can suggest hypoglycemia in a patient whose blood sugar is normal. Potassium moves the other way, leaking out of cells so that a delayed sample can suggest hyperkalemia, and clotting factors decay so that a delayed coagulation sample can suggest a bleeding tendency. Bacteria in urine multiply and can turn a small colony count into a large one. The time limits are part of the measurement, and the acceptable interval between collection and analysis must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Labeling is where the specimen stops being a biological sample and becomes information about a named person, and the rule is that the label is applied at the bedside, in the presence of the patient, at the moment of collection. The label carries at least two independent identifiers, such as the full name and the date of birth or the hospital number, with the date, the time, and the collector's identity, written in waterproof ink or printed from the hospital system. The commonest operator error in the whole chapter is to write labels in advance or carry a batch of pre labeled tubes to the bedside, which inverts the logic of identification. A specimen that arrives unlabeled, mismatched, or labeled after the collector left the bedside must be discarded and a new specimen obtained, however precious it is. The identifier fields, the labeling materials, and the discard rule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The request form or its electronic equivalent carries the clinical question, and without it a laboratory can report only numbers without meaning. In a hospital with a laboratory information system, the request is entered once and a barcode is printed that the analyzer reads directly, which removes the transcription step and a whole class of error. The characteristic alarm here is the barcode that will not read at the analyzer, which stops the specimen on the track until a person decides what it is, and a second is the rejection flag for a short or clotted tube. Before dispatch the collector confirms the fill line, the gentle mixing, the label, the matching request, and the absence of clots or hemolysis, and all of these criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Specimen collection is one of the most hazardous tasks in the hospital, because it places a sharp instrument into a patient who may carry a blood borne infection and then places the collector's hands near that instrument. Gloves are worn for every draw, with an apron and eye protection when a splash is possible, and the defenses are backed by vaccination against hepatitis B and a written procedure for after a needlestick. The sharp is never recapped by hand, bent, or left on a tray, but dropped into a puncture resistant container placed within reach before the needle is uncovered. The container is closed and replaced before it reaches its marked fill line. The fill line, the protective equipment, and the post exposure procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning is part of specimen collection, because the same trays, tourniquets, and work surfaces pass from one patient to another. The tourniquet is the object most often forgotten, since it touches the skin of every arm and is rarely washed, and it should be cleaned between patients or dedicated to one patient when an infection is present. Trays and holders are wiped with a compatible disinfectant, and blood spills are covered with absorbent material, flooded with fresh bleach solution, left for the stated contact time, and removed as clinical waste. The hands are washed or rubbed with an alcohol preparation before and after every patient contact, and gloves do not replace that step. The cleaning agents, their contact times, and the surfaces that tolerate them must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance of collection equipment is mostly a matter of time and temperature, and it is unglamorous work that prevents a great deal of waste. The refrigerator that holds specimens and reagents is checked against a thermometer twice a day and the reading is written down, and the characteristic alarm of such a unit is a temperature alarm that must be answered rather than silenced. The bench centrifuge is leveled, its buckets are loaded in balance, and its lid interlock is checked, because an unbalanced centrifuge vibrates, walks across the bench, and can release a cloud of aerosol. The stock of tubes and media is rotated so the oldest is used first, and the vacuum in each box is sampled occasionally, because a tube that has lost its vacuum fails at the bedside. The thermometer check interval, the temperature range, and the centrifuge service schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of this chapter are cheap individually and expensive collectively, and one missing item can stop a clinic. They include the tubes of every additive and size, the needles in their several gauges, the holders, winged sets, lancets, and capillary tubes, and the blood culture bottles with their broth. There are the swabs and transport media, the sterile urine jars with and without preservative, the stool and parasitology pots with fixative, the tissue pots and formalin, and the sputum jars. There are the cleansing agents, alcohol wipes, iodine or chlorhexidine applicators, gauze, tape, bandages, and gloves. There are the labels, barcode stock, request forms, transport bags, cold packs, insulated boxes, temperature loggers, sharps containers, and the spill kit, and each has an expiry date or shelf life that must be checked before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the pre analytical phase is the part of the laboratory that survives, because it needs no electricity, no analyzer, and no specialist. All the chemistry of the tubes, the sterility of the containers, and the arithmetic of the fill volumes still apply, but the supporting infrastructure is missing, since there may be no refrigerator, no centrifuge, no incubator, and no courier other than a person on a motorcycle. A specimen carried on a motorbike can still save a life, and the same specimen can arrive warm, hemolyzed, or mislabeled and waste the only chance the patient had. What the field gives up is redundancy and certainty, and what it demands instead is discipline, planning, and a written record of every step. The storage conditions, transport times, and substituted containers used in the field must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest field collection device is the ordinary syringe, because it works without vacuum and can be controlled by hand on a vein that a vacuum tube would collapse. The operator draws slowly, watching the barrel, and stops before the syringe is full, because pulling hard on the plunger across a small needle bursts red cells and releases potassium into the plasma. The blood is then transferred into a tube, and that step loses the most, because pushing blood through the drawing needle hemolyzes it, so the safer method is to remove the needle, cap the syringe, and use a transfer device or a gentle gravity transfer. If the tube contains an additive, the operator must fill it to the proportion the laboratory expects, because a tube filled by eye underfills the anticoagulant tube and distorts a clotting time. The syringe size, needle gauge, transfer method, and fill proportions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where the laboratory is days away and no cold chain exists, one useful field format is the dried blood spot, in which a few drops of blood are soaked into a card of absorbent filter paper and allowed to dry in the air. The physical principle is that the cells dry onto the fibers and the proteins and genetic material of parasites and viruses stay bound to the paper, so a laboratory far away can later punch out a small disc and elute the material into a liquid. The card must be filled with free flowing drops that soak through to the far side, must not be touched in the printed area, and must dry horizontally away from sunlight and insects before it is bagged with a desiccant pack. The drying time, the storage temperature, and the permissible interval before the card reaches the laboratory must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field cold chain is built from a vaccine carrier or a similar insulated box, a set of phase change packs, and a thermometer, and it succeeds or fails on the temperature inside rather than the appearance of the container. The thermometer is read at every handover and written in the log, so the receiving laboratory knows the temperature history and not merely the temperature at arrival. The hazard of the field journey is the long delay and the rough road, and the commonest operator error is to pack too little insulation or too many specimens for the packs to hold. The number of packs, the box loading, and the temperature log must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the field gives up is the backup specimen, the printed label, and the refrigerator, and what it demands instead is a set of habits a hospital can leave to the system. Since there is no second tube, the draw must be right the first time, and the collector decides before the needle is uncovered which tests matter most and which tube is filled first. Since there is no label printer, the label is written by hand at the bedside in waterproof ink with two identifiers, the time, and the collector's name, and the same details go into a bound specimen register. The label fields, the register contents, and the transport plan must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the field the safety hazards of collection are sharper because the defenses are thinner, and naming them is part of using the equipment. A needlestick in a clinic without a nearby supply of post exposure treatment is a life changing event, so the sharp is handled in one direction only, into a puncture resistant box improvised from a rigid sealed container if no commercial one exists. The characteristic alarms of this chapter are the temperature alarm of a refrigerator or transport logger, the imbalance alarm of a centrifuge, the positive alert of a blood culture instrument, and the rejection flag of an analyzer for a short or clotted tube. The protective equipment available, the post exposure procedure, and the alarm responses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, specimen collection is the pre analytical equipment of the laboratory, and its governing idea is that a specimen continues to change from the moment it leaves the patient, so the tube, the additive, the fill volume, the temperature, and the time are all part of the measurement. The evacuated tube works by pressure difference and is coded by stopper color, the additives preserve one property at the expense of others, the order of draw prevents cross contamination, and the fill line protects the ratio of blood to anticoagulant. Blood culture bottles are incubators whose sensitivity rests on the volume of blood and the cleanliness of the skin, swabs are samplers that must reach the right surface and travel in the right medium, and urine, stool, sputum, and tissue each demand their own container, preservative, and time limit. The label is applied at the bedside with two identifiers and an unlabeled specimen is discarded, while the transport box with its cold packs and its temperature log is the last defense of the result. The field substitutes a syringe, a hand labeled tube, a dried blood spot card, and a motorbike for that infrastructure, giving up redundancy and refrigeration and demanding a planned journey, a written register, and a draw that is right the first time. Every volume, temperature, time limit, and alarm threshold named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 32 — Hematology and Coagulation Analyzers

A hematology analyzer turns a tube of blood into numbers, and a coagulation analyzer times how long that blood takes to clot. Both are counting and timing instruments before they are clinical instruments, and a listener who understands the counting and the timing will recognize a wrong result before it harms a patient. This chapter describes the hospital laboratory versions first, with their reagents, waste, calibration, and maintenance, then the field versions, which are a microscope, a hand centrifuge, a hematocrit reader, and a careful pair of eyes. Every setting, temperature, incubation time, centrifuge speed, alarm threshold, and reagent expiry named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Blood is a suspension rather than a solution, and every measurement in this chapter depends on that fact. The cells are denser and less conductive than the plasma, they settle when left standing, and they change as soon as the sample leaves the vein. A tube for a full blood count contains a dried salt that removes calcium and stops clotting, and because that salt is fixed in amount, the tube must be filled to its marked line to keep the proportion correct. A short-filled tube is over-anticoagulated, an overfilled tube may clot, and a clotted tube can block the analyzer and produce a falsely low count, so the anticoagulant type and fill volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest counting principle is electrical impedance, which is easiest to picture as a narrow gate in a stream. The blood is diluted in a conducting salt solution and drawn through a small aperture with an electric current passing across it. A cell conducts poorly compared with that solution, so as it passes it displaces conducting fluid and briefly raises the resistance of the path, and that rise appears as a voltage pulse counted as one cell. The pulse height depends on how much fluid the particle displaced, so it is read as a measure of cell volume. The aperture diameter, the current, and the counting thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Two cells passing the aperture together produce one large pulse instead of two small ones, an error called coincidence, and the sample is wrapped in a sheath of the same salt solution so the cells are forced into single file along the center of the aperture. Platelets are counted in the same pass as the red cells but at a lower size threshold, so cell fragments, debris, or bacteria in the platelet window are counted as platelets. When an aperture begins to clog, the flow slows, the pulses distort, and the count falls, which is the moment to stop and clean rather than repeat the sample. The aperture size, the coincidence limits, and the platelet threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Many modern analyzers identify cells by flow cytometry, in which the diluted sample is squeezed into a single stream that passes one cell at a time through a focused beam of light. Forward scatter increases with the size of the cell, side scatter increases with the complexity of the cell interior, and fluorescence adds a third signal because stains that bind to nucleic acid or to particular proteins glow when the beam strikes them. Combining size, granularity, and fluorescence lets the instrument sort the white cells into their families and print a differential. The laser power, stain volumes, and gating boundaries must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Hemoglobin is not counted but measured by light, in a method called photometry. A measured volume of blood is mixed with a reagent that bursts the red cells and releases the hemoglobin, and the same reagent converts it into a stable colored compound whose intensity is proportional to the amount present. A lamp shines through the mixture at a chosen wavelength and a detector on the far side measures how much light survives the passage, so the darker the color the less light reaches the detector, and a cloudy or lipemic sample can bias the reading unless a blank is measured first. The wavelength, the reagent volume, and the conversion factor must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The analyzer is built around its sampling system, and the aspirating probe is the part the operator touches most. In open mode the probe is lowered into an uncapped tube and draws a measured volume; in closed mode it pierces the cap of a sealed tube, which protects the operator from aerosol but requires the correct cap and depth. The probe tip is wiped clean between samples, because a drop of one patient's blood carried into the next tube gives a wrong result to two patients at once, and the tubing that carries the sample onward must be free of kinks and air. The probe depth, the aspiration volume, and the carryover wash volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A full blood count analyzer consumes three or four liquids, and confusing them is a classic way to ruin a run. The diluent is the salt solution in which cells are counted, the lysing reagent destroys the red cells so the white cells and hemoglobin can be measured, the sheath fluid keeps cells in single file inside a flow cytometer, and a cleaning solution removes protein residue from the tubing and aperture. Each has a storage temperature, an expiry date, and a limit on how long it may sit on the instrument, and a warm or expired reagent drifts results without any obvious alarm. Everything it aspirates it must also discard, and that waste is a biohazard disposed of by the local infectious waste route, while some reagents are corrosive or contain cyanide, so the waste may be chemically hazardous as well as infectious. The storage temperatures, expiry rules, and waste handling must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The machine does not simply print numbers; it attaches flags, and the flags are the part that demands judgment. A flag may mean that a value falls outside a reference range, that the instrument could not classify the cells confidently, or that two measurements disagree. A delta check compares today's result with the patient's previous result and flags a change too large to be explained by biology, which is often the first sign that the wrong sample was loaded. Suspect flags for immature cells, abnormal lymphocytes, or fragments are the instrument's request for a stained film, and the operator reads them, decides which need a microscope, and records that decision, with the flag rules confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest operator error with a full blood count analyzer is to trust a result from a bad sample, usually a clotted or short-filled tube that someone decided to run anyway, or to mix the sample by shaking or let it stand for hours so that platelets clump or cells swell. The hazard that follows is a transfusion or a treatment decision made on a false number, and the error is invisible once the tube is discarded. The characteristic alarm is a clog or flow error, and a machine that alarms repeatedly on the same sample should be cleaned and the sample re-collected rather than forced through again. The acceptable sample age, the mixing method, and the action after a clog alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Daily maintenance of a full blood count analyzer is short but not optional, and it is the operator's work rather than the engineer's. The probe is wiped, the instrument is run through a cleaning cycle, and a background count is performed with diluent alone, which should return counts near zero; a rising background is the earliest warning of a dirty aperture or an expiring reagent. The waste is emptied, reagent levels are checked, and the previous run's flags are reviewed before the first patient sample, while at longer intervals the aperture is cleaned or replaced, the peristaltic pump tubing is changed before it flattens, and the instrument is calibrated. A neglected analyzer usually does not stop; it drifts, which is far more dangerous than a failure, and the cleaning cycle, background limits, and parts replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A result is only a number until it is proved, and the proof is a calibrator and a control. A calibrator has values assigned by a reference method, and calibrating anchors the instrument's calculations to a known sample, while a control has a known range and is run every day at a normal level and at least one abnormal level. The control values are plotted on a chart, and a value outside the accepted range, a run of values on one side of the mean, or a sudden shift all mean that patient results cannot be released until the cause is found. Calibration is repeated after a major part change, a change of reagent lot, or a failed control, and the calibrator values, control ranges, and acceptance rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When the analyzer raises a suspect flag, the reference method is still the microscope. A drop of blood is spread along a glass slide in a thin wedge, dried, and stained so that the white cells can be told apart by the color and shape of their nuclei and granules, and a technologist classifies a fixed number of white cells, traditionally 100, while noting the size and shape of the red cells and the platelets. A mechanical differential counter, a row of keys or a rotating dial that tallies each cell type, is still found on many benches because it prevents arithmetic errors. The film also reveals what no counter can, including malarial parasites inside the red cells, which is why the microscope has never been retired, and the stain quality and counting rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Before automated counters, every cell count was done in a counting chamber, and the method is still taught because it is the fallback when the machine fails. The chamber is a thick glass slide with a ruled grid of known area and depth, so the volume above each square is fixed, and a measured volume of blood is diluted by a known factor, sometimes in a fluid that also lyses the red cells when only the white cells are wanted. The mixture is drawn under a cover glass, the cells in a defined set of squares are counted under the microscope, and the count is multiplied by the dilution and divided by the volume counted to give a concentration. The errors are almost always in the dilution, the filling, or the distribution of the cells, and an overfilled or dried chamber gives a wrong answer with great confidence, so the chamber depth, dilution factor, and counting rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is the oldest hematology test still in daily use, and its principle is gravity. A tall narrow tube of fixed bore is filled with anticoagulated blood and stood perfectly vertical, and the distance the red cell column has fallen in 1 hour is the result, measured in millimeters. The rate depends on how readily the red cells stack into rolls, which depends on the proteins coating them, so a rise in fibrinogen or in the globulins makes the cells settle faster while anemia and a low temperature slow them. The test is crude and nonspecific, but it is cheap and sensitive to inflammation, and the tube dimensions, standing time, temperature, and reading method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Coagulation testing rests on a different physical principle, because the endpoint is not a count but a moment in time. Plasma is separated from the cells by centrifugation, and a reagent is then added that starts the clotting cascade while the instrument watches for the instant fibrin appears. The cascade is a chain of enzymes normally held in check, and each test bypasses part of the chain so that a defect in one region can be isolated; adding calcium restores what the anticoagulant removed, and adding a phospholipid surface or a tissue factor substitute supplies what the reaction needs. The time from the addition of the starting reagent to the formation of fibrin is the result, and the reagent volumes, incubation temperature, and starting point of the timer must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

One way to detect that fibrin has formed is to feel for it, and the mechanical method does exactly that. A small metal ball, a wire loop, or a plastic flag is moved through the plasma mixture, and the instrument senses the change in its motion when the mixture thickens from a liquid to a gel, while the magnetic method instead drives a small bead with a moving field and records the endpoint when fibrin traps it. These methods are robust in the presence of lipemia, jaundice, or slight hemolysis, because they respond to the physical change rather than to the light. Their weakness is that bubbles, a short sample, or a strand of fibrin from a badly collected tube can stop the moving part early and shorten the time, so the bead size, movement amplitude, and detection threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The optical method detects the clot by watching the light instead. A beam passes through the plasma mixture to a detector, and as fibrin strands form the mixture changes from clear to cloudy, so the light reaching the detector falls or the scattered light rises, and the instrument records the time at which that change crosses a set threshold. This method is gentle on the sample and lets several tests run at once from a small volume, but it is easily fooled by anything else that changes the clarity of the plasma. Severe lipemia, deep jaundice, much free hemoglobin, or a very anemic sample can all move the optical signal and produce a wrong time, so the path length, wavelength, and detection threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The prothrombin time measures the tissue factor pathway and is the standard way of monitoring therapy that reduces the activity of the vitamin K dependent clotting factors. A tissue factor preparation and calcium are added to the plasma, and the time to clot is recorded in seconds, so a prolonged time means that one or more of those factors is deficient or that an inhibitor is present. Because tissue factor preparations differ in sensitivity, the result is converted into an international normalized ratio, which compares the patient's time with the mean normal time and corrects for the reagent's sensitivity using a value assigned to that reagent, and this is the number used to adjust the dose of a vitamin K antagonist drug. The assigned sensitivity value, the mean normal time, and the therapeutic range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The activated partial thromboplastin time measures the contact pathway instead. A contact activator and a phospholipid substitute are added to the plasma, the mixture is incubated, and calcium is added to start the reaction, after which the time to clot is recorded; it screens for defects in the early part of the cascade and monitors therapy that enhances the action of antithrombin. The fibrinogen test measures the amount of the final raw material rather than the time, usually by adding a high concentration of thrombin to diluted plasma so that the time depends almost entirely on how much fibrinogen is present. A thrombin time adds thrombin alone and is prolonged by heparin or by a fibrinogen abnormality, and the reagent concentrations, incubation time, and reference ranges must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Platelet function testing asks a different question, not whether the clotting factors are present but whether the platelets respond. In one method platelets in plasma are stirred and a trigger substance is added, and the instrument watches the mixture become less cloudy as the platelets clump, because clumped platelets scatter less light than single ones; in another the clumping is detected electrically, because platelets sticking to electrodes change the current between them. A simpler screen draws whole blood through a small aperture coated with a trigger and measures how long the platelets take to plug it, which is called the closure time. These tests are sensitive to the age of the sample, to the anticoagulant, and to drugs that block platelets, so the trigger substances, sample age limits, and reference values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A coagulation analyzer is a small instrument compared with a full blood count analyzer, but it depends even more on its consumables and its temperature. It needs water of good quality to reconstitute frozen or lyophilized reagents, a refrigerator to store them, and a warm station held near body temperature for the reaction, usually 37 degrees Celsius, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Reagents are reconstituted in exact volumes, allowed to reach working temperature, and used within a stated time, because a partly degraded reagent lengthens or shortens every time it produces, and a blocked pipette biases every result in the same direction. Calibrators and normal and abnormal controls are run daily, and the control ranges and reconstitution rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest operator error in coagulation is to use a sample that is short-filled or collected into the wrong tube, because the ratio of blood to anticoagulant decides the result. An underfilled tube carries too much anticoagulant for the plasma and prolongs the time, while a tube that sat too long or was mixed badly may hold a small clot that consumes fibrinogen and shortens it. Drawing blood from a line that is running heparin, or filling the coagulation tube after a tube with another additive, contaminates the sample and produces a result that reflects the line rather than the patient. The characteristic alarm is a clot detection error or a short sample warning, and the correct response is a new sample drawn properly, with the fill volume, sample age, and collection order confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The centrifuge is the quiet workhorse of both hematology and coagulation, and its principle is the one that makes sediment settle in a river, made faster. Spinning a tube around a central axis subjects its contents to a force much greater than gravity, so denser material moves outward while lighter liquid stays nearer the center, and the force depends on the rotor radius and the square of the speed. Tubes are arranged in balanced pairs opposite one another and of equal weight, because an unbalanced load sets up vibration that can damage the rotor and throw a tube from its bucket. That vibration can crack a tube and release an aerosol of blood into the rotor chamber as the operator leans over it, so the lid is interlocked and must never be defeated. The speed, running time, rotor radius, and rotor life limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of this chapter are unglamorous and decisive. They include blood collection tubes of the correct size and additive, needles and holders, capillary tubes for microhematocrit and manual counts, glass slides and cover glasses, a Romanowsky type stain and its buffers, a counting chamber with its cover glass, cuvettes for coagulation, calibrators and control materials, cleaning solutions, and the disinfectant for the bench. Every one has a storage condition, an expiry date, and a rule about how long it may be used after opening, and stock is rotated so the oldest is used first, with every reagent lot number recorded with the control results so that a bad lot can be traced. The storage temperatures, expiry dates, and open-vial limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile clinic or a frontier hospital, this whole laboratory may be one wooden box and a bench by a window. The field version is a light microscope with a mirror or a battery lamp, a hand driven or small electric centrifuge, a hematocrit reader card or a ruler, a staining rack, and a supply of slides, capillary tubes, and diluting fluids. It gives up the automated count and everything that comes with it, including the machine differential, the flags, and the speed, so a single full blood count may take 30 minutes or more of trained attention, and what it demands instead is a good stain, a clean microscope, a steady hand, and a person who has counted enough cells to know when a number is plausible. The light source, centrifuge speed, and stain times must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The commonest field measurement is the hematocrit, and it can change a decision within minutes. A plain capillary tube is filled about three quarters full with blood, one end is sealed, and the tube is spun in a microhematocrit centrifuge for a fixed time, usually 5 minutes, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The tube is then laid on a reader card with a scale, and the height of the packed red cell column is read against the total column of blood, with the thin pale buffy coat of white cells and platelets ignored but noted when it is unusually thick. The common errors are an incompletely sealed tube, a tube not filled to the right length, too short a spin, and reading the level at an angle, so the fill length, spin time, and reader scale must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When the field clinic needs a white cell count or a differential, it falls back on the counting chamber and the stained film. The dilution is made with a pipette or a small measured tube, the chamber is charged, and the cells in the ruled squares are counted under the microscope, with the arithmetic done by hand and checked twice. The film is spread, dried, fixed, stained, and examined, and 100 white cells are classified one by one while the red cells are examined for shape, size, and parasites. The limits are real, because a count from one chamber, a film stained in humid air, and a sedimentation tube on a vibrating table all produce numbers that deserve caution, so the dilution, staining times, and counting rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Coagulation in the field is harder, because it is a timed test and time is what a busy clinic has least of. The manual method uses a small water bath or a heated block to hold the plasma and reagent near body temperature, a tube, a stopwatch, and a wire loop or wooden stick to lift the mixture and watch for the first thread of fibrin. The reagent is added at a recorded moment, the tube is tilted or the loop lifted repeatedly, and the endpoint is the first time the mixture no longer drips but forms a gel, so the result depends on the operator's eye, on the temperature of the bath, and on how evenly the mixing is done. This is why field coagulation is usually limited to tests that change immediate care, and the bath temperature, reagent warm-up time, and observation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the field version gives up is precision, speed, and the automatic check that catches an impossible result. What it demands is a trained person who can look at a film and see what is there, a reliable light source, clean water for stains and reagents, and a stock of unexpired consumables that survives heat and dust. The safety hazards are sharper in the field than in the hospital, because there is usually no biological safety cabinet, no sharps container at every bench, and no dependable infectious waste route, so blood is handled at arm's length, sharps go into a rigid puncture proof container, and the bench is disinfected after every session. The microscope is the fragile and expensive part, and it must be carried in a padded case, kept dry, and cleaned only with lens tissue, so the disinfectant concentration, sharps disposal, and microscope storage conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, hematology and coagulation analyzers are counting and timing instruments whose results rest on the sample, the reagent, and the daily proof that the machine is still correct. The hospital analyzer counts cells by impedance or by light scatter, measures hemoglobin by photometry, flags what it cannot classify, and depends on the operator to clean it, run the controls, and send a film to the microscope when the flags demand it. The coagulation analyzer detects the moment fibrin forms by mechanical, magnetic, or optical means, and it is only as reliable as the tube that was filled correctly and the reagent that was reconstituted correctly. The centrifuge, the microscope, the counting chamber, and the hematocrit reader are the same devices in the hospital and in the field, and in both settings the rule is the same: the number is not the patient, a doubtful result must be confirmed before it changes care, and every setting, temperature, time, and threshold used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 33 — Clinical Chemistry and Immunoassay Analyzers

Clinical chemistry and immunoassay analyzers are the instruments that measure molecules rather than cells, and that distinction explains how they are built. A hematology analyzer counts and sorts formed elements, while a chemistry analyzer asks how much of a dissolved substance is present in serum, plasma, urine, or another body fluid, and an immunoassay analyzer asks the same question about substances so dilute that ordinary chemistry cannot see them. The physical problem is that a molecule is invisible, so the instrument must persuade it to produce a signal. There are 3 great routes to that signal: a chemical reaction that creates color and therefore absorbs light, an electrical potential that appears across a membrane admitting one ion and refusing others, and a light-emitting label attached to an antibody that has captured its target. Each route converts an invisible quantity into a number that a photodetector or an amplifier can measure, and knowing which route an instrument uses tells the operator what will disturb it, what will drift, and what must be cleaned. This chapter describes the hospital-grade laboratory first, with its plumbing, its reagents, and its service needs, and then the field variant that must work where there is dust, heat, and no reliable refrigerator.

The workhorse of the chemistry laboratory is spectrophotometry, and its logic is easy to hold in mind. A lamp, either a tungsten halogen bulb or a light emitting diode, called LED, produces a broad beam; a monochromator or an interference filter narrows it to a band of wavelengths; the beam crosses a transparent cuvette holding the reaction mixture; and a photodetector measures how much light survives the journey. The instrument first measures a blank and then the sample, and compares the 2. What it calculates is absorbance, the logarithm of the ratio between the light that entered and the light that left, and the reason this quantity is used is that absorbance rises in direct proportion to the amount of colored substance in the light path. In plain words, twice the concentration absorbs twice the light, and a longer path through the liquid absorbs more. That is the Beer-Lambert relationship, and it is what allows a color change to be translated into a concentration. The wavelength chosen for a test, the incubation temperature of 37 degrees Celsius, and the path length of the cuvette must all be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Most molecules of clinical interest are colorless, so the reagent mixture is designed to turn the analyte into a colored product, or to consume a colored product at a rate that depends on the analyte. In an endpoint reaction the color develops fully and is read once, which is simple and robust; in a rate reaction the instrument reads the changing absorbance several times over a fixed interval and calculates the slope, which is how enzymes are measured, because an enzyme present in tiny amounts acts on its substrate again and again and its catalytic speed reveals its concentration. Many such reactions are coupled to the oxidation of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, which absorbs light strongly at 340 nanometers, so the disappearance of that absorption tracks the reaction. The common operator errors are physical rather than chemical: a cuvette with a fingerprint or a scratch, a bubble in the light path, a sample cloudy from fat, pink from released hemoglobin, or deeply yellow from bilirubin, and a reaction read before it has reached its proper point. A cloudy or discolored sample scatters and absorbs light on its own, so the result may be a plausible number that is simply wrong, and severe hemolysis can add substances that the reagent mistakes for the analyte. The characteristic alarm is the absorbance range or reaction error flag, which warns that the reading fell outside the range in which the mathematics still holds, and the exact limits and the correct response must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The second physical route is the ion-selective electrode, which measures an electrical potential rather than light and is used above all for sodium, potassium, and chloride. The heart of the device is a membrane permeable to one ion and nearly impermeable to all others, so a charge separation builds across it whose size depends on how much of that ion is present; a stable reference electrode completes the circuit, and a very high impedance amplifier reads the voltage between the 2. The relationship between voltage and concentration is logarithmic, which lets the electrode respond over a wide range but also means it must be calibrated often. Most instruments calibrate with 2 solutions of known concentration, one near the low end and one near the high end of the clinical range, and the resulting slope and offset convert voltage into a number. Some analyzers measure the sample directly while others dilute it first, and this difference matters enormously when a patient has very high protein or very high lipid levels, because the diluted measurement can report a falsely low sodium that is not present in the body. The membrane is also easily fouled by protein, by clot, and by air bubbles, and an electrode near the end of its life loses its slope and drifts, which appears as a calibration that will not hold. The electrode slope, the calibration voltage, and the operating temperature of 37 degrees Celsius must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The third architecture abandons liquid reagents and places the whole reaction in a thin film, and this is the dry chemistry slide. The slide is a small rectangle of transparent plastic carrying several layers: a spreading layer that distributes a drop evenly over a defined area, sometimes a scavenger layer that removes interfering substances, a reagent layer holding the enzymes and dyes, and an indicator layer where the color finally appears. The instrument applies a measured drop, usually about 10 microliters, incubates the slide, and shines light through the transparent support from below, reading the color by reflectance rather than transmission. Because the slide is the reaction vessel, there are no reagent bottles, no tubing to rinse, and no wash water, so the instrument can be small, quiet, and battery powered. The price is a narrower menu and a higher cost for each test, since every measurement consumes a manufactured slide. The characteristic operator errors are a drop too small or too large, an air bubble under the spreading layer, a finger touching the reagent surface, a slide taken from a pouch left open in humid air, and a slide used after its expiry date, and the analyzer usually answers these with an insufficient sample or slide error message rather than a number. The storage conditions, the sample volume, the incubation time, and the reflectance limits of each slide type must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Between the tiny dry slide and the enormous automated line sits the discrete cuvette analyzer, the instrument most hospital laboratories actually run. A robotic arm carries a sample probe that descends into the sample cup, senses the liquid surface, and aspirates a precise volume measured in microliters; a second probe adds one or more reagents; the mixture moves into a plastic cuvette, is warmed to 37 degrees Celsius, and is read by a photometer at one or more wavelengths. After the reading the cuvette is rinsed by a wash station and dried with a jet of air, or discarded if it is a single-use design. Behind the visible probes are peristaltic pumps, syringe pumps, valves, and stepper motors, and the precision of the whole instrument rests on those hidden parts. The characteristic hazards are a probe that strikes a cuvette because the mechanical position has drifted, a probe clogged by a fibrin strand from an incompletely clotted sample, and reagent carryover from one test to the next when the wash is incomplete. Because the sample is handled in open air, aerosols and spills are a real biohazard, and the operator should treat the sample area as contaminated and wear gloves and eye protection. The pipetting volumes, the incubation temperature, the wash volumes, and the level-sensing sensitivity must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The largest chemistry instruments are not single analyzers but automated lines, in which a track carries tubes between modules. The line begins with a sample handler that reads the barcode on each tube and records its position, then a decapper that removes the cap, a centrifuge module that separates serum, and an aliquoter that splits the sample into smaller cups for different destinations. Along the track stand chemistry modules, immunoassay modules, and sometimes a module for coagulation or for glycated hemoglobin, and at the end a refrigerated archive holds the finished tubes for later add-on testing. Throughput is measured in tests per hour and can reach several thousand on a large line, and the software decides which module receives a test, dilutes a result above the measuring range, repeats a result that failed a check, and adds a reflex test when an initial result crosses a rule. The great safety hazard of the line is misidentification, because a barcode read in the wrong orientation, a tube loaded into the wrong position, or a label smeared by condensation can attach one patient's result to another patient's name. The common operator errors are loading tubes the wrong way round, providing too little blood for the requested menu, using a tube type the line cannot process, and leaving a clot that blocks a probe downstream. The characteristic alarms are a track jam, a barcode unreadable message, and a sample not detected warning, and every threshold, speed, and alarm response must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

An immunoassay does not rely on color chemistry or on an electrode but on the selectivity of an antibody, and that selectivity is the whole basis of the method. An antibody is a protein produced by the immune system that binds one particular molecular shape, called an epitope, and ignores almost everything else. In the laboratory such antibodies are raised deliberately, either by immunizing an animal and harvesting its antibodies or by growing cells engineered to secrete one single antibody, and the result is a reagent that finds its target in a mixture of thousands of other molecules. This is essential because hormones, cardiac markers, and therapeutic drugs circulate at concentrations of nanograms or picograms per milliliter, far below the reach of ordinary spectrophotometry. The common formats are the sandwich assay, in which one antibody captures the analyte and a second labeled antibody binds a different part of it, and the competitive assay, in which a labeled copy of the analyte competes with the patient's own analyte for a limited number of antibody binding sites. In every format the bound material must be separated from the unbound before the signal is read, and an incomplete separation is a classic source of a falsely high result. The operator must also respect cross-reactivity, in which a similar molecule is mistaken for the target, interference from the patient's own antibodies, and the hook effect, in which an extremely high concentration overwhelms the capture and produces a falsely low reading. The interference limits and the dilution protocol must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The signal at the end of an immunoassay can be produced in 3 principal ways, and each carries its own failure modes. In the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, the detection antibody carries an enzyme, and after the unbound material is washed away a substrate is added that the enzyme converts into a colored product whose absorbance is read in a plate reader; the plate has many small wells, so dozens of samples can be run at once. In chemiluminescence the label itself emits light when triggered by a chemical reaction, and a photomultiplier tube counts the photons, which gives enormous sensitivity and a wide working range and needs no lamp or monochromator, but also makes the measurement sensitive to stray light and to contaminated reagent. In the lateral flow format the reagents are dried onto a strip of nitrocellulose, the liquid sample wicks along it by capillary action, a labeled antibody travels with it, and the captured complex forms a visible line at a fixed position, with a second control line proving that the strip worked. The lateral flow test is cheap, needs no instrument, and is ideal in the field, but it is only as good as its storage and its timing, because a strip read too early shows nothing and a strip read too late can develop a faint line that means nothing at all. The characteristic alarms of a laboratory immunoassay module are a calibration failure and a signal below the detection limit. The cutoffs, incubation times, wavelengths, and alarm responses for every one of these formats must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The analytes a chemistry analyzer reports are chosen because each answers a physiological question, and each method has its own quirks. Glucose is measured by an enzyme that oxidizes it and produces hydrogen peroxide, which then drives a second reaction that creates color, or by an electrode that measures the same reaction as an electric current; because red cells continue to consume glucose after the blood is drawn, the tube should contain a substance that stops that consumption, and otherwise the sample must be separated quickly. Creatinine, the marker of kidney filtration, is measured either by its reaction with alkaline picrate, the older method, or by an enzyme, and the older method is cheaper but disturbed by bilirubin, by ketones, and by several common drugs. Urea is measured by the enzyme urease, which splits it into ammonia and carbon dioxide, after which the ammonia is quantified, and because urea production depends on diet and hydration as well as on the kidneys the result is read alongside creatinine. Sodium, potassium, and chloride come from the ion-selective electrodes described earlier, while calcium and magnesium are measured by related electrode or dye methods. A single chemistry panel may therefore rest on 3 or 4 completely different physical principles at once, and the operator must know which method produced a result before interpreting an odd value. The reaction temperatures, incubation intervals, and method-specific interference notes must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The liver tests show how enzymes reveal organ injury. Alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase are measured by rate reactions in which the enzyme's own activity generates a color change, and their concentration in blood rises when liver cells leak; alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase are measured in the same fashion and point more toward bile ducts and bone. Bilirubin is measured by coupling it to a diazonium salt to form a colored compound, albumin by its binding to a dye that changes color when bound, and total protein by the biuret reaction, in which copper in alkaline solution forms a colored complex with peptide bonds. Cardiac markers are immunoassays, because troponin and the myocardial band of creatine kinase circulate in vanishingly small amounts, and a rising troponin over several hours is more meaningful than one value, which is why the timing of the second sample is written into every chest pain protocol. Hormones such as thyroid stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, cortisol, and human chorionic gonadotropin, and therapeutic drugs such as digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, and phenytoin, are also immunoassays, and for a drug the moment of sampling matters as much as the number, because a level drawn at the wrong time relative to the dose cannot be interpreted. The reference intervals, dilution rules, and interpretive cutoffs for all of these tests must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Calibration is the bridge between a signal and a concentration, and quality control is the proof that the bridge is still standing. A calibrator is a material with a known concentration, usually traceable to a national or international reference preparation, and the instrument measures it to build a relationship between signal and concentration; some tests need a single calibrator, some need a full curve of several points, and a new reagent lot or a replaced electrode almost always demands a fresh calibration. Quality control material is different from a calibrator: it is a sample with an assigned value that the instrument treats as if it were a patient, and it comes at more than one level, typically a normal level and an abnormal level. The laboratory runs controls at the start of every shift, after maintenance, after a reagent lot change, and after any calibration, and plots the results on a chart; a result that drifts or jumps triggers a defined rule, and by long convention a control more than 2 standard deviations from its mean is a warning while a larger excursion is a rejection. If a control fails, no patient result from that run may be reported until the cause is found and corrected, and the most damaging common error is the temptation to recalibrate until the control looks acceptable instead of finding the fault. Internal control proves only that the instrument is consistent with itself, so laboratories also join an external quality assessment scheme, in which unknown samples arrive from outside and the returned results are compared with those of other laboratories. The control limits, the accepted rules, and the corrective actions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The quiet requirements of a chemistry laboratory are reagents, water, and waste, and each can ruin results long before any electronic fault appears. Many reagents must be kept cold, typically between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, some must be frozen, and some arrive as a concentrate that is reconstituted and then remains stable for only a few days; most degrade with heat and light, and a bottle left on the bench overnight may give a result that is wrong in a direction nobody can predict. Reagents must never be topped up into a partly used bottle, because that mixes lots and invites contamination, and a reagent past its expiry date or changed in color should be discarded rather than used. Water is a reagent in its own right, since it dilutes samples, rinses cuvettes, and carries reagents, so it must be purified by distillation, by deionization, or usually both, and its purity is judged by electrical resistivity, commonly expressed in megohm centimeters, with bacteria and dissolved carbon dioxide removed as well. Waste is the other half of the equation, because the instrument produces a continuous stream of liquid containing patient sample, reagent, and cleaning solution, and this stream is both a biological and a chemical hazard that may carry heavy metals, azide, strong acid, or strong base. Waste must be collected in labeled containers, never poured into an ordinary sink without checking local rules, and the fill level watched because a full container will eventually shut the instrument down. The storage temperatures, the reconstituted stability limits, the water resistivity specification, and the waste handling rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

A chemistry or immunoassay analyzer rewards routine care and punishes neglect in ways that are easy to predict once the design is understood. Every day the operator should confirm that the water supply is flowing, the waste container has room, the probes are clean and undamaged, the reagent compartments are loaded correctly, and the controls have been run and passed before any patient sample is handled. Every week the instrument usually needs a cleaning or wash cycle, a check of the cuvettes or reaction cells, and a look at the lamp or detector readings; every month the syringes, seals, tubing, and filters deserve inspection; and once a year, or at the interval the maker states, the photometer is checked, the lamp and the peristaltic pump tubing are replaced, and the probe alignment is verified. The typical failure modes leave characteristic traces: a lamp near the end of its life produces rising blanks and noisy results; flattened pump tubing delivers a smaller volume than it should and shifts every result in the same direction; an aging ion-selective electrode loses its slope and reads low; a drifting incubation temperature disturbs every enzyme reaction measured by rate; and a partly blocked sample probe gives intermittent short samples that appear as random errors. The characteristic alarms are no water, waste full, low lamp intensity, temperature out of range, probe collision, and control out of range, and the operator must never silence an alarm without identifying what caused it. Each maintenance interval, lamp hour limit, temperature tolerance, and alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Long before the analyzer is involved, the fate of a chemistry result is decided by how the blood was taken and handled, and this pre-analytic stage causes more errors than any instrument fault. The patient should be fasting when the test requires it, the tourniquet should be released within about 1 minute, and the patient should not clench and relax the fist repeatedly, because that alone can raise the potassium measurably; the tube must be filled to its marked volume so the additive is correctly proportioned, and the order of draw matters because a trace of the chelating agent from a lavender-topped tube will lower calcium and raise potassium in the next tube. Hemolysis is the most common visible problem, since red cells broken by a narrow needle, by pulling too hard on a syringe, by shaking a tube, or by forcing blood through a needle release their contents, which raises potassium, raises lactate dehydrogenase, and interferes with many colorimetric reactions. Serum or plasma must be separated from the cells within the time the local protocol allows, because potassium leaks out of cells on standing and glucose is consumed by them, and some analytes, notably bilirubin, must be protected from light. The sample must then be centrifuged at the specified speed for the specified time, transported at the required temperature, and delivered with a label that the analyzer and the technologist can both read; sharps are never recapped by hand, and a blood spill is cleaned with gloves and a fresh disinfectant under local rules. Every time limit, centrifuge speed, storage temperature, and tube requirement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Once a result exists it must travel to the person who will act on it, and that path is part of the device's design. Most analyzers connect to a laboratory information system, which in turn feeds the electronic health record, called EHR, and the common language for that conversation is Health Level Seven, called HL7; results may also carry interpretive flags for hemolysis, lipemia, or icterus detected by the instrument itself. Modern software performs a delta check, comparing each new result with the patient's previous value and holding back any change larger than a defined limit for human review, and it may autoverify results that pass every rule so that the technologist examines only the exceptions. Critical values, those results so far outside the reference interval that they demand immediate action, must be communicated directly to a clinician and documented, and the thresholds defining them are set by the laboratory in agreement with the clinical services. The operator's final checks before release are therefore identity, plausibility, units, reference interval, and any flag attached to the result, because a perfectly accurate measurement attached to the wrong patient is more dangerous than no measurement at all. The delta check limits, the critical value thresholds, and the notification procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.
