A field clinic at the end of a long road cannot support the laboratory just described, so the field variant is built around simplification and self-containment. There is often no reliable mains electricity, no purified water system, no refrigerator that holds a stable temperature, no continuous supply of liquid reagents, and no service engineer within a day's travel, and the person running the test may be the same person who took the sample while other patients wait. The instrument that answers this is a small reflectance or electrochemical analyzer using sealed dry slides or single-use cartridges, in which every reagent needed for the reaction is already inside the package, so there is nothing to reconstitute, nothing to refrigerate after opening, and no liquid waste to manage. It runs on a rechargeable battery that can be charged from a solar panel, and it calibrates itself by reading a code printed on the cartridge or the slide packet, which removes the burden of a manual calibration curve. Whole blood from a finger prick or a small tube can often be applied directly, which saves the centrifuge and the pipette, and the menu usually covers glucose, creatinine, urea, a few electrolytes, and perhaps 1 or 2 enzymes. What it gives up is throughput, since samples are run a sample at a time, and also the wide menu, the automatic dilution of high results, the delta check against previous values, and the full program of daily quality control with several levels of material. What it demands in exchange is discipline about the operating temperature range, which for some devices is roughly 15 to 30 degrees Celsius, about shade and protection from dust and wind, about the exact sample volume, about the timing of the reading, and about keeping a written log of every result, control, battery charge, and error message. Each of those figures, and any control schedule the field site can sustain, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The device that does most of the field's chemistry work is the handheld glucose meter, and its physical principle is small enough to fit in a pocket. The strip contains an enzyme, usually glucose oxidase or a glucose dehydrogenase, plus a mediator molecule and 2 electrodes; when a drop of blood enters the strip, the enzyme oxidizes glucose and the mediator carries the electrons to the electrode, producing a current proportional to the amount of glucose present. Some meters use reflectance instead, reading a color change on the strip, but the electrochemical design dominates because it needs no optics and very little power. The strip is the fragile part: the reagents are dried onto it and are destroyed by moisture and heat, so the vial must be capped immediately, stored out of the sun, and never used past its expiry date, and the meter must be set to match the strip lot, either by a code chip, a keypad entry, or an automatic read of a code on the vial. The classical interferences are hematocrit and other blood constituents, because anemia can push the reading up and a very high red cell count can push it down, while ascorbic acid and severe dehydration distort it further, and extreme altitude and temperature change the chemistry as well. The common operator errors are a finger still wet with fruit juice, a drop too small to fill the strip, squeezing the fingertip so that tissue fluid dilutes the blood, an expired or heat-damaged strip, and a meter left uncoded for the strip in use. The characteristic alarms are a strip error, a low battery warning, a temperature out of range message, and a result flagged as below or above the measuring range, and the meter's error codes, the sample volume, the storage temperature, and the difference between whole blood and plasma readings, which is roughly 10 to 15 per cent, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Immunoassay in the field is usually reduced to the lateral flow strip, and that reduction is both its strength and its limit. A pregnancy test, a malaria test, a human immunodeficiency virus test, and several others are the same physical object: a plastic housing containing a nitrocellulose strip, a pad holding a dried labeled antibody, a test line, and a control line, driven only by capillary action. The strip must be stored within its stated temperature range, usually below 30 degrees Celsius and never frozen, and it must be kept dry, because heat and moisture destroy the dried antibodies; the result must be read within the exact window printed by the maker, since a line that appears later is meaningless. The limit is sensitivity, because a lateral flow test cannot detect the tiny concentrations a laboratory immunoassay measures, and it may be negative early in an infection when the laboratory test is already positive, which is why the timing of the sample relative to the illness matters as much as the test itself. For sodium and potassium an older field method survives in the flame photometer, in which a diluted sample is sprayed into a flame, the sodium and potassium atoms emit light at their own characteristic wavelengths, and a filter and detector measure that light; the method is fast but needs a combustible gas, a very stable flame, and careful dilution, so it carries a fire hazard and a hot-surface hazard. A battery-operated immunoassay reader for troponin and similar markers exists for clinics without a laboratory, but its reagents still need a cold chain, and that chain is the real constraint in the field. Without a daily program of quality control at several levels, a field site cannot claim the accuracy of a hospital laboratory, so the most it can do is run a control solution when one is available, send a split sample to a reference laboratory from time to time, and compare the 2 results in writing; a device that has been dropped, soaked, or overheated should be withdrawn until it can be checked, and a result near a decision threshold should be repeated or confirmed by a laboratory method. The storage temperatures, reading windows, detection limits, gas and flame settings, cleaning solutions, and transport conditions for referral samples must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

To summarize, clinical chemistry and immunoassay analyzers turn invisible molecules into measurable signals by 3 physical routes: the absorption of light by a colored reaction, the electrical potential across an ion-selective membrane, and the light or color produced by an antibody label. Hospital-grade instruments add plumbing, robotics, tracks, and software to gain throughput, menu breadth, and automatic checking, and in return they demand purified water, refrigerated reagents, waste handling, calibration, and a daily program of quality control before any patient result may be reported. Immunoassays extend the reach of the laboratory to hormones, cardiac markers, and drugs by exploiting the specificity of antibodies, whether in a plate, a chemiluminescent module, or a lateral flow strip. The field variant strips the instrument down to sealed dry slides, cartridges, and a handheld glucose meter, which gives up throughput, menu, and formal quality control while demanding discipline about temperature, sample volume, timing, dust, and battery charge. In both settings the safety hazards begin with the contaminated sample itself and with the misidentification that attaches a correct result to the wrong patient, and the characteristic alarms are the instrument's way of saying that a number cannot be trusted. The operator's real work is therefore not pressing the button but controlling the pre-analytic phase, checking the controls, watching the maintenance intervals, and knowing when to doubt a convenient result. Every setting, temperature, threshold, and interval mentioned in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

# Chapter 34 — Microbiology

The microbiology laboratory does not merely measure a substance already present in a specimen but persuades a living organism to show itself, by growing it, by watching how it feeds, and by testing what stops it. The work has three physical tasks, which are to keep an organism alive outside the body, to separate it from everything else in the specimen, and to measure its response to a drug. This chapter describes the hospital-grade equipment of those tasks, from the incubator, the anaerobic jar, and the media kitchen to the blood culture instrument, the identification and susceptibility benches, the molecular platform, the biosafety cabinet, and the sealed centrifuge. It then turns to the field variant of a microscope, a gram stain, and a trained eye, and every temperature, atmosphere, cycle, and alarm threshold named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Everything here rests on one idea, which is that a microorganism is a small chemical engine that runs only when its conditions are supplied. It needs water, a source of carbon and nitrogen, a correct temperature, the right gas mixture, and time, so the first job of the laboratory is to supply those in a controlled way. Growth becomes visible because one cell that divides repeatedly becomes a colony, and a colony is large enough to see, count, and touch, which converts an invisible population into an object. Identification exploits the fact that different organisms run different chemical reactions, so a substrate that changes color when consumed becomes a question whose answer is a clue, and susceptibility testing asks whether the organism can still grow while a drug is present. Every set point and incubation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The incubator is the simplest and most important machine in the department, and its principle is negative feedback. A temperature sensor reports the air temperature to a controller, the controller switches a heating element on or off, and a fan stirs the air so that every shelf sits at nearly the same temperature, while thick insulation and a well fitting door hold the heat in. The usual setting for clinical bacteriology is 35 to 37 degrees Celsius, close to the human body. A carbon dioxide incubator adds a second loop, in which a sensor measures the gas and a valve admits carbon dioxide to hold the atmosphere near 5 per cent, because organisms that cause pneumonia and meningitis need that gas on a primary plate. The temperature, the gas concentration, and the humidity of each incubator must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An incubator fails in ways that are quiet before they are loud, so the operator's check is a routine rather than an event. The door seal hardens and leaks, the fan slows, the sensor drifts, and the shelf nearest the door sits cooler than the shelf at the back, so the chamber must be mapped with an independent thermometer rather than trusted to its display. A high temperature alarm and a low temperature alarm are the characteristic alarms, and a carbon dioxide deviation alarm belongs to the gas incubator, but by the time one sounds, plates have often been at the wrong temperature for hours. The common operator error is to overfill the chamber, which blocks the fan and strangles circulation, and the next is to stack plates so thickly that the air cannot reach them. The alarm set points, the acceptable range, and the recording interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An anaerobic jar is a heavy sealed vessel that removes oxygen from the atmosphere around the plates. A gas pack inside, once its seal is broken, consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and the hydrogen then combines with the remaining oxygen on the surface of a palladium catalyst to form water, leaving the jar almost free of oxygen. A strip of indicator paper changes color to show that the conditions are correct, and the catalyst and the gas pack are the consumables that make the method work. The common operator error is a poor seal at the gasket or the lid clamp, which leaves oxygen inside and lets the anaerobic organisms die while the facultative ones grow and give a misleading picture. The gas pack type, the catalyst condition, the indicator reading, and the incubation time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Media preparation begins with water, a powdered nutrient base, and agar, a polysaccharide from seaweed that melts when hot and sets into a firm gel when it cools. The mixture must be sterilized, and the device that does it is the autoclave, whose principle is saturated steam under pressure. Steam above the boiling point of water carries latent heat, and when it condenses on a cooler load it releases that heat into the material, which coagulates the proteins of any organism present and kills it faster than dry heat at the same temperature. A typical cycle holds the load at 121 degrees Celsius for about 15 minutes, while a faster cycle may reach 134 degrees Celsius for a few minutes. The temperature, the pressure, the holding time, and the load arrangement of every cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Once the agar is sterile it must be cooled and poured, and the two devices here are a water bath and a pouring station. The molten agar is held in the bath at about 45 to 50 degrees Celsius, warm enough to stay liquid and cool enough not to injure the blood or the additives mixed into it, and it is poured into shallow dishes to a depth of roughly 4 millimeters. A mechanical pourer gives the same volume to every plate. A plate with bubbles, cracks, a wavy surface, or growth before use is discarded. The bath temperature, the volume per plate, the agar depth, and the drying time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The inoculating loop is a small wire with a handle whose physical job is to carry a known volume of liquid or a single colony from one place to another. A calibrated loop delivers a fixed volume, commonly 1 microliter or 10 microliters, so that the colonies that grow after streaking can be counted and multiplied into a concentration that quantifies the specimen. Disposable loops are molded in plastic and used once, while metal loops are re used after being heated to redness in a flame, which sterilizes them by burning away every organism on the wire. A metal loop must be allowed to cool before it touches the agar, and the commonest operator error in the department is to touch a hot loop to a plate, which kills the organisms and leaves a scar in the agar. The loop volume, the streaking pattern, and the sterilization method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The blood culture system is the most sensitive culture device in the hospital, and its principle is continuous surveillance rather than a single reading. A bottle holds nutrient broth, an anticoagulant so the blood does not clot, and often a resin or charcoal material that absorbs the antibiotics the patient is already receiving, with a headspace of gas above the broth. The bottle is incubated at 35 to 37 degrees Celsius with gentle agitation, and an instrument watches continuously for the physical signs of growth, which may be a change in the fluorescence of a sensor, a change in the pressure of the headspace, or a change in a color indicator. When growth is suspected it raises a positive alert, and a sample is taken for a gram stain and for subculture onto solid media, while the decisive variable is the volume of blood in the bottle. The incubation temperature, the blood volume, the number of bottles in a set, and the alert response time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The blood culture instrument has its own maintenance and alarms, and both belong to the daily round. The incubation block must be held at its set temperature, so a temperature fault alarm is characteristic, and a bottle not loaded alarm tells the operator that a specimen is not being watched as it should be. The consumables are the bottles, and a bottle past its expiry, stored too warm, cracked at the neck, or overfilled will not support growth or will flood the sensor. The commonest operator error is contamination by the skin, which produces a positive bottle growing an organism that lives on the skin rather than in the blood, and the next is to take only one set, when two sets from separate sites are needed to separate true bloodstream infection from contamination. the bottle expiry, the storage conditions, the fill volume, and the alarm responses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Identification by biochemical reaction is the classical method, and its principle is that an organism's enzymes are a fingerprint. A differential plate contains a substrate that changes color when it is attacked, so a fermented sugar produces acid and turns an indicator from red to yellow, a sulfur containing amino acid that is broken down releases hydrogen sulfide and blackens the medium, and an organism that makes urease turns a urea medium alkaline. A strip system multiplies the idea into a row of small wells, each holding a different substrate, and the pattern of color changes after incubation is read as a code matched against a database. The inoculum density, the incubation time and temperature, and the reading of each well must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The newest identification bench uses mass spectrometry instead of chemistry, and its principle is that the mass of a molecule can be measured by the time it takes to fly. A pure colony is mixed with a matrix compound and dried on a target plate, and a laser pulse vaporizes and ionizes the mixture, so the proteins of the organism become charged particles. Those particles are accelerated by an electric field and travel down a long tube to a detector, and the lighter ones arrive first, so the arrival time at each mass to charge ratio builds a spectrum of peaks characteristic of the species. The instrument compares that spectrum with a library of reference spectra, and it is fast, but it demands a pure colony, depends on a current library, and cannot always separate closely related species. The target preparation, the matrix, the laser energy, and the library version must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Susceptibility testing by disk diffusion is the workhorse of the hospital laboratory, and its principle is diffusion against growth. A paper disk carrying a measured amount of antibiotic is placed on a lawn of the organism spread evenly over the agar, and the drug dissolves and diffuses outward, so its concentration is highest near the disk and falls with distance. The organism grows everywhere except where the drug concentration exceeds the level that stops it, and the result is a circular zone of no growth whose diameter is the visible record of that balance. The diameter is measured in millimeters and compared with an interpretive table that converts it into susceptible, intermediate, or resistant, and those breakpoints follow current guidance and are revised as resistance changes. The inoculum density, the agar depth, the disk potency, the incubation conditions, and the breakpoints in use must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Where disk diffusion gives a category, the minimum inhibitory concentration gives a number, and its principle is to expose the organism to a series of drug concentrations and find the lowest that prevents visible growth. In broth dilution, a row of wells or tubes holds a doubling series of concentrations, each is inoculated with the same small number of organisms, and after incubation they are read for turbidity or for a color change that marks growth, and the first clear one is the answer. A strip carrying a gradient of drug gives the same result on an agar plate. Automated systems fill small cards with drug, incubate them, and read the growth optically, which shortens the work but hides the arithmetic inside a machine that can drift. The drug panel, the inoculum, the incubation time, and the breakpoints applied must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Molecular platforms find the organism by its genetic material rather than by growing it. The polymerase chain reaction works by thermal cycling, which is repeated heating and cooling of a reaction mixture. Heating separates the two strands of a piece of deoxyribonucleic acid, cooling lets short primers bind to the sequences they match, and a warm step lets an enzyme copy the strands, so each cycle doubles the target and 30 to 40 cycles turn a few copies into millions that a fluorescent signal can detect. Because the reaction copies whatever it finds, a trace of genetic material from a previous run can contaminate the next, so the physical separation of the preparation room from the detection room is part of the device. Cartridge-based systems close the process into a sealed disposable, so extraction, amplification, and detection happen inside, which reduces contamination, and the cycling temperatures, the number of cycles, the primer and probe concentrations, and the contamination controls must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The biosafety cabinet is the barrier between the technologist and the aerosol a culture can raise, and its protection depends on airflow rather than on a sealed box. Room air is drawn in through the front grille, filtered, and blown down over the work surface as a smooth curtain, while a high efficiency particulate air filter cleans the air that is exhausted or recirculated, and the inward flow at the opening keeps organisms from escaping toward the operator. The commonest operator error is to block the front grille with the hands or a pile of plates. The airflow alarm is characteristic, and the airflow set point, the filter certification, and the lamp timing must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The centrifuge is a hazard as well as a tool, and it earns its place because it concentrates organisms from a liquid so they can be seen or grown. Its principle is that a spinning rotor throws denser particles outward, so cells and organisms gather at the bottom of the tube while the liquid stays above them. The danger is that a broken tube, a loose lid, or an unbalanced rotor throws a fine aerosol of infectious material into the room, which is why sealed safety buckets with tight lids and rubber gaskets are used, and why the rotor is never opened until it has stopped completely. The imbalance detector is the characteristic alarm, and the rotor speed, the run time, the bucket and gasket condition, and the rotor retirement schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning the department is equipment work, because every surface and machine has a decontamination routine defined by its manufacturer. Bench surfaces are wiped with a disinfectant active against the organisms handled, spills are covered with absorbent material and flooded with disinfectant from the edge inward, and waste leaving the bench is autoclaved before disposal, since a discarded plate is a concentrated culture of whatever the patient carried. Incubators are emptied, cleaned, and dried on a schedule, water baths are drained and disinfected because a warm bath grows its own biofilm, and the centrifuge and the biosafety cabinet are cleaned after each session as well as on the maintenance schedule. The consumables that keep the chain intact include gloves, gowns, eye protection, disinfectant, spore strips and indicator tape for the autoclave, sterile plates and broth, transport media, swabs, saline, immersion oil, slides, stains, pipettes, and the sharps container. The disinfectant contact time, the spill procedure, the autoclave validation method, and the waste route must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Quality control in microbiology is harder than in chemistry, because the result is a living population and the reference is another living population. The laboratory keeps reference strains of known organisms and grows them alongside the patient's specimen, on the same medium and in the same incubator, to prove that the medium supports growth and that the tests behave as they should, and a disk diffusion test is controlled by a reference strain whose zone diameters are known. Thermometers are checked against a reference, loops and pipettes are verified, reagent and medium lots are recorded, and the temperature of every incubator and refrigerator is written in a log at fixed intervals. The common operator errors are to skip the control when work is heavy, to read a strip too early, and to trust a machine's identification without confirming it against a gram stain, and the control organisms, the acceptable zone ranges, the calibration interval, and the recording schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant of this department is not a smaller version of the hospital laboratory but a different idea. A mobile or frontier clinic rarely has an incubator it can trust, never has a mass spectrometer, and cannot run a susceptibility panel, so it gives up species identification and the prediction of resistance and asks instead a smaller set of questions that change treatment. What remains is a microscope, a set of stains, a flame or a battery lamp, clean slides, and a trained eye, and that combination can still answer whether there are acid fast bacilli in a sputum smear, whether cerebrospinal fluid shows organisms and cells, whether a wound smear shows a dominant organism and its shape, and whether a blood film shows a parasite. The field laboratory therefore trades depth for reach, and it demands a discipline the hospital can partly delegate to machines, which is careful collection, careful staining, patient reading, and an honest refusal to guess beyond the smear. Every reagent, stain time, and microscope setting named below must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The microscope is the central instrument of the field laboratory, and its principle is that the wavelength of light and the size of the opening that admits it set the smallest detail that can be resolved. The condenser focuses a cone of light onto the specimen, the objective lens collects the light that passes through it, and the eyepiece magnifies the image the objective has already formed, so magnification without adequate light and aperture produces a large and empty picture. The numerical aperture of the objective measures how wide a cone of light it can accept, and resolution improves as the aperture rises, which is why a drop of immersion oil is placed between the slide and an oil immersion objective, because the oil has nearly the same refractive index as glass and stops the light from bending away at the gap. A field microscope may be lit by daylight through a mirror or by a battery powered light emitting diode, and it must be carried in its case, kept dry, and cleaned of oil with lens paper after every session. The lamp, the condenser setting, the objective, and the immersion oil must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The gram stain is a sequence of dyes that sorts bacteria into two great groups by the structure of the cell wall, and every step has a physical reason. Crystal violet stains all cells purple, iodine is applied and forms a large complex with the dye inside the cell, and alcohol or a mixture of alcohol and acetone is used to decolorize. In a gram positive organism the thick mesh of peptidoglycan in the wall traps the dye complex and the cell stays purple, while in a gram negative organism the thin peptidoglycan and the lipid rich outer membrane let the complex wash out, so the cell becomes colorless and is counterstained pink with a dilute dye such as safranin. The result is read as purple or pink and as round cocci or rod shaped bacilli, in single cells, pairs, chains, or clusters, and the arrangement is itself a clue. The common operator errors are to decolorize too long, which turns gram positive organisms pink, and to make the smear too thick, which leaves the middle of the field a purple mass, and the dye sequence, the decolorizing time, the smear thickness, and the reading of the control slide must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field laboratory can still culture a little, and its substitutes for the hospital media kitchen are modest but real. A pressure cooker, a lidded pot, or a simple steamer can sterilize a small batch of agar, and a candle jar replaces the carbon dioxide incubator, because a lit candle in a sealed jar consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide as it burns out, leaving an atmosphere rich enough for organisms that need that gas. A warm cupboard or a thermos flask can hold a temperature close enough to body heat for a short incubation, though the temperature must be watched with a thermometer and not assumed. For tuberculosis the field method is the acid fast smear, and for malaria it is a stained thick and thin blood film read under the microscope. The field laboratory must also solve with discipline what the hospital solves with infrastructure, which is safe disposal of cultures and sharps, disinfection of the bench, fly proof storage, and a cool dark place for the reagents that need it, and the sterilization method, the jar atmosphere, the incubation temperature, and the storage conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hazards of the field laboratory are the hazards of the hospital laboratory with the protections removed, and naming them is part of using the equipment. Without a biosafety cabinet, the aerosol raised by an open culture, a flame, or a centrifuge is breathed in the same room, so the field worker uses gloves, a gown, eye protection, and a well ventilated space, and handles the most infectious material on an open bench only when nothing better exists. A centrifuge without sealed buckets is particularly dangerous, and it is safer to spin a capped tube in a shielded or hand powered device than to run an open rotor in a crowded room. The absence of susceptibility testing is a clinical hazard in itself, because treatment must then be chosen from local guidance and the appearance of the smear, and the honest clinician names that limit rather than pretending that a gram stain predicts resistance. The characteristic alarms of the field version are the autoclave pressure indicator and the thermometer in the incubation box, and the personal protective equipment, the ventilation, the spill procedure, and the local treatment guidance must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Between the two extremes stands the district laboratory, and its shape is instructive because most of the microbiology in the world happens there. Such a laboratory lives on its maintenance log, and the daily check is short but not optional, covering the temperature of every incubator, refrigerator, and water bath, the date and sterility of every batch of medium, the condition of the gas packs and the catalyst, the level of disinfectant, and the expiry of reagents, stains, and culture bottles. The failure modes to watch are the ones that produce a confident wrong answer rather than an obvious breakdown, which are an incubator that runs cool, a medium overheated during preparation, a stain diluted or contaminated, a loop that no longer holds its volume, and a breakpoint table years out of date. The recording interval, the acceptance limits for each check, and the replacement schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, the microbiology laboratory is the part of the hospital that grows and questions living organisms, and its governing principle is that an organism behaves only when its conditions are supplied, so temperature, atmosphere, nutrient, and time are the measurement rather than the background. The incubator holds a negative feedback loop at body heat and its gas variant adds carbon dioxide, the anaerobic jar strips oxygen with a gas pack and a catalyst, the autoclave kills with saturated steam under pressure, the calibrated loop turns growth into a number, and the blood culture instrument watches a bottle continuously so that the volume of blood in it becomes the decisive variable. Identification moves from color changing biochemical reactions to strip systems to mass spectrometry, susceptibility moves from the diffused zone of a disk to the number of a minimum inhibitory concentration and depends on breakpoints that follow current guidance, and molecular platforms find genetic material by thermal cycling while the biosafety cabinet and the sealed centrifuge contain the aerosol that all of it can raise. The field version gives up species identification and resistance prediction and keeps the microscope, the gram stain, the candle jar, the pressure cooker, and the trained eye, demanding instead careful technique, honest reporting, safe disposal, and a maintenance log kept by hand. The alarms to know are the incubator temperature and gas alarms, the airflow alarm of the cabinet, the imbalance alarm of the centrifuge, the positive alert of the blood culture instrument, and the autoclave pressure or cycle fault, and every temperature, atmosphere, cycle, and threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 35 — Point-of-Care Tests

Point-of-care tests carry the laboratory to the bedside, to the clinic bench, and to the tent where a patient has just arrived. The physical principle is always the same in outline: a chemical or immunological reaction happens inside a small disposable vessel, and the signal it produces becomes a number the operator can act upon. What changes is how much machinery is left behind. In the hospital laboratory the reaction occurs in a cuvette and a photometer or electrode reads it, while at the point of care it occurs in a strip or a cartridge and the reading may be a line the eye can see, a color matched against a chart, or a current measured by a pocket instrument. This chapter describes the hospital grade program with its governance, its connectivity, and its quality control, and then the field position, where these devices often are the only laboratory that exists.

The handheld glucose meter is the most familiar point-of-care device in medicine, and its principle can be pictured as a current produced by an enzyme. A single-use strip carries dried glucose oxidase or a glucose dehydrogenase, a mediator molecule, and at least 2 electrodes printed on plastic. When a drop of blood fills the strip, the enzyme oxidizes glucose and the mediator ferries the freed electrons to the electrode surface, so a current flows whose size is proportional to the glucose present. The meter applies a small voltage, measures that current, and converts it into a concentration using a calibration stored in its memory. Some older designs let the reaction produce a color and read it by reflectance, but the electrochemical design dominates because it needs no optics or lamp and very little power. The strip is the true reagent vessel, because everything that makes the reaction specific is dried onto it, and moisture, heat, and age destroy those reagents long before the plastic looks damaged. The operating temperature range, the sample volume, and the measuring range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Because strips are manufactured in lots that vary slightly, the meter must be told which lot it is reading, and this is the meaning of coding. The match is made by a code chip, by a number on a keypad, or by a code printed on the vial that the meter reads automatically, and a meter set to the wrong lot reports a number that is precise, plausible, and wrong. A control solution at one or more levels must be run at the interval the local program defines, whenever a new vial is opened, and whenever a result is doubted. The classic distortions are physical and hematological rather than electronic. Anemia lowers the red cell content and can push the reading upward, a very high red cell count or dehydration can push it downward, and ascorbic acid, high doses of acetaminophen, extreme altitude, and extreme temperature disturb the chemistry unpredictably. The control limits, the coding method, and the correction between whole blood and plasma readings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The common operator errors at the bedside are small and repetitive. A fingertip still wet with water, fruit, or alcohol dilutes the drop; a drop too small to fill the strip gives a low current; squeezing the finger hard expresses tissue fluid and dilutes the blood; a strip from a vial left open in humid air has absorbed its own destruction; and a strip past its expiry or left in a hot vehicle may never have been reliable. The characteristic alarms are a strip error, a low battery warning, a temperature out of range message, and a result shown as below or above the measuring range rather than a number, and each is a refusal to report rather than a reading to argue with. The operator must resist repeating the test on fresh drops until a preferred number appears, because that converts a measurement into a search for reassurance. The error codes, the sample volume, the storage temperature, and the response to each alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

In a hospital the glucose meter is not a loose object in a pocket but a managed instrument inside a program. Each meter is assigned to a unit, tied to its operator by a login or badge, and connected by a docking station or wireless link so that every result flows into the electronic health record, called EHR, stamped with the patient, operator, strip lot, and any quality control result that accompanied it. The program keeps meters cleaned and charged, distributes control material, records the training and competency of every operator, and periodically compares meter results with the central laboratory using the same blood sample, because agreement with the reference method is the only meaningful definition of accuracy at the bedside. The consumables are strips, control solutions, lancets, alcohol pads, batteries, and cleaning supplies, whose storage temperature and expiry are the program's constant concern. The connectivity standard most often used is Health Level Seven, called HL7, and the patient is identified by a barcode or radio frequency identification, called RFID, wristband rather than by asking the name again. The temperature limits, the comparison schedule, and the data fields required must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The rapid diagnostic test, which most people simply call a rapid test, is built on the lateral flow strip, and its principle is capillary action doing the work of a pump, a pipette, and a wash station. A plastic housing contains a strip of nitrocellulose, a pad holding dried labeled antibody, a test line where a capturing antibody is fixed, and a control line further along. When the sample is applied it wicks along the strip, rehydrates the labeled antibody, and carries it forward; if the target molecule is present, the labeled antibody binds it, the complex is caught at the test line, and a colored line appears. The control line catches antibody that traveled past regardless, and so proves that the liquid moved and the reagents were alive. Some tests work in the opposite way, with a labeled copy of the analyte competing for limited capture sites, so a strong test line means a low concentration, and the operator must know which format is in hand. The result is qualitative or semi-quantitative, which is why a lateral flow test cannot report a concentration as a laboratory immunoassay can. The reading time and the interpretation of each line must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The tests that matter most share this same body. A malaria test detects an antigen released by the parasite, a human immunodeficiency virus test detects antibody or antigen, a syphilis test detects antibody to the bacterium, a pregnancy test detects human chorionic gonadotropin in urine, a dengue test detects viral antigen or antibody, and a streptococcal test detects the group A carbohydrate. Storage is a condition of validity rather than a detail. The dried antibodies and the nitrocellulose are destroyed by heat and moisture, so the sealed pouch must be kept within its stated temperature range, often below 30 degrees Celsius and never below freezing, opened only immediately before use, and never left in a hot vehicle or a humid room. Expiry must be read on the pouch itself and not the carton, and a test that has been frozen, baked, or soaked should be discarded rather than tried. Reading must occur within the exact window printed by the maker, because a line appearing after the window may mean nothing, and a line absent at the closed window means the test is negative. The storage temperature, the expiry rule, and the reading window must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The operator errors that damage rapid tests are as consistent as the tests themselves. Too much or too little sample, a buffer volume guessed rather than measured, a strip read in poor light, a strip left on the bench while other patients are seen, and a result recorded from memory rather than from the strip are the ordinary failures, and the most dangerous habit is reading the strip again later and accepting whatever appears. A test with no control line is invalid, and a faint test line in a patient with a low probability of disease may be a false positive just as a clear negative in early disease may be a false negative. The safety hazards are the lancet, which belongs in a sharps container at once, the blood or urine on the strip, which is infectious material, and the used strip itself, which belongs in infectious waste rather than an ordinary bin. The characteristic alarms of the few readers that exist are a low battery warning, a temperature out of range message, and a device error, because the strip alone is silent and its only warning is the missing control line. The sample volumes, buffer volumes, reading windows, and waste rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Blood gas and electrolyte analyzers measure the gases, the acid base state, and the ions of whole blood with a cluster of electrodes rather than with light. A glass electrode measures hydrogen ion activity and therefore acidity; a Clark type electrode measures oxygen by letting it diffuse through a membrane and be reduced at a cathode, producing a current proportional to its partial pressure; and a Severinghaus type electrode measures carbon dioxide by letting it change the acidity of a thin bicarbonate film behind its membrane, and that shift is read as a partial pressure. Sodium, potassium, chloride, and ionized calcium are read by ion selective electrodes, and some instruments also measure hematocrit by conductivity, glucose and lactate by enzyme electrodes, and hemoglobin or bilirubin by photometry. The instrument must be calibrated before each measurement, and the calibrating solutions, wash, and gas mixtures are held inside the cartridge or reagent pack, which is why a blood gas analyzer can sit in an intensive care unit rather than a laboratory. The electrode temperatures, the calibration intervals, and the sample volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The accuracy of a blood gas result is decided mostly before the sample reaches the electrode. The syringe must hold the correct amount of heparin, because too much dilutes the blood and shifts the values, and the sample must be free of air bubbles, because air equilibrates with the blood and moves the oxygen and carbon dioxide readings toward room air. The measurement should be made quickly, and the sample kept cool if it must wait, because leukocytes and platelets continue to consume oxygen and produce carbon dioxide inside the syringe. A capillary tube filled from a heel or earlobe must be sealed and mixed without introducing a bubble, and the operator must record whether the patient was breathing room air or supplemental oxygen, and at what concentration, because a blood gas without that information cannot be interpreted. The common operator errors are a clotted sample, a bubble under the cap, a sample drawn into an ordinary tube instead of a heparinized one, and a specimen that waited on a warm bench through a shift change. The heparin concentration, the maximum delay, the storage temperature, and the acceptable bubble size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

A cartridge based blood gas analyzer removes most of the plumbing from the operator's view, but it does not remove the maintenance. Every cartridge holds its own calibrants, wash, and waste chamber, and it must be stored within its stated temperature range and used before expiry, with the first measurement after installation usually reserved for calibration or quality control rather than for a patient. The electrodes foul with protein and clot and must be cleaned or replaced on the schedule the maker gives; the sample probe clogs with fibrin; tubing and seals age and admit air; and a battery that has not been charged will interrupt a measurement exactly when it is needed. The characteristic alarms are a calibration failure, a sample not detected message, a clot detected flag, a temperature out of range warning, and a low battery or replace cartridge notice, and each demands a defined response before another patient sample is run. The cartridge storage conditions, the calibration and quality control schedule, the electrode life, and the response to each alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Troponin testing at the point of care is an immunoassay compressed into a cartridge or strip, and it exists because a cardiac marker is useful only if it is known while the patient is still in the emergency area. A quantitative device applies a measured volume of blood or plasma to a cartridge, lets a labeled antibody bind the cardiac troponin, captures the complex on a defined zone, and reads the signal by fluorescence or by an electrochemical or magnetic method, while a simpler qualitative strip produces only a line. The physical limits of the format are the source of its clinical limits. Sensitivity is lower than in a central laboratory, so a negative result early after the onset of pain does not exclude myocardial injury, and the test must be repeated at the interval the protocol defines while the patient is observed and an electrocardiogram, called ECG, is obtained. Cross-reaction, a very high concentration that overwhelms the capture, and poor temperature control all produce results that mislead. The decision cutoffs, the repeat interval, the storage temperature, and the handling of an invalid cartridge must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The coagulation meter that reports the international normalized ratio exists to manage anticoagulant therapy, and its physical principle is the detection of the moment blood turns from liquid to gel. A drop of capillary or venous whole blood is mixed with a thromboplastin reagent dried on a strip or held in a cuvette; the reagent activates the extrinsic clotting pathway, and the instrument detects the clot by a mechanical method that senses a small magnet or plunger, by an optical method that senses light scatter, or by an electrochemical method that senses the fall in current as the mixture solidifies. The time from the start of the reaction to the clot is the prothrombin time, and that time is divided by the mean normal prothrombin time of the reagent and raised to the power of the reagent's international sensitivity index, which yields the international normalized ratio and makes results comparable between laboratories and reagent lots. This arithmetic is why the reagent lot and the calibration matter so much, and why a meter and a strip must be treated as one system rather than interchangeable parts. The reagent sensitivity index, the calibration procedure, and the therapeutic range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The errors that distort a coagulation meter are partly the patient's and partly the operator's. Hematocrit changes the viscosity of the sample and shifts the result, so a very anemic or very polycythemic patient may need a different method; a drop obtained by squeezing the finger is diluted with tissue fluid; a strip that has been warm, moist, or expired has lost its reagent; and a sample from a line flushed with heparin will be altered. The operator must keep the meter clean, since dried blood on the strip channel and around the optical window is a common cause of failed readings, and must run the control solutions at the interval the meter provides rather than only when a result looks wrong. A result outside the measuring range, or inconsistent with the patient's dose history and previous values, should trigger a venous sample and laboratory confirmation rather than a change in dose. The characteristic alarms are a strip error, a temperature out of range message, a low battery warning, and a result flagged as out of range. The control schedule, the hematocrit limits, the measuring range, and the alarm responses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The urine dipstick is the oldest point-of-care test in continuous use, and it is a row of small reagent pads on a plastic strip, each pad carrying a different chemical system and each judged by a color. Glucose is detected by an enzyme and a dye that darken in proportion to the sugar; ketones by a nitroprusside reaction that turns purple; blood by the peroxidase like activity of hemoglobin, which produces a greenish blue color; protein by a dye that changes color when it binds albumin; nitrite by a diazotization that reveals nitrate reducing bacteria; leukocyte esterase by an enzyme reaction that reveals white cells; and bilirubin by a diazo coupling. The specific gravity pad works differently, using a polyelectrolyte whose apparent acidity changes with the concentration of ions. The color must be read at the exact interval the maker states, because the reactions continue and a pad read late deepens and overstates while a pad read too early understates. The reading interval, the lighting, and the interpretation of each pad must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Read by eye, the dipstick is cheap and everywhere, and it is also a device that punishes haste. The common operator errors are dipping the strip too long so that reagents from one pad run into another, dragging the strip along the rim of the container, reading the pads in dim or colored light, reading them at the wrong time, and comparing a wet pad against the chart on the bottle instead of blotting and holding it flat. A sample left standing at room temperature grows bacteria that consume glucose and raise the acidity, so an old specimen can be reported as sugar free when it was not, and a specimen contaminated by vaginal discharge or cleaning fluid gives a result unrelated to the urinary tract. A reflectance meter removes some lighting and timing variation and prints a record, which is a real advantage in a busy clinic, but the meter must itself be calibrated and cleaned, and urine on the optical window can damage it. The dip time, the reading window, the specimen age limit, and the meter's calibration schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

A hemoglobin meter answers a single question and does it almost anywhere, because anemia is common, blood donation programs depend on it, and a laboratory hemoglobin is not always available. The common hospital design takes a small volume of capillary or venous blood into a disposable cuvette that already contains a reagent, converts the hemoglobin to a stable colored form such as azide methemoglobin, and reads it photometrically through the cuvette wall; a second design measures whole blood by conductivity or photometry without dilution, and older color comparison scales still exist in field kits. The measurement depends on the blood being well mixed and the cuvette filled to its mark, because a short fill or a bubble in the light path changes the result, and the cuvette must be wiped clean on the outside but never the inside. The common errors are a drop from a squeezed finger, blood left to settle so that cells and plasma separate, a dirty or expired cuvette, and a meter read while it is still stabilizing. The sample volume, the cuvette storage temperature, the calibration interval, and the measuring range must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Connectivity turns a collection of small devices into a point-of-care system, and its purpose is that the result reaches the record with the right patient attached. A meter linked to the EHR through a docking station or a wireless network can transmit the value, the time, the operator identity, the device serial number, the strip or cartridge lot, and any quality control result that accompanied it, and that bundle is what allows a supervisor to audit the device later. When a meter cannot connect, the operator must write the result by hand, and handwriting is where identity errors are born, so the local protocol must define who transcribes, how the value is confirmed, and how the paper record is reconciled with the EHR. The data also feed the wider program, because transmission shows which meters produce results outside the expected range, which operators have not run controls, and which lot numbers are associated with failures. A result that arrives without an identity, or that is duplicated because a meter was docked twice, is a defect of the system rather than of the chemistry. The interface specification, the data fields, and the reconciliation procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Quality control is what separates a measurement from a guess, and at the point of care it has three layers. The first is built into the device, namely the control line on a lateral flow strip, the electronic self check of a meter, the calibration verification a cartridge performs when inserted, and the internal control solutions some instruments run automatically. The second is the external control material the operator runs deliberately, at more than one level where the program provides it, at the start of a session, after a new lot or cartridge, after the meter is dropped, and whenever a result matters a great deal. The third is external quality assessment, in which an outside body sends samples with unknown values and compares the answers with those of many other sites, and it is the strongest available check because it examines the whole local system rather than one instrument. The honest discussion belongs to the test that is convenient and wrong. A device used under pressure, without controls, with a strip stored in a hot room, and with a result never compared against the patient's appearance or a laboratory value will produce numbers believed because they are printed, and a falsely reassuring result can delay treatment as surely as a false alarm can cause harm. The control frequency, the acceptance rules, the quality assessment schedule, and the response to a failed control must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Point-of-care devices are maintained by a routine that fits into the clinical day, and the routine matters more here than in a laboratory because the device travels. Every day the operator should confirm the battery or mains connection, inspect the strip channel and optical window for dried blood and dust, check that strips or cartridges are within expiry and have been stored properly, and verify that the session controls have passed before the first patient is tested. Every week the instrument usually needs its outer surfaces cleaned with the disinfectant the maker approves, since alcohol and bleach damage some housings and optical parts, and the battery contacts, printer, and docking station deserve a look. The consumables list is longer than the device list, and it includes strips, cartridges, cuvettes, lancets, capillary tubes, heparinized syringes, control solutions, calibration codes, printer paper, batteries, disinfectant wipes, sharps containers, and the temperature log for whatever refrigerator or cool box holds the reagents. Storage temperature is the quiet variable that decides whether a strip still works six weeks later, so the refrigerator temperature, typically between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, must be recorded and watched. Every storage limit, cleaning agent, and replacement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

In a mobile clinic or a frontier health post, point-of-care testing is not an addition to the laboratory but the laboratory itself, and its limits must be named before its results are trusted. What the field position gives up is the menu, the throughput, the multiple levels of quality control, the refrigerated storage, the trained technologist, the service engineer, and very often the reliable electricity and connectivity that make a hospital program auditable. What it demands instead is discipline of a different kind. The device must be charged, usually from a solar panel or a vehicle, protected from dust and direct sun, and kept within its operating temperature range, which for many instruments is roughly 15 to 30 degrees Celsius; strips and cartridges must be carried in a sealed dry box and rotated so the oldest are used first; the operator must be trained and re assessed; and every result, control, error message, battery state, and storage temperature must be entered in a written log, because the log is the only substitute for the absent electronic record. The operating temperature range, the charging method, and the log fields must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Within those constraints the field bundle is usually small and chosen for robustness rather than range. It contains a handheld glucose meter with strips and control solution; lateral flow tests for the conditions that matter locally, which may include malaria, human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, pregnancy, dengue, and streptococcal infection; a urine dipstick bottle with a color chart; a hemoglobin meter or a color scale; sometimes a cartridge blood gas and electrolyte analyzer or a small coagulation meter where a generator, a refrigerator, or a cold chain can be sustained; and the consumables that make them work, including lancets, alcohol pads, capillary tubes, buffer vials, a timer, a thermometer, a sharps box, and disinfectant. The limits of this bundle are physical and must be spoken plainly. A lateral flow test negative early in an illness may become positive later, so a single negative result cannot rule out disease; a glucose reading altered by anemia or dehydration may mislead; a cartridge analyzer stored above its allowed temperature may fail without warning; and a device that has been dropped, soaked, or heated may produce numbers that look entirely normal. The operator must know which tests the site can do well, which must be sent to a reference laboratory, and when clinical judgment must override a printed number, and the menu limits, cold chain requirements, and referral rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any device is used on a patient.

The failure modes of point-of-care testing are worth naming as questions the operator can ask before every test: is the device calibrated or coded for the strip in use; is the strip or cartridge within expiry and has it been stored at the stated temperature and humidity; is the control solution in date and did it pass; is the sample the right kind, the right volume, and free of bubbles, clot, and dilution; is the patient identified by a wristband or record number rather than by assumption; has the reading been taken within the exact window; and is the result plausible against the patient in front of the clinician. The hazards that accompany these devices are equally concrete, and they include a sharps injury from a lancet or needle, a blood splash to the eye or mouth, a chemical burn from a reagent, an allergic reaction to a disinfectant, and the infectious waste that a used strip represents. All of these require personal protective equipment, called PPE, hand hygiene, and a waste stream that keeps used sharps and contaminated disposables out of ordinary refuse. The battery state, the strip storage conditions, the control schedule, and the waste rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

To summarize, point-of-care tests are the laboratory reduced until it fits in the hand of the person at the bedside, and each works by one plain physical principle the operator can picture. A glucose strip turns an enzyme reaction into a current; a lateral flow strip turns antibody binding into a colored line moved by capillary action; a blood gas analyzer turns the diffusion of gases and the selectivity of membranes into voltages and currents; a coagulation meter times the formation of a clot; a dipstick turns several small chemical reactions into colors; and a hemoglobin meter turns a blood pigment into absorbed light. The hospital version of these devices is embedded in a program of connectivity, training, control material, comparison with the central laboratory, and documented maintenance, while the field version trades that scaffolding for portability and must repay the loss with storage discipline, charging discipline, a written log, and an honest awareness of what it cannot measure. In both settings the governing rule is the same, because a convenient result is not the same as a correct one, and the value of a point-of-care test is decided less by the instrument than by the person who prepared the sample, respected the storage, ran the control, and asked whether the number matches the patient.

# Chapter 36 — Pathology and Blood Bank

Pathology and the blood bank look nothing alike, yet both rest on one idea: tissue and blood must be stabilized before they can be examined. The pathology laboratory turns tissue into a glass slide thin enough for light to pass, using chemistry, heat, wax, and a sharp blade. The blood bank keeps cells and fragile proteins usable outside the body, using cold, gentle motion, identity, and an unbroken temperature record. Both are chains, judged by the weakest link rather than the finest instrument. This chapter describes the hospital-grade machines of each department, then the field version. In the field, one refrigerator, one thermometer, and one log sheet carry the whole burden, and every setting, temperature, time, and alarm threshold named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The first step of pathology is fixation, and its principle is chemical cross linking. Formaldehyde in buffered water diffuses into the tissue and bonds proteins together, locking the structure of life in place. Diffusion advances only about 1 millimeter each hour, so a thick specimen fixes at its surface while its center stays soft. Blocks are therefore trimmed thin and fixed at about 10 parts fixative to 1 part tissue, a ratio and a time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The vapor irritates the eyes and airway and is a human carcinogen, so fixation belongs under a fume hood, and the common error is impatience, because a block fixed for an hour stays raw at its center while no alarm warns anyone.

The tissue processor replaces the water in a specimen with wax, because only a solid block cuts into slices a few micrometers thick. It moves cassettes through heated pots: alcohols remove water, a clearing agent such as xylene mixes with both alcohol and wax, and molten paraffin replaces the clearing agent. A schedule commonly runs overnight for 8 to 12 hours, a time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The vapors are the hazard, since xylene is flammable and neurotoxic and formaldehyde is a carcinogen, so the machine needs extraction and the operator needs personal protective equipment, PPE for short. Its characteristic alarms are a low reagent level, an over temperature condition, and a blocked drain, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The embedding station bridges processing and cutting, with a heated paraffin bath, a dispenser, a warm surface, and a cold plate. The operator orients the tissue in a mold, fills it with molten paraffin, and sets it on the cold plate, where the wax hardens around the chosen plane. The principle is support: the wax must resist the blade without shattering, and the tissue must lie where the pathologist needs to see it. The hazard is the burn, because the bath holds wax hotter than boiling water. The common errors are air trapped against the tissue and wax that is too hot, which shrinks as it cools, and the bath temperature and hardening time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The microtome gives pathology its name, and its principle is a precise advance. A block holder carries the wax block past a steel blade while a micrometer screw advances it a set distance each pass, lifting a ribbon of sections. The sections are usually 3 to 5 micrometers thick, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is the blade, which cuts to the bone in one movement, so blades are handled with forceps and the holder is locked whenever the hand leaves it. The common errors are a blunt blade, a section cut too thick, and a vibration called chatter, and the microtome has no alarm, so all of these must be recognized in the ribbon.

The cryostat answers questions that cannot wait a day for processing, and its principle is that freezing hardens tissue without chemical fixation. A fresh specimen is frozen on a chuck and cut inside a chamber held near minus 20 degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The surgeon can then have an answer in minutes about a margin or a lump. Cutting generates an aerosol of infectious material, so the operator wears gloves and a mask, works behind the window, and disinfects the chamber with a tuberculocidal agent afterward. The common errors are freezing too slowly, which grows ice crystals that tear cells, and setting the chamber too cold, which shatters the block, and the characteristic alarm is a chamber temperature alarm, confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The staining station gives the colorless section its contrast, because charged dyes bind oppositely charged structures. Hematoxylin, a basic dye, colors the acidic nuclei blue, while eosin, an acidic dye, colors the basic cytoplasm pink. A manual station is a row of dishes, and a rack of slides is dipped from dish to dish on a timetable of seconds and minutes, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The automated stainer performs the same journey with a robot arm and buys consistency at the price of complexity. The hazards are solvent vapors and the carryover of one reagent into the next, and the characteristic alarms are a low reagent level and a jammed carrier, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A stained section is fragile, and the coverslipper seals it under thin glass with a drop of mounting medium. The medium has a refractive index close to that of glass, so light crosses the coverslip, the medium, the section, and the slide with little scattering. A manual coverslipper demands a steady hand because the section dries in seconds, while the automated instrument places the drop, lowers the slip, and warms the slide. The hazard is the xylene based solvent, which needs ventilation, and the common errors are trapped bubbles, too little medium so the section darkens, and a slip placed off center, with drying time and volume confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The microscope turns a stained section into a diagnosis, and its principle is the bending of light by lenses. The condenser focuses light on the specimen, the objective forms a magnified image, and the eyepiece magnifies it again. Resolution is set by the wavelength of light and the numerical aperture, and a good light microscope resolves about 0.2 micrometers, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The oil immersion objective reaches its high aperture because a drop of oil, with the refractive index of glass, replaces the air above the slide. Eye strain and lamp heat are the everyday hazards, and a fluorescence microscope adds ultraviolet light that can damage the eye. The common errors are oil on a dry objective, a lowered condenser that destroys contrast, and a lens wiped with a dry tissue, and the microscope has no alarm, so the warning is the image itself.

The slide scanner converts a glass slide into a digital image, and its principle is a camera on a moving stage. The stage carries the slide under the objective in a raster pattern, the software focuses each field, and the tiles are stitched into one large image. The value is remote review, consultation, teaching, and an archive that cannot fade, and the price is a large file and a dependence on power, storage, and network. Identity is the hazard, because a scanner will digitize a mislabeled slide and the error travels into the record unquestioned, so a barcode is read and matched before the scan. The common errors are scanning a wet or warped slide, which throws the focus off, and omitting the daily calibration slide, and the characteristic alarms are a focus failure, a barcode mismatch, and a full storage warning, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The immunohistochemistry platform detects specific proteins, and its principle is the lock and key fit of an antibody to its antigen. An antibody binds its target, a second reagent carries an enzyme, and a colorless substrate becomes a colored deposit at the exact site. Many targets need antigen retrieval, in which heat or an enzyme reopens the cross links made by fixation, and the retrieval method and antibody dilution must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The platform is a heated humid chamber that dispenses reagents on a timed program, and it is unforgiving of a section that dries out, because drying concentrates salts and creates background staining. The chromogen, commonly diaminobenzidine, is a suspected carcinogen whose waste needs a defined route, and the characteristic alarms are a reagent level, a temperature, and a waste container full alarm, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The pathology laboratory is a chemical workplace as much as a clinical one. Formaldehyde is a carcinogen and an irritant, xylene is flammable and neurotoxic, the alcohols are flammable, and the acids used to soften bone are corrosive. All of them need bench extraction, closed containers, a spill kit, and a flammable storage cabinet, because the vapor is the danger. Personal protective equipment, PPE for short, means gloves chosen for the specific chemical, eye protection, and a gown, and the choice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is complacency with a familiar smell, because a nose that no longer notices formaldehyde is not protected from it.

The blood bank is a chain of temperatures and identities, and its principle is that cold slows living processes. Refrigeration slows the metabolism of red cells and the growth of bacteria, freezing suspends the decay of clotting factors, and constant motion keeps platelets from clumping. A unit held at the wrong temperature for the wrong time is wasted at best and dangerous at worst. The department is built around a refrigerator, a freezer, an incubator with an agitator, a refrigerated centrifuge, a thawing device, a crossmatching system, an irradiator, and a record tying every unit to a patient. Every temperature, time, and alarm threshold in this part of the chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the characteristic failure of a blood bank is quiet, discovered only when the unit hangs at the bedside.

The refrigerated centrifuge separates whole blood into components, and its principle is density under a spinning load. A bag held at a fixed radius and spun at high speed feels a force many times that of gravity, so red cells pack at the bottom and plasma remains on top. The chamber is held near 4 degrees Celsius because spinning generates heat and warming blood damages cells, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A heavy spin separates red cells from plasma, while a light spin first separates platelet rich plasma. Imbalance is the hazard, because a rotor carrying unequal masses at high speed can destroy itself and its bowl, and its alarms are an imbalance alarm and a lid interlock, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The blood bank refrigerator looks domestic and is nothing of the kind. Its principle is forced air cooling with a circulating fan, so every shelf stays within a narrow band instead of the wide swing of a household thermostat. Red cells are held between 1 and 6 degrees Celsius, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because below it cells freeze and above it bacteria multiply. Its defining feature is the alarm system: high and low temperature alarms, a power failure alarm, a door ajar alarm, and often a remote alarm repeated at a nursing station, all confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The temperature chart is the legal memory of the unit, and the common errors are silencing the alarm instead of answering it, storing food beside the blood, and overloading the shelves so that air cannot circulate.

Plasma is frozen because its clotting factors are proteins that lose activity at refrigerator temperature, and cold below the freezing point of the water in plasma suspends that decay. The storage temperature is minus 30 degrees Celsius or colder, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The freezer is a thick walled cabinet that depends on its alarm and its log exactly as the refrigerator does. The hazard is frost, which builds on the evaporator and acts as insulation, so the compressor runs longer and the cabinet warms without any fault until a limit is crossed. Its characteristic alarms are a high temperature alarm and a power failure alarm, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common errors are placing warm plasma into the freezer and stacking units against the walls.

Platelets are living fragments without a nucleus, they cannot be frozen, and they are therefore stored warm and moving. Their storage temperature is 20 to 24 degrees Celsius, and they rest on an agitator that rocks them gently and continuously, a temperature and a motion that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The principle is gas exchange and suspension, because platelets clump when they are still and the rocking lets oxygen reach them. Because they are stored warm and the bag has been entered, bacteria are the dominant risk, so the storage period is commonly limited to 5 days, a limit that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Its alarms are a temperature alarm and an agitation failure alarm, and the common errors are switching off the agitator during a power cut and stacking bags so the lower ones cannot move.

Frozen plasma must be returned to body temperature before transfusion, and the thawing device is where the cold chain meets the patient. Its principle is conduction, because heat passes from a warm medium into the bag until the ice becomes liquid, and the medium is held at about 37 degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.
