A water bath thaws quickly, but water is a contamination risk, so the ports of the bag stay above the surface and the bath is cleaned on a schedule. A dry plasma thawer uses warm plates or circulating air and removes that risk at the cost of a slower thaw. Overheating destroys the clotting factors the plasma was frozen to preserve, and its characteristic alarms are an over temperature alarm and a low water alarm, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Crossmatching asks whether the recipient's serum will destroy the donor's red cells, and the tube method shows the answer as clumping. Its principle is that an antibody binds two cells at once and bridges them into a lattice that settles as visible agglutination. The stages each have a purpose: an immediate spin detects the strong antibodies of the major blood groups, and incubation at 37 degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, lets weaker antibodies bind. Antihuman globulin then reveals antibodies that coated the cells without bridging them, which is why the cells are washed first. The hazard is clerical, because a sample from the wrong patient gives a perfect result for the wrong person, and no laboratory test can detect that mistake. The common errors are reading too quickly and missing a weak reaction, and shortening the wash so that free antibody consumes the reagent, and the tube method has no alarm, so the result is only as good as the hand holding the rack.

The gel column system replaces the tube with a card holding a column of gel beads, and its principle is filtration by size. Serum and cells are mixed and incubated above the column, and the card is spun; unagglutinated cells pass between the beads and form a button at the bottom, while agglutinated cells are trapped higher up. The height of the red cell layer reports the strength of the reaction, and because every card is spun for the same time at the same force the reading is less subjective than a tube. The common errors are a card with a broken seal or a bubble in the gel, the wrong volume of cells or serum, and a centrifuge not calibrated to the card setting, all confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard remains the human one, because a clean automated card invites trust, and it can only be trusted if the sample belongs to the patient on the label.

An electronic crossmatch replaces the physical mixing of serum and cells with a calculation by a validated computer system, and its principle is that compatibility can be proven from data when the data are complete. The system holds two independent blood group results from two separate samples, with the donor unit's group, and compares them by the rules of the major blood group and rhesus systems. The prerequisites are strict: two concordant results, no history of a clinically significant antibody, a current negative antibody screen, a validated system with secure identity and interfaces to the laboratory and the refrigerator, and a written procedure that returns to a serologic crossmatch the moment any prerequisite fails. The hazard is silent, because a wrong result here looks exactly like a right one, and the cause is a data entry error rather than a reaction in a tube. Its characteristic alarm is a mismatch flag that blocks the release of a unit, confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Some immunosuppressed patients can be attacked by the white cells in a donated unit, a complication called transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, and the irradiator prevents it. Ionizing radiation from a sealed source of cobalt 60 or cesium 137, or from a high energy X-ray tube, breaks the deoxyribonucleic acid of donor lymphocytes so that they cannot multiply, while red cells, platelets, and clotting proteins survive. The dose is in the range of 25 gray to 50 gray delivered to the center of the bag, and both the dose and the calibration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Irradiation is not sterilization, so it never replaces aseptic technique. The radiation is the hazard, so the source sits behind a shielded door interlock, the operator wears a dosimetry badge, and the characteristic alarms are a door interlock, a timer, and a source position alarm, each confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cold chain does not end at the blood bank door, and the transport box is a device in its own right. A validated passive shipper holds units between panels that change phase at a chosen temperature, so the box absorbs heat without letting its contents warm, and a data logger records the journey. The principle is thermal mass and insulation: the box is a battery of cold, with a capacity measured in hours at a stated outside temperature, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is the box opened at every stop, because each opening exchanges cold air for warm. The common errors are packing units that were not pre cooled, placing frozen packs in direct contact with red cells so they hemolyze, and sending a box without a logger, and acceptance limits at receipt must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Blood banking is a discipline of small routines, and the routines are equipment. Every refrigerator and freezer carries a thermometer whose calibration is checked against a reference on a schedule, because a thermometer reading 1 degree low lets a unit drift out of range while the log looks perfect. Every alarm is tested by simulating the fault, because an alarm that has never been heard is an assumption rather than a safeguard, and the test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The units that hold blood usually sit on an uninterruptible power supply, UPS for short, and on a circuit separate from the general lighting, so one breaker does not silence the department. The chart, the alarm log, the maintenance record, and the unit history are reviewed together, because a flat line at an impossible value is a broken pen rather than a stable cabinet, and signing a log that was not read is the common failure.

In a mobile clinic or a district hospital with no blood bank refrigerator, this department becomes one refrigerator, one thermometer, one log sheet, and the discipline that makes them work. The refrigerator is usually a domestic or pharmaceutical unit, and it must be understood as neither, because its thermostat swings widely, its coldest spot freezes red cells, and its door opens many times a day. The thermometer sits at the warmest usable point, found by trial with a second thermometer on each shelf, and the reading is written twice a day at fixed hours, with the range of 1 to 6 degrees Celsius confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The unit is dedicated to blood, kept locked, placed in the coolest room away from the sun and the generator, and never used for food, drink, or specimens. Because there is no alarm, the thermometer and the log are the alarm, and a missed reading is a gap in the safety of every unit inside. The field blood bank also needs a written plan for the power cut, naming who moves the units, where they go, and how long the door may stay closed, and that time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Transport in the field is usually a cold box carried by hand, by motorcycle, or on a bicycle, and it obeys the same physics as the hospital shipper. A vaccine carrier with frozen water packs and a lining of cloth or cardboard holds a few units for hours, provided the packs never touch the bags directly, because contact freezing damages red cells. The box has a budget of cold, and every opening spends some of it, so the most distant delivery is opened last. The hazard is heat, because a box left in the sun or a closed vehicle loses its reserve far faster than the plan assumed. The common errors are packing the box the night before, trusting a hand on the outside instead of a thermometer inside, and sending it without a written record of departure and arrival temperatures, and the packing arrangement and maximum journey time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field version of pathology is not a small histology laboratory, because no field clinic runs a processor, a microtome, and a cryostat. What it can do is the smear and the stained preparation, in which a drop of blood or a touch of a lesion is spread thinly on a slide, fixed in alcohol, stained, and read under a light microscope. The field microscope is often a robust monocular instrument with a mirror or a battery powered light emitting diode, LED for short, and it gives up automated illumination, multiple objectives, and the camera of the hospital instrument. The hazards are the flammable fixative and stain and the sharps used to make the smear, so the work happens on a clean surface with gloves and separated waste. The common errors are a smear that is too thick, a stain left on too long, and a pencil label that rubs off in transit, and the staining times and fixative choice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Anything that needs tissue architecture rather than single cells must travel, and the transport pot is the field pathologist's most important equipment. A biopsy is placed in a wide mouthed container of buffered formaldehyde at least 10 times its own volume, sealed, labeled with the patient's identity and the site, and packed so it cannot leak, and the volume ratio and fixation time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Fixation continues during the journey, so the tissue is being processed while the vehicle moves, and a specimen that arrives after two warm days is usually fixed even if not ideal. The hazard is the leak, because formaldehyde is a carcinogen and a spill inside a vehicle is a serious event. The common errors are a container that is too small, ink that runs, and a request form that travels separately from the specimen, and reagents must stay within their storage temperature and expiry, both confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Certain failures recur in these two departments often enough to be named as a group. The alarm that everyone silences and no one investigates, on a blood refrigerator or a tissue processor, is the most costly device in the room because it trains the staff to ignore the next alarm. The chart recorder with a flat line, the thermometer that was never calibrated, the gasket gone hard, and the condenser coils matted with dust are quiet failures that leave no trace until an audit or an accident. The refrigerator on a circuit switched off at night, the freezer that thaws and is quietly refrozen, and the thawed plasma returned to the freezer turn a cold chain into a story. In pathology the matching failures are the exhausted stain bath, the blunt blade, the processor interrupted by a power cut, and the cryostat disinfected with a chemical that does not kill mycobacteria, so the operator must check the reading, the date, the seal, the blade, and the reagent at the stated interval.

The consumables of this chapter are easy to overlook because they are silent and small. The histology bench depends on cassettes and lids, embedding molds, disposable blades, glass slides and coverslips, mounting medium, stains and solvents, antibodies and retrieval solutions, and paraffin itself, and every one carries a lot number and an expiry that must be recorded. The blood bank depends on crossmatch tubes or gel cards, reagent red cells, antiglobulin reagent, saline, blood bags and labels, irradiation indicators, loggers, thermometers, chart paper, and log sheets, and a reagent is part of the test, so an expired card changes the result rather than merely the supply. The routine maintenance an operator can do is short: clean the microscope lenses, change the lamp, defrost the freezer, clean the thawing bath, check the agitator motion, clean the centrifuge chamber, change the chart paper, and test the alarm. Cleaning the cryostat and the staining bench uses a tuberculocidal disinfectant and the manufacturer's named agent, with contact time confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and no operator should open a refrigeration circuit or a sealed radiation source.

To summarize, the pathology laboratory and the blood bank are both chains of preparation, and every link is a device with a physical principle behind it. Pathology fixes tissue by chemical cross linking, replaces its water with wax, cuts it on a micrometer screw, freezes it when speed matters, colors it with oppositely charged dyes, seals it under glass, and reads it through lenses whose resolution is set by wavelength and numerical aperture. The blood bank keeps cells and proteins alive by cold and gentle motion, separates them by density in a refrigerated centrifuge, proves compatibility by the bridging of antibodies or by validated data, and protects the immunosuppressed recipient with ionizing radiation. In the hospital these functions rest on narrow temperature bands, audited alarms, calibrated thermometers, and written records, while in the field they rest on one refrigerator, one thermometer, one log sheet, and a person who reads them at the stated hour. The hazards are formaldehyde, xylene, sharp blades, infectious aerosols, cold surfaces, and radiation, and the recurring errors are the silenced alarm, the uncalibrated thermometer, the unread log, the mislabeled specimen, and the overridden computer stop. The single habit that holds both departments together is confirming every number against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

# Chapter 37 — Operating Theatre Layout and Fixed Equipment

An operating theatre is not a room that contains equipment but a machine in its own right, built to keep living particles away from an open wound. Contamination always travels on a carrier, whether air, water, a hand, an instrument, or dust, so the room controls the carriers rather than the organisms. A wound is warm, wet, and exposed, and any organism landing on it may multiply, so the design excludes contamination rather than killing it after arrival. The theatre is therefore a system of zones, pressure steps, filtered air, cleanable surfaces, and limited traffic, and this chapter describes it in a well-resourced hospital and then in a mobile or frontier clinic where none of it exists.

The sterile field is a concept before it is a place, being the region of the patient, the drapes, the instruments, and the air directly above them that is treated as free of living organisms. Its boundary is held by gravity, by distance, and by materials: a sterilized drape kept dry, a gown and gloves worn by a scrubbed person, and a rule that treats everything below waist level and beyond the drape as unsterile. Because organisms are carried rather than walking, a dry cloth is a barrier only while it stays dry, since moisture wicks organisms from an unsterile surface to a sterile one. The commonest operator error is the unthinking one, the hand that adjusts a lamp above the wound or the tubing lifted back after trailing on the floor, and no alarm reports a broken field, so the circulating nurse watches the boundary.

A modern theatre is laid out as zones of decreasing contamination, and the layout itself is equipment. The outer transfer area receives the patient and stops street clothing, outside equipment, and family. The clean zone holds the scrub sinks and the closed storage of sterile supplies, while the restricted zone is the operating room itself, entered only by staff in theatre clothing, caps, and masks. A theatre that lacks these zones still works clinically and pays for the lack in surgical site infections, so the zoning and traffic rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the room is used for a patient.

The operating table holds an unconscious body in a chosen position for hours without injuring it and without shifting under the surgeon's hands. It is a column or pedestal carrying the weight to the floor, a top divided into sections, and a mechanism that raises, lowers, tilts, and flexes those sections. The hydraulic version pushes an incompressible fluid into a cylinder and holds position when the pump stops, while the electric version uses a motor with a screw or gear, quieter but slower and dependent on power. The joints between sections are the weak points where fluid leaks and skin can be trapped, and the maximum load and locking procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a patient is placed on the table.

The movements of the table each change what the surgeon can reach: Trendelenburg position lowers the head and raises the feet, lateral tilt rolls the table, and the kidney bridge arches the flank. The table also takes attachments, including arm boards, leg holders or stirrups for pelvic surgery, shoulder supports and straps that stop a patient sliding on a steep tilt, and a headrest for prone surgery. The positions these create, supine, prone, lateral, lithotomy, and sitting, carry mechanical hazards, because a patient who cannot report numbness can suffer a stretched nerve, pressure damage from a hard edge, or a fall from a table tilted before the straps are applied. Every pressure point, strap tension, and position limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the patient is positioned.

Before every case the table is checked in a fixed order, because the failure that matters happens after the patient is asleep and draped. The operator releases the brakes, runs each movement through its full range, listens for a change in the motor's note, looks for fluid under the column, and confirms that the table locks solidly. The foot switch is checked for a stuck button, since a table that keeps moving after the button is released is a serious hazard, and a table that drifts, sinks, or grinds is removed from service. Maintenance covers the hydraulic fluid and seals, the supply cord, and the battery that lowers the table when the mains fails, and the service interval and load test procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the table returns to use.

The surgical light exists because the eye needs far more light on a deep, wet, moving field than a room can provide, and its design follows from intensity and heat. Intensity is measured in lux, and any intensity setting, focus, or filter specification must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The halogen lamp is an incandescent filament in a gas-filled envelope, and most of its energy leaves as heat, so it needs a large housing and a heat filter and can still feel warm on the surgeon's neck. The light-emitting diode, or LED, lamp produces light at a semiconductor junction, wastes far less energy as heat, lasts much longer, and allows a flatter head, while both types use a reflector and a ring of lamps to reduce the shadow cast by the surgeon's hands.

The light head hangs from an arm with joints and counterweights, and a joint that has lost its friction lets the head drift over the field or drop without warning. The sterilizable handle at the center of the head, or the disposable cover over it, lets a scrubbed person reposition the light without touching the unsterile body of the lamp. The common operator error is to grab the unsterile arm, contaminating the hand and then the field, or to over tighten a joint until it strips, and a light that flickers, dims, or cuts out is repaired before the next case. Every theatre needs a tested backup of a battery lamp, a head torch, or a second ceiling light, and its charge state must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the room is used for a patient.

Ceiling pendants and booms bring gases, power, suction, and data to the point of use without a floor full of hoses, and they are the equipment most often overloaded. A boom is a column or articulated arm fixed to the structural ceiling, carrying outlets, gas hoses, sockets, and often a shelf for a monitor or pump. The load hangs from the building, so the ceiling fixing and each joint brake carry the whole weight, and a boom rated for a stated load must not also hold a pump, a monitor, and a heavy bag. The outlets are color coded and indexed by gas, and the common errors are to force a hose onto the wrong outlet with an adapter, to leave a joint unbraked, or to park the boom over the sterile field, so the load limit, brake test, and gas outlet check must each be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Ventilation is the part of the theatre that is invisible and works hardest and longest. Clean air is delivered at the ceiling, sweeps the room in a controlled direction, and leaves near the floor, carrying particles away from the wound rather than across it. Outdoor air is filtered, conditioned for temperature and humidity, and supplied at a rate measured in air changes per hour, which is how many times the whole volume of the room is replaced in an hour. Above the table the supply is usually a unidirectional or laminar flow field made possible by a high-efficiency particulate air filter, and the air change rate, filter efficiency, temperature, and humidity set point must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the room is used for a patient.

The pressure of the theatre relative to its corridor is a deliberate choice and one of the cheapest defenses against infection. The room is usually held slightly above the corridor, so that when a door opens the air flows outward, while for a patient with a contagious airborne infection the relationship is reversed and the room is held at a lower pressure so air is exhausted through a filter. The difference is small and is measured in pascals, and a difference that is too large makes doors hard to open and whistle, while one that is lost leaves the room at the mercy of the corridor. A pressure monitor with a gauge and an audible alarm is the standard way to know the state of the room, so the set point and alarm band must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator check on ventilation is short and is done before the first case and after every door has been opened. The gauge is read and written down, the alarm is tested with its test button, and the room is walked for a draught that should not be there, because a door propped with a chair or taped back defeats the pressure step completely. Filters load with dust, and a loaded filter lowers the air change rate while the fan works harder, so the pressure drop across the filter is monitored and the filter changed on a schedule. A ventilation failure during a case is serious, and the fallback is to stop if the case can be stopped, close the wound, and leave the room, while the filter change interval and pressure drop limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The electrical supply of a theatre is arranged differently from that of a ward, and the difference is a transformer. In the usual arrangement the room is fed by an isolated or ungrounded system, in which a transformer separates the mains so that neither of the 2 supply conductors is connected to earth and a single fault to earth cannot complete a circuit through a person. A line isolation monitor watches the leakage to earth and sounds an alarm when it crosses a threshold, and that alarm is a warning that the margin has been used, so equipment is removed until the leak is found. Critical circuits, meaning the table, lights, anesthetic machine, monitors, and life support devices, are usually backed by an uninterruptible power supply, or UPS, and by the emergency generator, and every threshold, battery condition, and generator test record must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Power and gas reach the patient through a clutter of cords and hoses, and that clutter is where the mechanical and electrical hazards of the room meet. A cord across the floor trips a person carrying a sterile tray, a cord under a wheel can be crushed and its conductors exposed, and a cord coiled around a metal rail can overheat. The common errors are the extension lead, the multiple adaptor, and the cord pulled out by its cable instead of its plug, all of which loosen the connection the safety of the device depends on. Every cord, plug, and strain relief is inspected before use, a damaged one is removed at once, and the inspection routine and the acceptance rules for borrowed equipment must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The anesthetic machine stands at the head of the table so that the person watching the patient, the breathing circuit, and the controls never has to turn away. It is connected to pipeline outlets or cylinders, its hoses run without a loop that can be tripped over, and its scavenging system carries waste gas out of the room to a safe discharge. It must be close enough that the circuit reaches the airway without tension, and its wheels are locked, because a machine that rolls during induction pulls the circuit and can dislodge an airway. The check before every case covers the gas supply and its alarms, the vaporizers, the circuit and its seals, the absorber, the ventilator, and the monitoring, and every pressure, flow, concentration, and alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Instrument tables are the working surface of the sterile field, and their arrangement is a matter of reach and gravity. The back table is the large draped surface where instrument sets are opened and laid out in the order they will be used, and the Mayo stand is a small table on a single pedestal brought over the patient for the current step. Because a drape is a barrier only while it is dry, a wet table is a contaminated table, so the tables are placed where the scrub nurse reaches the surgeon in one step and nothing passes over the open wound. The errors are to stack instruments so high that a hand knocks them, to leave a blade facing upward in a tray, or to lay a wet towel at the drape's edge, and the weight a table can carry must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Three smaller items complete the working field: the electrosurgical or diathermy unit, the suction source, and the receptacles that receive what the case discards. The diathermy unit sends a radiofrequency current through an active electrode to cut or coagulate tissue and returns it through a large return electrode on the patient's skin, so its placement and full contact are safety critical. Suction keeps the field clear of blood and irrigation fluid, so a blocked tip, a full canister, or a kinked tube stops the surgeon, and waste receptacles are placed where the discarding hand naturally goes, because a needle dropped into a general bin is an injury waiting to happen. A counts board records the sponges, needles, and instruments in the field, the counts are checked aloud before the wound is closed, and every energy setting, suction pressure, and alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Doors and the number of people in the room matter as much as the ventilation, because people are the largest source of the particles that carry infection. Every person sheds skin scales, and the rate rises with movement and talking, so a room filling with observers defeats the ventilation trying to clear it, while an open door destroys the pressure step and admits corridor air. The door therefore stays closed except for a patient, a trolley, or a needed supply, and the number of people is limited to those with a defined role while movement in and out is minimized. Caps, masks, and theatre clothing reduce shedding and are worn by everyone including visitors, and the traffic rules, dress requirements, and permitted occupancy must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The room is built of materials chosen so that it can be cleaned, and cleaning is a physical process rather than a ritual. Floors are seamless or coved where they meet the wall so dirt cannot collect in a corner, walls are smooth, and the table, booms, and housings are finished so a cloth passes over them without a seam to catch a soiled edge. Cleaning lifts organisms into a cloth or a solution and carries them away, which is why a surface wiped with a dirty cloth is redistributed rather than cleaned, and why the cloth is changed between areas. Between cases the room receives a turn over clean of the table, light handles, arm boards, and floor, and at the end of the day a terminal clean, while the cleaning agent, its dilution, and its contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning carries its own hazards and its own consumable list. Liquid pushed into a switch, an outlet, or the grille of a machine can bridge insulation and destroy the device, and a strong disinfectant can attack the plastic and the labeling of an instrument, so the agent is matched to the surface and a powered device is never sprayed. The consumables are easy to forget: light handle covers, sterile drapes, table pads and straps, gas hoses, suction canisters and liners, diathermy return electrodes, filter elements, and the caps, masks, and gowns worn by the staff. A theatre that runs well keeps a par level of each and checks a written list daily, because a missing handle cover or return electrode stops a case as surely as a broken light, and the storage conditions, expiry dates, and single-use policy must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Behind the daily turn over sits a maintenance program that only technical staff can perform, and that program is what keeps the fixed equipment fixed. Electrical safety is tested on a schedule, the earth path and leakage of each device are measured, and the line isolation monitor is checked against a known leak. The booms and light arms are inspected for ceiling fixings, brakes, and joints; the table for hydraulic leaks and its battery; the ventilation for air change rate and filter loading; and the gas outlets for identity, flow, and leaks. Each test has a pass value and a service interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, a register records what was done and by whom, and the failure mode most easily missed is the intermittent one.

The failure modes of the theatre itself are worth naming in advance, because the response must be decided before the pressure is high. If the table fails with a patient on it, the case is brought to a safe stopping point, the wound is packed and covered, and the patient is moved to a trolley with the position controlled by hand. If the light fails the backup lamp is deployed, if the ventilation alarm sounds the door is closed and the case is stopped if it can be stopped, and if the gas supply or suction fails the machine switches to cylinders and suction changes to a portable pump. If the mains is lost the emergency circuits and the uninterruptible power supply carry the critical devices, and every fallback and its trigger must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol in advance of the emergency.

In a mobile clinic or a frontier hospital the surgical need is the same and the architecture is absent, so the room and its discipline are improvised from different materials. The typical field theatre is a clean room with a table, a lamp on a stand, and sterile drapes processed locally, and its performance depends far more on the behavior of the team than on the building. It gives up the pressure cascade, the filtered unidirectional air, the isolated power, the booms, the adjustable table, the piped gases, and the central sterile supply. It demands instead a set of rules that substitute for the architecture, applied without exception, because there is no monitor to notice when they are broken, and when that discipline holds the field theatre can achieve acceptable surgical infection rates.

The first demand is a room separable into a clean area and a soiled area, and the separation can be as simple as tape on the floor. One end holds the table, the instrument table, the lamp, and the sterile supplies, while the other holds discarded sponges, used instruments, soiled linen, and waste, and the 2 ends never mix. A hand washing point with clean water, soap, and a means of drying stands at the boundary, windows and doors are screened so dust and insects are excluded, and a fan blows from the clean side toward the soiled side rather than across the wound. The room is cleared of clutter, because clutter is a reservoir of dust, and the layout rules for a given facility must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field operating table is often a plain wooden or metal table with a firm top, and because it does not articulate, position is made with pads, sandbags, folded linen, and straps. Trendelenburg position is achieved by propping the foot of the table and securing the patient, and every such improvisation is tested with the patient's weight on it before the case, because a prop that slips under a straining abdomen is a fall. The table is checked for stability, a level top, splinters or sharp edges that would press into skin under anesthesia, and the space beneath it for the surgeon's legs and the suction tubing. Padding is placed at the heels, elbows, shoulders, and head, a table that is too high or too low makes the surgeon work awkwardly, and the stability check and the load the improvised table can bear must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Lighting is the field constraint surgeons notice first, because the illumination of a hospital light cannot be matched by a lamp on a stand. The usual solution is a battery or solar charged light-emitting diode lamp on an adjustable stand, chosen because it runs cool, draws little current, and gives a bright white field from a small head. The stand is weighted so it cannot be knocked onto the patient, the lamp sits above and slightly to the side of the wound so the surgeon's head does not eclipse the field, and a head torch is the usual backup for deep work. The characteristic failure is not a burnout but a slow dimming as the battery discharges, so the charge state and spare battery are checked before the first incision, and the intensity and charging routine must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Sterile supplies are the hardest field constraint, because everything touching the wound must have been processed to a standard the room cannot verify. Where a central sterile services department is absent, instruments are cleaned and then sterilized by boiling in water for a stated time, by steam under pressure in a small autoclave or pressure cooker, or by a chemical agent where the material cannot tolerate heat. Boiling does not destroy every organism and does not leave instruments dry and wrapped, so a boiled instrument is used immediately, while a pressure cooker gives a genuine steam cycle when the air is driven out and the pressure held. The field therefore demands a written processing routine, a log for each cycle, and indicator strips or tape, whose time, temperature, and interpretation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Power in the field comes from a generator, a battery, or a solar array, and none behaves like the mains. A small generator can sag when a large load starts and can carry a waveform the device was not designed for, so sensitive equipment runs from a battery or a voltage stabilizer rather than the generator directly. There is no isolated supply and usually no line isolation monitor, so the defense against electric shock is a residual current device, a good earth connection to a rod driven into the ground, and the discipline of keeping water away from electrical equipment. Gases come from cylinders with a pin index and a regulator that is checked for identity and turned off when not in use, and the electrical arrangements and cylinder handling rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance in the field is a stock list and a habit rather than a service contract, because no engineer will arrive and no spare will be shipped in time. The stock includes spare lamps and charged batteries, spare gas hoses and regulators, spare suction tubing and canisters, seals for the sterilizer, cleaning agent, indicator tape, suture, gloves, and tools to repair a table. The habit is a daily check mirroring the hospital check in fewer steps, and the common error in a low-resource setting is to postpone a small repair until it becomes a large failure, or to fit a part that does not belong because the correct one is unavailable. Equipment is kept under cover, away from dust, moisture, rodents, and direct sun, with a named person responsible for it, and the spare parts list and storage conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The comparison between the 2 versions describes what each buys rather than which is better. The hospital theatre buys its low infection rate with filtered air, pressure control, isolated power, an adjustable table, piped gases, and a central sterile supply, at the cost of capital, energy, and maintenance. The field theatre gives up those systems and buys mobility, low cost, and independence from the grid, at the cost of a far greater reliance on the behavior of the team and the processing of instruments. The hospital version can fail in a way nobody notices, such as a loaded filter or a drifted pressure, while the field version fails visibly, such as a lamp that dims or a table that rocks, so it demands more discipline per case and not less.

To summarize, an operating theatre is a machine for controlling contamination and for holding a patient safely while the body is opened, and its fixed equipment serves those 2 purposes rather than decorating the room. The zones and the sterile field define where clean ends and dirty begins, the table positions the patient, the lights and booms bring light and services to the field, and the ventilation, the pressure step, the isolated supply, and the traffic rules keep the environment from loading the wound. The hospital version does this with architecture that must be maintained and monitored, while the field version gives up the architecture and substitutes discipline, a charged lamp, a stable table, a written processing routine, and a controlled room. In both settings the operator check, the cleaning, the consumable list, and the maintenance register are the parts no purchase order includes, and they decide whether the room helps the patient or harms the patient.

# Chapter 38 — Anesthesia Machines and Monitoring

Anesthesia is a controlled and reversible unconsciousness, and the machine that produces it mixes gases and moves them. A liquid agent evaporates into a carrier gas, and the concentration of that vapor produces unconsciousness, so the machine must make a mixture of known composition and move it into the lungs. Gases flow only when a pressure difference pushes them from a higher pressure to a lower one, so the compressed supply, the regulator, the needle valve, and the flowmeter create and measure that difference. The circuit turns a steady fresh gas flow into the rhythm of breathing, the ventilator replaces the patient's muscles, and the monitor reveals what is happening inside.

Anesthetic gases reach the machine from a pipeline or a cylinder, and the physics of each decides how it behaves as it runs low. A hospital pipeline delivers oxygen, medical air, and nitrous oxide at a working pressure of about 4 bar, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A full oxygen cylinder at room temperature holds gas at about 137 bar, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, so a regulator must lower the pressure first. The gauge reads pressure and not contents, so a cylinder reads full until the charge is nearly spent, and each cylinder connects through a pin index arrangement and a color code that admits only the correct gas. A crossed pipeline can deliver the wrong gas, and the oxygen failure alarm is the last defense, with the characteristic alarm a rising whistle followed by a shut-off of nitrous oxide, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Flowmeters turn a pressure difference into a readable number, because a float in a tapered tube rises until the gap around it passes the chosen flow. The reading is taken at the top of a ball or the widest edge of a bobbin, a convention that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A needle valve controls each gas, and the anesthetist sets the total flow and the oxygen proportion by eye, which is why the flowmeter is among the most misread instruments on the machine. A hypoxic guard links the valves so that the oxygen concentration cannot fall below about 25 per cent, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to reuse the flow settings chosen for one patient on a small child.

A vaporizer converts a liquid agent into a precise concentration of vapor, and its physics is evaporation from a saturated surface. A liquid anesthetic has a vapor pressure at room temperature, and gas passed over it becomes saturated at a concentration set by temperature and by the agent rather than by the flow. To deliver a concentration far below saturation, the vaporizer splits the fresh gas between a vaporizing chamber and a bypass, and a bimetallic strip opens the bypass as evaporation cools the liquid, which is temperature compensation. Each vaporizer is calibrated for one agent only, so its dial means nothing with a different liquid inside, and the wrong agent, an overfilled chamber, or a tipped vaporizer produces a concentration far above the setting. An interlock prevents two agents from being used at once, and a typical dial setting is 1 to 2 per cent, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to fill while the vaporizer is in use.

The circle system lets the patient breathe the same gas more than once, and it exists to save agent, heat, and moisture. Fresh gas enters near the patient, and the exhaled gas passes through an expiratory valve, a canister of carbon dioxide absorbent, a reservoir bag that stores gas between breaths, and an inspiratory valve back to the patient. An adjustable pressure limiting valve, also called the pop-off valve, releases the excess and sets the circuit pressure, and the unidirectional valves are the heart of the design, because a valve that sticks open or is fitted backwards lets exhaled carbon dioxide flow back to the patient. The absorbent, usually soda lime, removes carbon dioxide by a reaction of carbon dioxide, water, and calcium hydroxide that releases heat and leaves calcium carbonate, so the canister grows warm and the granules crumble as they are spent. Moisture is essential to that reaction, so a dried canister passes carbon dioxide, and the characteristic warning is a rising inspired carbon dioxide on the capnograph, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to trust the color of the granules alone.

When the circuit has no absorber it is called a Mapleson arrangement, and its physics is the physics of flow, because fresh gas must sweep the exhaled gas out before the patient breathes it again. The arrangements are lettered from A to F, and the Bain arrangement is a coaxial version in which fresh gas runs down a narrow inner tube to the patient while exhaled gas returns through the outer tube to a reservoir bag and an expiratory valve at the machine end. For spontaneous breathing the fresh gas flow must exceed the peak inspiratory flow, which may reach 20 to 30 liters per minute in an adult, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and for controlled ventilation a flow of about 70 milliliters per kilogram per minute is often quoted, a figure that must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The Bain circuit is light, warm, and easy to position, but it consumes large volumes of fresh gas, and a reversed inner tube turns it into a large dead space whose sign is a rising carbon dioxide and a falling saturation. The common error is to use a low flow suitable for a circle system in a Mapleson arrangement, because the rules of one circuit do not transfer to another.

Waste anesthetic gas leaving the expiratory valve is a hazard to everyone in the room, and scavenging collects it and carries it away. A scavenging interface sits between the circuit and the disposal system and contains a reservoir and relief valves, because the system may pull with active suction or the patient may push gas out faster than the duct can carry it. If the scavenging hose kinks or the vacuum fails, the reservoir bag fills and the circuit pressure rises, and the negative pressure relief valve exists so that the patient does not breathe against a suction that is too strong. Chronic exposure of theater staff to volatile agents and to nitrous oxide is associated with headache, fatigue, and reproductive harm, and the common error is to clamp a scavenging hose that keeps falling off.

The integrated ventilator is a machine inside the machine, and it takes over the work of breathing when the patient is paralyzed or deeply anesthetized. Most anesthesia ventilators are driven by compressed gas or by an electric motor and deliver a set volume or a set pressure at a set rate through the same circuit the patient has been breathing from. The direction of the bellows matters, because an ascending bellows rises when it fills while a descending bellows falls by its own weight, so a disconnected circuit can let a descending bellows cycle and look normal. The controls set the tidal volume, the respiratory rate, the ratio of inspiratory to expiratory time, the positive end-expiratory pressure, and the pressure limit, and typical adult values are a tidal volume of 6 to 8 milliliters per kilogram and a rate of 10 to 12 breaths per minute, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The high airway pressure alarm usually means a kink, a cough, secretions, or a stiff lung, while a low pressure alarm means a leak or a disconnection, and the common error is to silence the alarm and continue.

The machine is checked before every case, and the check is a physical examination rather than a ritual. The operator confirms that the cylinders are full and the pipeline hoses are connected, that the flowmeters move, that each vaporizer is filled, seated, and locked, and that the interlock prevents two agents at once. The breathing system is then tested for leaks by occluding the patient end and closing the adjustable pressure limiting valve, and a pressure of about 30 centimeters of water must hold for about 10 seconds, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The test finds the cracked gasket, the worn seal, the loose canister, the split reservoir bag, and the badly seated valve, and it must be repeated after any part of the circuit has been taken apart. The unidirectional valves are inspected, the absorber is checked for fresh granules, the scavenging hose is checked for kinks, the ventilator is cycled against a test lung, and the airway trolley, the suction, the drugs, and the resuscitation equipment are checked as one package.

Capnography is the measurement of carbon dioxide in the exhaled breath, and it reports that the tube is in the trachea, that the circuit is connected, and that the patient is producing carbon dioxide. The sensor works because carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light at a particular wavelength, and the amount absorbed is proportional to the number of molecules in the light path, so a chamber in the gas stream and a detector produce a continuous reading. The waveform has four parts, an inspiratory baseline near zero, a steep expiratory upstroke, an alveolar plateau that ends at the end-tidal value, and an inspiratory downstroke, and the number alone is almost useless without the shape. A tube in the esophagus produces no sustained waveform, a disconnection produces a flat line, and an exhausted absorber produces a baseline that never returns to zero. The end-tidal value is normally a few millimeters of mercury below the arterial value, a difference that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to read a low number as hyperventilation when the sampling line is blocked by water.

Pulse oximetry measures the oxygen carried by hemoglobin, and its physics is the different absorption of light by hemoglobin with and without oxygen bound to it. Oxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more infrared light and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more red light, so a probe that shines both wavelengths through a finger or an ear can calculate a ratio that corresponds to the saturation. The calculation uses only the pulsatile part of the signal, assumed to come from arterial blood, which is why motion, poor perfusion, cold, ambient light, and nail polish corrupt the reading. A saturation below about 90 per cent is a warning that the oxygen content of the blood has fallen sharply, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, yet the device cannot distinguish a patient who is not breathing from one who is breathing well, and the common error is to trust the saturation as a measure of ventilation when it measures oxygenation alone.

The gas analyzer measures the concentration of oxygen and of the volatile agent in inspired and expired gas, and it closes the loop that the flowmeter and the vaporizer dial leave open. A paramagnetic analyzer uses the fact that oxygen is drawn into a magnetic field while most other gases are not, and a fuel cell produces a current proportional to the oxygen it consumes, so each type ages and must be calibrated. The agent channel uses infrared absorption at wavelengths chosen for each agent, and some instruments identify the agent itself, which is how a vaporizer filled with the wrong liquid is detected before the patient is harmed. The characteristic alarms are the low inspired oxygen alarm and the agent concentration alarms, with thresholds that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to treat the analyzer as decoration and rely on the dials alone.

Depth of anesthesia monitoring tries to measure the effect of the drug on the brain rather than the amount of drug in the machine. A processed electroencephalography (EEG) monitor places a few adhesive electrodes on the forehead and reduces the cortical signal into a single index number between about zero and one hundred, with values lower than about 40 suggesting deep anesthesia and values higher than about 60 suggesting awareness, thresholds that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The raw EEG and the trend are more informative than the index, because muscle activity, electrical interference, and the surgical diathermy contaminate the signal, and some drugs including ketamine and nitrous oxide produce unconsciousness with a high index. The monitor is most useful during total intravenous anesthesia and in patients at high risk of awareness, and the common error is to deepen anesthesia to chase a number while the blood pressure falls.

The anesthesia monitor also watches circulation, temperature, and the return of muscle power, and each channel has its own physical principle. The electrocardiography (ECG) electrodes measure the small voltage generated by heart muscle as it depolarizes, so a change in the surgical field or in the depth of anesthesia is seen at once. Blood pressure is measured non-invasively by an oscillating cuff that detects the pulsation of the artery, or invasively by a catheter connected to a fluid column and a transducer that converts pressure into an electrical signal. A neuromuscular monitor stimulates a peripheral nerve and measures the muscle response, and a ratio of the fourth response to the first greater than about 0.9 is needed before safe extubation, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Temperature is measured by a probe in the esophagus, the nasopharynx, or the bladder, and a fall below about 36 degrees Celsius is worth treating, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Anesthetized patients lose heat quickly, and the warming devices that prevent it are as much a part of the machine as the ventilator. Heat leaves the body by radiation, convection, conduction, and evaporation from the wound and from the lungs, and anesthesia removes the normal defenses by dilating the blood vessels and by reducing the shivering response. A forced air warmer blows warm air through a disposable blanket over the patient, a resistive blanket uses electrical current in a carbon-loaded fabric, and a circulating water mattress conducts heat from below, while fluid warmers pass intravenous fluid or blood through a coil in a warm water bath or against a heated plate. A typical target is a fluid temperature near 37 degrees Celsius, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the hazards are a burn, an air embolism from a warmer that was not primed, and a damaged blood product from a heater that is too hot. The characteristic alarm is an over-temperature cutout, and a patient whose temperature rises instead of falls may have malignant hyperthermia, a rare reaction to a volatile agent or to succinylcholine that must be recognized early and treated with the specific drug and with active cooling.

Maintenance is a schedule of small tasks that together prevent most serious failures, and it begins with the daily check and the leak test already described. After each case the surfaces are wiped with the agent the maker approves, the water traps are emptied, the condensate is removed, the soda lime is changed when it is spent, and the breathing circuit, the mask, the filter, and the sampling line are reprocessed or discarded according to their labeling. Filters, circuits, reservoir bags, valve discs, gaskets, seals, and temperature probes are consumables with a stated life, and their replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a reused filter that has been wetted or autoclaved no longer filters. At intervals set by the maker, the vaporizers are serviced, the oxygen analyzer cell is replaced, the gas analyzer is calibrated with a known gas, the relief valves are tested, the battery is replaced, and the electrical safety of the machine is verified. The service record is part of the equipment, and the common error is to clean a machine with a dripping cloth so that fluid enters the electronics or the flow sensors.

The serious failures of the anesthesia machine fall into a small number of families, and naming them makes them recognizable. A failure of oxygen supply, from an empty cylinder, a closed valve, a crossed pipeline, or a plant shutdown, leads to a hypoxic mixture and a falling saturation, and the oxygen failure alarm gives the operator seconds to act. A failure of the circuit, whether a disconnection, a kink, a stuck valve, or an exhausted absorber, leads to a rising carbon dioxide or to no ventilation at all, and capnography shows it first. A failure of the vaporizer, from overfilling, tipping, wrong agent, or a defective temperature compensator, leads to a concentration far from the dial, and a failure of the ventilator requires immediate hand ventilation with a self-inflating bag. Fires and burns occur in an oxygen-rich atmosphere when the diathermy, a laser, or a spark meets alcohol-based skin preparation that has not dried, so the anesthetist must announce every change and keep the record in real time.

The field variant begins with the draw-over vaporizer, which works on the opposite principle to the hospital machine because the patient generates the flow. The patient breathes in through a low-resistance vaporizer and a one-way valve, drawing room air across the liquid agent, so no compressed gas and no electricity are required and the whole apparatus fits in a case. A self-inflating bag can be added to assist ventilation, and oxygen from a concentrator or a small cylinder can be enriched into the inhaled gas, but the concentration depends on the patient's minute volume, the temperature, the agent, and the altitude. The output is therefore less predictable than that of a plumbed machine, so the dial setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the hazards are hypoxemia, overdose when a high minute volume pulls more vapor than expected, and hypothermia from cold dry gas. None of these is announced by an alarm because there is no gas analyzer and usually no capnography, and the common error is to leave the patient unattended while the surgeon works.

Oxygen in the field comes from a concentrator, from cylinders, or from a small plant, and the concentrator manufactures the gas from room air. It works by pressure swing adsorption, in which air is compressed and passed through a bed of zeolite that adsorbs nitrogen in preference to oxygen, so the gas leaving the bed is enriched to about 90 to 95 per cent oxygen, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Two beds alternate so that the flow is continuous, and a compressor, a set of valves, intake filters, and a sieve bed are the parts that fail, usually because of dust, heat, and humidity. A concentrator delivers a limited flow, often 5 to 10 liters per minute, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it cannot drive a ventilator or fill a cylinder because it produces low pressure, which is a dangerous misunderstanding.

Where no machine exists at all, anesthesia is produced by drugs rather than by gas, and ketamine has carried most of the surgery performed in frontier clinics. Ketamine produces unconsciousness and profound analgesia while preserving the patient's own breathing and airway reflexes more than most agents, and it is given intravenously or intramuscularly at a dose that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Its limitations include a rise in blood pressure and heart rate, excessive secretions, emergence delirium, and the possibility of laryngospasm or vomiting, so a drying drug is often given first and suction and an airway kit must be within reach. Spinal anesthesia, regional blocks, and local infiltration are the other pillars of the field technique, and in all of them the operator must be trained and must stay with the patient, because there is no ventilator, no gas analyzer, and no alarm to call for help.

Monitoring in the field is reduced to the observations a trained person can make with the senses and with a few battery-powered devices. A precordial stethoscope taped over the upper chest or the sternal notch carries the breath sounds, the heart sounds, and the movement of air, and it is the cheapest continuous monitor in existence. A colorimetric carbon dioxide detector placed between the tube and the breathing bag changes color when carbon dioxide is present, because a pH-sensitive indicator reacts with the gas, so it confirms that the tube is in the trachea, though gastric contents can confuse it. A battery-powered pulse oximeter with a reusable probe gives the oxygen saturation and the pulse, and a manual blood pressure cuff, a watch, a thermometer, and a urine collection bag complete the set. The operator must record the observations at a fixed interval, usually every 5 minutes during a general anesthetic, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the trend is more informative than any single value.

The field equipment survives by simple maintenance and by planning for the part that will fail next. The draw-over vaporizer is drained, cleaned, dried, and stored upright with its filler capped, and the concentrator filters are cleaned after every dusty day and replaced at the maker's interval. Oxygen cylinders are checked for the hydrostatic requalification date fixed by national rules, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a cylinder is stored upright, secured, away from grease and flame, and never left with a regulator attached in transit. Batteries are charged whenever power is available, and the spare parts that matter most are the seals, the breathing tubes, the valve discs, the oxygen tubing, the fuses, and a spare pulse oximeter probe.

The comparison between the two versions is the heart of the matter, and the field version gives up a great deal and demands a great deal in return. The hospital machine gives continuous measurement of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and agent, a ventilator of known performance, a scavenging system, and a maintenance organization behind it, while the field kit gives up all of that for portability and independence from pipelines and mains power. What it demands instead is a trained provider who never leaves the patient, a disciplined oxygen supply, a pre-use check performed from memory with the same care as a printed list, and a plan for the three emergencies of apnea, hypoxemia, and cardiac arrest. The measure of safety is therefore not the amount of equipment present but the presence of a trained person who understands the physics, watches the patient, and expects the failure before it happens.

To summarize, the anesthesia machine is a gas mixer, a vaporizer, a breathing circuit, and a ventilator that together produce a controlled concentration of anesthetic vapor and move it in and out of the lungs. The gas arrives from a pipeline or a cylinder, the flowmeter proportions it, the vaporizer adds the agent, the circuit conserves it, the absorber removes the carbon dioxide, and the scavenging carries the waste away. The monitors are the other half of the machine, because capnography confirms the tube and the circuit, pulse oximetry follows the oxygen, the gas analyzer confirms the mixture, and the processed electroencephalogram estimates the depth. Every number named in this chapter, whether a pressure, a flow, a concentration, a temperature, or an alarm threshold, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The machine must be checked before every case, the circuit must hold pressure, and the consumables that filter, seal, and sample must be replaced on schedule rather than when they visibly fail. In the field, the draw-over vaporizer, the oxygen concentrator, the colorimetric detector, the pulse oximeter, and the drugs replace the plumbed machine, and what they demand instead is a trained provider who stays at the head of the patient and expects the failure before it happens.

# Chapter 39 — Surgical Instruments

A surgical instrument is a hand tool that concentrates the force of an arm onto a few square millimeters of tissue, and almost every instrument on a theater tray is one of a few simple machines. A scalpel is a wedge, a scissors is two wedges on a first-class lever, a hemostatic clamp is a spring lever with a ratchet, a forceps is a pair of pincers, and a retractor is a lever that holds tissue under tension. Each design answers the same questions: where the force enters, where the pivot sits, how the grip is shaped, and what the working end must do to the tissue it meets. A listener who sees instruments as levers, wedges, and springs will understand why a dull blade tears, why a long-handled scissors needs less effort, and why a ratchet that has lost its bite fails suddenly.

Every hinged instrument reads from the hand outward, with a handle or rings, a shank, a joint, and a jaw or blade. The handle is shaped for the glove and sets how much torque the wrist can deliver, and its flat sides stop it turning when it is wet. The shank sets the length of the lever, so a long shank gives reach into a deep cavity but also a long bending moment, which is why the longest instruments bend first at the joint. The joint, called the box lock, is the pivot and the weakest point, and it is where blood, saline, and cleaning fluid collect and where corrosion begins. The jaw or blade is the working end, and its shape is a compromise between grip and injury, sharpness and strength, and delicacy and durability. Fatigue and corrosion both start at the box lock and the tip, so the operator must inspect both before use, because a crack at the box lock can open under load and leave half of a clamp inside a wound.

The metal decides how an instrument behaves, and most surgical steel is a compromise between hardness and corrosion resistance. Stainless steel resists rust because chromium forms a thin oxide layer that seals the surface, and that layer repairs itself only when the metal is clean and exposed to air. Harder grades hold a keener edge but contain less chromium and corrode more easily, while softer grades resist staining but lose their edge sooner. Instruments are commonly made from a hardenable grade for cutting edges and a more corrosion-resistant grade for clamps and handles, and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) designation is the reliable way to know what has been supplied. Titanium is lighter, nonmagnetic, and highly corrosion resistant, which is why it is chosen for neurosurgical and ophthalmic work and for patients with a nickel allergy, but it is softer at the edge and easily scratched. Tungsten carbide inserts give a hard, long-lasting jaw, but the insert is bonded into the steel and can loosen or fall out, so a loose insert must be found before the wound is closed and every sterilization temperature and cycle named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The scalpel is the sharpest tool on the tray, and its physics is the physics of pressure, because cutting requires a pressure greater than the tissue's own strength and pressure equals force divided by area, so a blade ground to a very thin edge needs a light touch while a dull blade needs a heavy push. The handle is numbered by size and blade family, and the blade is numbered by shape, so the operator chooses a shape for the task rather than the largest blade available, with a small handle held like a pen for fine work and a large handle in the palm for long incisions. The blade is fitted with a needle holder and never with the fingers, must seat until it clicks, and must be checked with a gentle tug, because the loading motion is the commonest cause of a scalpel injury to the operator. The characteristic warning of a scalpel is not an alarm but a change in feel, since the blade begins to skate, the incision becomes ragged, and more force is required. The common error is to pass the instrument or discard it with a used blade still on the handle, and the safety rule is that blades are loaded and removed with a holder and dropped immediately into a sharps container.

Scissors cut by shear, and the two blades act as opposing wedges that slide past each other rather than meeting edge to edge. The length of the handles relative to the blades sets the mechanical advantage, so short blades on long handles multiply the force of the hand and give fine control, while long blades on short handles cut thick tissue in fewer strokes. A curved blade follows a plane of dissection without lifting the tissue, a straight blade cuts on a flat surface, and the tips are sharp on both blades, sharp on one and blunt on the other, or blunt on both. A suture scissors has short blades, one blunt or notched tip, and a shape designed to catch a thread without cutting the tissue beneath it, while a tissue scissors has longer, sharper blades and should never be used on suture. Cutting suture with tissue scissors notches the edge, and cutting tissue with suture scissors crushes rather than divides it, so the two instruments must not be substituted for each other. The characteristic warning of a scissors that is failing is that it chews, because the blades no longer meet along their whole length, and the common error is to force it through material heavier than it was designed for, which springs the blades apart permanently.

Forceps are pincers whose physics is the first-class lever, with the pivot at the box lock and the hand closing the shanks toward each other. A non-toothed forceps has ridges, a matte finish, or fenestrations that grip by friction over a broad area and is called atraumatic because the tissue it holds is not punctured, while a toothed forceps has small interlocking points that bite into tissue and prevent slipping. Toothed patterns are described by the arrangement of the teeth, so a 2 by 3 pattern and a 1 by 2 pattern are different instruments with different grip and different injury, and they are used on skin and fascia where grip matters more than gentleness. A vessel, a nerve, a bowel wall, or a delicate organ held in a toothed forceps is likely to be crushed or perforated, and the injury may not be obvious when it is made. The characteristic warning of tissue injury is a white or dusky mark that does not refill when the forceps are released, and the common error is to grip harder when tissue slips, when the answer is a better instrument rather than a stronger hand.

A hemostatic clamp is a spring lever with a ratchet, and the ratchet turns a squeeze of the hand into a lock that holds by itself. The shanks act as springs, the box lock is the pivot, and the jaws close as the ratchet catches one notch after another, so the number and spacing of the teeth set how tightly the jaws close. The familiar names describe different jobs: the mosquito is a very fine clamp for the smallest vessels, the Kelly and Crile carry grooves on the distal and the whole jaw, and the Rochester-Carmalt is a heavy clamp with long grooves for large vessels. A straight clamp is used on a surface, while a curved clamp reaches around a vessel or into a deep cavity where the tip must follow a curve. The Kocher carries teeth at the tip that penetrate and hold tissue, the Allis carries interlocking teeth that grasp a mass of tissue firmly, and the Babcock carries smooth fenestrated jaws that hold bowel or a tube without crushing it. A towel clip holds drapes either by piercing or without piercing, so the choice must match the surface beneath. The characteristic warning of a failing clamp is the click that no longer locks or a jaw that no longer meets at the tip, and the common errors are to use a penetrating clamp on bowel and to leave a clamp on a pedicle until the tissue beneath dies.

A retractor holds tissue away from the field, and its physics is tension and the distribution of pressure, because the pull on the handle is spread over the area of the blade. A broad blade therefore produces less pressure on any one point than a narrow blade carrying the same pull, which is why blade shape matters as much as the strength of the arm. Hand-held retractors are simple levers, a blade on a handle, sometimes with a lip or a rake of teeth to stop it slipping, and a malleable retractor can be bent by hand to fit a cavity. Self-retaining retractors turn tension into a frame, using a screw, a ratchet, or a spring to hold the blades apart without an assistant, in patterns for the abdomen, chest, spine, neck, and limb, and they free a pair of hands and give steady exposure. They apply force for as long as they remain in place, so prolonged retraction of the shoulder can stretch the brachial plexus and prolonged retraction of the abdomen can impair breathing and reduce the return of blood to the heart. The characteristic warning is a pale tissue, a changed pulse in the limb, or a change on the monitor as the retractor tightens, and the common error is to retract harder to see better instead of repositioning or releasing the blade.

The needle holder is a lever that grips a needle and transmits the turning force of the wrist to it, and it often decides whether a suture is placed cleanly. Its jaws are cross-hatched or fitted with tungsten carbide inserts to grip a smooth steel needle, and its ratchet or spring holds the needle while the surgeon regrips, with a ratcheted holder locking at one of several tensions and a spring-handled holder releasing as soon as the hand relaxes. The needle should be grasped at the junction of its shaft and curve, or across its middle, so that the curve follows the rotation of the wrist and the needle enters at right angles and leaves by the same arc. Grasping a needle at its point dulls the point, and grasping it at the very end of the curve gives no leverage and bends it with the first push. A needle holder is not a cutter or a hammer, and using it for those jobs burrs the jaws and ruins the grip on which every future suture depends. The characteristic warning of a failing holder is the needle that turns inside the jaws or springs free at the moment of the push, and the common error is to force a needle through tissue tougher than the needle is designed for.

A suction tip removes blood, irrigation, and smoke by negative pressure, and its behavior is set by the physics of flow through a tube. Flow rises steeply as the bore widens, because resistance falls with the fourth power of the radius, so a small increase in tip diameter gives a large increase in what it can remove, while a partial blockage by clot reduces the flow far more than it appears to. A large single-opening tip moves fluid fast where the field is wet, and a thumb hole lets the operator break the vacuum without lifting the tip from tissue. A fenestrated tip draws through many small holes behind a shield so that soft tissue cannot be pulled into one opening, and it is the safer choice around bowel or a graft, while a very fine tip blocks easily. The hazards are the tissue drawn into the opening and injured, the graft or nerve sucked against the tip, and the blood removed faster than it can be replaced. The characteristic warning of a suction problem is a change in its sound, a sudden silence, a hiss at a loose connection, or a canister reaching its limit, and the common error is to use the tip as a retractor or a probe.

Beside the cutting, grasping, and holding instruments is a group of quiet tools whose purpose is to feel, to part, and to guide. A probe is a rigid rod that transmits the sense of touch from tip to hand, so the operator can feel a stone, a tract, or a mass without seeing it, and a probe too flexible or too thick destroys the information it carries. A grooved director is a probe with a channel that guides a knife or scissors into a stricture so the cut follows the groove, and a dissector, a periosteal elevator, and a curette are variations on a shaped tip that follows a plane or scrapes a surface without cutting across it. A skin hook uses a very small sharp point and tension to hold skin without crushing it. The characteristic warning of a probe is the false passage, because a tip pushed with force can create the very channel it was meant to find, and the common error is to push instead of letting it follow the natural line of the tissue.

Surgical instruments are organized into sets, and the set is a device in its own right because it decides what the team can do without leaving the room. A basic set holds a scalpel handle and blades, a needle holder, a scissors, toothed and non-toothed forceps, several hemostatic clamps, and towel clips, while a major abdominal set adds long clamps, deep retractors, large scissors, suction tips, and a range of needle holders. Each specialty adds its own: vascular fine clamps and scissors, orthopedic holding and bone-cutting tools, obstetric long curved clamps and cord scissors, and ophthalmic, neurologic, and pediatric sets scaled to the tissue and the patient. Set contents are standardized and the tray is laid out in the same order every time so a missing item is noticed at a glance, and heavy instruments are never stored on top of fine ones because they bend them. The characteristic alarm of a surgical set is not a sound but a number, the instrument count, taken before the case, before a cavity is closed, before the skin is closed, and at the end, and a count that does not match is treated as a retained instrument until it is proved otherwise. The common error is to add an instrument to the field without telling the person who keeps the count, and every count threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Inspection is the operator's own check, and it must be done by the person who will use the instrument rather than assumed from the packaging. The first check is alignment, because the jaws of a clamp must meet along their whole length, a scissors must close smoothly to its tips, and a needle holder must grip a needle without the needle turning. The second check is the ratchet, which must lock at every tooth and release without sticking, because a ratchet that has lost a notch will open under the tension of a pedicle.
