The third check is for corrosion, and rust shows as a brown or black stain and pitting as small dark craters, either of which weakens the metal and shelters organisms from cleaning, so a stained instrument is removed from service rather than merely wiped. The fourth check is the box lock and screw, which must be tight but not frozen, because a loose screw lets the jaws wobble and a frozen joint hides debris, and the fifth is the cutting edge, tested on suture rather than on a finger. The characteristic warning of a hidden defect is an instrument that feels different, clicks at the wrong point, or shows rust inside the box lock, and the common error is to accept an instrument without looking at it, because packaging says nothing about alignment, sharpness, or a crack.

Lubrication and storage are the habits that decide how long a set lasts, and both are about water and friction. A film of the approved lubricant displaces water from the box lock and screw and lowers the friction of the joint, and the maker's instructions decide which lubricant may be used and which sterilization methods it can survive, while an unapproved oil attracts debris, may soften plastic, and can carry contamination into the joint. Instruments are stored dry, with ratchets open, on racks or trays that let air reach every surface, because an instrument closed on its own ratchet traps moisture and blood in the box lock. Heavy instruments are stored below fine ones, and fine instruments rest on a soft mat rather than bare metal, because the vibration of handling is enough to blunt a delicate edge. Every sterilization cycle, temperature, and holding time referred to in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a lubricant, a mat, or a packaging material can invalidate a cycle that looks correct, and the common error is to lubricate a stiff joint heavily when the correct remedy is cleaning and repair.

Reprocessing begins at the point of use, because blood and saline that dry on an instrument form a film that protects organisms and corrodes the steel. The instrument is wiped or rinsed of gross soil as soon as it leaves the field, kept moist during transport, and never left to soak in saline, because chloride ions pit stainless steel and the pits deepen with every cycle. In the reprocessing area, which in a larger hospital is the central sterile services department (CSSD), instruments are opened, disassembled where possible, and cleaned in an enzymatic or alkaline detergent chosen for surgical instruments, and the box lock, ratchet, and lumen of a hollow instrument need a brush because fluid alone does not reach them. An ultrasonic cleaner does the work a brush cannot, because sound waves create tiny bubbles that collapse against the surface and lift debris from joints and serrations, and it works only when the instruments are open and the solution is fresh, after which the instruments are rinsed with soft or deionized water because tap water leaves mineral deposits that stain the surface. Any instrument that fails inspection is set aside for repair or disposal before it is packed, since a defect that is packed becomes a defect that is used, and every cycle parameter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to soak instruments in a chlorine solution that is not compatible with stainless steel, producing pitting that appears weeks later on a tray that was thought to be clean.

The failures of surgical instruments fall into a few families, and naming them makes them recognizable before they reach a patient. Corrosion, from blood, saline, a chlorine soak, or a humid store, weakens the metal and shelters organisms, showing first as staining and then as pitting and cracking. Fatigue is the slow cracking of metal under repeated stress, and it begins where stress concentrates, at the box lock and at any scratch, so a clamp used thousands of times can fail with no visible warning. Deformation is the bending or springing of a shank or jaw by a force greater than the design allows, and a sprung instrument stays out of alignment even if it is straightened. Wear is the loss of the edge or the grip, and it shows as a scissors that chews, a needle holder that lets the needle turn, and a forceps whose teeth no longer interlock, and the consequences are a fragment left in the wound, a vessel that bleeds again, a needle dropped in the field, or tissue crushed beyond its design. The characteristic warning is a small click and a change in the feel of the tool, and the common error is to keep a favorite instrument in service long after it has failed its inspection.

The field version begins with a short list, because a mobile clinic cannot carry a theater's worth of trays and does not need them. A workable field set is a scalpel handle with a small stock of blades, 1 or 2 needle holders, 4 to 6 hemostatic clamps in straight and curved patterns, a toothed forceps, a non-toothed forceps, one scissors for tissue and one for suture, 2 or 3 retractors, a grooved director or probe, a suction tip if suction is available, and a handful of towel clips. This list covers the incision, the control of bleeding, the retraction of tissue, the placement of a suture, and the removal of a specimen, with fewer choices rather than fewer possibilities. What the field set gives up is the specialty tray, the self-retaining retractor that holds exposure without hands, the tungsten carbide insert that keeps an edge for years, the powered suction that clears a deep field, and the count system that catches a missing item before the wound is closed. What it demands instead is that the operator inspect every instrument before every case, sharpen or replace what is dull, and clean and sterilize the whole set without a central department, and it also demands disciplined improvisation, since a clean metal spoon can retract, sterile tubing can drain, a bent wire can probe, and strong clean thread can suture, but only when the substitute can be cleaned and will not break or leave a fragment. The characteristic warning in the field is unchanged, a clamp that does not lock and a scissors that chews, but there is no spare tray to reach for, and the common error is to begin with an instrument known to be doubtful because the patient is already asleep.

Sterilization in the field is a cycle that must be measured rather than believed, and every boiling time, pressure cooker temperature, and holding time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Boiling kills most organisms when the instruments are fully submerged and the water has boiled for the full time the protocol requires, and a lid keeps the heat in while a suitable additive may raise the temperature only if the protocol allows it. A pressure cooker sterilizes by steam under pressure above the boiling point of water, and its time begins only when the pressure is reached and the air has been driven out, because trapped air keeps the temperature below the target even though the gauge looks right. A hospital steam autoclave commonly runs at 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 minutes or at 121 degrees Celsius for about 15 minutes, and a field pressure cooker reaches about 121 degrees Celsius in roughly 15 to 20 minutes, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Drying matters as much as sterilization in a humid climate, because a wet instrument in a closed box rusts overnight, so the set is dried and given a thin film of approved lubricant, and scissors are sharpened only along the bevel on a fine stone because sharpening the flat side destroys the two wedges that must slide past each other. The common error is to shorten the boiling time when the queue of cases is long, because the number of organisms on a used instrument is not reduced by the hurry.

The comparison between the two versions is the heart of the matter, and the field set is not a lesser hospital set but a different instrument with different rules. The hospital version offers specialty trays, the best available alloys, self-retaining retractors, powered suction, a central reprocessing department with validated cycles, and a count checked several times around every operation. The field version gives up that depth of choice, that quality of steel, that freedom of the surgeon's hands, and that systematic accounting, and it accepts a set small enough to be carried in a bag and reprocessed in a pot. What it demands in return is an operator who knows why a clamp locks, why a scissors chews, and why a needle turns in a worn jaw, and who inspects the set with the attention a hospital gives to a printed cycle record, and whether the available instruments are good enough for the operation proposed. The measure of safety is not the number of instruments on the tray but the condition of each one, the discipline of the count, and the operator's willingness to reject a tool that is not fit.

To summarize, a surgical instrument is a simple machine, a wedge, a lever, a spring, or a pair of pincers, shaped so that the force of a hand becomes a controlled effect on tissue. Scalpels cut by concentrated pressure, scissors shear, forceps grip by friction or teeth, clamps lock with a ratchet, retractors hold tissue under tension, needle holders turn a needle through an arc, and suction tips move fluid by negative pressure through a bore whose flow depends steeply on its width. The metal matters as much as the shape, because hardness and corrosion resistance pull in opposite directions, and because fatigue and corrosion begin at the box lock and the tip and end an instrument's life without a visible warning. The safety of the tray depends on inspection for alignment, ratchet function, corrosion, and sharpness, on cleaning that reaches the joints and lumens, on drying and lubrication before storage, and on a count repeated until it matches. Every temperature, cycle, holding time, and count threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because an instrument is only as safe as the process that prepared it. In the field, a short set covers most surgery and gives up the specialty tray, the fine alloy, and the mechanical retractor for portability and independence, and what it demands instead is an operator who inspects every tool before every case, sterilizes by a measured cycle, and refuses to operate with an instrument that is not fit.

# Chapter 40 — Energy Devices

Surgery has always used a blade, and the energy device is the blade replaced by heat, by vibration, or by light. Radiofrequency electrosurgery passes an alternating current through the body and lets the resistance of the tissue turn that current into heat. Ultrasonic devices vibrate a blade tens of thousands of times each second so that friction generates heat at the point of contact. Lasers deliver light whose energy is absorbed by water or by pigment inside cells, and argon plasma coagulation carries current through a channel of ionized gas. A listener who understands where the heat is made, and how deeply it reaches, will recognize the moment when a device begins to injure rather than to treat.

Electrosurgery begins with an alternating current whose frequency is far above the range that nerves and muscles can follow. Tissue conducts because it holds dissolved salts and water, so a current passed through it stimulates a nerve until the frequency rises above roughly 100 kilohertz, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. At that point the ions can no longer follow the reversal, the stimulation disappears, and the only useful effect left is heating where the tissue resists the current. A modern generator therefore produces about 300 to 500 kilohertz, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Heating depends on current density, so a small electrode boils the water inside cells while a large electrode barely warms the skin, and this one idea explains the active tip, the return pad, and most electrosurgical burns.

In the monopolar configuration the current enters at a small active electrode, crosses the patient, and leaves through a large return electrode stuck to the skin. The active tip concentrates the current until the cells beneath it explode into steam, while the dispersive pad spreads the same current over a wide area so the skin stays cool. The current follows the path of least resistance rather than a straight line, so the pad must lie on a large muscle mass, clean and dry, with no hair, moisture, or bony point beneath it, and the exact placement and the adhesive supplied by the maker must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is the return electrode monitoring alarm, which measures the impedance of the pad circuit and stops the output when the pad is loose or missing, and the common operator error is to press a loose pad down instead of replacing it.

The generator shapes the current into two waveforms, and the difference between them is the difference between cutting and coagulation. A continuous cutting waveform with moderate voltage boils the water in cells and divides tissue along a clean line with little charring. An interrupted coagulation waveform leaves pauses for the tissue to cool, so proteins denature and shrink into a coagulum that seals small vessels, but the higher peak voltage needed spreads heat more deeply and less predictably. Typical settings lie between about 30 and 80 watts for cutting and between about 30 and 60 watts for coagulation, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to raise the power whenever bleeding obscures the field, because more power rarely improves a seal and often deepens the injury.

The bipolar configuration puts both poles into one instrument, so no return pad and no long path through the body are needed. The surgeon holds a forceps whose two insulated jaws carry the active current and the return, and current passes only through the small volume of tissue grasped between them. Because the path is short and the tissue is thin, the voltage is lower than in monopolar surgery and thermal spread beyond the jaws is limited to a millimeter or two, a distance that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, which makes bipolar forceps suitable near nerves, in the pediatric patient, in the patient with a pacemaker, and inside the laparoscope. The characteristic alarm is the impedance alarm that sounds when the jaws are shorted by a metal clip or by saline, and the common error is to grasp too much tissue so that only the outer surface seals and bleeding resumes when the jaws are released.

The generator is a box of power electronics that turns mains current into a controlled radiofrequency output, and everything the surgeon holds hangs from it. A handpiece cable carries current to the pencil, which is activated by a button or by a foot switch while a tone tells the whole team that energy is being delivered. The active electrode is a small metal tip, and the choice of blade, ball, needle, or loop decides whether the current is concentrated on a line, a point, or a surface. Pads, tips, pencils, cables, foot switches, and cords are consumables with a stated life, and their replacement intervals and reuse rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to run a handpiece cable under a trolley wheel and damage the conductor invisibly until a patient is burned.

The complications of electrosurgery are variations on one theme, which is current concentrated where it should not be. A return pad burn occurs when poor adhesion, fluid, hair, or a fold in the drape reduces the pad area, so current leaves through a small patch of skin and heats it. An accidental contact burn is classically caused by the pencil left resting on the patient or on a drape, because the weight of the handpiece can press the activation button, and a burn may also appear at an electrocardiography electrode that offers an unintended return path. The characteristic warning is often the smell of burning rather than any alarm, and the common error is to leave an active pencil on the sterile field without an insulated holster to hold it.

Fire is the most catastrophic complication, and it occurs because an oxygen-rich atmosphere turns an ordinary spark into an ignition source. The ignition triangle needs fuel, oxygen, and heat, and all three are routinely present: a drape or an alcohol-based preparation that has not dried, oxygen from a face mask or an open airway, and the active tip, a laser, or a hot wire, while nitrous oxide supports combustion as readily as oxygen. An alcohol preparation is the commonest fuel because its vapor is heavier than air and can pool under the drapes, so the preparation must be allowed to dry completely before the drapes are applied. When an airway fire occurs, the response is to stop the gas, remove the burning material, flood the area with saline, and secure the airway, because the injury is a burn of the trachea and not only of the surface, and the oxygen concentration used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Electrosurgery can interfere with implanted electronics because the device may read the radiofrequency current as the heart's own electrical signal. A pacemaker may inhibit its output while energy is applied, or it may sense nothing and pace at its own rate, which is usually harmless. An implanted defibrillator may read the interference as a lethal rhythm and deliver a shock, or it may be reprogrammed, so the device must be interrogated before and after the operation according to a plan made with the device clinic. Bipolar current is safer because it is confined between the jaws, pad placement must keep the current path away from the device and its leads, and the exact magnet behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to assume that a modern device is safe.

The laparoscopic route adds a hazard with no open-surgery equivalent, because the current may travel where the surgeon cannot see it. A monopolar instrument passed through a metal cannula is insulated, and a pinhole, a crack from repeated sterilization, or a break at the tip lets current leak to the cannula and from there to the bowel or the abdominal wall. Current can also be induced in a nearby cannula by capacitive coupling, or pass by direct coupling into another metal instrument that burns the tissue at its far end. These injuries happen outside the field of view and appear days later as a perforated bowel, so every laparoscopic electrode must be inspected with a magnifier under good light before it is passed, and the inspection standard and replacement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The generator performs a self-test each time it is switched on and refuses to deliver energy if a circuit fault, a missing pad, or an internal error is found. The display shows the selected mode, the power, and the pad status, and a return electrode monitoring alarm, a pad contact quality alarm, or an error code stops the case and must be understood rather than bypassed. A biomedical technician should measure the output into a test load, check the calibration of the displayed power against that measurement, verify the alarm thresholds, and perform an electrical safety test on the chassis and the patient circuit. The acceptable output range, the alarm thresholds, and the test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to keep using a generator whose display flickers or whose tone has become unreliable.

Much of electrosurgical maintenance is the inspection and testing of insulation, because the reusable active electrode, the laparoscopic instrument, and the handpiece cable all carry high voltage. A visual inspection with magnification under bright light finds the cracks, the charred spots, the pinched segments, and the exposed conductor that no electrical test can see. An insulation tester applies a high voltage between the conductor and a conductive probe moved along the shaft, a leakage current above the limit set by the maker condemns the instrument, and a continuity test confirms that the electrode and the cord conduct. The instruments that pass are stored straight or loosely coiled, never bent sharply, and never sterilized in a way the maker forbids, because heat and chemicals degrade insulation over time, and the acceptable leakage current, the test voltage, and the test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of electrosurgery follow the label and the instructions of the maker rather than habit. Return pads are single-use and must never be re-stuck, re-trimmed, or reused even when they look intact, because their adhesive and their conductive gel are designed for one application. Many tip electrodes and cables are reusable and must be cleaned of charred tissue with the approved method, dried, and inspected, and some tips can be steam sterilized while others cannot, because a tip whose insulation has been softened by the wrong process is a hazard. A non-stick coating that has worn away should be replaced rather than scraped with a blade, and the cleaning agent, the disinfection method, the sterilization cycle, and the permitted number of reuses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to stack hot electrodes so that the tips bend or the insulation is scored.

Ultrasonic surgery replaces electrical current with mechanical vibration, and its physics is the physics of friction. A stack of piezoelectric crystals expands and contracts when an alternating voltage at about 55,500 hertz is applied, a frequency that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The vibration travels along a metal blade whose tip moves a few tens of micrometers, and pressing that blade against tissue raises the temperature to between about 50 and 100 degrees Celsius, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, which is enough to denature protein and to seal small vessels without boiling water or charring. The same blade cuts when it is advanced and coagulates when it is held still, and because no electrical current passes through the patient the device avoids return pad burns and most interference with implanted devices.

The ultrasonic handpiece demands care in its assembly and its blade. The blade is tightened with the torque wrench the maker supplies, because a blade that is loose will not transmit the vibration and may overheat at the junction, while a blade that is overtightened can strip the threads. The blade is a consumable with a rated life measured in hours of activation or in numbers of procedures, and a worn blade loses its edge and its sealing ability, with the replacement interval and the activation limit confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The tip stays hot after the generator stops, so it must be placed in its holder and never laid on a drape or on the patient, and irrigation through or beside the blade cools the tip and clears the field. The characteristic alarm is the handpiece error or blade fault alarm, which appears when the blade is loose, when the connection is wet, or when the load is outside the expected range, and the common error is to clean a hot blade with a wet cloth, which warps it.

Vessel-sealing devices fuse the walls of a vessel into a permanent seal using pressure and heat. One jaw vibrates or delivers a bipolar current while the other applies pressure, and the combination melts the collagen and elastin in the vessel wall so that the two walls fuse together. The strength of a seal is described by the burst pressure the maker claims, often several times the systolic blood pressure, and the width of the seal and the largest vessel it can close, commonly up to about 7 millimeters in diameter, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A feedback system ends the cycle when the seal is complete and the generator sounds a distinct tone to mark the moment, but a seal that looks complete may fail later, so a large artery or a vessel under high pressure still needs a suture or a clip, and the common error is to release the jaws before the cycle tone sounds.

A laser is light that is monochromatic, coherent, and collimated, which means a single wavelength with all its waves in step, traveling in a narrow beam that spreads very little. Stimulated emission inside a medium causes each photon to trigger more photons of the same wavelength and direction, so the medium rather than the machine sets the wavelength, and the wavelength decides how deeply the light penetrates and what absorbs it. A carbon dioxide laser at about 10,600 nanometers in the far infrared is absorbed by water within a few cell layers, so it vaporizes superficially and is used for skin lesions, for the cervix, and for the airway. A neodymium yttrium aluminum garnet laser at about 1,064 nanometers penetrates several millimeters and coagulates deeply through a fiber, a holmium yttrium aluminum garnet laser at about 2,100 nanometers fragments stones, a potassium titanyl phosphate laser at about 532 nanometers is absorbed by hemoglobin and pigment, and a diode laser emits between about 800 and 980 nanometers. Every wavelength, power, and pulse setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The delivery system must match the wavelength, because glass and water absorb some wavelengths and pass others. A carbon dioxide laser travels through an articulated arm of mirrors or a hollow waveguide, while neodymium and holmium lasers travel through a flexible silica fiber that can be passed through an endoscope, and the fiber tip is fragile and burns back as it is used. The surgeon controls the spot size by focusing and the depth of injury by power density, which is the power divided by the area of the spot, so a smaller spot at the same power is far more intense. Eye protection is wavelength-specific and is not interchangeable, because goggles that block green light will not block invisible infrared, so everyone in the room, including the patient, must wear the correct protection, and the nominal hazard zone, the eyewear specification, the power, and the pulse settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A laser is managed as a controlled area rather than as a tool, with a warning light at the door, an interlock that stops the beam when the door opens, a key or code that prevents untrained use, and a nominated person responsible for its records. The beam must never be aimed at a shiny instrument, because the reflection is as dangerous as the direct beam, and the field must stay dry because a wet drape or a pool of fluid can reflect light and can also conduct heat. The greatest fire risk is the airway laser, where a tube or a gauze lies inside an oxygen-rich atmosphere, so the special tubes and the saline-filled cuff are used and the oxygen is kept as low as the saturation of the patient allows. Surgical smoke is produced by every laser and every electrosurgical device, and it carries particles small enough to reach the depths of the lung, together with benzene, formaldehyde, and the genetic material of the patient, so a high-flow evacuator with a filter must capture it close to the source, with its flow setting and filter replacement interval confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Argon plasma coagulation is a monopolar method that carries current to tissue without touching it, and its physics is the ionization of a gas. Argon flows through a probe at a few liters per minute, a high voltage between the central electrode and the tissue ionizes the argon into a conducting plasma, and the current follows that channel to the nearest earthed tissue and produces a superficial burn. The probe never touches the tissue, so nothing sticks and the tip does not char, and the injury is usually shallower than that of a laser or an ultrasonic blade, a depth that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The current still needs a return pad, and because argon is heavier than air and is not absorbed from the bowel it can distend a loop of intestine or cause gas embolism, so a probe used inside the gut must come with a plan for the gas it delivers, and the common error is to use it there without one.

A standard suction tip does not clear surgical smoke, because it captures only what passes close to its opening and the capture velocity falls with distance. The hospital-grade energy device is a small system rather than one box, and the operating theatre is built to support it. A grounded mains supply, often routed through an isolated circuit that limits the current of a first fault, feeds the generator from a dedicated socket within reach of the surgeon. The trolley also carries the smoke evacuator, the argon console, or the laser console, so the consumables that must be in the room before the case include correctly sized return pads, the tip electrodes for the planned mode, a spare handpiece cable, ultrasonic blades and their torque wrench, sealing cartridges, laser fibers, and smoke filters, and the socket, circuit, and accessory arrangement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant begins with the battery-powered thermal cautery, which is a different device from the electrosurgical generator even though it performs a similar task. Its physics is simple resistive heating, because a small battery drives a current through a fine wire tip whose resistance makes it glow dull red and char the tissue it touches. The instrument is a disposable pen with a button, a battery, and one or two wire tips, and it needs no mains supply, no return pad, and no generator, which is what lets it survive in a clinic without reliable electricity, but it cannot cut because its few watts only char the surface. The tip reaches several hundred degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it remains hot after the button is released, while its characteristic alarm is silence, because the device has no monitoring and no alarm, and the common error is to leave it switched on in a pocket or on a drape.

Where mains power exists, a small bipolar generator is the field instrument of choice, because it needs no return pad and confines the current between the jaws. Fine bipolar forceps seal a bleeding point in a thyroid, a scalp, or a limb with little deep tissue damage, and the same forceps can be reused for years if they are cleaned and their insulation is inspected. A compact generator can run from mains or from a small inverter connected to a vehicle battery, and the output depends entirely on the quality of that supply, with the voltage and the duty cycle confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, so a display showing a high setting may still not deliver the power a large monopolar case needs. The bipolar generator has the same impedance alarm as its hospital cousin, but an alarm helps only if someone recognizes it, and the common error is to trust a low-power machine with a vessel that needs a suture to hold.

Before any energy device is used, the operator must complete a short check that is the same in spirit everywhere. Confirm that the generator passes its self-test, that the pad is the correct size and firmly applied to clean dry skin away from the current path, and that the tip, cord, and foot switch are intact. Confirm that the planned mode and power match the tissue and the protocol, that the smoke filter is seated, that the correct blade or fiber is fitted and torqued, and that the active tip stays in its holder until the surgeon asks for it. Name the alarm that would stop the case, know what each message means, and confirm every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a check performed from memory is only as good as the memory behind it.

The field energy device gives up a great deal, and what it gives up is what the operator must replace with technique. It offers no monopolar cutting with a return pad, no argon plasma coagulation, no laser, no ultrasonic or sealing instrument, and usually no smoke evacuation, and it also lacks impedance monitoring, a patient circuit test, and often any electrical safety measurement. What it demands instead is a surgeon who can tie a ligature, who can control bleeding by pressure and packing, who inspects every reusable forceps for a broken jaw or a cracked insulator, and who keeps the cautery in its holder, together with a fire-safe field, a tested battery, spare tips, and the honesty to admit that a vessel too large for the instrument needs a suture rather than a longer press of the button. The hospital machine gives monitored current, a choice of waveforms and powers, a pad that reports its own contact, smoke evacuation, and scheduled maintenance, while the field kit substitutes the judgment of the surgeon for the feedback of the generator, and neither version is simply better, because an uninspected generator is more dangerous than a simple pen used with care.

The safety of any energy device rests on three habits that apply everywhere. Inspect the instrument and its insulation before use, keep the active tip in its holder and away from the patient when it is not in use, and understand the path the current will take or the heat will spread. A device that is understood can be used to its limit and not beyond it, while a device that is trusted without understanding will eventually injure someone. Every power, temperature, frequency, depth, and alarm threshold in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the numbers that suit one tissue and one patient may not suit the next.

To summarize, the energy devices of surgery replace the blade with heat, vibration, or light, and each works by concentrating energy at a small point and letting tissue convert it into a change. Electrosurgery passes a radiofrequency current above the range that nerves can follow, concentrates it at a small active electrode, disperses it through a large return pad, and shapes it into a continuous waveform for cutting or an interrupted waveform for coagulation, while the bipolar configuration confines the current between two jaws and needs no pad. The complications are pad burns, contact burns, fire in an oxygen-rich field, interference with a pacemaker or an implanted defibrillator, and the unseen injury from current that channels through a laparoscopic cannula or a defective insulation. Ultrasonic dissectors vibrate a blade so that friction seals and cuts, vessel-sealing devices fuse vessel walls under pressure and heat, lasers deliver a wavelength chosen for the depth of penetration, argon plasma coagulation conducts current through ionized gas without contact, and all of them produce smoke that must be evacuated rather than breathed. In the field the battery cautery and the small bipolar generator replace the hospital systems and give up cutting power, monitoring, and smoke control in exchange for independence from mains electricity, so what they demand is a surgeon who ties and packs and inspects, an understanding of the heat path, and the honesty to ask for a suture when the device has reached its limit.

# Chapter 41 — Endoscopic and Minimally Invasive Surgery

Minimally invasive surgery is surgery performed through a small opening rather than a long incision, and every device in this chapter exists to make that substitution possible. The clinical promise is easy to state, because less of the body wall is divided there is less pain, less bleeding, a shorter hospital stay, and a faster return to ordinary activity. The cost is equally easy to state, because the surgeon no longer looks directly at the tissue and no longer touches it directly either. The eye is replaced by a camera on a cable, the hand by a shaft tens of centimeters long, and the working space by a cavity that must be created and held open with gas. Three substitutions, and everything that follows is a consequence of them.

The telescope is the eye, and it works by relaying an image along a tube. Light from the tissue enters a small objective lens at the tip, which brings it to a focus inside the instrument. In the oldest design a series of small lenses carried that image to the eyepiece, losing brightness at every glass surface. The modern rigid telescope replaces the air spaces with solid glass rods separated by narrow gaps, so most of the path is glass and the image crosses fewer air-to-glass boundaries. Each rod acts as a light pipe, and because the light strikes the glass wall at a shallow angle it is reflected back inside rather than escaping, a behavior called total internal reflection. The result is a bright image delivered to a socket at the back of the telescope, where a camera head or an eyepiece can be attached.

The camera head converts that optical image into an electrical signal. At its center is a solid-state image sensor, a silicon chip covered with a grid of tiny light-sensitive cells called pixels. Each cell accumulates an electrical charge in proportion to the number of photons that fall on it, and the chip reads the charge out row by row many times each second to build a moving picture. A single-sensor camera uses one chip under a mosaic color filter, while a three-sensor camera splits the light with a prism and sends red, green, and blue to separate chips for cleaner color. The camera is white balanced before use by pointing it at a white surface and telling the electronics that this is white, so the colors of everything else can be corrected. The camera head and its cable are not immersible unless the maker states otherwise, and the permitted disinfection or sterilization method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Illumination comes from a light source on the trolley that sends light down a cable of glass fibers to the telescope. An older source used a halogen bulb, a later one a xenon arc lamp, and the newest a light emitting diode, or LED, array. The lamp is not merely bright but concentrated, and the end of the cable can reach a temperature high enough to burn tissue or ignite a drape if it is laid on the patient while the lamp is on. The cable is unplugged from the source, or the source placed in standby, whenever it is not in use, and its end is never left lying on the drapes. The lamp hour meter, the intensity setting, and the over-temperature and lamp failure alarms must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The laparoscopy tower is the rack that binds these parts into one machine. It holds the light source, the camera control unit, the monitor, the recorder, and often the insufflator on a wheeled trolley with a power strip and hooks for cable management. On a well-designed tower the monitor height is adjustable so that the surgeon's gaze and the axis of the instrument line up, because a screen placed too low or too far to one side causes neck and shoulder strain over a long case. The trolley also carries a spare lamp, a spare camera cable, and a spare light cable, because a dark screen during a dissection is an emergency. The recorder captures what the camera sees for teaching, audit, and defense, and it documents what was found and what was done. A high-definition camera feeding an older standard-definition screen wastes its resolution, and a long or damaged cable leaves shadow bars, color drift, or intermittent noise. The screen is cleaned only with a solution the maker permits, because alcohol and ammonia attack some surfaces and anti-glare coatings. The electrical safety of the tower, the viewing distance, the retention of recordings, and the permitted cleaning agents must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Making a working space is the central physical problem of laparoscopic surgery. The abdominal wall is a flexible tent over the organs, and unless it is lifted the cavity collapses and the camera sees nothing. The insufflator solves this by pushing gas into the abdomen through a needle or a port and holding a set pressure while a valve admits more gas to replace what leaks. Carbon dioxide is the gas of choice for three reasons, because it is highly soluble in blood, it does not support combustion, and it is cheap and widely available. Pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury and flow in liters per minute, and the insufflator reports both continuously. The target pressure, the maximum pressure, the flow rate, and the alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A pneumoperitoneum is not a neutral act, and its consequences follow from simple mechanics. Pressure inside the abdomen pushes the diaphragm upward, reduces the volume the lungs can expand, and raises the airway pressure the ventilator must generate. The same pressure compresses the large veins that return blood to the heart, so venous return falls and blood pressure becomes sensitive to position and fluid status. Carbon dioxide is absorbed across the peritoneum and must be removed by breathing, so its level in the blood tends to rise and the ventilator is usually adjusted to remove more of it. The head-down position used to let the bowel fall away adds its own effects on the heart, the lungs, the eyes, and the brain, and a patient with heart or lung disease tolerates all of this poorly. These effects are why insufflation pressure is kept as low as the surgery allows, and the pressure and ventilation settings for each patient must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The insufflator has a small vocabulary of alarms, and each one points to a different cause. A high pressure alarm sounds when the set limit is exceeded, and the usual causes are a blocked port, a kink in the tubing, a patient coughing or straining, or an over-enthusiastic attempt to create space quickly. A low flow or flow failure alarm suggests a leak, an empty cylinder, a closed stopcock, or a disconnected tube, and the first response is to look for the leak rather than to raise the pressure. Some insufflators warm the gas before it enters, which reduces fogging of the telescope, and that heater has its own over-temperature alarm. The common operator error is to silence an alarm and continue, and the pattern that must never be dismissed is a sudden rise in pressure with a fall in flow, because the tip of the needle or port may have entered a structure. The pressure limits, flow limits, heater temperature, and alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The most feared consequence of insufflation is gas embolism, in which carbon dioxide enters a vein or an organ and travels to the heart and lungs. It appears as a sudden fall in blood pressure, a fall in the carbon dioxide measured at the end of exhalation, a change in heart rhythm, and a mill wheel murmur that is rarely heard in time. The response is to stop the gas, release the pressure, give oxygen, and position the patient so that gas is kept away from the heart, and the exact steps belong in the local protocol. Subcutaneous emphysema, in which gas tracks into the skin of the chest and neck, usually follows a port that has slipped out of the cavity or a pressure that is too high. A capnothorax can follow a defect in the diaphragm, and the anesthetist is usually first to notice because airway pressures rise and oxygen saturation falls.

A trocar is the door through which everything else enters. It has three parts, a tip that opens the abdominal wall, a hollow sleeve that stays behind, and a seal at the top that closes around whatever passes through it. Disposable trocars usually carry a spring-loaded shield over a blade so that the blade retracts once the wall is crossed, and reusable trocars rely on a blunt obturator or a dilating tip that separates muscle fibers rather than cutting them. The seal is a slit valve, a duckbill, or a combination, and it has a side stopcock for gas. A port with a worn seal leaks continuously and makes the insufflator work harder, and a port that has lost its shield can injure the bowel. The insertion technique, the port size, and the condition of the seal must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Most serious injuries of laparoscopy happen at the first entry, because that entry is made without seeing where the tip is going. The classical error is to push a sharp trocar too hard in a patient whose bowel lies against the abdominal wall, and the injury may not be recognized until the abdomen is examined from inside. The alternative is an open entry in which a small incision is made layer by layer and the port is placed under direct vision, and this route is often chosen in patients who have had previous surgery and are likely to have adhesions. A port site later becomes a weak point, and a port larger than 10 millimeters is usually closed at its fascial layer to prevent a hernia. The first entry technique, the incision size, and the closure of each port site must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Telescopes are described by two numbers that the listener should be able to picture. The first is the angle of view, which is the direction in which the lens faces, so a telescope at 0 degrees looks straight ahead and one at 30 degrees looks forward and to one side, letting the surgeon sweep the view around the cavity by rotating the shaft. The second is the diameter, where a 10 millimeter telescope admits more light and gives a brighter picture and a 5 millimeter telescope fits a smaller port at the cost of brightness. A telescope is a delicate optical instrument inside a metal tube, and a bend of only a few degrees cracks the rod lenses inside, leaving a dark crescent or a blurred edge that no cleaning will remove. It is never used as a retractor, never dropped into a tray, and never left where an instrument can fall across it, and checking the image before every case is the cheapest quality test in the room. The angle and the diameter chosen for each procedure, and the inspection of the image, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The instruments of laparoscopy are recognized by function rather than shape, and each is a small hand at the end of a long shaft. Graspers hold tissue, dissecting forceps spread it, scissors cut it, hooks lift it, and needle holders drive a suture through it. A suction and irrigation probe clears blood and smoke, a clip applier places a metal or polymer clip across a vessel, and a specimen bag receives tissue that must be removed without spilling its contents. Electrosurgical probes, ultrasonic shears, and vessel-sealing devices have their own chapter, but their handles and shafts are made long for this route. The length of the shaft is a compromise, because a longer instrument reaches deeper but magnifies every tremor of the surgeon's hand and applies less force.

The shaft also hides a maintenance problem. Insulation covers the metal to protect the patient from current, and a pinhole in that insulation lets current escape at the point of contact and burn tissue nobody can see. Insulated instruments are tested with a dedicated insulation tester at a defined interval, and any instrument with a visible crack, a burned spot, or a loose connection is removed from service rather than repaired in the operating room. The moving parts of a reusable instrument need a lubricant that survives sterilization, and a stiff or gritty action warns that the instrument may fail during the case.

Staplers bring the closure technology of open surgery through a narrow port. A linear stapler lays two or three rows of staples and then cuts between them, which is how a length of bowel or a large vessel is divided without bleeding. A circular stapler creates a ring of staples and removes the tissue inside the ring, which is how two hollow organs are joined end to end. The staples must form closed loops rather than partly open ones, and a malformed staple leaks, so the fired line is inspected before the instrument is withdrawn. Each stapler accepts a reload of a specific length and staple height, and matching the reload to the thickness of the tissue is the difference between a secure closure and a leak. The staple height, the tissue thickness, and the number of firings allowed must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Taking tissue out through a small hole is its own problem. A specimen too large to pass through a port is placed in a retrieval bag, a thin plastic sack with a drawstring that is opened inside the abdomen, filled, closed, and pulled out through the port or a slightly enlarged incision. If the specimen is not bagged and it is malignant or infected, its cells or bacteria can seed the port site and the wound. A morcellator solves the size problem by cutting tissue into strips drawn out through the shaft, and it carries the specific hazard of spreading an unrecognized tumor through the abdomen.

Robot-assisted surgery is master-slave telemanipulation rather than an independent machine. The surgeon sits at a console, looks into a stereo viewer that shows two slightly different images for depth, and moves two master handles. A computer translates those movements into the motion of instrument arms docked to the patient, and it can scale a large hand movement into a small instrument movement, filter out tremor, and articulate an instrument wrist far beyond what a straight shaft allows. The system decides nothing and does not restore the sense of touch, so the surgeon works from vision alone. The instrument life, the arm alignment, and the console settings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cost of ownership is the least visible part of robotics and the hardest to justify, and it must be understood before a hospital buys one. The console and the arms are expensive, the instruments are consumables with a limited number of uses, and the training and the service contract continue to cost after the purchase. The failure modes are characteristic, and a communication fault between the console and the arms freezes the slave, so the immediate response is to remove the instruments from the patient while a second team stands ready to convert to open surgery. Docking is slow, the patient must be positioned rigidly, and a patient who moves can be injured against an arm that cannot feel them. The instrument use limits, the fault alarms, the emergency undocking procedure, and the conversion plan must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning is a physical process that must happen before sterilization, and its purpose is to remove the organic material that shelters microbes and blocks sterilants. Blood, fat, and protein dry into a film that water alone will not lift, so instruments are kept moist after use, pre-cleaned where they are used, and transported in a closed container to the reprocessing area. There the instrument is disassembled as far as it will go, because a box lock, a ratchet, or a screw joint hides soil that no steam will reach. Long shafts and hollow channels are brushed with a brush of the correct diameter, flushed with a detergent solution, and cleaned in an ultrasonic bath, where bubbles that form and collapse on the surface lift debris from the crevices. The detergent concentration, the water temperature, the ultrasonic cycle, and the rinse quality must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Telescopes and flexible instruments cannot be judged by the eye alone, and the leak test is the check that protects them. A leaking flexible endoscope takes fluid into its optical bundle and its electronics, and the damage appears as a foggy image or a dead section weeks later. The tester is a small hand pump that slightly pressurizes the sealed shaft, and the instrument is then immersed and watched for bubbles, which mark a hole in the outer sheath that must be repaired before the next use. Rigid telescopes are inspected by holding them to a light and looking along the barrel for a cracked lens, a loose lens, or moisture. Any loss of brightness, a color cast, a dark crescent, or a hazy spot means the telescope goes for repair.

Sterilization destroys the microorganisms that remain after cleaning, and the method must be matched to what the device can survive. Rigid stainless steel instruments and most rigid telescopes tolerate steam under pressure, with a typical cycle at 134 degrees Celsius for a few minutes at the autoclave's stated pressure, and that cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because exceeding the temperature or the time damages seals, cements, and lens mounts. Heat-sensitive instruments, camera heads, light cables, and flexible endoscopes require a low-temperature process such as hydrogen peroxide gas plasma, ethylene oxide, or a liquid peracetic acid system. A sterilized set goes into a container or a peel pouch with a chemical indicator and a process label, and the pouch is inspected for holes, dampness, and a broken seal before it is opened. The choice of sterilant, the cycle parameters, the aeration time, and the storage limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Everything that enters the abdomen is either sterile or it is a source of infection, and the consumables of laparoscopy are counted before the case and again after it. Trocars, clip appliers, stapler reloads, specimen bags, and suture on long needles all leave the sterile field and must be accounted for, and the count is reconciled before the patient leaves the room. Reusable instruments are stored dry and protected from one another in a way that lets air circulate, because instruments dropped together into a drawer are how a telescope is cracked. Single-use items are checked for the expiry date, the integrity of the package, and the correct size before the case, and a package that is damp or torn is not used.

The tower rewards a short scheduled inspection more than it rewards repair. The light cable is examined for broken fibers, which appear as dark spots that reduce illumination and as heat that concentrates at the damaged end. The camera cable is checked for kinks at the connector, the insufflator is checked against a calibrated pressure gauge, and the gas supply is checked for the correct cylinder and a full contents gauge before the list begins. The electrical safety of the trolley, including its protective earth and its insulation, is measured at a stated interval, and the battery of any cordless component is tested for capacity rather than voltage alone. The image chain is checked with a test target, so that a dimming lamp or a drifting white balance is found before it is discovered midway through a case. The inspection interval, the calibration tolerance, and the electrical safety limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the operator must check before the first case is a short list that prevents most disasters. The tower is powered, the lamp hours are within the maker's limit, the white balance is performed, and the image is confirmed sharp on the monitor. The insufflator shows the expected cylinder pressure, the tubing is connected the right way around, and the pressure and flow limits match the plan for this patient. The telescopes are inspected, the instruments are laid out in the order they will be needed, the ports are checked for intact seals, and the stapler reloads and clip appliers are matched to the planned steps. The diathermy return pad is on the patient, the alarm limits of the anesthetic monitor are set, and the team has spoken the patient's name, the procedure, and the side aloud.

In a mobile clinic or a district hospital without a laparoscopy tower, the same clinical problem is met with a fraction of the equipment. The light source becomes a battery-powered LED headlamp or a small battery light box attached to the telescope, and the monitor becomes a laptop or a small portable screen. The gas supply may not exist, so the surgeon works with a gasless technique or with a mechanical lifting device that raises the abdominal wall with a fan-shaped retractor held on an external frame. The ports and instruments are reusable and reprocessed on site, which shifts the burden from a supply chain to a cleaning and sterilization discipline. Each substitution changes what the operation can safely do, and the honest limit must be understood before the first incision.

Gasless laparoscopy is not a lesser version of the same operation but a different physical situation. Lifting the wall mechanically creates a smaller and more irregular space, and the surgeon must use counter-traction against the lifting device rather than relying on the even pressure of gas. The advantages are real where carbon dioxide is scarce, where anesthesia is light, or where the patient's heart and lungs cannot tolerate a pneumoperitoneum, because there is no gas to absorb and no pressure on the veins. Single-port surgery, in which the telescope and instruments pass through one opening, is possible with ordinary instruments, but the instruments cross one another, the camera and the hands compete for the same space, and triangulation is reduced. Both approaches demand more time and more patience, and both should be converted to an open operation without hesitation when the view is poor.

The field kit that works is small and unglamorous. It carries a rigid telescope with both a straight and an angled lens if both can be afforded, a battery light source with spare cells, a portable screen, 2 or 3 reusable ports, a basic set of graspers and scissors, a suction and irrigation syringe, a bipolar forceps unit, and a supply of suture and ligatures. Sterilization on site usually means steam under pressure if an autoclave is available, and if it is not, the honest option is to refer the patient rather than operate with instruments that cannot be made safe. The lack of a reliable sterilizer, the lack of smoke evacuation, and the lack of a second trained operator are the three limits that most often make a planned laparoscopic procedure unsafe. The available sterilization method, the instrument set, and the criteria for referral must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The last requirement of this chapter is not a device at all but a system of competence. Minimally invasive surgery is harder to learn than open surgery because the eye and the hand are separated, so the surgeon practices the new coordination on a simulator or a box trainer before testing it on a patient. The team rehearses the failures, including a lost image, a bleeding vessel that cannot be seen, a gas embolism, a stapler that misfires, and the decision to convert to open, and every member knows their role in each. Cases are reviewed for complications, conversion, port-site infection, and instrument failure, and the findings are fed back into training rather than filed away. The credentialing requirements, the simulator practice hours, and the complication review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, minimally invasive surgery replaces a long incision with a small port, and every device in the chapter exists to serve that single idea. A telescope relays an image by total internal reflection to a camera that turns light into an electrical signal, and a monitor returns that signal to the surgeon's eye. A light source illuminates the cavity, an insufflator holds it open with carbon dioxide at a pressure that must be kept as low as the operation allows, and the physiology of the pneumoperitoneum dictates much of what the anesthetist must do. Trocars, long-shafted instruments, staplers, and clip appliers do the work of the hand, while robotic arms add articulation and steadiness at a cost of ownership that must be planned for years in advance. Cleaning, leak testing, sterilization, insulation testing, and instrument counting are not housekeeping but the conditions that make the operation safe. Where no tower exists, a battery light, a portable screen, reusable ports, and a gasless lift can still serve, provided the team accepts the narrower view and refers early when the honest limits are reached.

# Chapter 42 — Orthopedic Equipment

Orthopedic surgery is the surgery of bone, and bone is unlike any other tissue that the instruments in this book are asked to cut. It is a composite of a flexible collagen scaffold and a hard mineral phase, and the two behave differently according to the direction of loading. Cortical bone, the dense outer shell, is strong along its length and much weaker across it, while cancellous bone, the spongy interior, crushes progressively rather than breaking cleanly. Every tool in this chapter exists because bone must be cut, drilled, reamed, held, or replaced. Each action is a contest between a hard brittle material and the soft living tissue around it, and a listener who grasps that contest will understand why these instruments are heavy, cooled, and unforgiving of haste.

The central problem of cutting bone is heat, because bone is alive and its cells die at temperatures an ordinary drill reaches in seconds. The energy of the rotating cutting edge becomes friction at the interface, and without cooling it raises the bone far above body temperature. Osteocytes, the cells that maintain the bone matrix, begin to die when the local temperature stays near 47 degrees Celsius for about one minute, so the bone is replaced by weaker tissue and an implant may loosen months later. The drill clears chips and heat only when it is sharp, when it turns fast enough to cut rather than rub, and when the surgeon uses light pressure. Irrigation with cool sterile fluid removes the remaining heat, and the common error is to lean on the drill and pause at one spot instead of withdrawing to clear the chips, so the temperature threshold and the irrigation routine must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Orthopedic power tools are grouped by how they make rotation. An electric tool turns a motor with current and gives steady torque from mains power, but it ties the surgeon to a cable. A battery tool carries its own chemical energy and trades power for freedom from the cord, which matters where the supply is unreliable. A pneumatic tool runs on compressed gas and is light and robust because it has no electric motor, but it needs clean dry air and its exhaust is cold and noisy. The saws add oscillation: the blade sweeps through a small arc many times each second, so its teeth engage rigid bone, plaster, or metal and retreat while soft tissue is pushed rather than cut, and typical saw speeds of 10,000 to 20,000 oscillations each minute must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cutting end of the tool is a consumable with a short life. Drill bits for bone are fluted, with helical grooves that carry debris out of the hole, and they are made of stainless steel or tungsten carbide, which holds an edge longer but is brittle. Burs are small rotating cutters for shaping, and their round, acorn, and tapered shapes decide whether they cut a hollow, a flat, or a groove. A modern quick coupling locks the shank with a ring, while an older keyed chuck needs a key that is easily lost. The hazards here are variations on one accident, in which a glove, a drape, a gown, a cable, or a strand of suture wraps around a spinning shank and pulls the surgeon's hand toward the bone, and the common error is to leave a handpiece on a drape with the trigger locked on.

Reaming enlarges a canal so that an implant of known size will fit, and it is done in steps rather than in one pass. The medullary canal is an irregular cavity lined with soft tissue, and a reamer is a rotating cylinder with spiral blades that shaves the wall as it advances over a guide wire. Each reamer is slightly larger than the last, and orthopedic sets are made in increments of 0.5 millimeters for many applications, a step that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A reamer pushed off the line of the canal thins one wall until the cortex cracks, and long reaming of a femur can drive marrow fat into the circulation and produce a fat embolism. The common error is to force a blunt reamer with heavy pressure, which produces heat, eccentricity, and a canal larger than the planned implant.

Traction applies a steady pull to a limb or to part of the skeleton, and its principle is that a continuous force balanced by countertraction can hold a fracture in alignment while it heals. The force comes from a weight on a cord over a pulley, and the countertraction is usually the weight of the patient's body against the bed. Skin traction is generally limited to about 5 kilograms, while skeletal traction carried by a pin through bone can reach 15 kilograms or more, and both limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A balanced suspension frame adds cords and pulleys so the limb can be lifted for care without losing its pull, and the pulleys must turn freely because friction destroys the calibration. The characteristic alarm is the clang of a weight reaching the floor, and the common error is to rest the weights on the bed for care, which silently removes the traction.

Skeletal traction begins with a pin, and the pin site is a decision about anatomy. A pin through the lower femur is used for fractures of the femur, a pin through the tibial tuberosity is used when the knee joint must be avoided, and a pin through the heel is used for fractures of the tibia. A threaded wire grips the bone better but is weaker at the thread, and a smooth pin can slide and loosen earlier, so the pin is drilled at low speed with irrigation, because a pin drilled hot leaves a ring of dead bone that becomes the entry point for infection. Both ends are held in a curved bow that spreads the load so the wire does not bend in the middle. Pin sites must be cleaned and dressed according to the local protocol, and any redness, discharge, or loosening must be reported at once, because a pin tract infection can track to the bone.

An external fixator turns the principle of traction into a rigid frame. Pins or wires are placed into the bone above and below the fracture, and rods and clamps connect them into a frame that holds the fragments from outside the skin and carries the load the broken bone cannot. A unilateral frame places pins on one side, a bilateral frame on both sides, and a circular frame uses thin tensioned wires on rings, with a wire tension of about 90 to 130 kilograms of force, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Because the metal never crosses the fracture inside the limb, the wound remains visible and can be inspected and dressed, which is the great advantage in the contaminated or the open fracture. The characteristic problem is the pin site, where a small discharge crusts, a red margin spreads, and a pin loosens. The common errors are to overtighten a clamp until the threads strip and to leave a clamp only hand tight, and both produce a frame that looks solid and moves under load.

Internal fixation moves the holding force inside the body, and its two families are the plate and the screw. A plate is a flat metal bar with holes that lies on the surface of the bone and holds the fracture by friction, by compression, or by bridging a comminuted zone, while a locking plate grips the screw heads so the assembly behaves as one rigid frame. A cortical screw has a fine thread for dense bone and is commonly 3.5 millimeters in diameter, and a cancellous screw has a coarse thread for spongy bone and is commonly 6.5 millimeters in diameter, so the exact diameters and lengths must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A screw is chosen so that its tip ends just beyond the far cortex, because a screw that protrudes can injure a vessel, a nerve, or a tendon. The common error is to use a worn screwdriver, which rounds off the head so the screw can neither be tightened nor removed, and the second is to mix metals from different makers, because two alloys in one wound corrode each other.

An intramedullary nail is a long metal rod inserted into the hollow center of a long bone, and it works because a splint along the axis shares load far better than a plate on the surface. The nail is introduced through an entry point at one end, passed across the fracture, and fixed with locking screws placed through holes near each end. The locking screws control rotation and prevent the fragments from sliding along the nail, and the pattern of locking decides how much load passes through bone and how much through metal. A nail can be inserted into a reamed canal, which allows a thicker nail but adds heat and marrow embolization, or unreamed, which is faster and gentler but limits the size of the nail. Wires are the thinnest implants, and the most feared complication of a Kirschner wire is migration, because one that is not bent or anchored can travel through tissue and has reached the heart and the great vessels, so the diameters and insertion techniques must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

All of these implants are placed with an instrumentation set, and the completeness of that set is a patient safety issue. A typical set holds the drill guide, the depth gauge, the tap, the countersink, the screwdriver, the torque-limiting handle, the reduction forceps, the bone holding forceps, and the mallet. The drill guide controls the angle and protects the soft tissue, the depth gauge measures the hole so the correct screw length can be chosen, and the torque-limiting handle stops the surgeon before the screw strips or the plate deforms. Implants arrive in sterile packages and must never be resterilized, never reused once opened, and must be recorded by the package label so the exact device and its lot can be traced later, and every screw and implant is counted at the end of the case because a retained implant is a never event. The common error is to substitute an instrument from another set, which fits loosely, slips, and damages the implant and the bone, and the second error is to leave the instrumentation in a tray of blood and bone for hours, which hardens until cleaning is impossible.

A tourniquet is a cuff wrapped around a limb and inflated until the pressure inside it stops the flow of blood in the arteries beneath. When that pressure exceeds the systolic pressure of the patient with a margin to spare, the artery is compressed and the limb becomes bloodless, which makes surgery possible and makes the tourniquet dangerous. A common upper limb pressure is about 250 millimeters of mercury and a common lower limb pressure is about 300 to 350 millimeters of mercury, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A common safe limit is 60 to 90 minutes for the upper limb and 120 to 150 minutes for the lower limb before the cuff is released for reperfusion, times that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is the pressure loss or leak alarm of the regulator, and the common error is to ignore it, because a cuff that has lost pressure no longer controls the field, so the operator must record the inflation time and must never allow an alcohol-based skin preparation to pool beneath the cuff and produce a chemical burn.

Not every tourniquet is a surgical instrument, and the difference matters when one is improvised in an emergency. A tourniquet used to stop catastrophic bleeding is a rescue device, and it must be wide enough to compress the artery without cutting into the skin and the nerve beneath it. The pressure under a band is the force divided by the area over which it is applied, so a narrow cord or a thin strap concentrates the same force into a tiny area and can injure the nerve even when it stops the bleeding. A field tourniquet should therefore be at least 5 centimeters wide, a width that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it is tightened with a windlass or a ratchet until the bleeding stops and no pulse can be felt beyond it. The common error is to apply a venous tourniquet, tight enough to block the return of blood but not the inflow, and the second error is to loosen the device periodically, because that releases the clot and restarts the bleeding.

A cast is a rigid shell that holds a limb still while bone or soft tissue heals, and its chemistry decides how it behaves in the hand. Plaster of Paris begins as calcium sulfate hemihydrate, a powder that becomes a paste when mixed with water, and the paste sets because the hemihydrate takes up water and recrystallizes into interlocking crystals of the dihydrate. The reaction releases heat, and that heat is the first hazard of casting, because a thick cast mixed with warm water can raise the skin temperature beneath it into a burn. The setting time depends on the temperature of the water, so lukewarm water of about 20 to 30 degrees Celsius gives several minutes of working time, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a wet plaster cast takes about 24 to 48 hours to dry fully, a period that must also be confirmed. The padding is part of the device, with a stockinette next to the skin, layers of wadding over it, and extra felt over the heel, the ankle, the knee, and the elbow, and the mold made while the cast sets produces the three-point fixation that resists the deforming force.

Synthetic casting material replaces the plaster crystals with a knitted fabric of fiberglass or polyester impregnated with a polyurethane resin, and the resin cures when it absorbs moisture. The synthetic cast is lighter than plaster of the same strength, it is radiolucent so a radiograph can see the bone through it, it tolerates water once cured, and it sets in minutes rather than in a day. A typical synthetic cast sets in about 5 to 20 minutes, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and because it gives less working time it must be applied by someone who has already planned the mold. The synthetic material is less forgiving of a poor mold, it can irritate the skin if the edges are rough, and it is harder to remove than plaster because a dull blade will not cut it cleanly. A splint is the same material laid along one or two sides of the limb over padding, and its great advantage is that it does not close the circumference, so the limb can swell without being strangled and a fresh injury is usually splinted rather than cast.

Removing a cast depends on one elegant principle. The cast saw has a stiff blade driven back and forth through a very small arc, so the teeth move fast but travel only a little in each direction. A hard, brittle material such as plaster or cured resin cannot follow that rapid reversal, so the teeth chip into it and cut a groove, while soft skin yields and moves with the blade instead of resisting it, so the blade does not cut it. The same principle makes the saw dangerous, because the blade still becomes hot from friction, and the shoe that rides on the skin can burn if the blade is dull or the operator presses too hard. The operator must use a sharp blade, must keep it perpendicular to the surface, and must stop whenever the patient reports heat, and the common error is to cut through the padding in one deep pass instead of lifting the cast away in stages, after which the limb is examined for skin damage and the neurovascular status is checked.

Arthroscopy looks into a joint through two small openings, and it works because a joint can be turned into a cavity. A rigid telescope built from glass lenses and a bundle of light-carrying fibers is passed through a portal into the joint, and sterile fluid is pumped in to distend the joint capsule so that there is space to see and to work. A typical irrigation pressure lies between about 40 and 60 millimeters of mercury, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a pressure that is too high drives fluid into the soft tissues and can produce a compartment syndrome. The second portal admits a shaver, which trims torn tissue, or a radiofrequency probe, which seals tissue with heat, or a hand instrument such as a probe. The characteristic alarm is the pressure or occlusion alarm of the pump, and the common error is to raise the pressure instead of checking whether the inflow cannula has left the joint, while the arthroscope, the camera head, the light cable, and the shaver handpiece are heat sensitive and must be sterilized by a low-temperature process whose cycle parameters must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The power tools and the arthroscopes are the most maintenance-hungry items in the orthopedic department, and most of their failures can be predicted. A battery pack is a set of cells whose chemistry decides its habits: an older nickel-cadmium pack loses capacity if it is repeatedly recharged before it is discharged, a nickel-metal hydride pack has less of that memory but loses charge while it sits, and a lithium-ion pack holds its charge well but must never be charged while it is hot from the sterilizer.
