A common hospital cycle for a wrapped handpiece is 134 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes in saturated steam, a cycle that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a battery must never be put through it, because steam destroys the cells and the sealed case. The chuck must be cleaned of bone dust, the flutes of the drill and the reamer must be flushed, and the moving parts must receive only the lubricant the maker specifies, because a general-purpose oil traps debris and gums the mechanism, so every failure must be recorded and the tool removed from service.

Cleaning decides whether sterilization will work, and orthopedic instruments are the hardest things in the hospital to clean. Bone, blood, fat, and cement harden inside cannulations, threads, ratchets, and chucks, and a sterilizer cannot penetrate a plug of dried tissue, so the instrument must be opened, dismantled where the maker allows, and flushed through every channel. Cannulated drills, cannulated screws, reamers, and suction tips are flushed with water in both directions, and the fine channels are cleaned with a brush of the correct size, all according to the local reprocessing protocol. The instruments then go through the cleaning and sterilization pathway of the Central Sterile Services Department, or CSSD, where the washer-disinfector and steam sterilizer cycles are validated and recorded, and the cycle parameters must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Burs, saw blades, drill bits, reamers, drapes, and tubing are consumables with a stated life, and a cutting edge that has lost its bite is replaced rather than sharpened. Bone cement is a two-part powder and liquid that polymerizes in the wound, and the reaction is strongly exothermic, with a peak temperature that can exceed 70 degrees Celsius, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the toxic monomer can cause a fall in blood pressure, so the anesthetist is warned before it is inserted.

Before any orthopedic case, the operator and the team run through the same list, and most of it targets the failure that would be worst at the worst moment. The power supply and the battery charge are checked, and at least one charged spare battery is on the trolley, because a drill that stops in the middle of a nail is a serious problem. The blades, burs, drill bits, reamers, and saw blades are inspected for sharpness, cracks, missing teeth, and correct fit in the chuck. The irrigation fluid, the suction, and the tourniquet are prepared and tested, with the cuff checked for leaks and the intended inflation time recorded on the anesthetic record. The implant set is matched against the planned procedure, the implants are checked for size, side, and package integrity, and the image intensifier is positioned with the lead apron, the thyroid shield, and the dosimeter worn by everyone in the room, because the radiation dose to the team is cumulative.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the same operations are done with far less, and the substitution changes the character of the work. The power drill may be replaced by a hand drill, a cranked or T-handled device that turns the bit by muscle alone, and by a mallet, which drives a pin through bone by impact rather than rotation. A hand drill gives up speed, controlled torque, and the irrigation pump that cools the bone, so the surgeon turns slowly and pauses often, and the drill is withdrawn at intervals to let the chips clear and the heat escape. The external fixator becomes the workhorse of the field, because it can hold almost any long bone fracture with pins and rods light enough to carry, and because it can be applied through a small incision under local anesthesia. The internal plate and the intramedullary nail give up their place to the external frame and to simple wires, because they demand a full implant set, a power drill, and an image intensifier that the field clinic does not have. The plaster becomes the universal immobilizer, and a carpenter's saw with a fine blade becomes the cast saw, which has no oscillation and no guard, so the operator must cut slowly with a finger between the blade and the skin, and sterility is kept with the smallest possible kit and instruments boiled or chemically disinfected according to the local protocol.

The field clinic also has its own safety hazards, and they are the hazards of the environment as much as of the device. A hand drill can slip and drive the bit into the surgeon's hand or into a vessel, so the limb must be held firmly on a stable surface and the line of the drill kept away from the body. A mallet strike that misses the pin strikes the hand, and a pin driven too fast can crack the bone, so the assistant must hold the pin steady and the surgeon must strike with control. Improvised traction using stones, sandbags, or water containers works by the same physics but cannot be calibrated, so the force is estimated, the skin is checked more often, and the local protocol decides how the weight is secured. An external fixator in the field is exposed to dust, mud, and rain, so the pin sites are cleaned at every opportunity and the frame is protected with a clean dressing. An open fracture in a field clinic carries a high risk of infection, so the wound is cleaned and debrided and antibiotics are given according to the local protocol, and where no image intensifier exists the reduction is judged by feel, by alignment, and by plain radiographs.

The failures of orthopedic equipment are rarely sudden and rarely mysterious, and a technician who knows the machine can often hear them coming. A battery that is losing capacity shows itself as a tool that slows under load before it stops, and a drill that is overheating smells hot at the housing. A blade that is dull requires more pressure and produces more dust and more heat, and a blunt reamer is the common cause of a canal that is too hot. A chuck that is worn slips on the shank and rounds it, so the bit no longer runs true and the hole is oversized. A tourniquet cuff that is failing leaks slowly, so its alarm sounds late in the case, and its tubing must be checked for cracks and its bladder for folds before every use. A cast saw with a dull blade burns the patient, and a cement stored too warm sets in the mixing bowl, so every failure must be recorded, because a device that has failed once will fail again.

To summarize, orthopedic equipment is a family of tools built around one hard, living material, and every design decision follows from that fact. Bone must be cut with sharp edges, at controlled speeds, under irrigation, because the heat of cutting kills the bone and a dead surface is a loose implant waiting to happen. Traction, splints, casts, and external fixators hold a fracture from outside, while plates, screws, nails, and wires hold it from inside, and each method trades one kind of control for another. The tourniquet buys a bloodless field with a measured pressure and a measured time. The cast saw cuts hard material while sparing soft tissue, and the power tools demand batteries that are never autoclaved. In the field the principles do not change but the apparatus does, and the hand drill, the mallet, the external fixator, and the plaster slab ask for skill, patience, and hygiene in place of power and imaging, so the operator must know the physical principle, must check the device before the case, must confirm every setting, pressure, temperature, and cycle against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and must recognize the failure before it reaches the patient.

# Chapter 43 — Sutures, Staplers, Meshes, and Hemostats

Every wound closed by hand is held by something that carries tension, and that task is the physics of a rope under load. Tissue heals by laying down collagen across a gap, but only while the edges stay in contact and the collagen matures. A closure device must bring the edges together, hold them against the forces that pull them apart, and keep holding while healing is weak. Four families answer that demand, the suture, the staple or clip, the mesh, and the hemostatic agent. A cough can place kilograms of force across an abdominal incision, so a closure that only looks neat may still fail.

The behavior of a suture is decided by what it is made of, whether the body dissolves it, and whether it is one strand or many. The useful strength of a suture is not its strength when implanted but the strength left after days or weeks in tissue. Absorbable materials lose strength as the body breaks the polymer apart, while non-absorbable materials keep their strength but stay as a foreign body. A monofilament is one smooth strand that slides through tissue easily and resists bacteria because there is nowhere to hide. A braided suture ties secure knots, but its interstices can harbor organisms and wick fluid along the strand.

A knot holds because friction between the strands resists the pull of the wound. A stiff, smooth monofilament has little friction, so it needs more throws and must be tied flat, while a soft braided material grips itself and needs fewer. The square knot, in which the strands cross left over right and then right over left, is the standard because it resists capsizing under load. A suture tied too loosely leaves the edges apart and one tied too tightly strangulates the tissue, so the throws must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Absorbable sutures are made from materials the body can dismantle, and they differ in how fast they lose strength. Catgut is made from the collagen of animal intestine, and its plain form loses strength within about seven to ten days while the chromic form holds for two to three weeks, intervals that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Synthetic absorbables are polymers broken down by hydrolysis, the reaction of the polymer with water, so their behavior is more predictable and tissue reaction is smaller. A braided synthetic such as polyglactin holds for two to three weeks, while a long-lasting monofilament such as polydioxanone retains strength for about six weeks. Absorbable materials suit tissue that cannot keep a foreign body, such as the urinary tract and the biliary tree.

Non-absorbable sutures are the permanent materials, chosen where strength must outlast healing. Silk handles superbly and ties securely, but it is braided, it provokes chronic inflammation, and it loses strength slowly over years. Nylon is a strong monofilament with low tissue reaction, but it is stiff and its knots tend to slip, so it needs several throws. Polypropylene is smoother and chemically inert, and it is the common choice for fine vascular work and for permanent reinforcement. Polyester is a strong braided synthetic, and stainless steel wire is the strongest and stiffest of all, used in sternal closure and in orthopedic work where nothing else holds.

A suture reaches the table as a sterile package, and everything about that package matters. It is delivered with a swaged needle that is pressed onto the strand instead of threaded through an eye. The swaged junction is stronger and smoother than an eyed needle, because it is the same diameter as the strand and leaves no doubled thickness to drag through tissue. The package states the material, the size, the needle type, the curvature, the length, and the expiry date, and those details must be confirmed before the pack is opened. A package that is torn or past its date must be discarded, and a suture cannot be reprocessed after it has been in tissue.

Suture sizes follow a convention that confuses almost everyone, because the numbers run in two directions from a central zero. A size written as zero is the reference, and sizes larger than zero are written as 1, 2, 3, and 4 and beyond, each step a thicker strand. Sizes smaller than zero are written as 2-0, 3-0, 4-0 and so on, each step a finer strand, and the finest microsurgical sutures reach 12-0. Beside this number stands a metric size, which is the diameter in tenths of a millimeter, so a 3-0 suture is about 0.2 millimeters across. The size for a given tissue must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Needles are where the closure meets the tissue, and the shape of the point decides what the needle does as it passes. A cutting needle has sharp edges that slice through dense tissue such as skin and fascia. A reverse-cutting needle puts the flat surface on the inside of the curve so the cut is directed away from the wound edge. A taper needle has a rounded point that spreads the fibers apart rather than cutting them, and it is used in bowel, blood vessel, and liver. The curvature is quoted as a fraction of a circle, and the choice depends on how much room the surgeon has to rotate the wrist.

The needle is the sharpest object in the operating room and it carries the greatest risk to the operator. A needle-stick injury can transmit bloodborne infection from a patient to a member of the team, and the risk is highest with a needle that has just been in a deep vessel. The safety hazard is a needle left loose on the field, handed from hand to hand, or forgotten on a drape. The common operator error is to reach for a dropped needle with bare fingers instead of a forceps and a sharps container. The recommended practice is the neutral zone, in which the needle is placed on a tray by one person and picked up by another so that no two hands ever hold it at once. The characteristic alarm is the sudden absence of the needle from its counted mat, and the needle count must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Suturing is a two-handed skill, and the instruments that support it are as important as the strand. A needle holder is a hinged clamp with a short, strong jaw and a ratchet. Its jaws are cross-serrated or fitted with tungsten carbide inserts that grip the needle without letting it rotate. The needle is grasped about two thirds of the way from the point for a curved needle, so enough length is exposed to pass through tissue but the grip is not on the sharp end. The holder is rotated through the arc of the needle rather than pushed straight, because pushing a curved needle follows a different path and tears the tissue.

A surgical stapler replaces the tied loop of a suture with a small piece of bent wire, and its physics is a controlled plastic deformation. The staple is a U-shaped piece of metal held in a cartridge, with a driver above it and an anvil below it that has two curved depressions. As the legs are driven down they curl inward and close into a B shape. That B shape matters, because the closed staple must be tight enough to hold the tissue but loose enough not to crush the blood supply inside its loop. The height of the finished staple is set by the thickness of the tissue and by the gap designed into the cartridge, so the tissue must match the stapler. The correct staple height must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a cartridge too short will crush thick tissue and one too long will not close thin tissue.

The stapler family divides by the geometry of the closure it makes. A skin stapler fires one staple at a time across an incision, and it is fast, strong, and well tolerated, though its staples must be removed later with a dedicated extractor. A linear stapler places rows of staples across a length of tissue and divides it with a blade in the same instrument, and it is used to close the stomach, the bowel, and the lung. A circular stapler fires a ring of staples around a circular knife, and it is the instrument of the colorectal anastomosis, where a donut of tissue is cut from the inside and two bowel ends are joined by a ring the surgeon can inspect. A linear cutter combines rows of staples with a knife on the same pass, and its reload cartridges come in lengths and colors. The cartridge code must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Staplers fail in ways that are particular to mechanical devices, and a misfire is often discovered only when the tissue is already divided. A cartridge that is not fully seated, a safety interlock that has not been released, or a piece of tissue caught in the mechanism will produce an incomplete staple line. A malformed staple has its legs splayed outward instead of curled inward, so it holds nothing and leaves a hole. The characteristic signals are the feel and the sound of firing, because a completed line gives a firm sweep of the handle and a distinct click. The safety hazard is a staple line across a hollow organ that later leaks, and the common operator error is to fire without confirming that the anvil and cartridge are aligned and the tissue lies flat. Reloads are single-use, and a partly fired cartridge must be discarded because its remaining staples are no longer in a known position.

Skin clips are the simplest form of staple, and they are a device that the ward nurse as well as the surgeon must understand. A clip is a piece of wire shaped into a wide squared U, and it is applied across the skin with an applier that holds the two ends and bends them inward, so the clip lies over the wound edges like a bridge. The advantage is speed and strength on a scalp, an abdomen, or a limb. Removal is done with a clip remover that hooks the center of the clip, squeezes the ends apart, and lifts it away, and the common operator error is to pull a clip out with a forceps and scissors, which tears the fresh wound. The interval between clips and the timing of removal must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Surgical mesh answers a different problem, because it does not close a gap but reinforces a wall that cannot be trusted to hold. The physics is the distribution of load, because a flat sheet spreads the tension of the abdominal wall across a large area instead of concentrating it where sutures pass through tissue. A synthetic mesh is a woven or knitted sheet of polymer, usually polypropylene, polyester, or expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, and the knit pattern gives it a pore size, which is the distance between the strands. A macroporous mesh has pores larger than about 75 micrometers, a dimension that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and it allows immune cells and blood vessels to grow in so the mesh integrates with the tissue. A microporous mesh bridges the gap effectively but allows bacteria to hide in its interstices where immune cells cannot reach them.

Meshes come in several families, and the choice between them is a bet about infection. Permanent synthetic meshes are the workhorses of hernia repair and abdominal wall reconstruction, and they are strong and durable, but once infected they usually cannot be saved and must be removed. Bacteria adhere to the polymer and form a biofilm that no antibiotic can reach. Biological meshes are made from animal collagen or human donor tissue, processed to remove the cells, and they act as a scaffold that the body repopulates and eventually replaces with native tissue. They are useful in a contaminated field, but they are expensive, weaker at the outset, and can stretch. Composite meshes combine a permanent layer for strength with an absorbable or anti-adhesive layer that faces the bowel, so the mesh does not adhere to the intestine.

Sutures can tack the mesh at the corners and edges, but each suture is a point of tension that can pull through. Tacks fired from a mechanical device hold faster but can injure a nerve or a vessel if placed blindly. Some repairs rely on the pressure of the abdomen to hold the mesh, with only a few absorbable tacks to keep it in place during healing, and tissue glue has its own role in the groin. The common operator error is to cut a mesh to fit the defect exactly, because the mesh must overlap the defect by several centimeters to carry the load. A mesh that touches the skin is contaminated and should not be implanted, so the sterile field is not broken until the mesh is in place.

A hemostatic agent helps blood to clot where a suture or a ligature cannot reach, and its physical principle is either to concentrate the clotting machinery, to provide a scaffold for the clot, or to press on the bleeding surface. A topical hemostat is a dry sheet, sponge, or powder placed on the bleeding area. It works by absorbing water from the blood so that clotting factors and platelets become concentrated at the surface. Oxidized cellulose and oxidized regenerated cellulose are acidic sheets that swell into a brown gel when they meet blood, and the acidity itself helps to denature proteins and start the clotting cascade. A gelatin sponge is a porous foam that holds many times its own weight in blood and provides a physical plug. A collagen sponge or a microfibrillar collagen powder works in a similar way, with a surface that attracts platelets.

The hazards of hemostatic agents come from two properties, which are that they swell and that they are foreign material. An oxidized cellulose or gelatin sponge swells as it absorbs blood, and a sponge left in a confined space such as the spinal canal, the orbit, or a closed joint can press on a nerve or a vessel. The resorbable sponges are broken down over weeks, but a large mass of them can become a nidus for infection. The common operator error is to pack a wound and close it without removing the excess, so the retained mass later mimics an abscess. A powder sprinkled into a blind bleeding cavity can also clump and swell, so it must be delivered to the bleeding point rather than poured in.

Beyond the passive agents stand the active ones, which supply the components of the clotting reaction rather than merely concentrating them. Thrombin is an enzyme that converts fibrinogen into fibrin, and applied with a gelatin or collagen carrier it forms a clot within seconds, but it is inactive in a patient whose blood has no fibrinogen. A fibrin sealant supplies both fibrinogen and thrombin in two syringes that meet at the tip, and the mixture forms a gel that glues tissue surfaces and seals small leaks. Topical powders and sprays are designed for the broad oozing surface of a burn, a liver bed, or a tumor resection, where no single vessel can be ligated. The characteristic signal of these products is the rapid formation of a firm clot, and their storage temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Bone wax is a special hemostat for bleeding from cut bone, and it is a device whose misuse is a classic error. The wax is a malleable mixture based on beeswax, and it works purely by mechanical tamponade. It is pressed into the open ends of bleeding vessels and the spaces of cancellous bone, blocking the flow without any clotting chemistry. The problem is that bone wax is not absorbed, so it remains in the bone forever, and it can interfere with the union of a fracture, act as a foreign body, and increase the risk of infection. The safety hazard is the patient who has wax left in a sternum or a long bone and later develops a chronic infection or a non-union. The common operator error is to smear wax across a whole bone surface instead of pressing a small amount into the specific bleeding point, so the amount used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Drains are the last element of a closure, because a closed wound that accumulates fluid under pressure will open or become infected, and a drain gives that fluid a path out. The simplest drain is a flat strip of soft rubber or plastic, called an open drain, which works by capillary action and gravity, so fluid flows along its surface into a dressing. A closed suction drain is a tube with holes along its end and a bulb or canister that maintains a gentle negative pressure, and the pressure difference is perhaps 50 to 100 millimeters of mercury, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The relationship between the drain and the closure is intimate, because the drain site is a hole in the sterile barrier and a path for bacteria. A drain is therefore brought out through a separate stab incision rather than the main wound where possible. The safety hazard is a drain that erodes, falls out, or stays too long, and the common operator error is to anchor it so loosely that it migrates or so tightly that it cuts the skin.

A drain is useful only while it is patent, and its failure modes are easy to miss. The tube can kink, the holes can be blocked by clot or omentum, the suction bulb can be left uncompressed, and the canister can fill so that the negative pressure is lost. Each of these turns an apparently working drain into a closed cavity with a foreign body inside. The characteristic signal of a blocked drain is a sudden fall in output while the wound swells and the patient becomes febrile. The common operator error is to flush the drain blindly with saline, which can push infection into the cavity rather than clear the tube. A drain is also a retained item if its anchoring suture is removed and the tube is forgotten, so it is counted with the sponges and the needles. The count at the beginning of the case, at the first closure of a cavity, and at the final skin closure is the standard that prevents a retained item.

The hospital-grade supply of closing materials depends on an infrastructure that a small clinic does not have. The central sterile services department receives the reusable instruments, cleans them of blood and tissue, inspects them, packs them with an indicator, and sterilizes them. A steam sterilizer at 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 minutes, or at 121 degrees Celsius for about 30 minutes, is the common cycle for wrapped instruments, temperatures and times that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A tightly wrapped or overfilled pack fails even when the sterilizer works, and a pack on a damp shelf loses sterility over time.

The consumables of this chapter are numerous, and each has a defined life and a defined failure. Suture strands and needles, staple cartridges, skin clips, clip removers, mesh sheets, tacks, hemostatic sheets and powders, bone wax, drains and canisters, needle counter mats, and sharps containers pass through a case once and are replaced. The reusable closing instruments, which include the needle holders, forceps, scissors, staple removers, and the staplers themselves, need their own care. Blood and saline left in the joint of a needle holder corrode the hinge, and a dropped stapler must be inspected and its alignment verified before use. Cleaning is with the approved detergent in an ultrasonic bath or by hand with a soft brush, followed by rinsing, drying, lubrication where the maker allows, and sterilization by the correct cycle. The characteristic sign of a worn needle holder is a needle that rotates in the jaws under load, and the replacement criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Before any closing material is used, the operator must perform a short series of checks that takes seconds and prevents the worst errors. The package must be intact, dry, within its expiry date, and marked with a sterilization indicator that has changed as expected. The strand must be inspected for fraying, for a kink that will weaken it, and for discoloration, and the needle must be firmly attached and straight, because a bent needle makes a curved path. A staple cartridge must be seated fully, must match the tissue thickness, and must be of the type the case plan calls for, and the stapler must be checked for the alignment of the anvil. A mesh must be opened only onto the sterile field and must never be touched by an ungloved hand, and each of these checks must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the mobile or frontier clinic the same needs are met with a much smaller inventory, and the first thing given up is the choice of material. The field kit usually carries one or two sutures only, most often a braided absorbable for deep tissue and a monofilament nylon for the skin. The size is chosen by the tissue rather than by a catalogue, with 2-0 and 3-0 for fascia and 4-0 for skin being a common range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The needles are more often reusable, and they are sharpened, straightened, and inspected between cases, so they are duller than a new swaged needle and demand more force and a firmer grasp. Where a manufactured suture is unavailable, the team may use a monofilament made for another purpose, but any substitution must be sterile, of a known diameter, and tested for knot security before it is trusted in a wound. The characteristic alarm of the field is the snap of a suture under tension, and the common operator error is to compensate for a dull needle or a weak strand by pulling harder, which tears the tissue.

The field variant of this chapter is less a device than a method, because sterile technique is what makes an affordable closure safe. Without a steam autoclave, the instruments and the reusable needles are sterilized in a pressure cooker at about 121 degrees Celsius for about 30 minutes, a cycle that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The sterile field is built from a boiled or chemically disinfected cloth, and the operator works with gloves if any are available and with a strict no-touch technique if they are not. Skin preparation with an alcohol or chlorhexidine solution, a clean drape, and a firm separation between the clean and dirty hands are the substitute for the missing operating room. The characteristic signal of a break in technique is a wound that becomes red and hot on the second or third day.

What the field clinic gives up beyond the choice of suture is the mechanical closure and the advanced reinforcement. A linear or circular stapler requires cartridges, calibration, and a supply chain, so the field surgeon performs a hand-sewn anastomosis with a continuous or interrupted suture, which is slower and demands more skill but needs nothing beyond a needle and a strand. Mesh is often unavailable or unaffordable, so a hernia is repaired by tissue approximation with a suture, which has a higher recurrence rate but leaves no foreign body and no biofilm to remove when it becomes infected. The hemostatic sheet and the fibrin sealant are replaced by pressure, by packing, by a ligature, and by the oldest agent of all, which is a hot instrument applied to a bleeding point. Adhesive strips and tissue adhesive become the field closure for a small clean laceration, and they spare the suture entirely when the wound edges can be brought together without tension.

The field variant demands more of the operator in three respects, which are skill, judgment, and stock discipline. A hand-tied knot must hold on the first attempt, because there is no assistant with a stapler to rescue a leaking anastomosis, and a wound closed under tension will fail in a patient who cannot return for a second operation. The judgment is about when not to close primarily, because a contaminated wound is better left open and packed than closed over an infection. The stock discipline is about expiry and storage, because a suture package that has been damp, sun-baked, or crushed in a vehicle is no longer guaranteed. The characteristic signal of poor stock control is a case that is underway when the last 3-0 strand is found to be frayed.

To summarize, closure is a mechanical bet placed on biology, because every strand, staple, mesh, and hemostatic plug must carry load only until the tissue can carry it alone. The material decides how long that help lasts, the needle and the instrument decide how cleanly it is delivered, and the knots and the staple line decide whether the help holds. Mesh and hemostatic agents extend the same principle to reinforcement and to bleeding, and both bring a foreign body whose infection and swelling must be respected. The hospital version buys certainty with cartridges, biological indicators, and a sterile supply chain, while the field version buys access with a needle, a reusable strand, and a sterilizing pot. In every setting, the operator's checks, the counts, and the confirmation of every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol are what turn the hardware into a safe closure.

# Chapter 44 — Surgical Drapes, Gowns, Gloves, and Counting Systems

A sterile field is not a place but a boundary, and the drapes, gowns, and gloves of an operating room exist to hold that boundary against two things that always travel together, microorganisms and fluid. A barrier resists that passage by two separate mechanisms, and confusing them is the origin of most breaches of technique. The first is a mechanical screen, in which a fabric stops a particle larger than its pores, and the second is a resistance to liquid, in which a surface repels water even where the openings are wide enough to admit it. A loosely woven cloth can screen dust and still allow a thin film of blood to wick through by capillary action, while a non-woven fabric can be nearly impenetrable to fluid and still fold into a pack the size of a hand. The consequence is that a barrier is only as good as its weakest point and only for as long as it stays dry, so a drape that is intact at the first incision can become a wet channel within minutes. Every decision about draping is therefore a decision about fluid, time, and contact.

The fabrics themselves fall into two families, and the difference between them is the difference between a net and a sheet. A woven textile is made by interlacing threads, so it has a regular grid of pores and a tendency to wick fluid along its threads from a wet area to a dry one. A non-woven textile is made by bonding fibers into a mat whose random orientation removes the straight capillary path that a woven cloth provides. Barrier performance is stated as a resistance to liquid under pressure, measured as the height of a column of water that the fabric holds before water appears on the far side, and as a weight in grams per square meter, and a surgical drape commonly falls between 20 and 60 grams per square meter, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The choice between a heavier and a lighter fabric is the choice between a stronger resistance to fluid and an easier drape that fails sooner when it is wet.

Drapes are shaped for the body part they cover, and the shape is a mechanical answer to a specific problem. A plain sheet is the universal barrier and is laid first to establish the field, a fenestrated drape carries a window that frames the incision, and a split drape opens along one edge so that it can be wrapped around a limb or a head without lifting what is already in place. An adhesive edge bonds the fabric to the skin, and its purpose is not comfort but the elimination of the gap through which fluid and organisms travel from unprepared skin to the wound. An aperture is often surrounded by a reinforced ring or a fluid collection pouch, which turns the window into a shallow basin and directs irrigation and blood away from the operator's feet. The operator must confirm after opening the pack that the drape matches the planned procedure, because a drape of the wrong shape invites improvisation at the worst moment.

Draping follows a direction, and the direction is always from the sterile toward the unsterile. The first sheet is placed at the incision and the field is enlarged outward, so that the operator never reaches across a covered area to place a new one. The drape is handled by its corners and its cuffs, and the hands stay inside the sterile boundary while the fabric unfolds under its own weight rather than being shaken open above the field. Once placed, the drape defines the rules of the room, because the table top is sterile, the hanging part below the table level is not, and the boundary between them must never be crossed by an instrument, a hand, or a cable. A drape that has been lifted and repositioned has lost its contact with the reason for its placement, and a drape over a patient who moves or breathes must be checked again. The common error is to reach over an unprepared area to retrieve a dropped instrument, which drags the sleeve across a contaminated surface, and the correct response is to step back and ask for a replacement.

The hazards of draping are fluid, fire, and concealment. Strike-through is the moment fluid reaches the far side of the fabric, and it converts the barrier into a bridge, so any wet spot or dampness felt through the glove is treated as a contamination of the field and covered with a fresh drape. Fluid collects in the folds of a drape and in the pouch of a fenestration, and a pool that sits against the skin macerates it, hides bleeding, and can spill when the patient is moved. An oxygen-enriched atmosphere under a drape is a fire risk when an energy device or a laser is used nearby, and it must be managed according to the local fire protocol, with every concentration, flow rate, and alarm threshold confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Cables and cords are laid over the drape rather than under it, because a cord that crosses the field can drag without warning. The characteristic warning of a draping failure is a change in appearance rather than a sound, a spreading wet area, a stain at the edge of an adhesive strip, or a gap that appears when the patient is repositioned.

A surgical gown is a personal barrier, and its performance is judged at the places where the body meets fluid. The fabric is rated by the level of liquid and viral penetration it resists, and the rating rises with the amount of fluid, the pressure behind it, and the duration of contact, with the highest level reserved for procedures that produce a large volume of blood under pressure. Reinforcement panels are added at the forearms and the chest because those are the surfaces that press against a wet field, and a gown is only as protective as the part of it that touches the patient. The closure runs down the back and is secured with ties, a hook-and-loop strip, or a wrap-around flap, and the back of the gown is never considered sterile because it is not designed as a barrier. Cuffs are usually knitted, which is comfortable and absorbent, and that same absorbency is why a saturated cuff must be changed rather than ignored.

The gown fails first where it is wettest, and the sequence of failure is predictable. Fluid wicks up a woven sleeve, spreads across a reinforcement panel, and reaches the skin at the forearm or the abdomen, often without the wearer noticing because the inner surface is already damp with sweat. A gown that is soaked at the front and the sleeves is no longer a barrier even though it is still intact, and the only remedy is to leave the field, remove the gown, perform hand hygiene, and put on a fresh one. The common error is to keep working in a wet gown because the case is nearly finished, and the second common error is to tie the gown at the front, which pulls the sterile front panel open and exposes the wearer. The characteristic warning is the cold, heavy feeling of a saturated sleeve and the visible darkening that spreads upward from the cuff, and both are signals to change rather than reasons to continue.

A surgical glove is a thin elastomer film that is stretched over the hand, and its protection depends on the film staying continuous under tension. Natural rubber latex is the most elastic of the common materials, so it conforms to the fingers, seals at the wrist, and recovers its shape after being stretched, but its proteins are the cause of the most serious glove allergy. Nitrile is a synthetic rubber that resists oils, punctures, and many chemicals better than latex and contains no natural rubber protein, which makes it the usual choice for the latex-sensitive wearer, though it is less elastic and tears more readily at a sharp edge. Vinyl is the least expensive and the weakest barrier, since it is stiff and tears easily. The strength of any film is stated as a tensile measurement, a resistance to puncture, and an average thickness that is often near 0.2 millimeter at the fingertip, and every such specification must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Gloves are supplied sterile and non-sterile, powdered and non-powdered, and the choice is a clinical decision rather than a matter of convenience. A sterile surgical glove is packed as a pair, sized to the hand, and put on by the closed technique so that the outer surface is never touched by bare skin, while an examination glove is supplied in a box and may be non-sterile. Powder was once used to make a tight glove easier to pull on, but the particles it leaves in a wound can provoke inflammation and adhesion formation, and the powder also carries latex protein into the air and into the tissues, so non-powdered gloves are now the standard wherever they are available. Size matters physically, because a glove that is too tight restricts the blood flow of the hand, tires the fingers, and tears at the cuff, while one that is too loose wrinkles at the fingertips and reduces the sense of touch. Double gloving adds a second film that can be removed when it is contaminated. The common error is to choose a glove by habit rather than by fit, and the characteristic warning of a failing glove is the sudden looseness, the damp feeling at a fingertip, or a visible tear at the web of the thumb.

The allergy problem is a hazard of the glove itself, and it takes two distinct forms that must not be confused. Immediate hypersensitivity to natural rubber latex proteins is a systemic reaction that can begin within minutes of contact and can progress to difficulty in breathing, a fall in blood pressure, and shock, and it is a medical emergency rather than a skin complaint. Delayed contact dermatitis is a reaction to the chemicals used to accelerate the curing of the rubber, and it appears hours later as redness and itching at the back of the hands. Powder increases the risk of the immediate form because it binds the protein and carries it into the air as an aerosol that a sensitive person can inhale, so a facility that cares for a latex-sensitive patient or worker should remove powdered gloves from the area entirely. The response to a known latex allergy is a latex-free environment, with nitrile or another synthetic glove for every person in the room. The characteristic warning is the itching, the rash, or the wheeze that appears soon after a glove is put on, and the common error is to dismiss it as dryness of the skin.

The cap, the mask, and the shoe cover are small barriers with specific jobs, and each has a physical reason for its shape. A surgical cap contains hair and skin scales so that they do not fall into the field, and it must cover the whole crown rather than sit on the back of the head. A mask filters the air that passes through it by three mechanisms, direct interception of larger particles, inertial impaction of particles that cannot follow the airstream around the fibers, and diffusion of the smallest particles, and a layer of electrostatic charge increases the capture of the fine ones, which is why a mask must not be crushed, folded, or wetted before use. A surgical mask is tested on particles of about 1 micrometer and is expected to capture a high proportion of them, and the exact efficiency figure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The mask works in two directions at once, protecting the wearer from a splash and the patient from the wearer's own respiratory droplets, and a mask worn below the nose, left hanging around the neck, or reused for a second case does neither. A valved mask makes exhalation easier but allows unfiltered air to leave, so it is not a substitute for source control in a sterile field.

The counting system is an accounting device, and it exists because a human being cannot see the whole of a wound and cannot remember every item that passes through it. Counting works by comparison, since a number recorded before the case begins is compared with a number recorded at fixed points during and after it, and that comparison is the only evidence available that nothing has been left behind. The items counted are the instruments on the tray, the swabs and sponges used to mop and to pack, the needles loaded onto holders, and the blades fitted to handles. A count is not a formality but a control, and its reliability depends on the same principle as any other measurement, namely that the same method is used every time so that a difference means something. The count must be written down rather than remembered, and the record must stay visible to both counters.

The count is taken at fixed moments, and the moments are chosen so that no item can leave the field unrecorded. The first count is taken before the incision, when the tray is complete and the field is still clean, and it establishes the number against which every later count is compared. The second is taken before a cavity or a deep layer is closed, the third before the skin is closed, and the fourth at the end of the procedure, and a local protocol may add a count when a new item is added or a member of the team changes. The scrub person and the circulating person count together, aloud, item by item, using the same order and the same names every time. Interruptions spoil a count, so the counting pair stops speaking to anyone else until the number is agreed. Swabs are counted by type and by number, needles are counted as loaded and as returned, and a needle that has been bent or broken is kept and counted as a separate item. Every count threshold and every check point a local protocol defines must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When a count does not match, the discrepancy is treated as a retained item until it is proved otherwise, and the proof is never the word of a tired person. The first action is to stop the closure, to keep the field and all the used materials untouched, and to recount the same category in the same way. The second action is a search of the field, the floor, the drapes, the suction canister, the trash, and the linen, and the third is a search of the patient, which is a clinical decision made by the surgeon. A radiograph is taken when the missing item is radiopaque and the search has failed, and the patient is not closed and the team is not dismissed until the item is found or its absence is established by an agreed method. The incident is documented with the item named and the times of each count. The characteristic alarm of the counting system is precisely this mismatch, and the common error is to accept a verbal explanation such as the swab is probably in the bin without looking in the bin.

A retained surgical item is called a never event because it should not happen at all, and its mechanism is always the same combination of a small object, a deep cavity, and a count that was believed rather than performed. A sponge is the commonest offender because it is soft, it changes shape when it is soaked, and it may be indistinguishable from the tissue around it once it is buried, while a needle, a blade, a screw, or a broken instrument tip can travel beyond the reach of a finger. The consequence is not merely a foreign body, since a retained sponge can cause infection, obstruction, and erosion into a vessel or a bowel. The radiograph is the instrument that finds such an item when the search of the field has failed, and its physics is the same absorption of X-rays that produces every other image. A radiopaque marker is woven into or bonded onto a surgical sponge so that it casts a distinct shadow, and the marker must be dense enough to be seen through the patient and the table. A single film of the whole operative area is taken, and in some protocols a second view is added in another direction, because an object can be hidden along one projection and revealed along another. The technique has limits, since a very small needle fragment or a non-radiopaque material may be invisible. Every exposure setting, projection, and detection threshold used in this search must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to accept an unread film as evidence that the field is clear.

Reusable drapes and gowns are reprocessed rather than discarded, and their life is limited by the gradual loss of the barrier that makes them worth keeping. The laundering cycle uses water at a temperature set by the protocol, commonly between 60 and 71 degrees Celsius, a detergent chosen for the fabric, and a rinse that removes the residue of both, and every temperature, concentration, and cycle time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Heat and mechanical agitation shrink the fibers, open the weave, and wear away any water-repellent finish, so a gown or a drape that has been through many cycles looks sound and still lets fluid through. Reusable woven textiles are inspected after every wash for holes, thin areas, broken seams, and lost ties, and the person inspecting must hold the fabric against a light to see the weave that the eye misses in a folded pile. Patches, darns, and replacements of ties and hook-and-loop closures are repairs of convenience rather than of barrier. The number of wash cycles a fabric can tolerate is stated by its maker, and the count of cycles must be recorded so that the item is withdrawn before its barrier fails.

Items labeled for single use are not designed to survive reprocessing, and the reason is physical rather than commercial. A single-use drape is often made from a light non-woven fabric whose fibers are bonded with a finish that is removed by detergent and heat, and a single-use gown may have a coating that cracks when it is dried and folded again. A single-use glove cannot be laundered, because the film absorbs the detergent, loses its elasticity, and develops pinholes that are invisible to the wearer, so a washed glove is a false barrier. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has set conditions under which some single-use devices may be reprocessed by a regulated third party, and those conditions include validation of cleaning, sterilization, and function. The World Health Organization advises against the reuse of single-use items wherever supplies allow an alternative, and the practical rule is that an item must be reprocessed only when its maker permits it and when the method has been validated. Every such permission and every cycle parameter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to treat a package that still looks intact as proof that the item inside is still sterile.

Sterile drapes, gowns, and gloves arrive in packs that are themselves devices, since the pack must let the sterilizing agent in, keep organisms out, and open without contaminating what is inside. The central sterile services department (CSSD) assembles the pack, adds a chemical indicator that changes with the cycle and a biological indicator where the protocol requires one, and records the load so that every item can be traced to the cycle that processed it. The pack is stored in a dry, cool, dust-free place, handled gently, and kept away from sunlight, because compression, moisture, and ultraviolet light all degrade the wrap and the contents. A pack that is dropped, punctured, damp, or past its expiration date is treated as unsterile. Opening the pack is a technique in itself, since the outer wrap is peeled back without reaching over the sterile contents, and the sterile person lifts the item from the inside of the wrap. A hospital steam autoclave for these packs commonly runs at 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 minutes or at 121 degrees Celsius for about 15 minutes, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic warning of a storage failure is a wrap that feels damp, a seal that has lifted, or a stain on the paper, and the common error is to use the last pack in the cupboard because the cupboard is empty.

The field version of the sterile field begins with the recognition that a mobile clinic cannot carry a sterile pack for every case and often has no autoclave at all. The drape becomes a woven cotton sheet or a length of cloth that is washed, boiled, dried in the sun, and folded for the next patient, and its barrier is weak because a woven fabric wicks fluid along its threads. What the field version gives up is the non-woven barrier with a measured resistance to liquid, the adhesive edge that seals to the skin, the fenestration that frames the incision, and the single-use pack that guarantees a known performance. What it demands instead is a discipline of its own, since the cloth must be washed with soap and clean water, rinsed, boiled for the full time the local protocol requires, often 15 to 20 minutes after the water returns to a rolling boil, and dried completely in direct sunlight or over a fire. That boiling time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a cloth that is merely warm is not sterile and a cloth that is still damp will grow organisms in storage. The field operator must also accept a smaller field and a shorter case, because the barrier is only trustworthy while it is dry. The common error is to hang a damp cloth in a closed cupboard overnight and to treat it as ready in the morning.

In the field, the gown is often a clean cotton gown or a plastic apron, and the glove is the item that decides how safe the case can be. A clean cotton gown can be washed and boiled and will serve as a barrier against gross contamination, but it is not a fluid barrier, so the wearer must avoid pressing against a wet field and must change it when it is soaked. A glove is the one item that must never be reused, because the film stretches, loses its elasticity, and hides pinholes that no eye can see, so a washed glove is a false promise of protection. What can be washed is the woven cloth, the cotton gown, the reusable instrument wrap, and the linen, and what must be burned is the single-use item that cannot be cleaned, including the used swab, the soiled dressing, and the used examination glove. What must never be reused is the needle, the blade, the syringe, the single-use glove, and the single-use drape or gown whose wrap has been opened, because their safety depends on a property that washing cannot restore. The characteristic warning in this setting is the same as in the hospital, a wet gown, a torn glove, and a count that does not reconcile, and the common error is to stretch a limited supply of gloves by reusing them.

Counting in the field is harder because there are fewer people and fewer items. A single operator may be both the scrub person and the circulating person, so the count must be written on a card or a board that stays in view and must be repeated aloud. The field count starts before the incision, is repeated before every closure, and is finished before the wound is dressed. The radiograph that a hospital uses to find a retained item is often unavailable, and when it is unavailable the operator must rely on a careful search, on the use of a fixed number of swabs with a known total, and on the rule that no closure begins until the count reconciles. Every count threshold and every local protocol for a missing item must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because the field version has no second system to catch what the first one missed. The common error is to count from memory at the end of a long day, when fatigue makes the number agree with what the operator hopes rather than with what is on the tray, and the characteristic warning is a swab that cannot be placed.

To summarize, the sterile field is a boundary that is held by drapes, gowns, and gloves, and it is defeated by fluid rather than by visible dirt. Drapes and gowns work as mechanical screens and as liquid barriers, and their performance is stated in grams per square meter and in a resistance to water under pressure, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Woven fabrics wick along their threads, non-woven fabrics block by random fibers, adhesive edges close the gap to the skin, and a dry intact barrier becomes a channel the moment fluid reaches the far side. Gloves are elastomer films whose protection depends on continuity and fit, and their materials carry different risks, with natural rubber latex able to cause an immediate and dangerous allergy while nitrile avoids the protein. Caps, masks, and shoe covers complete the barrier, and a mask protects in both directions only when it is fitted, dry, and worn over the nose and mouth. The counting system is an accounting device rather than a ritual, and it works by comparing a written number taken before the incision with numbers taken before the closure of a cavity, before the skin is closed, and at the end, with a mismatch treated as a retained item until a search and, where it is available, a radiograph prove otherwise. In the field, cloth is washed, boiled, and dried, the count is kept on a card by one pair of hands, and the glove is the one item that must never be reused, because a barrier that has lost its property cannot be restored by hope.

# Chapter 45 — Obstetrics and Neonatology

Obstetric and newborn equipment answers three questions, and each rests on a different physical principle. The first is how the unborn child tolerates labor, answered with reflected sound, and the second is how the uterus contracts and how birth progresses, answered by pressure against a belt or by a trained hand. The third is whether the newborn can breathe and stay warm, answered by pressure, radiant heat, convection, and light. A listener who understands these principles recognizes a failing machine before it stops working.

The handheld Doppler holds a crystal that vibrates at 2 to 3 million cycles per second, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Moving blood and moving valves reflect that sound at a slightly different frequency, so the device produces an audible whoosh and a rate. The probe is angled with gel to exclude air, and a flat battery is the characteristic failure, while the common error is to mistake the mother's pulse for the fetal heart. The cardiotocograph records the fetal heart rate and the contraction pattern together, so it is two instruments in one housing. One channel turns the Doppler signal into a rate, and the other uses a tocodynamometer, a strain gauge pressed against the fundus by a belt so that the changing curve of the abdomen becomes an electrical signal. The characteristic alarm is a loss of signal from a slipped belt or a dried probe, and the common error is to read a flat trace from slack belts as reassuring.

The trace is read as a baseline, a variability, accelerations, and decelerations. The baseline rate normally lies between 110 and 160 beats per minute, and variability of 5 to 25 beats per minute is reassuring, ranges to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Early decelerations mirror the contraction, variable decelerations fall and recover abruptly, and late decelerations begin after the peak and suggest a placenta short of oxygen. The characteristic alarm is a sustained rate below 100 beats per minute, a threshold to confirm in the same way, and the common error is to treat one number as a diagnosis. The external tocodynamometer measures only the changing shape of the abdominal wall, so it shows when a contraction happens but not how strong it is. An internal pressure catheter is a fluid-filled tube whose tip lies in the amniotic cavity, and it turns the pressure of that column into millimeters of mercury, though it can be used only after the membranes rupture and it carries the hazards of infection, bleeding, and perforation.

Fetal monitors are cleaned on the parts that touch the patient. The belts are wiped and hung to dry, because a damp belt becomes a reservoir of organisms, and each transducer face is cleaned with the agent the maker approves but never immersed or autoclaved, because water and heat destroy the crystal. Transducers, belts, cables, and leg plates are consumables whose replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to coil a cable tightly around the housing, which breaks the fine wires and produces an intermittent trace that looks like a problem with the fetus. A delivery bed is mechanics rather than electronics. The mattress sits on a frame raised and lowered by a hydraulic pump or an electric motor, and the backrest, head section, and leg supports adjust separately so that the mother can sit, lie back, or be placed with her legs in stirrups. A removable section at the foot opens a gap where the baby is received, and the hand grips and side rails support her between contractions, while the hydraulic pedal and the electric control must lower the patient quickly in an emergency.

The hazards of the delivery bed are mechanical. A bed whose brakes are off can roll while a woman pushes, and a frame that drops when a hydraulic seal fails can injure mother or attendant, while hooks, mattress gaps, and unlocked side rails are entrapment points. The schedule covers the seals or the motor and battery, the locking pins, and the brakes, with intervals to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to treat the bed as a storage shelf, which damages the mechanism and delays the next delivery. Forceps are two crossed levers whose fulcrum lies between the blades. Each blade curves to follow the head and the birth canal, and the shanks cross so that a pull on the handles becomes a controlled pull on the head, while an outlet forceps has a gentle pelvic curve, a mid-cavity instrument is longer, and a rotation forceps has a sliding lock for turning a head that faces the wrong way. The hazards are maternal tearing, nerve injury, and skull fracture, and the common error is to apply the blades blindly and then pull hard.

The vacuum extractor replaces grip with suction, and its physics is the difference between the pressure inside the cup and the pressure of the atmosphere. The cup is pressed against the scalp and a pump removes air beneath it, so the pressure difference holds the scalp and the skull, and a metal cup can rotate the head while a soft cup is kinder to the scalp but slips more easily. A typical working pressure is about 0.8 bar, roughly 600 millimeters of mercury below atmospheric pressure, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Traction is applied only during a contraction and along the axis of the canal, and the characteristic sign of failure is the cup detaching with a pop, while the common error is to continue after a detachment. Bruising or blood beneath the scalp warns of a subgaleal hemorrhage, which can hide a large loss of blood inside a newborn and is a reason to stop. A perished seal or a cracked cup holds on the gauge but not on the head, and the common error is to use either forceps or vacuum as a substitute for a decision that should have been made earlier.

An episiotomy is a controlled cut, and the instruments must be sharp and complete. The scissors are blunt-tipped and angled, so the blade can be introduced without cutting the baby or the rectum, and the repair set holds a needle holder, toothed forceps, tissue forceps, scissors, and a retractor. The repair is a knot, because the suture brings tissue together without strangling it, and deeper layers close first, while the hazards are a needle stick, a retained needle or swab, and a repair drawn too tight. The common error is to count needles only at the end. Delivery instruments are reprocessed in the central sterile services department (CSSD) or in a small unit following the same logic, which begins with cleaning rather than sterilization. Blood, tissue, and dried secretion are removed first, because no sterilizing agent reaches a covered surface, so instruments are opened, disassembled, and washed before packing. The sterilizer then uses steam under pressure, and a typical cycle for wrapped instruments is 134 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the common error is to release a load that has not passed its tests.

Suction clears the airway of a newborn by pressure difference. A bulb syringe produces a weak suction by hand, a trap collects material in a bottle while wall suction works, and a mechanical unit may run from a foot pedal or a battery, while the pressure must be limited because the lining of a newborn airway is delicate. A typical limit is 80 to 100 millimeters of mercury, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the hazards are a fall in heart rate, bleeding, and a collapsed lung, while the common error is to suction deeply and repeatedly after a normal birth. A radiant warmer heats a newborn by radiation. A heated element at the top emits infrared energy that crosses the air and is absorbed by the first surface it meets, the skin of the baby. The warmer is controlled by hand or automatically by a skin probe on the abdomen, and a typical servo setting holds the skin at about 36.5 degrees Celsius, to confirm in the same way, while its alarms announce a probe that has fallen off, a skin temperature that is too high, and a heater that does not respond. The common error is to leave a baby under it with the probe detached.

The bag and mask displace a known volume of gas. A self-inflating bag refills because its elasticity pulls it open, so it works even when no gas supply is connected, and a relief valve releases gas above a set pressure, typically 30 to 40 centimeters of water, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A newborn bag holds roughly 240 milliliters, and the mask is chosen by size so that it covers mouth and nose without covering the eyes. The characteristic sign of a poor seal is no chest movement and no rise in heart rate, and the common errors are an adult bag and a forgotten oxygen supply. An oxygen blender mixes air and oxygen to any concentration between about 21 and 100 per cent, to confirm in the same way. Too much oxygen narrows the vessels of the immature eye and damages the lung. Typical saturation targets are about 60 to 65 per cent at one minute and about 85 to 95 per cent by ten minutes, to confirm in the same way, and the common error is to leave the blender at its default while a probe on the right hand watches the oxygen.

The resuscitation area is checked before every birth, because a device found empty has already failed. The check covers the warmth of the platform, the gas supply and blender setting, the suction with its pressure limit, the bag and masks in the sizes needed, and a bag that refills briskly when squeezed. The airway set holds a laryngoscope with a straight blade, tubes of 2.5, 3.0, and 3.5 millimeters of internal diameter, a stylet, a carbon dioxide detector, and suction catheters. Expired consumables, discharged batteries, and a missing probe are the failures a checklist prevents, and the common error is to assume that someone else will carry the equipment in. An incubator makes a warm, humid, quiet, oxygen-enriched environment for a baby who cannot hold its own temperature. Its physics is convection and conduction, because a fan moves air over a heating element and through a water reservoir, and the warmed air circulates inside a double wall that reduces loss to the room. Typical settings are an air temperature near 34 degrees Celsius and a relative humidity near 60 per cent, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while its alarms announce a high temperature, a low temperature, a probe failure, and a power failure. The common error is to leave the hood ajar, which destroys the environment the machine has built.

Incubator maintenance fights water, dust, and organisms. The reservoir is emptied and refilled with sterile water, because a standing pool of warm water grows bacteria and can cause pneumonia in the infant, and the humidifier and tubing are cleaned or replaced at the maker's interval. The air filter is washed or changed, the fan is listened to for noise, the skin probe is checked against a reference thermometer, and the heater and thermostat are verified, while the mattress, porthole sleeves, probes, and tubing are consumables whose replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to set the alarm limits so wide that they never sound. Phototherapy treats jaundice by turning bilirubin into a form that can be excreted, and its physics is the absorption of light by a molecule. Bilirubin in the skin absorbs light most strongly between about 460 and 490 nanometers, which is blue-green, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the absorbed energy converts the pigment into water-soluble products that liver and kidney can clear. The source may be fluorescent tubes, a panel of light emitting diodes (LED), a halogen lamp, or a fiberoptic blanket, and the useful measure is not apparent brightness but irradiance, the power delivered per unit area in the blue part of the spectrum. A typical therapeutic irradiance is 30 microwatts per square centimeter per nanometer, to confirm in the same way, and the common error is to judge treatment by the color of the light.

Two things must accompany phototherapy. The eyes are covered with opaque shields fixed so that they cannot slip over the nose and obstruct breathing, and the shields come off at every feed and examination so that the eyes can be inspected. The baby loses water through the skin under the lamp, so feeding is increased, weight and urine output are followed, and the temperature is checked, while the lamps age and a tube that has run for its rated hours produces far less light than its label promises. An irradiance meter is the only honest check, and the common error is to hang the lamp at a convenient height without measuring the dose at the skin. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) keeps a newborn's lungs open between breaths, and its physics is a pressure held in the airway that prevents the small air sacs from collapsing at every expiration. A gas is made to escape against a known resistance, and the pressure that builds behind it does the work. In the bubble system the expiratory limb sits under a measured depth of water, so a tube held 5 centimeters below the surface produces about 5 centimeters of water of pressure, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A typical starting pressure is 5 to 6 centimeters of water, to confirm in the same way, and the common errors are a leaking mouth, oversized prongs, and a pressure raised to chase a low saturation.

Nasal continuous positive airway pressure depends on its interface and humidifier. The prongs are sized to fill the nostril without blanching it, and the cap and straps hold the interface without pulling the nose out of shape, while the position is changed and the skin inspected commonly every 4 hours, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The nasal septum is the structure at risk, because steady pressure on the columella produces necrosis that heals slowly. The characteristic alarm is a low or high pressure signal from the driver, and the common error is to accept a large leak and raise the flow instead of refitting the interface. Weight and length are recorded at birth, and the instruments that measure them are easily fooled. A digital infant scale uses a load cell whose resistance changes as it bends under a weight, and it is zeroed before each use and checked with a known weight at an interval to confirm in the same way. A spring scale is more robust in the field and less precise, and both types must stand on a hard level surface, while a measuring board has a fixed head piece and a sliding foot piece and the baby lies with the legs straightened. The common error is to weigh a baby in a wet diaper and a heavy blanket without subtracting the tare.

A newborn needs a thermometer accurate at the low end of the scale. A thermistor thermometer measures the change in resistance of a small bead as it warms, and it is the reference method in the axilla, where it stays long enough for the reading to stop rising, while an infrared thermometer estimates temperature from the radiation emitted by skin and is fast but misled by a cold surface, a draft, or a probe held too far away. A low-reading thermometer confirms hypothermia, because an ordinary clinical thermometer may not register below 35 degrees Celsius, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to accept a number that is still climbing. Keeping a newborn warm is a chain of small measures, and every link matters. The delivery room is warmed before the birth, the baby is dried at once with a warm towel while the wet towel is discarded, and a hat covers the head, the largest surface for heat loss. A skin-to-skin position on the mother's chest uses her body as the heater, and a typical delivery room temperature is 25 to 26 degrees Celsius, to confirm in the same way, while the characteristic warning is a temperature below 36.5 degrees Celsius, to confirm in the same way. The common error is to delay drying while attending to the mother.

The records are part of the equipment, and the obstetric record is where trace, drugs, times, and interventions meet. A partograph plots the dilation of the cervix, the descent of the head, the contractions, and the fetal heart rate against time, so that a labor which has stopped progressing appears as a shape on paper. An electronic health record (EHR) can display the same information continuously, but it brings its own failure modes, including a monitor that is not networked and a clock set wrongly. Every device here produces a number that a person must interpret, and the common error is to treat documentation as an administrative task to be finished after the clinical work. The field version begins with the clean delivery kit, assembled so that a birth can happen without a hospital. It contains a square of plastic sheeting, a bar of soap, two clean cloths, a sterile blade, two lengths of clean cord tie, and a pair of gloves. Its principle is hygienic rather than electronic, because the sheet separates the mother from the ground, soap and gloves break the chain of contact, and the blade and cloths keep the cord and the baby clean, while the common error is to open the kit days before the birth and store it in a damp place.

Where no kit exists, the same principles are assembled from what can be cleaned. A clean cloth or a piece of plastic serves as the surface, water that has been boiled and cooled is the cleanest fluid available, and a new razor blade that has been boiled cuts the cord. The attendant wears gloves if they exist and washes hands before and after if they do not, and the stump is kept dry and uncovered because traditional dressings are a common route to infection in a newborn. The common error is to reuse a blade or a needle, which passes blood-borne infection in both directions, and anything which cuts skin is used once and then disposed of safely. Kangaroo mother care is the field answer to the incubator, and its physics is the transfer of heat from one body to another by direct contact. A mother's chest is a warmer with a skin temperature near 37 degrees Celsius, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and its feedback loop is a living nervous system rather than a thermostat. A baby held upright between the breasts, naked except for a hat and a diaper, loses far less heat than a baby in a cot, and the position steadies breathing and encourages breastfeeding. The limits are a mother who is ill or unavailable and a baby who needs suction or oxygen or light, and the common error is to interrupt the contact for every weighing and examination.

Fetal monitoring in the field uses a trained hand and ear. A Pinard stethoscope is a wooden or plastic trumpet pressed against the abdomen, and it carries the fetal heart directly to the ear without electronics, so it never needs a battery and never fails silently. A handheld Doppler with a charged battery extends the range, and a fetoscope with a headband frees both hands, while the trace of the cardiotocograph is given up entirely, so the field counts the rate before, during, and after a contraction commonly every 15 to 30 minutes in the active phase, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is to listen for a few seconds and report a rate that was never counted. The field vacuum extractor is a hand-pumped device with a reusable cup, and it gives up the electric pump and the pressure gauge of the hospital model. Because the pressure is felt rather than displayed, the discipline is to build it slowly and test the hold with a gentle pull before any real traction. Traction is used only with a contraction and only until the cup detaches or a set number of pulls is reached, to confirm in the same way. Manual vacuum aspiration works from the same negative pressure made by a hand pump, and the common error is to use a cup that is too small or a pump whose seal has hardened.

Field newborn resuscitation is built around warmth, airway, and a bag, in that order. A self-inflating bag with a newborn mask and no gas supply delivers room air, which is an acceptable starting gas for most newborns, while oxygen from a concentrator is added when it is available. A bulb syringe or a mucus trap provides suction, a cloth dried in the sun provides the towel, and the mother's chest provides the warmer, so resuscitation can be conducted with the baby on the mother. The common errors are to forget to dry and cover the baby while ventilating, to use a bag meant for an adult, and to keep squeezing without a second person checking the heart rate.
