Jaundice in a place with no phototherapy unit is treated with sunlight, and the physics is the same absorption of blue light, though the dose is uncontrolled. The baby is placed in indirect sunlight near a window, lightly dressed so that as much skin as possible is exposed, and turned at intervals so that all sides receive light, while direct midday sun is avoided because the skin burns and the baby overheats. The eyes are shielded with the same care as under a lamp, and a baby who becomes lethargic or refuses to feed is referred rather than exposed longer. A fiberoptic blanket running from a battery or a small solar panel is a better field answer where it is available, and the common error is to believe that a few minutes of sun equal a night under a therapeutic lamp.

Continuous positive airway pressure in the field uses a bubble circuit and an oxygen concentrator. The circuit is assembled from a nasal interface, a length of tubing, a bottle of sterile water, and a gas source, and the depth of the expiratory tube below the surface sets the pressure, typically 5 centimeters of water, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The concentrator delivers a limited flow, so the blender that would control oxygen concentration is usually absent, and the only guide is a battery pulse oximeter with a newborn probe. The hazards are a pressure that drifts as the bottle is knocked or the water evaporates, a nose damaged by an ill-fitting interface, and a collapsed lung that is not recognized, and the common error is to leave the circuit for hours without measuring the depth. Reprocessing in the field is a choice among boiling, chemical disinfection, and single use. Boiling in clean water for a full 5 minutes kills most organisms but does not sterilize, because some spores survive, to confirm against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A chlorine solution is used for surfaces and for items that cannot be boiled, and its strength and contact time must be measured rather than guessed, while blades, needles, suture, and cord clamps are never reused. The common error is to add more chlorine to a solution that has lost its strength, because a disinfectant that still smells strong may be spent.

Field equipment survives when it is simple, repairable, and fed with the right consumables. A handheld Doppler needs a charged battery, a supply of gel, and a probe that is not dropped, while a suction unit needs clean tubing, a trap that is emptied and washed, and a filter that is changed. A radiant warmer needs a working probe, a spare element, and a power source that can carry its load. The spare parts worth carrying are those that stop a device completely, which are fuses, batteries, tubing, masks in two sizes, prong sets, probe covers, and a spare thermometer, and the common error is to stock a device without its consumables. The comparison comes down to what is measured and what is merely observed. The hospital has continuous cardiotocography, a servocontrolled warmer, a closed incubator with humidity, a metered phototherapy unit, a driven continuous positive airway pressure circuit, and a sterilization service, and each turns a clinical impression into a number. The field gives up all of that, and in exchange it gains portability, independence from mains electricity and piped gas, and the freedom to work in a house rather than a ward. What it demands instead is a trained attendant who counts the fetal heart, dries and covers the baby, keeps the cord clean, measures the water depth, and recognizes the signs that mean referral.

To summarize, the equipment of obstetrics and neonatology is a small family of instruments built on a few physical principles, which are reflected sound for the fetal heart, pressure for contractions and suction, levers and negative pressure for assisted birth, radiant heat and convection for warmth, and the absorption of blue light for jaundice. The hospital versions measure continuously and are supported by consumables, calibration, cleaning, and a sterile service, and they surround two patients with numbers that a trained person must still interpret. The field versions give up the monitor, the incubator, the metered lamp, and the driven circuit, and they demand instead clean hands, a warm cloth, skin-to-skin contact, a counted fetal heart, and a plan for referral. Every number named in this chapter, whether a pressure, a temperature, a wavelength, an irradiance, a sterilization cycle, or an alarm threshold, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety of the mother and the newborn rests less on the machines than on the operator who checks them, cleans them, understands why they work, and notices the alarm, the leak, and the error before harm is done.

# Chapter 46 — Pediatrics

Pediatrics takes every device in this book and asks one question, which is whether it is the right size for this body. A child is not a miniature adult made by uniform shrinking. The head of a newborn is large and heavy, so the neck flexes easily, and the airway is narrow everywhere and shortest at the larynx. The chest wall is soft, so it draws inward rather than expanding, and the work of breathing rises with every extra resistance. A child has a large surface for its mass, so heat escapes quickly and the small body cools in minutes. Size is therefore a physiological variable as powerful as any drug.

The first principle behind the pediatric airway set is that airflow resists narrowing with extraordinary force. Resistance rises steeply as the radius falls, in proportion to the fourth power, so halving the diameter multiplies resistance about 16 times. A newborn trachea is about the width of a drinking straw, and a swelling of 1 millimeter can halve the opening and multiply the work of every breath. The child then retracts the ribs, tires quickly, and stops feeding. This is why the operator chooses the largest device the child tolerates, not the smallest that fits, and why a small leak around a tube is often accepted as a margin against swelling. Every size, cuff pressure, and leak value named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The pediatric airway set is one family of devices graded by size. Face masks are chosen by rim diameter so the rim seals over the nose and chin without covering the eyes, and an adult mask will not seal on an infant face. Self-inflating bags come in about 250 milliliters, 500 milliliters, and 1600 milliliters, volumes that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Laryngoscope blades are straight or curved, and the straight blade is preferred in infants because it lifts the floppy epiglottis directly. Supraglottic devices sit over the laryngeal opening and help when the cords cannot be seen. Endotracheal tubes run from about 2.5 millimeters internal diameter in a premature infant to about 7 millimeters in an adolescent, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The bedside formula for an uncuffed tube equals the age in years divided by 4 plus 4, with a cuffed tube one half size smaller, and the result must also be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Once a tube is chosen, the problems move to the patient. A cuff seals the trachea with a small balloon that protects the lungs from stomach contents, but the balloon presses on the mucosal blood supply. A common target is about 20 to 25 centimeters of water, checked with a manometer, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A small child often needs no cuff, because the ring of cartilage below the cords forms a natural seal. The tube is fixed at a depth commonly about 3 times its internal diameter in millimeters, a rule that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarms are the high pressure and low exhaled volume alarms, and the common errors are to advance the tube into one bronchus, to fix it too loosely, and to let the tubing kink under the chin.

Vascular access in a child is a contest between a small target and a device that must not move inside it. Gauges rise as diameter falls, so a 24 gauge cannula is thinner than a 22 gauge cannula, and the smallest sizes used in newborns are 24 gauge and 26 gauge, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The veins of an infant are short, superficial, and easily blown, and the tourniquet is a finger or a soft band. The transilluminator makes these veins visible because hemoglobin absorbs red and infrared light far more strongly than fat and skin do, so a bright cold light pressed to the skin passes through the tissue. The blood-filled vein then appears as a dark line on a glowing background, and a hot lamp left on the skin burns a newborn in seconds. The common errors are to probe after the vein is punctured, to release the tourniquet too late, and to leave a cannula that is no longer needed.

When veins cannot be found, the marrow cavity becomes the route. The medullary cavity of a long bone is a sponge of marrow and vessels that does not collapse when the circulation fails, so it behaves as a vein that never closes. Fluid delivered there reaches the central circulation at a speed comparable to a peripheral vein. The needle is short and stout, about 15 to 18 gauge and 15 to 25 millimeters long, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. It enters the flat upper surface of the tibia below the knee, the lower femur, or the upper arm bone in older children. The hazard is a needle through the far wall, so fluid runs into the soft tissue and produces a compartment syndrome, which is why placement is confirmed by aspirating marrow, by free flow, and by watching the limb for swelling.

Fluids given to a child are measured rather than dripped, because the margin between enough and too much is narrow. The blood volume of an infant is only about 80 to 90 milliliters per kilogram, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A common starting bolus for shock is 10 to 20 milliliters per kilogram, and a common maintenance rule gives 4 milliliters per kilogram each hour for the first 10 kilograms, 2 for the next 10, and 1 thereafter, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The device that makes these volumes safe is the graduated burette, a chamber of 100 to 150 milliliters that holds only the intended amount, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An infusion pump adds control and raises alarms for occlusion, air, and end of infusion. The common errors are to hang a full bag on a gravity line, to leave a roller clamp open, and to override an occlusion alarm without looking at the limb.

The length-based resuscitation tape turns one measurement into a whole plan. In children older than a few months, body length predicts weight far better than age does, so a tape marked in length intervals can assign the child to a weight zone with useful accuracy. The tape is laid from the crown of the head to the heel, and each zone is printed in a color that repeats on the drawers of a resuscitation trolley. The correct tube, blade, bag, cannula, drug dose, and defibrillation energy are then found together. Defibrillation commonly begins at about 2 joules per kilogram, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common errors are to ignore the zone when it disagrees with a measured weight and to keep only one tape in the department.

Monitoring a child uses the same measurements as monitoring an adult, delivered through devices sized to a smaller body. The bladder of a blood pressure cuff should be about 40 per cent of the arm circumference and cover about 80 per cent of it, so a cuff that is too narrow reads falsely high and one that is too wide reads falsely low, and both figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The oxygen saturation probe passes light of two wavelengths through a translucent part of the body and compares how much of each is absorbed, because oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood differ in that absorption. A child needs a small soft pad for the finger, the toe, or the edge of the hand, and the characteristic alarm is the low saturation alarm, commonly set below about 90 per cent, a threshold that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common errors are a probe that is too tight, a probe on poorly perfused skin, and a reading accepted while the child moves. Cardiac electrodes are smaller and closer together than adult electrodes.

Temperature is the pediatric variable that kills quietly, and the physics of a small body explains why. Heat leaves by four routes at once, which are evaporation from skin and breath, conduction into a cold surface, convection into moving air, and radiation to cooler objects. A newborn loses heat by all four faster than an adult because surface area is large relative to the mass that produces heat. A newborn also cannot shiver effectively and has little insulating fat, so it burns brown fat, which consumes oxygen and glucose and fails quickly in a sick infant. Cold stress leads to a fall in temperature, a rise in oxygen consumption, a fall in blood glucose, and a metabolic acidosis that makes everything worse. The neutral thermal environment is the range in which the child holds a normal temperature with the least oxygen consumption, and for a small unclothed infant it commonly lies near 32 to 34 degrees Celsius of air with a skin temperature of about 36.5 degrees Celsius, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An infant warmer and an incubator are two answers to the same problem. A radiant warmer hangs a heated element above an open cot and warms the skin by infrared radiation without touching it, which allows full access but increases water loss. An incubator encloses the child in a chamber of heated circulating air, often with a double wall and a humidifier, which reduces evaporation but delays access and harbors bacteria in a poorly cleaned humidifier. Both devices in automatic mode are controlled by a skin probe containing a thermistor, a resistor whose resistance falls as its temperature rises. The characteristic alarms are the over-temperature, probe failure, and low temperature alarms, and each threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The most dangerous common error is a probe that has come loose and now measures the air, because the controller then drives the heater hotter while the alarm may stay silent.

Jaundice in a newborn is visible because bilirubin, the pigment released when red blood cells are broken down, accumulates in the skin and the whites of the eyes. Bilirubin absorbs blue and green light strongly, with a peak near 450 to 460 nanometers, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A transcutaneous meter flashes light into the skin and compares absorption at a wavelength bilirubin absorbs with one it does not. The device measures skin and not blood, so it is a screening tool affected by skin maturity, by the site, by the darkness of the skin, and by whether phototherapy is running. The hazard is a reassuring reading while the blood level rises, so a value near a treatment threshold must be confirmed with a laboratory measurement of a blood sample. The common errors are to use the meter during phototherapy, to measure over a bruised area, and to treat the number as a diagnosis.

An infant scale and a length board look simple, and they are the devices whose error propagates into every drug dose. Most modern scales use a load cell, a metal bar that bends very slightly under a load, with strain gauges whose electrical resistance changes as the metal stretches. An infant scale commonly reads to the nearest 5 or 10 grams with a capacity of about 20 kilograms, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A length board has a fixed headpiece, a sliding footpiece, and a scale in millimeters along its edge. Length is measured lying down until about 2 years of age and standing after that, and the two are not interchangeable because a standing child is shorter. The common errors are to weigh a child with a wet diaper without subtracting it, to record the wrong unit, and to plot a single point instead of the trend.

Nasal prong continuous positive airway pressure, or CPAP, keeps the small airway open by holding a positive pressure in it throughout the breath. The infant breathes through short prongs just inside the nostrils, and the expiratory limb is dipped into sterile water to a measured depth. The pressure needed to push a bubble out equals the depth of the tube below the surface, so 1 centimeter of depth gives about 1 centimeter of water pressure. A common setting is 4 to 6 centimeters of water with a flow of 6 to 8 liters per minute and oxygen adjusted by a blender, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pressure holds the pharynx and small alveoli open and reduces the work of breathing, but it can also distend the stomach or rupture an alveolus and produce a pneumothorax. The common errors are a large mouth leak that destroys the pressure, prongs that are too large and press on the nasal septum, and an interface left too long in one position.

A nebulizer turns a liquid medicine into a mist that a child can inhale, and the common jet type uses a stream of compressed gas. The gas is forced through a narrow opening, and the drop in pressure as it accelerates draws the liquid up a tube and tears it into droplets, which strike baffles that knock the large droplets back. The useful droplet size for the lower airway is roughly 1 to 5 micrometers, and the flow is commonly 6 to 8 liters per minute, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A child is treated with a small face mask rather than a mouthpiece, because a crying child deposits most of the drug in the nose and throat. A spacer, or holding chamber, is the simpler alternative for an inhaler, a plastic chamber that holds the puff as a cloud so the child can take several quiet breaths. The common errors are to let the mask sit away from the face, to forget to shake the inhaler, and to leave the cup unwashed.

Immobilization in a child means matching a rigid device to a soft and growing body. A cervical collar transfers the load of the head from the neck to the shoulders and chest, so its size is chosen by neck circumference and chin height. A collar that is too large lets the head fall forward, and one that is too small presses on the throat. Pediatric collars follow the shorter distance from chin to shoulder, and a hospital keeps a range from the smallest infant size upward, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A pediatric backboard carries extra padding and a head support so that the large head does not force the neck into flexion, because a rigid collar or a tight strap can obstruct the airway or raise the pressure inside the skull. The common errors are to place a folded towel behind the shoulders without checking that the neck is neutral and to move a child with a suspected spinal injury without a coordinated log roll.

Cleaning and reprocessing in pediatrics is harder than in adult practice because the devices are smaller and their lumens narrower. Sterilization kills but does not remove, so a device that reaches the sterilizer with dried blood in a channel comes out sterile and still carrying the material that shields the next patient. Pediatric circuits, masks, prongs, blades, suction catheters, and cannulae are therefore taken apart as far as the maker permits, rinsed at the bedside, and cleaned with a soft brush of the correct diameter. A common steam cycle for wrapped pediatric instruments is 134 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes, a cycle that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and many plastic circuits and soft masks cannot survive it and need the low temperature method their maker specifies. The consumables a pediatric ward must never run short of are the small gauge cannulae, the small masks and blades, the correct tubes, the small suction catheters, the oxygen tubing and prongs, the electrodes, the oral rehydration solution, and the smallest gloves. The common errors are to reuse a single-use item because it is the only one left and to mix parts from different size sets.

Preventive maintenance in a pediatric department is mostly about instruments that sense, because a device that measures wrongly is more dangerous than one that fails to switch on. Temperature probes, load cells, pressure transducers, oxygen sensors, and pulse oximeter probes all drift with age and abuse, and each has a stated interval for calibration or replacement that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A rechargeable battery loses capacity gradually, so a transport monitor or a syringe pump that once ran for hours begins to fail during a transfer. Tubing cracks at the connector, seals harden, filters block with dust, and an incubator humidifier grows a biofilm that rinsing will not remove once it has formed. The most insidious failure is a silent alarm, because a failed speaker or a limit that has been switched off lets the device sit quietly while the child deteriorates. The operator must test every alarm at the start of every shift and record every fault, because a monitor that has failed once will fail again.

Before any child is attached to a device, the operator runs a check that is shorter than the adult version but stricter, and the first item is size. The intended tube, mask, blade, bag, cannula, collar, and blood pressure cuff are laid out and compared with the child's measured length and weight, and a length-based tape is opened beside the bed. The oxygen source and tubing are checked for flow and connection, the suction is tested, and the self-inflating bag is squeezed to confirm that it refills and its valve works. Every monitor is switched on and allowed to complete its self-test, its alarm limits are set to the child's age rather than left at adult defaults, and the probe and electrodes are checked for a clean signal. The weight and length are recorded and the drug doses are calculated before they are needed, and the environment is prepared with a warm surface and a hat. Every setting, alarm limit, pressure, temperature, and drug volume used on a child must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the pediatric equipment list is rebuilt from the diseases that kill children. The hospital department is organized around diagnosis and surveillance, while the field clinic is organized around the few interventions that change the outcome, which are warmth, oxygen, oral rehydration, the first dose of an antibiotic, the treatment of malnutrition, and the recognition of a child who must be referred. The devices that survive are the simple ones, because a device with a battery, a sensor, and a circuit board cannot be repaired at a health post. The field version keeps the self-inflating bag with small masks, a manual suction device, a thermometer, a timer, and a scale, and it lets go of the servo-controlled incubator, the infusion pump, and the electronic monitor. What it gives up is precision and continuous surveillance, and what it demands instead is the trained hand and eye of a worker who measures, counts, and looks.

The mid-upper arm circumference tape is the single most useful piece of pediatric equipment in a field clinic. Its principle is that the circumference of the arm changes remarkably little between the ages of about 6 months and 5 years as long as the child is well nourished. Muscle and fat in the upper arm respond early to a shortage of food, so the tape measures the reserve, and the measurement is quick and repeatable in trained hands. The tape is marked in centimeters with colored bands, and cutoffs commonly used are 11.5 centimeters for severe acute malnutrition and 12.5 centimeters for moderate acute malnutrition, thresholds that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The measurement is taken on the left arm, midway between the tip of the shoulder and the tip of the elbow, and the tape is pulled snug without compressing the skin. The common errors are to read at the wrong point, to pull too tight, and to record the color band without the centimeter value, and a swollen arm from edema gives a falsely large reading.

A weighing scale in the field is usually a hanging spring scale, and its principle is that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force that stretches it. The child is placed in a sling suspended from the hook, and the pointer moves along a marked scale, and a scale of this kind commonly holds up to about 25 kilograms with graduations of 100 grams, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Its virtue is that it has no battery, and its weakness is that the spring can fatigue, the zero can drift, and the pointer can stick, so the worker must check the zero and hang a known mass from the hook. The hazards are a sling that tears, a struggling child, and a reading taken while the scale swings, and each produces a false weight that becomes a false drug dose. The common errors are to forget to subtract the sling and clothing, to read at an angle, and to record a single weight without plotting it.

Ready-to-use therapeutic food is the equipment of severe malnutrition, and it is a manufactured device with a specification, a package, a storage condition, and a failure mode. It is a dense paste of groundnut, milk powder, sugar, vegetable oil, and a vitamin and mineral premix sealed in a foil sachet. Its energy density of roughly 500 kilocalories per 100 grams means a small volume carries enough energy to rebuild a child who cannot eat a large meal, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A common sachet holds about 92 grams and is given in a scheduled number of sachets each day according to weight and protocol, an amount that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazards are contamination when the paste is shared, spoilage when the sachet is stored in heat, and the dangerous use of the food at home for a child with infection, poor appetite, or edema, who needs inpatient care. The oral rehydration solution is the companion equipment of diarrhea, a measured mixture of salts and sugar that uses sodium and glucose transport in the gut to pull water back into the body, and the common errors are to mix it too strong, to mix it too weak, and to use a dirty container.

The field version of the pediatric airway is a self-inflating bag in the smallest size with a set of masks, a manual suction bulb or foot-operated pump, and a straight blade if the worker is trained. There is no ventilator, so every breath is delivered by hand and the worker watches the chest rise and counts the rate. There is no infusion pump, so fluid is given by gravity through a chamber that counts drops, and the worker must know how many drops make a milliliter for that set. There is no electronic monitor, so the respiratory rate is counted for a full minute, the work of breathing is judged by rib recession and grunting, and the temperature is taken with whatever thermometer the clinic has. Warmth comes from the oldest device in pediatrics, the skin of the mother, where the naked child is placed upright between the breasts, covered, and held day and night, which is called kangaroo care. The field kit gives up servo control, continuous measurement, and the alarm, and it demands a trained hand, a second helper, a schedule, and the honesty to refer a child who is not improving.

The hazards of pediatric equipment in the field are mostly the hazards of improvisation and of the environment. An improvised spinal board is a plank or a door with cloth padding, and it works only if the head and neck are held in line and the child is strapped without pressure on the chest. Small instruments are usually sterilized by boiling in clean water for the time stated in the local protocol, which kills most organisms but does not destroy spores and does not remove protein. The failure modes of the field kit are predictable, because a bag valve sticks and does not refill, a mask rim hardens, a thermometer reads low as its battery fades, a scale zero drifts, and therapeutic food stored in the sun turns its oil. The operator must check each of these before the clinic opens and must know the referral criteria by heart, because the most important equipment in a frontier clinic is the vehicle and the decision to use it.

To summarize, pediatrics is the discipline in which size becomes a clinical decision, and almost every device in this chapter matches a machine to a body that is small, growing, and changing in proportion. The airway set is graded by diameter because resistance rises so steeply as a tube narrows, the tubes and cuffs are checked by measured values, and the length-based tape converts one measurement into a complete plan of sizes and doses. Vascular access uses the smallest cannulae and, when the veins fail, the marrow cavity, and every fluid is measured in milliliters per kilogram against a narrow margin. Blood pressure cuffs, saturation probes, and electrodes all carry a size that changes the reading, while the bilirubin meter and the transilluminator turn light into information about skin and veins. Warmth is a device in its own right, delivered by a warmer, an incubator, or the skin of a mother, and the scales and length boards that look trivial are the source of every dose. Whatever the setting, the operator must understand the physical principle, choose every item by size against the measured child, test the alarms before relying on them, and confirm every setting, pressure, temperature, cycle, and threshold against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 47 — Nephrology

The nephrology chapter gathers the machines that stand in for a kidney when the organ has stopped working. A kidney performs many jobs through about a million filtering units, and the ones that kill quickly are the removal of waste, the control of water, and the control of potassium. In physical terms it is a selective filter that runs blood at pressure against a membrane, letting water and small dissolved molecules pass while holding back cells and large proteins. When those filters fail, waste accumulates, the acid-base balance drifts, potassium rises to a level that stops the heart, and water overloads the lungs.

Every dialysis membrane works on two movements of dissolved particles, and those movements explain almost every setting on the machine. Diffusion is the movement of particles from a place of higher concentration to a place of lower concentration, and it needs only a gradient and a path through a membrane whose pores let water and small molecules cross while holding back cells and large proteins. Blood runs on one side of that membrane and a fluid called dialysate on the other, so urea and creatinine leave the blood at a speed set by the concentration difference, the membrane area, the membrane thickness, and the contact time. The second movement is convection, in which water is pushed through the pores and drags dissolved molecules with it, and that pressure-driven flow becomes ultrafiltration when it is used to remove water.

In a well-resourced hospital the kidney machine is a fixed installation rather than a portable object, standing beside a dedicated chair or bed. It is connected to treated water, to drainage, and to a reliable electrical supply, and it consumes single-use tubing, a filter, and prepared fluid. It needs a trained operator who can answer its alarms and a technician who can maintain the water plant and calibrate its sensors. The field clinic rarely has any of that, so the second half of this chapter describes peritoneal dialysis, which uses the patient's own abdominal membrane and a bag of fluid and asks for clean hands instead of a water plant.

The hemodialysis machine is a console with two fluid circuits, and those circuits meet only at the filter. The blood circuit takes blood from the patient, pushes it through the filter, and returns it, while the dialysate circuit makes a warmed fluid of the correct composition from concentrate and treated water. Between them sits the dialyzer, the membrane device where diffusion, convection, and ultrafiltration occur, and the pump that moves the blood is almost always a peristaltic roller pump. In that pump, rollers press a flexible tube segment against a curved track and push the trapped volume ahead of them, and a common blood flow is 200 to 500 milliliters per minute, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the characteristic failure is the pump segment that ruptures or walks along the track.

Pressure is measured at several points of the blood circuit because pressure tells the machine whether it is pulling or pushing too hard. The pressure before the pump falls when the access is poor or the line is kinked, while the pressure after the pump rises when the venous needle is misplaced or a clot is forming. The characteristic alarm is a high venous pressure alert, and the common error is to silence it without inspecting the needle, the line, and the filter in that order. The exact alarm limits for the venous and arterial lines must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The dialysate circuit begins with proportioning, the mixing of a concentrate with treated water in a ratio that most machines hold with two balancing chambers. The fluid is then warmed and stripped of dissolved air, because bubbles inside the dialysate compartment can blanket part of the membrane and reduce clearance. Conductivity is measured continuously as the quickest proof that the ratio is correct, since dissolved salts carry current in proportion to their concentration, and a typical value of about 13 to 14 millisiemens per centimeter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A mix that is too weak draws sodium out of the blood and one that is too strong drives sodium in and can damage red cells, so the conductivity alarm diverts dialysate away from the filter and must never be reset without checking the concentrates.

Dialysate must be warmed to body temperature, and a temperature near 37 degrees Celsius is normal, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Blood returned too cold causes shivering and a rise in blood pressure, while blood returned too hot damages red cells, so the heater is controlled by a thermistor and guarded by a thermal cutout. The characteristic alarms are the temperature alarm and the blood leak alarm, the second detecting blood in the dialysate if the membrane has ruptured. The common error is to drape a blanket over the machine vents, which overheats the electronics while the patient complains of feeling cold.

Ultrafiltration control decides how much water is removed, and it is the part of the machine most directly tied to the patient's wellbeing. A common maximum removal rate is 10 to 15 milliliters per kilogram of body weight each hour, and a common session target is the difference between the weight before the session and the dry weight agreed by the clinical team, both of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The machine removes fluid by making the outgoing dialysate volume greater than the incoming volume or by measuring the difference with a flow sensor, and removal that is too fast drops the blood pressure and causes cramping and fainting. The characteristic alarm is the ultrafiltration error alarm, which usually means the balancing chambers no longer agree with the set target, and the common error is to record an incorrect starting weight.

The venous line carries blood back to the patient, so it is the place where air must never pass. Air enters through a loose connection, an empty saline bag, an open syringe port, or a needle that has come out of the vessel while the pump keeps running. The machine guards against this with an air detector, a drip chamber that lets bubbles rise out of the blood, and a venous clamp that closes when the detector alarms, because a larger volume of air reaching the right side of the heart can block the pulmonary circulation and kill the patient within minutes. The characteristic alarm is the air detector alarm with the pump stopped and the venous clamp closed, and the common errors are to override the detector and to leave the drip chamber nearly empty.

The check before a session is a fixed sequence, and it is the operator's real protection against a machine that is quietly wrong. The machine runs a self-test of its pumps, valves, and sensors, and a pressure test then proves that the blood circuit holds and that the dialysate does not leak across the membrane. The conductivity and temperature are read against the prescribed values, the alarm limits are reviewed for this patient, and the operator confirms that the correct concentrate is connected to the correct port. Priming follows, in which the sterile blood lines and dialyzer are filled with sterile saline so that no air remains and no blood meets a dry surface, and the common error is to initial the check sheet without reading the values.

The dialyzer is the membrane device itself, and its usual form is a cylinder packed with thousands of hollow fibers through which blood flows while dialysate flows around the outside in the opposite direction, so the concentration difference is maintained along the whole length. The wall of each fiber is the membrane, made of regenerated cellulose, a modified cellulose, or a synthetic polymer such as polysulfone, and the fibers are potted at each end in resin so the two compartments stay sealed. The size of the dialyzer is given by its membrane surface area, typically 1.0 to 2.2 square meters, and the character of the membrane by its flux, which states how freely water and larger molecules cross, both of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A low flux membrane restricts the middle molecules, a high flux membrane passes them and far more water, and the common error is to knock or drop a dialyzer, because the potting can crack.

In many units the dialyzer is reprocessed and used more than once for the same patient, and reuse is a controlled process rather than a rinse. The fibers are flushed with clean water and then a disinfectant, the volume of the fiber bundle is measured against its first-use value, and the device is tested for membrane leaks before storage. A fall in fiber bundle volume beyond the local limit, a failed leak test, or a damaged header means the dialyzer is discarded, and each device is labelled with the patient's identity and the number of uses and never used for another patient. The common errors are to accept a dialyzer whose volume has fallen below the limit and to omit the test for residual disinfectant, and the acceptable number of reuses and the minimum fiber bundle volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The vascular access is the connection between the patient and the machine, and it is the component that fails most often. The best access is an arteriovenous fistula, created by joining an artery to a vein in the arm so that the vein receives arterial pressure and enlarges over weeks into a thick vessel that must mature before it is used, a period that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator checks it every session by feeling the thrill of turbulent flow and by listening for the bruit through a stethoscope, and a fistula that has lost its thrill, that hurts, or that keeps bleeding must be assessed before it is used again. The common error is to accept a weak thrill as normal, because a narrowing that is tolerated today can clot the access tomorrow.

The needles that puncture a fistula are large, because the flow must be high and the resistance low, and they are usually 14 gauge to 17 gauge, where the gauge number falls as the needle becomes thicker. The venous needle always points toward the heart, and each needle is inserted at a shallow angle with the bevel facing up, because a needle pressed against the wall reduces flow while one that has passed through it lets blood leak into the surrounding tissue. The common error is to cannulate the same spot at every session, which weakens the wall and produces an aneurysm, and the correct practice is to rotate the sites in a ladder pattern. The needle gauge, the insertion angle, and the rotation plan must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the characteristic alarm is a rising arterial pressure with a falling flow.

A dialysis catheter is a large bore tube placed in a central vein, usually the internal jugular vein, with two or three lumens so that blood can be withdrawn through one and returned through another. A tunneled catheter is passed under the skin to a cuff that anchors it and seals the tract, a non-tunneled one serves for days to weeks, and the lumens are locked between sessions with heparin or citrate whose concentration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The catheter is the access most likely to become infected, so the hub is scrubbed and the connection protected, and the common errors are to leave a clamp open, to let air enter, and to use the catheter for other purposes without a deliberate decision. When no fistula is possible, a graft of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE, is sewn between an artery and a vein, and its characteristic problems are a narrowing at the venous end and a pseudoaneurysm, so the common error is to press too hard after the needles are removed.

In a dialysis unit the water is not a utility but a clinical device, because the patient's blood meets it across a thin membrane many times each week. Ordinary drinking water carries chlorine, chloramine, calcium, magnesium, iron, bacteria, and bacterial fragments, so the treatment chain is a sequence in which each stage removes something the next cannot tolerate, usually a sediment filter, carbon tanks, a softener, and a reverse osmosis unit. The sediment filter traps particles, rust, and grit before they reach the finer stages, and the carbon filter removes chlorine and chloramine by adsorption onto activated carbon. The carbon stage is the most safety-critical of all, because those substances destroy red blood cells, so the water must be tested before every shift, and the test method and permitted concentration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A softener removes calcium and magnesium by ion exchange, passing the water through a bed of resin that holds those ions and releases sodium in their place. Hard water forms scale on the reverse osmosis membrane and reduces its output, so the softener protects the plant and also the patient, because calcium and magnesium in the wrong proportion can disturb the heart, and a hardness test of the water leaving the softener shows whether the resin is still working. The resin is regenerated by drawing brine from a salt tank through the bed, so the salt level must be checked and the tank kept clean, and the common error is to let the salt tank run dry, after which the resin is exhausted and hard water passes unnoticed. Reverse osmosis forces water at a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure through a membrane that rejects dissolved salts, producing purified product water and a stream of reject water carrying the impurities away, and the rejection rate and product flow must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Deionization passes water through ion exchange resin that replaces dissolved salts with water, and the resin is monitored by measuring the resistance of the water, because a fall means it is exhausted. Beyond the chain the water is stored in a tank and moved through a loop of piping to each machine, and that loop is itself a device that must be maintained. Stagnation, rough joints, dead ends, and warm spots encourage biofilm, a community of bacteria in a slime layer that disinfectant cannot easily reach, so the water is monitored by counting colonies and by testing for endotoxin, a bacterial fragment that produces fever and shock in the blood. Common action limits of below 100 colonies per milliliter for water used to prepare dialysate and below 0.25 endotoxin units per milliliter for the same water must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic failure is a biofilm that is invisible in the water, and the common errors are to continue past the capacity of the resin and to sample from a tap that is not the point of use.

Dialysate is made from two concentrates and treated water, and the reason for two is chemistry: the acid concentrate is acidic so that the bicarbonate in the other concentrate does not precipitate with the calcium and magnesium in the water. The bicarbonate concentrate is usually a powder dissolved on site or a ready liquid, it is the part most vulnerable to bacterial growth because it is a warm alkaline solution, and the machine mixes the concentrates at a fixed ratio that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The composition is prescribed for each patient, and potassium is usually set low because the session aims to remove the potassium a failing kidney has retained, with a common value of 2 millimoles per liter that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common errors are to connect the acid container to the bicarbonate port, to use a bicarbonate batch that has stood warm, and to use powder that has not dissolved completely.

Between patients the machine is cleaned and disinfected, and that schedule is part of treatment rather than housekeeping. The exterior is wiped with a compatible disinfectant, the blood pump and the ports are cleaned, and the internal fluid path is disinfected with heat or a chemical agent and then rinsed, with citric acid commonly used to descale the heater at a concentration and contact time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The machine is also a measuring instrument whose sensors drift, so the conductivity cell, the temperature sensor, the pressure transducers, and the ultrafiltration balance are calibrated against reference instruments on a schedule, and the blood pump is checked for the flow it delivers with the tubing in use. The common error is to skip the internal disinfection because the machine looks clean when the growth is inside the fluid path, and the second error is to treat the annual service visit as the only maintenance when the daily checks catch the drift.

Peritoneal dialysis uses the patient's own peritoneum as the membrane, and it is a fundamentally different device from a hemodialysis machine even though the physics are the same. The peritoneum is a thin moist membrane that lines the abdominal cavity and covers the organs, and it is richly supplied with blood vessels, so it is a dialysis membrane already inside the body. Dialysate is instilled through a catheter, left to dwell, and then drained, and during the dwell diffusion removes the small waste molecules while dwell time decides how complete that removal is, while fluid removal is produced by osmosis because the dialysate contains glucose at a higher concentration than the blood. The solution comes in a clear plastic bag, its glucose concentration is chosen for the amount of water to be removed, with common concentrations of 1.36 per cent, 2.27 per cent, and 3.86 per cent and common adult bag volumes of 1.5 to 2.5 liters, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to warm a bag in a microwave or in water that is too hot.

The transfer set is the tubing that joins the bag to the catheter, and the technique of connecting it is the single most important skill in peritoneal dialysis. In a twin bag system the sequence is drain, flush, and fill, and the flush step pushes any bacteria that touched the connector out of the fresh line before the new fluid enters the patient. The connector is disinfected, the clamps are opened in the correct order, and the hands never touch the sterile ends, because the peritonitis that follows a break in technique is the characteristic complication of this therapy and presents as a cloudy drained bag, abdominal pain, fever, and a loss of ultrafiltration. The first equipment step is to examine the drain bag, because turbidity is the earliest sign, the effluent is sent for a cell count and a culture, treatment is usually started before the culture returns using antibiotics given into the peritoneum through the catheter, and the common error is to attribute a cloudy bag to fibrin and to wait.

The catheter is a soft silicone tube with side holes near its tip and one or two polyester cuffs near the exit site, and the cuffs provoke fibrous tissue that anchors the catheter and blocks bacteria from tracking along its outside. The exit site is kept dry and undisturbed, a red, tender, or discharging exit site is an infection that must be reported at once, and the common error is to pull or rotate a new catheter, which disturbs the cuff and opens the tract to bacteria. The cycler automates the therapy while the patient sleeps, using a pump or valves, a heater plate for the bags, scales to measure what is drained, and a controller that runs a program of fills, dwells, and drains. The prescription sets the total volume, the number of cycles, the dwell time, and the final fill, and each of these along with every alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the characteristic alarms are the low drain volume alarm and the fill volume alarm, whose common cause is the catheter tip lying against the bowel.

Continuous renal replacement therapy, or CRRT, is dialysis delivered slowly and without interruption for a patient who cannot tolerate the blood pressure swings of standard hemodialysis. The patient is usually in an intensive care unit, and instead of removing two days of fluid in 4 hours the machine removes the same volume over 24 hours or more. The circuit is a set of tubing, a pump for blood, pumps for replacement fluid and effluent, and a filter much smaller than a hemodialyzer, and a common blood flow is 100 to 200 milliliters per minute, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The effluent rate is prescribed according to the patient's weight, a common prescription is 20 to 35 milliliters per kilogram each hour, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and unfractionated heparin or a regional citrate infusion keeps the circuit open. The characteristic alarm is a rising filter pressure or a falling effluent volume, and both mean the membrane is clotting, so the common error is to ignore a slow drift in the pressures until the filter fails.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the hospital-grade hemodialysis machine is almost never present, and the reason is infrastructure rather than cost. The machine needs a continuous supply of treated water that meets a strict chemical and microbial standard, a drain for hundreds of liters in a session, a stable electrical supply for several hours, a vascular access that can be cannulated with large needles, and a patient who can return three times each week for years. When any of those is missing the realistic answer is peritoneal dialysis, which needs no water plant, no electricity during the dwell, and no needle, but what it gives up is speed and clearance, because the peritoneum clears small molecules far more slowly than a dialyzer. What it demands instead is a clean room, scrupulous hand and connection technique, a reliable supply of bags and transfer sets, and a trained patient or family member; the manual exchange is performed with the bag hung above the patient, commonly 2 liters instilled, left to dwell for 4 to 6 hours, and then drained, repeated 4 times each day, figures that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The frontier clinic must also recognize what it cannot do, and the most important decision is when to refer. A patient who needs rapid removal of potassium, who has pulmonary edema from fluid overload, or who has taken a poison that requires fast clearance cannot be treated by slow peritoneal dialysis and must reach a hemodialysis unit. In the meantime the clinic restricts fluid and potassium intake, gives medicines that remove potassium through the gut, treats the cause of the kidney injury, and watches the heart rhythm, because the conservative care of acute kidney injury is itself a set of equipment decisions from accurate urine collection to a reliable scale. The clinic must know its referral pathway in advance, and the indications for starting dialysis and for urgent referral must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of nephrology are heavy, bulky, and perishable in ways that make stock control a clinical matter. The dialyzers, blood lines, fistula needles, saline, concentrates, disinfectants, and peritoneal dialysis bags each have a shelf life and a storage condition, and the peritoneal dialysis bags must be kept cool, upright, and out of direct sunlight, while a bag that has frozen or been stored hot must be discarded. The concentrates have a limited life once opened or once mixed, the bicarbonate is the most perishable of all, and the reverse osmosis membranes, the carbon, and the ion exchange resin are consumables of the plant whose stock must be tracked as carefully as the supplies at the bedside. The minimum stock level, the storage temperature, and the shelf life of each item must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is to order only the visible items and to forget the filters and the salt that keep the water plant alive.

To summarize, the machines of nephrology do outside the body what a kidney does inside it, and they do it by moving dissolved particles across a thin membrane. Hemodialysis depends on a peristaltic blood pump, a proportioning system, a dialyzer chosen for its surface area and flux, a vascular access, and a water plant whose carbon stage is the difference between safe treatment and hemolysis. Diffusion removes the small waste molecules, convection and ultrafiltration remove the middle molecules and the accumulated water, and every pressure, temperature, conductivity value, and alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The operator's duties are decisive: the pre-session test, the chlorine test before the first patient, the trend of the pressures, the inspection of the drain bag, and the refusal to silence an alarm whose cause has not been found. Peritoneal dialysis is the device that travels, because it uses the patient's own membrane and demands technique instead of infrastructure, while CRRT serves the unstable patient in the intensive care unit, and in every setting the rule is to understand the physics, check the machine, and treat the patient rather than the alarm.

# Chapter 48 — Gastroenterology

The gut is a muscular tube some 7 to 9 meters long, folded into the abdomen and reachable from either end only through a narrow opening. It is collapsed when empty, dark inside, wet, and constantly moving, so a physician who wants to look at its lining cannot do so from outside the body. Gastroenterology solved this problem with instruments that travel into the tube itself, carrying light in and an image out. Every device in this chapter is a variation on that single idea, and every hazard follows from the fact that the instrument is in contact with living tissue for the whole of its journey.

The physical principle is total internal reflection. Light traveling through a glass fiber strikes the boundary between glass and air at a shallow angle, and instead of leaving the fiber it is reflected back inside, so light can be guided around bends with little loss. The first flexible gastroscopes used one bundle of fibers to carry light to the tip and a second, carefully ordered bundle to carry the image back, and the image bundle worked only because each fiber kept the same position at both ends. The modern instrument replaces the image bundle with a small solid-state sensor at the tip, wired back through the shaft, so the picture arrives as an electrical signal while illumination still comes from fibers. This division, fibers for light and a wire for the image, explains why a damaged endoscope may lose brightness while keeping a perfect picture, or lose part of the picture while the illumination remains.

At the operator's end sits the control section, the only part the examiner touches. Two large wheels bend the tip up and down and left and right, and each has a lock that holds a position while the hands do something else. A set of valves admits air to open the collapsed gut, admits water to wash the lens, and applies suction to clear fluid and hold tissue. The insertion tube runs from this section to the tip, a thicker umbilical cord reaches the light source and the processor, and a small biopsy port admits forceps, snares, and needles. The tip angle, the air flow, and the water flow must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The upper endoscope, often called the gastroscope, passes through the mouth and esophagus into the stomach and the first part of the small intestine. Its working length is usually about 100 centimeters, its insertion tube about 9 to 10 millimeters, and its working channel about 2.8 millimeters, wide enough for biopsy forceps but not for every therapeutic accessory. The shaft is marked at intervals so the examiner can judge how far the tip has traveled, and the markings are read as the instrument is withdrawn rather than as it is pushed. A thinner pediatric instrument of about 5 to 6 millimeters gives comfort at the cost of a smaller channel, and a therapeutic instrument of about 12 millimeters carries a channel wide enough for a clip or a snare. The sizes, the depth of insertion, and the accessory that fits the channel must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The colonoscope is longer and thicker because the colon is longer, more folded, and entered from below. Its working length is typically 130 to 170 centimeters and its tube about 12 to 13 millimeters, and it must negotiate a mobile, looping organ that can be pushed ahead of the tip. The examiner steers by torque as much as by tip deflection, and a loop in the sigmoid or the transverse colon is recognized and removed before the tip can advance, because pushing harder against a loop only stretches the bowel and risks a perforation. Many instruments offer variable stiffness, in which a cable or a rotating collar stiffens the shaft so that it transmits force instead of folding. The stiffness setting, the insertion technique, and the degree of air insufflation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The small intestine lies between these two reachable zones and is the hardest part of the gut to see. Balloon enteroscopy solves the reach problem with an overtube that carries an inflatable balloon, and sometimes a second balloon on the endoscope itself, so that the two surfaces grip the bowel wall alternately. The examiner advances the scope, inflates the overtube balloon to hold the bowel, advances the overtube, deflates, and repeats, effectively pleating the intestine onto the instrument. This reaches depths the older push enteroscope could not, at the cost of a long procedure and a real risk of mucosal injury from the repeated gripping. The balloon pressures, the inflation sequence, and the maximum insertion depth must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The duodenoscope is the most specialized and the most dangerous instrument in the endoscopy unit, and its shape explains why. It looks sideways rather than straight ahead, so that the examiner can see the far wall of the duodenum and the small opening where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter. At its tip sits a small hinged lever called the elevator, which lifts the tip of a catheter or a wire so that it can be aimed into that opening, and because a side-viewing instrument cannot see the path ahead, it is passed under direct vision with a straight-viewing scope or with fluoroscopy. The elevator and its recess are the heart of the contamination problem, because they are difficult to brush and they trap fluid, biofilm, and bacteria that survive an ordinary cycle. Duodenoscopes have transmitted resistant organisms between patients even when the reprocessing steps appeared to have been followed, so they require a stricter, documented, sometimes cultured routine that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The light source is a separate box on the trolley that sends concentrated white light down the fiber bundle. Older units used a halogen lamp, later ones a xenon arc lamp that is closer to daylight, and newer ones a light emitting diode, or LED, array that runs cooler and lasts longer. The end of the light cable and the tip of the endoscope become hot during a long procedure, and a scope left switched on against a drape or the patient's skin can burn, so the source is placed in standby whenever the instrument is not in the patient. The lamp has an hour meter so its aging can be predicted, and the unit usually carries a lamp failure alarm and an over-temperature alarm, and the intensity setting, the standby behavior, and both alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The processor turns the sensor's electrical output into a picture and controls the appearance of that picture. It synchronizes the readout of the sensor, corrects the video signal, sets white balance so that tissue colors are rendered as the examiner expects, and sends the result to a monitor. Advanced processors add optical or digital contrast enhancement, in which selected wavelengths make surface vessels and mucosal patterns stand out, because early cancers often change the pattern of blood vessels before they change color. Magnification, either optical by zooming the lens or digital by enlarging the image, is useful only when the surface is clean and the tip is close, since enlargement of a blurred image is still blurred. The enhancement mode, the magnification, and the balance procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The monitor sits at eye level on the trolley so that the examiner's head and the screen do not fight each other for hours, and it must be bright enough to be read in a lit room, since a dim screen hides exactly the subtle findings the examination is for. The recording system captures the live image, still photographs, and often the video of the whole procedure, with the patient's identifiers attached, and stores them in the picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, which is the hospital's image store. Stills and video may be exported in the standard medical imaging format called Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine, or DICOM, so they can be reviewed beside radiology. The retention period, the labeling convention, and the export format must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An endoscope can only look, and everything that treats is an accessory passed through its channel, so these accessories are consumables that must match the channel and the task. Biopsy forceps are flexible cables with two small cups that are closed by a handle, and a dull forceps crushes rather than cuts, producing a specimen the pathologist cannot read. Snares are loops of wire opened around a polyp and tightened while electrical current is applied, and they come in different shapes and diameters for different lesions. Injection needles are thin retractable needles used to inject a solution beneath the mucosa or beside a bleeding point, and injecting too deeply or too superficially defeats the purpose. These accessories are usually single use, because reuse after cleaning removes the lubricant, blunts the cups, and leaves protein in a joint that cannot be cleaned, and the size, the electrical settings, and the reuse policy of every accessory must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Bleeding inside the gut is controlled with devices that either mechanically pinch the vessel or heat it closed. A through-the-scope clip is a jaw opened outside the patient, advanced along the channel, pressed onto the bleeding point, and released, leaving a permanent or slowly absorbed clasp across the tissue. Thermal therapy uses a probe with a heated tip, a bipolar probe that passes current through the tissue between two electrodes, or a jet of ionized gas that conducts current to the surface without touching it, and all three coagulate by raising the tissue temperature until the proteins denature and the vessel seals. Too much energy desiccates the tissue until it chars, and a charred surface hides the vessel that is still bleeding underneath, while a spurting artery needs a mechanical or injection method before or instead of heat. The energy level, the application time, and the probe selection must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Capsule endoscopy removes the shaft altogether. The patient swallows a capsule the size of a large vitamin, which contains a lens, a light source, a battery, a transmitter, and a small antenna, and which passes through the gut by the ordinary movement of the bowel. The capsule photographs the mucosa as it travels and sends the images to a recorder worn on a belt, so the examination needs no sedation, no insufflation, and no insertion, and the patient walks around while it happens. Its limits follow from its design, because it cannot steer, wash the surface, biopsy, treat, or send back anything but images, and the retention of a capsule in a narrowed segment is the characteristic serious complication. The battery life, the recording interval, and the exclusion criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Endoscopic ultrasound puts a high-frequency sound transducer on the tip of an endoscope, so that the wall of the gut and the organs immediately beyond it can be seen without the intervening gas and bone that spoil an external scan. High frequency gives fine detail but shallow penetration, so a probe at 12 to 20 megahertz images a few centimeters while a lower frequency reaches further, and the examiner chooses the compromise that fits the question. Radial probes sweep a circle around the shaft and produce an image like a slice across the gut, while linear probes look forward along the shaft and leave a path for a needle to pass into a lymph node, a cyst, or a pancreatic mass. The tip is coupled to the tissue with a water-filled balloon or by filling the gut with water, because sound does not travel through air, and the frequency, the balloon volume, and the needle path must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Everything that enters the gut is contaminated with blood, mucus, and a dense population of bacteria, and the instrument is hollow, long, and heat-sensitive, so it cannot simply be steamed. Reprocessing a flexible endoscope is a chain of steps in which each one protects the next, and a break anywhere in the chain leaves a device that looks clean and is not. The chain begins at the bedside, within minutes of the instrument leaving the patient, because delay lets blood and mucus dry into a film that later steps cannot lift. The insertion tube is wiped, the channel is flushed with detergent solution, and air is passed to expel the fluid before the scope travels to the reprocessing room. The interval allowed before bedside cleaning, the detergent concentration, and the flush volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A flexible endoscope is a sealed tube, and the single most important test of its integrity is the leak test. The scope is pressurized with air at a low pressure through its leak test port and then submerged in water, and any breach in the covering, the bending section, or the channel walls releases bubbles that show where the damage is. The test is done before immersion cleaning so that water is not drawn into a punctured channel, where it would reach the electronics and the optics and destroy the instrument, and it is repeated whenever the scope has been struck, bitten, or used on a patient with a sharp foreign body. The test pressure, the immersion time, and the required response to bubbles must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Manual cleaning comes before any machine, because a disinfectant cannot penetrate a layer of dried organic matter. The scope is fully immersed in a basin of detergent solution and every external surface is wiped, including the control section, the insertion tube, and the bending section, with attention to the rough areas where the covering is bonded. Every channel is brushed, including the suction channel, the air and water channel, the biopsy channel, and the elevator recess on a duodenoscope, and the brush is pushed through until it emerges at the far end before the bristles are pulled back. The brush diameter must match the channel, because a brush too small does not touch the walls and a brush too large jams and can scratch the lining, and the brush itself is a contaminated item that must be cleaned or discarded between scopes. The brush sizes, the number of passes, and the detergent contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The washer-disinfector automates the part of the chain that humans do inconsistently. The scope is placed in a tray with its channels connected to ports on the machine, and the machine pumps detergent, rinse water, and disinfectant through the lumens at a controlled flow, temperature, and time, so that every internal surface sees the chemical rather than only the outside. Some machines also test for channel blockage by measuring flow, and a channel that no longer accepts the expected flow is flagged. The cycle is only valid if the connectors are correctly attached, the channels are not occluded, and the chemicals are at the correct concentration, because a cycle that runs with a loose connector washes the outside of the scope and leaves the inside untouched. The cycle parameters, the flow check, and the connector configuration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

High-level disinfection is a chemical process that kills all bacteria, most viruses, and fungi, and leaves some bacterial spores, which is why it is not called sterilization. The chemistry most often used is a dialdehyde solution, usually glutaraldehyde, which cross-links the proteins of the microbial cell, while ortho-phthalaldehyde is less irritating to the airway and peracetic acid acts by oxidizing and is often used in automated processors. Concentration, temperature, and contact time act together, and a dilute or cold or short exposure may fail even though the instrument was submerged. Test strips confirm that the active concentration is above the minimum effective value, the solution is discarded after its stated reuse life or sooner if the strip fails, and the room must be ventilated because the vapors irritate the eyes and the airways. The concentration, the temperature, the contact time, the test method, and the ventilation requirement must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Drying is not cosmetic, because a drop of water left in a channel is a place where bacteria multiply between patients. After disinfection the scope is rinsed with water of a defined quality, purged with air, and often flushed with alcohol, which mixes with the remaining water and evaporates with it. The instrument is then hung vertically with its valves removed, in a cabinet that circulates filtered air through the channels and keeps the surfaces dry. The cabinet is a device in its own right, with a filter, a fan, and sometimes a timer and a record of when the scope was placed inside, and its purpose is to prevent the regrowth that happens in a damp, closed space. Storage time has a limit, and a scope stored beyond it is reprocessed before use, and the rinse water quality, the drying time, the cabinet airflow, and the maximum storage time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Endoscopy equipment speaks in alarms, and each one points to a different part of the chain. The processor alarms on lamp failure, on overheating, and on a disconnected scope or cable, and a dark monitor during a procedure requires a spare lamp and a spare scope rather than a repair attempt on the patient. The reprocessing machine alarms on low disinfectant concentration, on a blocked channel, on low temperature, and on an incomplete cycle, and the only correct response to an incomplete cycle is to repeat the whole cycle rather than to release the scope. The storage cabinet alarms on loss of airflow or a saturated filter, while the leak tester simply shows bubbles. The alarm behavior, the response to each alarm, and the records to be kept must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The common operator errors in gastrointestinal endoscopy are few and expensive. The first is to advance against resistance, because the gut wall is thin and a loop that will not straighten is a warning rather than an obstacle, and a perforation may be silent at the moment it happens and declared later by pain, fever, and a rigid abdomen. The second is to insufflate without limit, because distension is uncomfortable and in a patient with a weak wall it can cause a perforation, so the abdomen is watched as the examination proceeds. The third is to pass an accessory through a channel that is too small or a needle that is too short for the lesion, and the resulting jam damages both the accessory and the lining. The fourth is to silence an alarm or accept an incomplete reprocessing cycle because the list is long, and that shortcut is how a clinic transmits infection. The resistance that should stop the advance, the insufflation limit, the accessory and channel match, and the alarm response must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic failures of a flexible endoscope are physical, and most are visible before they are dangerous. A bite from a confused patient cracks the covering of the bending section, and the leak test then bubbles, admitting fluid into the optics so the picture fogs or dims permanently. A channel punctured by a needle or an over-sized accessory leaks during the leak test and later cannot be properly cleaned, because fluid bypasses the lumen walls. A broken fiber bundle shows as black dots in the image, and the number of dots only grows, while the angulation mechanism can lose its range or become stiff so the tip no longer reaches the angle needed to see a flexure. Each finding has a defined action, whether removal from service or continued use with a limitation, and the acceptance criteria for each must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of an endoscopy unit are as important as the instruments, and running out of one stops the list. Every patient needs a bite block to protect the instrument from the teeth, a lubricant, and often a topical anesthetic for the throat. The unit needs suction canisters and tubing, basins and detergents for manual cleaning, channel brushes in several diameters, leak testers, and the disinfectant with its test strips. There are specimen containers with fixative, labels that survive the fixative, and a documented chain from the patient to the pathology laboratory, plus the accessories themselves, forceps, snares, needles, and clips, each with an expiry date and an intact package. The staff who reprocess the instrument wear personal protective equipment, because the detergent, the disinfectant, and the patient's secretions all splash, and the stocking levels, the expiry checks, and the storage conditions of every consumable must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field position begins with a hard fact, which is that a flexible endoscope is one of the least field-friendly devices in medicine. It needs a light source, a processor, a monitor, clean water, a disinfectant, a drying cabinet, and a trained person to reprocess it, and none of those are present in a tent at the end of a road.
