Reprocessing in neurosurgery is dominated by delicate geometry, because micro-instruments, dissectors, and drills have narrow channels, hinges, and fine tips that trap blood and bone dust. Cleaning begins immediately after use, before the debris dries, and instruments are opened, disassembled where possible, and cleaned in an ultrasonic bath before inspection under magnification. Steam sterilization is the standard, commonly 134 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes in a vacuum cycle or 121 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes, and the operating microscope cannot be steamed, so it is covered with a sterile drape. The cycle, the load configuration, and the drying step must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and instruments whose tips no longer meet are sharpened or rejected.

Preventive maintenance is mostly electrical safety, calibration, and consumable life tracking. The biomedical technician verifies the leakage current and the protective earth of every line-powered amplifier, checks pressure transducers and nerve stimulators against a reference, and tests every alarm function. The air compressor or gas supply that drives the drills needs its filters changed and its dryer working, since water in the line destroys bearings, and each handpiece has an hours-of-use limit after which it is serviced or retired. The maintenance intervals, the calibration tolerances, and the acceptance criteria after repair must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the operator checks before every use is a short list that catches most disasters. The patient is identified, and the procedure and side are confirmed aloud with the team. The machine passes its self-test, the electrode impedances are acceptable, and the pressure transducer is leveled and zeroed. The drain stopcocks and chamber height are correct, the drill runs true in the air with a secure hose, and the microscope is balanced with its light shuttered. The clip board and the instrument count are started before the incision, so the specific checks and the documentation they require must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant of this chapter is defined by what is missing. There is no computed tomography scanner in many district hospitals, no magnetic resonance imaging, no neuronavigation, no operating microscope, no air-driven drill with a clutch, and no sterile processing department with validated cycles. What remains is the burr hole, the catheter, the fluid column, a hand drill, a good light, and a trained hand. The equipment that survives is the equipment that works without mains power, without compressed gas, and without a supply chain, so the field clinician must be honest about which problems can be treated where.

The field EEG is a reduced instrument that is still useful for the questions it can answer. A battery-powered amplifier with 8 or 16 channels can be carried in a case and set up on a table, with reusable disc electrodes held on with saline-soaked pads or paste. A clear seizure pattern, a marked asymmetry, or the electrical silence of a severe injury can still be identified. The instrument gives up the full montage, the video, the prolonged recording, the exact electrode placement, and the artifact rejection of a hospital system, so its findings are suggestive rather than definitive. The channel count, the electrode type, and the interpretation limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Field EMG and nerve conduction use a handheld stimulator and a simple amplifier and are most valuable for locating a divided nerve in a limb injury. The field external ventricular drain is improvised from a ventricular catheter, sterile tubing, and a graduated container held at a measured height. The zero point is marked on the bed frame or the wall beside the patient's ear with tape and a pen, and the height above it is measured with a ruler or tape. Without a transducer there is no continuous waveform and no alarm, so the pressure is inferred from the height and the patient is watched for drowsiness, vomiting, and a falling level of consciousness. The reference mark, the chamber height, and the volume drained must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field burr hole is the central procedure of frontier neurosurgery. Without a clutch perforator, the surgeon uses a hand-turned brace and bit or an electric drill with a sterile bit, applies light and intermittent pressure, and stops the moment the resistance changes. Bone is cleared with a curette rather than driven through, because the dura and the brain lie a few millimeters beyond the inner table. The site is prepared with an antiseptic solution and draped, local anesthetic is infiltrated, and the hole is enlarged only as much as the task requires. The preparation, the anesthesia, and the draping routine must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because sterile technique is more demanding in a tent than in a theater.

Some patients must be transferred, and saying so early is part of good equipment practice. A falling level of consciousness, a new focal weakness, a suspected aneurysm, or an open fracture of the skull with brain visible needs imaging and a neurosurgeon, and no amount of improvisation replaces either. The transfer is planned with the airway secured and the drain clamped so it cannot siphon. Images travel badly, so a copy on a storage device or a photograph of the scan is sent with the patient, and the receiving center is spoken to before departure. The transfer criteria, the clamping rules, and the observation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Field sterilization is the weakest link in the whole chain, and the honest clinician treats it as such. Where there is no steam autoclave, instruments may be boiled, which kills most organisms but does not reliably kill spores and is not sterilization. A chemical soak may be used instead, but its concentration cannot be verified and it irritates the eyes and the airways. A burr that cannot be sterilized should be single use if possible, and a catheter that cannot be guaranteed sterile should not be placed in the brain. Where a real autoclave is available, a common cycle is 134 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes or 121 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes, and the cycle and its monitoring must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Power and environment shape the field equipment more than the clinical task does. A battery-powered amplifier, a rechargeable drill, and a headlamp remove the dependence on mains electricity, but their batteries must be charged from a generator that may deliver unstable voltage. Heat, dust, humidity, and altitude change the behavior of motors, compressed gas supplies, and electronics, and a device rated for a clean room may fail in a tent. Instruments intended for these conditions should be simple, mechanical where possible, repairable with ordinary tools, and supplied with spare batteries and seals rather than a service contract. The storage temperature, the charging routine, and the cleaning limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic alarms of this chapter are few, and each one means something specific. An electrode impedance alarm means a contact has failed or dried, and the response is to fix the electrode rather than silence the channel. A pressure alarm or a suddenly flat waveform on a drain means a blocked catheter, a bubble, a disconnection, or a patient who has moved, and it is answered by checking the patient first and the tubing second. A drill that slows, heats, or changes pitch has a supply, bearing, or burr problem and must be stopped, so the threshold of every one of these alarms must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, neurology and neurosurgery ask machines to do two difficult things at once. They must detect signals smaller than the noise around them, and they must work inside a closed space where a millimeter of error or a drop of contamination can be permanent. The hospital-grade versions use differential amplifiers and averaging, transducers leveled to a bony landmark and zeroed to the atmosphere, and navigation and frames that translate an image into a patient. They add microscopes that light the bottom of a narrow corridor, drills that cut bone and spare the dura beneath, and implants such as clips, shunts, and stimulators that must be chosen, counted, programmed, and verified. The field versions keep the burr hole, the drain, the measured fluid column, and the careful observation, and they give up the imaging and the validation that make the complex operations safe. The clinician who understands why the fluid column measures pressure, why averaging reveals the evoked response, and why a clip must never be reused will use the simplest version of this equipment correctly and will know when the honest answer is to transfer the patient.

# Chapter 52 — Urology, Gynecology, and Wound Care

This chapter gathers three fields that share a physics before they share a corridor. Urology and gynecology both work through natural openings into cavities that are normally collapsed, so both depend on instruments that distend a soft-walled space enough for a lens and a tool to work inside it. Wound care works in the other direction, on a cavity that is kept open to drain while its surface is sealed against the air, and its central machine controls pressure across a film. In all three the outcome depends on lumen size, applied pressure, and the cleanliness of a long narrow channel.

The urinary tract is plumbing with a chemical factory at one end and a valve at the other. Each kidney makes urine continuously, and the urine leaves through a funnel called the renal pelvis and then through the ureter, a muscular tube about 25 centimeters long that pushes it downward in small waves. That tube is narrowest at three points, where it leaves the kidney, where it crosses the pelvic blood vessels, and where it enters the bladder, so a stone usually lodges at one of them. The bladder stores urine at low pressure and empties by contraction, and the urethra is the outlet. When the path is blocked, pressure rises behind the blockage and travels back to the kidney, which is why so much urological equipment exists simply to relieve pressure, and the catheter size and drainage technique must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Most instruments in this field are measured on the French scale, and the scale is worth understanding rather than memorizing. A single French unit equals one third of a millimeter of external diameter, so 18 French is about 6 millimeters across and 30 French is 10 millimeters across. A change of 2 French is therefore a real change in the bore, and a tube that passes easily at one size may tear the lining at the next, because the urethral wall is thin and its blood supply is easily compressed. A catheter that is too small drains poorly, and one that is too large presses on the lining and can cause a stricture months later. The size chosen and the balloon volume that comes with it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cystoscope is the eye of urology, and its shape follows from the fact that the urethra is a curved tunnel with no view of its own walls. A rigid instrument is a metal tube carrying a lens system and a light, and it is passed with the patient's legs supported and the urethra well lubricated. Beside the telescope runs a working channel for a catheter, a wire, or a small forceps, and a separate channel admits irrigation so the bladder can be filled and blood washed away until the lining is visible. A flexible instrument replaces the rigid lenses with a bundle of fine glass fibers or a chip camera at the tip, so it follows the curve of the urethra without leverage. The diameter, the angle of view, and the irrigation flow must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A rigid cystoscope is assembled from parts that must match exactly, and a mismatch is the first thing to check. The sheath is the outer tube, with a blunt obturator filling its lumen during insertion so that no sharp edge can catch the lining, and a seal at the near end stops irrigation running over the operator's hands. Forcing the instrument when resistance is felt can create a false passage or perforate the bladder, and over-distension causes pain, bleeding, and fainting. Every pass of the instrument carries bacteria upward, so disinfection and technique are the real infection control. The over-temperature alarm of the light source is the characteristic alarm of the system, and the light output, the temperature limit, the sheath size, and the alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The resectoscope is a cystoscope given a cutting loop, and it removes tissue from inside the bladder or the prostate by sliding a wire loop across the surface while a high-frequency current passes through it. The current concentrates at the thin wire and raises the temperature of the tissue in contact with it until the cells separate, and a lower current density produces coagulation instead of division. The loop sits on a spring carriage worked by the thumb, so the cut is a controlled sliding movement, and the speed of that movement decides whether the surface is clean or charred. A continuous flow sheath has inner and outer tubes so irrigation enters through one and leaves through the other, keeping the view clear while bleeding continues. The loop size, the current, and the irrigation rate must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The irrigation fluid is a safety decision, because the choice follows from the electrical circuit. A monopolar loop needs a non-conducting solution such as glycine, sorbitol, or mannitol, and those dilute fluids behave like water when they are absorbed; a bipolar loop keeps the current between two electrodes at its tip, so ordinary salt water is safe. Absorption happens because the open veins of the resected surface are bathed in fluid under pressure, and a large absorbed volume of a dilute solution lowers the blood sodium and can cause confusion, nausea, visual disturbance, seizures, and death, a pattern known as transurethral resection syndrome. A monopolar generator also supervises the large return pad on the patient's thigh, and it sounds a return electrode alarm when the contact is poor, which is a warning of a skin burn rather than a nuisance. The fluid, the resection time, the pressure, the pad position, and the alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The urethrotome treats a stricture, which is a scar that narrows the urethra into a tight ring. The instrument places a blade at the narrow point and draws it through the scar in controlled cuts, so the ring is opened and the channel widened; a laser fiber or a knife under direct vision does the same work another way. A blind instrument carries a graduated scale along its shaft, so the operator reads how deep the blade has advanced instead of judging by feel. Cutting too deeply opens the erectile tissue around the urethra and causes severe bleeding or a fistula, while cutting too little lets the stricture narrow again. This is a purely mechanical device with no alarm of its own, so the only warnings are resistance and blood, and the blade depth, the instrument size, and the intended incision length must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An extracorporeal lithotripter breaks a stone with a shock wave made outside the body and focused on the stone. Most machines make that wave by discharging a spark across a gap under water, by driving a metal plate with a magnetic pulse, or by contracting a piezoelectric array, and most focus it with an ellipsoid reflector that has two focal points. The patient is positioned so the stone sits at the second focus, and the energy is concentrated there while the tissue along the path is largely spared. Some machines time each shock to the heart rhythm so that it avoids a vulnerable phase of the cardiac cycle. The number of shocks, the energy level, and the coupling of the water cushion to the skin must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Intracorporeal lithotripsy carries the energy to the stone through a probe or a fiber. A pneumatic probe fires a small projectile at the stone, an ultrasonic probe vibrates it apart and sucks the fragments away, and a laser fiber delivers light that water and stone absorb, creating a tiny plasma bubble that drills and cracks the stone. The laser is the most versatile, because a thin flexible fiber reaches almost any stone, and its energy is set in joules per pulse and its rate in pulses per second, so a typical setting might be 1 joule at 10 hertz, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazards are a fiber fired against the ureter wall, a fragment driven into tissue, and a laser triggered outside the field of view. A lithotripter also reports coupling, water, and calibration faults, and it usually refuses to fire rather than fire at the wrong energy; the common error is to raise the energy instead of repositioning the fiber.

Urodynamic equipment asks not what a structure looks like but how it behaves while it fills and empties. Two fine catheters, one in the bladder and one in the rectum or vagina, each connect by a column of fluid to an external pressure sensor, and the machine records bladder pressure and abdominal pressure against time. Because the two pressures are recorded together, the pressure made by the bladder muscle itself can be found by subtracting the abdominal pressure from the bladder pressure. A pump fills the bladder at a controlled rate, a flowmeter weighs the urine as it leaves, and surface electrodes record the electrical activity of the pelvic floor. An air bubble flattens the trace, a catheter tip against the wall records a false pressure, and a sensor not zeroed at the level of the pubic bone drifts, so the filling rate, the pressure limit, the calibration, and the alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The urinary catheter is the most common device in this field, and its physics explain both its usefulness and its dangers. A Foley catheter is a flexible tube with two channels, one draining urine and one inflating a small balloon near the tip with sterile water, so the balloon holds it in the bladder. A three-way catheter adds a channel for irrigation fluid, which is used after bladder surgery or when clots must be washed out, and a coudé catheter has a curved tip that can be steered past an enlarged prostate. Catheters are made of latex, silicone, or polyvinyl chloride, and the material decides how stiff the tube is, how long it may stay in place, and whether a patient with a latex allergy can tolerate it. The size, the material, the balloon volume, and the intended dwell time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The balloon must never be inflated until urine returns, because a balloon filled inside the urethra tears the lining and creates a false passage. Lubricant reduces friction and pain, and in a man the penis is lifted to remove the curve of the urethra before steady gentle pressure is applied; pushing against resistance is the common error that causes the injury. The drainage bag hangs below the bladder so urine runs downhill and never flows back, and a dependent loop of tubing where stagnant urine collects is a defect to correct, not a detail of tidiness. Every day an indwelling catheter remains raises the chance of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection, so it is removed as soon as it is no longer needed and the closed circuit is never opened to take a sample. An electronic urine meter may carry a full-bag alarm, and its alarm volume, bag capacity, and emptying interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When the ureter itself is blocked and a catheter cannot pass, pressure is relieved with a tube placed directly into the kidney. A fine needle is guided into the collecting system under ultrasound or X-ray, a guidewire is threaded through it, and a pigtail catheter is passed over the wire and coiled in the renal pelvis, where a locking thread keeps it from falling out. A ureteric stent takes the other route, running inside the ureter from kidney to bladder with two curled ends that give it the name double J. Both are quiet devices whose failures are noticed by their consequences: a blocked or dislodged nephrostomy stops draining and the kidney distends, and a stent left in place for many months becomes encrusted and may break when it is finally removed. The diameter, the length, the fixation, and the planned removal date must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and every stent belongs in a register.

The urological equipment of a frontier clinic is chosen by what can be cleaned without a machine and repaired with ordinary tools. A rigid cystoscope with a battery handle, a set of metal sounds, catheters in every size, a manual irrigation syringe, and a supply of sterile water and gel carry most of the urgent work, which is the relief of retention and the drainage of an obstructed kidney. Stones are managed with analgesia and referral unless a portable lithotripter is available, because the machine is heavy and needs power, water, and a trained operator for every session. The clinic gives up diagnostic endoscopy and gives up urodynamics entirely, and in exchange it demands a stricter rule about which patients are kept and which are sent onward. What is never improvised is prolonged irrigation with tap water into an open bladder or prostate, because the fluid is absorbed and the electrolyte disturbance can kill; the sterilizer cycle and the chemical disinfectant contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Gynecology begins with the speculum, the simplest and most misunderstood instrument in the specialty. Its purpose is to hold the vaginal walls apart so the cervix can be seen, and it does this with two blades that open like a beak when the handle is squeezed, held by a screw or a ratchet so the operator's hands are free. Blades come in different lengths and widths, from a narrow instrument for a postmenopausal patient to a wide one for a woman who has delivered, and the choice follows from what the examination requires. A metal speculum is reusable and sterilized between patients, while a plastic one is single use, which matters where reprocessing is unreliable. The size, the material, and the sterilization or disposal method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a speculum that is cold, dry, or roughly inserted is remembered for years.

The speculum has no gauge and no alarm, so all of its safety lies in technique. It is inserted closed and angled along the axis of the vagina, and it is opened only after it is in place, because opening it early catches the vulva and the urethra; the screw is then set so the blades cannot close on the cervix. A lubricant is used when it is appropriate, but not when a cervical sample is being taken, because the gel dilutes the specimen. The colposcope goes further by magnifying the cervix under a strong light, using two eyepieces on a long arm to give a three-dimensional view from 20 to 30 centimeters away, and a green filter that makes the blood vessel pattern stand out. Dilute acetic acid turns abnormal tissue white, and iodine stains mature tissue dark while leaving abnormal areas unstained; the magnification, the light level, the acetic acid concentration, and the reading time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A colposcope is an optical instrument on a movable stand in a room used for many purposes, which is exactly the combination that damages it. Its lenses are cleaned only with a soft cloth and a solution the maker permits, its joints and counterbalance are checked, and a spare lamp is kept on hand because the usual warning of lamp failure is a dimming image rather than a sudden blackout. The common operator error is to mistake normal immature tissue that whitens with acetic acid for a lesion, or to examine without enough light and magnification and record a confident normal finding. Tissue is taken whenever the view is abnormal, using a punch forceps with two sharp opposed jaws, or a thin spoon for the endocervical canal, and the physical action must be a clean shear rather than a tear because a dull instrument crushes the specimen beyond interpretation. The sampling site, the fixative, and the label on each pot must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hazard of cervical biopsy is bleeding, because the cervix has a generous blood supply. Pressure from a swab usually stops it, with a silver nitrate stick or a cauterizing paste ready, and a suture or a vaginal pack is the next step; a dark discharge and light bleeding for a few days are normal, while fever and heavy bleeding are not. The hysteroscope looks into a cavity whose walls touch one another, so its central problem is distension rather than view. A sheath carries fluid in and lets it out, and the pressure of that fluid holds the cavity open; salt water is used for a bipolar instrument, while a monopolar electrode needs a non-conducting medium that behaves like water if it is absorbed. The distension medium, the inflow pressure, the flow rate, and the maximum fluid deficit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The most serious complication of hysteroscopy is an absorbed fluid load, because the uterus has an open venous drainage that accepts distension fluid under pressure. A large absorbed volume of a dilute non-conducting medium lowers the blood sodium and can cause confusion, nausea, visual disturbance, and seizures, while a large absorbed volume of salt water overloads the circulation and fills the lungs. The defense is to count what goes in and what comes out continuously, to keep the inflow pressure as low as the view allows, and to stop when the deficit reaches the limit set for that patient, because a woman with heart disease tolerates far less than a healthy one. The distension pump carries a fluid deficit alarm and an over-pressure alarm, and both are stop signals; the inflow pressure, the deficit limit, the flow rate, and the alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The loop electrosurgical excision procedure removes the abnormal transformation zone with a thin wire loop carrying a high-frequency current, and its value lies in the control the wire gives over depth and shape. A loop is chosen so that one pass removes the lesion and a margin of normal tissue while leaving a specimen the pathologist can read. The current is a blend of cutting and coagulation, with a low voltage and a high current density at the wire, so the tissue divides with little thermal damage at the edge; too slow a pass cooks the specimen and too fast a pass cuts without sealing the small vessels. The generator also supervises the return pad on the thigh and sounds a pad alarm if the contact becomes poor, and the smoke is removed by an evacuator close to the field because it carries fine particles and chemicals. The power, the loop size, the pad position, the smoke evacuation, and the alarm behavior must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cryotherapy destroys tissue by freezing it, and the mechanism is the formation of ice inside and between the cells. A probe cooled by a gas that expands through a small nozzle, usually nitrous oxide or carbon dioxide, is pressed against the cervix, and the expanding gas absorbs heat from the metal tip through the Joule-Thomson effect. The ice ball ruptures cell membranes and stops the small vessels, and the cycle is repeated as a freeze, a thaw, and a second freeze, because the second freeze kills more cells than the first. Thermal ablation reaches a similar result with a probe held at about 100 degrees Celsius, and its temperature, contact time, and probe size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Both methods destroy tissue in place, so they are used only for a small, fully visible lesion confirmed non-invasive by biopsy, and never when cancer is suspected.

The gynecological field kit is built around the eye and the hand rather than around electricity. A set of specula, a good lamp, dilute acetic acid, and a trained examiner will find most visible cervical lesions, and the technique of inspection after acetic acid is deliberately taught because it needs no machine at all. A battery-powered colposcope or a magnifying loupe improves the view, and a portable thermal coagulator running from a battery or a small inverter can treat a lesion in a clinic with no reliable mains supply. The clinic gives up cytology, histology, and the precise excision a loop provides, and in exchange it demands a rigid referral rule for anything that looks invasive, bleeds on contact, or extends into the canal. The disinfectant concentration, the contact time, and the sterilizer cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Wound care rests on a principle that is physiological rather than mechanical, because a wound heals best in a moist, warm, clean environment. Cells migrate across a moist surface, while a dry scab forces them to travel underneath it, and a wound allowed to cool and dry loses the enzymes that drive repair. Modern dressings therefore control moisture rather than dry the wound out, and the choice follows from how much fluid the wound produces and whether the surrounding skin can tolerate being wet. Clean water or salt water at low pressure removes loose debris, and the force of the irrigation matters more than the solution, because a high-pressure jet drives bacteria into the tissue while a gentle flow washes them away. The irrigation pressure, the solution, and the dressing choice must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The instruments of wound care are simple and mostly about seeing and cleaning. A probe measures the depth and direction of a tract, forceps remove loose debris, and a scalpel or curette takes away dead tissue, with good light and a measuring tape as important as the blade. Sharp debridement is a controlled surgical act and is never done blindly in a wound over a vessel, a tendon, or a joint, and the dressing that follows must not macerate the surrounding skin or press on a bony prominence. The wound is measured and described at each visit, with its size, depth, base, edges, and the state of the surrounding skin, because that record shows whether the treatment is working. The common error is to leave a dressing in place because it looks clean while the wound underneath deteriorates, so the dressing is lifted and the wound inspected on the schedule the protocol sets; the cleaning agents, the debridement technique, and the dressing interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Negative pressure wound therapy is the most technical device in wound care, and it turns an open wound into a closed system under a controlled subatmospheric pressure. The wound is filled with an open-celled foam, covered with a semipermeable film that sticks to the surrounding skin, and joined by a tube to a pump that removes air and fluid; the film lets water vapor escape while keeping air and bacteria out, so the seal is what makes the system work. The usual range is a negative pressure of 75 to 125 millimeters of mercury, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pressure gradient draws the wound edges together, pulls fluid from the tissue, and increases blood flow to the wound bed, while the mechanical deformation of the cells appears to stimulate granulation tissue. The foam also gives the new tissue a scaffold, which is why the choice of foam is not arbitrary.

The system has four parts, and each can fail in its own way. The foam is either a black open-pored polyurethane sponge with pores between roughly 400 and 600 micrometers, used for most granulating wounds, or a white denser polyvinyl alcohol sponge with smaller pores, used where the wound is painful or the tissue fragile; the pore size and material must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The film must overlap the skin by several centimeters on every side and must not be stretched across a crease or a joint, because a wrinkle becomes a leak. The tubing carries fluid to a canister that must be seated correctly, and the pump runs in continuous or intermittent mode with set cycle times, carrying a leak alarm, a canister full alarm, a blockage alarm, and a low battery alarm, each naming a different physical fault. The pressure, the mode, the cycle times, the canister size, and the alarm thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The most serious hazard of negative pressure wound therapy is hemorrhage, because the negative pressure can erode a blood vessel in the wound bed, and a patient taking an anticoagulant can bleed catastrophically into the dressing. Foam is never placed in direct contact with an exposed large vessel, a graft, or a fresh anastomosis, and a bleeding wound is an emergency rather than a dressing problem: the pressure is stopped, the dressing removed, and direct pressure applied. Infection and retained foam are the next hazards, so every piece of foam is counted and recorded and the dressing is changed on schedule rather than when it begins to smell. The common operator error is to keep raising the pressure to overcome a leak instead of finding it, and the pressure setting, the dressing interval, and the alarm responses must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A frontier clinic can sometimes build a version of this therapy from what it owns, and the honest account must say what such a system cannot do. The improvisation uses sterile gauze or foam in the wound, a flat drain or small tube laid over it, an adhesive film sealing the dressing to the skin, and a wall suction or portable suction unit with a regulator, and the pressure is judged by the gauge and by bubbling in the canister rather than by a pump that measures it. It removes fluid and holds the surface under some negative pressure, but it has no leak compensation, no fluid measurement, and no alarm at all, so a blocked tube or a lost seal is silent and the therapy is simply not happening. The dangers are an uncontrolled suction pressure, a hemorrhage nobody is warned about, a vacuum line contaminated with wound fluid, and a dressing left unchanged too long. The improvised system must never be used over a vessel, and the delivered pressure, the seal, the suction setting, and the observation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

All three fields carry the same reprocessing burden, and the fragile instruments at the center of it are the ones most often damaged by cleaning. Rigid telescopes, cystoscopes, and hysteroscopes are leak tested before immersion, because fluid entering the optical tube destroys it, and the test takes less time than the repair it prevents. Reusable metal instruments are cleaned before blood dries, inspected for cracks and stiffness, lubricated where the maker requires it, and sterilized in a cycle set for the load, a typical steam cycle being 134 degrees Celsius for 3 to 4 minutes, a number that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Single-use devices are not reused even when they look intact, because their materials were never designed to survive cleaning and their internal channels cannot be inspected. Flexible scopes are hung vertically to drain and dry, since a scope stored wet grows a biofilm that no later disinfection will remove; the cleaning agents, the test method, and the storage conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Maintenance across this equipment is mostly inspection, and the inspection is mostly of the parts that touch the patient. Light cables lose fibers and grow dim, camera cables break at the strain relief, seals and gaskets harden and leak, balloons weaken and burst, pump tubing stretches and delivers a wrong volume, and suction regulators drift so that the number on the gauge is no longer the number delivered. A preventive schedule names what is checked daily, monthly, and at service, and each check is recorded in a logbook that belongs to the device rather than to the ward. The consumables that must never run out are the ones that stop a procedure in its middle: sterile water for balloons, lubricant, biopsy pots and fixative, return pads, smoke filters, foam and film, and canisters of the right size. A recurring theme of this chapter is that the most dangerous failures are silent, since a catheter that no longer drains, a forgotten stent, an absorbing uterus, and a dressing that has lost its seal all look normal while they fail; the maintenance interval, the spare parts list, and the calibration method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, these three fields meet in the physics of soft tubes, closed spaces, and controlled pressure. Urology sees with the cystoscope and the resectoscope, distends with irrigation, cuts with controlled current, fragments stones with focused energy, measures function with pressure catheters, and drains with catheters, nephrostomy tubes, and stents sized on the French scale. Gynecology examines with the speculum, magnifies with the colposcope, takes tissue with sharp forceps, distends the uterus with a measured fluid, and destroys small lesions with a wire loop, with cold, or with heat. Wound care keeps a wound moist, cleans it gently, and where the wound is large or slow, seals it and applies negative pressure through foam and film. In each field the hospital version is a system of pumps, sensors, sealed circuits, and trained reprocessing, while the field version trades that machinery for portability and gives up measurement, alarm, and certainty in return, demanding stricter selection, closer observation, and a written protocol instead.

# Chapter 53 — Rehabilitation and Physiotherapy

Rehabilitation equipment restores function by rearranging force rather than by killing a microbe or replacing a molecule. A cane, a brace, and a prosthetic foot take a load that a damaged limb can no longer carry and pass it to a structure that can. A therapy unit adds energy to tissue as an electrical current or a mechanical vibration, and the tissue answers with a sensation, a contraction, or a warming. The therapist is a technician of leverage, alignment, and dose, and the equipment makes a correct dose repeatable. This chapter covers walking aids, wheeled chairs, orthoses, prostheses, therapy units, exercise frames, and measuring tools, first in a hospital and then as they are made and repaired far from a workshop.

Every walking aid begins with the relationship between the base of support and the center of gravity. A standing person is stable when a vertical line dropped from the center of mass falls inside the area bounded by the feet. Walking is a controlled fall caught by the next foot before balance is lost, and a damaged limb, a painful joint, or a weak muscle reduces the force available to catch it. An aid enlarges the base of support, adds a point of contact that shares the load, or carries force to the floor through a rigid column instead of through the leg. The height of that column and the condition of its tip decide whether the device helps the patient or betrays the patient.

The cane is the simplest column, a single shaft with a handle and a rubber tip. Its handle usually sits at the wrist crease with the arm relaxed, leaving the elbow bent about 20 to 30 degrees, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Holding the cane on the side of the weak leg is the most common operator error, because the cane belongs in the hand opposite the weak limb where it forms a tripod with the affected foot. The tip is a consumable that hardens, wears flat, and loses its grip on a wet floor, and a worn tip is a fall waiting to happen. An axillary crutch is set so its pad rests about 5 centimeters below the fold of the armpit, a distance that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazard of that type is pressure in the armpit, where the radial nerve and the axillary vessels pass, and prolonged pressure produces numbness, a weak wrist, and the palsy that carries the crutch's name. A forearm crutch with a metal cuff is lighter but demands more arm strength, and the operator checks the gap, the elbow angle, and the rubber tips before every walk.

The walker converts the patient into a four legged structure, which is why it goes to the person with the poorest balance. The frame widens the base of support in front of the body, so a forward lean is caught by the frame rather than by a single stick. A rollator adds wheels so the frame is pushed instead of lifted, and its height follows the rule of the wrist crease, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazards are a wheel that rolls because the brake was not set, a folding hinge that collapses because it was not locked, and worn tips that slide on a polished floor. The characteristic failure is a stretched brake cable, which leaves the lever feeling firm while the wheel turns freely, and the common error is to load the frame before the brakes are set. The operator rocks the frame, tests both brakes, and inspects the tips and locking clips before the patient stands.

The manual wheelchair is a chair on two large rear wheels and two small front casters, and its behavior comes from the wheel and axle. A large wheel climbs a threshold more easily because each turn carries it further, while a small caster accelerates more easily. The seat width is chosen so the hips clear the side frames by about 2 centimeters on each side, and the depth so the front edge stops just behind the knee crease, with both measurements confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Moving the rear axle forward makes the chair easier to push and more likely to tip backward, so almost every frame carries an anti tip device and a pair of wheel locks. The wheel lock is a parking brake, because it holds a chair already at rest and must never be relied on to slow a moving chair on a slope. The common error is to transfer a patient into a chair whose locks are loose or whose armrest is raised, so the check before each transfer is the locks, the anti tip devices, the upholstery, and the footrests.

Maintenance is what keeps a wheelchair rolling, and it is a small and unglamorous routine. Tire pressure is checked with a gauge rather than by thumb, because a soft tire increases rolling resistance and damages the rim, and the correct pressure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The spokes are squeezed in pairs to find the loose ones, the axles are turned by hand to feel for rough bearings, and the wheel locks are adjusted to bite the tire when engaged. The common errors are to inflate from a compressor without a gauge, to leave the chair in the rain, and to ignore a front caster wobble that grows into a seized bearing. The consumables are tires, inner tubes, bearings, hand rims, armrest pads, footrests, and upholstery, and a workshop that holds them keeps a chair in service for years. The operator confirms the tires and locks each day, and the technician inspects the frame and axles at an interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cushion under the patient is a clinical device, because the physics of pressure injury is pressure multiplied by time. Sitting drives body weight through a small area over the ischial tuberosities, and the soft tissue is compressed between bone and seat until its blood supply closes. A cushion spreads the load over a larger area and reduces shear, the sliding force that stretches and closes small vessels. Foam cushions are cheap, gel cushions stay cooler, air cell cushions float the pelvis on many small pockets, and a contoured cushion keeps the pelvis from sliding forward. The common errors are to substitute an ordinary pillow, to over inflate an air cushion until it feels firm like a ball, and to cut a hole in a cushion in the belief that it removes pressure over a sore. The cover is cleaned between patients, the foam is checked for collapse, and any cleaning agent and its contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The powered wheelchair adds motors, a controller, and a battery to the same frame. Electrical energy in the battery becomes torque in the motors, so the controller sends a current proportional to the joystick deflection and the motors answer with a defined force. Most chairs run on a 24 volt battery pack, and the charging voltage and time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is the low battery warning, usually a repeated beep with a flashing indicator, and the common error is to ignore it until the chair stops on a slope with the patient aboard. Sealed lead acid batteries release hydrogen while charging and must be charged in a ventilated place away from a flame, while lithium packs carry a fire risk if punctured, overheated, or charged with the wrong charger. The operator checks the battery gauge, the joystick, the motors, the freewheel levers, and the tires before every journey, and the chair is secured with four point tie downs in a vehicle.

An orthosis is a shell that holds a body segment in a chosen position, and its action is explained by three point fixation. A force is applied at the apex of the deformity and two opposing forces on the far side, so the segment is held in a corrected line and the brace replaces the pull of a muscle or a ligament. Materials are chosen for stiffness, weight, and the ability to be shaped, and they include plaster, thermoplastic sheet, polyethylene, polypropylene, carbon fiber, aluminum, steel, leather, canvas, and foam. A custom brace is made over a positive model of the limb, which is poured from a cast taken with the limb corrected, and the heated sheet is vacuum formed over that model before the edges are smoothed and the straps and hinges are fixed. The forming temperature varies with the material and must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazards are pressure over a bony prominence, which can produce a sore that a patient with impaired sensation does not feel, and a joint held in the wrong position until a contracture sets in. The common error is to apply a brace over a wrinkled sock, because a fold becomes a hard ridge under load.

The orthoses are named for the joints they cross. An ankle foot orthosis controls the ankle so the toes clear the ground during the swing phase of walking, and it is used when the foot drops. A knee ankle foot orthosis extends the shell to the thigh with a knee hinge, and it is used when the knee is unstable or the limb must be protected from weight bearing. A spinal orthosis limits a movement, unloads a vertebra, or reminds the patient to keep the spine in a safe range. The fitting check is the skin at every edge, the circulation beyond the brace, and the position of the joint. The common errors are a shell too tight at the calf, a hinge placed away from the axis of the knee, and a strap tightened to hide a bad fit rather than to hold the shell.

A prosthesis replaces a missing part, and the socket is where the physics becomes clinical. The residual limb is held in a rigid cup, and body weight passes through soft tissue to the socket wall, so the shape of that wall and the distribution of load decide whether walking is comfortable or impossible. A total surface bearing socket spreads the load over the whole limb, while a patellar tendon bearing socket concentrates it on tolerant areas and relieves sensitive ones. Suspension holds the socket on the limb with suction through a one way valve, a pin that locks into a liner, a silicone sleeve, or a belt around the waist. A liner is a soft interface of silicone, gel, or foam, and woven socks are added in thin layers as the limb shrinks after amputation. The common error is to add several socks at once, which lifts the limb and produces a piston motion that damages the skin.

The components above and below the socket decide the quality of the gait. A prosthetic knee may be a single axis joint, a polycentric linkage that folds in a more natural path, or a microprocessor knee that measures load and angle many times each second and adjusts the resistance to bending. A prosthetic foot may be a solid ankle cushion heel design that mimics the roll of the foot, or an energy storing foot of carbon fiber that returns energy at push off. The pylon joins the foot to the knee or socket, and the adapters allow the angle and rotation to be adjusted. Alignment is set on the bench, standing still, and walking, and the therapist reads the gait for a lean, a pelvic drop, a wide step, or a rotation that betrays a wrong angle. The characteristic problem is a limb a few millimeters too long or too short, and every alignment value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A prosthesis needs daily care, and the skin is the instrument that reports its condition. The liner is washed with a mild soap, rinsed, and dried completely, because sweat and salt left on the surface irritate the skin and degrade the gel. The socket is wiped out and allowed to dry, the suspension sleeve and valve are checked for tears and a proper seal, and the foot and knee are inspected for cracks and loose bolts. The safety hazard is a fall from a loss of suspension or a locked knee, and the common error is to keep walking on a red and painful limb because the prosthesis feels too good to leave off. The volume of the limb changes through the day, so socks are adjusted in thin layers, and the correct thickness and wearing schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Therapeutic electricity is applied through electrodes on the skin, and the physics begins with current and resistance. A current passing through tissue can depolarize a nerve, and the result depends on the amplitude and shape of the pulse rather than on total energy. The gate control theory explains one common use, because comfortable sensory impulses carried by large fibers reach the spinal cord and reduce the transmission of pain signals carried by small fibers, so transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation floods that gate with sensation. A motor level current instead depolarizes the motor nerve and produces a visible contraction that retrains a weak muscle. Typical settings include a pulse width of 50 to 250 microseconds and a frequency of 80 to 120 hertz, and all of these values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is a contact warning when an electrode has lifted and the current density under the remaining pad has risen.

The hazards of electrical therapy are burns, skin irritation, and unexpected muscle contraction, and most come from a poor electrode or an impatient operator. Two electrodes of different sizes concentrate current under the smaller one, a dried out pad raises resistance and heats the skin, and a metal implant, a pacemaker, or an implanted defibrillator can carry current along an unintended path. Electrical stimulation is avoided over the carotid sinus and throat, over the eyes, over the abdomen in pregnancy, over infected skin, and across the chest of a patient with a pacemaker, and each contraindication must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The electrode pad is a consumable, and its adhesive gel dries, collects dirt, and stops conducting evenly, so it is replaced when it no longer sticks. The common errors are to raise the amplitude before the patient is ready, to reuse a pad that has lost its gel, and to leave a connected patient without a clear view of the control.

Ultrasound therapy turns electricity into mechanical vibration, and the conversion happens in a ceramic crystal that changes shape when a voltage is applied to it. That oscillation passes into tissue through a coupling medium, producing a gentle deep warming from absorption plus a mechanical stirring called cavitation that moves fluid and may alter the behavior of cells. The frequency decides how deep the energy reaches, with about 1 megahertz for deeper tissue and about 3 megahertz for a superficial target, and the exact frequency and intensity must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Intensity is prescribed in watts per square centimeter, commonly from 0.5 to 2, and treatment may run from 5 to 10 minutes, with both values requiring confirmation against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The transducer is kept moving in slow overlapping circles, because a stationary head deposits its energy in one place and can burn the periosteum, and the common errors are a head held still and a treatment started with no coupling gel. Ultrasound is avoided over a pregnant uterus, a malignancy, the growth plates of a child, the eyes, the gonads, a pacemaker, and a blood clot, and these exclusions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Other modalities fill the same role with different physics. Shortwave diathermy uses a radiofrequency field to heat deep tissue by making ions and water molecules rotate, and its hazard is a burn from a cable that touches the skin or from metal in the field. A paraffin bath warms a hand or foot by conduction, with the wax held at about 50 to 54 degrees Celsius, a temperature that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Cryotherapy removes heat with ice or cold packs, and the safety hazard is a cold burn from prolonged contact, so a barrier cloth is always used. Intermittent compression inflates a sleeve around a limb in cycles to move edema, and traction pulls the spine with a measured force, both requiring settings that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm on a motorized unit is an obstruction or overload signal, and the common error is to leave a patient attached while the therapist leaves the room.

The exercise equipment of a rehabilitation gym is built around controlled weight bearing and controlled movement. Parallel bars are two rails at hand height that let a patient practice standing and stepping while both hands take part of the body weight, and they are set at the wrist crease, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A standing frame supports a patient upright with straps and a table, allowing weight to pass through the bones as a mechanical stimulus and a rehearsal for standing tolerance. A tilt table raises a patient from lying toward standing in measured steps, letting the circulation adapt gradually for someone who cannot yet stand. The safety hazards are a fall in blood pressure during the tilt, a patient who faints against the straps, and a frame that moves during a transfer, so the patient is strapped at the chest, hips, and knees. The common errors are to leave the tilt table wheels unlocked and to leave a strapped patient unattended, and the rate of tilt and maximum angle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Measurement is the other half of the department, because a treatment that cannot be measured cannot be justified or corrected. A goniometer is a protractor with two arms, and it measures a joint angle when the fulcrum sits over the joint axis and the arms lie along the fixed and moving segments. A tape measure records limb girth, length, and swelling from a fixed landmark with the same tension each time, so numbers can be compared across visits. A hand dynamometer measures grip strength by compressing a spring or a hydraulic cell, and a volumetric tank measures the water displaced by a swollen hand as the most sensitive test of edema. Outcome measures turn function into a number, such as a timed walk over a set distance or a count of the activities a patient can perform without help. The common errors are to measure from a different landmark each time and to record a number that flatters the patient, and the landmark and testing position must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables of a rehabilitation department are quiet but constant, and a shortage stops treatment as surely as a broken machine. Electrical therapy needs self adhesive electrode pads, lead wires, and conductive gel, and ultrasound needs coupling gel, paper towels, and transducer covers. Brace and prosthetic work consumes plaster bandage, stockinette, thermoplastic sheet, padding foam, leather, rivets, buckles, hook and loop straps, adhesive, and thread. Wheelchairs consume tires, tubes, bearings, brake cables, and upholstery, and walking aids consume rubber tips of several diameters. Cleaning is a clinical act, because the same plinth, exercise bar, and cushion are used by many patients in one day, and shared equipment is a surface that hands, skin, and clothing touch. Hard surfaces are wiped with detergent and then with a disinfectant, and the surface is kept wet for the contact time stated on the label, which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Fabric is the difficult item, because a cover may be wiped while the foam inside cannot be washed, so a fluid resistant cover and a barrier sheet are used, and electrical equipment is never sprayed or immersed.

Maintenance here is mostly inspection and adjustment rather than repair of electronics, and its greatest enemy is the assumption that a simple mechanical device cannot fail. The daily round covers the rubber tips, brake levers, wheel locks, straps, buckles, hinges, electrode leads, cables, and the battery gauge of every powered item. The scheduled round covers wheel bearings, caster stems, spoke tension, upholstery, frame bolts, the tilt table lock, and the calibration of the therapy timer at an interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A workshop holding tires, tubes, bearings, tips, straps, and fuses returns most equipment to service the same day, and every repair is recorded with its date, part, and the person who did it. The safety hazard is a device returned to the ward without a test, and the common error is to tighten every bolt on a wheelchair so hard that the frame cracks at the hole. Any device that has been dropped, soaked, or involved in a fall is taken out of service and inspected before it is used again.

The field version begins with what is absent, because the constraint shapes every choice. Electricity may come only from a solar panel, clean water may be a walk away, plaster of Paris may be the only molding material, and no spare part may lie within a day's travel. The clinician chooses not between a good device and a lesser one, but between a device that can be maintained locally and no device at all. A locally made brace is built from plaster, wood, leather, canvas, metal strip, or heated plastic pipe, and each material has a character the maker must respect. Plaster is cheap and molds directly on the limb, but it is heavy, softens when wet, and cannot be adjusted once set, while leather and canvas are repairable but stretch and trap moisture. A metal strip from a barrel hoop can be bent into a rigid upright, and a plastic pipe heated in water can be flattened into a shell, though the temperature must be judged by eye. The common errors are a brace made too tight because the limb will swell, a rivet or cut edge left where it presses the skin, and a fit done without teaching the patient where to look for redness, and the review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The wheelchair that survives a village is usually built from bicycle and motorcycle parts, because those parts already have a supply chain. A rough terrain chair may run on three wheels with a bicycle front wheel and two rear wheels so it can be pushed along a dirt path, and a hand powered tricycle may use a chain and crank so the rider propels it with the arms. The advantages are enormous, because a punctured tube, a worn tire, a snapped cable, and a dry bearing can all be repaired by the mechanic who fixes bicycles in the market. What is given up is adjustability, light weight, and sophisticated seating, since the frame is welded to one size and the seat is often a wooden board or a canvas sling without a pressure relieving cushion. What is demanded instead is a stock of bicycle tires, tubes, bearings, and spokes, a pump and a set of cone spanners, and a mechanic taught how the wheel locks and anti tip devices work. The safety hazards are a missing lock, a soft tire, a sharp edge on the seat, and a frame cracked at a weld, and the operator checks all of them before the chair leaves the clinic.

A field prosthesis is a compromise between a good socket and a material that can be shaped without a workshop. The common approach is to take a plaster cast of the residual limb, pour a positive model, and form a socket in polypropylene over that model, which yields a socket fitted to the individual limb with only a heat source and simple tools. Alignment is then set by eye and by watching the patient walk rather than with a measurement jig, so the prosthetist looks for a lean, a pelvic drop, a wide step, and a rotation, and adjusts the angle, height, and rotation of the foot in small steps. What is given up is the precision of a modern alignment system and the durability of a laminated frame, and what is demanded instead is a longer fitting session, repeated visits as the limb changes shape, and a supply of liners, socks, and suspension materials. The common errors are to fit a socket before the swelling has settled, to leave a rough edge inside the socket, and to send the patient home without a written appointment for the first review. The interval between reviews and the sock schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The therapist who improvises is not practicing a lesser medicine but a different logistics, and the principles of dose and safety still govern. When a therapy unit fails or the current is off, treatment becomes exercise, manual therapy, heat from a hot water bottle wrapped in cloth, cold from a river, and a graded program of walking and strengthening with weights made from bottles filled with sand. A parallel bar becomes two lengths of pipe lashed to a frame, a plinth becomes a firm table, and a mirror becomes the visual feedback that a hospital would provide with an electrode and an electromyography, or EMG, display. The safety hazards are a hot water bottle that burns a numb limb, an improvised weight that falls on a foot, and unsupervised walking practice near a step or a drain, so the therapist stays within arm's reach and checks the skin after every session. Transfers of heavy patients without a hoist also injure the therapist's back, so a mechanical lift or a sliding sheet and enough hands are used instead. Every improvised device is recorded with its material, its dimensions, and the date it was checked, and the supervision interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, rehabilitation equipment restores function by changing the way force moves through the body, so a cane widens the base of support, a brace applies three point fixation, a socket spreads the load of walking, and a therapy unit delivers a measured dose of electrical or mechanical energy. In a well-resourced hospital these devices come with casting ovens, vacuum forming, microprocessor knees, calibrated ultrasound, and a maintenance workshop, and they depend on a steady supply of pads, gel, straps, tires, bearings, plaster, and thermoplastic sheet. In a field clinic the same principles are met with plaster, leather, heated pipe, bicycle parts, hot water, and the hands of a therapist who improvises, and the price of that improvisation is a longer fitting, a closer follow up, and a constant demand for local repair. Whichever setting applies, the operator checks the tips, the brakes, the straps, the hinges, the electrodes, the gel, and the skin before use, and every setting, pressure, temperature, energy level, treatment time, and alarm threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A device that is inspected, measured, documented, and cleaned keeps a patient walking, while a device assumed to be safe because it is simple will eventually fail under the weight of a person who trusted it.

# Chapter 54 — Mental Health Units

Every other chapter here describes a machine, while this chapter describes a room that acts on a patient. Its most important component is the absence of something, because a person in acute distress looks for an anchor above the body and a line to reach it. A ligature concentrates the whole weight of the body onto a band a few centimeters wide, which compresses the vessels to the brain and the airway. Nothing in that mechanism needs a special instrument, so this equipment is mostly a set of decisions to deny the mechanism its parts. A room without an anchor, a cord, or a breakable edge changes what a crisis can become before any clinician arrives. Every fixture here exists because a patient in crisis is an engineer of the nearest available material.

The ligature point is the first object to understand. A suspension point must hold a falling body, resist cutting the line, and stand high enough that the feet leave the floor, and hooks, door tops, rails, and grab bars all qualify while remaining ordinary furniture. The load is not the resting weight of the patient but a dynamic load several times greater, because a sudden drop turns motion into a sharp pull. Ligature-resistant hardware removes the hook shape, replaces it with a flat plate or a steep slope, and releases at a defined load, and that rating must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before installation. The common operator error is to see an odd piece of design rather than a safety device and to add a familiar hook beside it. The characteristic alarm here is not electronic, because it is a patient's unannounced absence from where the observation schedule expects them.

Door hardware is where most ligature points are created by accident. A lever handle, a coat hook on the back of a door, a closer arm, and the gap between door and frame all offer purchase, and the top edge of a door is a classic anchor because it is strong and above head height. Ligature-resistant doors use a continuous hinge line, a handle sloping inward at 45 degrees or more with no gap behind it, and a closer set in the floor or inside the frame. A door must also open outward or be openable against a patient who is pushing it closed, and the anti-barricade leaf resolves that conflict with a second set of hinges. Observation panels are the other half of the design, because a door that protects privacy also blocks the view, so a vision panel is set at a height that lets a standing adult see the whole room, and its obstruction from the inside by a poster or tape is an emergency rather than a housekeeping problem. The characteristic alarm is furniture dragged across a floor behind a closing door, and the team must open the way in without entering the narrow space between a pushing patient and a moving leaf.

The surfaces carry the same logic, because every projection, shelf bracket, and exposed pipe is a potential anchor. Ligature-resistant design flattens the room into recessed shelving, flush light fittings, ceiling-mounted fixtures, and sanitary ware set into the wall. The glazing must survive an impact without producing fragments that can cut or be swallowed, and here the physics of glass matters. Ordinary annealed glass breaks into large sharp shards, laminated glass holds its pieces on a plastic interlayer and stays in its frame, and polycarbonate does not shatter but deforms and scratches. The unbreakable pane is always a compromise, because the toughness that resists a fist also resists a rescue tool, and every glazed panel must be assessed for what it protects and what it prevents. The characteristic failure is a cracked pane reported and not replaced, because a crack becomes a cutting edge as it propagates, and the replacement criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Furniture is designed against two threats at once, because a chair can be thrown and a bed can be barricaded. A chair that can become a weapon has a heavy frame, a removable leg, or a hard edge, and a chair that can barricade can be wedged under a handle or stacked against a doorway. The safe answer is furniture heavy, formed in one piece, and rounded, or furniture light enough to be harmless and unable to become a projectile. Beds follow the same rule, with a solid platform, no cavity for hidden objects, no exposed bolt to unscrew, and no rail for a line, while a mattress has no removable cover and no spring that can be pulled out. The common operator error is to bring an ordinary visitor chair in for a conversation and leave it there. Every item must therefore be checked for loose fasteners, torn covers, and new sharp edges on each maintenance round.

Everything described so far assumes that a human being is looking, and here observation is the practice that turns the room into a working device. Observation places a patient where a member of staff can see them at a defined interval, and its equipment is a sight line. The corridor is angled so a nurse at the desk can see into every room, and the panel, the window, and the light are arranged so a patient standing, sitting, or lying on the floor is visible from one point. The common operator error is to trust the plan on the drawing rather than the view at eye level, because a new notice board or a parked trolley can block a sight line an architect once verified. The characteristic failing is an observation sheet signed without the patient having been seen, and the observation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Camera systems are the electronic form of observation, and they obey the optics of any lens. A camera has a field of view, a resolution, and a light sensitivity, and a wide field that covers a corridor leaves each face small, while a narrow field identifies a face and leaves blind spots behind a door and under a bed. Infrared illumination lets a camera see in darkness without a visible lamp, which is exactly why it can watch a sleeping patient without disturbing them. The safety hazard is the belief that the camera replaces the human round, because a lens cannot see a ligature being prepared in a space it does not cover. The common operator error is to reaim a camera to avoid a privacy complaint and to create a blind spot over the bed, and the retention period and the resolution setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the system is relied upon.

Alarms here are mostly about movement rather than physiology. A nurse call button is placed where it can be reached from the bed and the floor, is wired so a break in the circuit is itself an alarm, and is shaped so its cord cannot be removed and used as a ligature. Wander and exit alarms detect a patient crossing a doorway by a pressure mat, an infrared beam, or a radio tag, because an unsecured door is both a flight risk and a traffic risk. Bed and chair sensors detect a patient leaving a surface, and they serve those at risk of falling as well as those at risk of self-harm. The characteristic alarm is a repeating tone at the staff station, and the common operator error is to silence it at the panel instead of answering it at the room. Every alarm threshold, sensitivity setting, and delay must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, because a sensor tuned to ignore small movements will also ignore a patient who has stopped moving.

The seclusion room is the most heavily engineered space in the unit, and its purpose is to hold one person safely while a crisis passes. The room is stripped to the essential, with a bed fixed or set at floor level, a mattress that cannot be torn, a ligature-resistant toilet and washbasin, and a light behind a sealed diffuser. An observation panel and often a camera give a continuous view, and the door is a heavy anti-barricade leaf with a lock releasable from outside. The physical principle is that the fewer objects and edges a room contains, the smaller the number of ways a person can be hurt, and the clinical use is to reduce stimulation until the patient can return to the open ward. The physical dangers are not only self-harm, because a patient may fall from the bed, swallow a piece of the mattress, become dehydrated, or deteriorate from a medical cause mistaken for agitation, so the observation interval, the vital sign interval, and the maximum duration of seclusion must all be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is a silence that is too complete, and staff must learn to find that silence more alarming than noise.

Restraint equipment is used only when a person is at immediate risk, and every item in it is a compromise between control and harm. A soft limb holder is a cuff of padded fabric that spreads the pull of a limb over a wide area so the skin and nerves beneath it are not cut, while a rigid cuff concentrates the same force and injures. The mechanism of restraint injury is pressure and position, because a wrist restraint that is too tight compresses the median nerve and the artery beside it, and a patient left face down has the abdomen pressed into the mattress and the diaphragm unable to descend. Restraint asphyxia is the name of the death that follows, and it can happen quickly and quietly without a struggle, which is why position matters more than the tightness of any single strap. The common operator error is to secure a patient prone because it is the easiest way to control them, and the second error is to leave the room because the patient has gone quiet. Every restraint must be inspected for worn stitching, frayed webbing, a bent buckle, and a lock that does not turn, and the maximum continuous time in restraint must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Because the danger is positional, the check is positional before it is numerical. The patient must be turned so the chest and abdomen are free, the head is raised, and the airway is clear, and this is repeated often enough that any change is noticed. Vital signs are then recorded, including the pulse, the respiratory rate, the blood pressure, the oxygen saturation, and the color and warmth of each restrained limb. The circulation of a restrained wrist or ankle is judged by comparing color, warmth, and capillary refill with the other side, and a limb that is cool, pale, or numb means the restraint must be released and the finding reported. The characteristic alarm is a falling oxygen saturation or a rising respiratory rate in a patient who looks settled, and those numbers are a warning about position rather than a psychiatric change. Records must show the time, the position, and the findings at every check, and the check interval and the trigger values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazard is documentation that describes a check that never happened, because it conceals the only evidence that a patient was deteriorating.

Everything that can be swallowed, burned, or used as a cord must be removed from a room where a patient is at risk. The list is longer than a glance suggests, and it includes matches and lighters, plastic bags, batteries, small magnets, coins, glass, razors, scissors, needles, medications, alcohol-based hand rub, aerosol cans, and cleaning fluids. Shoelaces, belts, drawstrings, scarves, and the cords of headphones and chargers are ligature material, and the physical principle is that an ingestible object becomes a weapon once it is swallowed while a cord becomes a noose once one end is tied above the body. The common operator error is to search a room thoroughly at admission and never again, although patients accumulate objects over the days that follow. Searching is itself an equipment task, because a hand search depends on a written list and on consistency, while a walk-through metal detector finds only a metallic object in a pocket.
