The safety hazard is the false sense of completeness a detector creates, because glass, plastic, ceramic, and bone are invisible to it, and the sensitivity setting and the test procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Lighting and power are part of the safety equipment, not merely the comfort of the room. Light fittings are sealed behind diffusers so no lamp or cable can be reached, and the emergency circuit keeps a corridor lit when the mains supply fails, which is the moment a dark ward becomes most dangerous. A corridor at night needs enough light for a nurse to see a patient from the doorway while remaining dim enough for sleep, so the lighting level must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An uninterruptible power supply protects the nurse call system, the door alarms, and the records, and the batteries of every portable alarm and torch must be tested on a schedule. Water and sanitation carry their own mechanisms, because an anti-ligature tap has a smooth body, a short lever, and no exposed pipe, and a thermostatic mixing valve holds a fixed outlet temperature so a patient cannot be scalded, with that temperature confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the valve is set. The safety hazard is a socket outlet inside a patient room, and the characteristic alarms of these services are a door alarm that does not sound when the door opens and a bathroom that has gone quiet.

Not all equipment here is defensive, because therapeutic activity equipment gives the patient a way to discharge tension and rebuild the routine of a day. Its design must satisfy the therapeutic purpose and the safety rules at once, and that double requirement decides every purchase. Art materials must be washable, non-toxic, and free of solvent, and the shared scissors and needles of a sewing group must be counted out, counted back, and locked away like any other sharp. Sensory items, including weighted blankets, textured fabrics, soft balls, and rocking seats, work through the physiology of the nervous system, because deep pressure and rhythmic movement stimulate the large sensory fibers and the balance organs, which is thought to calm the arousal that drives agitation. Weighted blankets must be light enough that a patient cannot be trapped beneath one, and the weight and the supervision required must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to leave a well-intentioned craft material or a weighted item in a room overnight, where it becomes the material of the next crisis.

Outdoor space is therapeutic equipment made of ground. A garden, a courtyard, or a secure terrace provides daylight, fresh air, and the change of scene that lowers agitation, and access to it is one of the most effective measures in the unit that involves no medication at all. Designing it safely means applying the rules of the room to the open air, so there is no cord, no high anchor point, no climbable wall, and no tool left in a shed. The characteristic alarm of an outdoor area is a gate signal or a missing patient report, and the gate release and the supervision ratio must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The safety hazard is garden equipment such as a hose, a rope, a spade, or a watering can left outside because it seems harmless in daylight. The operator check before any group goes out is a slow walk of the ground that removes everything a patient could tie, climb, or swallow.

De-escalation is the practice that makes most of the equipment unnecessary, and it is worth describing as a technique rather than a virtue. The physical principle is that agitation rises when a person feels trapped, unheard, or overwhelmed by noise and light, and it falls when the environment becomes predictable and the person regains a measure of control. A clinician who speaks slowly, stands at an angle rather than face to face, keeps the hands visible, offers a choice, and moves to a quieter space is adjusting the same variables the room was designed to control, only faster. The common operator error is to begin with the alarm and the restraint team and to treat talking as the delay before the real intervention, when talking is the intervention and the restraint team is the failure. The characteristic alarm is a raised voice or a sudden change in the pace of speech, and it should trigger an environmental change and a second staff member rather than a stronger physical response.

Documentation is equipment in this field, because the observation chart, the risk assessment, and the restraint record carry a patient's safety from one shift to the next. The chart must be simple enough to complete at the bedside and complete enough to show the time, the position, the behavior, and the vital signs at each check. The risk assessment must name the specific hazard for the specific patient, because a form that says only that the patient is at risk of self-harm tells the next nurse nothing that can be acted upon. The common operator error is to copy the previous entry, which turns the record into fiction and hides a change a fresh observation would have caught, and the characteristic alarm of a failed system is a discrepancy between what the chart claims and what the camera shows.

Maintenance in this environment is a safety activity that looks like housekeeping. The routine round checks every ligature point in every room, which means the door top, the handle, the hinge, the hook, the rail, the tap, the shower fitting, the light, the bed frame, the mattress seam, and the edge of every panel. A fixture is tested by loading it and by looking at it, because a fixing loosened by repeated dynamic load may still look intact, and the inspection interval and the test load must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Glazing is examined for cracks and failed seals, and a cracked pane is replaced rather than patched, while door closers are adjusted so a leaf does not slam and a lock that sticks during an emergency is a hazard of its own. A maintenance record matters as much as the maintenance, and the common failure is a log signed as complete while a new coat hook has been installed by a contractor. The operator must also watch for the quiet change, whether it is a new notice board or a new bedside table, because each of those can reintroduce the anchor point the room was built to remove.

Cleaning and disinfection here serve infection control and searching at the same time. The cleaning chemical must be effective against the organisms of the ward while remaining safe for the surfaces in use, and the concentration and the contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. An alcohol-based product left in a room is a flammable hazard as well as an ingestible one. Consumables are deliberately few, and that is a design decision rather than a shortage, because paper towels, soap, laundry, and incontinence pads are each a potential plug, a potential cord, or a potential fire load. A bin liner is a suffocation hazard, so a bin is small, fixed to the wall, and emptied at every round instead of being lined with a loose bag. Bed linen is checked for tears because a torn sheet can be twisted into a cord, and restraint padding, replacement webbing, spare buckles, and breakaway rings of the hook-and-loop type are stocked, while the common operator error is to leave a cleaning trolley unattended in a corridor, where it offers both a chemical and a cord.

Failure modes in this field often take the form of a system that works exactly as designed and is still wrong. A camera clean and focused can be aimed at the wrong part of the room, an alarm that sounds correctly can be silenced at the panel, a correctly fitted restraint can still leave a patient prone, and a correctly locked door can keep help outside when it is needed inside. The deeper failure is organizational, because a ligature-resistant room can be defeated by one new object, a careful policy by one rushed shift, and a written risk assessment by a patient whose presentation has changed since it was made. The characteristic alarm of an organizational failure is a near miss that nobody reports, and a near miss is the cheapest warning a unit will ever receive. The physical failure that must never be missed is a cracked panel, a loosened fixing, or a missing screw, because those are the quiet beginnings of the next serious event, and the reporting threshold and the review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant of this chapter is not a portable machine, because it is an ordinary room in a general ward, a health center, or a tent in which an extraordinary risk has arrived. There is no anti-ligature hardware, no observation panel, no camera, and no seclusion room, so the nurse must build the unit out of what the building already holds. The work begins with a walk through the room at the height of a patient, taking down every projection that can be taken down, because an ordinary ward is full of cords, poles, and lockers that nobody has had reason to see as a risk. The patient is then moved near the staff station where a nurse can see the whole room, and every cord, belt, shoelace, scarf, and charger is removed and handed to the family or locked away. The bed is lowered or the mattress is placed on the floor, the frame is inspected for a projecting bolt, hook, or rail, and a family member or trained attendant stays in the room, with the shorter check interval for that patient confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

What the field version gives up is the certainty of the engineered room, because it loses the tested fixing, the sealed light, the locked door, the camera, and the alarm, and it replaces all of them with attention from a workforce that is present and a plan shared with the family. A low-resource unit can improvise the hardware with cheap material, using a smooth board over a projecting bracket, a shortened curtain with breakaway rings of the hook-and-loop type, a plastic chair instead of a metal one, and a mattress without a removable cover. The field unit must also hold the medical equipment a behavioral emergency can demand, because a crisis can end in a seizure, a head injury, an overdose, or the shallow breathing that follows sedation. Oxygen, a self-inflating bag with a mask, suction, a glucose meter, and a means of measuring the pulse and blood pressure must be within reach of the room, and if a sedative is given the dose and observation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is to give a sedative and then leave the patient alone because the ward has gone quiet, and the characteristic alarm is snoring respiration in a patient who was shouting a moment before.

The physical space of a field unit has to be chosen before it can be adapted. A tent offers no ceiling anchor and no lock, so the risk shifts to the frame, the guy ropes, the mosquito net, and the tent poles, all of which must be examined with the same eye that would examine a door, while a general ward offers lockers, bed rails, window frames, and curtain tracks that can be removed, lowered, or covered. Lighting matters in the field as much as in the hospital, because a lamp, a torch, and a candle are all sources of fire and of cord, and a battery lantern hung beyond reach is safer than a kerosene lamp on the floor. The family presence that substitutes for an observation panel must be explained, because a relative who does not understand the task will sleep through the event they are there to prevent. Training and rehearsal belong in the same inventory, because a team that has rehearsed a restraint, a seclusion, and a medical emergency will use less force and recognize deterioration sooner, with the frequency of the rehearsal confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, a mental health unit is a building engineered against the physics of the cord, and its equipment is a set of deliberate absences: no anchor above the body, no cord within reach, no edge that cuts, no door that can be barricaded, and no blind spot that hides a patient from the people responsible for them. The hospital version invests in ligature-resistant fixtures, laminated glazing, anti-barricade doors with vision panels, cameras and movement alarms, a stripped seclusion room, restraint equipment with its positional checks, and the therapeutic materials that give a patient another way to spend a crisis. The field version gives up the tested hardware and buys back safety with presence, a room stripped by hand, a mattress on the floor, a family member at the bedside, and a schedule that is actually kept. In both versions the decisive instrument is the same, because the equipment can only remove the means and the staff must remove the opportunity, and every interval, load, and threshold mentioned in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 55 — ICU Setup

An intensive care unit, or ICU, is not a room full of machines but a single bed space repeated, and each bed space is a complete life-support system for a patient who has lost the ability to regulate breathing, blood pressure, temperature, or consciousness. The organizing principle is distribution, since gases, electricity, vacuum, water, data, and alarms each arrive at a fixed point beside the bed, and each delivery has a source, a path, a terminal, and a failure mode. A ventilator without oxygen, a monitor without power, and a suction unit without vacuum are only furniture. A listener who understands the distribution can diagnose most trouble in an ICU before touching any device.

The design of one bed space begins with geometry, because the machines occupy the floor long before they occupy the patient. A common arrangement leaves about 60 centimeters of clear floor on both sides of the bed, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, but the principle is that a nurse must reach every port, line, and airway from either side while a second rescuer works without stepping over the first. The bed is positioned so the patient's head and chest stay visible from the central desk, because direct sight is the fastest detector of a disconnection or a change in skin color. Storage and the monitor shelf are placed so that no cable crosses the walking path. Lighting comes in layers rather than one bright ceiling fixture, because the room must brighten at once for a procedure and dim at night while the staff still read the monitor.

Medical gas reaches each bed space through a piped system whose principle is that a central source is held at high pressure and regulated down at the point of use. A central plant feeds pipe that passes a zone valve and a regulator to a terminal unit matched to one gas. The connectors of oxygen, medical air, and vacuum are deliberately made non-interchangeable, and the wall color code is a convenience rather than the safety mechanism, so a faded label is a hazard worth reporting. Piped oxygen is commonly delivered at about 4 bar at the terminal, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the flowmeter then reduces it to the few liters per minute the patient receives. The characteristic alarms are the low pressure alarm on the area panel and the high pressure alarm of the plant, and the common error is connecting a device to the wrong terminal because the fittings look similar in poor light.

Electricity follows the same logic, and its principle is that current must have a complete path and a deliberate return. Each bed space draws from circuits sized for its load, and critical care sockets are typically divided into ordinary mains sockets and sockets backed by an uninterruptible power supply, or UPS, with a further set on the emergency generator. The backed socket is the one a life-support device should occupy, because the battery carries the load through the seconds before the generator starts, and its runtime must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The serious hazards are an overloaded socket strip, a cord across the floor, and a damaged plug, and the common error is unplugging a ventilator to charge a telephone.

Everything needed in the first minute must be within arm's reach, because the interval between recognition and action decides the outcome of a resuscitation. The bedside stock holds gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, alcohol hand rub, suction catheters, syringes, saline flushes, gauze, tape, electrode pads, specimen tubes, and a sharps container. Consumables are grouped by purpose rather than by delivery, so the airway items are together and the vascular access items are together, and each group is restocked after use. The cupboard stays closed, dry, and out of direct sunlight, because many items are degraded by heat, humidity, or ultraviolet light, and storage conditions and shelf lives must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is a cupboard filled at the front with items that expire next year while the item needed tonight sits empty at the back.

The alarm system is the sense organ of the unit, and it exists because a monitor can measure while only a human can respond. A bedside monitor raises its own tone and light, a central station repeats the alarm at the desk, and a nurse call system carries a patient request to the same place, so no single alarm depends on one listener. The serious hazard is alarm fatigue, the dulling produced by hundreds of non-actionable signals each day, and the common errors are widening a limit to silence a nuisance and silencing an alarm without looking at the patient. Alarm limits and the escalation interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a unit should audit which alarms actually fire.

The ventilator takes over the work of breathing, and its principle is positive pressure. A normal breath is drawn in by negative pressure as the diaphragm descends, but a ventilator pushes gas into the airway, so the pressure inside the chest rises above the pressure around it. The machine creates that push with a blower or a compressed gas supply, controls it with an inspiratory valve, measures flow and volume near the airway, and ends the breath when a set volume, pressure, or time is reached. Because the gas is pushed, pressure and volume are what injure the lung, and overdistension together with the repeated opening and closing of small air sacs explains why ventilation can itself cause harm.

The prescribed settings keep the lung open without stretching it, and common starting points are a tidal volume of 6 to 8 milliliters per kilogram of predicted body weight, an end-expiratory pressure of 5 to 10 centimeters of water, and a plateau pressure below about 30 centimeters of water, all of which must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A common operator error is reading the exhaled tidal volume without checking that the circuit is not leaking or the tube is not partly blocked, because the machine reports what it measures rather than what the patient received. The characteristic alarms are the high airway pressure alarm, the low tidal volume alarm, the apnea alarm, and the oxygen concentration alarm, and each names a cause found by looking at the patient, the tube, and the circuit in that order. The safety hazard of a silenced ventilator alarm is a patient who is no longer being ventilated while the room stays quiet.

The ventilator is only as good as the disposable circuit that carries its gas, and those consumables are the breathing circuit, the humidifier chamber or heat and moisture exchanger, the closed suction catheter, the water traps, and the bacterial filters. Condensation collects at the low points of the circuit, where it can be tipped into the airway or can block the flow sensor, so the traps are drained and the circuit is routed so water runs away from the patient. Cleaning follows the manufacturer's instructions, because the housing and screen tolerate a wipe while the internal flow sensor and valves do not tolerate fluid at all. Preventive maintenance replaces the internal battery, recalibrates the oxygen and flow sensors, and tests the alarms on an interval that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic failure of neglect is an oxygen sensor that drifts low, so the machine delivers less oxygen than it displays.

The bedside monitor is a small computer that translates several physical signals into one picture. The electrocardiogram, or ECG, measures the tiny voltage generated by heart muscle through skin electrodes, and its trace appears only when electrode, gel, and skin form a stable conductive path. Pulse oximetry shines red and infrared light through a fingertip and calculates oxygen saturation from the different absorption of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, which is why motion, cold fingers, nail polish, and poor perfusion corrupt the number. Invasive pressure measurement uses a fluid-filled catheter joined to a strain gauge transducer, and the pressure wave moves the diaphragm of the gauge, changes its electrical resistance, and becomes the waveform on the screen.

The monitor is useful only when its alarm limits suit this patient rather than the defaults, and its characteristic alarms are the low oxygen saturation alarm, the low blood pressure alarm, the high heart rate alarm, and the asystole or lead-off alarm. The common errors are accepting default limits designed for a different patient, leaving a probe on a finger that has been cold and still for hours, placing electrodes over bone or scar tissue. Electrodes dry out and must be replaced before the trace becomes noisy, because a wandering baseline is a signal about the hardware rather than the heart, and a transducer is leveled at the height of the right atrium and zeroed before its pressure is believed. The skin under every electrode and probe is inspected each shift, and the housing and cables are wiped with the approved disinfectant, with alarm limits and cleaning contact times confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Infusion pumps exist because gravity cannot deliver a precise volume against resistance, and their principle separates them into two families. A volumetric pump moves fluid with fingers or a peristaltic rotor that squeezes a dedicated giving set, so the volume delivered equals the number of squeezes multiplied by the volume trapped in the tubing. A syringe pump drives the plunger of a syringe with a lead screw, so the volume equals the cross-sectional area of the barrel multiplied by the distance traveled. Both devices infer a problem from pressure, because a rising pressure at the pump means resistance downstream while a falling pressure means a line has come apart or a vessel has been lost. The characteristic alarms are the occlusion alarm, the air-in-line alarm, the syringe empty alarm, and the low battery alarm, and the common error is clearing an occlusion alarm without tracing the line from pump to patient.

The consumables are the dedicated giving set or syringe, the extension set, the filter where one is required, and the label, and they are not interchangeable between pump families because tubing diameter is part of the calibration. The hazard of a mismatched set is silent underdelivery or overdelivery, since the pump counts its own strokes and trusts the tubing it was told to expect. Free flow is a second hazard, because a set removed from a volumetric pump can siphon its container into the patient by gravity unless the roller clamp or anti-free-flow mechanism is closed. Every pressure limit, bolus volume, and drug library entry must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is overriding the library when a concentration is unusual.

The dialysis machine in an ICU is most often a continuous renal replacement therapy, or CRRT, device, whose principle is slow convection across a filter rather than the fast diffusion of a hemodialysis session. Blood is drawn from a central catheter by a peristaltic pump, pushed through a hemofilter whose membrane passes water and small molecules, and returned to the patient, while replacement fluid and an effluent pump remove the ultrafiltrate. A common prescription is an effluent rate of 20 to 35 milliliters per kilogram each hour with a blood flow of 100 to 200 milliliters per minute, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The installation demands treated water if the machine prepares its own fluid, a drain for the effluent, dedicated power, and a circuit of tubing, a filter, replacement fluid, and an anticoagulant. The characteristic alarms are the filter pressure alarm, the transmembrane pressure alarm, and the air detector alarm, and the common error is ignoring a slow upward drift of pressure until the filter clots.

The ICU bed is itself a machine whose principle is a set of electric actuators that raise and lower the platform and articulate the back and knee sections. The low position is the safest, because a patient who falls from a low bed is injured less, and the brakes are applied whenever the bed is stationary, because a rolling bed drags lines and tubes. The special mattress answers a different problem, namely that sustained pressure above the capillary closing pressure stops blood flow to the skin and produces a pressure injury, so an alternating pressure mattress inflates and deflates groups of cells in a slow cycle to move the contact points. A common cycle is about 10 to 20 minutes, a figure that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common errors are leaving the mattress pump unplugged, covering the surface with a thick pad, and forgetting the cardiopulmonary resuscitation release.

Suction removes what the patient cannot clear, and its principle is a pressure difference. A vacuum pump or a venturi driven by compressed gas lowers the pressure in a canister and a tube, and the higher pressure of the atmosphere then pushes secretions toward the lower pressure. The regulator sets the vacuum and a float valve protects the pump from overflow, so the characteristic alarms are the canister full alarm and the low vacuum alarm. The safety hazards are a vacuum set too high, which tears and bleeds the airway mucosa, and prolonged suction, which removes oxygen along with secretions and can drop the oxygen saturation and heart rate. The common errors are suctioning on a schedule rather than on need and leaving a canister near full, while the vacuum level for an adult, a child, and a neonate differs and must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The resuscitation trolley is a portable collection of everything needed in the first minutes of a cardiac arrest, sealed so that a missing item is visible before it is needed. It carries a defibrillator, airway equipment including a laryngoscope, blades, tubes, and a self-inflating resuscitation bag with masks, suction, intravenous access and fluids, drugs. The defibrillator's principle is the storage of energy in a capacitor and its sudden release through pads on the chest, which sends a current across the heart that depolarizes the muscle at once and allows the natural pacemaker to resume control. A common adult energy setting for a biphasic device is 150 to 200 joules, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common errors are expired pads, a battery that has never been load tested, and a seal broken weeks ago. The characteristic alarm is the self-test failure of the defibrillator, and the trolley is checked and recorded at the start of every shift.

Behind the wall the ICU depends on a plant the staff rarely see, and its reliability is built from ordinary maintenance. The medical gas plant holds the source, the changeover manifold, the regulators, and the alarm panel that warns the desk when a bank runs low, and a zone valve allows the gas to be isolated. The electrical plant includes the substation, the generator, the UPS batteries, and the distribution boards, and the generator is tested under load at intervals rather than merely started, because an engine that starts and then fails on load is a dangerous illusion of readiness. The heating, ventilation and air conditioning, or HVAC, plant holds temperature, humidity, and pressure relationships, and in critical areas it changes the air often enough to dilute contamination, with room pressure and air change rate confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarms of the plant are the gas pressure alarm, the generator failure alarm, and the UPS low battery alarm, and the common error is treating these distant alarms as the technician's business.

Isolation capability is a property of the room rather than the patient, and its principle is the control of air and contact. An airborne infection needs a room held at negative pressure relative to the corridor, so air flows in and leaves through a filtered exhaust instead of drifting into the hall, and that pressure difference is small enough that an open door or a blocked grille can reverse it without any alarm being heard. A contact or droplet infection needs something simpler, namely a barrier, dedicated equipment, and a place to remove personal protective equipment, or PPE, before leaving the room. The curtain is the most familiar barrier and also the most contaminated object in the unit, because it is touched before and after patient contact and cleaned far less often than the bed rail, so it is changed on a schedule or whenever it is soiled. The negative pressure, the air change rate, and the curtain change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the common error is opening the isolation door to improve the ventilation.

The consumables of critical care are the most visible cost and the least visible risk, because each has a shelf life, a storage condition, and a single-use rule. Oxygen masks and nasal cannulas, suction catheters and canisters, ventilator circuits and filters, infusion sets and syringes, central line dressings, electrodes and transducers, gloves and gowns, and drainage bags all expire, and stock that is not rotated becomes unusable at the worst moment. Single-use items are never reprocessed in a critical care area, because a residual contaminant in a device that touches blood or airway is not worth the saving. The minimum stock level for each item is set from the daily use rate and the resupply lead time, and the storage temperature, humidity, and expiry of each item must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common error is hoarding a private drawer of supplies, which hides real consumption and empties the shared shelf.

Cleaning and maintenance decide whether the equipment still is the device the manufacturer tested. Between patients the bed space receives a terminal clean, in which the mattress and cover, the bed rails, the monitor, the pump, the ventilator housing, and every touched surface are cleaned and then disinfected with a product whose contact time is respected, since a sprayed surface that dries in seconds has not been disinfected. Curtains and cloth surfaces are changed or laundered rather than wiped, and a mattress cover with a crack or a stain is replaced because fluid inside the foam cannot be removed. Preventive maintenance is scheduled by the biomedical technician, who tests electrical safety, calibrates pressure and flow sensors, replaces batteries, and records every intervention in the equipment register. The cleaning agent, its dilution, and its contact time, together with every calibration tolerance and service interval, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A well-run ICU plans for its own failure, because every supply it depends on can stop. The failure modes that matter are a power failure, a gas failure, a vacuum failure, a water failure, a network failure, and the failure of a single machine, and each has a rehearsed answer rather than an improvised one. When power fails the UPS carries the ventilator and the monitor for a measured time while the generator starts, and if it does not start the nurse switches to the self-inflating resuscitation bag and a portable oxygen cylinder, which is why that bag is checked and why the cylinder is never empty. When the gas plant fails the bed space is transferred to cylinder supply and the flow is calculated against the remaining pressure and the patient's demand, while a network failure sends the unit back to a paper chart prepared before the electronic health record, or EHR, goes dark. The operator's check at the start of a shift covers the bedside equipment, the oxygen and suction outlets, the alarm limits, the drugs, the defibrillator, and every running infusion, and the alarms, battery runtimes, and cylinder durations must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The equipment assumes a staffing model, and this is where machines and people must be counted together. A ventilator, a monitor with continuous alarms, and several infusion pumps extend the senses and the hands of a nurse but cannot act, so the unit assumes a nurse who reaches the bedside within seconds and a second trained person for every resuscitation. A common model assigns one nurse to one unstable patient and one nurse to two stable patients, and any such ratio must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The equipment also assumes competence rather than presence, so staff must be trained on each machine and drilled on the failure of power, gas, and airway. The common error is adding a bed without adding a nurse, and the serious hazard of understaffing is an alarm that sounds at a desk where nobody is sitting.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the intensive care unit is usually three beds made from an ordinary room, and the first decision is selection rather than construction. The room must be close to the entrance so a deteriorating patient can reach it and a referral vehicle can reach the door, and it must have a solid floor, a roof, light, enough electrical supply for the devices that matter, and at least one opening for ventilation. The design principle is unchanged, namely that every bed needs power, oxygen, suction, monitoring, and the consumables for the first hour, but in the field each of those is a separate object rather than a wall fitting. What the field gives up is the central station, the piped gas, the continuous vacuum, the building alarm, and the specialist who arrives with a spare part. What it demands instead is a disciplined order of assembly, a written plan for every failure, and staff who have rehearsed that plan.

The order of assembly starts with power, because nothing else can run without it. A generator, a battery bank with an inverter, or a solar array with batteries is sized from the sum of the loads, with the ventilator, the suction, and the lights counted first, and any such calculation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Oxygen comes next as cylinders with a regulator and a flowmeter, and the amount available is finite, because a full cylinder holds a known volume at a known pressure and its duration equals that volume divided by the flow the patient is receiving. Suction follows, either an electric unit on the generator or a foot operated pump that needs no power, and every bed must have one. The common error is placing the beds before the utilities and then running extension cords and oxygen tubing across the floor, which is both a trip hazard and a source of accidental disconnection.

Monitoring in the field is assembled from handheld devices rather than a central station, and the principle is to cover the measurements that change a decision. A handheld pulse oximeter, a manual blood pressure cuff with a stethoscope, a thermometer, and a disciplined count of respiratory rate and level of consciousness form the minimum set, and a single transport monitor is shared between beds. Ventilation may be a self-inflating resuscitation bag used continuously by a nurse, a simple turbine ventilator on its own battery, or a continuous positive airway pressure, or CPAP, device for a patient who is breathing but cannot maintain oxygenation, and any pressure or flow setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Consumables are laid out in one place per bed, with gloves, airway items, intravenous supplies, dressings, and drugs counted before the shift, because in a three-bed unit a missing item is a walk to the store.

The most important field equipment is the plan for the patient the unit cannot hold, because a three-bed intensive care exists to stabilize and refer rather than to finish. The order of assembly is therefore a clinical order as well, namely choose the room, secure the power, position the oxygen, establish the suction, place and brake the beds, set up the monitoring, prepare the airway and ventilation, stock the consumables, write the chart and fix the communication route, and only then accept a patient, with every device setting confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. What the field gives up in precision it must recover in vigilance, so the nurse to patient ratio is often one to one or one to two, and tasks are shared among assistants and family members trained for specific roles. The characteristic limitation is that a patient needing invasive monitoring, prolonged mechanical ventilation, or CRRT cannot be managed there.

To summarize, the intensive care unit is a distributed life-support system built around one bed space, in which gases, power, vacuum, water, data, and alarms arrive at a fixed point and the machines are only as reliable as the building behind them. The ventilator pushes gas and can therefore injure the lung, the monitor translates electrical and optical signals into a picture and can therefore mislead, the infusion pump counts strokes and trusts its tubing, the CRRT circuit clears slowly across a membrane, and the mattress, the suction, and the resuscitation trolley each answer a physical problem with a characteristic alarm and a common error. In the hospital the unit rests on piped gas, backed power, central alarms, isolation, a deep stock of consumables, and a staffing ratio that assumes a responder within seconds. In the field the same care is assembled from a chosen room, a sized power supply, cylinders, manual suction, handheld monitoring, and a plan to refer, and the rule in both settings is the same, namely understand the physics, check the device at the start of the shift, and treat the patient rather than the alarm.

# Chapter 56 — Emergency Department Equipment

An emergency department receives patients whose diagnosis is unknown, so its equipment must support a decision before it supports a treatment. The problem is sorting, because twenty people may arrive within an hour with complaints that range from a sprained ankle to a ruptured aorta, and attention and machines must be divided in proportion to risk. Every device has two jobs at once, to measure something quickly and to make that measurement visible to whoever decides next, so the room shortens the distance between the patient and the next action. The department is built around time, because the interventions that save lives in trauma, stroke, sepsis, and heart attack lose their value as minutes pass, and this chapter describes the hospital arrangement before the field version, where a table, a light, and a bag do the work of a building.

Triage is the first instrument, and its principle is that scarce attention is allocated by a rule rather than by the order of arrival. A scale takes a few variables, such as the ability to walk, the respiratory rate, the oxygen saturation, the heart rate, and the level of consciousness, and combines them into one level that says how soon the patient must be seen. A five-level arrangement is common, from a patient who needs resuscitation at once to one who can safely wait, and every threshold between the levels must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The scale asks the same questions in the same order for every patient, which keeps the last dramatic case from coloring the present judgment, and the commonest error is to grade behavior rather than physiology.

The tools at the triage desk are chosen for speed rather than precision. A pulse oximeter shines two wavelengths of light through a fingertip and compares how much of each is absorbed, because oxygen-rich blood absorbs the two differently. A reading below 90 per cent is a common trigger for immediate assessment, and that figure and every other threshold in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A thermometer reads infrared energy, a blood pressure cuff measures the pressure at which an artery in the arm is occluded and released, and a glucose meter reads a current produced when glucose reacts with an enzyme on a strip, so a reading below 3.9 millimoles per liter in a confused patient changes the plan.

The trauma bay follows one rule, that everything needed in the first 10 minutes must be reachable without stepping away from the patient. The patient lies on a bed that can be raised, tilted head down, and dropped flat in seconds, and working surfaces sit on both sides because two teams must work at once. A hard board or backboard gives a firm surface for chest compressions and spinal precautions, because a soft mattress absorbs the force the hands intend for the heart. The overhead light illuminates a deep wound without the operator's head casting the crucial shadow, so a boom-mounted light with a sterile handle is used, and suction, oxygen, the monitor, the defibrillator, and the airway trolley are mounted so a hand finds them by habit.

The trauma bed is chosen for access and for compatibility with imaging. It is narrow enough that a rescuer can reach across the patient, and a radiolucent section under the torso lets a film cassette or a fluoroscope be positioned without moving the patient. The head drops away so the airway can be managed from above, and the side rails fold flat so a board can slide underneath. The commonest error is to leave a backboard in place after the resuscitation, and the second is to imagine that lying on a board immobilizes the neck without a collar and blocks.

The surgical light gathers light from a lamp through a fiber bundle or a light-emitting diode array and focuses it with a reflector, so it delivers a bright beam with little heat at the wound. The patient monitor measures several signals at once, and its alarms are the department's early warning system, so a repeated alarm must be treated as data rather than as noise. A repeated lead-off tone means an electrode has lost contact, while a low saturation tone means a real physiological change until proven otherwise, and every alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The commonest error is to silence the alarm and walk away, which turns a warning into silence.

The rapid infuser turns the trauma bay from assessment into treatment, and its physics is pressure applied to a warmed fluid. A bag hung on a pole flows by gravity at a slow rate, so the machine uses a pump to push fluid through wide-bore tubing and a heater to bring it close to body temperature. A typical device delivers several hundred milliliters per minute and warms the fluid to about 38 degrees Celsius, and every flow rate and temperature setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Warming matters because large volumes of cold fluid make the patient colder and cold stops the clotting enzymes, and the commonest error is to connect the set to a narrow cannula that cannot carry the flow, while the characteristic alarms are air in the line, occlusion, and a heater fault.

Suction removes blood, vomit, and secretions by creating a pressure lower than the pressure in the airway, and the vacuum is usually set between 80 and 120 millimeters of mercury for an adult, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The airway trolley carries laryngoscopes, blades in several sizes, tracheal tubes, supraglottic airways, a bag and masks, and a carbon dioxide detector, arranged so the hand moves in the order the procedure is performed. A chest drain set contains a large-bore tube and a sealed drainage bottle that lets air and fluid leave the chest while preventing air from returning, and a drain on suction uses about 20 centimeters of water below atmospheric pressure, a setting that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic alarm is a swinging column that stops moving, which means the tube is blocked or the lung has re-expanded.

Access to imaging is part of the equipment of the bay, and the resuscitation room is its twin, because moving or keeping a patient is itself a clinical risk. A portable X-ray machine can be brought to the bed, while a machine for computed tomography, or CT, and one for magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, cannot, so the department has a short, wide route to the imaging suite. The resuscitation room is optimized for the medical arrest, with a fixed hard table, the monitor and defibrillator on one side so a single operator controls both, and a large clock facing the team. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, is recorded through adhesive electrodes, and its principle is that the heart's electrical activity reaches the skin as a small voltage that the machine amplifies and traces against time.

The defibrillator belongs in both rooms, and its principle is the capacitor, two conducting plates separated by an insulator that store charge and release it across the chest in a few thousandths of a second. The stored energy is measured in joules, and a typical adult biphasic shock delivers 120 to 200 joules, an energy level that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The pads are adhesive electrodes that both sense the rhythm and carry the shock, so their gel must be moist and their expiry date current, because a dried pad burns the skin and conducts poorly. An automated external defibrillator, or AED, removes the rhythm decision from the operator and shocks only when its algorithm recognizes a treatable rhythm, and the characteristic sounds are a rising charge tone, a discharge, and a steady low-battery tone.

The difficult airway cart answers the patient whose larynx cannot be seen, and it is organized as a sequence of escalating options rather than as a box of tools. It holds a video laryngoscope with a camera at the blade tip, which shows the cords on a screen, and it holds supraglottic airways, bougies, stylets, a surgical airway kit, and a carbon dioxide detector. Confirmation of any airway placement is by watching the chest rise, listening over both lungs and over the stomach, and detecting exhaled carbon dioxide, which is the only sign not shared with an esophageal placement. A waveform capnograph displays about 35 to 45 millimeters of mercury when the tube is in the trachea, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the commonest failure is a dead battery in a handle left switched on.

Spinal immobilization holds the injured column in the position it already occupies, because a fractured vertebra can injure the cord when the head moves. A rigid cervical collar supports the chin and the occiput and limits forward and backward bending, but it does not stop rotation, and it must be sized to the patient rather than stretched to fit. A spine board is a flat rigid surface with straps and head blocks, and its purpose is to transfer a patient as a single unit, not to serve as a bed for hours. The log roll turns a patient onto the side while the spine stays in line and needs at least three people, and the commonest error with a collar is a size that is too large, which lets the chin sink and the neck flex.

Splints, traction devices, and pelvic binders treat the fractures that bleed, and their physics is alignment, compression, and the reduction of movement at a broken surface. A rigid splint holds a limb in the position found and stops the bone ends from grinding, while an inflatable splint presses evenly and is light enough for a bag, though it can lose pressure with a slow leak. A traction splint pulls the lower leg lengthwise against a padded ring at the groin, which reduces a fractured femur and relieves the pain and bleeding that muscle spasm produces. A pelvic binder is a wide strap applied around the hips at the level of the greater trochanters, and it closes a disrupted pelvis, a maneuver that can stop venous bleeding that would otherwise fill the abdomen, and every strap tension and traction force must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Minor procedures have their own tray, and the suture set has barely changed in a hundred years because its principle is mechanical. It contains a needle holder, fine forceps, scissors, a scalpel handle, a syringe for local anesthetic, and a bowl for cleaning solution, and the suture is a thread with a sharpened end that pulls the wound edges together while the body heals beneath. The needle is curved so it can be rotated through tissue along the arc of its own shape, which is why the needle holder grips it at the middle and turns the wrist rather than pushing. Suture material is chosen by how long the wound needs support, and the size and type must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the commonest error is to close a wound that should be left open, because a contaminated wound closed tightly becomes an abscess.

Casts hold a reduced fracture still, and their chemistry is a setting reaction that gives off heat. Plaster of Paris becomes a paste when mixed with water and then hardens as crystals form, and the reaction releases heat, so a thick cast can become uncomfortably warm and, rarely, burn the skin. Synthetic tape sets by a different reaction, is lighter and stronger, and becomes permeable to water once cured, and a typical plaster sets in 5 to 10 minutes, so every setting time and thickness must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The cast is applied over a stockinette and padding and is split if the limb swells, because a cast that is too tight stops the blood and becomes a compartment syndrome, and the commonest error is to leave a finger or a toe unpadded over a bony prominence.

Point-of-care testing brings the laboratory to the bedside, and its principle is that a small disposable sensor is calibrated against a known reference so a whole instrument fits in a hand-held device. A blood gas analyzer passes a tiny sample across electrodes that generate a voltage proportional to the acidity, the carbon dioxide, and the oxygen, and it reports values such as an acidity between 7.35 and 7.45, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A lactate strip measures a chemical produced when tissue lacks oxygen, and a raised value in a patient with infection signals that the circulation is failing before the blood pressure does, while a test for troponin detects a protein released by injured heart muscle. The commonest error with all of these is a sample that is clotted, diluted, or delayed, which produces a number that looks authoritative and is wrong.

Ultrasound in the emergency setting became a piece of bedside furniture, and its principle is that a crystal changes shape when an electric field is applied and generates a pressure wave that reflects from every boundary. The machine measures the time each echo takes to return and builds a picture of the interfaces, so fluid, bone, and soft tissue appear differently because they reflect differently. A low-frequency probe penetrates deeply and a high-frequency probe resolves fine detail, so probes are chosen for the question, and a typical abdominal probe works between 2 and 10 megahertz, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The applications include looking for free fluid in the abdomen, judging the size of the aorta, and guiding a needle into a vein, and the hazard is that a negative scan is treated as certainty.

Eye and ear examination sets address two small spaces that hide serious disease, and their instruments share the principle of a light channel and a magnifying lens. An ophthalmoscope projects a beam into the eye and lets the examiner look at the retina through a hole in a mirror or a beam splitter, and the pupils must be dilated or the room darkened to see past the iris. A slit lamp produces a thin sheet of light and a microscope on a common axis, which reveals a foreign body or an ulcer that a penlight misses. An otoscope funnels light down a speculum into the ear canal and is braced against the patient's head, and a foreign body is removed with a moistened swab or a small needle under magnification, never with a jet of water if the object may be a battery.

Documentation equipment and the tracking board are the department's memory, because a patient in a crowded room becomes invisible unless an object stands for that patient. A whiteboard or a digital tracking board lists every patient with the location, the complaint, the triage level, the assigned clinician, and the results that have returned, so the whole room shares one picture of who is waiting. Notes on paper, labels for specimens, and the electronic health record, or EHR, carry the clinical information, and the department must be able to document when the network fails. The commonest error is a result seen on a screen and never recorded or handed over, so the finding exists only in one person's memory, and every scanning, labeling, and identity check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The consumables make the machines useful, and because the department treats the undifferentiated patient, its stock must cover almost every possibility at once. The core list runs from gloves and other personal protective equipment, or PPE, through cannulae, syringes, needles, giving sets, and fluid bags, to dressings, sutures, splints, catheters, specimen containers, and the forms that record care. Sharps containers must sit within arm's reach of every place a needle is used, because the commonest injury is a needle recapped by hand or left on a tray. Suture cartridges, chest drain tubes, airway tubes, and defibrillator pads all carry expiry dates, and stock is rotated on a first in and first out rule, while restocking happens after every patient rather than at the end of a shift, because a missing item is discovered at the worst possible moment.

Cleaning and reprocessing follow the logic of every department, which is that visible soil must be removed before disinfection can work. Reusable instruments such as laryngoscope blades, forceps, scissors, and specula are cleaned with a brush and an enzymatic detergent, rinsed, inspected, and then disinfected or sterilized by a validated method. A common steam cycle is 134 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes or 121 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, and those cycles must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Surfaces touched by many hands, such as trolley tops, monitor cables, and bed rails, are wiped between patients, and a chlorine solution of 0.5 per cent available chlorine with a contact time of 10 minutes is used for blood spills, a concentration and time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, while the commonest error is to wipe a device with a cloth that is already dirty, which moves organisms rather than removing them.

Maintenance is a scheduled program involving a biomedical technician, because a device that is never used still ages and the department cannot test everything at the moment of need. Defibrillators are checked for delivered energy and battery condition, monitors for calibration and alarm accuracy, infusion devices for flow accuracy, and ultrasound probes for lens cracks and cable damage. Suction and oxygen regulators are checked against a known gauge or leak tested, and every battery is tracked by the date it was installed, and the intervals for these checks must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The commonest maintenance failure is not a broken machine but an absent record, because a device whose last test cannot be found is treated as untested, and a technician should keep a small stock of the parts that fail most.

The failure modes that matter most appear during a resuscitation and turn out to have been present for weeks. A laryngoscope whose battery was left switched on is dead when it is needed, an oxygen cylinder used for transport was never exchanged, defibrillator pads whose gel has dried adhere poorly, a suction canister left full produces no vacuum, and a monitor whose alarm limits were set to unreachable values is effectively silent. The characteristic alarms each mean something specific, so a monitor repeats a lead-off tone, a defibrillator gives a low-battery tone, a rapid infuser alarms on air or a heater fault, a suction unit blocks at the canister float, and an infusion pump signals an occlusion. Every one of those thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the commonest operator error is to silence an alarm without naming its cause, which turns a warning into silence.

What the operator must check is a short, fixed routine performed at the start of every shift rather than when the patient arrives. The defibrillator is switched on and allowed to run its self-test, the pads and their expiry dates are inspected, the monitor is checked against a simulator or a known signal, the oxygen cylinders are weighed or their gauges read, the suction is run against a sealed test cap, the laryngoscope light is switched on, the bag is squeezed to test its valves, and the drugs are counted. The seal on the resuscitation trolley is read against the log, and a cart whose seal number does not match is treated as tampered. Every reading and threshold in this check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the commonest error is to check the front row of a drawer and the labels that face outward, since the items that fail are the ones that cannot be seen.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the emergency department is not a building but a system a person carries, and its principle is that the sorting function must survive the loss of every wall and pipe. The fixed furniture becomes a sturdy table that can be wiped, a battery or kerosene lamp with a bright focused beam, and a flat surface for instruments, and the rest is a set of bags that one or two people can lift. The hospital's spatial memory, in which a hand knows which drawer holds the airway and which holds the drugs, is replaced by a written inventory and a fixed order inside each bag, because a soft bag has no compartments that keep an item in place. Power comes from a battery or a small generator, water comes from a container, and oxygen comes from a cylinder rather than a wall outlet, so every device must be chosen for independence from infrastructure, and every pressure, flow, energy, and temperature setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Triage in the field does the work of the building, because there is no separate room in which the stable can wait and the unstable can be treated. The system is a printed scale or a set of colored cards, and the first decision is whether the patient can walk, which sorts the many minor cases from the few serious ones in a single minute. The next decisions use the same variables as the hospital scale, the respiratory rate, the heart rate, the ability to respond, and the presence of severe bleeding, and the color assigned determines the order of treatment. The colors correspond to actions rather than diagnoses, from treat now through treat soon and can wait to beyond the resources available, while the commonest error is to treat the loudest patient first and a written tally substitutes for the tracking board.

The field bag is built around weight and the questions that will actually be asked, and its contents compress the trauma bay. It holds a small monitor or a hand-held oximeter, a portable defibrillator with adult and pediatric pads, a bag and masks in several sizes, oral airways, a supraglottic airway, suction that is manual or battery driven, a small oxygen cylinder with a regulator, splints, a pelvic binder, dressings and tourniquets, a suture set, a few drugs, and laminated checklists. The weight is the central design problem, because a bag that is too heavy is left in the vehicle, so the kit is built around what one person can carry for a kilometer over rough ground, and drugs are chosen for stability in heat and carried in an insulated pouch. Every dose, energy level, and flow setting in the bag must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the bag is sealed after each restock so its seal number can be checked like a closed drawer.

The field variant gives up a great deal, and an honest list of the losses is more useful than optimism. There is no CT scanner and no MRI scanner, no laboratory on site, no blood bank, no rapid infusion device, no piped suction, no wall oxygen, and usually no capnograph to confirm a tracheal tube, so the clinician must decide with the hands, the eyes, and a few numbers. What remains is the clinical examination, a small number of tests, an ultrasound probe if one is carried, and the judgment to move the patient toward the hospital rather than wait for equipment to arrive. Maintenance is built around weather rather than a calendar, because heat shortens battery life and softens pad adhesive, dust clogs suction filters, humidity corrodes contacts, and vibration loosens connectors, so batteries are charged whenever power is available and the state of charge is written on a tag each day.

Reusable instruments are cleaned of all visible soil and then disinfected or sterilized by a method validated in that setting, and the cycles used must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Because the field has fewer alarms, the operator must supply the monitoring by repeating observations at fixed intervals and writing them down, and some interventions cannot be improvised at all, so the field clinician must know that boundary before the patient arrives. A kit that is checked once a week is not checked, and the person who carries it must confirm that every expiry date and setting inside it is still valid. A discharged defibrillator is an empty bag with a handle, so the battery state is the first thing checked and the last thing recorded, and a bag that has never been opened in a drill is only a collection of unverified assumptions.

To summarize, the equipment of the emergency department exists to sort the undifferentiated patient and to shorten the time between arrival and the right treatment. The trauma bay and the resuscitation room hold a hard bed, an overhead light, a monitor, a rapid infuser, suction, an airway trolley, a chest drain set, and a route to imaging, arranged so every device sits within reach of the role that needs it. Splints, collars, boards, and binders hold the injured body still, suture sets and casts protect the wounded part, and point-of-care tests and ultrasound bring the laboratory and the image to the bedside. In the field the building becomes a table, a light, and a bag, and the operator supplies the monitoring the alarms would otherwise provide. Whatever the setting, the discipline is the same: know the order of the kit, check the seal, confirm every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol, watch the patient and the clock, and restock before the next arrival.

# Chapter 57 — Transport and Pre-Hospital Equipment

The physical problem of transport is that a device must keep working while the ground beneath it moves, so every transport device is built around stored energy and restraint. A hospital machine draws power from a wall socket and gas from a pipeline, while a transport machine carries its own battery and cylinder and must survive being lifted, dropped, and braked. The second principle is inertia, because a vehicle in a sudden stop keeps its contents moving until something stops them, and the force on a loose object rises with the square of its speed. A transport device is therefore a compromise between the capability of a ward machine and the mass and power that one person can carry. That compromise explains the small screen of a transport monitor and the short cylinder life of a portable ventilator.

An ambulance is a family of vehicles separated by how much medicine they deliver while moving. The simplest is a van or pickup with a flat floor and one stretcher, a vehicle for carrying rather than treating. The most capable is a box vehicle with a permanent oxygen supply, a suction line, mains power from an inverter, and room for two clinicians beside the stretcher. The layout principle is that everything must be reachable from a seated or kneeling position, because the vehicle is a treatment room that is falling over. A bulkhead separates the cab from the patient compartment, and the layout of any class must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the vehicle is placed in service.

Securing is the least glamorous and most important task in the vehicle, and it rests on a calculation of deceleration. A stretcher and patient may weigh well over 100 kilograms, and the restraint must hold many times that in a crash, so fittings are rated in multiples of the load rather than by how firm they feel. The correct fittings are rails, brackets, and quick-release cradles tested to a stated load, and those values must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A cylinder is doubly dangerous because its regulator can shear off and turn it into a rocket, so it travels in a bracket with the valve protected. The commonest error is the hurried departure in which the last item is placed on the bench and never strapped, so a pre-departure check in which every item is touched and named is the only reliable defense.

The wheeled stretcher, or cot, is the central object of the vehicle, and its principle is a platform on a linkage that can be raised, lowered, and locked. The frame carries a mattress on a hinged backrest, the undercarriage collapses for loading, and side rails keep the patient from rolling off. The cot locks into the floor by a capture mechanism, and an unlocked stretcher is a heavy object on wheels that will travel forward in a crash. The commonest error is failing to hear the click of the floor lock, and the warning is a mechanical indicator that the crew must check by pulling the stretcher back before driving. The height, load rating, and locking procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the mattress must be wiped and the straps inspected after every patient.

A spine board is a rigid slab that turns the whole body into a single unit so that the injured spine is not bent. A body on a soft surface flexes at every bump, concentrating movement at an unstable fracture, so a rigid platform spreads the load and limits relative motion between vertebrae. A scoop stretcher applies the same principle in two halves that slide under the patient and lock together, allowing a casualty to be lifted without being rolled onto the side. The commonest error is leaving the patient on the hard board long after transfer, because a rigid surface concentrates pressure on the sacrum, heels, and back of the head and can cause a pressure injury within hours. The correct sequence, the board's weight limit, and the interval before the patient is moved off it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the straps and blocks must be checked for cracks.

The vacuum mattress is a bag of small beads that becomes a rigid shell, and its physics is friction between grains. When the air is withdrawn, outside pressure presses the beads together, friction rises sharply, and the bag hardens into the shape of the patient around whom it was molded, which distributes pressure far better than a board. The hazard is a slow leak, because a mattress that has lost its vacuum looks inflated and feels firm at the edge while the middle has gone soft, and the patient can shift unnoticed. The check is therefore a vacuum gauge or a firm hand at the start and end of transport, and a softened mattress must be repumped or replaced. The required vacuum level and pump strokes must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the valve and cover must be inspected for punctures and wiped between patients.

A transport monitor is a ward monitor asked to shrink, and what it gives up reveals its physics. It measures the electrocardiogram from adhesive skin electrodes, the blood pressure by an inflatable cuff, the oxygen saturation from the differing absorption of red and infrared light, the breathing rate, and often the carbon dioxide in the exhaled breath. The electronics are packed into a sealed case with a battery, and the screen is small while the alarms must be heard over an engine and a siren. The hazard is motion artifact, because every bump produces a false reading and every loose electrode a false alarm, and the commonest error is to silence the alarm instead of correcting the cause. The upper and lower alarm limits, the alarm volume, and the interval between charges must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The monitor must be strapped to its bracket, because an unsecured monitor is a heavy object in a crash.

A transport ventilator generates a breath without a hospital pipeline, and the way it does so defines its limits. A ward ventilator may use piped gas pressure to drive a bellows or turbine, so it has unlimited gas and mains power, while a transport ventilator makes its own pressure with a small turbine, piston, or compressed-gas injector and therefore spends battery charge or cylinder gas for every breath. The settings are the same family as a ward machine, a volume or pressure for each breath, a rate, a positive end-expiratory pressure, and an oxygen concentration, and every value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is disconnection during movement, and the characteristic alarm is a low-pressure or apnea alarm announcing a circuit that has come apart. The commonest error is to watch the screen rather than the chest, and every ventilator must be checked with a test lung before it leaves the station.

Portable oxygen is stored energy in its most concentrated form, and its arithmetic governs every transport plan. A cylinder holds gas at high pressure, and the usable volume equals the water capacity multiplied by the gauge pressure, so a small cylinder holds far fewer liters than its size suggests. A flow of 15 liters per minute through a reservoir mask empties a small cylinder in minutes, while 2 liters per minute through a nasal cannula may last an hour, and both flows must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The regulator reduces cylinder pressure to a safe working level, and the flowmeter shows the rate as a ball in a tapered tube, read at the top edge of the ball and not its middle. The hazard is a cylinder that is only half full, and the warning is a gauge falling faster than the flow should allow or a low-pressure whistle. The commonest error is to transport a patient on a cylinder never weighed or checked, and a spare cylinder must always be secured upright as part of the equipment.

Portable suction provides the same pressure difference as a wall vacuum line, but makes it with its own pump or with a human hand. A battery unit uses a diaphragm or rotary pump to draw air from a canister, and a manual unit uses a piston or bellows squeezed by the operator, so the suction lasts as long as the operator's arm. The vacuum is measured in millimeters of mercury, and a typical adult setting is between 80 and 120 millimeters of mercury, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A float valve rises as the jar fills and shuts the suction path to protect the pump, and the characteristic alarm is the sudden loss of vacuum when it rises. The hazard is a canister filling during transport with no one watching, and the commonest error is to keep suctioning through a full jar and drive fluid into the pump. The catheter must be measured against the patient and the vacuum released between passes, and the battery, canister level, and tubing must be checked before every shift.

An infusion pump in a moving vehicle fights gravity, and its physics differs between a syringe pump and a volumetric pump. A syringe pump drives a plunger at a controlled rate with a leadscrew, accurate and compact but limited to one syringe, while a volumetric pump squeezes tubing with a rotating cam or fingers and can run for hours from a bag. Both depend on a battery and both must be secured so that the pump and bag move with the patient rather than across the compartment. The specific hazard of a syringe pump is free flow, because when the syringe is removed the plunger can be pushed by gravity and the drug runs uncontrolled, so the line must be clamped before changing the syringe. The characteristic alarms are occlusion from a kinked tube or positional cannula and air in line, which demands that the line be cleared. The rate, alarm thresholds, and battery duration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the commonest error is to hang the pump on a hook never designed to carry it.

The transport defibrillator is the same capacitor device used in resuscitation, but it must work on a patient lying on a moving stretcher. The physics is charge stored on two plates separated by an insulator and released across the chest in thousandths of a second, with energy measured in joules and a typical adult biphasic shock between 120 and 200 joules, an energy level that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is that the operator or stretcher may be in contact with the patient when the shock is delivered, so the command to clear must be spoken and obeyed even in a cramped space. The characteristic alarms are the rising charge tone and the low-battery tone, and a self-test failure when the unit is switched on means that the device must be withdrawn from service. The commonest error is a pad whose gel dried in a hot vehicle, and the device, pads, and battery must be checked at the start of every shift.

A cervical collar is foam and plastic that limits neck movement, and its principle is to stiffen a joint by wrapping it in a shell. It reduces flexion and extension reasonably well and rotation less well, so it aids immobilization but does not replace manual in-line stabilization while it is applied. Collars are sized by the height from shoulder to jaw, and a collar of the wrong height either fails to support the head or pushes it into a harmful position, so size and fitting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hazard is a collar applied too tightly, which presses on the neck veins and can raise pressure inside the skull, and the second is pressure injury where the rim presses on the chin, the shoulders, or the back of the head. There is no alarm, which is why the collar must be reassessed and the skin under it inspected. The commonest error is to fit the collar first and stabilize the neck afterwards.

A traction splint pulls a broken thigh into line, and its principle is a balance of forces across the fracture. A fractured femur is surrounded by powerful muscles that shorten the limb, and that shortening increases pain, bleeding, and damage to nearby vessels and nerves, so the splint pulls at the ankle and takes counter-traction against the pelvis. Counter-traction is taken on an ischial pad or half-ring, and tension is applied by a ratchet or windlass with a strap around the ankle. The hazards are pressure on the perineum or the foot and a limb that is over-pulled, so the pulse, color, and sensation in the foot must be checked before and after application. There is no alarm, and the check is the operator's hand and eye, which is why this device fails silently in unpracticed hands. The traction force, pad position, and reassessment interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A pelvic binder is a wide band wrapped around the hips to close a fractured pelvis, and its physics is circumferential compression. A broken pelvis can open like a book, and the widening increases the pelvic volume so that blood pools there in liters, while a binder across the greater trochanters reduces that volume and can limit the bleeding. The correct level is the greater trochanters, the bony points at the widest part of the hips, and a binder placed too high does nothing and may press on the abdomen.
