The safety hazard is the open burning of PVC at low temperature, which is also the common operator error in a resource-limited setting. The stack temperature, the gas residence time, and the emission limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before waste containing chlorinated plastic is burned.

The incinerator has its own operating ritual, its own consumables, and its own characteristic alarms. The load is weighed, the chamber is charged in the order that puts wet waste below dry waste, the burners are watched until the chamber reaches temperature, and the ash is raked out only when the unit has cooled. Consumables include the fuel, the igniters, the refractory lining that slowly crumbles, the temperature probe, and the ash container, and a failed probe is the commonest cause of a unit that is reported as too cold. The characteristic alarm is a high temperature or a combustion air fault, and each of those thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the unit is run. The safety hazard is the ash, which can still contain sharps and heavy metals, and it is handled with gloves and buried or encapsulated rather than scattered.

Burial is the alternative where incineration is not available, and the hospital pit is an engineered structure rather than a hole. The pit is lined with concrete or with compacted clay to slow the movement of liquid into the ground, it has a cover that keeps out rain and animals, and it is fenced and locked. Its bottom is kept well above the water table, and its distance from any well or borehole is set by the local rules, and those distances and the depth must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the site is dug. The safety hazard is the pit that is dug into porous ground near a drinking water source, and the common operator error is to leave the pit open between rounds of filling. The depth, the lining, the cover, and the separation from water are the whole design.

Mercury is a small-volume hazard with a disproportionate consequence, and it appears in thermometers, blood pressure instruments, and some laboratory devices. Liquid mercury evaporates at room temperature, so a spill that looks like a few shiny beads becomes an invisible vapor that accumulates in a warm, still room. The cleanup removes the visible metal with a rigid card, a syringe, or an aspirator, seals it in a labeled container, and then treats the area with a sulfur powder or a commercial amalgamating agent before ventilation. The safety hazard is the vacuum cleaner, which heats the metal and blows fine droplets and vapor into the air, and the common operator error is to sweep with a broom, which breaks the beads into smaller ones. The spill kit contents, the ventilation time, and the vapor exposure limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a spill is handled.

Cleaning is not only a patient-facing activity, because the waste room, the trolleys, the bins, and the treatment plant must be cleaned on a schedule of their own. A bin is washed with detergent and disinfectant after each emptying, the trolley is wiped after each route, and the floor of the store is washed at least daily, and the concentration and the contact time of the disinfectant must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol. Sharps containers are never rinsed or reused, because rinsing exposes the worker to the contents and reusing a container defeats its single-use lock. The safety hazard is the cleaning staff who handle waste without personal protective equipment, and they are the group that receives the least training and the most exposure. The cleaning schedule, the disinfectant, and the protective equipment requirement must be confirmed against the local protocol before the task begins.

The people who handle waste need protection, and that protection is a system rather than a pair of gloves. Personal protective equipment for waste handling includes heavy gloves, an apron or a gown, eye protection, and a mask where dust or aerosol may be produced, and boots where liquids may spill. Vaccination against hepatitis B is offered to every worker with a risk of sharps injury, and the coverage is recorded, because a vaccinated worker who is injured has a very different outcome. The safety hazard is the assumption that general waste is harmless, and the common operator error is to handle a bag without knowing which category it belongs to. The protective equipment specification, the vaccination schedule, and the post-exposure protocol must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the worker begins the task.

Records are what turn a set of good habits into a system that can be audited. Every bag and container carries the date, the ward, the category, and the name of the person who closed it, so that a problem at the plant can be traced back to its source on the ward. The treatment plant records the weight or the number of containers received, the cycle parameters, the operator, and the destination of the residue, and the incinerator log records the temperatures and the burn times. The safety hazard is a treatment record that is filled in at the end of the day from memory, and the common operator error is to record the intended temperature rather than the observed one. The record fields, the retention period, and the audit frequency must be confirmed against the local protocol before the log is used as evidence.

The whole chain fails in characteristic ways, and a manager who knows them can find the weak link before an outbreak does. The failures are mixed bags at the ward, overfilled sharps containers, a leaking trolley, an unlocked store, a cold incinerator, an open pit, and a treatment log that is complete but untrue. Each of these failures is small in itself, and each one defeats a large investment downstream, because the system is a chain and the chain is only as strong as its cheapest link. The safety hazard that runs through all of them is the false confidence of a tidy-looking ward where the invisible segregation is wrong. The operator must check the bag, the lid, the fill line, the lock, and the label in that order, and the local audit criteria must be confirmed against the local protocol before the system is judged.

The field variant begins where there is no treatment plant, no separate store, and often no reliable electricity, so the system is built from what is available and must be simple enough to survive a busy day. The principle does not change, because hazard still flows from the concentrated stream into the dilute one, but the containment and the destruction are now the work of a drum, a fire, and a hole in the ground. A mobile clinic on a four-wheel drive vehicle may produce only a few hundred grams of sharps in a week, while a district hospital may produce a hundred times as much, so the scale decides the design. What the field gives up is the certainty of a validated cycle, and what it demands instead is discipline with distances, temperatures, and time. Every figure in this half must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used.

Segregation in the field is harder because there may be only one bin, so the categories are carried by the container rather than by the color. A field clinic that cannot supply a different bin for every category uses a small number of clearly marked containers, one for sharps and one for everything that must be burned, and it teaches the staff the two rules that matter most. The first rule is that a sharp never enters a bag, and the second is that a dressing with blood never enters the ordinary refuse. Where color-coded bags are available, the local code is posted at the bin and the national code is followed, and where they are not, a word or a picture on the lid takes its place, and the choice of scheme must be confirmed against the local protocol before it is taught. The safety hazard is the untrained volunteer who has never been told which container is which.

The field sharps container can be a manufactured puncture-resistant box or an improvised one, and the improvised version must be judged by the same physical tests. A rigid plastic bottle with a screw cap, a thick cardboard box lined with tape, or a metal tin can all work if a needle cannot pass through the wall and the opening cannot admit a finger. The container is closed permanently when it is three quarters full, reinforced with tape around the lid, and labeled with the word sharps and the date, and that fill limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol. The safety hazard is the bottle so soft that a needle passes through its side and into the leg of the person carrying it, and the common operator error is to keep using a container because it is not yet visibly full at the top. The closed container is kept in a locked place until it can be treated or buried.

Where a manufactured autoclave is unavailable, the field sterilizer for waste is often a pressure cooker or a small drum heated over a fire, and its principle is the same steam under pressure. The waste is placed in a perforated inner container so that steam reaches the whole load, the lid is clamped, and the unit is held at a temperature and a time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a load is accepted. In practice the operator watches a pressure gauge or a weighted valve together with a clock, because a load that has not reached the temperature has not been treated. The safety hazard is the sealed vessel that is opened while it is still under pressure, and the common operator error is to fill the unit so full that the steam cannot circulate. The treated waste is then buried, or placed well away from the working area.

Chemical treatment survives in the field because it needs only a bucket and a supply of disinfectant, and it is best suited to liquid waste and to small solid items that can be soaked. The waste is drained, the disinfectant is prepared at the correct strength, and the items are fully immersed for the full contact time, and both the strength and the time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol. A hypochlorite solution loses its strength in heat and sunlight, so the stock is kept in a closed, dark container and made up freshly rather than stored for weeks. The safety hazard is the concentrated solution splashed on the skin or in the eye, and the common operator error is to add waste to a bucket and then pour in disinfectant without measuring either the volume or the concentration. The solution is never used for sharps, because it does not remove the puncture hazard.

The field incinerator is usually built rather than bought, and a common design is a brick or mud-brick chamber with a metal grate, an air inlet, and a chimney, sometimes with a secondary combustion zone made from a stacked drum. A simpler version is a metal drum with holes punched around the base for air, set on stones so that the fire draws from below. The principle is unchanged, since fuel and oxygen produce heat, and the heat must reach the waste for long enough to consume it. The safety hazard is the structure that collapses while it is hot, and the common operator error is to load the chamber with wet or tightly packed waste so that it smolders and smokes. The chamber dimensions, the air inlet size, the loading rate, and the burn time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the unit is fired.

The field incinerator is the place where the chlorine problem becomes a daily reality, because the same drum that burns dressings also burns tubing, and the smoke from a smoldering fire carries hydrogen chloride and can help form dioxins. The operator keeps the fire hot and the fuel dry, loads in thin layers, and never burns chlorinated plastic unless the design has a secondary combustion zone that reaches the temperature the process needs, and that temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol. The ash is treated as hazardous, because it holds heavy metals, unburned sharps, and concentrated salts, and it is buried in the same pit as infectious waste rather than spread on a garden. The safety hazard is the operator who stands in the smoke plume, and the common operator error is to use the incinerator to dispose of aerosol cans or sealed containers. The operator must keep the chimney clear and the area downwind of patients.

The field pit is the heart of the low-resource system, and its design is a problem of distance and water rather than of concrete. The pit must not contaminate the well, and contamination happens through groundwater, through surface runoff, and through insects and animals that carry material from the pit to the house. The safe distance depends on the soil, the depth of the water table, and the slope of the ground, so a pit dug in sand near a shallow well is a very different proposition from a pit in dry clay far above the water table. The pit is sited downhill and downwind of the water source, and the distance is measured in meters from the well rather than in paces from the door, and that separation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the site is chosen. The safety hazard is the pit dug in a depression where rainwater collects and then flows toward the water point.

The construction of the field pit follows a small set of rules that can be taught in an afternoon. The pit is dug at least 2 meters deep and 1 meter wide, with a raised lip or a mound around the opening so that surface water runs away, and a cover that is kept closed and locked, and these dimensions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before digging begins. The bottom is not lined with a material that will rot, and a clay soil is its own lining, while the sides are kept as vertical as the ground allows so that the pit holds its volume. The pit is filled in layers, and a layer of soil is added periodically to cover fresh waste and reduce flies and odor, and when the pit is nearly full it is sealed and a new one is dug. The safety hazard is the person who climbs onto the crust of a full pit, and the common operator error is to use a pit as a general dump for every kind of waste.

The placenta pit is a separate and often shallower structure in many field maternity units, and it exists because the placenta is a large, soft, and readily scavenged object. It is dug near the delivery room but away from the water source and the kitchen, it is lined or built with a concrete ring, and it is closed with a heavy lid, and its depth, its lining, and its separation from water must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used. The placenta is dropped in without a container, or in a bag that will decompose, and a layer of soil is added after each delivery so that the surface is never left open. The safety hazard is the animal or the scavenger that pulls a placenta out of an uncovered pit, and the common operator error is to place the structure uphill of the well because it is closer to the ward. The pit is emptied or replaced when its contents reach the marked level.

Mercury still appears in field equipment, and in a setting without a spill kit the response is improvised but the principle does not change. The visible beads are collected with a piece of card, a damp cloth, or a plastic syringe, and the collected material is sealed in a glass or heavy plastic container with a lid, while the room is aired by opening windows and doors rather than by heating it, and the ventilation time must be confirmed against the local protocol. A paste of sulfur powder or a fine zinc dust is spread over the area where the beads were, and the surface is wiped rather than swept. The safety hazard is the person who handles the mercury with bare hands and then eats without washing, and the common operator error is to burn the broken instrument with the rest of the waste, which sends the mercury into the air. The spill response must be confirmed against the local protocol before the device is used.

Transport and security in the field are governed by the same downward flow as in the hospital, but the distances are longer and the vehicles are fewer. Waste is carried in a closed container or a tied bag, it travels on a route that does not pass through the food store or the patient waiting area, and it is delivered to the pit or the incinerator on the same day it is generated where possible, and that interval must be confirmed against the local protocol. The safety hazard is the bag that is left overnight in the corner of a room where children sleep, and the common operator error is to reuse a bag for laundry after it has held waste. Where waste must be stored, it is kept locked, and the key is held by a named person rather than kept in a drawer.

What the field variant gives up is measurable and worth naming, because a clinic that borrows the hospital standard without the hospital infrastructure fails at both. It gives up the validated cycle, the continuous temperature record, the engineered emission control, the dedicated store, the one-way corridor, and the trained waste handler whose only job is waste. It gives up the certainty that a bag marked infectious has actually been treated, and it gives up the audit trail that would prove it. The safety hazard of the field system is not that it is crude but that it is unverified, so the operator must rely on the observable evidence of temperature, time, and distance instead of on a printout. The field limits of temperature, time, and separation must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before they are trusted.

What the field variant demands instead is discipline and a small number of unbreakable rules, because it cannot demand expensive equipment. It demands that a sharp never leaves the hand uncontained, that a placenta never lies open, that a pit is never dug before its distance from water has been measured, and that a fire is never left burning unattended. It demands that somebody is named as responsible for the pit, the drum, and the store, even when that person has four other duties. It demands a stock of sharps containers, rigid enough to reach the fill line, and a supply of fuel and disinfectant that is ordered before it runs out. The safety hazard is the system that works because one person remembers it, and the common operator error is to depend on that person never being absent.

Consumables run through the whole chain, and their absence stops it more often than any mechanical fault. The list includes liners in the correct colors, ties, labels, sharps containers, rigid pharmaceutical containers, disinfectant, fuel, ash containers, heavy gloves, aprons, eye protection, and the covered trolley. A ward that runs out of yellow liners invents a substitute, and the substitute is usually a black bag that carries infectious waste into the general stream. The safety hazard is the improvised container that fails under load, and the common operator error is to order consumables after the last one is used rather than at the reorder level. The stock levels, the reorder points, and the storage conditions for each consumable must be confirmed against the local protocol before the supply is relied upon.

The operator has a short daily list of checks, and each check exists because its failure has already caused an incident. At the start of the shift the operator confirms that every bin has a liner and a lid, that every sharps container is below its fill line and locked, that the trolley is clean and covered, and that the store is locked and its floor dry. Before a burn the operator confirms that the chamber is clear, that the fuel is dry, that the air inlets are open, and that the wind will carry the smoke away from patients. After treatment the operator confirms the temperature and the time on the record, the condition of the ash, and the closure of the pit or the store, and each recorded figure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the load is released. The safety hazard the list prevents is the ordinary one of a missing lid or an unlocked door.

Alarms and indicators are fewer in waste management than in most equipment, but they exist and they must be learned. The incinerator may signal a high temperature, a flame failure, or a combustion air fault, and the autoclave may signal a low temperature, a low pressure, or an incomplete cycle, and each of those thresholds must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the machine is trusted. The treatment log is itself an indicator, because a run of identical numbers written in the same hand is a sign that the record has stopped reflecting the process. The safety hazard is the alarm that is silenced and then forgotten, and the common operator error is to reset a fault without finding its cause. The operator must know which alarms stop the cycle and which only warn.

Training is the only part of the system that cannot be bought outright, and it must be repeated because staff move. The training covers the categories and the local color code, the fill line, the assembly of the sharps container, the route, the storage limit, the treatment parameters, and the response to a spill or an injury. It is delivered at the point of use rather than in a classroom, and it is checked by observation rather than by a signature on a sheet, because a person who cannot assemble a sharps container correctly has not been trained. The safety hazard is the confident worker who learned the system in another country and applies its color code here, and the local code must be confirmed against the local protocol before it is taught.

Waste minimization is the cheapest form of waste management, and it belongs in this chapter because the smallest stream is the easiest to handle. Buying only what will be used, choosing reusable items where reprocessing is safe, replacing mercury devices with electronic ones, and segregating carefully at the bedside all reduce the volume that must be treated. The hospital can also recover clean paper, cardboard, glass, and some plastics through a controlled route, provided that the route is genuinely separated from the clinical stream and that the workers are protected. The safety hazard is the recycling program that quietly becomes a channel for contaminated material to leave the hospital, and the common operator error is to place a recycling bin next to a waste bin without a rule that tells them apart. The separation rules and the worker protection for any recovery scheme must be confirmed against the local protocol before it starts.

To summarize, waste management is the reverse supply chain of the hospital, and it is engineering, chemistry, and habit in equal measure. Hazard is concentrated in a small part of the mass, so segregation at the moment of generation is the practice that makes every other step possible, and the person holding the item is the only one who can perform it correctly. The hospital-grade system answers the problem with color-coded bins, rigid sharps containers, separated routes, a locked store, steam autoclaves, microwave units, chemical baths, and a two-chamber incinerator whose gas is kept hot long enough to be clean. The field system answers the same problem with a limited set of marked containers, an improvised puncture-resistant box, a pressure cooker over a fire, a brick or drum incinerator, and a pit whose depth and distance from the well are the whole safeguard. In both settings the safety hazard is the same, an item that escapes its category or its container, and the common operator error is the same, a decision made at the end of the shift instead of at the bedside. The characteristic alarms are few, a high temperature or an incomplete cycle or a failed flame, and the operator must check the bag, the lid, the fill line, the lock, the route, the fire, and the pit every day. Every number in this chapter, whether it is a temperature, a pressure, a holding time, a depth, or a separation, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used, because the written figure is only a starting point and the local ground is the final authority.

# Chapter 64 — Dressings and Wound Care Supplies

A dressing is not a cover laid over a wound but a controlled environment built on top of it. Broken skin has lost its barrier, and the wound beneath is a wet, warm, active surface that both needs protection and produces fluid. The task of a dressing is to hold that surface at the right moisture, the right warmth, and the right protection while the body repairs itself. Every material in this chapter answers three physical questions, which are how fast water vapor passes through it, how much fluid it absorbs, and how firmly it sticks to what lies beneath. Once those behaviors are clear, the choice follows from the wound rather than from the shelf.

Repair proceeds through overlapping phases, and each imposes a different demand on the material. Bleeding stops first as platelets and fibrin seal the broken vessels, and inflammation follows as white cells clear debris and bacteria, producing the warm, wet, red wound that a dressing must tolerate rather than suppress. New tissue is then built as fibroblasts lay down collagen and capillaries grow into the wound bed, and the scar matures over months. A wound that stays too dry forms a hard crust and heals slowly, while one that stays too wet softens and its edges break down. The target is a moist but not soggy wound bed, and the dressing is the instrument that maintains it.

The quantity that describes a film is its moisture vapor transmission rate, the mass of water vapor crossing a given area in a given time. An impermeable cover traps sweat and wound fluid until the skin beneath softens and breaks down, while a fully permeable cloth lets the wound dry and cool. A semipermeable film sits between the two, passing water vapor while blocking liquid water and bacteria, and that selective passage is the reason such films exist. Warmth matters as well, because cells divide and enzymes act faster in a warm environment, so the balance of vapor loss, absorption, and insulation separates one dressing class from another.

Transparent films are thin adhesive sheets of semipermeable polyurethane that behave as a second skin, letting the operator see the wound without disturbing it while they shed water, and they suit a shallow, clean, minimally draining wound or the securement of a vascular access site. Their weakness is that they absorb nothing, so fluid collects beneath them and lifts the adhesive until the film floats free, and they should not be stretched over a joint or placed on fragile skin, because the pull can shear the epidermis when they are removed. A hydrocolloid is different in kind, an adhesive wafer of a gel-forming powder with an elastomer and a polymer pressed onto a foam or film backing. When it meets wound fluid it absorbs water, swells, and forms a soft, yellowish gel that keeps the wound moist and slightly acidic and bathes the surface without sticking to new tissue, so removal is painless. Hydrocolloids suit a shallow, low to moderate draining wound and a pressure injury that is not infected. The wear time for either material must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A foam dressing is a sheet of open-celled polyurethane with a waterproof backing, and its physics is the physics of a sponge. The open cells draw fluid from the wound surface by capillary action and hold it in the body of the sheet, so the wound stays moist while the surrounding skin stays dry, which lets a moderately draining wound go for several days. It comes in adhesive and non-adhesive forms, and the non-adhesive form goes under a separate cover so that it does not injure fragile skin. A hydrogel is the opposite answer, a sheet or tube of water-based gel that gives water back to a dry wound, cooling the surface, rehydrating dead tissue, and softening the dry crust that must be removed before healing can proceed. Because it adds moisture rather than absorbs it, a hydrogel must not be used on a heavily draining wound, where it would float away. The wear time and change criteria for both must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Alginates are non-woven fibers spun from the polysaccharides of brown seaweed, and they absorb many times their own weight in fluid. As they absorb, the calcium ions in the fiber are exchanged for sodium ions in the wound fluid, which turns the fiber into a soft gel that conforms to the wound bed, holds the fluid, and can be lifted out in one piece with forceps, so alginates suit a deep cavity with heavy drainage. Hydrofibers are spun from cellulose rather than seaweed and swell on contact with fluid into a coherent gel that holds fluid and bacteria within it and does not break apart, so the dressing can be removed complete. A hydrofiber tends to hold drainage against the wound rather than lock it away, so it is often covered by a foam that absorbs the fluid passing through, and it suits a moderately to heavily draining cavity. The characteristic error is to pack either material so tightly that it dries against the wound edge and becomes painful to remove, so the size, the packing density, and the wear time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Silver-containing dressings carry a metal that is toxic to bacteria, and their principle is the slow release of silver ions into wound fluid. Silver ions attach to the bacterial cell wall and to its genetic material, disrupting the organism in several ways at once, and the metal may be held as a salt, a complex, or nanocrystalline silver, so two dressings that look identical may behave very differently. Silver suits a wound that is infected or heavily colonized, and prolonged use on a clean wound can delay healing and stain tissue, so the duration of therapy and the change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Medical honey is a concentrated sugar solution with low water activity that draws water out of bacteria and generates a small amount of hydrogen peroxide as it is diluted. It also pulls fluid from the tissues and lifts dead tissue away in a process of autolytic debridement, so it suits a sloughy or malodorous wound and a superficial burn. The dressings are prepared as sterile, irradiated honey, because ordinary table honey can carry spores and must never be placed in a wound, and the quantity to apply must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Charcoal dressings contain activated carbon, which is carbon treated to open millions of tiny pores and so to present an enormous surface area. Odor molecules from a necrotic or infected wound are adsorbed onto that surface as they pass through the sheet, and the dressing simply holds them. Because charcoal alone does not absorb fluid well, it is usually combined with a foam or an absorbent layer, and the assembly is covered by a waterproof backing that keeps the odor inside. Charcoal acts on the smell and not on the cause, so it must never be used to hide an odor that signals spreading infection, and the change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Gauze is woven cotton or a cotton and polyester blend, and it is the oldest and most flexible wound material in the cupboard. Its open weave is permeable to air and fluid, it can be cut to any shape, and it works by absorption and by the mechanical removal of debris when it is lifted away, which is why plain woven gauze dries a wound and adheres painfully as it dries. The family includes flat pads, ribbon and rope forms for packing a cavity, and loose swabs for cleaning, while cotton wool is a mass of carded fibers with no weave that sheds fibers into a wound and belongs on intact skin and never inside a cavity. The most serious hazard is the swab left inside a wound, which is why swabs used in an operating field are counted and why a counted swab must never leave the field unrecorded.

Adhesive tapes are the invisible half of wound care, and their physics is a balance between stickiness and the strength of the skin they hold to. Tape is a backing with an adhesive layer, and the backing may be paper, fabric, foam, or transparent film, while the adhesive may be acrylic, rubber-based, or a soft silicone. The peel force rises with the time the tape has been in place, because the adhesive flows into the microscopic roughness of the skin and the bond matures, so repetitive removal strips the outermost layer of skin, an injury called medical adhesive-related skin injury. Tension during application produces shear and blistering, and prolonged contact can cause irritation or allergy. The common operator error is to tear the tape away in one fast pull, when the correct method is to loosen the edge, support the skin, and pull the tape back slowly along itself.

Bandages are the devices that apply force to a limb, and that force follows a simple relationship in which the pressure under a bandage depends on the tension in the fabric and on the radius of the limb. A narrow limb or a tightly wrapped bandage produces a much higher pressure than the same bandage on a broad limb, so a bandage on a thin ankle can be dangerous while the identical technique on a thigh is gentle. Crepe is a lightly elastic cotton bandage that holds a dressing and gives light support, while a short-stretch compression bandage resists the calf muscle as it pumps and gives a high working pressure during walking that suits a venous ulcer. A long-stretch elastic bandage gives a steadier resting pressure but loses tension and can be applied too tightly by an inexperienced hand, and a tubular bandage is a knitted tube applied with an applicator that holds a dressing without tape on fragile or allergic skin. The type, the number of layers, and the target pressure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The safety hazard of any compression bandage is that it can reduce blood flow below the level the tissue needs. Pain, numbness, tingling, pallor, or a cool foot after application are signs that the pressure is too high, and the bandage must be removed and reapplied immediately. The pressure is also uneven where the bandage crosses a bony prominence or where layers overlap, and these are the places where skin breaks down. The common operator error is to add a second bandage to a limb that is already swelling, so the pressure climbs with every layer. The characteristic check is the observation of the toes and the distal pulses before and after application, and the frequency of that check must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleansing is the removal of debris, bacteria, and dead tissue from a wound surface, and its physical principle is dilution and flow, because a stream of fluid loosens material and carries it away. The volume of fluid matters more than the strength of any additive, and the World Health Organization and every modern wound guideline recommend clean water or normal saline for most wounds. Normal saline at 0.9 per cent sodium chloride matches the salt concentration of body fluid, so it neither draws water out of cells nor pushes water into them, and that concentration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Antiseptics kill bacteria but also kill the fibroblasts and keratinocytes rebuilding the wound, so a strong antiseptic on a clean healing surface can slow repair, and hydrogen peroxide, iodine, and chlorhexidine are therefore reserved for a contaminated or infected wound or one being prepared for a procedure. The concentration and contact time of every antiseptic must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Debridement is the removal of dead tissue, and its principle is that dead tissue is a barrier between the wound and the healing cells and a culture medium for bacteria. Removing it lowers the bacterial load, exposes the living tissue underneath, and lets the wound edges advance. Sharp debridement with a scalpel or scissors is the fastest and most complete method, and it demands the most skill and the clearest understanding of where living tissue begins, with bleeding from a hidden vessel as its characteristic hazard. The instruments are few, including a fresh blade, curved scissors or a tissue nipper, a spoon-shaped curette drawn across the bed to scoop softened tissue, and forceps and a probe to find the depth of a cavity. Each is used once and either discarded or reprocessed, and a sharp curette or blade is handled as a sharps hazard throughout, with the size of the instrument and the depth of the pass confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Enzymatic debridement applies the chemistry of digestion to dead tissue, and the agent is a preparation of a protein-digesting enzyme, most often collagenase, which acts on the collagen of dead tissue and spares the living tissue around it. The wound must be moist for the enzyme to work, so it is applied under a dressing that keeps it in contact with the surface. It is useful where sharp debridement is unavailable, not tolerated, or unsafe near a tendon or a major vessel, and the frequency and quantity must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. Autolytic debridement is the body's own digestion of dead tissue, and it is simply the maintenance of a moist environment that lets the wound's enzymes act, while larval therapy uses sterile fly larvae that liquefy and ingest dead tissue and secrete substances that inhibit bacteria. Larval therapy is offered where other methods have failed and with a clear explanation, with the product, duration, and containment dressing confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Negative pressure wound therapy applies a controlled suction to a wound through a porous interface, and its principle is the removal of fluid together with the mechanical deformation of tissue. A foam or a gauze interface is cut to the shape of the wound, covered by an adhesive film, and connected by a tube to a pump that holds the wound below atmospheric pressure, which draws fluid out, reduces swelling, and pulls the wound edges together while the film seals the surface from contamination. Foam is easier to cut and to seal and distributes pressure across the wound, while gauze is more conformable in a deep or irregular cavity and can be placed in a tunnel. The pressure is typically held between about 60 and 125 millimeters of mercury, a range that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A wound that is actively bleeding, that contains dead tissue not yet removed, or that holds exposed bowel or a major vessel is not a candidate for negative pressure wound therapy until those conditions are resolved. The machine has a small display and a set of alarms the operator must know by ear. A leak alarm sounds when the suction cannot hold the set pressure because the film seal has failed, and the characteristic sign is a hissing edge and a dressing that no longer dimples, while a blockage alarm sounds when the tube is kinked or filled with clot. A canister alarm sounds when the container is full or its seal is not seated, and the canister is the part most often mismanaged, because it must be seated and sealed correctly or the leak alarm sounds and therapy never begins. The alarms, their thresholds, the pressure setting, and the canister replacement rule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An ostomy appliance is a dressing for a stoma, and its physics is the management of a seal against a moving, wet, irregular surface. A stoma is a loop of bowel brought through the abdominal wall, and it has no nerve endings at its surface but bleeds easily. The appliance must hold an adhesive barrier against the skin, collect the output without leaking, and protect the surrounding skin from the enzymes in the effluent, and the barrier must match the stoma in size and shape and be cut to fit closely, because skin exposed to effluent becomes raw and painful within hours. A one-piece appliance combines the barrier and the pouch and is replaced as a unit, while a two-piece appliance joins the pouch to a separate barrier with a flange or a ring so the pouch can be changed without disturbing the barrier. Fittings include paste and rings to fill a crease, powders to dry a weeping area, belts to support a heavy appliance, and deodorants, and the correct barrier size and wear time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The common operator error with an ostomy appliance is to cut the barrier opening larger than the stoma to avoid rubbing it, because that leaves a ring of unprotected skin that the effluent will digest. The safety hazard is a leak left in place, because enzyme-rich output strips the skin within a day, and once the skin is broken the seal becomes harder still. The characteristic sign of a failing seal is itching or burning under the barrier, and the patient is the best detector of it. Teaching the patient to measure the stoma, to cut the barrier, and to inspect the skin is the part of ostomy care that lasts beyond the hospital, and the teaching and review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A wound is measured so that its progress can be judged, and the measurement is useful only if it is repeatable. The three dimensions are length, width, and depth, with length at the longest axis from head to toe and width at right angles to it, while depth is measured with a sterile probe at the deepest point and the amount of undermining is recorded by clock position. Photography is powerful and needs discipline, because a consistent camera distance, a scale marker, a color reference, and the same lighting make two images comparable while a casual snapshot misleads. The patient must consent, and the images must be stored under the same privacy rules as the rest of the record, within the electronic health record or another secured system. The written record carries the date, the site, the measurements, the appearance of the wound bed, the type and quantity of drainage, the odor, the state of the surrounding skin, and the dressing applied.

Dressings are consumables with dates, and their storage is part of their safety. Each class has an expiry date on the package, and a sterile package that has been wet, crushed, or opened is no longer sterile regardless of the date. Stock is rotated so that the oldest package is used first, and new deliveries are placed behind the existing stock. Storage should be clean, dry, out of direct sunlight, and within the temperature range the maker states, because heat and moisture degrade adhesives and some silver and honey products. A damp or hot stockroom can ruin a whole shelf of dressings while every date remains valid.

The hospital-grade half of wound care is not a single machine but a supply chain and a trained team. A wound care service, often led by a specialist nurse, chooses the formulary, sets the assessment schedule, and teaches the ward staff which dressing belongs to which wound, while the pharmacy or the central store holds the stock and the central sterile services department handles the reusable scissors, forceps, probes, and curettes. The ward keeps a dressing trolley restocked on a schedule, and documentation flows into the electronic health record so that the photograph, the measurements, and the product used follow the patient. The trolley is wiped with the approved detergent between patients, and the scissors and the probe are cleaned and steam sterilized at 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 minutes, a cycle that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The reusable instruments are inspected for rust, for a loose joint, and for a blunt edge, and the storage area is inspected for damp, for pests, and for expired stock, with the inspection frequency confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Failure in wound care rarely announces itself as a broken machine, and the characteristic signals are on the patient rather than on a display. A dressing that has lifted at the edge, a rim of fluid, a rising odor, a wound that has enlarged since the last assessment, or skin that is red and softened around the wound are the alarms of this field. The safety hazard is the wound concealed under a dressing for too long, so that an infection or a deterioration is discovered late, and the common operator error is to leave a dressing in place because it still looks clean when the interval has passed. Before a dressing is changed, the hands are cleaned, personal protective equipment is worn, the old dressing is removed slowly, and the wound is assessed before it is cleaned, because cleaning changes the appearance that was just recorded. The new package is checked for an intact seal, for a date within its life, and for the correct product, and only then is the dressing placed, secured without tension, with every step and product confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the mobile or frontier clinic the wound formulary is short, and the skill is in using a small set of materials well. The shelf usually holds plain gauze, cotton wool, adhesive tape, saline, a mild antiseptic, a few petroleum-jelly dressings, and perhaps a foam or a hydrocolloid if the supply chain has delivered one. The choice is made by the wound rather than by the catalogue, so a clean surgical wound needs only a dry or lightly moist gauze cover while a sloughy and wet wound needs frequent gauze changes, and the dressing that costs nothing and heals is not one product but a method, because a wound kept clean, moist, and undisturbed will close even under a simple cover. Where the manufactured product is absent, the field team improvises, so a piece of clean plastic film can serve as a semipermeable cover, a petroleum-jelly gauze as a non-adherent interface, a thin clean foam as an absorbent layer, and a clean plastic bag as a holder. Any improvised material must be clean, must not shed fibers into the wound, and must never stick and tear when it is removed, and the characteristic error in this setting is to spend a scarce advanced dressing on a wound that needed only cleaning and time.

Cleansing in the field is done with the best water available, and the volume and the method decide the outcome. Boiled and cooled water or clean saline is poured or gently irrigated over the wound, and a syringe with a soft tip provides a controllable stream. Sharp debridement is performed only by a clinician who can see where the living tissue begins, with a fresh blade and good light, because a deep cut in poor light can open a vessel or a tendon. Where a wound is too painful or too deep for sharp work, a moist dressing and time will soften the dead tissue for a later session, and the instruments are boiled or pressure-cooked between uses, with the timing of that cycle confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Compression for a venous ulcer in the field is achieved with a short-stretch bandage or a carefully applied elastic wrap whose pressure is judged by the patient's comfort and the color of the toes, because the same cloth on two different limbs produces two different pressures. The field variant also demands more of the operator in stock discipline and in judgment about when to refer. Adhesives fail in heat, silver and honey products lose their properties, and a dressing stored in a hot vehicle may be useless before its printed date, so the stock is kept in the coolest, driest place the clinic has and inspected at each use. The characteristic alarm of the field is a wound that smells worse and grows larger despite regular dressing, which means that the diagnosis, the debridement, or the referral has failed rather than the dressing. The common operator error is to keep changing the dressing and never reassess the wound, and what the field gives up is the advanced foam, the silver sheet, the negative pressure pump, and the engineered ostomy range, which all need a supply chain, storage, and training that a mobile clinic cannot sustain. In their place the team relies on gauze, water, and a moist, clean, undisturbed wound, and on a paper chart with a drawn wound map and a dated photograph.

To summarize, a dressing is an environment rather than a cover, and every class in this chapter is defined by how it handles water, how much it absorbs, and how it meets the skin. The wound decides the material, the material decides the interval, and the interval decides whether the wound is left moist and undisturbed long enough to heal. The hospital version buys choice with a formulary, a sterile supply chain, a trained wound service, and an electronic record, while the field version buys access with gauze, water, a clean cover, and disciplined judgment. In both settings the hazards are the same, which are a dressing left too long, a seal that fails, skin torn by adhesive, and pressure that starves the tissue. The operator's assessment, the measurement, the honest documentation, and the confirmation of every product, pressure, and interval against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol are what turn a shelf of materials into safe wound care.

# Chapter 65 — Catheters, Tubes, and Drains

A catheter, a tube, and a drain are three names for one idea, which is a deliberate channel between a cavity inside the body and a container outside it. Fluid always moves from a region of higher pressure toward a region of lower pressure, and the tube gives that movement a defined path. A bladder that cannot empty, a stomach that will not drain, and a chest cavity filled with air are the same physical problem in different places. What makes these devices difficult is not the flow but the fact that the tube is a foreign body crossing skin and mucosa, so each one trades a drainage problem for a risk of infection, injury, and blockage. This chapter describes the hospital-grade devices with their infrastructure and consumables, and then the field variants that a mobile or frontier clinic can keep in stock. Every setting, pressure, and volume named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied to a patient.

The behavior of every tube follows from a few facts about flow. Flow through a narrow channel rises steeply as the channel widens, so a small increase in internal radius produces a large increase in drainage. Flow falls as the tube lengthens, and it falls again when the fluid is thick or full of debris. This is why a catheter can seem adequate at insertion and fail once the fluid becomes purulent. The operator who understands this examines the channel and the fluid, not only the number on the wrapper.

The simplest driving force is gravity, which costs nothing and never fails, and a container placed below the patient creates a column of fluid whose weight pulls the contents out of the cavity. Suction adds force when gravity is not enough, as with a thick wound or a pleural space that must be kept expanded. Suction carries its own hazards, because a vacuum strong enough to move fluid is also strong enough to injure mucosa and pull tissue into the openings of the tube. Air, not force, is what carries most secretions, so an occluded opening defeats a powerful pump. Every suction level must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Materials decide how a tube behaves in tissue and how it can be reprocessed. Latex is soft, cheap, and elastic, but it provokes allergy in some patients and stiffens and cracks with age. Silicone is smoother, more inert, and tolerates heat, which makes it the material of reusable catheters and long-term tubes. Polyvinyl chloride, usually shortened to PVC, is the stiff, clear plastic of most single-use suction catheters and feeding tubes, and it softens at body temperature. Polytetrafluoroethylene, usually shortened to PTFE, appears as a slippery coating and as a chemically inert guidewire surface. The safety hazard is a latex tube in a sensitized patient, where the reaction can be sudden and severe.

Sizing follows two different traditions, and confusing them is a common and dangerous error. The French scale describes the outer circumference in millimeters, so a catheter of 16 French has an external diameter of about 5.3 millimeters, and one French equals one third of a millimeter. Needle and cannula gauges run the opposite way, with a larger number meaning a smaller diameter. Because a French number measures the outside, two catheters of the same size can carry very different flows if their walls differ in thickness. Sizing and the corresponding flow must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a device is chosen.

Three habits keep every tube in this chapter safe, and they apply in a teaching hospital and in a tent alike. The tube is secured so that normal movement cannot pull it out or push it in, its depth is marked and recorded, and it is reviewed every day for the moment it is no longer needed. A tube left in place because nobody remembers why it is there is the most common reason for a hospital-acquired infection. Within hours of insertion a film of protein coats the plastic, and bacteria settle into it and produce a slime that shields them from antibiotics and disinfectants. That biofilm is why a catheter can be sterile at insertion and infected a week later without any break in technique, and why the reliable treatment is removal. The characteristic sign is undramatic, usually fever or cloudy urine, and any new fever in a patient with a tube must be treated as possibly tube-related.

Urinary catheters are the most numerous tubes in any hospital, and their purpose is to keep the bladder empty when the patient cannot do it. The urethra is a soft muscular channel and the bladder is a muscular bag, so the design problem is to hold a soft tube in a moving organ without letting it fall out. The familiar balloon catheter solves this with a small balloon near the tip, inflated inside the bladder after the tip has passed the sphincter, so that the tube cannot be withdrawn. The two-way catheter has one channel for drainage and one for the balloon, while the three-way catheter adds a channel for irrigation when the bladder contains blood clots. The curved-tip catheter, whose bent end lets the operator steer past an enlarged prostate, is passed with a slight rotation, and the intermittent catheter has no balloon at all and is removed as soon as the bladder is empty. Adult sizes run from about 12 French to 18 French, and that size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The retention balloon is inflated with sterile water through a small side channel, and the volume is chosen for the catheter and the situation. A typical adult balloon holds 10 milliliters, while a larger balloon of 30 milliliters is used after some prostate operations to press on the bladder neck. Air must never be used, because air compresses and leaks and the balloon can deflate and let the catheter fall out. The most serious error is inflation before the tip is confirmed to be inside the bladder, which tears the urethra and creates a false passage. Overinflation is the second error, because it can rupture the balloon so that its fragments must be retrieved. The balloon volume and the inflation medium must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Insertion is a sterile procedure, and the sterile field is not a formality. The meatus is cleaned, sterile lubricant is applied to the tip, and the catheter is advanced gently until urine flows and then a little further so the balloon clears the sphincter. The safety hazard is urethral trauma, which begins with bleeding and can end with a stricture that narrows the channel for life. The common operator error is to push against resistance instead of stopping, withdrawing slightly, and asking for help. A catheter that will not pass is a reason to call a more experienced clinician, not a reason to push harder, and the technique and lubricant must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the procedure.

Once the catheter is in place, the drainage system matters as much as the catheter. The bag hangs below the level of the bladder so that gravity and not backflow moves the urine, the tubing avoids dependent loops where stale urine pools, and the junction between catheter and tubing stays closed. Meatal care is gentle washing with water and soap, and vigorous antiseptic scrubbing does more harm than good. Blockage is the quiet failure, and it announces itself through the chart rather than through an alarm, with falling output, suprapubic pain, and a tender bladder. Encrustation is the usual cause, because minerals deposit on the tube and slowly narrow the lumen, and gentle irrigation with sterile saline may restore flow. Irrigation must never be forced, and the drainage position, the emptying schedule, and the irrigation volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Catheter-associated urinary tract infection is the principal hazard of this device, and it is largely preventable. Organisms travel along the outside of the catheter, through the lumen, or across a broken junction, and they find a surface already coated with biofilm. Every extra day of catheterization multiplies the risk, which is why the removal date should be decided at insertion. The signs are fever, cloudy or foul urine, suprapubic pain, and confusion in an older patient. The characteristic alarm is not a sound but a reading, because the monitor may show a rising temperature or a falling blood pressure before anyone looks at the urine. The indication for the catheter and the review interval must be confirmed against the local protocol before the device is left in place.

In a mobile or frontier clinic, the hospital-grade catheter and its closed drainage system are often replaced by clean intermittent catheterization. A clean single-use catheter, or a reusable silicone catheter that is washed, boiled, and stored dry, empties the bladder several times a day and then leaves no foreign body behind. What this gives up is convenience for the staff and the continuous measurement of output, and what it demands is clean water, a way to boil, a private place, and a patient or family member who can be taught the technique well. When the urethra cannot be used at all, a catheter may be placed directly through the lower abdominal wall into the bladder, which bypasses an obstruction but risks bleeding, bowel injury, and leakage around the site. The tract of such a catheter takes time to mature, so it must not be changed early by an inexperienced hand. The reuse interval, the disinfection method, and the first change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Nasogastric tubes are the simplest tubes in the hospital and among the most dangerous when misplaced. A nasogastric tube passes through the nose, down the back of the throat, and into the stomach, where it drains the stomach, decompresses it, or delivers liquid feed by gravity and slow drip. Sizes run from about 8 French for a fine feeding tube to 18 French for a wide drainage tube, and the larger the tube the better it drains and the more it irritates the nose, throat, and stomach. Polyvinyl chloride is stiff enough to pass and cheap enough to discard, while silicone or polyurethane is softer and more suitable for feeding over weeks. A weighted tip contains a small heavy bead, usually of tungsten, that helps the tube sink and stay in the stomach, while an unweighted tube relies on the movement of the stomach to carry it along. A fine-bore feeding tube often carries a stiff guidewire to help it pass, that wire must be removed before the tube is used, a nasojejunal tube is longer and sits beyond the stomach in the small bowel, and these sizes and materials must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Confirming that a nasogastric tube is in the stomach and not in the lung is the single most important check in this chapter. The tube can pass through the throat into the trachea, and feeding through such a tube delivers liquid directly into the airway and kills the patient. Auscultation of a whoosh of air over the stomach is unreliable and must not be used as the only test. The reliable bedside test is to aspirate a small amount of fluid and measure its acidity with an indicator strip, because stomach fluid is acidic and lung fluid is not, while radiography remains the reference method when there is any doubt. The safety hazard is the misplaced tube, the common operator error is trusting the whoosh, and the characteristic alarm is the patient coughing, choking, or desaturating during insertion. The acidity threshold and the confirmation method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before feed is given.

Maintenance keeps a nasogastric tube working and keeps the patient safe. The tube is secured to the nose or cheek with tape or a commercial holder, and the mark that shows its depth is checked at every shift, because a tube that has slipped inward can enter the airway and a tube that has slipped outward pours feed into the throat. The lumen is flushed with water before and after every feed and every medicine, since dried feed and crushed tablets are the usual causes of blockage. Medicines are given one at a time with a flush between, and the tube is never used as a drain and a feed line at the same time. Long-term tubes cause sinusitis, sore throat, and erosion of the nostril, so the tube is moved from one nostril to the other when the protocol allows. The securing method and the flush volumes must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The field variant of enteral feeding gives up the pump and the sterile packaging and demands patience. A fine-bore feeding tube with a guidewire may be unavailable, so a larger nasogastric tube is used and tolerated less well. A gravity drip is made from a bag, a bottle, or a syringe barrel held above the patient, and the rate is set by the height of the column and a simple clamp rather than by a machine. The safety hazard is the uncontrolled fast feed, which can cause aspiration, vomiting, and diarrhea, so the container is never hung more than a set distance above the stomach. What this variant demands instead is a person who watches the patient during the feed, because no alarm will announce the complication. The drip height and the feed volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A rectal tube is a short, soft tube passed through the anus into the rectum to release gas or to deliver an enema. Its physical action is simple decompression, because trapped gas and fluid move down a pressure gradient when a path is offered. The tube is soft and usually has a rounded tip and side holes, and it is passed only a short distance and never forced. The safety hazard is perforation of the rectum or the sigmoid colon, which is a surgical emergency and is more likely in a thin, frail, or inflamed bowel. The common operator error is to insert the tube too far or to leave it in place for hours, which erodes the mucosa. The insertion depth and the dwell time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A chest drain rests on one of the most elegant principles in medicine, because the lungs are elastic and want to collapse while the chest wall springs outward, and the two are held together by a thin film of fluid in the pleural space. When air or blood enters that space the film is broken and the lung pulls away from the wall, so a chest drain restores the coupling by removing the air or fluid and then preventing anything from returning. The water seal is the key, because fluid bubbles out through a column of water while the water rises back and blocks the path inward. Suction is added only when the lung needs help to re-expand, and its level must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied.

Chest drains differ in size, shape, and stiffness, and the choice follows the fluid and the patient. The straight large-bore tube is the traditional drain for blood and thick fluid, and adults often receive 28 French to 36 French. The angled tube has a bent tip that helps it reach around the lung or into a pocket, while the pigtail is a thin curled catheter of 8 French to 14 French placed for air or simple fluid, which is much less painful. Small-bore drains are increasingly used for pneumothorax, while large-bore drains remain necessary for hemothorax and empyema. The size, the shape, and the insertion technique must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the drain is placed.

The drainage system is a set of chambers that each perform one job. The collection chamber receives the fluid and lets the volume be read from the side. The water seal chamber shows the pressure of the pleural space as a small movement of water called tidaling, which rises and falls with breathing, and if tidaling stops the tube is blocked or the lung has re-expanded. The suction control chamber sets the amount of negative pressure that reaches the chest, usually by bubbling air through a column of water, and continuous bubbling in the water seal means air is still leaking. The suction level and the water seal depth must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before suction is applied.

The hazards of a chest drain begin at insertion and never really stop. The trocar, a sharp point on some large tubes, can injure the lung, the liver, the spleen, or the heart, which is why many clinicians now use a blunt technique with a guidewire. Dislodgement is the next hazard, because air can rush back into the chest through the open tract and produce a tension pneumothorax. Clamping a bubbling drain is a common and dangerous operator error, since it traps air that is still leaking and converts a controlled situation into an emergency. The characteristic alarm is the sudden deterioration of the patient, with falling oxygen saturation, rising heart rate, and a shift of the trachea. The insertion technique and the clamping rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Daily chest drain care is mostly observation and documentation. The dressing at the skin is kept clean and occlusive, the tube is secured so that a turn in bed cannot pull it, and the tubing is kept free of loops and never lifted above the chest. Milking or stripping the tube to move clots is traditional but can generate very high negative pressures, so it is done only when the local protocol allows and never routinely. The output is measured and described, including its color and whether it is blood, pus, or serous fluid, because the rate of bleeding guides the decision about surgery. The insertion site, the drain depth, the swinging, the bubbling, and the volume are recorded at every shift, and the dressing type and measurement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The field variant of chest drainage strips the system down to a tube and a one-way valve. The collection chamber, the water seal, and the suction control are replaced by a small flutter valve that lets air and fluid out of the chest and closes against the flow back in. The whole device is light, needs no electricity and no water, and can be taped to the chest wall, which makes it usable during transport and in a tent. What it gives up is the ability to measure suction and to see tidaling, so the clinician loses two important signs. What it demands instead is careful observation of the patient and of the drain, because the valve will not announce a blockage. The valve specification and the drain size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Abdominal drains clear the space left by surgery, infection, or injury, and they work by gravity, by capillary action, or by suction. The flat latex strip drain is a soft ribbon with no lumen that relies on capillary action and gravity, and it is usually placed through a separate stab wound and covered with a dressing. The firm cylindrical drain is a perforated tube with a rounded tip that keeps a track open so fluid can enter along its length. The closed suction drain connects a perforated tube to a compressible bulb reservoir, which is squeezed flat so that it draws fluid out and holds it in the bulb. The pigtail drain is a thin curled catheter locked into a cavity with a suture and drained by gravity or gentle suction. Each design has a different removal rule, because a flat strip can be pulled early while a suction drain must be withdrawn gradually, and the dwell time and removal technique must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Abdominal drain care is a study in watching what comes out. The output is measured and described, and a sudden change from serous fluid to blood, bile, or bowel content is a signal that requires an urgent decision. The common operator error is to advance a drain that has been pulled outward, because pushing it back can carry skin organisms deep into the wound. Another error is to leave a drain in place because the output has stopped, when a stopped drain may mean the cavity is empty or that the holes are blocked against tissue. The safety hazard is erosion, where a rigid drain presses on a blood vessel or the bowel and slowly cuts into it. The output chart, the securing method, and the removal criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The T-tube drains the biliary tree after surgery on the bile ducts. It is shaped like the letter T from which it takes its name, with a short crossbar that sits inside the duct and a long limb that exits through the abdominal wall. The crossbar keeps the tube in place without a balloon and holds the duct open while it heals. Bile flows out through the long limb into a collection bag, and the volume and color of that bile tell the clinician whether the duct is patent. The tube is usually left for days to weeks and then removed, because the track from the duct to the skin must mature before the tube is pulled. The removal time and the clamping trial that precedes it must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A tracheostomy tube is a short curved tube placed through an opening in the front of the neck directly into the trachea. It bypasses the upper airway and is used when the airway is blocked, when long-term ventilation is needed, or when secretions cannot be cleared. The outer cannula is the main tube that sits in the trachea, the inner cannula is a removable liner that can be taken out and cleaned, and the obturator is a smooth guide used only during insertion and then removed. A cuff is a balloon near the tip that seals the trachea so that air from a ventilator does not leak past the tube, and the flange and ties hold the whole assembly at the neck. The cuff target is a pressure of 20 to 25 millimeters of mercury, or about 25 to 30 centimeters of water, measured with a dedicated manometer, and that pressure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The cuff is a seal and not a tourniquet, and its pressure must be kept within a narrow range. The capillaries in the tracheal wall are perfused at a low pressure, and a cuff that presses harder than that pressure stops the blood supply and damages the mucosa. The safety hazard is the overinflated cuff, which leads to tracheal stenosis, fistula, and necrosis, often noticed only after the tube is removed. The common operator error is to inflate the cuff by feel or by the number on the pilot balloon instead of using a gauge. The cuff pressure and the measurement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The characteristic emergencies of a tracheostomy are decannulation, blockage, and bleeding. Decannulation means the tube has come out of the trachea, and if the tract is not yet mature the stoma may close within minutes. Blockage is usually caused by dried secretions in the inner cannula, which is why the inner cannula exists and why it is cleaned on schedule, and bleeding may come from the stoma, from the tracheal mucosa, or from a vessel eroded by the tube. The ventilator announces trouble with a high-pressure alarm when the tube is blocked and a low-pressure alarm when the cuff leaks or the tube is displaced. The operator must check the ties, the cuff pressure, the inner cannula, and the patency of the tube at every shift, and every alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Routine care keeps a tracheostomy safe, and it begins with suctioning. A sterile catheter removes secretions that the patient cannot cough out, and humidification is essential because the nose no longer warms and moistens the air, so a heat and moisture exchanger or a saline instillation is used according to the protocol. The stoma is cleaned and the dressing changed, and the ties are replaced by two people, one holding the tube while the other works, because a tube released at the wrong moment is a lost airway. A spare tube of the same size, a smaller tube, a suction device, and a bag and mask are kept at the bedside at all times. The suction depth and the humidification method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The field variant of the tracheostomy and its care is defined by what can be kept clean and what can be improvised. A reusable metal tube with no cuff is common, because it is durable, easy to boil, and less likely to be damaged, but it cannot seal the airway for positive-pressure ventilation. Humidification may fall back to instilling a few drops of sterile saline and relying on the patient's own cough, and the inner cannula is cleaned by hand with a brush and then boiled or soaked in disinfectant. What this gives up is the precision of a cuff and the convenience of a disposable inner cannula. What it demands instead is a caregiver trained to clean, to suction, and to recognize blockage before the patient becomes exhausted, and the cleaning method and the instillation volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A suction catheter is a thin, flexible tube with a small opening at the tip and a side hole, and it removes secretions from the airway by connecting to a vacuum source. The physical principle is that airflow, not force, carries the mucus, so the catheter needs an opening that lets air move past the tip. The thumb port at the proximal end controls the suction, because while the port is open air enters and the vacuum at the tip is low, and when the thumb covers the port the vacuum acts. The catheter is chosen so that it does not occupy more than about half the internal diameter of the airway or the tracheal tube, because a catheter that fills the lumen blocks the air the patient needs. Suction is applied only while the catheter is withdrawn with a gentle rotation, the pass should last no more than about 10 to 15 seconds, and the patient is allowed to recover between passes. The safety hazard is hypoxia during a long or repeated pass, the common operator error is to apply suction while the catheter is advanced rather than withdrawn, and the characteristic alarm is the falling oxygen saturation on the monitor. The catheter size, the vacuum level, and the pass duration must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The field variant of suction replaces the wall vacuum and the electric pump with a hand or foot pump, a large syringe, or a simple mouth-operated device with a trap. The principle is unchanged, because a partial vacuum is still created by expanding a chamber. A foot-operated pump gives a more sustained vacuum than a syringe and is preferred for thick secretions, while a large syringe attached to the catheter clears a small amount of mucus but demands two hands and cannot be repeated quickly. What this variant gives up is the steady, adjustable vacuum of a hospital wall outlet. What it demands instead is a second trained person and a reliable method of cleaning the device between patients, and the vacuum produced and the cleaning method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The consumables that surround these tubes are as important as the tubes themselves, and a ward that runs out of them stops being able to use its catheters safely. Sterile gloves, sterile lubricant, and antiseptic solution are needed for every insertion, and sterile water or saline is needed to inflate balloons and flush lumens. The correct syringe is needed to inflate a balloon without overpressure, while securing devices, tape, and skin barrier protect the skin and hold the tube. Drainage bags, canisters, and clamps handle what leaves the body, and specimen containers, indicator strips, and labels support the tests and the documentation that make a tube auditable. Stock levels, expiry dates, and storage conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Reprocessing applies to the reusable minority of these devices, and the rules are stricter than for almost any other item. A reusable silicone catheter or metal tracheostomy tube must be cleaned of all visible soil before disinfection or sterilization, because a film of protein protects organisms from both. Sterilization by steam in an autoclave at 121 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes, or at 134 degrees Celsius for a shorter cycle, is the usual method for heat-tolerant items, and those cycle figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.
