Single-use catheters are labeled for one use, and reusing them, even with careful cleaning, carries a real risk of infection and of material failure. The safety hazard is the device that looks clean but hides biofilm in a lumen, and the common operator error is to shorten the contact time when the ward is busy.

Documentation is what turns a set of tubes into a safe system. Every insertion is recorded with the type of device, the size, the date and time, the depth or the marking, the indication, and the name of the operator. Every shift records the output, its color and character, the condition of the site, and any complication, and every removal records the date, the reason, the condition of the tube, and whether a specimen was sent. The safety hazard is a tube whose record has been lost, because the next clinician cannot judge whether it is old, infected, or misplaced. The common operator error is to chart the tube only at insertion and then trust memory, and the record format must be confirmed against the local protocol.

The failure modes of tubes are few and they repeat across every device in this chapter. Occlusion happens when the lumen fills with clot, feed, encrustation, or secretions, and dislodgement happens when the securing fails or the patient pulls the tube. Migration happens when the tube moves inward or outward and no longer sits where it was placed, and infection happens when the foreign surface meets organisms and a biofilm forms. Erosion happens when a rigid tube presses on tissue for long enough to injure it, while kinking and leaking are the mechanical failures, and a kinked tube behaves exactly like a blocked one. Every one of these has a sign that a careful observer can find before the patient is in danger.

At the start of every shift, the operator must walk the tubes in their care and check them one by one. The securing is tested gently by hand, the depth mark is read and compared with the record, and the drainage system is checked for position, kinks, and dependent loops. The site is inspected for redness, swelling, discharge, or bleeding, and the output is read and charted with its character. The balloon or cuff is checked if the protocol requires it, and the emergency equipment for a tracheostomy or a chest drain is confirmed to be present and working. Anything that has changed since the last shift is reported in the handover, and the review interval must be confirmed against the local protocol.

Competence with these devices is not memorizing a size chart but understanding a principle and recognizing a failure. A clinician who knows why a balloon holds and why a water seal works will notice when either stops behaving normally. In a low-resource setting the deeper problem is usually the supply chain rather than the skill, because a ward with no catheters, no lubricant, and no bags cannot deliver safe care no matter how well it is staffed. The practical response is to standardize on a small range of sizes, to keep a documented reserve, and to train one person per shift to manage the stock and the records. The reserve level and the resupply interval must be confirmed against the local protocol and the manufacturer's instructions before a shortage is discovered at the bedside.

To summarize, a catheter, a tube, or a drain is a controlled path for fluid, and its behavior follows from pressure, lumen size, and the properties of the material. The hospital-grade version surrounds the tube with sterile technique, closed drainage, calibrated suction, and a chart that records every change, and it depends on clean water, electricity, and a supply chain. The field version replaces that infrastructure with clean intermittent catheterization, gravity, a flutter valve, a hand pump, and a trained caregiver, and it gives up measurement and margin in exchange for portability. Every one of these devices is a foreign body, so the universal rules are to secure it, to record it, to watch it, and to remove it as soon as the need has passed. The hazards that matter most are infection, dislodgement, blockage, and erosion, and the operator errors that cause them are pushing against resistance, trusting a whoosh, clamping a bubbling drain, and inflating a balloon before the tip is in the bladder. The alarms, where they exist, are the falling oxygen saturation, the high and low ventilator pressure alarms, and the rising temperature, and none of them replaces the nurse who looks at the tube. Every setting, pressure, volume, and cycle figure in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

# Chapter 66 — Collection and Drainage Systems

Every tube in a hospital ends somewhere, and the collection and drainage system is the apparatus that decides where. Its physical job is to move fluid away from the patient along a path that is downhill, one way, and closed, so that the fluid reaches a reservoir instead of the bed, the wound, or the worker. The clinical use follows the physics, since a reservoir below the source drains by gravity, a reservoir above the source can run backward into the patient, and a circuit open to the air invites organisms inward. This chapter describes the hospital-grade systems that collect urine, wound fluid, stool, bile, and respiratory secretions, and then the field variants assembled from bottles, bags, and buckets. Every setting, pressure, volume, temperature, and replacement interval named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

Three physical ideas govern almost every collection system. The first is that a liquid finds its own level, so a reservoir hung below the patient drains by gravity alone and needs no pump. The second is that flow follows the pressure difference between two points, so a suction source simply makes the downstream pressure lower than the atmosphere. The third is that a one-way valve turns a tube into a one-way street, because a flexible membrane closes against reverse flow and opens with forward flow. When these ideas are respected the system is passive and reliable, and when one is violated the reservoir becomes a source of infection or the suction becomes a source of injury.

A closed system is one in which the fluid never meets the air of the room between the patient and the reservoir. Every opening in the circuit is a doorway through which organisms can travel against the intended direction of flow, and an open system has such a doorway at the catheter connection, at the bag mouth, and at the emptying spout. A closed system keeps a continuous path from the patient to a sealed reservoir and is emptied through a port that can be disinfected before and after use. The difference to infection has been measured, and it is the reason that modern urine drainage, wound drainage, and suction collection are all designed as closed circuits.

Hospital urine drainage begins at the indwelling urinary catheter and ends in a collection bag, and every part between them belongs to the same closed circuit. The catheter sits in the bladder, a length of wide-bore tubing carries the urine away, and the bag hangs on the frame of the bed below the level of the bladder. The tubing is wide because urine contains mucus, clots, and sediment, and the bag is transparent so that the color and volume can be seen without opening the circuit. A common adult night bag holds 2,000 milliliters, and that capacity must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the bag is hung.

A well-designed bag carries features the operator must recognize by sight and by touch. The inlet has a drip chamber, which lets the nurse see that urine is flowing rather than pooling, and the non-return valve below it closes when the bag is lifted. The sampling port is a needle-free access point where a specimen may be drawn after the port has been disinfected. The outlet tap at the bottom is the emptying spout that must never touch the floor or the measuring jug, and a vent when present lets air leave the bag as it fills.

The leg bag is a smaller reservoir strapped to the calf or the thigh so that a mobile patient is not tied to the bed. Its capacity is typically 500 milliliters, and that volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the bag is fitted, because a leg bag fills faster than its bearer expects. The physics does not change with the size, so the bag must still hang below the bladder level, and a leg bag strapped high on the thigh can push urine back into the bladder. The common operator error is to leave it in place for days without emptying or inspecting it, so that the straps dig into the skin and warm urine sits against the leg.

The night bag is the larger reservoir used while the patient sleeps, and it is usually connected to the leg bag through a link or joined directly to the catheter for the night. The correct routine is to empty the leg bag first, then disconnect at the catheter with a disinfected connection, then attach the night bag, and then leave the circuit undisturbed until morning. The safety hazard is the night bag hung on the bed rail above the bladder, which turns the bag into a reservoir that can siphon backward. The bag must be positioned below the bladder and above the floor, and that position must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the patient settles for the night.

Urine left in a bag is not sterile, and the reservoir is the warmest and quietest place in the system for organisms to multiply. Bacteria travel upward along the tubing from the bag toward the bladder, and the mucus layer that lines the catheter gives them a surface to climb. The longer a bag stays in place the more biofilm accumulates on its walls, and biofilm resists both antibiotics and disinfectants. The bag is therefore a consumable with a defined life, and the interval at which it is replaced varies with the manufacturer and the local protocol, so that interval must be confirmed before the system is changed. The clinical sign is urine that turns cloudy, foul, or bloodstained, and the characteristic event that follows is fever, so every bag must be treated as a device with an expiry.

The urometer is a graduated chamber inserted between the catheter and the collection bag so that urine output can be measured hour by hour rather than guessed. Its principle is that a narrow column of fluid magnifies the height of a small volume, so a few milliliters spread over a wide bag become a readable number in a tall chamber. A typical urometer holds 200 to 500 milliliters, and that capacity, together with the reading interval, must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the first measurement is taken. The device has no electrical alarm, so its alarm is the number that falls outside the expected range and stays there.

Hourly urine output is one of the earliest signals that a patient is losing circulation volume, developing kidney injury, or recovering from either. A fall in output that persists is the characteristic alarm of this device, and a sudden rise may signal the return of kidney function. The common operator error is to read the bag instead of the chamber, which averages away the very change the urometer was fitted to detect. The second error is to leave the tubing looped below the bladder, so that urine pools in the loop and the hourly reading lags behind the patient. The third error is to open the chamber valve without recording the volume, which erases the measurement permanently, so the tubing, the chamber, and the connection must be checked before every reading.

An ostomy pouch solves a problem that no valve can solve, because a stoma has no sphincter and the bowel empties on its own schedule. The physical principle is adhesion rather than control, since a sealed pouch is stuck to the skin around the stoma and the seal, not a muscle, prevents the output from reaching the clothing and the wound. That seal must hold against moisture, movement, and the digestive enzymes of the effluent, which is a demanding combination for any adhesive. When the seal fails the effluent contacts the skin, and the resulting excoriation is painful, slow to heal, and difficult to attach a new pouch to.

Ostomy pouches come in two fundamental arrangements, and the difference is where the adhesive lives. A one-piece pouch carries the adhesive wafer on the back of the bag, so the whole pouch is removed and replaced at every change. A two-piece system has a flange, also called a baseplate, that adheres to the skin, and a separate pouch that clicks or sticks onto it, so the pouch may be changed while the baseplate stays in place for several days. A typical wear interval is 1 to 3 days for a one-piece pouch and up to 7 days for a baseplate, and those intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol for the individual patient. The common operator error is to cut the aperture by eye, which leaves a crescent of exposed skin that the effluent will find within hours.

Stoma care uses a small pharmacy of barrier products whose physics is the creation of a dry, protected surface. A barrier ring or a strip of barrier paste fills the crease between the stoma and the surrounding skin, so that the adhesive meets a level surface rather than a valley. A barrier powder absorbs moisture on skin that is already weeping, and it is dusted on and sealed with a barrier film before the pouch is applied. The safety hazard is skin denuded by repeated removal of adhesive, and the common operator error is to apply a new pouch over wet skin, so the choice of product and the wear interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Emptying a pouch is a small operation with a large effect on the patient's comfort. The pouch is emptied when it is about one third full, because a heavy bag pulls on the adhesive and a full bag can lift the seal away from the skin. The character of the output carries clinical information, because a colostomy produces formed stool, an ileostomy produces a loose and enzyme-rich effluent that is corrosive to skin, and a urostomy produces urine. The safety hazard for the worker is the splash of ileostomy effluent into the eye, and the common operator error is to flush a pouch into a hand basin rather than a toilet, so the emptying routine and the disposal route must be confirmed against the local protocol.

Wound drainage uses the same physics as urine drainage, but the fluid is blood, serum, and lymph, and the collection vessel is often a canister under suction. A closed wound drain is a perforated tube placed in the wound bed and brought out through a separate incision, and it is attached either to a compressible bulb reservoir or to a flat drain joined to a spring-loaded cylindrical evacuator. The bulb or the spring holds a small negative pressure, which pulls fluid from the wound into the reservoir and keeps the wound edges together. A typical bulb reservoir holds 100 to 150 milliliters, and that volume must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the drain is activated.

Measuring wound drainage means recording the volume, the color, the consistency, and the odor, because each of these carries a different message. The volume is read from the graduations on the reservoir when the drain is emptied, and the empty volume is subtracted to obtain the output. A rising output of bright blood is the characteristic alarm of a wound drain, and it demands immediate attention because it may signal a bleeding vessel. The common operator error is to compress the bulb and then reconnect it without restoring the vacuum, so that the drain lies in the wound doing nothing, and the acceptable output volume and the action limits must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The suction canister is the reservoir that stands between the patient and the vacuum source, and its design protects both the patient and the machine. It is a rigid jar of 1,000 to 3,000 milliliters, usually with a lid that carries an inlet for the patient tubing, an outlet to the regulator, and a float or shut-off valve that rises when the canister is full. A hydrophobic filter or a float closes the outlet before liquid can be drawn into the vacuum line, because fluid reaching the pump damages the machine and aerosolizes infectious material. A disposable liner fits inside the canister so that only the liner and its tubing are discarded, while the rigid outer jar is cleaned and reused. The fill line is usually marked at three quarters of the height, and that limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the canister is put into service.

Measuring what a suction canister holds is more difficult than it looks, and the difficulty is a recognized source of error. The canister often stands on the floor or hangs below the eye of the nurse, and the graduations are read at an angle that distorts the level. The safety hazard is the overflow valve that fails, so the canister overfills and the fluid reaches the regulator and the pump. The characteristic warning is a change in the sound of the suction or the whistle of a float valve as it closes, and an electronic regulator may add a low-vacuum alarm, so the measurement method, the fill limit, and the alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A specimen trap is a small container inserted into the suction line so that a sample of secretion is captured before it is diluted in the canister. The trap has three ports, one from the patient, one to the suction source, and one that is sealed and used to send the specimen to the laboratory. The common operator error is to insert the trap upside down or to let it lie on its side, so that the specimen is drawn straight through and the trap arrives at the laboratory empty. The second error is to fill the trap so completely that the secretion is aspirated into the tubing and contaminates the whole circuit, so the trap must be labeled at the bedside and the labeling rule confirmed against the local protocol.

Stool and bile collection each have their own container and their own timing, and both are less trivial than they appear. A formed stool specimen is placed in a clean, wide-mouthed container with a tight lid, and a small quantity is sufficient for most tests, while a liquid stool may need to be transported within a short interval because the organisms and parasites in it change as it cools. Bile is collected after biliary surgery or when a T-shaped tube is placed in the common bile duct, and it follows the same gravity and closed-circuit rules as urine, with the bag hanging below the patient and the daily volume and color recorded. The safety hazard is the container that leaks in transit, and the common operator error is to collect stool from a bedpan after it has mixed with urine, so the label, the storage temperature, and the transport interval must be confirmed against the local protocol.

Emptying a collection bag or canister is the task that puts the worker in closest contact with the fluid, so the technique matters as much as the device. The person empties the reservoir into a designated toilet or sluice, wearing gloves and a plastic apron, and eye protection when a splash is possible. The spout is kept below the rim of the receiving vessel and never allowed to touch it, and the spout is wiped with a disinfectant after emptying and before it is closed. The hands are washed after the gloves are removed, and the gloves are removed without touching their outer surface. The safety hazard is the splash of urine or wound fluid into the eye or onto broken skin, and the common operator error is to carry an uncovered jug of fluid through a corridor, so the receiving vessel, the disinfectant, and the disposal route must be confirmed against the local protocol.

Some collection hardware is disposable and some is reusable, and the two demand completely different handling. A disposable bag, liner, or trap is used once and discarded into the infectious waste stream, and it must never be rinsed and returned to the shelf. A reusable rigid canister, rack, or trolley is cleaned of visible soil, then disinfected with a chemical agent such as a hypochlorite solution at a measured concentration and contact time, then dried and stored inverted. If a reusable item is to be sterilized it is processed by steam, and a common cycle is 134 degrees Celsius for a short hold, and that temperature, that hold time, and the chosen method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol. The safety hazard is the canister that is wiped but not cleaned inside, because dried protein shelters organisms, and the common operator error is to top up a disinfectant bath rather than replace it.

A collection system consumes a steady stream of small items, and their absence stops the system as surely as a broken pump. The list includes drainage bags of several sizes, leg bags with straps, catheter securement devices, non-return valves, tap caps, canister liners, hydrophobic filters, specimen traps, ostomy pouches, barrier rings, barrier powder, adhesive remover, wound drain reservoirs, and the labels that identify every one of them. These items must be stored clean and dry, away from direct sunlight, and rotated so that the oldest stock is used first. The expiry date matters most for the sterile items and for the adhesives, because a barrier that has passed its date may not stick and a sterile bag stored damp may no longer be sterile. The safety hazard is the ward that improvises a missing part with a non-sterile substitute, and the common operator error is to store bags beside a heat source, so the par levels, the storage conditions, and the expiry rules must be confirmed against the local protocol.

The failure modes of a collection system are mostly quiet, and the quiet ones are the dangerous ones. A bag can leak at a seam, a tubing connection can separate, a non-return valve can stick open, a tap can be left open, a canister float can jam, a filter can become wet and block the suction, and a catheter can be pulled out by a confused patient. The characteristic alarm of the electrically driven part is the low-vacuum alarm of the regulator, which sounds when the circuit is blocked or disconnected and the pump cannot reach its set pressure. The mechanical canister warns of fullness with the whistle or the click of a float valve, and the gravity bag has no alarm at all, so its warning is the wet sheet or the swollen leg. The safety hazard common to all of them is fluid that reaches the vacuum pump or the electrical socket, and the common operator error is to silence an alarm without finding its cause, so the alarm limits and the response to each alarm must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

The operator who starts a shift with a collection system should be able to answer a short list of questions about it. Is the reservoir below the source and above the floor, is the tubing free of loops and kinks, is the connection secure, is the non-return valve working, is the tap closed and capped, and is the volume inside the bag recorded? For a suction system the questions add the level of the canister against its fill line, the condition of the liner, the seal of the lid, the setting of the regulator, and the patency of the filter. For an ostomy they add the condition of the skin, the fit of the aperture, and the age of the baseplate. The answers are best written down, because a system checked by memory alone is a system checked only on the days when nothing is wrong, so the check and the corrective action must be confirmed against the local protocol.

The field variant of these systems keeps the physics and discards the plumbing. Where a hospital has wall vacuum, sterile bags, and a sluice, a mobile or frontier clinic has a bottle, a length of tubing, a bucket, and a hand pump. What the field gives up is convenience, measurable accuracy, and the assurance of a sterile circuit, and what it demands instead is discipline, improvisation, and a clear understanding of what the substitute cannot do. Every substituted component must be checked for the property it is meant to provide, because a bottle that leaks does not drain and a bag that is not closed does not protect.

Field urine collection usually means a bottle or a plastic bag hung on the bed frame at the foot of the mattress. A clean bottle with a hole in the cap and a short length of tubing can serve as a closed reservoir, and it must hang below the bladder and be emptied at a fixed interval, and that interval must be confirmed against the local protocol. A mobile patient has no leg bag and no catheter strap, so the reservoir is carried in a cloth bag or held in the hand, and the tubing is secured to the thigh with tape. The safety hazard is the container hung above the patient, which allows urine to run back into the bladder, and the common operator error is to rest the container on the floor beside the bed where it is kicked over.

Field suction relies on a hand pump, a foot pump, or a battery-powered pump rather than a wall vacuum line, and the reservoir is usually a bottle in series with the pump. The principle is unchanged, because the pump lowers the pressure in the bottle and the secretion travels from the patient into the bottle, while a float or a simple trap prevents the liquid from reaching the pump. The vacuum is generated by strokes of the pump, so the suction is intermittent and the operator must watch the secretion rather than trust a gauge. The safety hazard is fluid drawn into a manual pump, which cannot be cleaned internally and becomes a reservoir of organisms, and the pressure setting and the maximum suction must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

An ostomy patient in the field often manages with a plastic bag and adhesive tape, and the substitution demands more of the patient rather than less. A clean plastic bag is cut to fit the stoma, the skin is washed and dried thoroughly, and the bag is fixed with a wide tape that overlaps the skin by a comfortable margin. The bag is changed as soon as it leaks, because effluent left against the skin causes excoriation within hours, and the interval between changes must be confirmed against the local protocol. The safety hazard is the reuse of a bag that has been rinsed but not disinfected, and the common operator error is to cut the aperture too large, so the worker must teach the patient to inspect the skin at every change.

Field wound drainage is often an open drain and a gauze dressing rather than a closed suction canister, and the measurement becomes an estimate. A strip of latex or silicone is placed in the wound and covered with an absorbent dressing, and the dressing is changed when it is saturated, so the output is judged by the number of dressings rather than by a volume. The safety hazard is the drain that is pulled out when the dressing is changed, and the common operator error is to pack the wound so tightly that the drain cannot function. The character of the fluid still matters, so the worker records the color and the smell, and the drain type and the dressing change interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Sample collection and disposal complete the field system, and both are steps where improvisation carries the greatest risk. A suction specimen can be caught in a small sterile bottle placed in the line, and the bottle must stand upright and be sealed immediately after the sample is taken. Stool is collected in a wide-mouthed jar with a lid and kept out of the sun, while bile from a T-shaped tube is collected in a bottle hung below the patient and changed with the same care as a urine bag. Disposal means pouring urine and wound fluid into a latrine or a soak pit and never into a stream, a well, or a garden, while bags, liners, and traps are buried or burned as infectious waste. The safety hazard is the child or the scavenger who finds a discarded bag or a needle, and the common operator error is to label a container at the end of the round, so the burial depth and the separation distance from water must be confirmed against the local protocol.

In the hospital, disposal is designed to keep the fluid and the container on separate paths, and maintenance keeps both paths working. The fluid is emptied into a sluice or a dedicated hopper that discharges to the sanitary sewer, while the container is placed in the infectious waste stream, and a canister liner is closed with its own lid and discarded as infectious waste. Trolleys and racks are cleaned on a schedule, regulators and pumps are tested for the vacuum they can hold, and reusable parts are inspected for cracks, worn washers, and loose lids. The safety hazard is the reusable canister stored wet, because a wet filter blocks the suction and a wet jar grows organisms, so the sluice design, the vacuum test value, and the filter replacement schedule must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

To summarize, a collection and drainage system is the far end of every tube, and it decides whether the fluid leaving a patient is contained or released into the ward. Gravity, a pressure difference, and a one-way valve are the physical ideas that make these systems work, and a closed circuit is the design choice that keeps organisms from traveling back toward the patient. The hospital version provides graduated bags, urometers, sealed canisters with liners and overflow valves, specimen traps, ostomy pouches with engineered barriers, and a waste route that separates fluid from container. The field version provides a bottle, a bag, a hand pump, and a bucket, and it gives up accuracy and sterility in exchange for availability, while demanding more discipline from the person who empties it. In both settings the safety hazard is the splash and the reflux, the common operator error is the broken circuit and the unrecorded volume, and the characteristic alarm is often the absence of one, so every setting, volume, pressure, and replacement interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is used on a patient.

# Chapter 67 — Disposable Textiles and Linens

Cloth is equipment, and it is the equipment that a hospital touches more often than any other. A sheet lies under every patient, a gown covers every body, a towel dries every hand, and a drape defines the sterile field in every operation. The physical principle that governs all of them is simple. A woven textile is a lattice of threads, and between the threads there are gaps, so the fabric behaves as a selective barrier whose performance depends on the size of the gaps, on the surface chemistry of the fiber, and on the pressure applied from one side. When the gaps are small and the fibers repel water the cloth keeps liquid out, and when the gaps are wide or the liquid is pushed hard the cloth lets it through. Every clinical property of linen, from absorbency to barrier protection to warmth, follows from that geometry.

Three physical ideas carry the whole subject, and an operator who holds them can predict how a textile will behave. The first is capillary action, the tendency of a narrow space to draw liquid along itself against gravity, which is why a cotton towel wicks water away from skin and why the same property pulls contaminated fluid through a gown that has been wetted. The second is strike-through, the passage of liquid through a fabric under pressure, which is why a drape that repels a splash may still leak when a wet instrument rests on it. The third is the difference between a liquid barrier and a particle barrier, because a tightly woven cloth may stop droplets while still letting airborne organisms settle through. These ideas explain why two textiles that look identical from a meter away can perform completely differently against infection.

Textiles reach the patient in two forms, and the title of this chapter names only one of them. Disposable textiles are made from non-woven fiber, used once, and discarded, and they dominate the operating theatre, the isolation room, and the emergency department because they arrive sterile and leave as waste. Reusable textiles are woven from cotton or from a cotton and polyester blend, washed and reprocessed many times, and they remain the backbone of beds, wards, and clinics because they are cheaper over a thousand uses and gentler on the skin. The same chapter must therefore describe both, since a ward typically runs on reusable linen while its theatre runs on disposables, and the choice between them is decided by barrier performance, cost, laundry capacity, and the reliability of supply. The consumable side of the subject, the soap, the chemical, the bag, and the thread, matters as much as the cloth, because a laundry without consumables is a room full of dirty fabric.

Bed linen is a system rather than a single object, and each layer has a task. The mattress cover is the barrier that keeps body fluids out of the mattress foam, where they would be impossible to remove and would feed organisms for years. The fitted sheet is the working surface, smooth so that it does not crease under a pressure area and closely fitted so that it does not ruck and wrinkle. The draw sheet is a narrow sheet placed across the middle of the bed under the patient, and it exists so that two or three staff can slide a patient rather than lift, which protects both the patient's skin and the worker's back. The pillowcase covers the pillow, the underpad absorbs small amounts of urine or wound fluid, and the top sheet and blanket regulate warmth. A missing mattress cover or a torn fitted sheet is therefore not a cosmetic fault, because it defeats the barrier and the friction control of the whole bed.

The material of bed linen is chosen for two properties that pull in opposite directions. Cotton absorbs water readily, feels cool and soft against skin, and tolerates repeated hot washing, but it wrinkles, it shrinks, and it dries slowly. Polyester cotton blends resist wrinkling, dry quickly, and hold their shape, but they absorb less and they can feel hot and clammy against a feverish patient. The hospital therefore keeps a mixed inventory, and the operator learns to match the cloth to the patient rather than to the shelf, giving the absorbent cotton to the patient who sweats and the quick-drying blend to the ward whose dryer is overloaded. The common operator error in this small decision is to use a plastic-backed underpad directly against the skin, which traps moisture and macerates the skin within a few hours.

Patient gowns are textiles with a designed failure point, because they must open for examination and close for dignity. The standard gown ties at the back of the neck and at the waist, which allows a clinician to expose the chest, the abdomen, or the back with one movement, and the pediatric gown does the same in a smaller size with a brighter print. A gown that has lost its ties is no longer a gown, because the patient holds it closed with one hand and the examination becomes a struggle for both people. The common operator error is to keep a torn gown in circulation because it still covers the patient, and the result is a garment that falls open during transport in a corridor. The safety hazard that follows is a fall, because a patient who is holding a gown cannot use both hands for the walker or the rail, so the ties must be checked at every change.

Towels and blankets are the warm, bulky part of the inventory, and their bulk is exactly why they carry organisms from one patient to the next. A bath towel is used wet, left damp, and shared by habit in some wards, and a warm damp cloth held against skin is an efficient way to transfer organisms. The blanket is worse, because a heavy blanket is washed less often than a sheet, sits in contact with skin for hours, and is often shaken over the bed, which releases a cloud of fibers and organisms into the air of the room. The physical remedy is the same in every hospital, which is that towels must be single use per patient and blankets must be covered by a sheet or replaced by a washable cover. The thermal blanket used in the operating theatre or the warming cabinet adds another rule, because the warming cabinet temperature and the blanket's heat setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operating theatre uses textiles that are engineered rather than merely washed, because the drape defines the boundary between sterile and non-sterile space. A surgical drape must resist the striking through of blood, irrigation fluid, and saline under the weight of instruments, it must not shed lint into an open wound, and it must not burn when a cautery device touches it. Reusable theatre drapes are woven tightly from a polyester and cotton blend, often with a reinforcement layer at the working area, and they are inspected for holes after every wash because a pinhole becomes a channel for fluid. Disposable drapes are built from non-woven fiber and are supplied sterile in a pack, and their barrier performance is graded against a formal scale so that a drape for a short procedure is not used for a long one. The specific grade, the weight, and the fluid resistance required for each procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the pack is opened.

The structure of a non-woven textile explains its performance. Instead of interlaced threads, the fabric is a mat of fibers bonded by heat, by pressure, or by a chemical binder, and the fibers may be continuous filaments or short staple strands. A common three-layer construction places a layer of strong spunbonded filaments on each side of a layer of fine meltblown fibers, and the fine middle layer is the barrier while the outer layers carry the strength and the softness. A woven reusable drape achieves its barrier with a high thread count and a calendered surface, which flattens the threads and closes the gaps between them. The trade is written into the physics, since the tighter and denser the structure the better the barrier and the poorer the breathability, so a gown that protects completely also traps heat and moisture next to the surgeon.

The laundry flow is the part of the subject that decides whether clean linen is genuinely clean, and its governing rule is that dirty linen and clean linen must never share a path. The building is divided into a soiled side, where linen arrives, is weighed, sorted, and loaded into machines, and a clean side, where it is unloaded, dried, ironed, folded, and stored. The boundary between the two sides is a physical barrier, usually a wall with a pass-through washer or a doorway that only one direction of travel crosses, and the workers change garments or wash hands when they cross it. The one-way route exists because a clean sheet carried back through the soiled room is contaminated by the air and the surfaces around it, and no amount of folding will undo that. The common operator error is to walk a clean trolley into the soiled area to save a trip, and that single trip defeats the entire design of the plant.

The route in detail begins at the bedside, where the used linen is placed into a bag without being shaken or sorted. The bag is closed, carried on a dedicated soiled trolley that never carries clean goods, and delivered to the soiled linen room. There the load is weighed, because weight is the currency of a laundry contract and the trigger for the wash formula, and it is sorted only if the local protocol permits sorting before disinfection. The linen then enters the washer, passes through the wash stages, and emerges on the clean side, where it is transferred to a dryer, then to an ironer or a folding table, and finally into a clean linen store. A clean trolley with a closed or covered top then carries it to the ward, and the ward stores it in a cupboard that is used for nothing else. Every setting, weight, and cycle time along that route must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the plant is run.

Segregation begins where the linen is removed, and the categories are usually marked by the color of the bag. General ward linen, linen from an infectious patient, linen contaminated with blood or body fluid, and theatre linen are the common groups, and each demands a different handling and sometimes a different wash formula. The color code itself is local, so a green bag means one thing in one hospital and something else in the next, and the operator must therefore learn the code of the building rather than of the profession. Shaking soiled linen is the cardinal error, because it releases a cloud of fibers, dust, and organisms into the face of the person doing it, and that cloud settles on the floor, the trolley, and the clean doorway. The linen must be lifted with gloved hands, folded inward on itself if it is heavily soiled, and dropped into the bag without being compressed or fanned.

Thermal disinfection is the killing of organisms by heat, and its principle is that proteins and membranes lose their shape when they are held above a certain temperature for long enough. The relationship between temperature and time is a trade, so a higher temperature needs a short hold and a lower temperature needs a long one. A common thermal disinfection cycle holds the load at 71 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes, and a gentler cycle holds it at 65 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes, and both of those figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a cycle is selected. The temperature is measured at the coldest point that the machine can reliably control, and the hold time begins only when that point reaches the set value, which is why a display that shows the set point is not evidence that the load was disinfected. The characteristic alarm of this equipment is a cycle abort, because the controller did not see the set point reached or held, and the load must then be treated as soiled and reprocessed.

Chemical disinfection is used for fabrics that cannot take heat, and its principle is that an oxidizing or surface-active chemical damages the organism's proteins, its membrane, or its genetic material on contact. The common agents are chlorine-releasing compounds, peracetic acid, and quaternary ammonium compounds, and each has a spectrum of activity that is narrower than heat and a sensitivity to soiling that heat does not have. A chlorine-releasing solution is typically made up to a concentration measured in parts per million of available chlorine, and it must remain in contact with the fabric for a defined number of minutes, and both the concentration and the contact time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The critical point is that a heavy soil load consumes the chemical before it reaches the organism, so chemical disinfection is a second step after cleaning and never a substitute for it. Chlorine also attacks cotton and damages the fibers, so repeated chemical disinfection shortens the life of the linen and leaves it thin and grey.

A modern wash process is a sequence rather than a single immersion, and each stage has a task. The prewash removes the bulk of the soil in warm water and is often drained before the main wash begins, because soil carried into the main wash neutralizes the detergent and the bleach. The main wash carries the detergent and sometimes a bleach at the temperature and the time that the formula demands, and the intermediate rinses remove the chemical before the fabric is exposed to the next one. The final rinse removes every trace of detergent and disinfectant, and a souring agent may be added to bring the fabric back to a skin-friendly acidity, followed by a softener that makes the cloth pleasant to handle. The operator must understand that the rinse is not a formality, because a sheet that smells of chlorine or of soap irritates the skin of the next patient.

Detergent dosing is the daily judgment of the laundry, and it is measured rather than guessed. The main wash normally uses an alkaline detergent, often with enzymes that digest protein and fat, and the formula may add an oxygen or chlorine bleach for stain removal and a souring agent for the final rinse. An automatic dosing pump draws the chemical from a container and injects the set volume into the machine, and the pump is calibrated at intervals, because a worn pump delivers less chemical than the display claims. Under-dosing leaves soil and organisms on the fabric, and over-dosing leaves a residue that irritates skin, damages fibers, and wastes money, so the dose must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol for the machine and the water supply. The common operator error is to top up the dosage by eye when the linen still looks grey, which hides the real problem, which is usually hard water, an overloaded machine, or a failed pump.

Water hardness is the invisible variable that decides how much detergent a laundry really needs. Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium, and those ions react with soap and with detergent to form an insoluble scum that deposits on the fabric and inside the machine. Hardness is quoted as a concentration in milligrams per liter of calcium carbonate or in parts per million, and the value for a given supply must be confirmed against the local water test and the manufacturer's instructions before the wash formula is fixed. Soft water allows a smaller dose of detergent and a cleaner rinse, so a laundry that has switched to a softened supply and kept the old formula will over-dose and leave residue. The physical signs of hard water are grey, stiff, and scratchy linen, a white scale on the heating elements, and a machine that needs more energy to reach its temperature.

Drying is the removal of the water that the rinse left behind, and its physics is that warm air carries moisture away while the fabric gives it up. A tumble dryer forces heated air through a rotating load, and the temperature and the cycle length are chosen for the fiber, because cotton tolerates more heat than polyester and an overheated synthetic load can shrink, glaze, or even melt. Over-drying damages every fiber and consumes energy, so the machine is judged on whether the load leaves dry rather than bone dry, and the temperature setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a load is started. Ironing adds heat, moisture, and pressure together, and a flatwork ironer passes a sheet between a heated cylinder and a padded roller so that a large item is pressed in one movement. The hazard of the ironer is the same as the hazard of any hot surface, which is a burn to the hand or the forearm, and the safety guard and the emergency stop must be tested at the start of every shift.

Transport is where clean linen is most easily lost, so the equipment that moves it is designed around the separation of clean and dirty. A soiled trolley is a closed or lidded container that holds bagged linen and is washed or disinfected at the end of the route, and a clean trolley is a separate cart with shelves and a cover that carries folded linen from the store to the ward. The two are never the same cart, and the clean cart never enters the soiled room, because a cart that has been in the soiled room carries organisms on its wheels and its frame. A ward linen cupboard must be dry, dust-free, and used only for linen, because a cupboard that also holds cleaning chemicals or a dripping mop bucket will spoil the stock above it. Radio-frequency identification, or RFID, tags sewn into reusable linen allow a laundry to count and trace its stock, and the technology turns the invisible loss of linen into a number that can be managed.

Linen from an infectious patient demands special handling from the moment it leaves the bed. The linen must be bagged in the room, at the point of use, without being sorted or shaken, and the bag must then be closed and labeled before it leaves. If the outside of the bag is contaminated, a second bag is placed over the first, and the outer bag is removed on the clean side of the boundary so that the contaminated surface never travels further. The worker wears personal protective equipment, or PPE, including gloves and an apron, and performs hand hygiene after the bag is closed, because the organisms on linen are carried on the hands rather than in the air. The most serious hazard in this whole chapter is the sharp that a patient or a clinician has left in the linen, because a needle hidden in a sheet can pierce a hand during bagging, and every bag must be handled as though a sharp were inside it. A puncture-resistant container for sharps must stand beside the bed, and the operator must never compress a bag of linen with the hand or the knee.

The characteristic alarms of this equipment are the alarms of the machines that wash it, and the operator must learn them by sound and by sight. A washer-disinfector announces a failed disinfection cycle with a buzzer and a flashing fault indicator, and the cause may be a door that unlocked early, a heating element that did not reach its set point, a dosing pump that delivered no chemical, or a drain that did not empty. The door interlock alarm is a safety alarm, because it prevents the door from opening while the drum turns or while the water is hot, and defeating that interlock is a serious hazard to the operator. The alarm threshold and the response to every one of these faults must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the plant is run, and the rule for a failed cycle is always the same, which is to reprocess the load as soiled rather than to reason about how clean it might be. A laundry that silences its alarms to keep the flow moving is a laundry that is disinfecting nothing.

The stock level that a ward needs is a calculation rather than a feeling, and it is built from consumption. A ward measures its linen use per patient per day, usually in kilograms, and multiplies that figure by the number of beds and the number of days that the laundry cycle takes, adding a safety margin for the ward's peak demand. The result is the par level, the quantity that must be on the shelf at the start of a shift, and a stock that falls below it is the quiet alarm of this chapter, because the shortage is noticed only when a bed is being made. The par level must be recalculated when the ward's case mix changes, when the laundry's turnaround time lengthens, and when a new procedure adds to the demand, and the figures used must be confirmed against the local protocol and the manufacturer's instructions for the textile before the order is placed. A ward that holds too much linen is as badly managed as a ward that holds too little, because an overfilled cupboard buries the oldest stock and encourages it to be damaged and lost.

Theft and loss consume a linen inventory faster than wear, and the loss is usually invisible until a count is taken. Sheets leave a hospital as cleaning rags, as dust covers, as paint cloths, as car covers, and as fabric for uniforms, and a proportion of every inventory simply disappears into the community around the gate. Some of the loss is innocent, since linen that is heavily contaminated is discarded with the waste and linen that is used to clean a spill is thrown away, and some of it is not, and the management response must distinguish the two without insulting the staff. Physical controls include a locked store, a signed issue book, an annual or quarterly count against the register, and the RFID tag that makes the loss of a single item visible. The operator's part is to report a shortage early and to resist the habit of stashing a private reserve of clean linen in a cupboard, because a hidden reserve distorts the par level and creates the shortage that the next shift suffers.

Failure modes in textiles are mostly slow and visible, which is a gift to the operator who looks. Lint and pilling appear first, because the surface fibers break and ball up, and a pilled sheet is abrasive against skin and sheds particles into the air. Holes and thin patches follow, and a hole in a theatre drape is a barrier failure, a hole in a sheet is a route for fluid to reach the mattress, and a hole in a gown is an exposure for the wearer. Lost ties, broken buttons, and torn hems are mechanical failures, and chemical damage from repeated over-bleaching shows as a fabric that has lost its body and tears along a line rather than at a point. Damp storage produces mildew, which leaves a musty smell and dark spots that washing may not remove, and a load stored wet in a warm room can grow organisms on the cloth itself. The most dangerous failure is the retained object, because a sharp or an instrument that reaches the laundry in a sheet can injure a worker, and a lost instrument reaches the patient as a missing count.

The operator's checks before linen reaches a patient are short, physical, and decisive. The item is held up to the light, which reveals a thin patch or a pinhole that the eye misses at arm's length. The ties, the seams, and the hems are pulled gently, because a stitch that has rotted will part under a light tug rather than during the night. The cloth is felt for dampness and smelled for chlorine, mildew, or detergent, since a residue is a chemical exposure for the next patient. The barrier side of a drape is inspected for a breach, and the load is inspected for a sharp before it is handled with bare hands. Every item that fails a check is removed from circulation and routed to repair or to waste, and the item that is quietly returned to the shelf is the item that fails at the worst moment.

The field variant begins where the laundry plant ends, and it changes the equipment rather than the principle. A mobile or frontier clinic has no boiler, no tunnel washer, no dryer, and often no piped hot water, so the wash happens in buckets and basins, by hand, with whatever soap is available, and the drying happens on a line in the sun. The physics is unchanged, because organisms are still removed by mechanical action, by detergent, by heat, and by drying, but every one of those parameters is now uncontrolled and depends on the judgment of the person doing the work. What the field variant gives up is certainty, since it cannot prove a temperature, a contact time, or a concentration, and what it demands instead is discipline, because a hand wash done carelessly produces linen that looks clean and carries organisms.

Hand washing is organized so that the water itself does not become the contaminant. The practical arrangement is three containers: the first holds warm soapy water for the wash, the second holds clean water for the first rinse, and the third holds clean water with a disinfectant or the hottest water available for the final rinse. The items are worked from the least soiled to the most soiled, so that the wash water is not loaded with blood before the sheets arrive, and each item is agitated, rubbed, and scrubbed against itself or against a board rather than merely dipped. The soap does the chemistry, because its molecules lift oil and soil from the fiber and hold them in suspension so that the rinse can carry them away, but the mechanical work does most of the physical removal. The common operator error is to keep adding soap to water that has already turned grey, which raises the load of suspended soil and redeposits it on everything in the basin.

Water quantity and water quality are the two limiting resources, and both must be managed deliberately. A single basin used for a whole ward's linen becomes a suspension of organisms after the first few items, and each later item is dipped in that suspension rather than cleaned. The rule is to change the wash water when it becomes visibly soiled, to keep the final rinse water clear, and to dry the items in a way that does not return them to the ground. Where water is scarce, the clinic may prioritize the items that touch a wound or a newborn and use a smaller volume with a longer scrub, and that choice must be confirmed against the local protocol for the clinic before it is adopted. The last rinse should be clean enough to drink if the item is to be used on broken skin, which is a standard that most field laundries cannot meet and must therefore acknowledge.

Disinfection in the field is improvised from heat or from chemicals, and each route has a cost. Boiling an item in water for 10 minutes kills most organisms, and the time and the temperature must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the method is relied upon, because a pot that is not fully boiling is not boiling at all. A pressure cooker used as a small autoclave is a genuine sterilizer for drapes and gowns when it reaches its working pressure for the required time, and that pressure and time must likewise be confirmed before use, and the operator must remember that a folded, tightly packed load may not be penetrated by steam. A chlorine-releasing solution is the common chemical route, and its concentration and contact time must be confirmed before use, and the solution must be made fresh because chlorine loses its strength in light and in warm storage. The honest limit of chemical disinfection in the field is that a visibly soiled cloth consumes the chemical and comes out looking bleached rather than made safe.

Drying in the sun is the field method that is most often trusted and least often understood. Sunlight contains ultraviolet radiation, which damages the genetic material of organisms, and the sun also supplies heat and desiccation, which together reduce the load on the surface of a cloth. The effect, however, is confined to the surfaces that the light reaches, so an item hung in a thick fold, dried in the shade of a wall, or left through a humid overcast week loses the benefit while it still looks dry. The cloth must be spread open, turned after a time, and hung where air moves on both sides, and the line must be high enough that animals and dust cannot reach it. Ironing with a hot iron, where an iron and power exist, adds direct heat and pressure to the same surface and is a valuable second step. The operator must therefore treat sun drying as a real but partial intervention, useful exactly in proportion to how much of the cloth the sun actually touched.

What soap and sun do to an organism must be stated honestly, because the field worker will make decisions on the answer. Soap does not sterilize a cloth, and it does not reliably kill the organisms it removes, so its contribution is the removal of soil and the physical carriage of organisms into the rinse water. Sunlight does not sterilize a cloth either, and it acts only where the light strikes, so it cannot be relied upon for a folded bundle or for a cloudy day. The combination of washing, rinsing, thorough drying, and heat reduces the number of organisms greatly and is adequate for bed linen, towels, and gowns on a general ward. It is not adequate for a drape that will lie in an open wound or for a pack that will enter a body cavity, and the clinic that needs those items must obtain them sterile from a central service or produce them in a pressure cooker cycle with a validated load. The truthful field statement is therefore that hand laundering makes linen clean and safe for ordinary contact, and that sterile textiles remain a separate supply problem.

Field storage and transport are governed by the same separation as the hospital, even though the containers are simpler. Clean linen is kept in a closed cupboard or a cloth bag hung from a beam, away from the floor, the wall, and the cooking fire, and soiled linen is kept in a separate bag that is emptied and washed rather than reused damp. Where plastic sheeting replaces a mattress cover, it is wiped and dried between patients and inspected for tears, and where an underpad is unavailable it may be improvised from several layers of cloth placed over a plastic sheet, with the cloth layer changed as soon as it is wet. Disposable theatre textiles are the field supply that cannot be improvised, so their stock is counted and reserved for the procedures that genuinely need a barrier. The field checks before use are the same as the hospital checks, which are to hold the item to the light, to feel for dampness, to pull at the seams, to look for a hole, and to look for a sharp.

To summarize, textiles are equipment made of thread, and their behavior follows from the gaps between the fibers, which decide whether a liquid passes, wicks, or stops. The hospital runs a laundry that separates soiled from clean along a one-way route, disinfects by heat at a held temperature or by a chemical at a measured concentration, doses detergent against the hardness of its water, rinses away every residue, and dries and stores the result in a place that stays dry. The ward keeps a par level for each textile, counts what it uses, and accepts that theft, wear, and contamination will consume the stock whether or not anyone admits it. The field clinic replaces the plant with buckets, soap, a scrubbing motion, a line in the sun, and where possible a boiling pot or a pressure cooker, and it gains mobility and loses certainty. In both settings the operator is the last barrier, and the checks that matter are the same ones, which are to look for the hole, feel for the damp, smell the residue, and never trust a cloth that has not been checked against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

# Chapter 68 — Labels, Wristbands, and Documentation Supplies

Hospital care is held together by marks on surfaces, and a wristband, a specimen label, a medication label, and a log sheet are the same device in different clothes. Each is a durable mark that carries a fact from where it was established to where a decision is made, and the principle is adhesion plus legibility, because a mark works only if it stays attached to the right object and remains readable until that object is used. When the mark fails the failure is silent, and the harm appears later as a wrong drug, a wrong blood unit, or a wrong patient. Ink is a pigment or a dye in a solvent that sinks into the paper or sits on the surface as a layer that can be rubbed away, while the substrate and the adhesive decide whether the mark holds on skin, glass, plastic, or cold metal. Every material, temperature, humidity level, and storage interval named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is relied upon.

The hospital-grade identification band solves one problem with one physical trick, because it cannot be removed and refitted without being destroyed. It is closed with a single-use snap, a one-way rivet, or an adhesive overlap whose backing tears, so moving it to another person leaves visible evidence, while a reusable strap with a buckle can be moved in silence. Adults usually wear a soft strap of vinyl or a flexible polymer printed to resist water, alcohol hand rub, soap, and body oils, while newborn and pediatric bands are narrower, softer, and often made of a spun-bonded synthetic paper that will not cut a delicate limb. Placement is part of the function, because a band that cannot be seen will not be checked, so the band goes on a visible limb and may be duplicated on another site. The fit must allow one finger beneath the strap and must not slide over the hand, and that fit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the band is fastened.

An adult band carries at least the patient's full name and a unique record number, and many hospitals add the date of birth, the sex, and the admitting service. The unique number matters more than the name, because names repeat and names are misspelled under pressure, while a generated number is never reused. Printing must be large enough to read at arm's length in dim light, and characters must not be abbreviated, since an abbreviation creates a second name that only some staff will recognize. The band is checked before every medication, every transfusion, every specimen, and every procedure, and the check is made against a second source rather than against the band alone. A band that is read and agreed with itself proves nothing.

Children grow, they pull, and they are often uncooperative at the moment of application, so pediatric bands are smaller and are placed on an ankle as often as a wrist. The safety hazard is a band tight enough to press on a small vessel, so the limb is inspected at every shift for swelling, color, and marks. A newborn has no trustworthy name in the first hours, so two bands are placed on the baby and a matching band is placed on the mother, all carrying the same number. A band applied later is a weaker record because the interval is unaccounted for, and the characteristic alarm is a number on the baby that does not match the number on the mother. The placement method and the matching routine must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the first band is closed.

Alert bands carry a warning rather than an identity, and they are a convenience with a serious trap. A red band commonly means allergy, a yellow band a fall risk, and a purple band a resuscitation preference, but the meanings are not universal and change between hospitals and countries. The physical hazard is that color is read faster than text and is therefore trusted more, yet color vision deficiency affects a substantial minority of men and dim ward lighting alters every hue. A color must therefore never be the only carrier of the warning, and the condition must also be written on the band or in the record. The local color scheme and its meanings must be confirmed against the local protocol before any alert band is applied.

Band failure is usually a slow process rather than a dramatic event. Direct thermal printing fades with heat, sunlight, friction, and alcohol, so a band that was legible in the morning can be pale by the evening, while the plastic strap stretches with edema and repeated pulling until it slides over the hand. A band that is too tight leaves an indentation that can progress to skin breakdown, and a band cut by hand leaves a sharp corner that scratches the patient and the worker. The characteristic alarm is a mismatch between the band and the record, and the common operator error is to write a new band from the old band instead of from the record, which copies an error forward. Every band must be inspected at the start of a shift and replaced when it is illegible, damaged, loose, or has been removed.

A barcode is a pattern of dark bars and light spaces that a machine converts into characters. The scanner illuminates the pattern with a light-emitting diode or a laser, a photodetector measures the light that returns, and the dark bars absorb while the light spaces reflect, so the returning signal rises and falls in a rhythm that the decoder reads. The pattern works only if the contrast is high, the bars are sharp, the quiet zones at each end are clear, and the whole symbol lies inside the scanner's field, and a checksum makes a misread fail loudly rather than pass in silence. At the bedside the scan is a second reader of identity, because scanning a medication and then a band forces two independent records to agree before a drug is given, and a specimen tube is scanned against the band while the needle is still in the arm. Where scanning is used, the local policy must define when it is required and what to do when it fails, and that policy must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A scanner is a small optical instrument and it needs the care of any other lens. The window collects dust, adhesive residue, and the sticky film left by a label peeled from a gloved hand, and a scratched or cloudy window produces the failed reads that staff blame on the labels. The housing is wiped with a soft cloth and an approved cleaner and is never soaked, while the cable, the connector, and the battery contacts of a cordless unit are checked for wear and charge at the start of a shift. The characteristic alarm is the single low beep or the amber light of a failed read, and the common operator error is to keep scanning the same label instead of inspecting it. The cleaning agent and the maintenance interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Radio-frequency identification replaces the visible pattern with an invisible conversation. A tag holds a small chip and an antenna, a reader emits a radio field, the field induces a tiny current in the antenna, the chip wakes, and it answers by modulating the field it reflects, so a sealed tag needs no battery and no window to scratch. The read range depends on the reader's power, the antenna design, the orientation of the tag, and the material around it, because metal reflects the field and water absorbs it. Common bands are the low frequency near 125 kilohertz, the high frequency near 13.56 megahertz, and the ultra high frequency between roughly 860 and 960 megahertz. Any frequency named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the system is installed.

In a hospital the technology is used to count rather than to read, so it tracks pumps, trolleys, instruments, and linen as they pass a doorway. Its worst property is that it fails quietly, since there is no beep when a tag is not seen, only an absence in a list, and an absence is easy to mistake for a correct count. A tag can be detached, left on a shelf, or moved to another object, and the system will still report it as present, while two tags in the field at once can collide so that neither is reported. The common operator error is to treat a successful read as proof that the physical object is correct, rather than as proof that a tag was in range. The correct discipline is to reconcile the electronic list against a visual count at defined intervals, and that interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A label printer is a device that applies heat to a controlled pattern. In thermal transfer printing, a printhead of many tiny heating elements presses against a ribbon, the heated spots melt a wax or resin coating, and the coating transfers to the label stock beneath, so a wax ribbon smears while a resin ribbon resists abrasion and solvents. Direct thermal printing skips the ribbon and darkens a chemically treated paper with heat alone, which is convenient, but the image fades with light and heat and disappears entirely on a hot dashboard. The stock has a face material, an adhesive, and a liner, and the adhesive may be permanent, removable, or a medical grade made for skin and for cold surfaces, so the wrong choice either falls off a specimen tube or tears the skin of a newborn. The print resolution, the ribbon type, and the adhesive must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a printer is put into service.

Printer maintenance follows the path of the heat. The printhead is cleaned with an approved swab and a recommended solvent, because its hard coating is removed by an abrasive cloth, and the platen roller beneath it collects adhesive and paper dust until a flat spot produces a light band across every label. The ribbon path is checked for wrinkles, since a wrinkled ribbon leaves pale streaks and wastes stock. The characteristic failure is a label printed at the wrong position or split across two labels, and the common operator error is to adjust the tension without recalibrating the printer. Stock control is a clinical activity here, because a hospital that runs out of band stock or specimen labels improvises, so the par level is set from measured use plus a reserve the night shift can reach. The cleaning agent, the calibration routine, the storage temperature, and the shelf life must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A specimen label is the identity card of a biological object, and it must carry enough to survive every hand that touches it. The minimum set is the patient's full name, the unique record number, the date and time of collection, the type of specimen and the site it came from, the tests requested, and the identity of the collector. The label is attached to the container rather than to the lid alone, because the lid is the part most often swapped between tubes. The adhesive sticks when it can wet the surface it meets, which is easy on dry glass and hard on a cold, wet, or dusty tube, so the surface is dried, the label is pressed firmly from the center outward, and the adhesive is never touched with a gloved finger. The data set required by the receiving laboratory must be confirmed against the local protocol before a specimen is dispatched.

A mislabeled specimen is a special kind of harm, because the error is invisible when it is made and irreversible when it is discovered. Two tubes drawn at the same bedside and labeled away from the patient can be exchanged, and the exchange appears only when a result contradicts the patient in front of the clinician. The physical barrier is printing at the bedside, because a label produced at the moment of collection cannot be moved to another patient without the act being noticed, and where bedside printing is unavailable the rule is to label one tube at a time, in the room, with the patient's band in view. The common operator error is to pre-label a batch of tubes before the round begins, which separates the label from the person for the whole round. The characteristic alarm is a laboratory result that does not fit the patient.

A medication label must carry everything another person would need to give the dose safely if the preparer were suddenly unavailable. That list includes the drug name, the strength and the total dose, the diluent and the final volume, the route, the date and time of preparation, the expiry after preparation, the storage requirement, the patient's identifiers, and the initials of the preparer, with warnings for high-alert drugs and for drugs that look or sound like another. The most dangerous label in a hospital is the missing one, because a syringe without a label and a basin of clear fluid without a label both ask a future person to guess. The common operator error is to believe the drug is obvious because the preparer remembers it, which is true for the preparer and useless to everyone else. The correct habit is to label the container before drawing up the drug, and the exact list, the expiry after preparation, and the label size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

A log sheet is a device that converts a measurement into evidence, and a refrigerator log is the clearest example. It records the temperature of a cold space at a stated time with the initials of the reader, and a complete entry carries the date, the time, the temperature with its unit written out, and a note of the action taken when the value was outside the accepted range. A vaccine or a blood product can be damaged by a single excursion above or below its range, and the damage may not be visible in the vial. A hospital may use a continuous recorder or a data logger with its own display and audible alarm, and the thermometer must be checked against a reference at defined intervals because an uncalibrated instrument records a comfortable fiction. The characteristic alarm is an out-of-range temperature, an audible beep, or a gap in the record, and any of the three requires a documented response. The failure modes of a paper log are human, and the classic is retrospective filling, in which a week of readings is written at one sitting with one pen and one posture, while a missing sheet breaks the series and leaves the fate of the contents unknown. The accepted range, the reading interval, the alarm threshold, and the calibration interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol.

Consent and chart forms record a decision and a clinical course, and a consent form is not the consent itself, because consent is a conversation and the form is the evidence that the conversation occurred. The common form is a pre-printed sheet with a carbonless copy, in which pressure from a pen ruptures microscopic capsules of dye and transfers the writing to the sheet below, while a modern version is printed from the record and carries a barcode so that the signed page is matched without retyping. The hazards live in the details left blank, because a form signed by the wrong patient, a form dated later, and a form signed by a relative without documented authority can all invalidate the record. The patient must have capacity and must receive the information in a language and at a level they understand, so an interpreter is required when the clinician and the patient do not share a language. Paper records are also a physical problem that outlives the stay, because paper is hygroscopic, mold grows on it in a warm and humid room, and light fades the ink while rodents eat the paper and the glue on the spine, so access is controlled, retention is decided by law, and destruction must be documented when the period ends.

Digital documentation moves the record into a network, where it is faster to find and easier to lose. The electronic health record holds orders, results, medication administration, and notes, and it is backed by servers, a network, and a power supply protected by an uninterruptible power supply and a generator. The characteristic failure is the screen that will not load, and its alarm is often a silence, because no printer sounds and no label appears until a task cannot be completed. The correct response is a rehearsed downtime routine with paper forms in a known place, a defined way of numbering the paper record, and one person responsible for reconciling paper against the digital record afterward. The common operator error during an outage is to postpone documentation on the assumption that the information will be remembered, and the downtime procedure, the printed forms it requires, and the reconciliation interval must be confirmed against the local protocol before the system is used on patients.

The field variant begins where the network, the printer, and the reliable mains supply end. A mobile or frontier clinic has no server to fall back on, no barcode scanner, and often no electricity at the moment a record must be made, so the system is reduced to paper, ink, and a discipline that substitutes for the machine. What it gives up is speed, searchability, and the automatic cross-check that a scan provides.
