The temperature band, the conditioning time, the pack arrangement, and the maximum transit time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The driver in this system is not a courier but a member of the clinical team, and the argument of this chapter depends on that claim. The driver knows the roads, the river crossings, and the villages, so the driver is the only person who can give a realistic arrival time, and that time is a clinical fact because it decides whether a specimen is still valid. The driver carries the requisition, the stock card, and the return load, which may be a specimen, a broken device for repair, an empty cylinder, or a patient, and the handover of that load matters as much as the handover of a drug. The characteristic alarm in this half of the chapter is a telephone call that does not connect, because the vehicle has left network coverage and the clinic waiting for a cold box cannot know whether it is 1 hour or 1 day away. The commonest operator error is treating the trip as a transport task rather than a clinical one, so the cold box rides in the open bed under the sun and the delay is never reported. The route plan, the communication schedule, the custody record, and the cold chain log must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

At the frontier clinic the receiving dock is a doorway, the store is a cupboard, and the ledger is a stock card written by hand. The principles still hold, and the small scale sharpens each of them: the count must be done at the handover, the package must be inspected for tears, damp, and expiry, and the temperature indicator on a cold item must be read before the box is accepted. Storage space is the binding constraint, so the clinic cannot hold a large buffer and must hold a small quantity chosen for the diseases it actually treats, which makes the par level an act of clinical judgment. A solar powered refrigerator keeps the cold chain without fuel, but it depends on a battery, a controller, and a panel that must be kept clean, and its failure is silent until the temperature is checked. The storage temperature, the refrigerator alarm setting, the stock review interval, and the lock and key procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic failure of field logistics is a cold chain that breaks without anyone noticing, and its anatomy is worth following. The vehicle breaks down, or the road floods, or the fuel runs out, and the box sits for 6 extra hours in air that is 38 degrees Celsius or hotter. The packs melt, the internal temperature climbs, and the load arrives looking exactly as it did when it left, which is why the indicator or the recorder is not optional equipment. The decision that follows is the hardest part of the chapter, because the vaccine, the insulin, or the blood product may still be usable or may be a danger, and the decision must come from the recorded temperature, the product instruction, and the local protocol rather than from hope. The commonest operator error is opening the box repeatedly along the route to check on it, since every opening shortens the life of the load, and the second is adding warm packs at the last stop. The temperature trace, the excursion rule, the discard procedure, and the reporting route must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant gives up the machine and demands the human body, and the substitutes are older than the hospital. A 2 wheeled hand cart, a wheelbarrow, a bicycle with a trailer, a motorcycle with a box, a boat, a pack animal, and a person carrying a shoulder bag are all legitimate transport where no vehicle can pass, and each imposes its own limit on weight and fragility. A long lead time changes the par level completely, because a clinic resupplied every 12 weeks must hold enough for 12 weeks plus the delay, and it must also decide in advance which items it will share with a neighboring clinic when one of them runs short. The safety hazards are the ones that run through this chapter, which are the sharps in the wrong bag, the cold box in the sun, and the cart pushed past its load limit. The load limit, the packaging rule, the sharing agreement, and the review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The return direction of field logistics carries specimens, and a specimen is a load with a clock attached. A sample of blood, sputum, or water leaves the clinic in a container that must not leak and must not become a hazard to the person carrying it, so it travels inside a primary container, a secondary container with absorbent material, and a rigid outer box. The requisition with it must identify the patient, the test, and the time of collection, because a specimen that loses its identity must be repeated, and the characteristic failure is a box that arrives with a broken tube and a soaked label. The field system also needs its own maintenance, and the toolkit is small and specific: a spare wheel, a jack, a pump, wire, fuses, hand tools, tape, and a printed manual in the local language, because a repair that depends on a telephone call waits for coverage. The packaging specification, the temperature range, the maximum transit time, and the spare parts list must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator's part in logistics is smaller than in most chapters of this book, but it is not zero, and it can be stated as a short round. At the start of a shift the responsible person checks the par level on the shelf against the stock card, checks the expiry dates of the items nearest the front, checks that the emergency cart is sealed and that its seal number matches the record, and checks that the sharps container is below its fill line. During the shift every issue is written on the card at the moment it is made, because a movement remembered later is a movement lost. The person reports the fault before it becomes a failure, which in logistics means reporting the empty shelf, the damaged cart, the leaking tube carrier, and the warm cold box while there is still time to correct them. The par level, the expiry check, the seal number, the fill line, and the temperature band must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, logistics is the movement of things, and it is a clinical system rather than a housekeeping one. The hospital holds a central store because arrivals and consumption follow different rhythms, and it distributes stock by requisition or by topping each department up to a par level that must be calculated rather than guessed. Pneumatic tubes move a sealed carrier on air pressure, automated vehicles follow a path on the floor, elevators separate clean from dirty traffic, and carts carry stores on wheels, while clean and dirty routes never cross. Receiving and inspection are the gate, the stock card is the memory, and maintenance keeps the unglamorous machinery of movement alive. In the field the whole apparatus collapses into a truck, a cold box, and a driver who belongs to the clinical team, and what the field variant gives up in machinery it demands back in fuel, spare parts, honest paper records, and judgment about a broken road. Every chapter of this book depends on this one, because a device with no consumable, no spare, and no delivery is a device that does not exist, and the patient who pays for that failure is never the person who ordered the stock.

# Chapter 75 — Maintenance and Troubleshooting

Maintenance is the management of wear, and troubleshooting is the disciplined reading of its symptoms. Every physical device changes as it is used, because bearings lose their lubricant, seals harden, solder joints crack from thermal cycling, filters load with dust, batteries lose capacity, and sensors drift as their materials age. These changes do not announce themselves, and they accumulate quietly until a device crosses from working to not working, often during the busiest hour of the ward. Maintenance intervenes before that crossing, and troubleshooting finds the cause rather than the symptom after it has happened. This chapter describes its subject twice, first the hospital-grade program of schedules, work orders, calibration, and a biomedical engineering department, then the same discipline rebuilt in a frontier clinic from a toolkit, a manual, and a telephone.

Wear is a physical process with identifiable mechanisms, each with its own signature. Abrasion removes material where two surfaces slide, which is why cables fail where they bend and pump tubing wears thin where rollers squeeze it. Fatigue cracks metal that flexes repeatedly, so a bracket breaks after many small movements. Corrosion eats contacts and connectors where moisture, salt, or cleaning fluid collects, and its result is an intermittent fault that appears and disappears. Thermal cycling opens solder joints as a device warms and cools, while battery chemistry ages with every charge and every hour spent hot.

The pattern of failure over the life of a device is usually drawn as a curve with 3 regions. Early failure comes from manufacturing defects and shipping damage, the middle region is a long plateau of low failure, and the final region is wear-out, when failures rise steeply and each repair buys less time than the last. Preventive maintenance keeps a device on the plateau by replacing parts with a known life before they reach wear-out. A hardened seal changed during planned downtime costs a predictable part and a few hours of labor, while the same seal failing during a dialysis session costs a contaminated machine and a disrupted treatment. The schedule exists rather than the repair because prevention is cheaper, safer, and more controllable, and every interval and replacement life named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A preventive maintenance visit is a defined set of actions rather than a vague inspection. It begins with the history, because the technician reads the log before touching the machine, and then inspects housing, cables, connectors, seals, filters, and labels. Moving parts are cleaned and lubricated, fasteners are checked for torque, worn items with a known life are replaced, and the interior is cleared of dust that traps heat. The device is then powered and tested for its measurement, its output, and every alarm and safety interlock. The work is recorded with the parts used, the measurements taken, and the next service date, because the characteristic failure of a program is not the missed repair but the maintenance performed without testing the alarms.

The schedule is generated from the recommendations of the manufacturer, the intensity of use, the environment, and the clinical criticality of the device. A ventilator running continuously in a humid intensive care unit ages far faster than the same model used intermittently in a recovery room, and a device in a dusty or coastal clinic ages faster than one in a climate-controlled store. Criticality is the other axis, because a device whose failure would immediately endanger a patient is served on the shortest interval the maker allows, and the schedule is written into the equipment register so that the next service date travels with the machine. A schedule that is never reviewed becomes fiction, so it should be audited against real failure data at least once a year, a period that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The work order is the unit of maintenance work and the record that it happened. It identifies the device, the reporter, the symptom in the reporter's own words, the priority, the technician, the parts used, and the measurements obtained, and priority is assigned by clinical risk. The log becomes valuable only when it is read as a series of events, because a device repaired repeatedly for the same complaint is not unlucky but failing, and the pattern itself is the diagnosis. The history reveals causes a single visit cannot see, such as a pump that fails whenever a particular nurse sets it up.

The user-level check is the most repeated maintenance action in the hospital and the one with the largest effect. Before a device touches a patient, the operator confirms that it is the correct device, and that it has not been tagged out of service. The physical state is inspected for cracks, exposed conductors, crushed tubing, moisture, and cleaning residue, and power, battery charge, the self-test result, and the presence, fit, and expiry of consumables are confirmed. Settings are checked against the patient in front of the operator rather than the previous patient, and alarm limits are set deliberately and provoked once so that the operator knows the alarm can sound. Any failure means the device is removed, tagged, and reported, and every check interval, battery threshold, and alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

When a device misbehaves, a fixed sequence prevents the random swapping of parts that wastes time and hides the true cause. The sequence is power, connection, consumable, setting, calibration, alarm, and each step is cheaper and more likely than the next. Power comes first, so the operator confirms that the outlet is live, the plug is seated, the cable is undamaged, and the device has charge. In a hospital this includes checking whether the socket is fed from the normal supply or the emergency circuit, and whether an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is in bypass or has a discharged battery. A blown fuse, a tripped breaker, or a cord strained against a bed frame accounts for many apparent failures, so the tester used for this check must itself be verified.

Connection comes second and means every junction between device and patient or supply. The operator checks that tubing is seated and uncrimped, that connectors are locked, that gas fittings sit on sound washers, and that nothing is compressed by a bed rail or a door. A loose connector can look like an internal failure, because the machine reads an open circuit or a low pressure and reports it as a sensor or supply problem. The consumable comes third and is the most frequent single cause of apparent failure, whether it is an empty reagent pack, an expired test strip, a blocked filter, a worn sensor, or a canister whose float has sealed. The operator checks identity, expiry, fit, and remaining capacity before concluding that the device has failed, and all consumable specifications, expiry dates, and replacement intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Setting comes fourth, and it is where the assumptions of the operator are most often the fault. A healthy device can still produce a wrong result because it is in the wrong mode, set for the wrong patient size, using the wrong units, or carrying limits left from the previous patient. A ventilator in the wrong mode or a monitor using an adult algorithm on a newborn behaves within specification while delivering the wrong therapy. The operator therefore compares every displayed setting against the written order and the patient rather than against memory, and checks the units with particular care. When two people use a device, the setting should be read back aloud, and all modes, limits, units, and patient-size selections must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Calibration and verification are different acts, and confusing them is a serious error. Calibration establishes the relationship between what a device displays and the true value it measures, by comparing it with a traceable reference and recording the difference, after which adjustment changes the device so that the two agree. Verification is the simpler check that the device still reads within its stated tolerance, using a reference whose accuracy is known and adequate, so a device can pass verification and still be uncalibrated in the formal sense. Drift is the slow change in the link between a physical quantity and the electrical signal that represents it, and it is why calibration is repeated, because a strain gauge loses its bond and an optical source dims. The devices that most need calibration are those whose numbers become decisions, such as defibrillators, infusion pumps, ventilators, gas analyzers, and laboratory analyzers, and every tolerance and calibration interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Verification and calibration require instruments that are themselves trustworthy, and this is where a hospital program meets its limits. Test equipment must be calibrated against a reference that is traceable, step by step, to a national or international standard, and each step must be documented with a date and an uncertainty. Where no traceable reference exists, a clinic can cross-check one device against another, keep a dedicated reference instrument, and write the limitation down, because a cross-check between two equally drifted devices proves only that they agree. An uncalibrated device used knowingly is a named risk while the same device used unknowingly is a trap, and all reference accuracies and recalibration intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Spare parts determine whether maintenance is a plan or a hope, and their lead times decide the real downtime of every device. A critical spare is a part whose absence stops the device and for which no substitute exists, such as a proprietary sensor, a circuit board, a door gasket, or a pump head, and a consumable ordered today may arrive in 3 months, after the season in which it was needed has passed. The store therefore holds a minimum stock of critical spares set by lead time and failure rate. Consumables deserve the same discipline because they are the true constraint on care, since a hospital can own 20 ventilators and treat only 6 patients if it holds circuits and filters for 6. The dangerous design is the device that accepts only one proprietary consumable from one supplier, and a cannibalized part must be recorded with its donor and condition, so all stock levels and shelf lives must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Repair against replacement is an economic and clinical decision. The questions are whether the repair restores the specified performance, whether parts arrive in useful time, whether the cost is a sensible fraction of an equivalent replacement, and whether the maker or the regulator has withdrawn the device for safety. The cost of an old machine includes not only parts but downtime, power, obsolete consumables, and staff time, so a device that is cheap to buy can be expensive to keep. A device becomes unsafe to keep when its failure could harm a patient and cannot be reliably repaired, such as cracked insulation, an alarm that no longer sounds, a radiation output beyond tolerance, or a swelling battery. Such a device must be removed at once and stored where it cannot quietly return to the ward, and every tolerance, energy limit, and test date must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Planned downtime is the arrangement that keeps care running while a device is out of service, and it must be made before the device fails. The tools are redundancy, substitution, scheduling, and a written clinical fallback: a second device of the same type, a manual method the staff have practiced, a loan from another department, or a temporary referral of the patient. The schedule should place maintenance in the quietest hours the ward has, and the clinical team must know in advance what to do when the machine is unavailable, because improvisation during a crisis is not a plan. No maintenance may begin on a device that has no fallback unless a clinician has agreed the risk, and all downtime limits, backup capacities, and substitution rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The handover between shifts is where a fault that is not yet a failure is either caught or lost. A device that makes a new noise, runs warmer, takes longer to charge, or reads differently from yesterday is not yet broken, and the person who noticed it holds the most valuable information in the building. The handover must carry device status as deliberately as patient status, naming what is in use, what is out for repair, what is borrowed, and what is merely suspect. The report should name the device, the exact symptom, when it started, and what makes it worse, because a note that the pump is acting strange cannot be acted upon. Reporting early is a clinical skill built on knowing what normal looks like, and the common operator error is to assume that someone else has already reported it, which is how a warning becomes an incident.

The biomedical engineering department is the memory and skill of the institution for maintenance, and it is a partner rather than a repair shop. It receives new equipment, performs acceptance testing, keeps the register, schedules preventive maintenance, calibrates what it can and contracts what it cannot, repairs what is repairable, investigates incidents, trains users, manages spare parts, and recommends decommissioning. It works best when it is included at the moment of purchase and told about near misses. Its most valuable product is the trend, which is the model that fails repeatedly, the cleaning method that damages a surface, and the training gap that keeps producing the same user error. A hospital rarely performs all of its own maintenance, so the boundary between in-house work and vendor work must be drawn deliberately, and every service contract, response time, and warranty condition must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Electrical safety testing is a distinct branch of maintenance because it protects the patient from a hazard with no smell and no sound. The physical principle is leakage current, the small current that escapes from a device through insulation, capacitance, and protective components to earth or to the patient. A device with intact insulation and a sound earth leaks an amount too small to matter, but a cracked housing, a pinched cable, or a broken earth can route current through a patient who is connected to the machine. The test measures the resistance of the protective earth and the leakage current under normal and single-fault conditions and compares them with the limits the standards specify, and the general standard for medical electrical equipment is maintained by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). Every limit and test interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and a device that fails is removed from service immediately.

The room is part of the machine, and much of what looks like device failure begins in the environment around it. Heat shortens the life of every electronic component and battery, so cooling fans, filters, and air paths must be kept clear and the room kept within the temperature range the maker specifies. Dust blocks filters, raises the internal temperature, and can conduct electricity across a circuit board, while humidity corrodes contacts and static discharge damages sensitive electronics. Clean water is part of the specification for sterilizers, analyzers, humidifiers, and dialysis machines, because dissolved minerals scale internal surfaces and alter each process. Cleaning is itself maintenance, and its principle is that soil, salt, and protein must be removed before any disinfectant can work, because organic material shields the organisms beneath it and consumes the chemical meant to kill them.

Several hazards cross every device in this chapter and must be named where maintenance meets them. Electrical shock from a faulty lead or a broken earth is the oldest hazard. Fire is the second, and it hides in dust, in blocked cooling, in a lithium battery that has swollen, and in a device left running under a pile of linen. A swelling battery is an imminent fire and must be removed from the building rather than stored on a shelf, and it must never be punctured, crushed, or charged again. Radiation sources, lasers, and high-energy devices bring hazards that no untrained person may approach, and every safety limit and test criterion must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Alarms are the account a device gives of its own condition, and their classification tells the operator how fast to move. A high-priority alarm signals an immediate threat to the patient and demands an immediate response; a medium-priority alarm signals a condition that needs prompt attention, while a low-priority alarm can wait. A technical alarm, sometimes called a device alarm, is the machine reporting its own fault rather than the patient, such as a sensor failure, a calibration due notice, an occlusion, or a low battery. Alarm fatigue is a maintenance problem as much as a human one, because badly set limits produce so many alarms that the staff stop hearing them, so every threshold setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The common operator error is silencing an alarm and continuing, which converts a warning into an unnoticed event, and a device whose alarm cannot be provoked must be removed from service, because an untested alarm is a safety system of unknown state.

In a mobile or frontier clinic the entire hospital maintenance structure disappears, and the same clinical needs must be met from a toolkit, a manual, and a telephone. The field variant gives up the biomedical engineering department, the maintenance management system, the calibration laboratory, and the spare parts store, and in exchange it demands that the clinician become the technician, the record keeper, and the supply chain. The physical principles do not change, because wear, drift, corrosion, and battery aging happen just as fast in a hot, dusty room and often faster. What changes is who notices and who acts, which is why the field program is built from simple tools, short written routines, and a strict distinction between what may be repaired locally and what must be sent away.

The field toolkit is deliberately small, and its contents are chosen by the faults that actually occur. A typical kit holds screwdrivers, hex keys, pliers, a small wrench set, a multimeter, a soldering iron, spare fuses, cable ties, a knife, a headlamp, and self-amalgamating tape, in a case that can be carried on a motorcycle. It also holds the small consumables that decide whether a device runs, including fuses of the correct rating, O-rings and washers, tubing, batteries, and the filters the manual names. The multimeter is the most important instrument in it, because it turns a guess about power into a measurement, and the person who uses it must know how to check a supply, a fuse, and a cable. The kit must be inspected after every use and restocked before the next trip, and fuse ratings, battery types, and part numbers must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The service manual is the second half of the field toolkit, and it must be obtained at the time of purchase rather than sought after the first failure. The operator manual explains the daily checks, the alarms, and the cleaning that is allowed, while the service manual gives the fault codes, test points, adjustment procedures, and parts lists that turn troubleshooting into a method. Where the manual is missing, the fault codes and the wiring diagram should be copied, photographed, and kept with the device, because the original will not survive a clinic without electricity or files. The clinic should also keep a bound logbook that records every check, fault, repair, and part replaced, and any specification or fault code must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied to a patient.

The technician reached by telephone is the substitute of the field clinic for the engineering department, and the relationship must be built before it is needed. A named regional technician, a service line of the maker, or an experienced colleague at a district hospital can often diagnose a fault from a description and a photograph, and the value of that call depends on the quality of the report. The caller should have the device name and number, the fault code, the exact symptom, what was checked, and what the display shows, and should be standing at the machine with the manual open. The clinic should also agree in advance who may authorize a repair and who pays for a part, and every adjustment advised by telephone must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field preventive maintenance routine is performed by the clinical team on a fixed cycle, built from the tasks the manual allows. Each day the operator checks power and battery, cleans what may be cleaned, inspects cables, tubing, and connectors, and confirms that the alarms can sound. Each week the filters are cleaned, the moving parts inspected, and the battery cycled and charged. Each month the device is opened only as far as the manual permits, dust is cleared from vents and boards, fasteners are tightened, and battery capacity is estimated from the run time it actually delivers. The routine demands discipline because no engineer will arrive to enforce it, and honesty because a skipped filter is invisible until a device overheats or a patient is harmed, and every cleaning method, filter interval, and battery cycle must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Improvisation is sometimes the only repair available, and it is legitimate when it stays inside the manual and restores a specified function. It becomes a hazard when a fuse is replaced with wire, an alarm is disconnected, or a part is substituted without knowing its rating, because a device that appears to work is not the same as a device that works. What the field variant demands instead of infrastructure is training, judgment, and a tiered repair system that keeps decisions at the lowest competent level. The first tier is the user, who cleans, checks, changes consumables, and reports; the second is a trained clinic technician, who replaces modular parts and performs the tests in the manual; the third is the district workshop, which handles board-level repair and calibration; and the fourth is the maker or its agent, which handles warranty and sealed systems. Each tier needs a written description of what it may do, because a clinician who opens a sealed radiation device out of necessity can create a far worse hazard than the original fault, and the clinic needs a stock of the modular parts that the first two tiers consume.

Training is a component of the device, and maintenance training is what makes the rest of the program possible. Its purpose is to build a working mental model in the operator, so that the person understands what the device is doing, what normal looks and sounds like, and what early failure looks like. A good handover covers the start-up sequence, the daily and weekly checks, the meaning of the settings, the alarms and their correct responses, the cleaning that is allowed, and the faults that require a technician rather than a nurse. It should be practical and repeated, with a competency check rather than a signature on an attendance sheet. At least one person on every shift should be a designated superuser who can teach others and who knows whom to call, and any device whose training needs are unclear must be clarified against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

Documentation is what turns a collection of machines into a managed system, and it is also what protects patients when something goes wrong. The equipment register, maintenance log, calibration certificate, and training record form the legal and clinical history of the device, and they are the first things requested after an incident. That history also makes a recall possible, because a safety notice from a manufacturer can be acted upon only if the affected serial numbers and their locations are known. Underneath every schedule and every log is a human arrangement, and the failures that repeat are usually failures of ownership, because the machine that drifts between rooms, loses its accessories, and is discovered with a fault nobody reported is not badly designed but unowned. A culture of maintenance is built by making the report easy and never punishing the person who names a fault that turns out to be minor, and every record retention period and recall procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

To summarize, maintenance is the management of wear and troubleshooting is the disciplined reading of its symptoms, and together they keep a device trustworthy when a patient needs it. Wear arrives through abrasion, fatigue, corrosion, thermal cycling, and battery aging, and it follows a curve whose far end is reached by every machine used without attention. The hospital-grade program answers with a schedule built from risk, a written work order, a log read as history, calibration against traceable references, spare parts held against lead time, planned downtime, and a biomedical engineering department included early and told about near misses. The field variant gives up that structure and demands a toolkit, a service manual, a telephone relationship with a technician, a short written routine, and the judgment to know which repairs restore a device and which only hide its fault. In both settings the same sequence governs the first response to a fault, which is power, connection, consumable, setting, calibration, alarm, and the most valuable instrument is the operator who knows what normal looks like. Every setting, interval, pressure, temperature, energy level, and alarm threshold mentioned in these pages must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

# Chapter 76 — Regulation, Standards, and Quality

A device reaches a patient only after passing through rules that decide whether it may be sold, what it must prove, and who may repair it. Those rules exist because a leakage current, a burst pressure, and a sterilization temperature are measurable facts. A regulation is the agreement that somebody measures those facts before a patient is exposed. Every setting and threshold named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is relied upon.

A regulation is law, published by a government or by a delegated body, and it carries a penalty that can reach the withdrawal of a product. The authority registers devices and their makers, inspects factories, samples products, and can order a recall. A directive sets a required result and leaves each country to write its own law. A standard is a voluntary technical document that becomes binding only when a regulation refers to it.

Approval rests on the principle that a safety claim is a measurable quantity. Insulation is tested by raising the voltage across it until breakdown, and earthing by measuring the resistance of the earth path. A housing is dropped, a seal pressurized, a tube pulled apart, and a package held at a controlled temperature and humidity. Each test yields a number, and the approval file is the record of those numbers.

Classification is the regulator's first sorting decision, because the evidence demanded rises with the risk. A tongue depressor may need only registration and a truthful label. An infusion pump or a dialysis machine usually needs examination by an independent conformity assessment body. The highest class covers devices that sustain life, that are implanted, or that can kill when they fail.

Approval follows one of several pathways, each giving the object a different degree of scrutiny. A low-risk device may be self-declared by its maker. An intermediate one may be cleared by showing equivalence to a device already marketed. The strictest one needs clinical data, a factory inspection, and a renewable certificate, and its class and pathway must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase.

For the hospital, the practical output is a bundle of paper that the buyer should demand and keep. It includes the certificate, the declaration of conformity, instructions in a language the staff read, the service manual, and the name of the local representative. A device that arrives without this bundle is not a bargain, because the hospital inherits obligations nobody else will meet. The documents and the retention period must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before acceptance.

Traceability is the thread that runs from the factory to the patient and back again. A maker assigns a lot number to a production run and a unique identifier to many items, and the hospital records that number at the point of use. For a consumable the log sheet is what allows a contaminated batch to be found before it reaches anyone else. For an implant the record goes into the patient's file, so a failure found years later is traced to the exact device.

The characteristic failure of traceability is a missing number rather than an alarm. When the lot is not recorded, a recall cannot find the patient who received the batch. The common operator error is to leave the lot field blank because the ward was busy. The same omission hides a failed sterilization cycle and fluid stored too warm.

Standards are easier to hold in mind when they are grouped into families. The first is electrical safety, which governs insulation, earthing, leakage current, and alarms. The second is gas and medical supply, which governs cylinders, valves, connectors, regulators, and the identity of the gas. The third is sterility and biocompatibility, and the fourth is quality management, with risk management and usability supplying the reasoning the others assume.

The electrical safety family is written so that a device can be tested on a bench. The general standard for medical electrical equipment requires protection against electric shock and separation between the mains circuit and any part a patient can touch. Collateral standards cover electromagnetic disturbance, radiation, and alarms, while particular standards add tests for each device type. The test values and the retest interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a device is passed.

The gas and medical supply family exists because a cylinder is a pressure vessel and a connector is a safety device. Its standards fix the shape of cylinder valves and the pin index arrangement that prevents an oxygen regulator from fitting a nitrous oxide cylinder. They also fix the color and label of a cylinder, the pressure rating of a pipeline, and the terminal unit at the bedside. The valve types, colors, pressure ratings, and flow ranges must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a cylinder is connected.

The sterility family asks whether a device can be reliably freed of living organisms. The answer is proved by validating a process against a known bioburden and expressing the result as a probability of a surviving organism, called the sterility assurance level. That validation is physical, because the maker measures temperature, pressure, humidity, and duration at the coldest point of the load. The parameters and the sterility assurance level must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a process is adopted.

The biocompatibility part of the family asks whether materials that touch the body cause harm. It is tested by extracting substances from the material and exposing cells and living tissue to them. The search is for toxicity, irritation, and sensitization, and in blood-contacting devices for effects on clotting and red cells. A material that passes one test can still fail another, which is why the intended contact matters.

The quality management family governs the maker rather than the object. The central standard requires a documented system covering design, purchasing, production, inspection, storage, servicing, complaints, and corrective action. Its purpose is not paperwork for its own sake, but the ability to reproduce a safe device and to find the cause when one fails. A factory that cannot trace its components cannot investigate its defects, and the procedures and audit interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the system is trusted.

A separate standard governs risk management and supplies the reasoning the other families assume. The process identifies every foreseeable hazard, including electric shock, mechanical injury, contamination, radiation, and use error, and estimates the severity and probability of each. Controls are applied in a fixed order, which is to remove the hazard by design, then to guard against it, then to warn, and only last to rely on training. A warning is the weakest control invented, and the acceptability criteria must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the risk file is accepted.

Standards also govern how a person and a device meet, and this family explains more accidents than any other. Usability standards require the maker to find the steps where a reasonable user is likely to slip, and to design the interface so that the correct action is the easy one. They govern the shape of connectors, the position of a button, the wording of a label, and the priority of an alarm. A flow control that turns the wrong way or a gas connector that fits the wrong gas is a hazard built into the product.

The bodies that write these documents are international, regional, and national. The International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission write the international standards, with the electrotechnical commission taking the electrical field. National member bodies such as the American National Standards Institute and the British Standards Institution adopt and sometimes strengthen the text. The World Health Organization publishes guidance and lists of essential equipment that carry particular weight where no national framework exists.

A standard is only paper until somebody independent confirms that a maker can meet it, and that confirmation is called accreditation. Accreditation is granted to the laboratories and certification bodies that perform the tests. A test report is meaningful only when the laboratory can show that its instruments trace back through a chain of comparisons to a national measurement standard. That chain is why a calibration certificate names the reference and the uncertainty, and the traceability must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a report is relied upon.

Where a national framework exists, the hospital operates inside it and its duties follow from that. It must buy devices that are lawfully on the market, store and use them as instructed, and keep records that allow an item to be found again. It must report adverse events within the required time, act on a recall, maintain and calibrate as the maker requires, and train everyone who operates the device. The duties and the reporting deadlines must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any change is made.

The hospital must also avoid the quiet modifications that void an approval. A homemade adapter, a substituted fuse, a repaired circuit board, a bypassed interlock, or a software setting changed beyond its permitted range can remove the device from the protection of its certificate. Such a change is usually made to keep a machine working during a shortage, and it converts an approved device into an unapproved one. The permitted modifications and the parts that must be original must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any work is performed.

Adverse event reporting, often called vigilance, is the system by which a failure in the field reaches the people who can correct it. A reportable event is usually a death, a serious injury, or a malfunction that could have caused either if it recurred. The maker must investigate the cause and report to the national authority, which may then circulate the finding to every user. The system depends on the person closest to the event, because a device that failed on a night shift leaves the ward unexamined unless somebody writes it down.

The weakness of every vigilance system is under-reporting. The person who noticed is busy, the form is long, and the device seems to work again after a restart. A report that is not made allows the same fault to reach the next patient, and a culture that works punishes nobody for reporting. The common operator error is to describe the problem in conversation rather than in the system, which informs three colleagues and nobody who can fix it.

A recall is the action taken when a device already in use must be corrected or removed, and recalls arrive in degrees that reflect the danger. The most serious concerns a device that will probably cause serious harm or death and demands immediate action, including stopping use and contacting patients. The intermediate degree concerns a device that may cause temporary or reversible harm. The least urgent concerns a violation unlikely to cause harm that must still be corrected.

The notice is usually a field safety notice from the maker, and the clinic's procedure should be fixed in advance. Affected items are identified by serial or lot number, quarantined in a locked and clearly labeled place, and removed from use. Everyone who might use them is informed, and they are returned or corrected as instructed. The quarantine location and the removal deadline must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the notice arrives.

The characteristic alarm of this chapter is not a sound but the arrival of a notice that nobody reads. The recall letter in an unopened envelope, the message filtered into a spam folder, and the telephone message taken by someone who has since left are all the same failure. Each of them has kept a known-dangerous device in use. The defense is a named person who receives notices, a second who covers that absence, and one log in which every notice is entered and closed.

Post-market surveillance is the continuing collection of information after approval, and it is how a slow failure is discovered at all. The maker must gather complaints, service records, literature, and registry data, and periodically judge whether the balance of benefit and risk has changed. An artificial joint or a heart valve may fail only after several years and several thousand patients. Implant registries link the device to the outcome, and an implant card in the patient's hand lets a clinic find the person when a design is found to fail early.

The quality system inside a hospital mirrors the maker's system, and it begins with written procedures. A standard operating procedure states who does what, in what order, with what equipment, and what record is produced. Document control keeps only the current version in circulation, because a ward following an outdated procedure is following no procedure at all. The content, the version control, and the review interval must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the system is called complete.

An internal audit checks the system against its own rules, while an external accreditation survey checks it against an outside standard. A good surveyor follows a real patient through the building rather than reading a folder in an office. The purpose of all this paper is to protect the patient rather than the institution, and the test of a record is whether it would help the next patient. The common failure is the retrospective entry, written days later to fill a gap in a log, which turns a record into a fiction and hides the drift it was meant to reveal.

Quality control is the daily proof that a process still works, and it differs from quality assurance, which is the design of the system that makes the process reliable. A laboratory runs a control sample of known value before patient samples, plots the result on a chart, and stops the analyzer when the control falls out of range. A sterilizer proves each cycle with a chemical indicator and, at a defined interval, with a biological indicator containing harmless spores. The control limits, the acceptance rules, and the incubation conditions must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before results are released.

The characteristic alarm of quality control is the failed control, and the common operator error is to repeat the control until it passes. That does not repair the process, but selects the lucky result and hides the drift that caused the failure. The correct response is to stop and look for the physical cause, which may be an expired reagent, a dirty probe, an aged lamp, or a shifted temperature. Results that stay inside the limits while drifting steadily one way are also a warning, and the trend rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a result is reported.

Calibration and its traceability are the bridge between the hospital and the national measurement system. To calibrate is to adjust a device until its reading agrees with a reference, while to verify is to check that the reading already agrees. The reference used must itself be traceable, which means it has been compared, through an unbroken chain, to a national standard. The hazard is the device that reads confidently and wrongly, and the calibration interval and tolerance must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a result is trusted.

Maintenance is a regulatory obligation and not merely a service preference. The schedule the maker publishes is part of the conditions under which the device was approved, and skipping it can shift liability to the hospital when a patient is harmed. The work must be recorded with the date, the person, the parts used, and the measurements taken. The common failure is a repair that restores function without restoring safety, such as a fuse replaced with a higher rating or an earth wire left disconnected inside a closed housing.

Consumables carry their own regulatory burden, and it is often heavier than the burden on the machine. A single-use device is marked as such because the maker has shown that it is safe once, not that it can be cleaned, sterilized, and used again. Where reprocessing is permitted, it is permitted only through a validated process with documented cleaning, inspection, sterilization, and traceability, and the liability moves to whoever reprocessed it. Expiry dates are part of the approval, and the reuse status and expiry rules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any item is reused.

Compatibility is a physical property that a purchasing decision can quietly destroy. A maker validates its machine with particular consumables, and a third-party set may look identical while differing in internal diameter, wall stiffness, filter pore size, or the material that touches the fluid. Any of those differences can change the delivered dose or the behavior of an alarm. The substitute often appears to work for a hundred uses before it fails, and the compatibilities must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a substitute is introduced.

Cleaning and disinfection are regulated because a device that is not clean is not the device that was tested. Reprocessing instructions are part of the approval file, and they specify the cleaning agent, its concentration, the contact time, the temperature, the rinsing, and the drying. The physical failure is often invisible, because a channel that is not brushed keeps a biofilm and a connector that is not dried grows organisms in the moisture. The concentrations and contact times must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any device is reprocessed.

The hazard of poor cleaning is greatest in devices with narrow lumens, hinges, and rough surfaces, which is why flexible endoscopes and jointed instruments are the classic examples. The characteristic sign is the positive culture or the failed adenosine triphosphate test that arrives days after the procedure. A detergent that is too dilute does not lift the soil that protects the organisms, and a disinfectant that attacks the housing destroys the device it was meant to protect. Cleaning is therefore a device specification as much as a housekeeping task.

Complaints and failure modes are the raw material of quality, and a hospital that reviews them learns what no audit will teach. A single report of a cracked housing is an anecdote, while twelve reports of the same crack in the same model are a pattern. The pattern is what justifies a repair campaign, a change in training, or the withdrawal of a device. The investigation should ask what the device, the user, and the environment each did, because a fault attributed to the operator is often a design fault that made the error easy.

The common mistake is to record the complaint as a work order and close it when the device is returned, losing the trend that would have revealed the defect. The person at the bedside is the last and cheapest layer of the whole system. Before a device is used, the operator should confirm that it is the correct device, that its label and serial number match the register, and that the consumables are within expiry and of the approved type. During use the operator should watch for a warm plug, a new noise, a drifting reading, and an alarm that appears more often than it used to.

In a well-resourced hospital this whole structure is carried by people and by the consumables that the quality system itself requires. A quality unit keeps the procedures and the audit calendar, a biomedical engineering department keeps the register and the calibration schedule, and an infection prevention team validates the cleaning. Calibration certificates, reference standards, log sheets, labels, indicator strips, control samples, and training records are all consumables of the system. Service contracts are the usual place where the regulatory promise is broken, and a contract should name the response time, the parts included, and the documentation to be left behind.

Beyond the reach of this structure, the same clinical need is met by equipment that arrives with none of it, and regulation becomes a local practice rather than a national system. The field clinic usually receives its devices by donation, by ministry allocation, or by purchase in a market with no enforcement. The paperwork a hospital takes for granted is often absent, incomplete, in a language nobody reads, or written for a different model. What the field clinic gives up is the independent check on the design, the guarantee of spare parts, and the certainty that consumables will exist next year.

What it demands instead is judgment exercised before acceptance and the willingness to refuse. The device may be built for a voltage and frequency the local supply does not deliver. It may need a gas whose fittings do not exist locally, or water of a purity the clinic cannot produce. Its consumables may be proprietary and unavailable, and its service manual may never have been sent.

The question a receiving clinic must ask before accepting anything should be asked before the truck is unloaded. Can the device run from the power that actually exists here, and does it tolerate the swings and the outages? Can its consumables be obtained for the next several years, and at a price the clinic can pay? Is there a manual in a language the staff read, and a service manual for the technician? Are spare parts available, and is there someone within reach who can fit them?

When the device is accepted, the clinic must build the traceability the maker did not provide, and the substitute is a paper register kept honestly. Each item receives a local asset number painted or engraved on the case, and a line in a bound book records its origin, arrival date, serial number, condition, and responsible person. A photograph of the maker's plate and of the plug is a cheap copy of the information a lost manual would have carried. For consumables the lot number and the expiry are written on the log sheet at the point of use.

Vigilance in the field means using whatever channel exists rather than waiting for a formal one. The district health office, the regional referral hospital, the visiting technician, and the professional network are all part of the reporting route. A telephone call written down the same day is a valid report where no form exists. The field recall is the hardest case, because the notice must travel a road the device already travelled in the opposite direction.

A recall may arrive by radio, by a message to the district office, by a courier on a motorcycle, or by a colleague who heard about it at a meeting. The procedure that works must be decided in advance, with a quarantine shelf that is physically separate and clearly labeled. One person checks every notice against the register, and a recalled item leaves use on the day it is identified. The common failure is the notice filed with the intention of acting on it later, and the item used in the meantime.

The field quality system is small enough to be held by one person and must be written down anyway. One trained staff member keeps the equipment register, the log sheets, the maintenance calendar, and the file of instructions, and is given the time to do it. The daily checks match a hospital's, with the refrigerator temperature read and written, the sterilizer cycle recorded, the concentrator output checked, and expiry dates scanned. A short written procedure in the local language turns a habit into a standard that survives the departure of the person who wrote it.

Calibration and maintenance in the field rest on comparison, on the toolkit, and on the technician, and the honest statement is that the traceability chain is short. A device can be verified against a second device known to be good, a thermometer against an ice point and a boiling point, and a scale against a known mass. The physical principle is the same as in the hospital, because a measurement is only as good as the reference it is compared against. The common error is to adjust a device that is only slightly out rather than to record the deviation and watch for drift.

Cleaning, consumables, and failure modes in the field obey the same rules with fewer safeguards behind them. A chlorine solution mixed by hand must be measured, because a solution that is too weak does not disinfect and one that is too strong corrodes metal. A pressure cooker used as a sterilizer can be effective only when the cycle is timed, the temperature is reached, the air is removed, and an indicator proves the result. The consumable supply is the true constraint on every device, and the characteristic failure in the field is silence, because a device with no battery monitor has no low battery alarm.

The final field obligation is the same as the first, which is to decide before accepting rather than to repair afterwards. A receiving clinic that asks the hard questions, refuses what it cannot sustain, writes down what it owns, and reports what it sees has built a quality system out of paper and habit. That system protects patients as surely as an accreditation certificate does. The certificate is not the safety, because the safety is the physical test, the written record, and the person who reads the record.

To summarize, a regulation is the law that decides whether a device may be sold, a directive sets the required result and leaves the law to each country, and a standard becomes binding when a regulation refers to it. The standards that matter cover electrical safety, gas supply, sterility, quality management, risk, and usability. Approval is only the beginning, because traceability, adverse event reporting, recalls, calibration, maintenance, and cleaning continue for the whole life of the device. A hospital carries that structure with departments, contracts, and records, while a field clinic replaces it with a register, a log sheet, a trained person, and the discipline to refuse what it cannot sustain.

# Chapter 77 — Equipment in Low-Resource Settings

This is the chapter where the two halves of this book meet, because equipment in a low-resource setting is the same machine asked to work without the invisible system that surrounds it in a large hospital. A device is never a self-contained object but the visible end of a chain that begins with energy, clean water, gas, sterile supplies, spare parts, documentation, and a trained person. The physical principle is a continuous flow in which energy enters, work is performed, and consumables are used, and if any one link is broken the flow stops whether or not the machine looks intact. A ventilator with no oxygen, a sterilizer with no power, and an analyzer with no reagent are all, in the only sense that matters, broken. Understanding the chain rather than the box is the skill this chapter teaches, and it explains why the same need is met by very different hardware depending on where the patient lies. The chapter therefore describes the subject twice, first the hospital-grade system inside its maintained envelope and then the field variant that survives on what is physically present.

A machine is an island of order in a world that tends toward disorder, and every function it performs costs energy and material that must be replaced. Seals harden, lubricants dry, filters load, batteries lose capacity, calibration drifts, and metal corrodes, and these processes continue whether the device is used or merely stored. Maintenance is therefore not a repair after failure but the routine replacement of the small consumable parts of order before they are exhausted. A device that is not maintained rarely fails suddenly; it declines quietly, and the decline is usually invisible to whoever reads the number on its display. A machine without a maintenance plan is already in a slow failure, and the plan must name who does the work, with which parts, at what interval, and with what record. All maintenance intervals and calibration frequencies named in this chapter must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital-grade half of this book describes devices inside a support envelope that someone is paid to maintain. The building supplies stable electrical power, piped medical gases and vacuum, filtered air, purified water, drainage, steam, and a sterile processing department that returns instruments clean and packaged. A stores system holds consumables and rotates them before expiry, a biomedical workshop calibrates and repairs, a service contract brings the maker's technician, and the clinical staff are trained and supervised. The device is designed for exactly this envelope, and its tolerances for temperature, humidity, dust, and voltage are stated on the assumption that the envelope will hold. When it holds, the machine is reliable, and that reliability is a property of the system rather than of the box. The field variant is defined by what it loses from this list rather than by what it is.

The envelope is a set of physical conditions, and each one carries a number in the device documentation. Ambient temperature, relative humidity, airborne dust, altitude, supply voltage, supply frequency, and the depth and duration of power interruptions are all specified, and a device moved outside its stated range may fail at once or merely become inaccurate. A machine rated for a temperate clinic can overheat in a tropical room where the air is hot and wet, because heat cannot leave a cabinet when the surrounding air is already warm and moisture condenses on cold surfaces. Dust settles on cooling fins, blocks filters, and coats circuit boards, while humidity corrodes contacts and creates leakage paths across insulation. The stated operating temperature, humidity range, voltage tolerance, and frequency tolerance of every device must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital-grade chains for consumables and maintenance are the parts clinicians notice least and depend on most. Single-use items arrive in sealed packaging with a lot number and an expiry date, are stored in a controlled store, and are issued against a requisition, while reagents, electrodes, and sensors are kept within their temperature range and watched with a log. Preventive service is scheduled at intervals taken from the maker's documentation, calibration is performed against traceable reference standards, and a device that fails a test is removed from service rather than returned to the ward with a warning. The whole apparatus depends on trained biomedical technicians, on spare parts held in stock, and on purchasing that treats the cost of ownership rather than the purchase price as the real cost. Remove the technicians, the standards, or the parts, and the service program becomes a folder of unsigned forms.

A low-resource setting is not defined by geography or poverty alone but by the thinness of that support envelope. It is a place where power is intermittent, where clean water is carried rather than piped, where the nearest calibrated reference standard is a long journey away, and where a consumable may take months to arrive if it arrives at all. The same ward may hold a modern device and a broken generator, and the device will be judged by the generator. The term covers a rural health post with a solar panel, a district hospital with a failing grid, a mobile clinic on a truck, and a field hospital set up after a disaster, and the common feature is that the machine must survive on what is physically present. In such a setting the clinical question and the logistical question become one, because a treatment that cannot be repeated next week is not a treatment the clinic can honestly offer.

Equipment donation is the largest single source of unusable hardware in low-resource settings, and the reason is that the gift is usually chosen by the giver rather than the receiver. A well-meaning institution, a maker clearing a product line, a charity, or a surplus program assembles devices that are no longer wanted, and the receiving clinic accepts because refusing appears ungrateful. The machines arrive without manuals, without spare parts, without the consumables that fit them, and sometimes without a single person trained to use them. They may be built for a different voltage, frequency, gas connector, or language, and the incompatibility is discovered only when the crate is opened. The result is not care but the appearance of care, paid for in storage space, staff time, and the false confidence that the need has been met.

Walk into the back room and you see the anatomy of a failed donation. Along one wall stand ventilators with cracked circuits and missing sensors, their screens dark, beside infusion pumps whose proprietary tubing no longer exists and dialysis machines whose water treatment was never installed. On the floor are centrifuges with seized bearings, sterilizers with corroded chambers, X-ray units whose tubes have expired, and an ultrasound console whose probe cable was cut by a door. In the corner are boxes of consumables for machines that left the clinic years ago, their packaging faded and their dates long past, and a shelf holds manuals in a language no one reads. Every object in that room consumed money, freight, and hope on the way in, and it stands there because no one asked the questions that would have stopped it.

Incompatibility is physical, and it begins with electricity. A device built for a supply of one frequency will run fast or hot on another, and a motor, a compressor, or a centrifuge designed for the wrong waveform can overheat, vibrate, or fail. A device built for one nominal voltage may be destroyed by a surge or may refuse to start on a supply that sags, and the plug on its cord may not fit the socket at all. Gas connectors differ between countries, so a machine that needs a particular oxygen inlet may be impossible to connect without an adapter that no one stocks. Consumables are often proprietary, which means the device is useless without an item that only the maker supplies, and the supply route may be closed by cost, distance, or policy. Frequencies, voltages, connector standards, and consumable specifications must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any donated device is accepted.

Refurbished equipment occupies the middle ground and carries a middle risk. Refurbishment can be genuine, with worn parts replaced, software updated, performance tested, and a warranty given, and it can also be a coat of paint over a machine whose internal wear is unknown. A refurbished device has a history that cannot be fully verified, so its remaining life, its calibration, and its failure mode are estimates rather than facts. Proprietary software locks, activation codes, and dealer-only service tools can make an otherwise sound machine impossible to repair locally, and a device whose maker has withdrawn support may never receive another spare part. The purchase price is lower than new, but the total cost of ownership may be higher because the first repair needs an imported assembly that takes months to arrive. The condition, the warranty, the availability of parts, and the service arrangements must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase.

Needs assessment is the discipline that prevents the dead machine room, and it is performed before the crate is opened rather than after. The first question is clinical: which patient, with which condition, will this device treat, and is that condition actually common here? The second is operational: who will operate it, who will be on duty at night, and who will be accountable when it fails? The third is logistical: is the power compatible, is the consumable affordable for years, is a spare part obtainable, and is a technician within reach? The fourth is institutional: does the device duplicate something already present, and does the clinic have the space, security, and budget to keep it running? If any answer is no, the correct decision is to decline the device and, where possible, to ask instead for training, consumables, or a service contract.

Refusing a gift is difficult because it feels like refusing help, and the courage to do it is a clinical skill rather than a social failing. The refusal is easier with a written policy, adopted before any donation arrives, that states what the clinic can accept and what it cannot, so that the decision belongs to the institution rather than to the individual on the loading dock. The policy names the required voltage, frequency, gas connectors, language of the manual, availability of consumables, and the presence of a service plan, and it requires a signature from the person who will maintain the device. A polite refusal can be paired with a specific alternative, such as a request for a different device, for spare parts, or for the funds to train a technician. The person who accepts an unsupported device has, in effect, agreed to maintain it forever without the means to do so.

Robustness begins with temperature, because heat is the commonest killer of electronics in the tropics. A device dissipates its waste heat into the surrounding air, and the rate of transfer depends on the difference between the temperature of its components and the temperature of the room, so a hot room narrows the margin and a blocked vent removes it. Battery chemistry is temperature sensitive too, because heat accelerates the permanent loss of capacity while cold reduces the available current, so a battery that reads full in the afternoon may refuse to start a compressor in the early morning. Dust and humidity compound the problem, because dust absorbs moisture and moisture carries dust into places it should not reach; particles insulate cooling surfaces, clog filters, abrade bearings, and bridge contacts, while condensed water on a circuit board causes leakage currents and corrosion. A device intended for a hot, dusty climate should be rated for the ambient temperature, humidity, and dust it will actually meet, and those ratings must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The practical defenses are shade, ventilation, sealed enclosures with clean filters, a cover when the device is idle, and the habit of never opening a case in a dusty room.

Electrical supply in a low-resource setting is rarely a steady wave at the nominal voltage. It sags when a large load switches on, surges when that load drops, flickers as connections arc, and may change frequency as a generator governor hunts, and a supply shared with welding equipment, pumps, and air conditioners carries disturbances a hospital-grade device was never designed to tolerate. A transformer or a motor responds with heat, vibration, and torque that vary with the square of the voltage, which is why a compressor or a centrifuge is more vulnerable than a simple lamp. Electronic devices are protected by a voltage stabilizer, a surge protector, or a line conditioner, and each of these is itself a device that can fail and must be maintained. The acceptable voltage range, the frequency range, and the type of protection required must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A power interruption tests the whole chain, and the behavior of a device during the gap between the loss of mains power and its restoration decides whether a patient is harmed. Some devices simply stop, which is safe if the clinician knows and dangerous if the clinician does not; others switch to an internal battery, continue for a defined period, and then stop with an alarm; others restart automatically and may resume in an unexpected state. An uninterruptible power supply holds a battery and an inverter and carries the load for a short time, long enough to finish a critical action or move the patient to another supply. A generator takes several seconds to start and settle, and a device that cannot tolerate that gap needs a battery between it and the wall. The runtime, the transfer time, the battery test interval, and the alarm threshold of any backup supply must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The field variant of this chapter is the clinic that has accepted the chain is thin and has chosen its equipment to match. Its power comes from a solar panel, a battery, and an inverter, with a small generator as a last resort, and its devices are chosen for low current draw and tolerance of a sagging supply. Its oxygen comes from a concentrator driven by that power or a cylinder refilled at a distant plant, and its suction comes from a foot pump or a battery pump when the wall has no vacuum. Its sterilization is a pressure cooker or a small electric autoclave when power allows, and its laboratory is a set of tests that need no cold chain and no analyzer. The field clinic gives up speed, throughput, and the ability to run several complex procedures at once, and in exchange it gains the ability to keep working when the grid does not. What it demands instead is routine: batteries charged, filters cleaned, consumables counted, and every machine tested before the patient arrives.

The consumable is the true constraint on any device, because it must be bought again and again while the machine is bought once. A device is a lock and its consumable is the key, and when the maker controls the key the clinic's ability to treat patients depends on a supply route it does not own. The recurring cost of consumables, reagents, electrodes, tubing, filters, and test strips usually exceeds the purchase price over the life of the device, and a budget that covers only the purchase has funded a demonstration rather than a service. The practical test before buying anything is to ask whether the consumable can be obtained next month, next year, and after the donor has gone home. Where the answer is uncertain, the clinician should prefer a device whose consumable is generic, locally produced, or reusable under a defined protocol. The cost, availability, shelf life, and storage conditions of every consumable must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is adopted.

Clinics that cannot rely on a single supplier develop strategies, and each carries a risk. Standardization on a few device families reduces the variety of consumables that must be stocked and makes training and repair easier, but it also creates dependence on the one supplier chosen. Generic consumables may fit and perform correctly at a fraction of the price, or they may fit loosely, leak, or deliver the wrong volume, and the difference is often invisible until a patient is harmed. Reuse of items labeled for single use happens wherever supply is short, and it is safe only when the item can be cleaned, disinfected or sterilized, inspected, and confirmed to function, and when the protocol is written and followed. Reprocessing a catheter, a filter, or a sensor beyond its designed life introduces infection, inaccurate measurement, and sudden failure, and the decision must never be left to improvisation at the bedside. Reuse protocols, cleaning agents, sterilization cycles, and maximum reuse counts must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Cleaning and reprocessing are the unglamorous core of safe equipment use, and they compete for the same scarce inputs as everything else. Cleaning removes visible soil and the organic film that protects microorganisms, and it must precede disinfection or sterilization, because a sterilizer cannot penetrate a crust of dried blood. Disinfection with a chemical depends on the concentration, the contact time, and the temperature, and a reused bath that has become dilute or dirty may look correct while doing nothing.
