Water is the hidden input of this work, because hard water leaves scale that harbors soil and blocks fine channels, water carrying organic matter recontaminates what has just been cleaned, and water of the wrong acidity corrodes metal. Sterilization by steam depends on saturated steam under pressure reaching every surface for a defined time, and many hospital cycles use 134 degrees Celsius for a short hold or 121 degrees Celsius for a longer one, values that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. A chemical indicator and a biological indicator are the evidence that the cycle worked, and a sterilizer with no indicator, no log, and no maintenance produces confidence rather than sterility. Every disinfectant concentration, contact time, rinse water quality, sterilization temperature, pressure, and holding time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Training is the difference between a machine that is used and a machine that is merely present, and it must be planned at the same time as the purchase. The operator manual explains the controls, the setup, the meaning of the alarms, and what to do when one sounds, and it is useless if it exists only in a language the staff do not read or in a file no one can open. The service manual is a different document and contains the maintenance schedule, the calibration procedure, the spare parts list, the circuit descriptions, and the fault codes; it must be obtained at purchase, because years later the maker may no longer supply it and the local technician will need it more than ever. Training must be repeated, because staff move and memory fades, and a single session at installation does not survive a change of shift, let alone a change of staff. A written quick guide in the local language beside the machine, and one named person responsible for training, keep the knowledge alive after the trainer has left. The training required and the interval for refresher training must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Local repair capacity is the most valuable and most neglected asset in the system, because a clinic that repairs its own equipment is independent in a way no stock of spare machines can match. The technician needs tools, a multimeter, a test load, reference standards, a workspace, light, a computer, and access to the internet where it exists; more importantly, the technician needs the service manual, a stock of the parts that wear, and the authority to take a device out of service. Training a technician on a specific machine is far cheaper than importing a technician for every fault, and a person who repairs a device in the clinic learns its behavior in a way no course can teach. The alternative to local repair is cannibalization, in which one machine is dismantled to keep another alive, and while this can be a legitimate last resort it is also how a fleet of four devices becomes a fleet of one. The spare parts to hold in stock, the test equipment required, and the documentation needed for repair must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase.

The failure modes of a low-resource setting are often quieter than those of a well-resourced one, and quiet failure is the more dangerous kind. A device may run but drift out of calibration, so that its readings are systematically wrong while the machine appears healthy; a flowmeter may stick, a scale may read low, a thermometer may lag, and a pump may deliver less than its display promises. A device may fail intermittently, working in the morning and stopping in the afternoon heat, which leads to the false conclusion that it has been repaired when it is merely between failures. A device may be missing a small part no one can name, such as a washer, a fuse, a battery cover, or a sensor cap, and that trivial absence stops a substantial machine. A device may also fail because its consumable is exhausted, which the operator mistakes for a fault and which no amount of repair will solve. The characteristic alarms here include the low battery alarm no one can hear, the alarm whose message is in a foreign language, and the alarm silenced so often that the staff no longer register it, and every alarm threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The operator's check before every use is short, and it is the only thing standing between a hidden fault and a patient. It begins with the power source: that the plug is seated, the cable is not frayed, the supply is live, and the battery holds enough charge for the expected task, followed by switching the device on and confirming that it completes its self test without an unexplained error. Next comes the physical condition of the device and its accessories, the tubing, seals, cuffs, probes, and connectors, which must be intact, clean, and correctly fitted. Then the consumables are checked for correct type, intact packaging, and an unexpired date, and the settings are compared with the clinical requirement rather than with the last patient's convenience. The alarms are tested where the device allows it, because an alarm that cannot sound is worse than no alarm at all, and the result is written in a log the next shift can read. When any check fails, the device must be taken out of service, tagged, and reported rather than used with a private mental reservation.

Some equipment survives in a low-resource setting, and the reasons are consistent enough to serve as a design brief. The survivors are simple, with few settings and few parts, so a fault is visible and a repair is possible with common tools; they are mechanical where the function permits it, because a hand pump, a gravity infusion set, a manual resuscitator, and a spring-loaded scale have no electronics to fail and no battery to charge. They are modular, so a failed component can be replaced instead of the whole device, and they share consumables with other machines so that the store carries one kind of tubing rather than six. They tolerate a wide temperature range, a dusty room, and a sagging supply, and they accept generic consumables that can be bought in the local market. This is also the case for owning less, because every extra machine consumes power, space, security, training, consumables, and the technician's attention, and attention is the scarcest resource of all. A clinic that owns three complex devices and cannot maintain any of them treats fewer patients than a clinic that owns one device and maintains it flawlessly, since a device that is present but unreliable is worse than an absent one because it invites decisions based on false information. The proper test of a purchase is not what the device can do in a demonstration but what it will do in this clinic on an ordinary Tuesday.

Judgment at the point of purchase is the discipline this chapter is trying to teach, and it reduces to a few questions asked honestly and in advance. What clinical problem will this device solve, and how often does that problem occur here? Who will operate it, who will clean it, who will calibrate it, and who will repair it when it fails? What does it consume, where does that consumable come from, and can the clinic pay for it for the next five years? What does it need from the building, in power, water, gas, air, or space, and does the building actually provide it? What happens during an outage, and what is the plan if the device stops in the middle of a procedure? The answers define the total cost of ownership, which is the purchase price plus the consumables plus the training plus the spare parts plus the eventual disposal, and it is this total, not the price on the invoice, that decides whether the clinic can afford the device at all.

To summarize, equipment in a low-resource setting is the same medicine practiced against a thinner support envelope, and the machine is only the visible part of a chain that includes energy, consumables, documentation, spare parts, and trained people. The hospital-grade half of every chapter assumes that chain, and the field half rebuilds it from solar power, batteries, hand pumps, generic supplies, and local skill. Donated and refurbished equipment fails when it is incompatible, unsupported, or unrepairable, and the answer is a needs assessment before acceptance and the courage to refuse a gift that would cost more than it gives. Robustness means tolerance of heat, cold, dust, humidity, and a swinging voltage, and behavior during an outage that the clinician can predict. Consumables are the true constraint, maintenance and cleaning are the true work, and the operator's check before every use is the true safeguard. The equipment that survives is simple, modular, repairable, and modest in its demands, and the wisest clinic is often the one that owns less and keeps it working.

# Chapter 78 — Emerging Technologies

This chapter is different from every other chapter in this book, because its subject has not yet settled. The physical principles underneath them are already fixed, and a listener who grasps those principles can judge a new machine without waiting for the literature to agree. Every emerging technology in medicine is built from a small set of physical events, in which a photon is captured, a current is measured, a material is deposited, or a battery is discharged. The clinical promise sits on top of those events, so when the promise outruns the physics the device fails in the field rather than in the advertisement. This chapter keeps the discipline and the two halves of the rest of the book, and it ends by returning to the patient.

A demonstration proves that a thing can work once, in a room chosen for it, with the person who built it standing nearby. A device proves that it works every time, in a room it did not choose, in the hands of someone who did not build it and cannot repair it. The distance between those two statements is crossed by repeatability, calibration, documented failure modes, spare parts, consumables, training, and a regulatory pathway. A device must survive the hundredth patient on the hottest afternoon of the year, when the operator is tired and the cupboard is nearly empty. The question is therefore not whether a technology can work, but what it demands to keep working, counted in power, consumables, connectivity, training, and maintenance skill before it is bought.

Artificial intelligence begins with the fact that an image or a signal is a grid of numbers, and a pattern in those numbers can be learned from examples. A learning program is shown many such arrays with the answer a clinician gave, and it adjusts millions of internal weights until its own answers match those examples closely enough. The result is not a written rule but a statistical surface that responds to shapes, edges, and textures. Screening and triage follow directly, because both sort many normal studies from a few abnormal ones. The same mathematics makes the device excellent on images resembling its training examples and unreliable on images that do not, and it cannot tell the difference by itself.

In a well-resourced hospital, artificial intelligence usually arrives inside the imaging chain rather than as a separate box. The hospital-grade version therefore depends on infrastructure that has nothing to do with intelligence, because it needs a fast network, large storage, calibrated displays, and an electronic health record that can receive the result. Its validation problem is the hard part, because a program tested on one population and one machine can lose accuracy when either changes. Demonstrations report accuracy on a curated set, while a device must report its performance on the patients who actually arrive, and any stated accuracy, confidence threshold, or alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant is a program on a telephone or a small laptop, often without a network, because connectivity in a frontier clinic is intermittent and expensive. It gives up the large training sets, the calibrated display, and the continuous updates of the hospital version, and it demands disciplined use instead, meaning a defined population, a defined task, and a written record of which version was used for which patient. It also demands a path to referral, because a tool that raises suspicion without a route to confirmation creates anxiety rather than care, and the software version and model date must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The characteristic hazard of a diagnostic learning program is a confident wrong answer rather than a crash. It is delivered in the same clean font as a correct one. Automation bias is the operator error that follows, because a reader who sees a flag looks for confirmation and stops looking for what the flag did not mention. The device may fail silently when its input changes, so an image with a folded edge, a foreign body, or a poor exposure can produce a result that is fluent and false. There is rarely a traditional alarm, and that absence is itself the safety problem, because listeners expect a machine to announce its own uncertainty. The honest practice puts a quality check before the analysis, refuses to report when the input is out of specification, and treats every result as a second opinion rather than a verdict. The operator must check the image, the stated confidence, and the clinical picture together, and any rejection threshold or confidence value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Wearable monitoring rests on the fact that the body emits signals a small sensor can capture at the skin. A light emitting diode shines light into tissue and a photodetector measures how much returns, and because oxygenated and deoxygenated blood absorb light differently the pulsation of arterial blood becomes a signal from which heart rate and oxygen saturation are derived. An accelerometer measures acceleration in 3 axes and infers steps, posture, tremor, sleep, and falls, while a pair of electrodes measures the small voltage of the heart or the brain. Each measurement is a physical quantity converted into a number, and each is vulnerable to motion, poor contact, heat and cold, and the placement of the sensor. A consumer wearable and a medical monitor may use the same physics and still differ enormously in calibration and in what their numbers mean.

The hospital-grade wearable is a telemetry device, and it is inseparable from the infrastructure that receives it. A small transmitter on the chest sends an electrocardiogram to a central station through a dedicated wireless network that covers the ward, and the station applies alarm limits, stores the trend, and routes the signal to a monitor at the desk. Batteries are managed as a consumable with a defined life and a charging routine, and electrodes are replaced on a schedule because their gel dries. The safety hazard is an alarm that does not reach a human being, whether because the network has a dead zone, the battery died, or the alarm limit was set outside the protocol. The common operator error is to silence an alarm without resolving it, and the characteristic response is a technical alarm that the staff learn to ignore, so alarm limits, battery replacement intervals, and electrode change schedules must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant is a telephone paired with a low-power sensor, and a patch that records a single-lead electrocardiogram continuously and is read later gives up real-time alarms but can diagnose an intermittent rhythm in a patient who lives far away. It demands a system for retrieving the data and a person responsible for reading it.

Three-dimensional printing is the construction of an object layer upon layer from a digital model, and the physical principle differs with the method. In material extrusion, a heated nozzle lays down a bead of melted polymer that fuses to the layer beneath as it cools, so the strength of the part depends on the print parameters and the bond between passes, and those parameters must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. In vat photopolymerization, a light source cures a liquid resin one thin slice at a time, giving fine detail but requiring washing and a final cure under light. In powder bed fusion, a laser or an electron beam melts particles of metal or polymer into a solid, which produces strong parts for instruments and implants but demands an inert atmosphere, trained operators, and expensive powder. The clinical use follows from customization, because a shape can be made for one patient rather than chosen from a catalog.

In a hospital, three-dimensional printing appears in 3 places that carry very different risks. The next is the orthosis or external aid, a splint, a brace, or a prosthetic socket shaped to the patient, which must fit, tolerate cleaning, and bear load without cracking. The most demanding is the sterile guide or implant, which must be made from a validated material, printed in a controlled environment, cleaned, and sterilized by a cycle proven not to distort it, because a printed part is not sterile merely because it looks clean. Its layered surface harbors organisms more readily than a machined surface, so material lot, print parameters, and the sterilization method must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any printed object touches a patient. The field variant is a small extrusion printer in a district workshop, and its most valuable product is a spare part rather than a device. A knob, a bracket, a battery cover, a tube clamp, or a tray insert can be copied from a broken original and printed in a tough polymer, which can return a machine to service that would otherwise wait months for an imported piece. It gives up dimensional precision and material certification, and it demands dry filament, a stable power supply, a spare nozzle, and a person who can draw or scan the broken part accurately, while the operator must remember that a printed substitute inside a breathing circuit or a pressure vessel is a hazard rather than a repair.

Surgical robotics begins with teleoperation, in which the surgeon's hands move a master control while a slave mechanism inside the patient reproduces the motion. The link is electronic, so the motion can be scaled down, filtered of tremor, and given more degrees of freedom than a human wrist, while the camera gives a magnified three-dimensional view. The physical principle is the same as any remote manipulator, because position and force are sensed at one end, encoded, transmitted, and recreated at the other, and every joint adds a place where calibration can drift. The clinical gain is precision in a confined space and steadier hands during long procedures, and the cost is measured in purchase price, in a dedicated theatre, in a service contract, and in consumable instruments with a defined number of uses. The characteristic hazard is not the robot moving by itself but the loss of force feedback, which lets a surgeon push harder than intended because the hand feels nothing, and the characteristic alarm is a system fault that halts the instrument in mid-move, so any instrument use limit, calibration interval, and force threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant of robotics is almost nothing, and honesty requires saying so, because a machine that needs a stable floor, conditioned air, a trained engineer, and a service visit from another country does not belong in a frontier clinic. What the field clinic should take from robotics is not the robot but the principles it embodies, which are a stable adjustable table, bright and shadowless light, reliable suction, good instruments, and a second trained pair of hands. The field variant needs some way to confirm what it suspects.

Telemedicine is the transport of clinical information rather than of the patient, and its physical basis is the conversion of a measurement into a signal. Sound becomes a stream of numbers and an image becomes a grid of numbers, and both are compressed by discarding what the eye and ear are unlikely to notice, then transmitted and rebuilt at the other end. Three physical quantities decide whether the encounter works, which are bandwidth, latency, and stability. Bandwidth limits how much can be sent, latency is the delay between sending and receiving, and stability is whether the connection holds long enough to finish. A narrow question over a slow link works, while a moving image of a heart needs a better one. Bandwidth, latency, and image resolution requirements must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital-grade telemedicine system is a room or a cart with a camera, a microphone array, a display, a codec that compresses and decompresses the signal, and a network connection with reserved capacity. It is tied into the picture archiving and communication system so that images can be shared, and into the electronic health record so that the encounter is documented where the rest of the chart lives. The characteristic alarm is a connection or quality warning, and the common operator error is to proceed through poor audio rather than stop and fix the link, because both parties tend to be polite about it. The safety hazard is a decision made on incomplete information, which is why the receiving clinician must state what could not be seen or heard, and connection quality thresholds, camera resolution, and audio levels must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant is usually a telephone, sometimes a very small satellite terminal, and occasionally a radio link on the very high frequency or ultra high frequency bands where no telephone network reaches. It gives up the dedicated room, the codec, the clear image, and the reliable link, and store-and-forward messaging, in which a photograph and a short history are sent and an answer returns later, is often more robust than a live call. What it demands is a disciplined package, namely a measured set of observations, a clear photograph with a scale, a short written question, and a named person at the far end who will answer, because the common operator error is to send an image with no scale, no orientation, and no history.

A modern telephone contains a computer, a camera, a microphone, an accelerometer, a light sensor, a radio, and a touch screen, and any of these can be turned into a medical instrument by software, which is why the telephone is the most consequential emerging device in this chapter. The regulation problem is that most applications escape scrutiny entirely, because they are distributed as general-purpose software and make claims that fall outside the definition of a medical device. A step counter, a menstruation tracker, and a mood diary are consumer products, while a program that calculates a drug dose, interprets a rhythm strip, or photographs a lesion for diagnosis is making a medical claim and should be regulated as a device, whether or not it is. The listener should ask 3 questions of any clinical application, which are what claim does it make, on what data was it tested, and who is accountable when it is wrong. In the hospital, the application that survives is the one wired into the record and the workflow, and the hospital-grade version is managed by the institution with version control and a policy on photographs of patients. The field variant is the opposite, a large unmanaged collection of applications installed by individuals, and what it gives up is institutional oversight. The safety hazard is a dose or a threshold read from an unvalidated application, and the common operator error is to trust a familiar interface over a printed protocol, so the application version, data source, and any calculated value must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Solar power begins with the photovoltaic cell, a slice of semiconductor in which arriving light frees electrons and creates a voltage across a junction, so the current that flows is proportional to the light falling on the panel. A charge controller sits between panel and battery to prevent overcharging and to manage the discharge, and an inverter converts the stored direct current into the alternating current that most hospital equipment expects. Battery chemistry decides how the system behaves, because a lead acid battery is cheap and heavy and tolerates abuse poorly, while a lithium iron phosphate battery stores more energy for its weight and lasts more cycles, but it costs more and must be protected from heat and deep discharge. Panel rating, controller settings, battery type, and inverter capacity must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital-grade solar installation is an engineering project, an array on a roof or a frame sized from a measured load profile, coupled to a battery bank in a ventilated room, integrated with the mains supply, and monitored so that a failing string or a degrading battery is noticed before the ward goes dark. The field variant is a single panel, a small controller, and one battery, sized to run lights, a telephone charger, a refrigerator for vaccines, and perhaps an oxygen concentrator during daylight, and it demands that the clinic know its consumption in watt hours per day before it buys anything, with those load figures confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The characteristic failure is not the panel but the battery, which ages quietly, and the common operator error is to add a load without adding capacity. The low-voltage alarm on the controller is the characteristic warning that the battery is being drawn down. Battery capacity, depth of discharge, and charge controller voltage setpoints must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Sterilization innovations aim at the same goal by new physical routes, because heat and steam damage many modern instruments. Hydrogen peroxide vapor sterilizes at a low temperature by oxidizing the proteins and nucleic acids of organisms, but it requires a sealed chamber, a specific concentration, and a material compatibility check, since some polymers and some long narrow channels resist the vapor. Ultraviolet light damages the genetic material of organisms and is useful for surface and water disinfection, but it travels in straight lines and shadows protect whatever it does not reach. The verification principle matters most, because a sterilization cycle is only trusted when a biological indicator has been killed and a chemical indicator has changed, since the machine's own display cannot prove sterility by itself. The characteristic alarm is a cycle failure that aborts the run and leaves the load unsterile. Cycle temperature, hydrogen peroxide concentration, exposure time, and the biological indicator incubation period must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The field variant is mostly the old technology used well, which is a pressure cooker or a small autoclave heated over whatever fuel is available, with the air removed, the load arranged so that steam can penetrate, and the cycle timed and recorded. It gives up the low-temperature chemistry, the sealed chamber, and the automatic control, and it demands that the operator understand the difference between steam and air, because a chamber full of air is a chamber that is not sterilizing, while solar disinfection of water and simple heat-based disinfection of small items remain limited and verifiable only by careful process control.

Delivery by unmanned aircraft is a problem of energy and distance, because lift costs power continuously and the power is carried in a battery whose mass reduces the payload the aircraft can lift. A rotor turns electrical energy into thrust, the aircraft climbs against gravity, and the range is set by the battery capacity divided by the rate at which it is consumed, so range, speed, payload, and wind are traded against one another. The clinical use is the movement of small, light, urgent, and perishable things, such as a blood sample from a remote clinic to a laboratory, a unit of blood or a vaccine in the other direction, or a rapid diagnostic test that must be read within a short window. Payload mass, flight range, wind limit, and battery state of charge must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The hospital-grade program looks like an airline, with a route survey, a designated landing area, a maintained fleet, trained pilots, and a maintenance log. The field variant is a single aircraft flown by a trained health worker between two fixed points, and it gives up the fleet, the spare parts, and sometimes the cold chain, while gaining a route that no road can match during a flood. It demands a charging routine, a protected landing pad, a container that keeps the specimen cool, and a written protocol for what happens when the aircraft fails or the wind rises, while the safety hazard is a machine with stored energy falling from height near people and the common operator error is to launch with a partially charged battery.

An honest assessment of any emerging technology begins by separating 3 categories. The first is hype, a device that works in a demonstration and cannot be sustained, and whose total cost of ownership is never stated. The second is nearly ready, a device that works in a limited, well-defined task under conditions a district hospital can meet. The third is buy now, which is unglamorous and often invented long ago, and which will still be working when the exciting device is in the back room. The test that sorts them is a set of plain questions, which are what powers it, what does it consume, what does it cost to maintain, who repairs it, how is it cleaned, what does it do when the network fails, and what is the evidence in a setting like mine. A device that cannot answer all of those questions has not yet become equipment, and its performance claims, operating conditions, and maintenance intervals must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase.

For a remote clinic this year, the honest shopping list is short and mostly boring. Reliable solar power with a properly sized battery and a charge controller is the first purchase, because it decides whether anything else can run. A robust oxygen concentrator with a maintenance plan, a set of pulse oximeters, a working refrigerator or cold box for vaccines with a temperature log, and an autoclave that can be repaired locally follow closely behind. So does a telephone with a data plan and a link to a referral hospital, and so does an inventory system that tracks consumption. The exciting items, the diagnostic learning software, the printer, and the delivery aircraft, come after, and only when the questions about power, consumables, maintenance, and training have answers. This is not timidity but arithmetic, because the purpose of equipment is to be working on the day the patient arrives, and the purchase specifications and consumable requirements for each item must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before purchase.

Emerging technology does not escape the maintenance rules of the rest of this book, and in some ways it makes them harder. Firmware and software must be updated, and an update can change an alarm limit, a user interface, or an algorithm without changing the case, so the version in use must be recorded and the changed behavior taught. Batteries are the most common hidden consumable, because their capacity falls with every cycle and with every hour spent hot, and a device that ran all day when new may run half a day a year later. Sensors, electrodes, probe covers, filters, and printer filament all expire or degrade, and each has a replacement interval that must be written into the maintenance plan. Cleaning is its own hazard, because a sealed electronic device tolerates a wiped surface and not a soaked one, and a disinfectant correct for a metal instrument can cloud a plastic screen or corrode a connector. The device's cleaning method, battery replacement interval, and software update procedure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use. The invisible component of every emerging device is data, and data has physical requirements that a remote clinic may not meet, because it must be stored with enough capacity, transmitted with enough bandwidth, protected from loss and unauthorized access, and retained long enough to be useful without becoming a liability. A remote monitoring program that sends information to a distant server creates a duty of confidentiality in 2 places at once, so the hospital-grade answer is a governed system with access controls and audit trails, while the field answer holds as little data as the task requires and deletes it when the reason for holding it has passed.

Every device in this book, old or new, ends in the same place, which is a person lying on a bed or sitting in a chair with a question about their own body. A new technology that cannot be explained to the patient, that cannot be cleaned between patients, or that cannot be repaired within reach is not an advance for that patient, however elegant its mathematics. The listener who has followed this book now holds a method that outlasts any particular machine, which is to find the physical principle, name what the device consumes, identify what can fail and how that failure announces itself, and confirm every number against the manufacturer and the local protocol. That method will still be valid when today's emerging technology is ordinary and when something not yet imagined has taken its place. The patient is the reason for the whole inventory, and the equipment exists to serve the patient rather than the reverse.

To summarize, emerging technology is not a separate kind of medicine but the same physical events arranged in new ways, and it must be judged by the same questions that judge an autoclave or a syringe. Artificial intelligence learns patterns from examples and fails when the examples no longer match, so it must be validated where it is used. Wearables turn the light, motion, and voltage of the body into numbers that require a reader and a rule. Three-dimensional printing makes a custom shape from a digital model and is trustworthy only as far as its material and its sterilization. Robotics buys precision at a cost few clinics can carry, telemedicine trades distance for bandwidth, telephone applications mostly escape regulation, and solar power, new sterilization chemistry, and delivery aircraft each add reach while adding a new dependency. What a clinic should buy this year is power, oxygen, cold storage, and repair capacity, and what it should treat with suspicion is any device whose consumable, spare part, or repair cannot be named, because every one of these machines exists to serve a patient and the measure of the technology is whether the patient is better served.

# Appendix A — Visual Atlas of Equipment by Department

This appendix exists because a photograph cannot be heard, and a spoken atlas must do what a picture does. It fixes in the listener's mind where each machine stands, what it looks like from the doorway, and which sound identifies the room from the corridor. The walk follows a patient's route through the emergency department and its trauma bay, the ward, the operating theatre, the intensive care unit, the delivery room, the laboratory, the imaging suite, the central sterile services department, the pharmacy, the laundry, and the morgue. In every room the fixed equipment comes first, because it belongs to the building, and the movable equipment comes second, because it can be borrowed or lost. Every setting, pressure, temperature, and alarm threshold named here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device is used on a patient.

The emergency department announces itself from the corridor by layered sounds, the beep of a monitor, the chime of a call bell, the hiss of oxygen, and the gurgle of a vacuum canister. Its fixed equipment sits within reach of a standing team, so the resuscitation bay carries oxygen and vacuum at the head of the trolley, a ceiling light, a socket strip, and a leaded screen. On wheels it holds the crash cart with sealed drawers, the monitor, the defibrillator, the airway trolley, the suction unit, and the trauma bay's collars, boards, rapid infusion device, and chest drain set. A serious hazard is the unsecured oxygen cylinder, which becomes a missile if it falls and shears its valve, and the common error is silencing an alarm without looking at the patient first. The characteristic alarms are the defibrillator self-test beep and the monitor low oxygen saturation tone, and every defibrillator energy setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a shock is delivered.

The general ward is the quietest department that still holds a machine at every bed, identified by call bells, chattering infusion pumps, and a monitor alarm whose lead has loosened. The fixed equipment of a bed space is the bed frame with its motor and brake, the mattress, the overhead light, the oxygen, air, and vacuum outlets, and the call bell on its coiled cord. The movable equipment is the monitor, the infusion pumps on their pole, the suction canister, the walking frame, and the portable oxygen cylinder on its stand. The principle of the bed is mechanical advantage, because a small motor turns a screw that lifts a heavy patient with a force no nurse should provide by hand. A serious hazard is the gap between the side rail and the mattress, where a frail patient can be trapped by the neck, and the common error is hanging a pump on the side rail; every pump rate and alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the infusion begins.

The atlas of a bed space is incomplete without the drawer beside it, because consumables are what the ward consumes fastest. That drawer holds gloves, alcohol swabs, dressings, tape, a tourniquet, specimen tubes, a glucose meter with its strips, and the paper for the observation chart. The clean utility room stores sterile packs and intravenous fluids, while the dirty utility room holds the sluice and the bin for contaminated waste, and the two must never be treated as one. Cleaning follows a rule of direction, because the cloth moves from the cleanest surface to the dirtiest and never back, and the nurse's start-of-shift check runs the bed through its range, tests the brake, checks the outlets for leaks, and draws the suction against a thumb. A serious hazard is the reusable device that is wiped but not disinfected, and the common error is trusting an outlet nobody has tested; every vacuum setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied.

The operating theatre lies behind a changing corridor, and its approach is a sequence of rooms rather than one door, with street clothes outside, scrub suits in the middle zone, and the sterile inner zone where the masked team stands. The room announces itself by the hum of ventilation, which is reassuring because filtered air is pushed down from the ceiling and swept out near the floor. Its fixed equipment is the table that tilts and breaks under power, the large lights on articulated arms that fill the shadow of a hand, and the pendant carrying oxygen, air, vacuum, and anesthetic gas scavenging. Its movable equipment is the anesthesia machine, the monitor, the electrosurgery generator with its return electrode, the instrument tables, and the counts board. A serious hazard is fire in an oxygen-enriched field when electrosurgery is used near the face, and the common error is beginning the case before the counts are recorded; every electrosurgery power setting must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the first cut.

The intensive care unit is a ward in which every bed is a life-support station, recognized by a chorus of alarms punctuated by the rush of a ventilator and the click of an infusion pump. Its fixed equipment is the bed space itself, with oxygen, air, vacuum, and sockets, some on an uninterruptible power supply, a monitor arm, a ventilator bracket, and lighting that can be dimmed. Its movable equipment is the mechanical ventilator, the monitor, the stack of infusion pumps, the continuous renal replacement machine, and the resuscitation trolley. The principle of the unit is distribution, because every machine at the bedside is fed by a pipe, a wire, or a battery that begins far away in a plant room, and consumables are used once and discarded. A serious hazard is alarm fatigue, the gradual deafening that leads a team to silence the single alarm that matters, and the common error is changing a ventilator setting without a second reader; every ventilator setting and alarm limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied and again before transport.

The delivery room sits close to the operating theatre, because a normal birth can become a surgical one in minutes, and it is identified by the beat of a fetal heart and the thin cry of a newborn. Its fixed equipment is the delivery bed with its leg supports, the procedure light on an arm, the radiant warmer with its heater and skin probe, the oxygen, air, and vacuum outlets, and a resuscitation table with a firm surface. Its movable equipment is the fetal monitor, the portable ultrasound, the vacuum extractor, the forceps, the cord clamp, the sterile pack, and the neonatal transport incubator. The principle of the radiant warmer is that heat reaches the baby by radiation without touching it, and the skin probe closes a control loop so the heater responds to the baby rather than to the room. A serious hazard is the newborn left uncovered under a cooler that has not been switched on, and the common error is failing to dry and stimulate the baby; every warmer temperature and heater output must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the first delivery of the shift.

The laboratory is a room of benches, announcing itself by the whine of centrifuges, the clatter of an analyzer, and the alarm of a refrigerator that has drifted warm. Its fixed equipment is the bench with its sink, the fume hood, the biological safety cabinet that draws air away from the worker, the gas and vacuum taps, the analyzer, the refrigerator and freezer, and the eyewash. Its movable equipment is the centrifuge, the microscope, the pipettes, the tube racks, and the specimen bags. The principle of the centrifuge is that spinning a tube makes the dense cells settle outward while the lighter plasma stays behind, and the safety cabinet keeps the worker out of the aerosol a tube produces when it is opened. A serious hazard is blood splashed onto a bench or into the eye, and another is the needle recapped by hand, while the common error is accepting an unlabeled specimen, which must be discarded; every temperature limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a specimen is stored. Behind its own locked door, the blood bank is built around cold and identity, with refrigerators for red cells, a freezer for plasma, a platelet agitator, and a tag that ties every unit to one patient.

The imaging suite is a corridor of similar rooms that behave very differently, so each is identified by its fixed hardware rather than by a label. The radiography room holds a floating table, a tube on a ceiling or floor mount, a collimator that shapes the beam, and a console behind a leaded screen. The computed tomography room, called a CT room, holds a large ring-shaped gantry with its rotating tube and detector array and a sliding table, while the magnetic resonance imaging room, called an MRI room, holds a magnet that is always on and a control room behind a shielded door. The ultrasound room holds a console, a display, and a rack of probes, and the principles differ, because radiography depends on differential absorption while computed tomography reconstructs slices and ultrasound times returning echoes. A serious hazard in the magnetic room is the field itself, because a forgotten cylinder can be pulled across the room with lethal force, and the common error is skipping the implant questionnaire; every field strength, exposure setting, and probe output must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a patient is examined.

The central sterile services department, called CSSD, is the one place where the flow runs in a single direction, and its atlas is a corridor rather than a room. Soiled instruments arrive at the dirty end and move through a receiving bench, a washer-disinfector or ultrasonic bath, an inspection bench, a packaging table, a sterilizer, and finally the clean store. Its fixed equipment is the sink with its long handle and air break, the washer-disinfector, the ultrasonic bath, the drying cabinet, the autoclave with its chamber and door, and the hand wash basin at the boundary. Its movable equipment is the basket, the tray, the perforated container, the instrument rack, the transport trolley, and the biological indicator that proves a cycle worked. The principle of the autoclave is that saturated steam under pressure gives up its latent heat as it condenses on a cooler instrument, and that heat coagulates the proteins of every microorganism, but the principle fails when air remains trapped and insulates the load. A serious hazard is the wet pack, whose wrapper can carry organisms through itself, and the common error is overloading the chamber; a common cycle is 134 degrees Celsius for 3 to 4 minutes, and nothing leaves the clean end without a lot number, an expiry, a chemical indicator, and a signature, so that temperature and time must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before any load is released.

The pharmacy and the general store are rooms about preservation and control, recognized by the hum of a refrigerator and the beep of an automated dispensing cabinet. Their fixed equipment is the shelving, the refrigerator that holds drugs between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, a range to be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before anything is stored, the freezer, the safe for controlled substances, and the dispensing cabinet whose drawers open only for an authorized user. Their movable equipment is the medication trolley, the delivery box, the cold box with its ice packs, the thermometer, and the logbook that records every temperature. A serious hazard is the look-alike label, where 2 ampoules of nearly identical appearance hold very different drugs, and the common error is placing a vaccine against the freezer compartment, where it freezes and is silently destroyed. The characteristic alarm is the refrigerator temperature alarm, commonly set to sound near 8 degrees Celsius, and that threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the unit is trusted.

The laundry is entered at the soiled end and left at the clean end, and it is identified from the corridor by the thud of a washer, the hiss of steam, and the smell of hot linen. Its fixed equipment is the soiled chute, the industrial washer loaded at one end and unloaded at the other, the dryer, the ironer, the boiler that supplies steam, the ventilation that carries moisture away, and the hand wash basin at the barrier. Its movable equipment is the bag, the trolley, and the cart that carries clean linen to the ward. The principle of thermal disinfection is that heat kills microorganisms when the temperature is high enough and held long enough, so a common wash cycle reaches 71 degrees Celsius for at least 3 minutes, a temperature and holding time that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a load is released. A serious hazard is the needle left in a sheet, which injures the worker who shakes it out, and the common error is mixing soiled and clean linen on one trolley.

The morgue is the last room on the walk and the quietest, recognized by cold, stillness, and the low hum of refrigeration. Its fixed equipment is the bank of refrigerated cabinets with their sliding trays, the ventilation that keeps air moving out, the floor drain, the washable walls, the identification table with its light, and the locked cabinet for the property of the dead. Its movable equipment is the trolley with its cover, the body bag, the identification tag, and the register in which every entry is signed. The principle of the cabinet is the same as any refrigerator, because cold slows decomposition and the body is stored near 4 degrees Celsius, a value that must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the cabinet is loaded. A serious hazard is misidentification, which is a legal and emotional catastrophe rather than a clinical one, and the common error is accepting a body without a tag checked twice against the register; the characteristic alarm is the cabinet high temperature tone, and the silence of a door left open matters more, because memory is not a record.

Now the atlas must be compressed, because the same walk in a mobile or frontier clinic passes through 1 or 2 rooms instead of 12 departments. The clinic announces itself differently, by the click of a solar charge controller, the whir of a generator, the flutter of a tent wall, and the voices of a queue, and its rooms are defined by time rather than by walls. The consultation corner holds a table, 2 chairs, a blood pressure cuff, a thermometer, and a pulse oximeter, while the treatment corner holds the same table in the afternoon with a tray of sterile instruments, a pressure cooker, a sharps box, and a bucket of chlorine solution. The ward corner is a mattress with a mosquito net, a bedpan, a suction foot pump, an oxygen cylinder with its regulator, and a hand-held monitor if the clinic owns one, and the delivery corner adds a sterile pack, a cord clamp, and a radiant lamp. The laboratory corner is a bench with a microscope, a centrifuge, a rapid diagnostic test for malaria, and a cold box, and the pharmacy corner is a locked cabinet with a thermometer and a logbook, so the discipline that replaces the walls is cleaning between patients, a single direction for soiled and clean items, and a written morning check.

The field clinic gives up redundancy first, and what it demands instead is a plan for every single point of failure. It has 1 oxygen source, 1 suction device, 1 sterilizer, 1 light, and 1 vehicle, so a broken part stops a service rather than slowing it. The power system is its own small plant, with a solar panel, a charge controller, a battery, and an inverter, and the battery is the weakest link because it is cycled every day, so its state of charge must be read each morning. A serious hazard is the petrol generator run indoors or beside a window, because its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas that is invisible, odorless, and lethal, and another is the extension lead that feeds a sterilizer and a heater from 1 circuit. The common error is leaving a device switched on overnight and draining the battery the next day depends on, and the characteristic alarms are the inverter low voltage warning and the charge controller fault light; every charging voltage and battery threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the system is trusted with a patient.

On the field the most dangerous substitution is the one that looks like sterilization and is not, so the atlas must name it plainly. A pressure cooker can genuinely sterilize a wrapped load when the air is driven out and the timing is respected, while a pot of boiling water kills most bacteria and leaves the spores that cause tetanus and gangrene alive. A chemical soak in a chlorine solution or a glutaraldehyde substitute is high-level disinfection rather than sterilization, and it fails when the solution is too weak, too old, or in contact for too short a time. A serious hazard is the instrument rinsed in a bucket of water after disinfection and reused at once, and the common error is topping up the disinfectant instead of replacing it, while the morning check covers the power, the oxygen pressure, the suction, the sterilizer, and the cold box temperature. The clinic also carries a second atlas inside its vehicle, where a stretcher locks into a floor track and an oxygen cylinder, a suction unit, a monitor, a defibrillator, and a spine board are each strapped so a sudden stop does not turn them into projectiles; every sterilization temperature, disinfectant concentration, and cold box limit must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the clinic opens.

To summarize, a visual atlas of a hospital is a walk in which each room is recognized by what is bolted to it, what stands on wheels, and what it sounds like from the corridor. The emergency department keeps oxygen, suction, monitor, and defibrillator within a single step, the ward repeats one bed space many times and lives on consumables and cleaning, the theatre arranges lights, table, gas scavenging, and a sterile field around one wound, and the intensive care unit is a distributed life-support system whose machines depend on pipes and wires that begin elsewhere. The delivery room holds a warmer beside the bed, the laboratory and blood bank turn a specimen into a number while guarding identity and temperature, the imaging suite makes radiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and ultrasound each demand a different habit, and the sterile services department is a one-way flow in which cleaning decides whether sterilization can work. The pharmacy, the laundry, and the morgue are rooms of preservation, identity, and record, while the field version is not a smaller hospital but a different arrangement in 1 or 2 rooms, where the same need is met by a pressure cooker, a foot pump, a solar battery, and a cold box; in every room the rule is the same, namely understand the principle, name the hazard and the common error, learn the alarm, and confirm every setting against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before the device touches a patient.

# Appendix B — Quick-Reference Tables: Tube Colors, Needle Gauges, Catheter Sizes, and Oxygen Delivery Devices

This appendix gathers the numbers a clinician reaches for most often. Here are blood tube colors, needle gauges, catheter sizes in French, oxygen device flows and concentrations, suture sizes, glove sizes, and tube sizes by age. Each is a convention rather than a law of nature. Every figure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before a device is used on a patient.

Color coding deserves a warning before any table. A color is a symbol, and the same closure color may carry different additives in different hospitals. When the color and the label disagree, the label wins, and an ambiguous label means the tube is discarded. The operator who trusts color alone may draw into the wrong additive, and the only alarm is a result that does not fit the patient.

Blood clots because platelets and clotting factors respond to a foreign surface. An additive either interrupts that response or accelerates it, so the additive decides which measurement the sample can support. A tube with a clot activator yields serum, while one with an anticoagulant yields plasma or whole blood. Gentle mixing matters as much as chemistry.

A light blue closure holds sodium citrate, which binds calcium, and it is used for coagulation testing. A red or gold closure holds a clot activator or nothing, and it yields serum for chemistry. A green closure holds lithium or sodium heparin for chemistry and blood gas. A lavender or purple closure holds ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid for blood counts, and a pink closure holds the same additive for blood bank work. A gray closure holds sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate for glucose, and a yellow closure may be sterile for culture. Every closure color and additive must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The order of draw protects the most fragile test, and its logic is contamination. The needle that fills every tube can carry additive into the next one, so culture bottles come first, then the light blue coagulation tube, the serum tube, the heparin tube, the lavender count tube, and finally the gray glucose tube. The common error is drawing the coagulation tube after an anticoagulant tube, and underfilling the light blue tube is the second. Underfilling destroys the fixed ratio of 1 part citrate to 9 parts blood, and these figures must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

In the hospital the vacuum tube sits in a chain of infrastructure. Tubes arrive in sealed trays with lot numbers, needles are single use in shielding holders, and pneumatic transport carries specimens to a centrifuge. Consumables include the tourniquet, swab, sharps container, bedside label, and transport bag. The characteristic failure is a broken chain, such as a label on the wrong tube or a specimen left too long on a counter.

The field variant gives up the vacuum and everything that depends on it. A syringe and needle fill a plain tube or one whose additive was dried in at the clinic, and the operator judges the fill against a mark. Without a centrifuge the serum may separate by gravity before a journey to a laboratory hours away. It demands clean technique, immediate labeling, and knowledge of which tests delay will ruin.

Tubes expire, so the operator checks the date, the vacuum, the color, the printed additive, and the request label. Storage is upright at the stated temperature, out of sunlight and away from radiators, because heat ages the additive. Mixing is gentle inversion a few times and never shaking, since shaking releases potassium and hemoglobin. The failure modes are a lost vacuum, a cracked tube, a clotted specimen, and a hemolyzed specimen.

The gauge of a needle runs backwards, because it describes the outer diameter of the shaft. A larger number means a smaller needle, so 14 gauge is large-bore and 27 gauge is fine. Flow rises with the fourth power of the internal radius, so a slightly wider needle carries far more fluid. That is why a patient in shock receives blood through a short, wide cannula, and why the right length reaches the intended tissue without passing through it.

The larger bores serve volume and speed. A 14 gauge and 16 gauge needle serve rapid transfusion, and 18 gauge serves donation, surgery, and a patient who may need resuscitation. A 19 gauge to 21 gauge needle covers most adult injections and intravenous starts, and 22 gauge is the compromise for difficult veins. A 23 gauge to 25 gauge suits children and subcutaneous injections, while 26 gauge to 27 gauge serves intradermal and fine dental work.

Hub colors are only a memory aid, and they vary by maker. The common teaching pairs 14 gauge with orange, 16 gauge with gray, 18 gauge with pink, 20 gauge with yellow, and 21 gauge with green. It continues with 22 gauge with black and 23 gauge with blue, so a color may serve more than one size. The printed size must always be read, and every gauge must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

Hospital practice surrounds the needle with safety hardware. Standardized hubs, needles that retract or shield after use, blunt fill and filter needles, and needle-free connectors all reduce risk. The used needle goes into a rigid sharps container never more than three quarters full. The safety hazard is the sharps injury, the common error is recapping by hand, and the characteristic alarm is the occlusion alarm of a pump when a needle or cannula blocks.

In a frontier clinic the needle is scarce, so syringes are boiled and needles are sharpened on a stone. One needle may serve several doses from a multi-dose vial, which multiplies the risk of infection. The field gives up the engineered safety device and demands a flame, a clean surface, a puncture-proof container closed when full, and a rule that a needle is never bent, broken, or recapped. The operator checks package integrity, shaft straightness, bevel sharpness, and fit, and discards any needle that drags.

Catheter size uses the French scale, where one French unit equals one third of a millimeter of external diameter. A 16 French catheter therefore measures about 5.3 millimeters across. The number describes the outside, which must pass through a narrow opening, while flow depends on the inside. Two catheters of equal French size may drain differently if their walls differ in thickness, and the rule for suctioning is a catheter no wider than one half of the internal diameter of the airway.

Urinary catheters follow patient size. A newborn takes 5 French to 6 French, an infant 8 French, a small child 10 French, and a school-age girl 12 French. An adult woman takes 12 French to 14 French, an adult man 14 French to 16 French, long-term drainage 16 French to 18 French, and irrigation after surgery 20 French to 24 French. Nasogastric tubes run from 5 French in a premature newborn to 16 French in a large adult, suction catheters from 6 French to 14 French, central venous catheters from 4 French to 8 French, and chest drains from 12 French for air to 40 French for blood and pus. Every size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

A catheter too large presses on the urethra or airway and causes pressure necrosis that can leave a stricture, while one too small leaks and blocks. The common error is to confuse the external French size with the drainage channel, and the second is to overinflate a retention balloon. The characteristic alarm is the occlusion alarm of the pump or the absence of drainage where drainage is expected. The response is to check the tube for kinks and the bag for position before forcing any fluid.

The hospital-grade catheter is sterile and single use, with a kit of gloves, drape, antiseptic, lubricant, bag, and securement. The drainage bag is a closed system whose port is wiped before sampling, and it is kept below the bladder. Urine meters, leg bags, and overnight bags are separate consumables. Traceability records the date of insertion, the size, the balloon volume, and the inserter.

In the field the catheter is often reusable, and silicone tolerates boiling better than latex. Clean intermittent catheterization may be the only option where sterile kits cannot be supplied. The field gives up the closed bag and demands cleaning of the meatus, clean water, drying, and storage in a sealed container. Any improvised container must stay off the floor and be washed on a schedule.

The checks that keep a catheter working are position and hygiene. The operator confirms securement without traction, tubing that runs downhill with no loop below the bag, and a bag below the bladder. The failure modes are blockage by sediment, leakage, cloudy or foul urine, and pain suggesting the balloon has migrated. The bag is emptied on schedule, the sampling port is wiped, and the catheter and tubing junction is never opened unnecessarily.

Every oxygen device raises the fraction of inspired oxygen above the 21 per cent found in room air. A low-flow device delivers oxygen into the upper airway and lets the patient's own breath pull in the rest. The achieved fraction then depends on how fast and how deeply the patient breathes, so the printed numbers are approximations. A reservoir device holds oxygen ready for the next breath, an entrainment device mixes oxygen with room air in a fixed ratio, and a leaking mask delivers less than its label promises.

A nasal cannula runs at 1 to 6 liters per minute, giving roughly 24 to 44 per cent. A simple face mask runs at 5 to 10 liters per minute for roughly 35 to 55 per cent, and it must never run below 5 liters per minute or the patient rebreathes exhaled carbon dioxide. A venturi mask entrains room air to hold a set fraction, commonly 24 to 60 per cent. A nonrebreather mask adds a reservoir bag, runs at 10 to 15 liters per minute, and can approach 90 per cent. High-flow nasal therapy warms and humidifies 30 to 60 liters per minute, while continuous positive airway pressure, shortened to CPAP, and bilevel positive airway pressure, shortened to BIPAP, add pressure rather than only oxygen.

Oxygen accelerates fire, so no oil, grease, or petroleum product may touch a regulator, valve, or mask, and no one may smoke nearby. The common error is opening a flow meter to maximum on a nasal cannula in the belief that more flow means more oxygen, when the gas mostly leaks and dries the mucosa. The second error is letting a humidifier bottle run dry. The characteristic alarms are a low oxygen concentration alarm on a concentrator, a low saturation alarm on the oximeter, and a mask leak alarm on a CPAP device. Every flow and fraction must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital system begins at a bulk tank or piped medical gas and reaches the bed through a wall outlet that fits no other gas. The flow meter, regulator, humidifier, tubing, and mask are consumables, and the outlet pressure is reduced to the required liters per minute. Blenders mix oxygen with compressed air, analyzers verify the mixture, and alarm panels warn of low pipeline pressure. A backup cylinder stands at every bed, and the outlets are checked on a documented schedule.

The field variant is built around the concentrator, the cylinder, and conservation. A concentrator draws room air through a filter, compresses it, and passes it through a sieve bed that holds nitrogen, usually delivering 1 to 10 liters per minute at a concentration that falls as the flow rises. A cylinder holds a fixed volume, so its life is calculated from the pressure gauge and the flow. The field gives up the pipeline, blender, and analyzer, demanding charged batteries, spare filters, and a plan for a patient who needs more than the concentrator can make.

Maintenance means washing or replacing the concentrator filter on schedule, because a clogged filter starves the sieve bed and lowers concentration. Sieve beds are replaced after their stated hours, and flow meters are checked against a known standard. Tubing and masks are single patient items replaced when soiled, and humidifier bottles are emptied and dried between patients. The operator checks cylinder pressure, every joint, the mask seal, and the patient's saturation, and listens for the low concentration alarm.

Suture size is written as a number with zeros, and the zeros run opposite to ordinary counting. Size 0 is the starting point, 2-0 is finer than 0, and 5-0 is finer still. Diameter decides tensile strength and tissue drag, so a thread strong enough for fascia cuts delicate skin. A knot holds by friction, so a stiff monofilament needs more throws than a soft braided thread, and braided threads carry fluid by capillarity.

A size 2 or size 1 suture carries the largest loads, such as fascial closure and ligation of major vessels. A size 0 suture serves the abdominal wall, a 2-0 serves fascia and bowel, and a 3-0 serves bowel and small vessels. A 4-0 suture is the usual choice for skin, and a 5-0 is used on the face and hand. A 6-0 suits fine facial work and pediatric skin, while 7-0 to 10-0 belong to microsurgery. Every size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use, and the choice of absorbable or nonabsorbable material is made at the same time.

The hospital-grade suture arrives sterile in a foil packet with a needle swaged to the thread, a lot number, and an expiration date. The needle is counted with every other sharp before the wound is closed and again before the patient leaves the room. The characteristic alarm is a count discrepancy, which stops the closing until the item is found or the wound is explored. Absorbable sutures lose strength as the body breaks them down, while nonabsorbable sutures hold until removed.

In a frontier clinic the suture cabinet is small and every packet is counted. The field gives up the wide selection of needle shapes and the certainty of factory sterility, so a single sterile monofilament may serve many tasks. The operator must know the strength of what is in hand. The checks before use are packet integrity, needle sharpness, absence of rust, and the match between needle and tissue, and a suture stored in heat or damp should be suspected.

A glove is a thin membrane between two environments, and material, thickness, and fit decide its performance. Latex is degraded by petroleum-based creams, light, and heat, nitrile resists many chemicals, and vinyl is the weakest barrier. Thickness, often given in thousandths of an inch, decides how long the membrane survives abrasion. Fit decides whether the wearer can work, since a tight glove tears and a loose glove reduces feeling.

Glove size is measured as the circumference of the hand around the palm at its widest point, just below the knuckles. That circumference in inches is the size number, so a hand 7 inches around takes a size 7 glove. A hand 6 inches around takes size 6, about 15 centimeters, and size 8 is about 20 centimeters, with half sizes between. The wrist to fingertip length decides forearm coverage, and the size on the box must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The hospital routine is to select the correct size, perform hand hygiene before donning, and change gloves between patients. Double gloving is used where sharp injury is likely, and indicator gloves reveal a puncture as a dark spot beneath the outer glove. The safety hazard is latex allergy, which ranges from a rash to a life-threatening reaction, so a latex-free alternative must be available. The common error is wearing one pair from patient to patient, and in the field gloves are washed and reused when supply fails. Gloves are stored away from sunlight and heat, and the operator checks the cuff for tears and the membrane for pinholes.

Nasogastric and endotracheal tubes are both chosen by age, and in both cases the number is a compromise. Airflow falls steeply as internal diameter falls, so a small tube demands more pressure to move the same gas. The tube must be small enough to pass without injury and large enough to do its work, and that margin is narrow in a newborn. Length is measured from nose to earlobe to breastbone for a nasogastric tube and checked after placement for an endotracheal tube.

A nasogastric tube is usually 5 French for a premature newborn, 6 French to 8 French for a term newborn, and 8 French for an infant. A small child takes 10 French, an older child 12 French, and an adolescent or small adult 12 French to 14 French. A large adult takes 14 French to 16 French, and lavage after poisoning may call for 16 French to 18 French. A wide tube drains faster but is harder to pass and more likely to erode, while a fine tube is comfortable but blocks. Every size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

An endotracheal tube is usually 2.5 millimeters to 3.0 millimeters of internal diameter for a premature newborn. A term newborn takes 3.0 to 3.5 millimeters, an infant 3.5 to 4.0 millimeters, and a toddler 4.5 to 5.0 millimeters. A school-age child takes 5.5 to 6.0 millimeters and an adolescent 6.5 to 7.5 millimeters. An adult woman commonly takes 7.0 to 7.5 millimeters, and an adult man takes 7.5 to 8.5 millimeters. For a child older than two years, the uncuffed size in millimeters equals the age in years divided by 4 and then plus 4, and every figure must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The shared hazard of both tubes is misplacement. A nasogastric tube in the airway can deliver feed into a lung, and an endotracheal tube in the esophagus delivers no breath. The common error with an endotracheal tube is pushing it too far, sending it into one main bronchus and collapsing the other lung. A cuff inflated above the pressure the mucosa tolerates causes ischemia, so cuff pressure is measured with a gauge. The characteristic alarms are the ventilator high-pressure alarm for a blocked tube, the disconnect alarm when it loosens, and the falling saturation on the oximeter.

Daily tube care is a set of small checks that prevent large failures. The operator compares the depth marking with the depth recorded at insertion, listens to both sides of the chest, and checks cuff pressure. Oral care, suctioning with a catheter no wider than one half of the tube, and rotation when the protocol allows reduce secretion and infection. The consumables at hand are a spare tube, a smaller tube, a suction catheter, a cuff syringe, a bite block, and an oxygen source. The failure modes to fear are blockage, disconnection, displacement, and erosion from a tube pressing on one spot too long.

To summarize, the colors, gauges, French sizes, flows, suture sizes, glove sizes, and tube sizes in this appendix are agreements rather than facts of nature. The physical principles are stable: a smaller bore carries less flow, an additive changes what blood will do, and a French number measures the outside while drainage depends on the inside. An oxygen fraction depends on flow and seal, a suture holds by friction, and a glove is only as good as its fit. The hospital versions wrap these principles in packaging, traceability, alarms, and consumables, while the field versions demand skill, cleanliness, and improvisation. In every setting the safe habit is to read the label, name the hazard, count the sharps, and confirm every figure against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before it is applied to a patient.

# Appendix C — Crash Cart and Department Checklists

A checklist is a device made of words, and its physical principle is that it moves a sequence out of a tired human memory onto a surface that does not fatigue. Working memory holds only a handful of items at once, and under the noise and urgency of a resuscitation it holds fewer, dropping the quiet items such as the second dose, the battery, and the suction. A written or spoken list turns recall into recognition, so the person checking confirms what the list names instead of remembering what to look for. A list also fixes an order, and order matters because suction precedes ventilation and ventilation precedes drugs. The list is not a substitute for judgment but a floor beneath it. Every number in every list here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The crash cart is a box on wheels designed to be found, opened, and emptied in a defined sequence. It is a cabinet with a flat top, several drawers, and four casters, one or two of which lock, and the top carries a defibrillator and a surface for drawing drugs. Each drawer is dedicated to one phase of resuscitation so that the hand goes to a known place without searching, and a numbered seal passes through the handles with its number written on a log. That seal is the cart's memory, because a broken seal means the cart must be checked before it is trusted, while a matching number means only that no one has opened it. The characteristic failure is the sealed cart that is empty inside, restocked with the wrong sizes or holding drugs that expired quietly in the dark. The daily check exists because a seal never proves the contents are correct, and the check interval and inventory list must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The cart is opened in the order the resuscitation opens the patient: airway, breathing, circulation. The top drawer holds airway equipment, meaning a laryngoscope with working batteries and a spare set, blades, endotracheal tubes, a stylet, a supraglottic airway, a self-inflating resuscitation bag with several mask sizes, oral and nasal airways, and a carbon dioxide detector. The second drawer holds oxygen tubing and masks, a nasal cannula, a manual suction unit with catheters, and spare canisters and tubing. The third holds drugs in the order they are likely to be drawn, usually a first-line cardiac arrest drug, a vasopressor, an antiarrhythmic, atropine, a benzodiazepine, dextrose, and naloxone. The fourth holds intravenous catheters, intraosseous needles, tourniquets, antiseptic swabs, syringes from 1 to 20 milliliters, needles, and tape, while the fifth holds larger items such as a difficult airway kit, a chest drain set, and obstetric supplies. The pediatric cart differs in scale rather than shape, with smaller blades, tubes, masks, and bags, weight-based drug cards on the lid, and a length-based tape for estimating weight, and every size, dose, gas flow, and energy setting here must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The daily check and the shift check are two rituals with two different jobs. The daily check is the deep one: it verifies each drawer against its inventory, reads every expiry date, runs the defibrillator self-test, confirms battery charge and a spare battery, checks oxygen cylinder pressure and suction function, and compares the seal number with the log. The shift check is the fast one, confirming only that the seal is intact, the cart is in its place, the defibrillator shows ready, and the log is signed. The seal system assigns a number and a signature to a moment, so the next person can tell whether the cart has been opened since it was verified. The common operator error is to break the seal, remove one item, and reseal the cart without restocking, or to sign the log without touching the cart, which transfers blame to the next person. A cart whose seal number does not match the log must be checked completely, and the check interval, seal numbering convention, and self-test threshold must be confirmed against the manufacturer's instructions and the local protocol before use.

The code checklist runs from the first compression to the debrief.
